name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Chris McGowan, Dave Dawson share plans to lower fuel costs at 4th District debate
description: In the first 4th Congressional District of Iowa debate, candidates offered their own solutions to lower gas prices but also expressed concern about cuts to the federal gas tax. The race to succeed U.S. Rep. Randy Feenstra is between Republican Chris McGowan, the Siouxland Chamber of Commerce president and a veteran, and Democrat Dave Dawson, […]
text:
Former Democratic state Rep. Dave Dawson will face off against Siouxland Chamber of Commerce President Chris McGowan, a Republican in the Iowa 2026 4th Congressional District race. (Photos courtesy of the Dawson and McGowan campaigns)In the first 4th Congressional District of Iowa debate, candidates offered their own solutions to lower gas prices but also expressed concern about cuts to the federal gas tax.
The race to succeed U.S. Rep. Randy Feenstra is between Republican Chris McGowan, the Siouxland Chamber of Commerce president and a veteran, and Democrat Dave Dawson, who previously served as prosecutor in the Woodbury County Attorney’s Office and as a state lawmaker.
Though the seat is open, the 4th Congressional District has long been a conservative stronghold in Iowa. While other congressional races in the state are considered hotly contended in the upcoming Nov. 3, 2026, election, the 4th District seat is rated by political forecasters as a “solid” Republican seat.
As the two candidates faced off in a debate Wednesday evening hosted by KTIV in Sioux City, they emphasized their commitment to having a “civil” discussion while discussing their disagreements on policy proposals. McGowan said he and Dawson have talked before, having met over the summer at the Woodbury County Fair, “and both of us had a very civil conversation and agreed to run campaigns that were rooted in civil discourse and respect.”
Both McGowan and Dawson agreed that Congress needed to take action to lower costs — including finding ways to lower high fuel costs — but presented different approaches on how to achieve this goal.
McGowan said he believes increasing U.S. energy production is key to lowering costs across the board for Iowans, including on groceries and other goods.
“We have to remember that every good place in the stream of commerce travels via truck, trailer, air, train, and the fuel costs associated with that transportation has become ridiculously expensive,” McGowan said. “… One of the most impactful things that we can do, and the Republicans have been talking about for decades, is to maximize the production of energy at home, to make sure that we are the leading provider of energy in the world, and that we rely on domestic energy sources, not international. When we do that, and we drill, and we produce energy, and we lead the world in energy production, those prices are certain to come down.”
The Republican candidate said completing the Keystone XL pipeline project would bring in needed oil. The project has faced significant pushback and delays due to U.S. environmental concerns and disputes over the use of indigenous land, but Trump said in August he is seeking to revive the project.
“Unfortunately, for political reasons, the opposition party killed that project,” McGowan said of the Keystone XL pipeline. “Now, they cited environmental concerns and other concerns. But the reality is if we had access to that today, we wouldn’t be paying the prices that we’re paying at the fuel pump, so we have to begin to look further into the future rather than one election ahead.”
But Dawson said the best way to reduce fuel costs was to end the U.S. war with Iran. He criticized his opponent for not taking a position on the U.S. continued presence and military action in Iran during a time when some of McGowan’s children are deployed as members of the U.S. military.
“I have prayed for his children who are deployed and may be serving overseas related to this conflict,” Dawson said. “But it’s important to me that we not put American lives at risk … Why are we in the Middle East fighting a war that isn’t our war to fight? We have no imminent threat to our country, and we need to focus on fixing the problems here at home. The billions of dollars that have already been spent on this war could be better directed, fixing our roads, fixing our bridges, fixing our broken and ailing healthcare system where people have faced cut after cut over the last year with regards to healthcare funding.”
McGowan said that as someone who is not a current member of Congress, he did not have access to classified information about the war and the decisions made by the military.
“I do think it would be premature and perhaps a little irresponsible for me to comment without having access to that data,” he said. “But, like my opponent and so many other Americans, I hope that we will have a speedy and quick resolution to this conflict in Iran.”
While lowering fuel costs was a top priority, both Dawson and McGowan expressed potential cncerns suspending the federal fuel tax — a proposal other Iowa candidates from both parties running in the 2026 election have backed.
McGowan said he was “certainly open to a conversation in Congress with other members to say, ‘we’ve reached the point where we have to provide relief to the consumer, so let’s consider suspending the federal gas tax.'” However, he said, “if you do that, you have to recognize that the infrastructure is going to suffer enormously.”
“We’re increasing the amount of trucking and traffic — people who travel on Highway 20 or Interstate 80 in the 4th Congressional District know that these are very heavily traversed roads,” he said. “So we have to be careful about taking those dollars away.”
Dawson also said he believed discussions on suspending the federal fuel tax should include discussions on how to provide other funding sources for roads and infrastructure.
“It’d be important to make sure we have the funding we need to fix the roads and bridges in Iowa,” Dawson said. “We have some of the worst quality roads in bridges of all the states in the United States. So if we are going to cut taxes, we need to make sure we understand that there’ll be consequences to that.”
However, Dawson said he did not believe suspending this tax would not significantly lower fuel costs.
“Really, what’s important at the federal level, though, is cutting the federal gas tax will not address the huge increase that has happened with gas prices,” Dawson said. “… A more than 25% increase in gas prices would not be affected by cutting the federal gas tax. You really need to get to the source of the problem, which is ending the war in Iran.”

name: Mississippi Today
title: Christa Pike is alive a day after Tennessee’s failed attempt to execute her, her lawyers say
authors: By Kim Chandler and Kristin M. Hall, Associated Press
description: May Martinez, left, mother of murder victim Colleen Slemmer, walks out of Riverbend Maximum Security Institution during a stay of the planned execution of Christa Pike, Wednesday, Sept. 30, 2026, in Nashville, Tenn.
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
NASHVILLE, Tenn. — Christa Pike was in critical condition but receiving “lifesaving care” at a hospital, her lawyers said Thursday, a day after she survived a failed attempt to execute her for the 1995 murder during what Tennessee’s governor called a “deeply disturbing” procedure.
Pike was taken to the hospital Wednesday night after she received a double dose of the drug Tennessee uses to execute prisoners but survived. Her lawyers said they were told her condition is critical, but they didn’t know specifics.
This photo provided by the Tennessee Department of Correction shows Christa Pike on Jan. 12, 2023.  Credit: TDOC via AP
“Christa is alive right now. We don’t have a sense of her prognosis or much update on her health at the moment,” attorney Randy Spivey said during a news conference. “But we know she is alive right now and receiving lifesaving medical care.”
Attorney Steve Ferrell said Pike feared there would be complications with the lethal injection because of a lifelong blood disorder that made it tough to get needles into her veins.
“Throughout her life, she’s explained to us that she had trouble having blood drawn,” Ferrell said.
Spivey said he counted at least seven needles that were used in her left arm alone.
“Ms. Pike was not just cooperative but was helping to instruct the people placing the IV lines” as to where they might put them,” Spivey said. “She told them over and over, please try higher on my shoulder.”
Pike’s lawyers said the failed execution amounted to “torture,” and they called for her death sentence to be commuted.
An execution fails
The state tried to execute Pike by lethal injection, but neither the initial nor backup dose of pentobarbital killed her and she was still snoring when the execution chamber’s microphone was cut off more than an hour into the attempt. She was later taken to a hospital for treatment.
At one point during Wednesday night’s execution attempt, she asked prison officials if her arm was supposed to feel that way, though it’s unclear if it was after the first dose entered her body, as officials don’t share that information. Later, more than an hour after the process began and nearly 30 minutes after a backup dose of pentobarbital was administered, she could be heard snoring loudly.
On Thursday, Republican Gov. Bill Lee indefinitely postponed Pike’s execution and Tennessee’s lone remaining one that had been scheduled for this year. He also ordered an independent review of what happened, calling it “deeply disturbing.”
But Pike’s lawyers said such a review would be insufficient.
Pike, 50, was sentenced to death for a murder she committed at age 18. She would have been the first woman executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years.
An appeals court stopped the lethal injection an hour before it was scheduled to begin, but the U.S. Supreme Court overturned that stay hours later.
It was the second time this year that Tennessee was unable to complete an execution, though in the other case, officials couldn’t find a suitable vein for an IV line so the drugs weren’t administered.
May Martinez, whose daughter was murdered by Pike and her boyfriend and who traveled to Nashville to watch the execution, told NBC News that “it was a mess.”
Governor halts another 2026 execution
The failure, which one death penalty expert described as unprecedented, led Gov. Bill Lee to order a review and to indefinitely postpone Pike’s execution and Tennessee’s lone other one that had been scheduled for this year. It also reignited the debate over the state’s execution procedures, including its single-drug lethal injections.
“There are very few answers this morning. It’s very early,” Lee told reporters Thursday at an unrelated event, noting he had received no updates on Pike’s condition. “The people of our state deserve to have those questions answered.”
He called what happened “deeply disturbing” and said it appeared prison staff followed procedure.
Pike, 50, had been scheduled for execution Wednesday morning for the killing she committed at age 18 and would have been the first woman executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years. An appeals court stopped the execution an hour before it was to start, but the U.S. Supreme Court overturned that stay hours later.
Officials gave Pike two doses of pentobarbital, her attorneys said in court filings late Wednesday. The drug has been used in executions in multiple states and by the federal government, but there have been concerns raised about the potential for “unnecessary pain and suffering.”
The Tennessee Department of Correction said in a statement that it “followed every step of the State’s lawful, established execution protocol approved by the Attorney General’s Office.”
Tennessee changed its execution method two years ago
Tennessee announced in 2024 that it was switching from a three-drug series for lethal injections to the single drug pentobarbital. That came more than two years after the state abruptly halted the execution of Oscar Smith and acknowledged it had failed to ensure its lethal injection drugs had been tested properly.
Robin M. Maher, executive director of the Death Penalty Information Center, said what Pike experienced is “singular and unparalleled” in that she survived long enough to be moved to a hospital.
Seven other people have survived medical problems due to an execution team’s failure to access a vein to administer lethal injection drugs, but no one has stayed alive after receiving the drugs used in such executions, she said.
Executions in the U.S. have fallen sharply since the beginning of this century amid growing public opposition and concerns about the costs and the drugs used. But the number of executions nearly doubled last year behind a record increase in Florida.
Pike would have been the 30th person executed in the U.S. this year.
Pike was awake in the execution chamber
Strapped to a gurney in the execution chamber, Pike described herself as at peace.
When asked if she had any last words, Pike said several things, including, “I’m at peace. I’m ready to be free. … This is a happy day.”
But she remained awake, and at one point complained about the feeling in her arm. The chamber’s curtains were closed, suggesting it had been five minutes since the first dose was administered. But they were reopened three minutes later.
An hour after officials first raised the curtains, witnesses reported that a second dose of pentobarbital was administered. Pike could still be heard snoring behind a closed curtain until the microphone was cut off almost 30 minutes later.
Lawyers for Pike filed an emergency motion with the Tennessee Supreme Court seeking to immediately halt and stay the execution, saying she was in “unnecessary agony” and the procedure violated her right to be executed free of cruel and unusual punishment. They also filed motions with two other courts.
Last May, Tennessee officials called off the lethal injection of Tony Carruthers, who was convicted of kidnapping and killing three people in 1994, after executioners tried for over an hour but failed to find a suitable vein for a backup IV line.
Pike didn’t deny her role in the killing
Pike and her boyfriend were convicted of the fatal stabbing of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, a classmate. The killing stoked fears of Satan worship because of a pentagram carved on Slemmer’s body.
Pike’s boyfriend wasn’t eligible for the death penalty because he was 17 at the time of the killing and received a sentence of life in prison. He was denied parole last year.
Pike didn’t dispute that she helped kill Slemmer, but supporters argued that Pike’s age at the time of the murder, her mental illness and her allegations of severe sexual abuse should be considered. She was diagnosed with bipolar disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder after the killing.
“It took me numerous years to even realize the gravity of what I’d done,” she once said.

With contributions from Associated Press writers Jeffrey Collins in Columbia, South Carolina; Ed White in Detroit; Russ Bynum in Savannah, Georgia; Hallie Golden in Seattle; Hannah Schoenbaum in Salt Lake City and John Seewer in Toledo, Ohio.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: State-licensed nurse faces charges of animal neglect in Linn County
description: An eastern Iowa nurse who has worked for the state is facing animal neglect charges after police allegedly found two emaciated dogs, one already dead, on her property. In April 2026, police applied for a search warrant at the Cedar Rapids property of 33-year-old Laura Brynn Stowe. In their application, the police cited concerns that […]
text:
(Photo by simpson33 via iStock / Getty Images Plus)
An eastern Iowa nurse who has worked for the state is facing animal neglect charges after police allegedly found two emaciated dogs, one already dead, on her property.
In April 2026, police applied for a search warrant at the Cedar Rapids property of 33-year-old Laura Brynn Stowe. In their application, the police cited concerns that four animals — a rottweiler named Ginger, a pitbull named Lex, a Yorkshire terrier named Macy and a cat named Stella — were being neglected or abused.
According to the warrant application, an animal control officer went to the property on April 21, saw there was a water-utility disconnect notice on the door, but was unable to contact Stowe, who was allegedly living in Iowa City at the time.
The following day, an animal control supervisor went to the property, heard a dog inside barking, and saw several sun-faded packages left on the porch of the house.
On April 23, an individual allegedly gave police photos she had taken through a sliding glass door to the Stowe property. According to police, the photos showed trash and animal feces covering most of the interior floor visible from the door. That same evening, the animal control supervisor returned to the house, but again was not able to locate or speak to Stowe.
On April 24, armed with a warrant, police entered the house and seized one rottweiler and one deceased terrier. The available court records make no mention of any other animals in the home at that time.
Two months later, the City of Cedar Rapids filed a civil petition against Stowe, asserting that police had obtained evidence, including a video, of a dog being abused by Stowe’s minor children. While it’s not clear from the available court records whether the dog at issue is the rottweiler the city had seized in April, the city sought the court’s permission to have the allegedly abused dog placed for adoption. The case was dismissed a short time later after Stowe agreed to relinquish ownership of the animal.
By that time, the Linn County Attorney’s Office had criminally charged Stowe with two counts of animal neglect resulting in serious injury or death.  Prosecutors alleged Stowe failed to provide food and water for the two dogs police had seized in April.
The deceased terrier “was malnourished to the point that officers could see its bone structure coming out of its skin,” prosecutors stated, and an examination indicated the dog had likely died of starvation.
The rottweiler “appeared to be malnourished and unfed for a significant period of time” and “the residence was covered in feces” while the dogs were left without access to food, water or suitable shelter, prosecutors alleged.
Stowe has pleaded not guilty to the two criminal charges. A hearing on the matter is scheduled for Oct. 7, 2026. The Iowa Capital Dispatch was not able to reach Stowe for comment.
State records indicate Stowe is a licensed practical nurse who has worked for the state. In 2023, the Iowa Board of Nursing fined Stowe $400 and suspended her license for one month for failing to demonstrate completion of continuing-education requirements and failing to respond to board inquiries on the matter.
State records indicate that in the 2024-25 fiscal year, Stowe began working for the Iowa Department of Corrections as a nurse.

name: VTDigger
title: Brattleboro Memorial Hospital promotes its financial consultant to post of interim CEO
description:
David Sanville’s appointment comes a year after the southeastern Vermont healthcare hub reported a multimillion-dollar deficit and the subsequent departures of two top executives.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Brattleboro Memorial Hospital promotes its financial consultant to post of interim CEO.
text:
The Brattleboro Memorial Hospital campus on Belmont Avenue. Photo by Kevin O’Connor/VTDigger

Brattleboro Memorial Hospital has named the former chief financial officer of Windsor’s Mt. Ascutney Hospital and Health Center as its new interim CEO.
David Sanville, who recently has helped the Brattleboro hospital deal with a multimillion-dollar deficit, stepped into his new role at Thursday’s start of the 2027 fiscal year, the facility’s board of directors announced.
“David brings extensive experience in hospital finance and operations, as well as a deep understanding of the challenges facing community hospitals,” board Chair Chloe Learey said in a statement. “He already knows BMH, our people and our community, and we are grateful that he has agreed to take on this important leadership role as we search for a permanent CEO.”
Sanville has worked as a healthcare administrator for more than 30 years, not only at Mt. Ascutney but also at Gifford Medical Center in Randolph and Central Vermont Medical Center in Berlin. 

Brattleboro Memorial Hospital interim CEO David Sanville. Courtesy photo

He will replace acting co-CEOs Tony Blofson and Elizabeth McLarney, two doctors who have shared the post for the past year and now will serve as senior advisers.
Sanville’s appointment comes after former President Christopher Dougherty exited without explanation in November and former Chief Financial Officer Laura Bruno departed amid similar silence in December.
Acting hospital leaders have blamed recent deficit spending on past administrative and accounting problems. 
Two weeks ago, state regulators at the Green Mountain Care Board adopted fiscal year 2027 budgets for the state’s 13 other general acute-care hospitals, only to level-fund the Brattleboro facility until it clarifies its proposal “given all the changes and some of the inconsistencies we’ve seen,” care board Chair Owen Foster said. 
The southeastern Vermont healthcare hub, operating on a $130 million annual budget, has forecast a $7.1 million deficit for the 2027 fiscal year that began Thursday. That would follow a $33.6 million operating loss for the fiscal years 2017 through 2025 and an estimated $9.5 million shortfall for the 2026 fiscal year that ended Wednesday, it reported in a state filing.
Even with improvement measures, the hospital doesn’t anticipate breaking even on an overall annual budget until the 2028 fiscal year at the earliest.

text:
Officials have extended Georgia's annual oyster season closure because the water is warm, raising the risk of dangerous bacteria. (Caila Brown)This coverage is made possible through a partnership between WABE and Grist, a nonprofit environmental media organization.
Georgia is extending the annual closure of the oyster harvest season because of unusually warm ocean temperatures. Officials say the closure, which usually ends September 30, will continue until the water is safe for wild oysters.
It’s common knowledge in coastal areas: avoid raw oysters in the summer because warm water lets dangerous bacteria flourish. Georgia shuts down wild oyster harvesting from June through September every year to keep people safe. But this year, for just the second time, the state is extending the closure because the water is still too warm. 
“I think it’s a pretty known thing. We had a very hot summer,” said Dominic Guadagnoli, who manages the Georgia Department of Natural Resources shellfish and water quality program. “And also, we didn’t have, thankfully, any major storms. Usually the major storms, even tropical storms, will cool waters down.”
In 2018, the state extended the closure for several weeks until ocean temperatures cooled, he said.
The state has made a major change since then, implementing a formal system for farming and harvesting of oysters. That means that now, the restrictions only apply to wild oysters. Using floating gear, farmers can control the conditions for the oysters they raise, making them safe to harvest and eat throughout the closure season.
“Our oysters have to stay submerged for two weeks before we harvest them,” said Laura Solomon, owner of Tybee Oyster Company. “That means that they’re continuing to sit in the water, filtering, and in the shade of our floats, and all of those things. So they’re never just sitting in the sun.”
Solomon’s firm is one of three in the state with a permit to harvest during the closure under the new regulations.
Officials are closely monitoring the ocean temperature and will reopen the harvest as soon as it’s safe, Guadagnoli said.

It seeks monetary damages for each violation of Florida law plus an injunction against [[...]
text:
Dr. Joseph Ladapo is shown with Gov. Ron DeSantis on Sept. 21, 2021. (Photo by Michael Moline/Florida Phoenix)Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier filed a lawsuit Thursday against Pfizer Inc., alleging unfair and deceptive marketing of Pfizer’s COVID-19 vaccine.
The suit, filed in state trial court in St. Lucie County, also names Albert Bourla, the company’s chairman and CEO.
It seeks monetary damages for each violation of Florida law plus an injunction against future violations.
“Pfizer’s conduct misled Florida consumers when they were making some of the most sensitive health decisions of their lives. Ultimately, Pfizer’s misconduct rests on the paternalistic assumption that Florida consumers could not be trusted with the truth about Pfizer’s products. That offensive assumption is anathema to the principles underlying the Florida Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act (‘FDUTPA’),” it asserts.
Uthmeier denounced the company in a video posted on X.
In response, Pfizer issued a written statement.
“We are proud to have developed the COVID-19 vaccine in record time in the midst of a global pandemic and saved countless lives. The representations made by Pfizer about its COVID-19 vaccine have been accurate and science-based, and the Company stands behind the safety and efficacy of its vaccine. Pfizer believes that the state’s allegations have no merit and will respond to the suit in due course.”
“Pfizer is deeply committed to the well-being of the patients it serves. Since its initial authorization by FDA in December 2020, the Pfizer-BioNTech COVID-19 vaccine has been administered to billions of people, demonstrated a favorable safety profile in all age groups, and helped protect against severe COVID-19 outcomes, including hospitalization and death.”
Florida’s complaint recalls the scary time when Americans confronted a new virus that filled hospitals and impelled government leaders to close nonessential businesses, including in Florida initially.
Gov. Ron DeSantis later changed course, easing business restrictions and surrounding himself with COVID skeptics including Joseph Ladapo, whom the governor installed as Florida surgeon general.
“Florida citizens faced an unprecedented level of uncertainty” and “worried about how to protect their loved ones and themselves from a previously unknown virus” and resulting “once-in-a-generation economic shock,” the complaint reads. The company “bet big” its mRNA vaccine, it adds.
To overcome skepticism over the novel vaccine, the company undertook an intensive marketing campaign attesting to the vaccine’s safety, the document continues.
“Pfizer was not content merely to promote its own narrative. It also sought to quash any dissent that might impact consumer demand — like calling those who dared to question Pfizer’s public claims ‘criminals.’”
At the same time, the complaint says, Pfizer’s “record-breaking profits rested on deception and falsehoods. While Pfizer was insisting to consumers that the vaccine posed no material safety risks — and while it actively sought to discredit those who said otherwise — Pfizer was aware of data reflecting serious safety risks that it hid from the public.”
In January 2025, a Florida statewide grand jury found no evidence that COVID-19 vaccine manufacturers broke federal or state laws when making and distributing the shots. That was more than two years after DeSantis asked the Florida Supreme Court to assemble it to investigate alleged wrongdoing related to the COVID-19 vaccines.
The report did criticize what it considered too-close relationships between regulatory agencies such as the Food and Drug Administration and Pfizer and Moderna.

description: A north-central Iowa attorney has been sentenced to six months in federal prison for healthcare fraud in attempting to assist a client in qualifying for Medicaid. U.S. District Court Judge Leonard T. Strand imposed the prison sentence against Timothy Anderson, 67, of Garner, last month, calling the lawyer’s actions “obviously fraudulent and illegal.” Strand[...]
text:
(Main photo by simpson33 via iStock / Getty Images Plus; seal courtesy State of Iowa)A north-central Iowa attorney has been sentenced to six months in federal prison for healthcare fraud in attempting to assist a client in qualifying for Medicaid.
U.S. District Court Judge Leonard T. Strand imposed the prison sentence against Timothy Anderson, 67, of Garner, last month, calling the lawyer’s actions “obviously fraudulent and illegal.” Strand also fined Anderson $25,000, and ordered him to pay $184,274 in restitution to Iowa Medicaid.
Anderson pleaded guilty last year to one count of false statements relating to a healthcare matter. Citing that plea, the Iowa Supreme Court recently ordered that Anderson’s Iowa law licenses be temporarily suspended, with the suspension to continue until he shows good cause for reinstatement.
At his October 2025 plea hearing, Anderson admitted that as an Iowa-licensed attorney, he provided financial services to elderly clients hoping to qualify for Medicaid that would pay for nursing home care. Eligibility for the Medicaid program typically hinges on one’s assets since it’s designed to pay for care for those who can’t afford it. In determining the assets and resources of individuals and their spouses, one automobile is typically excluded from consideration, regardless of its value.
Court records show that one elderly couple Anderson assisted in 2021 had more than $400,000 in assets, including a 2020 Chevrolet valued at $30,000, but was hoping to have Medicaid pay their nursing home expenses while passing their remaining assets on to their heirs.
Iowa Medicaid determined the couple would have to either reduce their assets by $300,000 or spend that amount of money on excluded assets — such as a car.
Anderson later admitted that in October 2021, he deposited a $186,000 check from the couple into his personal savings account and transferred the certificate of title to his 1961 Rolls Royce Phantom V to them. Just two days before that transfer, Anderson had been driving the Rolls Royce when he was involved in an accident that rendered the car inoperable.
On Nov. 4, 2021, Anderson later acknowledged, he gave Iowa Medicaid a series of documents to qualify the husband for Iowa Medicaid benefits.  The documents reflected the couple’s ownership of the Rolls Royce and indicated it had a fair market value of $194,000.
Iowa Medicaid rejected the application, and the Federal Bureau of Investigation launched an investigation that resulted in the criminal charge and guilty plea.
Anderson declined to comment on the case when contacted by the Iowa Capital Dispatch, but his attorneys told the Iowa Supreme Court recently that Anderson “fully appreciates the significance of his misconduct” and is remorseful.
“Mr. Anderson has had an exemplary record of good conduct,” they told the court. “Additionally, Mr. Anderson has cooperated with the government, cooperated with the Attorney Disciplinary Board, self-reported his conduct, has begun to make efforts to transfer his practice, has not had any complaints since his self-report, and has conducted himself in an honorable fashion.”

name: Mississippi Today
title: Farm worker, 24, dies of heat exposure in North Mississippi
description: Sweet Potato Harvest — 2017
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
A north Mississippi farm worker died of extreme heat exposure in early September amid one of the hottest summers in recent state history. 
Obed Azahel Hernandez Perez, a 24-year-old man from Mexico, died Sept. 8 from prolonged heat exposure while harvesting sweet potatoes, according to Chickasaw County Coroner Larry Harris. In an email, Harris said the Mississippi Department of Agriculture and the federal Occupational Safety and Health Administration are investigating the incident.
OSHA began an inspection on Sept. 9 into a worker heat-related death at Alexander Farms LLC, a Vardaman sweet potato farm owned by Ryan Alexander near the Chickasaw County and Calhoun County border. It’s the first death inspection conducted by Mississippi’s only OSHA office that was listed as heat-related this year. 
An OSHA Eastern Regional spokesperson said in an email to Mississippi Today that she was unable to immediately respond to questions about the incident. 
Mississippi has some of the most dangerous working conditions in the country. In 2024, workers in Mississippi died at a higher rate than anywhere except Wyoming, according to the most recent U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics Data. 
This year was Chickasaw County’s hottest summer since 2011, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. The temperature in nearby Calhoun City reached a high of 98 degrees Fahrenheit, according to federal data. 
When Mississippi Today called Alexander Farms, an employee acknowledged the death but said she wouldn’t get into the details before hanging up the phone. The company didn’t respond to an email asking what Hernandez Perez’s job was, how long he had worked there and how the farm protects employees from heat-related dangers.
An Alexander Farms job application on the U.S. Department of Labor website says that the company planned to hire 117 seasonal farm workers this fall. The farm worker responsibilities include “all duties involved in planting, growing and harvesting corn, soybeans and sweet potatoes.” 
On the application, listed duties include stooping and kneeling to pick vegetables, removing weeds, carrying bags of potatoes weighing up to 50 pounds and driving trucks and tractors. Alexander Farms lists the pay at $12.50 per hour, with a deduction of $1.15 per hour for immigrant workers who stay in company housing. 
The job’s start date was about two weeks before Hernandez Perez died. Debbie Berkowitz, a former chief of staff for OSHA, told Mississippi Today that heat-related deaths are common when seasonal employees first begin their jobs. 
“They’re not acclimated to do this work in high heat,” Berkowitz said. 
Both the federal and Mississippi governments have few heat protections for workers. In 2024, the Department of Labor proposed a federal rule that would’ve required companies to provide their employees with shade or air-conditioning, cool drinking water and regular rest breaks whenever the felt temperature was over 90 degrees Fahrenheit. It also would’ve required employers to acclimate new workers to high heat conditions and create plans to quickly spot heat illnesses.
Two years after the rule’s initial proposal, OSHA has yet to finalize workplace heat standards. Last November, U.S. Rep. Mark Messmer, a Republican from Indiana, proposed a bill to ban OSHA from ever implementing it. 
Jordan Barab, a former deputy assistant secretary for the federal agency, told Mississippi Today that national workplace heat regulations could have saved Hernandez Perez’s life. 
“If that had become a standard and the employer was in full compliance with that standard, that worker would likely be alive today,” he said. 
Some states implement their own workplace heat standards, but Mississippi isn’t one of them. The state uses federal workplace health standards and is one of five states that doesn’t have its own labor enforcement agency. 
Other Mississippians, experiencing health effects tied to increasingly hot summers,  may have died of heat exposure on the job, according to Barab. Berkowitz said it’s common for heat-related workplace deaths, like Hernandez Perez’s, to be undercounted. Workers exposed to high temperatures can die with little public notice and no follow-up investigations. 
“There’s no press, nobody knows about it,” Berkowitz said.
Harris, the Chickasaw County coroner, said Hernandez Perez’s body has been transported back to Mexico.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Living with bears in Anchorage: We can do better
description: News that 20 or more bears have been killed in Anchorage this year, mostly because they’ve gotten into the habit of eating human trash, is both disheartening and infuriating. People who live in the municipality, like elsewhere in Alaska, have long known what steps to take to minimize bear-human conflicts. At the top of the […]
text:
A dumpster outside an Anchorage residence was tipped over by a bear in the summer of 2026. (Photo courtesy Bill Sherwonit)News that 20 or more bears have been killed in Anchorage this year, mostly because they’ve gotten into the habit of eating human trash, is both disheartening and infuriating.
People who live in the municipality, like elsewhere in Alaska, have long known what steps to take to minimize bear-human conflicts. At the top of the list: keeping garbage away from bears.
Making matters worse is the fact that local businesses that provide bear-resistant trash “carts” and dumpsters to their customers are part of the problem. A recent news story published by the Anchorage Daily News, indicates that two companies that provide the bear-resistant containers ran out of them.
This is both hard to comprehend and unacceptable. Keeping an adequate supply of the carts and dumpsters should be an essential part of the business plan, part of the cost of doing business. That should also be something the municipality demands, simply because it’s a key part of the solution to this problem.
I can personally speak to another part of the problem. Because we have renters, my girlfriend and I keep a dumpster on our property. For years, the dumpster had heavy, metal lids. This spring, for some inexplicable reason, Alaska Waste replaced those metal lids with much more flimsy plastic ones. In retrospect, we should have insisted then that the metal ones be re-installed. That was our mistake. We didn’t.
On Sept. 7, a large black bear tipped over our locked dumpster, an impressive feat. It then easily flicked aside the plastic lid without undoing the lock, and pulled several bags of trash from the dumpster, scattering it across our yard. We went outside and made enough noise to chase the bear away, then cleaned up and re-bagged the mess and stashed it inside a workshop building.
Because we had no immediate way to put the dumpster upright, we parked Jan’s 2000 Honda SUV in front of it, thinking that would keep the bear from getting to the trash that remained inside.
We were wrong. At 3 a.m. the next morning, the bear returned and shoved Jan’s car aside—an even more impressive feat—while putting a large dent in the front of the car, along with some claw marks. And the bear then had no problem once more flipping the plastic top aside to pull out more garbage before again being chased off.
Thanks to one of our renters and his daughter, the dumpster was righted the next day. That same morning we called Alaska Waste to request it fully empty the dumpster and replace the plastic lids with metal ones.
I can’t say for sure that heavy metal lids would have kept the bear out of the dumpster, but they would have offered some resistance, maybe enough that the bear would have given up.
For Alaska Waste to use ridiculously lightweight plastic lids in a part of town that bears frequent is inexcusable, an example of worst, not best, practices. This must change. And if the company won’t do so on its own, the municipality must take appropriate action.
The ADN story noted that the Alaska Department of Fish and Game, municipality, trash-hauling companies and others “discuss challenges involving bears and unsecured trash” and other related issues through the Anchorage Bear Committee. The ABC was established in 2001 and I attended several meetings in its early years.
I’ve fallen out of touch, but in my experience the committee does good and necessary work. Maybe its members need to revisit the responsibilities of local trash-pickup companies, the parts of Anchorage where bear-resistant carts and dumpsters are required and the need for greater enforcement.
People like to talk about “problem bears,” but as I’ve noted many times over the years, the problem starts with people.
As bear researchers have long emphasized, bears are smart critters and fast learners. And they are “opportunistic omnivores,” always on the lookout for an easy meal. It doesn’t take but a time or two of getting into our species’ garbage—and also our bird feeders, dog food, chicken coops and other sources of food—to adapt their own behavior to take advantage of the easy pickings.
When Fish and Game’s wildlife managers determine that a bear has become “food conditioned” to trash or other human foods, they’re considered a public-safety threat and targeted for “removal.”
Thus the saying, “A fed bear is a dead bear.”
It’s telling that of the 20 local bears killed through Sept. 27, “All but one were killed because they sought out ‘unsecured attractants,’” according to Fish and Game regional supervisor Cynthia Wardlow.
We humans like to boast about our species’ intelligence, but when it comes to bears—and many other matters—our smarts are too often outweighed by ignorance, laziness, stubbornness, intolerance and prejudice.
Here in Anchorage, all of us can do better, from individuals to businesses, government agencies and city leaders.
It’s been said many times before: living with bears can be challenging. But if we wish to coexist with the animals—and past surveys have indicated a large majority of residents do—then we’ll do what’s necessary to reduce conflicts and live more peacefully with bears.
Lately, it seems, we haven’t been doing nearly enough.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Double-digit health insurance increases will hit individual and small group plans in 2027, again
description: Hundreds of thousands of Minnesotans are facing significantly more expensive health insurance next year. The average increase for individual and small group insurance plans is 17% for 2027, the state’s Department of Commerce announced Thursday, raising costs for the 203,000 and 184,000 Minnesotans covered by individual and small group plans respectively. Ind[...]
text:
(Getty Images.)Hundreds of thousands of Minnesotans are facing significantly more expensive health insurance next year.
The average increase for individual and small group insurance plans is 17% for 2027, the state’s Department of Commerce announced Thursday, raising costs for the 203,000 and 184,000 Minnesotans covered by individual and small group plans respectively.
Individuals and their families who are not covered by their employer or by public programs — like Medicare, Medicaid (called Medical Assistance in Minnesota) and MinnesotaCare — buy individual plans from health insurers through MNsure, the state’s Affordable Care Act marketplace. Many people using MNcare can get discounts on their insurance premiums — what people pay upfront to be insured — if they make below a certain income.
Minnesota health insurance rates ballooning in 2026

The rate hikes come at the same time as significant shifts in the individual marketplace from federal policy: Republicans blocked Democratic efforts to extend “enhanced” premium discounts — delivered through tax credits — into 2026, resulting in the amount of discounts and the number of people who can receive those discounts to drop this year. (People can also buy individual health plans outside of MNsure, though they would be unable to get tax credits to offset premium costs.)
Health insurers have raised rates by double digit increases for two years in a row. Last year, individual rates went up 22%, while rates for small groups — which refers to businesses with fewer than 50 people — went up an average of 14%. Increases in the year before that were less extreme.
In a press release, Julia Dreier, the Department of Commerce’s temporary commissioner, attributed the eyewatering cost spikes to “broad changes across our health care system,” including the high prices of medical visits and drugs, people using more healthcare, and “the growing role of profit-driven entities in the delivery and financing of care.”


Only some health insurance companies are approved to sell coverage to individuals and small groups. The Department of Commerce releases the average rate increases for each health insurer, which range from 10% to 21% for 2027. HealthPartners, in the individual market, and UnitedHealthcare, in the small group market, both posted average increases exceeding 21%.
The same day the rate increases were announced, health economists from the University of Minnesota and the University of Southern California spoke at a state Senate human services committee hearing about how hospital consolidation drives up healthcare prices, which in turn drives up insurance prices. Mergers are being proposed at what Erin Conti of the Minnesota Attorney General’s Office called a “breakneck pace” in 2026, with a new merger announced just this week between Essentia and HealthPartners, two Minnesota-based health systems.
Glenn Melnick, a professor at USC, referred to increasingly expensive insurance premiums as a “hidden tax” in employment-based health insurance, where health insurance premiums are either taken out of paychecks or paid by employers, both resulting in lower pay for workers.
Melnick also noted that as insurance rates balloon, the same rate increases refer to larger and larger dollar amounts over time, making it more difficult to curb costs. In other words, since health insurance premiums are so expensive, even 10% growth now means families need to shell out — or sacrifice in wage growth — an additional couple thousands of dollars for higher insurance premiums every year.
Melnick and other health economists point to high hospital prices as a major driver of healthcare prices and, by extension, insurance prices. “If we don’t control hospital spending, we’re not going to effectively control overall healthcare spending,” Melnick said.
The increases come in the heat of midterm elections, and candidates were quick to blame the opposition for the ballooning costs, often in broad terms.
Republican House Speaker Lisa Demuth, who is running for governor against Democratic Sen. Amy Klobuchar, released a statement: “There is one person in this race responsible for the rising cost of health insurance: Amy Klobuchar. Twenty years ago U.S. Senate candidate Amy Klobuchar promised us lower health insurance costs, but they have skyrocketed over the two decades she’s been in Washington DC.”
Klobuchar, Minnesota’s senior senator, also released a statement. She blamed healthcare cuts from President Donald Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act for the rate hikes: “Minnesotans cannot afford a governor whose only plan for their health care is to double down on the Trump policies that are making healthcare more expensive and out of reach in our state and across the country.”
Klobuchar also reiterated her promise, if elected governor, to enact state-level tax credits if federal enhanced premium tax credits aren’t restored.
The Minnesota Council of Health Plans, the trade group for health insurers here, released a statement attributing cost increases to high prices and usage of medical services and prescription drugs.
The trade group also pointed to administrative changes by the Department of Commerce requiring insurers to cover 24/7 in-home nursing care, though neither the trade group nor the Department of Commerce clarified where exactly those changes stood by the time of publication.
Insurers had covered 24/7 in-home nursing care for 15 years, following a 2010 state law requiring them to cover medically necessary nursing care. For 2026 plans, though, some insurance companies placed caps on how much in-home care a person could receive. Bipartisan legislators tried to remove those caps in the 2026 legislative session, but failed to pass a bill. Sen. Liz Boldon, DFL-Rochester, an author of that bill, said that she’s still waiting for plans to be released to see if the Department of Commerce has indeed required insurers to cover 24/7 in-home nursing care.
“For them to say that they are increasing rates because of this care is nonsense to me, because they have been covering it for the last 16 years,” Boldon said in a phone call. “It is not a new thing.”
An analysis from the Peterson Center on Healthcare and KFF found that across the country, ACA marketplace insurers proposed a median increase of 15%, largely driven by higher prices of medical care.
Open enrollment for individuals shopping for health insurance begins Nov. 1.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Democrats’ ad links Ty Masterson to Sam Brownback; Kansas GOP nominee claims it’s a ‘lie’
description: Tax-policy legacy of former Kansas Gov. Sam Brownback is drawn into fray of gubernatorial race between Cindy Holscher and Ty Masterson.
text:
Sen. Ty Masterson, the Kansas Republican Party's nominee for governor, claims a new attack ad from the Democratic Governor's Association misrepresents video clips from 2017 and 2023 to smear his affiliation with former Gov. Sam Brownback and Brownback's disastrous 2012 overhaul of state income tax policy. In this June 1, 2026, image, Masterson chats with reporters as his wife, Marlo, looks on. (Photo by Baya Burgess/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — The Democratic Governors Association’s latest ad for Kansas gubernatorial candidate Cindy Holscher alleges Republican nominee Ty Masterson claimed a key role in shaping income tax cuts that cast the state into a budget abyss rather than promote economic growth.
Holscher, the Democratic nominee, has sought throughout the campaign to link Masterson with former Gov. Sam Brownback, especially his tax reform catastrophe. The DGA’s ad stresses that theme. Masterson, after reviewing the DGA’s commercial, declared it a “lie.”
The new DGA digital ad pointed to video of a 2017 Kansas Republican Assembly meeting in which Masterson referenced authorship of tax legislation signed by Brownback in 2012 to lower individual income tax rates and shield more than 300,000 business owners from state tax liability. Brownback’s objective was to kill off the state’s income tax and spark a supply-side economic renaissance.
During the Republican Assembly gathering, the DGA ad shows Masterson saying: “The Brownback plan, which by the way, I wrote.”
The DGA commercial included Masterson’s remark in 2023 on High Plains television that Brownback wasn’t the author of the 2012 tax legislation, but “just got blamed for it.”
Johanna Warshaw, deputy communications director of the DGA, said political connections between Masterson and Brownback should be clear to voters ahead of the Nov. 3 election.
“The Masterson agenda is the Brownback agenda,” she said. “No matter how hard Ty tries to distance himself from his role in the failed Brownback experiment, the truth is he wrote the disastrous plan — and he was caught admitting it on tape. Kansans across the aisle do not want to go back to the disastrous Brownback days of four-day school weeks and businesses fleeing the state.”
 
Masterson: It’s a ‘lie’
In response, Masterson said the DGA misrepresented his role in developing the 2012 income tax package. He said the DGA created a deceptive narrative by weaving together snippets from Republican Assembly and High Plains appearances that occurred six years apart. A key piece of video from the Republican Assembly was drawn from Masterson’s comments just over one hour into the forum.
Masterson said he specifically referred during the Republican Assembly to his idea from 2007 or 2008 to use a portion of state revenue increases to buy down the state’s income tax rates. At the Statehouse, such a mechanism has been called a ratchet.
Here is a longer version of Masterson’s qyote: “The original ratchet had nothing to do with the Brownback plan, which by the way I wrote back in 2008, maybe, or seven, I don’t know. All it did was, as long as you had growth in your revenues, a certain portion would ratchet your income tax down.”
Masterson, the Kansas Senate president who has represented Andover in the Legislature for 20 years, said the DGA’s ad perpetrated a “lie” and “they got caught.”
“They have video of me talking about my plan and saying it had nothing to do with the Brownback plan,” Masterson said. “So, they chopped up my own sentence and stitched together a fake video to change the meaning. When you have to doctor a video to make your opponent say something he never said, you’ve admitted you can’t win on the truth. Cindy Holscher’s allies are lying to Kansans, and they should be ashamed and embarrassed.”
 
Tax reform history
In terms of the 2012 tax cut, Brownback referred to the policy overhaul as an “experiment,” but he promised Kansans the changes would deliver an “Pulp Fiction”-style adrenaline shot to revive the state’s sluggish economy. It failed to inspire extraordinary growth in Kansas. From 2013 to 2016, Kansas’ gross domestic product expanded 4.8%. That was less than half the national average of 11.9% for the period.
The law did slash state revenue by nearly $1 billion. Without adoption of equivalent spending cuts, the result was multiple years of state budget shortfalls. The Legislature became desperate to balance the budget and ended up retaining what was to have been a temporary hike in the statewide sales tax. State lawmakers rapidly expanded the state’s borrowing, cannibalized the Kansas Department of Transportation’s budget and interfered with appropriations to K-12 public schools and social service programs.
Masterson served as chairman of the Senate Ways and Means Committee during this period and was partially responsible for advancing gambits aimed at preserving the Brownback tax agenda.
In 2017, a bipartisan coalition of legislators including Holscher but not Masterson voted to spike much of the Brownback tax program. The bill raised individual income tax rates and abolished the business tax loophole. Brownback vetoed the bill, but was overridden. Masterson characterized the repeal bill as “a piece of garbage.”
Democratic gubernatorial nominee Cindy Holscher says her Republican opponent, Ty Masterson, is linked to controversial tax policy signed by Gov. Sam Brownback in 2012. Holscher voted with a bipartisan coalition in 2017 to repeal Brownback’s tax agenda, while Masterson opposed the bill. Here, Holscher waves at the Kansas State Fair in Hutchinson on Sept. 12. (Photo by Jill Hummels for Kansas Reflector)
 
Holscher’s view
During the 2026 campaign, Holscher has sought to connect Masterson’s politics to the legacy of Brownback, who at one time was the most unpopular governor in the nation.
During the Kansas State Fair debate with Masterson, Holscher declared her GOP rival the equivalent of “Brownback 2.0.”
“Under Brownback, Kansas public schools cut Fridays and ended the school year early,” said Holscher, a state senator from Overland Park. “Kids lost learning time. Teachers permanently left the profession. It took our state years to recover. Ty Masterson championed that experiment. Now he wants to repeat it. Ty Masterson equals Brownback remastered.”
Global Strategy Group, which regularly works with Democratic candidates and the DGA, says Brownback has remained unpopular. The pollster says 64% of those surveyed viewed Brownback negatively, while 21% viewed the former governor positively.
The Legislature in 2025 adopted a ratchet for lowering individual and corporate income tax rates in Kansas, despite a veto by Gov. Laura Kelly. The trigger for adjusting rates was tied to whether the treasury received revenue above an inflation-adjusted baseline.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Healey touts Wu endorsement to start October push
authors: Colin A. Young I State House News Service
description: The governor and mayor, both Democrats and each the first woman elected to the chief executive positions in the state and city, are not known to have a close political connection.
text:
BOSTON MAYOR MICHELLE WU formally endorsed Gov. Maura Healey and Lt. Gov. Kim Driscoll for reelection Thursday morning, citing a “partnership to build a Boston and a Massachusetts that work for everyone.”
The governor and mayor, both Democrats and each the first woman elected to the chief executive positions in the state and city, are not known to have a close political connection. They backed opposing candidates in two of last month’s Democratic primaries for state Senate seats and Healey, a former Boston resident who now lives in Arlington, declined to say whether she supported Wu the day before Wu’s mayoral primary against Josh Kraft a year ago.
“I’m grateful for our work together — from a historic summer that delivered economic impact throughout our neighborhoods, to lowering costs, building more housing, keeping residents safe, and expanding opportunity throughout the Commonwealth,” Wu said in a statement provided by the Healey campaign. “I look forward to continuing to work alongside the Healey-Driscoll Administration to keep delivering results, defending our communities, and creating the future we deserve.”
Healey called Wu “such a fantastic partner and a true champion for the people of Boston” and referenced this summer’s era of good feelings around the World Cup and other popular events. “Coming off a great summer for Boston and our whole state, I’m so grateful to have worked side-by-side with her to deliver for our communities,” Healey said of Wu.
In a Tuesday social media video titled “Good luck to the Red Sox tonight!” Republican gubernatorial candidate Mike Minogue took a jab at both Healey and Wu. The short starts by showing a clip of Healey and Wu being booed on the field at Fenway Park this April and displays the message, “Looks like fans want someone else up to bat” before Minogue turns towards the camera in what appears to be a Star Trek captain’s chair.
Healey and Wu plan to be available to the press later Thursday. The pair are scheduled to celebrate new retrofits and renovations at Otis Elementary School in East Boston at 11:30 a.m.

name: Georgia Recorder
title: Proposal requiring Georgia election workers to ‘shuffle’ ballots at the polls fails to find support
description: A last-minute proposal that would have required poll workers to manually “shuffle” ballots before scanning them in an effort to prevent bad actors from identifying how Georgia residents voted failed to advance Thursday at a special-called meeting of the State Election Board. Election workers and advocates said the proposed rule would be impossible to impleme[...]
text:
State Election Board member Salleigh Grubbs, a top Georgia GOP official who was appointed to the board last year, speaks during a February board meeting held in Barrow County. Maya Homan/Georgia RecorderA last-minute proposal that would have required poll workers to manually “shuffle” ballots before scanning them in an effort to prevent bad actors from identifying how Georgia residents voted failed to advance Thursday at a special-called meeting of the State Election Board.
Election workers and advocates said the proposed rule would be impossible to implement before the November midterms and would likely create more problems than it solved.
Georgia’s voter registration deadline is approaching. Here are five things you need to know.

State Election Board member Salleigh Grubbs, a top Georgia GOP official who was appointed to the board last year, argued that emergency rules were needed to uphold Georgia’s constitutionally required ballot secrecy rules. Her proposal would require voters to place their completed ballots into “secure boxes” rather than ballot scanners, which voters use to submit their printed ballot. Under Grubbs’ proposal, ballots would later be scanned by poll workers rather than the voters themselves.
Thursday’s meeting was called to consider Grubbs’ proposal. 
“We cannot continue on the same path with these kinds of vulnerabilities,” Grubbs said. “It must be addressed before the November election so that we can continue on to secure all future elections.”
Janelle King, Georgia Election Board member. Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder
But other members of the board appeared more skeptical. Janelle King, the board’s vice chair, said she worried that the proposal would likely generate more fear and distrust among voters.
“I also have major concerns about dropping our ballots into a secured box and then having other individuals scan my ballot,” she said. “How do I know that in the shuffling something doesn’t fall out?”
Anne Dover, the Cherokee County elections director, raised concerns that counties could struggle to recruit poll workers if the proposal were approved.
“Elections officials are put in a very difficult position,” she said. “We’ve been accused of fraud. We’ve been accused of being criminals. Our poll workers have been accused of doing things they shouldn’t do, and this atmosphere just gets worse for us as elections officials and poll workers. And I’m afraid we will lose poll workers if something like this is mandated, because they’re going to feel that pressure not to make a mistake.”
The change would also be extraordinarily expensive for counties, Dover said. Cherokee County’s policies mandate that at least three poll workers be assigned to monitor ballots. The cost of hiring enough poll workers to have three people monitoring ballots at every early voting location across the county, she said, would require an extra $80,000 for the midterm elections.
Lawmakers mull cybersecurity concerns as they prepare for overhaul of Georgia’s voting system

Ballot images have been public record in Georgia since 2021, and records dating back to 2024 are available online at the secretary of state’s website. In August, a Princeton University researcher claimed that he was able to use artificial intelligence to tie thousands of voters to specific ballots with relative certainty by putting publicly available data through an AI tool.
In July, Election Director Blake Evans issued guidance to county election workers instructing them to redact ballot record numbers before uploading them to the secretary of state’s website to prevent ballots from being traced back to specific voters. At Thursday’s meeting, VotingWorks executive director Ben Adida, whose company also manufactures election equipment, said the secretary of state’s office had successfully addressed election security concerns.
But some election activists have maintained that Georgia’s system contains critical security issues and are urging the state to take action ahead of the midterm elections. Early voting begins on Oct. 13.
Last week, the Georgia Republican Party and Republican National Committee penned a joint letter to the board raising concerns about Georgia’s voting equipment software in light of the Princeton researcher’s findings and also called on the board to “seek any federal technical assistance required to complete a certified upgrade” of the state’s voting equipment.
Georgia election panel asks Trump administration to help push for election system updates

On Monday, members of the board approved a resolution urging the secretary of state’s office to update the state’s voting machine software and calling on the U.S. Department of Justice and U.S. Department of Homeland Security to step in to ensure that the update takes place.
But Carolyn Roddy, the board’s GOP appointee and sponsor of the resolution, said she shared board members’ concerns about ballot secrecy, but that Grubbs’ proposal went too far.
“I’m not in favor of putting election officials through the ringer on this thing,” she said Thursday. “I think that it will cause incredible conflict that will deter us from other missions.”

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: NC receives first $45.2M payout from Meta child safety settlement
description: North Carolina Attorney General Jeff Jackson said Thursday the state has received its first $45.2 million payment from Meta, owner of Facebook and Instagram, as part of a multistate settlement over allegations that the company’s social media platforms harmed children.  The payout is the first installment of a settlement that could bring up to $645 […]
text:
A bipartisan group of  29  attorneys general allege the tech giant Meta deceived the public about the addictive nature and the harms of their product.
(Photo: Getty Images) North Carolina Attorney General Jeff Jackson said Thursday the state has received its first $45.2 million payment from Meta, owner of Facebook and Instagram, as part of a multistate settlement over allegations that the company’s social media platforms harmed children. 
The payout is the first installment of a settlement that could bring up to $645 million to the state by 2035. The state is guaranteed at least $451 million, with an additional $194 million available if other major social media companies, including YouTube and TikTok, agree to safety measures. 
The state legislature will decide how to spend the money. Jackson has encouraged lawmakers to direct the money toward funding crisis helplines for children and funding after-school and summer programs. 
He also suggested using the money to hire additional school health officials amid shortages of counselors, social workers and nurses in North Carolina’s school systems. 
Meta to pay North Carolina up to $645 million in landmark settlement

“This settlement is about holding Meta accountable and protecting children,” Jackson said. “Not only does it require Meta to make major safety changes to its platforms, but it brings hundreds of millions of dollars to our state.”
Jackson announced the settlement with Meta in August after North Carolina and 32 other states sued the company in 2023. 
The states alleged that Meta designed Facebook and Instagram to increase the time children spent on their platforms while downplaying the risks and collecting data from minors without parental consent. 
State officials also cited the company’s internal documents and raised concerns about features such as autoplay, push notifications and infinite scrolling, which they said were designed to increase engagement. 
The settlement requires Meta to strengthen measures keeping children under 13 off Facebook and Instagram and give parents more control over teen accounts. 
Jackson said teens can expect to see several changes to their accounts in the coming months: 

Under the changes, teens will have a new default two-hour daily limit. Once they reach that limit, their accounts will time out, restricting access to their feeds and scrolling. Access to direct messages will still be allowed. 
Meta will also implement an anti-scrolling feature that will pop up every 15 minutes to discourage continuous app usage. 
Feeds will be blocked from midnight to 6 a.m. each night and notifications will be disabled from 10 p.m. to 7 a.m. Notifications will also automatically turn off on Facebook and Instagram during school hours on weekdays during the school year. 
Like counts and post reactions will be turned off by default, and beauty filters will be removed on the platforms to limit potential harm to children’s self-esteem and self-image. 

The remaining payments to the state will be made through the next decade, with installments scheduled each Jan. 15 beginning in 2027.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: South Dakota Supreme Court says father doesn’t have a right to police records about son’s death
description: The South Dakota Supreme Court ruled this week that a father doesn’t have a right to obtain investigation records he wanted about his son’s death. Ryan Pyle, age 37, went missing in August 2020, and his remains were found in November of that year near the Snake Creek Recreation Area in South Dakota, near the […]
text:
The entrance to the South Dakota Supreme Court at the state Capitol in Pierre. (Photo by Joshua Haiar/South Dakota Searchlight)The South Dakota Supreme Court ruled this week that a father doesn’t have a right to obtain investigation records he wanted about his son’s death.
Ryan Pyle, age 37, went missing in August 2020, and his remains were found in November of that year near the Snake Creek Recreation Area in South Dakota, near the city of Platte. Law enforcement believed he died of hypothermia. His father, Brian Pyle, believed the death may have involved foul play.
Brian Pyle asked a lower court to force the release of reports and records from the investigation into his son’s death. The lower court said no. The South Dakota Supreme Court affirmed that decision. 
“The State had no duty to disclose criminal investigative information, nor did Pyle have a clear right to access such information,” wrote the court. 
Pyle’s argument for access included pointing to Marsy’s Law, the South Dakota constitutional amendment passed by voters in 2016 that establishes a formal bill of rights for crime victims. But the court said the record had not proven that a crime occurred, and that Brian “is not a ‘victim,’ as the term is defined under Marsy’s Law, and therefore Marsy’s Law is not applicable.”
Even if Marsy’s Law applied, wrote the court, “none of the nineteen enumerated rights in Marsy’s Law direct or compel the State to disclose investigative reports or records.”  
South Dakota law also specifically exempts law-enforcement investigation records from public disclosure requirements.

name: Colorado Newsline
title: Victor Marx isn’t running for Colorado governor. He’s running for state pastor.
description: Victor Marx has made some spectacular headlines. The Republican nominee for Colorado governor can’t say how many people he’s killed. He claims to have participated in extraordinary exploits overseas as part of his ministry but refuses to substantiate what appear to be tall tales. He performs exorcisms — over the phone, even. He faces allegations […]
text:
Victor Marx, the Republican nominee for Colorado governor, speaks at the 2026 summer conference of the Colorado Water Congress in Steamboat Springs on Aug. 19, 2026. (Photo by Chase Woodruff/Colorado Newsline)Victor Marx has made some spectacular headlines.
The Republican nominee for Colorado governor can’t say how many people he’s killed. He claims to have participated in extraordinary exploits overseas as part of his ministry but refuses to substantiate what appear to be tall tales. He performs exorcisms — over the phone, even. He faces allegations of campaign finance violations. A Daily Beast report this week highlighted Marx’s own accounts of committing physical violence against his wife and young son.
It’s easy for voters to get the impression Marx is little more than “a liar and a fraud,” as put by Kyle Cark of 9News during a candidate debate.
Marx’s wild claims deserve every bit of the scrutiny they’ve received. But that attention has obscured an essential quality of his campaign, the one that could be the most disastrous were he to become the chief executive of Colorado: his extreme faith. A Christian pastor, Marx makes no attempt to hide his vision for political leadership, which to him is indistinguishable from religious leadership. Based on his behavior and rhetoric, he appears to be running for lead Christian pastor of Colorado, not governor.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
A striking moment during that Clark-moderated debate came at the end, when the three GOP primary candidates were invited to give closing remarks. Marx closed his eyes and prayed. Many politicians pray, nothing wrong with that. But Marx’s decision, in that setting, to fill that crucial time with a public Christian prayer, instead of trying to persuade voters that his plan for the state’s highest political office was superior, signaled to viewers that God was his platform.
It also foreshadowed more explicit expressions of Christianity’s improper place in his campaign. During a Fox31 interview in August, anchor Matt Mauro asked Marx what he’d do to make Colorado more affordable.
“I’m going to consecrate the state back to God,” Marx said. “We need to lead to help our state with integrity and a moral code, and that’s how we’re going to get it back on track.”
An investigation by 9News of Marx’s activities in the last 15 years “indicates that his work casting off demons is at the center of his $7.5 million per year ministry, All Things Possible, and can fairly be described as his life’s work,” Clark wrote. He added, “The ministry leader says casting off evil spirits is his greatest achievement.”
Earlier this month, the campaign called on supporters to participate in a 21-day fast, based on Biblical principles.
“This is not just an election, but this is a spiritual battle against the forces of wickedness,” Eileen Marx, Victor’s wife, said in a video announcement about the fast. In another video about the fast, Eileen said, “We believe God’s going to heal Colorado.”
It’s hardly unusual for politicians to proclaim their faith, but it is unusual for them to stake their entire campaign on their faith.
The implications for Colorado are profound. Marx’s Christianity is not only fundamental to his life and campaign, but it bears odd and extreme qualities that could make a wreck of state policy. Take abortion. Coloradans again and again have supported abortion rights. In 2024, they voted to enshrine abortion rights in the state constitution. But Marx, based on his faith, would try to reverse the amendment, as he alluded to in the Fox31 interview. He has a long history of extreme rhetoric on abortion.
Last month, Marx earned the endorsement of Andrew Wommack, a national religious figure. Since Marx made a big deal about the endorsement, saying he was “incredibly honored” to receive it and lauding Wommack for “encouraging Christians not simply to believe their faith privately, but to live it boldly,” it’s reasonable to assume Marx is sympathetic to Wommack’s advocacy for the Seven Mountains Mandate, which says Christians should rule over all aspects of society.
Colorado faces pressing problems. The state budget is buckling under multiple increasing pressures, especially those related to healthcare costs. Housing remains unaffordable. Environmental crises abound.
Scripture might offer fortitude. It doesn’t offer solutions. Those will come from research, facts and earthly debates. But Marx is all piety and no policy.
