name: Kansas Reflector
title: Kansas GOP files complaint against Democrat. She says, ‘Let the timing speak for itself.’
description: TOPEKA — A Kansas Republican Party leader accused a Democrat’s campaign of tainting a congressional race and violating federal election law because of her ties to a nonprofit she co-founded. The complaint filed Wednesday by Kansas GOP executive director Rob Fillion alleges Katy Tyndell, a Democrat who is running in the 4th District against Republican […]
text:
Katy Tyndell appears for a March 13, 2026, podcast recording at the Kansas Reflector newsroom in Topeka. (Photo by Sherman Smith/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — A Kansas Republican Party leader accused a Democrat’s campaign of tainting a congressional race and violating federal election law because of her ties to a nonprofit she co-founded.
The complaint filed Wednesday by Kansas GOP executive director Rob Fillion alleges Katy Tyndell, a Democrat who is running in the 4th District against Republican U.S. Rep. Ron Estes, used her nonprofit’s email list to promote her campaign, coordinated with the nonprofit to sponsor a debate and solicited an endorsement from a public figure who appeared at nonprofit events.
“I can’t speak for Ron Estes or tell you what he is worried about,” Tyndell said, “but I’ll let the timing speak for itself.”
She said the Kansas GOP’s allegations are false.
Tyndell is one of four founders of Leading Kansas, which designated itself as a nonpartisan 501(c)4 nonprofit. It is billed as a civic engagement organization. One of Tyndell’s fellow founders is Noah Taylor, who ran in the Democratic primary for U.S. Senate.
Tyndell said she stepped away from her leadership role at the nonprofit when she launched her campaign and has been “extremely careful” to keep the two separate.
“I have not used Leading Kansas’ email lists, Slack channels, social media, programming, or other organizational resources to run my campaign, and we have taken care not to put campaign materials into Leading Kansas communications,” she said.
A news release from the Kansas GOP said Fillion requested the Federal Election Commission immediately investigate Tyndell’s campaign to determine whether it accepted forbidden in-kind contributions and cease the campaign from doing so in the future “before it further taints” the race.
“Instead of building her campaign on her own, she used Leading Kansas’ resources to reach voters and advance her candidacy,” Fillion said. “That is not civic engagement. It is an illegal in-kind contribution. It is an attempt to inject undisclosed dark money into a federal race and to treat a nonprofit she controls as an arm of her campaign.”
The complaint pointed to March 29 and April 20 emails from Tyndell’s Leading Kansas address “announcing her congressional campaign and soliciting continued engagement while she remained tied to the group.” Tyndell said those emails were “completely ordinary” communications from the beginning of her campaign to say she was stepping back from her leadership role with the nonprofit. 
“If the Kansas Republican Party genuinely believed there was some serious violation, it is curious that they waited until Sept. 30 — months after these events and coincidentally the very day I’m scheduled to host a large town hall event in Sedgwick County — to raise it,” Tyndell said.
The complaint also called out a July 17 candidate debate sponsored by Leading Kansas and an endorsement from Michael Fanone, an officer who was at the U.S. Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021, and appeared earlier this year at Leading Kansas events in Wichita and Lawrence. It accused her campaign of linking Leading Kansas programming in Facebook posts to her candidacy.
Kansas GOP’s vice chair, Andy Hooser, accused Tyndell of using Leading Kansas as “a slush fund.”
“Democrats never stop lecturing everyone else about dark money and ‘saving democracy.’ Then they turn around and run their own candidate using a dark money group she still controls. This is the Democrat playbook: one set of rules for them, another for everyone else,” Hooser said. “The law applies to Democrats too.”
Tyndell wrote commentary for Kansas Reflector before she declared a run for public office. Kansas Reflector does not publish commentary from elected officials. 
“It’s unfortunate that Ms. Tyndell, who has contributed to the Kansas Reflector, seems to be using her influence in dark money groups to prop up her campaign, but that’s best left to the FEC to investigate these serious allegations brought forward by the Kansas Republican Party,” the Estes campaign said in an emailed statement. 
The Kansas GOP filed a similar complaint against the Democratic U.S. Senate candidate, the Rev. Adam Hamilton, and his United Methodist church, Resurrection. The state Republicans accused Hamilton, who at the time hadn’t officially filed to run for office, of improperly using church resources to “advance his political ambitions.”
The outcome of that complaint, which was also filed with the FEC, is unclear.

name: Nevada Current
title: Former police chief hopes to oust incumbent in Henderson mayor race
description: After nearly winning re-election outright during the June primary, incumbent Henderson Mayor Michelle Romero will face the former Henderson Police Chief Hollie Chadwick in the general election.  The election comes amid a recent ethics complaint against Romero alleging a conflict of interest stemming from her consultant work and the businesses she has represe[...]
text:
Hollie Chadwick, Michelle Romero. (Candidate photos)After nearly winning re-election outright during the June primary, incumbent Henderson Mayor Michelle Romero will face the former Henderson Police Chief Hollie Chadwick in the general election. 
The election comes amid a recent ethics complaint against Romero alleging a conflict of interest stemming from her consultant work and the businesses she has represented coming before the city council. 
Chadwick announced in May 2025, months after being terminated by the city, that she was challenging Romero in order to bring transparency and accountability to the Henderson City Council.
A candidate who receives a majority of the vote in nonpartisan primary races wins the election outright, but Romero, who faced four challengers in June, received 49.75% of the vote, roughly 29,000 votes.
Chadwick received 23% of 13,432 votes during the election. Adam Price, who also ran and received 21% of votes, endorsed Chadwick following the primary. 
Before entering office Romero launched a consulting firm. She was elected to represent ward 1 in 2019. 
In 2022, she was elected mayor, winning the race outright during the primary with more than 70% of the vote.
Following this year’s primary election, Price, president of the Henderson Democratic Club, filed a complaint with the Nevada Commission on Ethics about Romero, alleging that her consulting work with developers that come before the city is a conflict of interest. 
Romero has disputed the accusation, saying she has abstained from voting on items related to consulting work. 
The Las Vegas Review-Journal found she has also repeatedly abstained from voting on issues related to Las Vegas Paving Corp because her son and husband work for the company.  
In a previous interview with Nevada Current, Chadwick said people liken Henderson City Council to high school because of the drama, adding it was “setting the wrong tone for the community.”
Romero pushed back on the allegation the council doesn’t get along, telling The Nevada Independent that council meetings run “smoothly and effectively” and arguing that collaboration is why Henderson scores high when it comes to quality of life. 
On her website Romero says that “transparency in our government is paramount,” adding that “I believe it is critically important for elected officials to actively respond to questions and concerns; which I have done and will continue to do throughout my service.”
Chadwick is running under the promise to bring more transparency to the city, previously telling Current that elected officials shouldn’t “just give a little sound bite and not give the meat and potatoes.”
“Our city deserves a leader who listens, acts, and understands the importance of trust between government and the people,” Chadwick said on her campaign website. “It’s time to bring authentic leadership that puts you first.” 
Chadwick, who was appointed chief of police in May 2023 and terminated two years later without cause, has  faced scrutiny in her previous position. 
A 2023 Las Vegas Review-Journal investigation found Chadwick cleared the disciplinary record of a detective who was accused of using the N-word and calling Black, latino and LGBTQ people “savages” and “garbage.” The Review-Journal noted at the time she “fled when a reporter tried to ask her a question at a public event.”
The Current previously reported that the city police supervisors’ union filed a complaint with the Nevada Employee Management Relations Board in 2024, alleging Chadwick denied overtime resulting from union leave provisions in Nevada law and the city’s collective bargaining agreement. 
Romero had far out-raised Chadwick as of July 15 campaign finance reports. She had $700,000 on hand at the end of June; Chadwick had nearly $3,000
Culinary Union, Vegas Chamber, and Southern Nevada Building Trades Unions are among the organizations that endorsed Romero. Chadwick is endorsed by the Nevada Voter Alliance, the Nevada Narcotic Officers Association, and Nevada Teamsters.

 Catching Our Eye

• SNAP. The Ohio Newsroom’s Kendall Crawford is reporting, “Ohio will lose an estimated $38M to administer SNAP. Metro areas will be hardest hit.”
The federal government will pay less to help Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Programs run starting on Thursday.
Historically, SNAP administrative costs have been shared by the federal government and the state. But, under the Trump administration’s HR1, or “One Big Beautiful Bill,” the portion the federal government covers will go down.
On Oct. 1, the federal government will cover 25% of administrative costs, rather than 50%.
Around 1.4 million Ohioans are enrolled in the program that provides low-income people monthly funds for groceries.
• Minimum wage. WTOL’s Dave DeNatale is reporting, “Ohio’s minimum wage will increase starting on Jan. 1, 2027.”
The minimum wage in Ohio will increase to $11.40 per hour for non-tipped employees and $5.70 per hour for tipped employees beginning on Jan. 1, 2026.
According to the Ohio Department of Commerce’s Bureau of Wage and Hour, the minimum wage will apply to employees of businesses with annual gross receipts of more than $420,000 per year, an increase from the current $405,000 threshold.
Currently, Ohio’s minimum wage is $11 per hour for non-tipped employees and $5.50 per hour for tipped employees.
• Paper products. WBNS’ Kristen McFarland is reporting, “Chillicothe paper mill prepares to restart production.”
The former Chillicothe paper mill is back in the spotlight as paper production is set to return just one year after the mill shut down.
The new owners, U.S. Paper Mill LLC, are currently manufacturing and selling nitrile gloves and other personal protective equipment at the site.
The company said it is now hiring employees as it prepares to restart paper production.

title: Put the AI servers within sanctuaries
description: This summer, while University of Michigan leadership defended a proposed data center with Los Alamos National Laboratory, my family gathered for my late sister Rachana’s birthday at a different kind of infrastructure. Decades ago, my parents partnered with Michigan State University to establish the Rachana Rajendra Serenity and Bird Sanctuary, a 78-acre natu[...]
text:
No Data Centers sign in Howell, Michigan | Photo by Jon King/Michigan AdvanceThis summer, while University of Michigan leadership defended a proposed data center with Los Alamos National Laboratory, my family gathered for my late sister Rachana’s birthday at a different kind of infrastructure.
Decades ago, my parents partnered with Michigan State University to establish the Rachana Rajendra Serenity and Bird Sanctuary, a 78-acre nature preserve in East Lansing to honor their daughter’s life, which transitioned too soon. Rachana, whose name in Sanskrit means creation, was an electrical engineer who also loved nature.
For years, in anguish, I appreciated this urban refuge as a family tribute to Rachana. But it is also an example of the kind of public sanctuary that Michigan could create around AI data centers. Such an integrative space could uplift both the economy and the ecology if only public officials used imagination, leverage, and the state’s extraordinary tradition of innovation and commitment to its natural resources.
The hyperscale University of Michigan proposal is currently designed as the epicenter of an extractive site whose harms to surrounding communities will span from toxic stress to toxic chemicals.
Fifteen miles from U-M/Los Alamos, another massive data center construction site is unfurling. At $56 billion and 21 million square feet, Saline’s Stargate “Barn” is Michigan’s biggest construction project. But the billionaire investors behind this project now also want to dump their wastewater into the Saline River.
Construction underway on Related Digital’s hyperscale data center in Saline Township, Michigan on June 20, 2026. (Photo by Jon King/Michigan Advance)
Technology leaders who are publicly urging “pacing the frontier” on AI itself should prioritize creating more sustainable, life-centered value from campuses drawing a nuclear reactor’s worth of power.
Imagine how slowed and discerning development could build these campuses with safe, non-toxic materials and contain industrial waste on-site. The State of Michigan can foster pioneering collaborations between entrepreneurs and its pre-eminent educational institutions — including MSU’s ecological expertise (from the nation’s first land-grant college) with U-M engineering innovations  — to transform each data center blueprint into an economically-robust-ecological sanctuary.
Imagine if, together, Michigan minds build a regenerative star within a nourishing universe: a data campus that captures and uses its own rainwater, recycles its cooling water, generates more solar, wind, and geothermal energy than it consumes, and feeds the surplus back to neighborhoods. The biodiversity-balanced buildings would be ringed by refuges of native food forests, waterfalls, ponds, parks, streams, and community gardens.
Admittedly, such technological utopias don’t yet exist and most data center acreage does not usually begin with ecological abundance. Even simpler ecosystems like Rachana’s sanctuary can take generations to flourish. But precedent exists to slow down. Minnesota offers a baseline framework. Pennsylvania has restricted new data center construction, and New York’s Executive Order 62 has paused hyperscale projects pending review.
In England, major developments are required to enhance land by 10 percent with Biodiversity Net Gain laws and be accountable for at least 30 years with independent ecological audits paid for by the investors.
Here at home, more government and university policymakers should follow the lead of Ypsilanti Township Supervisor Brenda Stumbo and Congresswoman Debbie Dingell, who blocked the U-M project’s power and water and called on U-M to pause. I ask Michigan policymakers to use their own leverage to integrate community voices to dream, drop rushed plans, and, eventually, develop better.
I love Michigan deeply, and most Michiganders do; it is one of the most beautiful places in the country, a state whose natural resources are our united pride.
As a result, standards for balancing economic development with the natural riches of the people’s peninsula must be higher here.
In Graeme Base’s children’s book “Uno’s Garden,” a village expands from a forest. Soon, nearly every creature, and wonder, disappears. The villagers must try to restore balance with the remnants.
Interpretive sign inside the Rachana Rajendra Serenity and Bird Sanctuary, (Photo from Anuja Rajendra)
I hope Michigan does not have to lose the wellbeing of its people or the wellspring of its wildlife to learn the lesson. The population of Kirtland’s warblers, songbirds that nest primarily here, declined 34% between 2021 and 2025. Michiganders fight for the Karner blue butterfly, celebrate the comeback of the lake sturgeon, and value the countless silent species with their own claims on this land.
Data centers are inevitable (any building with servers is one) and artificial intelligence has the potential to unlock life-saving secrets about the natural world. I’m not an anti-technology person; however, when billionaire investors offer pennies on the parcel, Michigan should ask for more and build hyperscale campuses that people will yearn to visit like forest-bathing sanctuaries.
My sister Rachana simultaneously engineered signals and appreciated soil. Her essence still emanates through the streets, streams, and yes, electrical signals, across Michigan. A metal sign at the entrance of the sanctuary reminds visitors of the interconnectedness of all things. “When we try to pick anything out by itself, we find that it is hitched to everything else in the universe,” says the quote by naturalist John Muir.
Let’s ensure our peninsula  continues to be a haven where life energy flows for eons – not only through our souls but through our built environments.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Missouri adds new paperwork requirements to food assistance as federal penalties loom
description: Since receiving a letter from the Missouri Department of Social Services Sept. 1 containing “an important notice” about his federal food assistance, Andrew Dallas has struggled to ease his mind.  Dallas, 63, of Arnold, who was diagnosed with epilepsy after a childhood head injury, can’t work or drive, and he depends on disability benefits and […]
text:
Starting Oct. 1, the Department of Social Services will require Missourians applying to receive or renew their eligibility for SNAP food benefits to provide documents verifying their housing, utility and dependent care costs, as well as financial resources including money in bank accounts (Photo by Justin Sullivan/Getty Images).Since receiving a letter from the Missouri Department of Social Services Sept. 1 containing “an important notice” about his federal food assistance, Andrew Dallas has struggled to ease his mind. 
Dallas, 63, of Arnold, who was diagnosed with epilepsy after a childhood head injury, can’t work or drive, and he depends on disability benefits and the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance program, previously known as food stamps, to get by. 
Skipping meals, Dallas told The Independent, can trigger his seizures. Without SNAP, he said, “I wouldn’t be able to get the food I need to keep myself going.”
Starting Oct. 1, the department will require Missourians applying to receive or renew their eligibility for SNAP to provide documents verifying their housing, utility and dependent care costs, along with financial resources including money in bank accounts. 
“Failure to provide requested verification may result in your SNAP application being rejected or SNAP case being closed,” the letter says. “If you do not submit expense verification, we cannot include these expenses in determining your eligibility and benefits level.”
The department says the additional paperwork is intended to reduce Missouri’s SNAP payment error rate before a federal law begins requiring states with high error rates to shoulder a share of benefit costs.
Whether the new verification requirements will significantly reduce Missouri’s overall error rate is unclear. The state’s own data shows the expenses targeted by the new requirements were responsible for only a small fraction of Missouri’s SNAP payment errors last year. Nearly half of the dollars improperly paid or withheld resulted from inaccurate wage and salary information.
And advocates worry the new requirements could create another kind of problem not reflected in the payment error rate: eligible Missourians losing benefits because they cannot produce the paperwork or the state fails to process it.
In an email to The Independent, Baylee Watts, the department’s media director, said federal law does not require states to verify all of those expenses and resources to determine SNAP eligibility, but the department is opting for additional documentation requirements ahead of a key change included in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act passed by Congress last July.
Starting Oct. 1, 2027, states with SNAP payment error rates of 6% or higher will have to pay between 5% and 15% of benefit costs. States can use their error rate from fiscal year 2025 or fiscal year 2026 to determine their benefit cost share for the first year.
Missouri’s error rate in federal fiscal year 2025, from October 2024 through the end of September 2025, was 8.67%, according to data released by the U.S. Department of Agriculture. That could put Missouri on the hook for $150 million in fiscal year 2028, according to an estimate by the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities. USDA will release SNAP payment error rates for the current federal fiscal year, which ends Sept. 30, in June 2027.
Andrew Dallas, 63, of Arnold, worked for years as a jeweler but had to stop because his seizures were triggered by the sound of the machinery in the shop. Dallas, pictured here in 2019, worries he won’t be able to meet new documentation requirements to keep his SNAP benefits (photo provided).
Watts said the department required SNAP participants to document expenses and resources until 2001.
“The department is reinstating verification as part of its broader effort to reduce payment errors and prepare for the state share requirement” in the federal law, Watts said.
Five Missouri food security and legal advocacy organizations last week urged the department to delay or cancel the planned SNAP documentation requirements in a Sept. 22 letter to Mandi Adams, director of the department’s Family Support Division. 
The signatories — Legal Services of Eastern Missouri, Empower Missouri, the Missouri Budget Project, the GLO Center, which is an LGBTQ community center in Springfield, and A Red Circle, a community organization based in north St. Louis County — argued the planned changes could increase Missouri’s SNAP error rate and deprive eligible low-income Missourians of benefits.
“The department claims that these changes will ‘safeguard resources for households who truly need them,’” the letter says, quoting a statement from Adams in a department press release. “In fact, it will cause thousands of low-income Missourians to lose the nutrition assistance they ‘truly need’ to feed their families.”
In an Aug. 18 webinar hosted by the American Public Human Services Association, Jeremy Bowman, the department’s deputy director of intergovernmental relations, said the state’s SNAP error rate had been “holding steady right at 5.9%.” 
“We don’t even want to jump up that little tenth of a percent,” Bowman said. “We just need to keep that to a low.”
Watts confirmed that 5.9% “was Missouri’s state-reported payment error rate for a portion of federal fiscal year 2026” but cautioned that Missouri’s official error rate won’t be released by USDA until June 2027.
 Error rate

A department report obtained by The Independent shows that the largest source of errors in federal fiscal year 2025 was inaccurate wage and salary information. Shelter and dependent care costs ranked fifth and sixth.
Out of a sample of 101 cases with payment errors totaling $25,397, almost half — $12,156, or 47.9% — stemmed from inaccurate wage and salary data. Incorrect information about dependent care costs accounted for $1,025 or about 4% of over- and underpayments. Inaccurate shelter costs accounted for another $1,010.
States are required to review statistical samples of households participating in SNAP — active cases — and households whose cases were denied, suspended or terminated — negative cases — and submit that information to the U.S. Department of Agriculture.
Only active cases are used to calculate states’ payment error rates. That means the measure captures benefits that were too high or too low, but not eligible applicants who were wrongly denied or recipients whose benefits were improperly terminated.
Watts said in a Sept. 25 email that the state’s quality control reviews “consistently identify unverified resources and household expenses as primary contributors to SNAP administration errors and overpayments.”
Asked how that characterization squared with the federal fiscal year 2025 data obtained by The Independent, Watts said that while “wage and salary information accounted for the largest share of error dollars” that year, “shelter expenses, dependent care expenses and countable resources also contribute to payment errors.”
Watts said the department is addressing errors from inaccurate wage and salary information by investing in technology to verify that data, including a database called The Work Number, and by enhancing staff training.
 Duty to assist

Federal law requires state agencies to assist households in obtaining required verification when they are cooperating with requests for information.
In their letter to Adams, advocates expressed concern that the department won’t be able to process the extra paperwork created by the new requirements — and that when Missourians struggle to obtain requested documents, department staff won’t be able to help.
“Overburdened caseworkers will now have to process voluminous additional paperwork and are more likely to make mistakes, creating the very errors the department claims these changes are intended to prevent,” the letter says.
Christine Woody, food security policy manager for Empower Missouri, told The Independent the bigger concern is what happens when paperwork problems knock eligible people off the program. 
The department is “already very limited in their staff, so if that paperwork does not get accounted for, the family will most likely be terminated from the program, and then they’re not counted as an error,” Woody said. “But those are eligible families that need these benefits and could get these benefits based on their income and their resources.”
Watts said that if households provide initial documentation that doesn’t meet the department’s requirements, they will receive a formal request for information from the division, “providing participants with a clear designated timeline to submit the necessary records.”
Instructions and resources for participants on SNAP verification requirements will be posted on the department’s website, Watts said.
The additional requirements come as the department continues to struggle with paperwork processing and helping Missourians navigate applications and renewals for public benefits.
Of the more than 333,000 Missourians who lost Medicaid coverage from January 2025 and February 2026, nearly 92% were procedural terminations, meaning the department could not determine whether they were still eligible because of missing forms, incomplete information or other paperwork problems.
A federal court ruled in May 2024 that long wait times and automatic disconnections from the department’s call center illegally deprived eligible Missourians of SNAP benefits by preventing them from completing interviews required to verify and maintain their eligibility. 
A federal appeals court in August asked the district court to consider whether to narrow Judge Douglas Harpool’s order, including requirements that the department ensure that no more than 20% of SNAP applications are denied for failure to interview and that 90% of callers wait no more than 20 minutes to speak with a staff member.
In June 2026, the most recent month with reported data, 24% of SNAP denials were for failure to complete an interview, and 72.3% callers waited no more than 20 minutes.
Dallas is one of the plaintiffs in that case. In 2023, when he tried about 10 times to reach the call center for help filling out his SNAP recertification paperwork, he was repeatedly disconnected.  When he was put on hold, he was told there were 234 callers ahead of him, according to court documents.
Now Dallas, who experiences confusion and struggles to focus due to his disability, worries he won’t be able to navigate the new SNAP verification process. 
“The stuff they’re requiring makes it seem like I require a secretary to go through my files,” Dallas said. “This is a lot of stuff. It’s overwhelming.”
“All I’m doing now anymore,” he said, “is worrying.”

name: Nevada Current
title: Prosecutor challenges incumbent judge in Clark County District Court Department 29
description: Clark County District Court Judge Jacob Reynolds faces a challenge from prosecutor Alex Quagge in the race for District Court Department 29. Reynolds says attorneys who think he owes them favors that he failed to deliver are behind the effort to elect his opponent. “I think some people got upset that I didn’t rule their […]
text:
Alex Quagge, Jacob Reynolds. (Candidate photos)Clark County District Court Judge Jacob Reynolds faces a challenge from prosecutor Alex Quagge in the race for District Court Department 29. Reynolds says attorneys who think he owes them favors that he failed to deliver are behind the effort to elect his opponent. 
“I think some people got upset that I didn’t rule their way when they thought I should have, and so now they’re running somebody against me,” Reynolds told the Current. “That’s their right. They want to get somebody who aligns with their business interests. My business is to be fair.” 
Reynolds is speaking of A Coalition for a Fair and Qualified Nevada Judiciary, which has endorsed Quagge. The group is made up of about 20 firms that generally represent plaintiffs, such as personal injury attorneys.
“I’m just not a judge who grants favors,” Reynolds said. “I took a large pay cut to get this job, and if I lose this election, I’ll go back to making more money. I’m not intimidated by people who want to try to intimidate me.”
Quagge says he chose to challenge Reynolds because he spoke with attorneys and others and “a number of people were not happy. Ultimately, that’s why I picked this race. I think it’s important for everybody to believe in the judiciary.” 
Quagge is a prosecutor for the Clark County District Attorney. He served in the same capacity in Carson City. He also served in the U.S. Army JAG Corps. 
“I have a lot of trial experience, both as a prosecutor and as a defense attorney,” he said. “I’m taking multiple trials to verdict, and I think that I would make good, fair, and legally sound rulings.” 
This is Quagge’s first bid for office.
Reynolds first ran for the bench in 2020 and lost to Tara Clark Newberry. In 2023, Gov. Joe Lombardo appointed him to Dept. 29. The following year his opponent dropped out of the race and he ran unopposed.
Of the 189 attorneys who evaluated Reynolds in the Las Vegas Review-Journal’s Judging the Judges 2025 survey, 73% said he should be retained. His highest score was for administrative ability while his lowest score was for legal ability. 
“When I saw the rating I was very happy with it because 50% of the people that come in front of me, I tell ‘no.’”
Reynolds doesn’t put too much stock in the ratings. 
“One of the comments said I need to be tougher on crime, and I’ve never handled a criminal case,” he stated. “These people have never been in front of me, obviously, or they’re just doing this maliciously.”
Dept. 29 currently has a civil docket. Reynolds says he has “no criminal background at all,” and doesn’t think judges need to be equipped to handle all types of cases. 
Of 33 cases that have been appealed, Reynolds’ rulings have been deemed in error in six cases. 
“People have donated to me that haven’t donated to any judge ever because I 
bring that civil experience, and I think the civil bar has appreciated getting a fair shake,” he said. “We desperately need judges who have a background in civil law. The great majority of our judges have criminal experience.”  
Quagge says he’d like to preside over a split docket if he’s victorious. 
He says he’s not concerned about exhibiting prosecutorial bias. 
“I’d really be looking at rehabilitation,” Quagge said. ”The motivations behind crimes are often housing instability, untreated mental health issues, or untreated substance abuse that lead somebody to spiral. Ideally, that would all get treated on the front end.”
Quagge says he believes it’s “important for judges to have empathy for everybody in the courtroom, to include the criminal defendant.”
His goal, as a veteran, is to one day preside over the district’s Veteran Treatment Court, which he says is highly effective but could use more resources. “A lot of times we would run into maybe not enough bed space for inpatient treatment, or not enough providers. The system is overloaded.” 
As of July, Quagge had raised $145,000 and had about $110,000 in the bank. 
He is endorsed by Senate Majority Leader and candidate for attorney general Nicole Canizzarro, Clark County Commissioner Tick Segerblom, and Clark County District Attorney Steve Wolfson, his boss.
He’s also endorsed by PLAN Action, Nevada National Organization for Women (NOW) PAC, veterans groups, and a number of labor organizations, including Culinary Local 226, SEIU Nevada, AFL-CIO, Southern Nevada Central Labor Council, and Teamsters Nevada.
Reynolds raised $483,000 as of the July reporting period and had $370,000 on hand.
“I’m just trying to raise as much as I can to be successful in the race,” he said. 
His endorsements include a dozen law enforcement unions, the Asian American Group, Hispanics in Politics, the Latin Chamber of Commerce, Veterans in Politics, Laborers 720, and the Third Branch PAC, which states on its website that it’s bipartisan, but is funded exclusively by the Nevada Republican Club. 
Reynolds says he was invited to interview by Pauline Lee of the NRC, but was unaware the PAC is funded by a Republican organization. 
“It’s my understanding they try to make it a bipartisan effort,” he said. 
Early voting begins Saturday, Oct. 17.

name: Nevada Current
title: Corporations keep finding new ways to gouge us. Our laws must catch up.
description: Every day, companies find better, and sneakier, ways to reach deeper into our wallets. They trap us in subscriptions, bury fees until checkout, use algorithms to collude with competitors, and mine our personal data to charge us the most we’re willing to pay. With each trick and tactic, companies are reinventing the ripoff right under […]
text:
They trap us in subscriptions, bury fees until checkout, use algorithms to collude with competitors, and mine our personal data to charge us the most we’re willing to pay. (Getty Images)Every day, companies find better, and sneakier, ways to reach deeper into our wallets.
They trap us in subscriptions, bury fees until checkout, use algorithms to collude with competitors, and mine our personal data to charge us the most we’re willing to pay. With each trick and tactic, companies are reinventing the ripoff right under our noses. And, as families strain under the rising cost of living, these practices are coming for every line of the household budget.
Algorithmic price fixing is one of the most powerful tools in that arsenal. Price-fixing no longer requires a smoky back room. Today, technology can do CEOs’ dirty work for them. From rent to gasoline, this algorithmic price-fixing playbook is wreaking havoc on family budgets.
In June, a class-action lawsuit in California alleged that AI-powered pricing tool Kalibrate helped more than 1,700 gas stations coordinate and inflate prices at the pump. Drivers paid a hefty price, as Kalibrate allegedly pushed gas prices up by as much as 30 ​cents a gallon in some markets — a roughly $4 billion dollar dent in Californians’ budgets. Similar schemes could well be underway in other states.
Meanwhile, in the rental market, the blockbuster RealPage lawsuit alleged that the company’s leasing software pooled landlords’ data and spit out rent recommendations that helped landlords raise rents in lockstep. In some buildings using RealPage, rents jumped by as much as 33 percent in a single year — more than eight times the increase in a comparable building that didn’t use the software.
Another weapon in the gouger’s arsenal is dynamic pricing. Americans are familiar with prices that fluctuate when supply is scarce — say, seats on a plane or rooms at a hotel. But today, companies are pushing the practice well beyond contexts of scarcity.
For example, shoppers might find that sunscreen and bottled water have changed prices overnight in Las Vegas hotel lobby shops. And as stores like Walmart and Kroger install electronic shelf labels across thousands of stores, the infrastructure for high-frequency dynamic pricing in brick and mortar shopping is taking shape.
And companies aren’t just changing prices at high speed, they’re changing prices based on who’s shopping. Surveillance pricing, or the tactic of using personal data to squeeze each consumer to their breaking point, is being deployed all across the market.
Shoppers who are near a Target, for example, have been charged higher prices than those shopping at home. And on platforms like Booking.com, users from wealthier cities may see higher prices for identical hotel rooms. Companies have stopped merely pricing products. Now, they are pricing people, too.
Shoppers know the deck is stacked in corporations’ favor, and they’re tired of being spied on and ripped off.
A reckoning over what Americans are owed in the modern marketplace is long overdue. The market has changed at warp speed, but our guardrails haven’t kept up. Without new protections, the price tag we’ve taken for granted for more than 100 years is at risk of extinction.
In my new book Gouged, I offer one path forward: the Shoppers’ Bill of Rights.
From ensuring that the price you see is the price you pay to banning surveillance pricing to giving mom and pops on Main Street a fair shot against the big box stores and requiring AI assistants to act in shoppers’ best interest, it lays the baseline for a fair marketplace, putting simple guardrails around the technologies, tricks, and traps that companies are using to gouge us.
Lawmakers in some states are already taking strides independently, with roughly 90 bills introduced to counter these unfair pricing tactics in just the last two years.
But we shouldn’t settle for leaving shoppers vulnerable if they step across the street or cross state lines. Putting food on the table and a roof over your head is hard enough without greedy corporations squeezing you for all you’re worth. A Shoppers’ Bill of Rights would be a good place to start to restore the basic bargain between shoppers and corporations.
This commentary was originally published in OtherWords.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Animal welfare groups criticize response to bird flu outbreak at Utah mink farm
description: After reports of a bird flu outbreak at a mink farm in Utah emerged, animal welfare advocates are describing the state’s response to it as “dangerously lax.” Details about the outbreak are still publicly unclear. A spokesperson for the Utah Department of Agriculture and Food said that “due to the limited reach and ongoing nature […]
text:
The first case of avian flu in mink was diagnosed in Utah this summer. (Photo courtesy of Animal Wellness Action)After reports of a bird flu outbreak at a mink farm in Utah emerged, animal welfare advocates are describing the state’s response to it as “dangerously lax.”
Details about the outbreak are still publicly unclear. A spokesperson for the Utah Department of Agriculture and Food said that “due to the limited reach and ongoing nature of the outbreak, we are unable to answer some questions that are too specific about the case in order to protect the privacy of the producer.”
However, records from the U.S. Department of Agriculture show seven cases of avian influenza among captive mink in Salt Lake County collected and confirmed in August — though the data may be incomplete, the agency said in its website. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Animal Wellness Action and the Center for a Humane Economy, two advocacy groups, criticized the lack of information released to the public, including the mink population of the affected farm, whether there was mink-to-mink transmission of the virus, its source, or any worker exposure findings.
“This isn’t an obscure infection in an isolated wild animal,” Wayne Pacelle, president of Animal Wellness Action and the Center for a Humane Economy, said in a news release. “It occurred among intensively confined mink, animals with a documented history of amplifying respiratory viruses and providing opportunities for viral evolution. Americans deserve to know what happened and what government found.”
In 2020, COVID-19 killed about 12,000 mink in Utah, one of the top mink producing states in the country. 
The bird flu outbreak is the first of its kind documented in the country, according to the Animal Welfare Institute. The group found through a public records request to the Utah Department of Agriculture and Food that the affected farm was expecting to lose about 80% of its mink to the disease, and that officials were uncertain on the appropriate protocol to contain the virus.
Without a standard to quarantine the farm, an official said: “our only options at this point are to watch them die or get emergency vaccine approval.” 



Let us know what you think...


 


Leon Page, a Utah Department of Agriculture and Food public information officer, said that because this is the first avian influenza outbreak in mink in the country, there isn’t an existing precedent for treatment or response. 
“However, (Utah Department of Agriculture and Food) staff also do everything they can during the process to support producers and make sure that we maximize safety and minimize damage wherever we can,” he said.
But animal rights groups were not reassured.
“It only takes one unlucky mutation of this dangerous virus to trigger a human health crisis, and we can no longer ignore the threat posed by disease proliferation on mink farms,” Kate Dylewsky, assistant director of government affairs at the Animal Welfare Institute said in a release. “The failure of state and federal officials to prepare for this scenario, or to implement important biosecurity measures in response to the outbreak, demonstrates how mink farming operates with almost no oversight, compounding the threat to the public.”
The agency informed the Utah Department of Health and Human Services of the case while it investigated the possibility of transmission to humans, “which has not yet proven to be a high risk,” Page said. The department also issued a “verbal hold” to the facility rather than a legal quarantine, before officials continued their investigation.
Similar cases in other countries were solved through depopulation instead of quarantines, “so there is also little international precedent for a protocol that doesn’t immediately resort to depopulation,” he said.
The options the department has contemplated for the outbreak are depopulation, quarantine and vaccination, Page said. But the latter can only be approved by the U.S. Secretary of Agriculture Brooke Rollins, not by state departments.
“Because (avian flu) in mink is new to the US, research is limited, and there is little guidance for dosage or efficacy in mink specifically,” Page said. “If approved, the vaccine would be released to the state veterinarian and tracked closely by that office to ensure there was no diversion to poultry, dairy cattle, or other farms. USDA is having internal discussions on when they can or would allow vaccinations.”

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: We need to work together to preserve our vessel — earth
description: A close friend of mine during my time at the University of Minnesota in Duluth earned money for school by working on a ship carrying iron ore pellets from Minnesota ports on Lake Superior to steel mills along the lower Great Lakes. My roommates and I would slip down to the terminal whenever his ship […]
text:
A freighter ship traveling on Lake Superior requires constant maintenance to remain seaworthy. (Photo by Getty Images)A close friend of mine during my time at the University of Minnesota in Duluth earned money for school by working on a ship carrying iron ore pellets from Minnesota ports on Lake Superior to steel mills along the lower Great Lakes. My roommates and I would slip down to the terminal whenever his ship docked in town to surreptitiously chat with him while he and the other deckhands maneuvered the large vessel back and forth along the wharf to even out the loading of the cargo.
I once asked him how he and his fellow crewmembers occupied their days out on the open water between the hectic loading and unloading at ports. He shrugged and replied: Every hour of every shift was spent monitoring, repairing, scrapping, painting and cleaning. The aggregation of all sorts of necessary tasks, large and small, kept the ship seaworthy. 
We all grasp the importance of maintenance, although it’s easier acknowledged than accomplished since it requires investments of time and money now in exchange for future benefits. Cars require regular checkups and servicing, lest they fail us at moments that can be inconvenient or even disastrous. Homes have all sorts of needs that if ignored can  make them uninhabitable.
We all accept the necessity of maintenance when we can get our heads around the scope of the tasks, whether that involves taking care of our personal property or — with quite a bit of prodding — maintaining big shared infrastructure projects, such as our country’s electrical grid, interstate highways or air traffic control system. 
But we all now face a far greater maintenance task that challenges our capacity for comprehension and thus our ability to act.
This planet that sustains all 8.2 billion of us should be perceived as a remarkably complex and intricate ship. But this ship travels through the vastness of space without any ports of call, no reprovisioning of supplies, and no stops for the removal of wastes. You board this ship when you are born and disembark when you die. The only input from beyond the ship is energy from the sun, which powers the physical, chemical and biological infrastructures that sustain us all.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
This planetary ship has been an astonishingly favorable home for life for a very long time. We have built a vast global human enterprise on the expectation that earth’s infrastructure will always deliver the services on which we depend, while we simultaneously degrade that very infrastructure. We are changing the composition of the atmosphere and thus altering how it and the ocean below it behave. We are altering the chemistry of the ocean and thereby damaging its capacity to support fisheries. We are dramatically reducing biodiversity everywhere and hence decimating our ability to improve the genetics of our crops against diseases and pests.
We must now acknowledge the daunting implication that our planet’s infrastructure is declining in its capacity to support us. It can be easy to dismiss reports from those responsible for monitoring our planet’s infrastructure that things are amiss, especially when some political leaders won’t acknowledge the seriousness of our current situation and actively deny that there is anything that needs to be done and instead seek to divide our earth ship into spheres of influence.
Imagine being a passenger on a vessel where different factions seek to establish domains over various portions of it, dismissing the fact that its infrastructure cannot be divided up. The ship either functions as a whole or eventually fails to function.
Some of our current leaders mistakenly claim that doing the work of slowing and ultimately reversing the decline in our planet’s infrastructure is too difficult and too expensive. We deserve leaders willing to champion our ambitions. Great infrastructure empowers great human achievement. Doing the work of repairing our planet’s deteriorating infrastructure will unleash the greatest flourishing of human creativity and enterprise we have ever witnessed.
We now live on a human-dominated plant. The future of earth will be determined by human decision making; either by default or by design, either by accident or by intention. Together, let’s imagine, design and realize a more secure and prosperous climate future.

title: Wolves in SE Washington pack to be killed ‘incrementally’ by state officials after livestock attacks
description: The director of the state’s Department of Fish and Wildlife this week authorized the “incremental” killing of wolves in southeastern Washington with a goal to stop attacks on livestock.  Agency officials could not say how many wolves would be killed, but said other nonlethal measures would not be appropriate for the situation.  The order is […]
text:
A wolf in Yellowstone National Park. (Photo by Jacob W. Frank/National Park Service)The director of the state’s Department of Fish and Wildlife this week authorized the “incremental” killing of wolves in southeastern Washington with a goal to stop attacks on livestock. 
Agency officials could not say how many wolves would be killed, but said other nonlethal measures would not be appropriate for the situation. 
The order is the second this month that calls for killing wolves in the Couse pack. On Sept. 17, the department killed an adult male. Since then, at least one member of the pack attacked again. 
Over the last 10 months, members of the Couse pack have attacked livestock at least seven times, with four confirmed fatalities, the state says. The attacks affected two livestock owners. The state offers reimbursement for livestock owners whose animals have been killed by wolves. 
In December, the Couse pack had at least five members, according to the department’s annual wolf report. Department staff say that full pack removal is not the goal. 
“The number of wolves ultimately removed is dependent on the size of the pack and which animals are removed,” a department spokesperson said in an email.
Critics say the department isn’t transparent about its kill orders, also known as lethal removals, and say it prioritizes livestock owners over the state-endangered grey wolves. 
“Alarmingly, its public notice states neither how many wolves may be killed nor when the order expires,” said Francisco Santiago Ávila, science and advocacy director at Washington Wildlife First. “Publicly, this is an open-ended authorization, and an extraordinary measure toward a state-endangered species.”
Gray wolves in Washington are considered endangered under state law. Though gray wolves in the eastern third of the state were federally delisted in 2011, legal protections still apply to the entire state. 
“When killing fails, more killing is not science; it is a preference,” Santiago Ávila said in an email. “Both wolves and the Washington public deserve better.”

name: Missouri Independent
title: Republican attacks on the Missouri Supreme Court may just be the beginning
description: I was baffled when I saw that Missouri Secretary of State Denny Hoskins, represented by Attorney General Catherine Hanaway, had asked a federal district court for an injunction against the Supreme Court of the State of Missouri.  Why would they risk infuriating the court that they regularly appear before with a weird gambit in federal […]
text:
The Missouri Supreme Court building in Jefferson City, as photographed Sept. 10 (Annelise Hanshaw/Missouri Independent).I was baffled when I saw that Missouri Secretary of State Denny Hoskins, represented by Attorney General Catherine Hanaway, had asked a federal district court for an injunction against the Supreme Court of the State of Missouri. 
Why would they risk infuriating the court that they regularly appear before with a weird gambit in federal court that was certain to fail? A gambit the U.S. Supreme Court had already indicated would fail?
Hoskins and Hanaway asked a single district judge to order the Missouri Supreme Court to halt contempt proceedings against Hoskins for his failure to abide by its order to conduct the midterm elections using Missouri’s 2022 map, rather than a further gerrymandered map passed by the legislature in 2025. Voters will have the opportunity to reject or approve the 2025 map in November.
The court had already indicated its displeasure with Hoskins in a lengthy footnote in that decision. Hoskins had argued that it was too late to switch back to the 2022 map because we used the 2025 map in the August primary. 
But as the court explained at length, Hoskins created that problem himself.
Hoskins appealed the order to use the 2022 map to the U.S. Supreme Court, which declined to reverse it. 
Missouri Republicans still wouldn’t take “no” for an answer. U.S Rep. Bob Onder and state Sen. Rick Brattin, filed a new case in federal court seeking an order directing Hoskins to use the 2025 map. Instead of defending the Missouri Supreme Court’s decision, Hoskins and Hanaway badmouthed it and consented to an order directing Hoskins not to use any map but the 2025 map.
Hoskins announced that he was forced to follow the federal court order he had asked for and directed election officials to use the 2025 map. What he should have done, as the Missouri Court explained when finding him in contempt, was nothing. He should have sought further direction from the court rather than treating the federal order as a command to put the 2025 map into effect.
The U.S. Supreme Court quickly stayed the federal court’s order. Though the U.S. Supreme Court had twice deferred to the Missouri Supreme Court on this issue of Missouri law, Republicans went on the attack against the unanimous, Republican-dominated Missouri Supreme Court.
Hoskins tweeted a post from President Trump calling the court’s ruling horrible and ridiculous, and himself accused the Court of igniting a constitutional crisis. Hoskins said of the judge who wrote the opinion: “She’s never run an election.” 
Hanaway went on a media tour criticizing the court. She excoriated it for its “unprecedented” ruling, despite the fact that she and Hoskins had created the unprecedented situation.
Members of the State Senate sent a letter to the chief justice threatening impeachment of any judge who voted to find Hoskins in contempt—which, it turned out, would mean all of them. 
In a filing asking the U.S. Supreme Court for a third time to put the 2025 map in place, Hanaway accused the Missouri Supreme Court of injecting chaos into the election, blaming the court for the delay and confusion caused by Hoskins’ actions. This, as one legal analyst noted, seems to be “a real issue of candor.” Lawyers, after all, have a professional duty of candor to courts.
At first, I thought this was an exceedingly stupid performance for President Trump, who demanded new maps. They knew they would lose, but this was the kind of fight Trump wanted to see.
But what I first thought was performative stupidity is something more sinister. Hanaway’s willingness to torch her good will and credibility with the court, and Republicans’ open threats, are extremely ominous. It says to me that they have abandoned trying to persuade the court and are instead trying to delegitimize it — laying the groundwork to dismantle it. 
A likely target is Missouri’s method of selecting judges known as “The Missouri Plan,” which has been adopted by over 30 other states. A nonpartisan commission selects three candidates, the governor chooses one and judges later face retention elections. 
The attacks on the court and calls to dismantle it are a rejection of the fundamental premise that the judiciary is a co-equal branch of government. Republicans want to make the judiciary a subservient branch that can be counted on to rule based on what MAGA wants rather than the law. That is an authoritarian rejection of our system of government.
Hanaway and Hoskins attacked the Missouri Supreme Court despite knowing the law wasn’t on their side. As the U.S. Supreme Court put it: “Given this Court’s two prior orders in this litigation, [this] should come as no surprise.” In a sharply worded order, the U.S. Supreme Court put the lower federal courts and Missouri officials who sought to evade its rulings in their place. 
This was a victory for the rule of law, despite the unconscionable waste of tax dollars spent fighting Missourians and the embarrassing national spectacle. But the danger hasn’t passed. Expect the judiciary to come under not just rhetorical, but legislative attack here as has happened in other states.
Fortunately, the Missouri Plan is in the Missouri Constitution. So they can try to take our courts, but those seeking to remake them will once again have to face the voters — and Missourians have gotten pretty savvy about politicians’ attempts to gut our rights.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Bill would give $60M in state aid to NJ farmers who lost crops in April freeze
description: An April freeze ravaged early-blooming fruit crops, with over $300M in losses projected in New Jersey. Lawmakers propose giving farmers $60M in grants.
text:
An April freeze ravaged early-blooming fruit crops, with over $300 million in losses projected in New Jersey. Several legislators propose giving farmers $60 million in state-funded grants to help them recover. (Photo by Dana DiFilippo / New Jersey Monitor)New Jersey farmers whose fruit crops were damaged or destroyed by an unexpected four-day freeze last spring could apply for grants to help them recover their losses under new legislation that would earmark $60 million in state funding for such relief.
The late-April cold snap zapped peach, apple, pear, cherry, and other early-blooming trees, as well as shrub, vine, and ground crops like blueberries, strawberries, and grapes at farms both statewide and throughout the eastern U.S. from Virginia to Michigan. Many growers lost 30% or more of their fruit crops, with some reporting total losses. Officials estimated damages in New Jersey would top $300 million.
Assemblywoman Dawn Fantasia (R-Sussex) applauded the state and federal response, with both Gov. Mikie Sherrill (D) and the U.S. Department of Agriculture making statewide disaster declarations that cleared the way for farmers to apply for emergency loans and other relief assistance.
But in the weeks afterward, farmers called for direct financial aid, with many saying the freeze was the most catastrophic of their lifetimes. So Fantasia recently introduced a bill that would allocate $60 million for grants impacted farmers could apply for, with priority given to those hardest hit. The bill would require the state agriculture secretary to report within a year how the money was spent and advise if more aid is needed.
Seven Republicans signed on to co-sponsor the bill. Sen. Parker Space (R-Sussex), who’s also a farmer by trade, will sponsor the bill in the upper chamber, Fantasia said.
Fantasia said $60 million in aid for farmers is far from the controversial budget add-ons that annually bloat the state budget and make GOP legislators howl in protest.
This year, state budget appropriations critics deride as “pork” included $500,000 for pickleball courts and millions for other “really beautiful things that are absolutely wants and not needs,” Fantasia said. Farm relief “is not a want. It’s a need,” she added.
Farming has a sprawling footprint in New Jersey, she said. Almost 10,000 farms generated nearly $1.5 billion in sales in 2022, federal data shows. They employ about 25,000 farmworkers, the bill says.
“We can sure as hell take $60 million from the general fund and give it to an industry that spans the entire state and brings in over a billion dollars to the state of New Jersey,” Fantasia said. “We’re talking about people’s livelihoods and ability to keep jobs and stay in their homes.”
April’s freeze came as farmers already were struggling with rising labor, fertilizer, and fuel costs. Some smaller farms rely on a single season for their annual income, prompting industry observers to predict the freeze would force some growers to cut staff, sell off acreage, or quit farming altogether.
For those reasons, Fantasia expects legislators from both sides of the aisle will support the bill.
“There’s no question here: Severe losses happened. No product to sell. Devastating to the economy. Devastating to the jobs in New Jersey. I think it’s a no-brainer,” she said.
Hunterdon County farmer John Melick lost much of his peach, apple, cherry, plum, and pear crops to the April freeze.
Crop insurance has helped him recover, he said. But he welcomes any assistance the state wants to offer the fruit-growing industry, noting it would be most beneficial for smaller farmers, those without diversified crops, and the few who couldn’t afford or thought they didn’t need crop insurance.
“It’s not going to put me out of business if I don’t get it, but I won’t turn it away either,” Melick said of state aid.
He’d be more excited for Trenton’s intervention if legislators could control the weather, he joked, because the recent rainy stretch has kept customers away.
“I’m hoping for sunny weekends for October, so that the 30% crop that I do have I can sell to pick-your-own customers,” Melick said. “When it rains every Saturday and Sunday, they’re not coming out.”

name: WyoFile
title: Things that last
description:
Stories — built from relationships with one another, with our environment, with a higher power — make us who we are and write the legacy we leave behind, columnist Walt Gasson reflects.
The post Things that last appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Opinion

We were up long before the first gray on the eastern horizon. We attacked the biscuits and gravy and bacon and spuds like there would be no lunch, because there wouldn’t be. 
We worked hard until it was dark. And after dinner, we headed for home — two hours away. When the day was young and full of promise, we were full of words and laughter. But now, it was very quiet in the truck. We were just toughing it out to get home to a warm bed. When that big full moon came up over the Powder River country east of Buffalo, my heart went east to meet it, and suddenly, somehow, it was 1979.
I was young then, and this hard and broken country was a friend to me. A young kid with his first real job, I became friends with the Basque guys who ran sheep in the Powder River breaks. Second- and third-generation sheepmen, they knew the juniper draws, the canyons and badlands from horseback, and they knew the history of the people. Most of them weren’t big talkers, but in time they began to tell me their stories. They told me about their families — the Falxas and Harriets and Irrigarays and Iberlins and more. They told me, too, about the ones who went belly-up — the people who left when lamb and wool prices tanked, or maybe when they just couldn’t listen to the wind one more day. When I’d ask about that old cabin on Powder River or those old broken-down corrals on Cat Creek, they’d tell me about the people who moved on to some other place, some other life. This one was just too hard. 
The next morning, I was up and gone again before the sunrise. I think it’s one of the blessings of being a gentleman of a certain age that I seldom linger in bed much anymore. But that same full moon was setting now over Chalk Mountain, an image so stunning that only God or Charles Marion Russell could have created it. And again, my heart went out and my mind went back to those old guys who knew the place so well, and who kindly allowed me to learn it from them: Bob Meer, Martin Lee Sullivan, Louie Irene and the rest. And just like in the Powder River country, there were stories of the people — the people who stayed and the people who left. Each of those people left behind them the relics of their time here. The lodgepole logs cut with an axe and trimmed with a drawknife, the juniper posts and the root cellar hand dug into the side hill all remain as testimony to their hopes and dreams. 
They say the winners get to write the history, the losers just quietly move on. But when I think back now on those old faces and those old places, I think that each had something to teach me. Something about optimism in the face of overwhelming odds, something about courage in the face of possible failure, something about being willing to work hard for your family and their future. In a time of artificial intelligence, social media influencers and cultural superficiality, maybe we have to be reminded about things that last.
For me, the things that last are almost all about relationships:

My relationship with God. Not everyone feels like they need one. But I do. I grew up in my mom’s church. I left it for a different church, and I stayed with that one for several years. But I’ve come to the conclusion that the best relationship with Deity is a simple one. I need a church like a moose needs a hat rack. 


My relationship with Kim. We’ve been married for 53 years, a couple for 56. It’s fair to say that we’ve faced our fair share of challenges in that time. It’s more important to say that we’ve faced more than our fair share of joy. And that’s mostly because of Kim. She is, without a doubt, the finest human being I’ve ever known. She’s kind, intelligent, and deeply committed to her family and friends. She has an unerring moral compass. In a truly difficult situation, she is always absolutely outstanding. She is the great love of my life.


My relationships with our kids and grandkids. We have a son and three daughters. They’re magnificent people. They are fifth-generation Wyomingites, and they wear their love for the Cowboy State proudly. Perhaps even more important, they are committed to making this a better place, now and in the future. They’re strong, compassionate people who love wholeheartedly. They have given us wonderful grandchildren. Some of those grandkids have made a conscious decision to stay here. Others have followed their dreams to other places. All of them are kind, intelligent and hardworking.


My relationship with the land. I don’t remember a time in my life when I wasn’t in love with wild things and wild places. I think I came here that way. But more importantly, I came here to a family with deep roots in the mountains and deserts of western Wyoming. I spent most of my life caring for what’s left of the greatest part of the interior west, and learning the stories of the land and the people. I’ve tried to use my thoughts and words to inspire others to do the same.

When I move on from this life, I hope these relationships will be my legacy, my gifts to the future. They are real and true. They are the things that matter, the things that last.

name: WyoFile
title: The plight of the pronghorn: Part 2
description:
The lackluster recovery of the Sublette Pronghorn Herd after the killer winter of 2022-23 whispers of trouble on the range, writes guest columnist Chris Madson.
The post The plight of the pronghorn: Part 2 appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Editor’s note: This is Part 2 of a look at the Sublette Pronghorn Herd. For Part 1, click here.
Yesterday, we examined how pronghorn herds typically recover after a difficult winter. Now, let’s examine a more recent example.

Opinion

Since we’re focused here on the Sublette Herd, let’s consider some of the recent fawn-doe ratios. After the winter of 2022-23, the ratio subsided to 47 fawns per 100 does, an expected consequence of the poor condition of the herd’s females. In the fall of 2024, it rose to 68:100, a moderate recovery. In 2025, it hit 70:100. Is this really “better than average?
In the 10-year span between 1973 and 1982, the Sublette Herd averaged almost 82 fawns per 100 does, with a peak as high as 96:100. In the 1970s, other pronghorn herds in Wyoming produced well over 100 fawns per 100 does. One of the more troubling statistics from the record of the Sublette Herd is the ratio from 2022, the year before the killer winter — that year, there were only 55 fawns per 100 does in the herd.
In fairness, local biologists say that four out of the last six winters in Pinedale country have been “bad” for pronghorns. That may well be, and those winters may offer at least a partial explanation for the lack of a “bounce” in the Sublette Herd. But I’m troubled when I compare fawn-doe ratios from the good old days of pronghorn abundance in the 1970s and 1980s with the numbers today. Take just one other example, the Medicine Bow Pronghorn Herd a hundred miles east of the Sublette Herd. In the decade between 1975 and 1984 — even after the devastating effect of the winter of 1983-84 — the Medicine Bow Herd averaged 80 fawns per 100 does. Between 2016 and 2025, that average dropped to 67 fawns per 100 does.
Enough numbers. Today’s game managers can’t be blamed for assuming that the mean of the last 10 years of data reflects some sort of normal state against which the current year’s estimates can be measured. They’re dealing with a new normal. What, precisely, is “new” about it? Weather, for one thing. We’ve seen four killer winters in the Green River country over the last six years. That’s something new. And, between those winters, we’ve seen a remarkable succession of drought years — without adequate forage, a pronghorn herd simply won’t “bounce.” 
I’m tempted to deliver a sermon on climate change here, but, even if we took Bill McKibben’s advice and treated the climate challenge with the single-minded focus we used to win World War II, we wouldn’t see any improvement in the plight of the pronghorn for decades. 
We can only change what we can change. The “Path of the Pronghorn” has finally been pried open — the migration corridor for a single herd of Wyoming’s pronghorns. There are other corridors in other parts of the state, just as critical to the well-being of migrating big game but poorly defined and beset with obstacles, both physical and political. Clearing the way for the migrants is important but only if the destinations on either end provide the animals with what they need. Of all the implications of the low fawn-to-doe ratios, this one may worry me the most. 
How much forage do we leave for our pronghorns: on the summer pasture, along the migration corridors, down on the critical winter ranges? The fawn counts suggest it isn’t much, probably not enough to sustain the herds at the numbers some of us knew 50 and 60 years ago. If we want those thriving herds again, we need to feed them. According to the BLM’s own data, a vast area of the public range is in fair-to-poor condition. No small part of this is due to a long history of abuse. If we care about pronghorns and much of the rest of our wild heritage, we need to stop that abuse and set about healing the damage.
And, while we’re considering how much livestock the range can really support, we need to turn our attention to the management objectives that have been set for many of our big game herds as well. Just one example: The current objective for the Sublette Pronghorn Herd is 48,000 animals. It will take a hell of a “bounce” to return that herd to the size it attained in the 1970s. It’s worth asking whether that objective is even achievable and sustainable in current conditions. As much as many of us would like to believe it’s possible, ongoing weather patterns and grazing regimes may not allow it. If that’s true, then our efforts to reach the current objective may only damage the habitat that remains. Hard data on the condition of the animals and their habitat could define the dimensions of this issue, but only if we care enough to collect and act on it.
Hunting is not the problem here. The length and timing of hunting seasons, the size of the buck harvest, the number of licenses we issue have little, if anything, to do with the sluggish production of pronghorn fawns in the last 20 or 30 years. Unfortunately, the only management tools state biologists really have to influence pronghorn populations are hunting seasons and license allocation. 
The real solutions are controlled by other state and federal entities whose political agendas are set by a host of special interests with little or no interest in pronghorns or any other wildlife. They can be swayed only by massive public outcry. The success of the campaign to open the Path of the Pronghorn shows what is needed, but one migration corridor is just the barest beginning. If we really want to get back to “better than average,” we’ll have to feed our pronghorns better, and that’s not likely to happen until the public at large demands it.
