title: Ohio’s next education fight could be over how kids learn math
description: This story was produced by The 74, a non-profit, independent news organization focused on education in America. Ohio officials are tackling the math struggles of students with an effort resembling its science of reading push, but have yet to deal with perhaps the most fundamental issue — how instruction should change. That decision won’t come […]
text:
Students work in a math class at Wasatch Junior High School in Salt Lake City in March 2024.(Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)This story was produced by The 74, a non-profit, independent news organization focused on education in America.
Ohio officials are tackling the math struggles of students with an effort resembling its science of reading push, but have yet to deal with perhaps the most fundamental issue — how instruction should change.
That decision won’t come until next April when the Ohio Department of Education and Workforce chooses between competing visions of how math should be taught and names textbooks and other learning materials low-scoring schools will be forced to use.
In the meantime, schools will be in a holding pattern of what lessons to use while advocates and state education officials duel behind closed doors over which approaches win out.
With Ohio’s math scores still below pre-pandemic levels, the Ohio legislature and Gov. Mike DeWine passed a law this summer that mirrors Ohio’s 2023 law mandating the use of the science of reading in classrooms by requiring schools to better track math skills and give students extra help.
The new law also requires elementary school teachers to show they are proficient in math skills before they can teach math.
But unlike the science of reading law which sets a clear path for how schools should teach, there is no consensus — both nationally and in Ohio — on how students can best learn math, with ongoing debate nationally between a self-proclaimed science of math movement and more holistic approaches favored by many educators.
The differences in math approaches are nuanced — simplified by some as focusing on teaching concepts versus teaching procedures — and have not become a full public debate in Ohio, at least not yet.
But educators are watching cautiously as the Ohio Department of Education and Workforce follows the model of the reading law and creates a list of “high quality” math textbooks and other learning materials by April 2027.
Most schools can still pick their own textbooks, but an estimated 450 schools with low test scores will have to use only books from that list.
The department won’t clear up concerns by saying which studies or resources will guide its evaluation of materials. Asked by The 74, if the science of math was under consideration, the department did not respond, only saying it is still in the planning stages.
“It would be premature to speculate on those details,” the department told The 74.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.Both the state superintendents association and the Ohio Federation of Teachers union said during debate over the law they oppose letting the state, not each local district, decide what to use.
Ohio’s math teachers also object to the state taking that control.
“I don’t like the state telling me I have to use a certain textbook,” said Mike Lipnos, president of the Ohio Council of Teachers of Mathematics.
Lipnos wants the state to follow a state math learning plan he helped create last year that prioritizes teaching math concepts and making sure students develop problem-solving and reasoning skills. But he sensed some opposition within the department to the plan and worries the state will instead approve science of math books he believes teach math as a set of procedures to memorize.
His organization has criticized the science of math as trying to “capitalize” off of the science of reading.
“We want to say clearly to all mathematics stakeholders that OCTM rejects the outdated and inappropriate instructional practices that are being repackaged and promoted as some sort of new ‘scientific’ ideology,” the group states on its website.
The science of math wasn’t an issue in debate over the bill: Backers did not testify and have not made any public comment. University of Texas professor Sarah Powell, leader of the movement, also told The 74 she is not talking with Ohio officials to promote her approach.
The movement’s website calls criticisms like Lipnos’ a “misconception.” While backers favor teacher-led lessons with explicit instruction on how to solve math problems — prioritizing them over lessons on concepts that Powell has said can “ waste students’ time” — they say schools need a balance.
How schools teach reading has become a major issue nationally in the last several years, with the majority of states passing laws mandating use of phonics-heavy science of reading lessons. Low math scores on the 2022 National Assessment of Educational Progress then focused states’ attention on math.
Ten states have passed policies to change math instruction just this year, said Lindsey Henderson, the senior policy director for math of the ExcelinEd nonprofit education advocacy group.
ExcelinEd has identified 11 ways it believes states can improve math, such as having math coaches, teaching math at least 60 minutes a day, or making sure students can take advanced math classes. Alabama, an early adopter of some of the policies, leads the way with eight of the 11 approved and Ohio, as one of the ten states setting math policies this year, is also a leader in the effort, Henderson said.
But Henderson and other experts concede that math research is a few years behind where reading was when the science of reading caught on.
“Math doesn’t have a nice short term like the science of reading, and everybody knows what it means and everybody knows where to look for the research,” Henderson said.
The Center for Reinventing Public Education, another nonprofit research and advocacy group, characterized the two sides of the “math wars” as favoring “traditional” teacher-led classes as opposed to “reform-oriented” classes in which student exploration takes priority.
In a recent survey of states, CRPE found that as of late last year 18 states and Washington, D.C., have passed math policies, “many of which emphasized priorities associated with the science of math.”
But the report notes that both sides claim to be “evidence-based,” which makes it hard to decide what’s best.
“The Science of Math has not achieved the academic and professional consensus that the Science of Reading eventually did, and the gap matters,” the report states. “Whether the field will eventually reach comparable agreement, remains unclear.”
In Ohio, the bill enacted this summer by the Ohio legislature and Gov. Mike DeWine comes as just 55 percent of students across all grades scored as proficient or better in math in 2025, while more than one in four scored at the lowest level, the state equivalent of F grades on state tests.



“This problem has not developed overnight, but its severity grows ever more prevalent as students who were knocked off track by the impact of the pandemic, or who were already struggling academically, continue to be promoted to the next grade despite showing very clear signs of needing significant intervention,” said State Sen. Andrew Brenner, the law’s author and chair of the Senate Education Committee.


The law passed this summer has drawn praise for several changes, including requiring tutoring of students who struggle, schools where fewer than 51% of third graders score proficient in math to develop a plan to improve and letting high-scoring middle school students combine seventh and eighth grade math into one year and start algebra in eighth grade.
The bill has been praised widely for calling attention to math and for taking steps to help improve math skills.
The law falls far short of Ohio’s 2023 science of reading bill in a few important ways, however. The reading bill budgeted over $160 million to pay for new teaching materials and teacher training, while the math bill provides no new money.
The reading bill also mandated that teachers learn the basics of the science of reading, while the math law only requires the Department of Education and Workforce to develop training by December.
Good training in how to teach math is considered crucial by wide-ranging advocates, including ExcelinEd, Lipnos’ math teachers association and its national organization.
The portion of the law that could lead to debate going forward — the requirement that the Ohio Department of Education and Workforce approve a list of “high quality instructional materials” in math — did not spark much discussion during hearings for the law.
In the end, the final law calls for all schools required to set math improvement plans — the 450 schools with fewer than 51% of students testing as proficient in math on state tests — to use only state-approved books and other materials.
And unlike with the reading law, which specifically banned some discredited teaching approaches and mandated phonics-heavy lessons, the law offers no definition of “high-quality.” The new Ohio law only requires that books help students build their math skills toward mastery.
The department declined to answer questions from The 74 about whether schools are using bad textbooks, whether bad books are leading to bad scores or which methods of math teaching need to be added or cut.
“That’s precisely the gap,” Steve Dackin, the department’s director told The 74 by email.
“Historically, the Department has not been able to collect data on math materials, and there is currently no approved list to compare materials against in Ohio,” Dackin said. “As a result, we are not in a position to characterize what districts are using.”
Dackin and the department declined to say what it would base its “high
quality” judgment on, saying only that books should have “coherent learning progressions, strong alignment with standards, embedded assessments that inform instruction and help teachers identify student needs, and evidence-based strategies that create more opportunities for students to engage deeply with core concepts.”
“It’s not about stopping certain materials,” he said. “It’s about ensuring classrooms use resources that truly support strong instruction.”

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: The federal tax credit as a boon for public schools?
description: Starting in January, Americans can “donate” $1,700 to a “scholarship granting organization” (or SGO) and get every penny back on their federal taxes. The program, created in last year’s reconciliation bill, was sold as a way to subsidize private school tuition. But because school vouchers like these are strikingly unpopular with the public, supporters have [[...]
text:
The U.S. Education Department said it will start garnishing wages from student borrowers in default. (Catherine Lane/Getty Images)Starting in January, Americans can “donate” $1,700 to a “scholarship granting organization” (or SGO) and get every penny back on their federal taxes. The program, created in last year’s reconciliation bill, was sold as a way to subsidize private school tuition.
But because school vouchers like these are strikingly unpopular with the public, supporters have added a new pitch: public schools can cash in too.
In Ohio, we have witnessed a smaller version of this experiment for five years. We are seeing how this plays out.
In 2021, Ohio created its own tax credit of up to $750 per person for donations to SGOs. Most of the money goes to families already sending their children to private schools. But a few public school districts have tried to take advantage of the program to pay for full-day kindergarten, which Ohio does not require. State law lets schools charge tuition for it.
Kindergarten, the foundation of a child’s education, is being paid for through a tax-credit fundraiser, one voucher at a time. Some Ohio families pay more than $3,000 for all-day kindergarten, so a few communities have formed SGOs to help cover the cost. A suburban school district in Northeast Ohio, Nordonia Hills, started the state’s first public school SGO, raising about $252,200 this year, ensuring every family could access all-day kindergarten.
This approach works best in wealthier communities like Nordonia, where people are more likely to have the tax bills, time and know-how to redirect their money. The federal program is built the same way, with even more strings attached.
First, the money doesn’t go to schools, nor are income limits fair. Vouchers must go to eligible students from households earning up to 300% of their area’s median income. In Nordonia Hills, the income eligibility cutoff will be $276,000 a year; in the even wealthier suburb of Hudson, families making up to $494,000 will be eligible. In East Cleveland, a struggling inner-ring suburb that does not have an SGO, the cutoff will be $75,000. SGOs cannot send checks to a district or school to hire a reading teacher, fix a roof, or run an after-school program for everyone. It can only pay for things a specific student would otherwise be charged for. The only way a public school “benefits” is by charging families. A district that offers free kindergarten, free technology, free field trips and free instrument rentals gets nothing unless they start charging. Switching to fees opens a door for voucher money, but hands a new bill to every family.
Second, running one of these programs is a big job. Under the U.S. Treasury Department’s preview of the forthcoming rules, SGOs must spend at least 90% of their income on vouchers, verify each family’s income, and complete annual audits and IRS reporting. Many school foundations do too many other things to qualify and would likely need to start a brand-new nonprofit. The school district gets nothing for invoicing, tracking and paperwork.
Private schools already have financial aid offices, donor lists and accountants, meaning they’re already ahead.
Third, this program will reward communities and families that already have more. Because of community wealth, SGOs in Hudson and Nordonia Hills can raise more donations than urban and rural districts. Rather than creating a more equitable system, this program will exacerbate disparities between districts – an inevitable outcome when a public good is funded through individual effort.
None of this is free. Every dollar credited back to a donor is a dollar of federal revenue gone, money that could go to special education, low-income schools, or school meals. Ohio’s state credit alone cost nearly $27 million in 2023. Meanwhile, by one estimate, Ohio’s current two-year budget left public schools $2.75 billion short of its own school funding formula while spending $2.4 billion on private school vouchers. President Donald Trump’s federal voucher program could cost the federal budget as much as $51 billion annually.
About eight in 10 Ohio children attend traditional public school districts that shouldn’t have to become fundraisers, fee collectors and paperwork processors to get crumbs from a program designed for someone else. And children shouldn’t need a voucher to learn and grow in a welcoming and well-resourced public school.
States that haven’t opted in to Trump’s voucher program should think hard before they do. States that have, like Ohio, should not mistake this program for a school funding plan. The real answer is for Ohio to meet its constitutional duty to fully fund public schools, and for Congress to keep its own promises, starting with the special education funding it pledged 50 years ago.

title: Former Tosa cop Mensah given $95,000 in PTSD claim
description: The Wauwatosa Common Council approved a $95,000 settlement on Tuesday night for Joseph Mensah, the former Wauwatosa police officer who killed three people while on duty during his five years on the force. The settlement stemmed from a workers compensation claim for PTSD.  The city said that Mensah filed the claim a few years ago, […]
text:
Then-Detective Joseph Mensah testifies before the Senate Committee on Judiciary and Public Safety in early 2025. (Photo by Isiah Holmes/Wisconsin Examiner)The Wauwatosa Common Council approved a $95,000 settlement on Tuesday night for Joseph Mensah, the former Wauwatosa police officer who killed three people while on duty during his five years on the force. The settlement stemmed from a workers compensation claim for PTSD. 
The city said that Mensah filed the claim a few years ago, Fox6 reported. The money will come through the city’s workers compensation fund. Mayor Dennis McBride said that the settlement was reasonable “to put the matter behind us.” 
The Wisconsin Examiner’s Criminal Justice Reporting Project shines a light on incarceration, law enforcement and criminal justice issues with support from the Public Welfare Foundation.
Attorney Kimberley Motley, who has represented the families of two people killed by Mensah, said that she wasn’t surprised, given Mensah’s history, that he has mental health issues. Motley emphasized that the families of people killed by Mensah had to fight  for justice and compensation through the courts, whereas Mensah has received multiple payouts from the city. McBride said that “whatever happened in 2020 or earlier, that’s actually a different matter. So, although I understand the feelings of the Cole family, it’s really an unrelated matter at this point.”
The details of Mensah’s PTSD diagnosis and the work-related trauma that triggered it are not public.
The $95,000 settlement comes on top of $125,000 awarded to Mensah as part of a severance agreement when he left the Wauwatosa Police Department in 2020. As protests mounted against him earlier that year, Mensah also accumulated more than $78,000 in GoFundMe donations. Meanwhile, Mensah remained on paid leave from the police department while the investigation into Cole’s shooting continued. He is also pursuing a separate duty disability claim.
Mensah’s severance agreement included a waiver stating that the city was “irrevocably and unconditionally” released and discharged “from any and all grievances, claims, demands, rights, damages, costs, losses, suits, actions, causes of action, attorney’s fees and expenses of any nature whatsoever …” A city of Wauwatosa spokesperson said in an email to the Wisconsin Examiner that under state law workers compensation is a separate matter and that an employee’s right to pursue workers compensation for a work-related injury cannot be waived or bargained away in a separation agreement.
Mensah’s departure from Wauwatosa amid protests following the killing of George Floyd in Minneapolis. In February of that year, Mensah shot 17-year-old Alvin Cole, his third fatal shooting. Mensah shot Cole during a foot chase as the teen fled Mayfair Mall with his friends after an altercation involving a gun. Mensah said that Cole pointed a gun at him. Witnesses offered conflicting accounts. 
Protesters gather in Wauwatosa’s city hall to call for Officer Joseph Mensah to be fired and arrested in 2020. (Photo by Isiah Holmes/ Wisconsin Examiner)
Four years earlier in 2016, Mensah killed 25-year-old Jay Anderson Jr. Mensah said that Anderson was sleeping in his car alone in a park late at night, when he awoke and reached for a gun beside him on the passenger seat. Less than a year before killing Anderson, Mensah shot and killed 29-year-old Antonio Gonzales, who was intoxicated and brandishing a sword when officers arrived at his home.
The Milwaukee County District Attorney’s Office declined to charge Mensah after any of the shootings. In 2021, after a John Doe hearing a circuit court judge found that probable cause existed to charge Mensah with homicide by negligent use of a dangerous weapon. Special prosecutors later declined to pursue the charges. In 2025, Mensah testified  before the state Legislature in support of a bill prohibiting John Doe hearings for police officers who kill citizens on duty. 
Mensah was the target of two federal civil trials brought by the Cole family. Both trials ended in hung juries, and Mensah reached a confidential settlement with the family. Another civil lawsuit involving the Anderson shooting is currently on appeal. 
After leaving Wauwatosa, Mensah was hired at the Waukesha County Sheriff’s Department. He resigned as a detective in 2025, between the two Cole trials, and said he was leaving law enforcement altogether. His file from the sheriff’s department states that at times Mensah was congratulated for being professional and compassionate on calls. Other times, supervisors needed to follow up with Mensah for not showing up to court trials, being difficult to reach by phone, missing appointments and not properly analyzing and cataloging evidence. He attempted unsuccessfully to become a drug task force officer. In his employee biography for the sheriffs department, dated January 2021, Mensah said that “the events surrounding my resignation with Wauwatosa PD were unfair, unfortunate, and unjust,” but that he put that chapter behind him.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Thousands of immigrants in Maryland to lose Medicaid coverage under H.R. 1
description: Treatments for cancer, diabetes and other conditions could be disrupted for up to 4,500 Maryland residents who will no longer qualify for Medicaid under a federal rule that takes effect Thursday that will disqualify people for Medicaid based on immigration status. It’s just one of the provisions that kick in Thursday under the federal “One […]
text:
Members of CASA rally in Annapolis in 2023 in favor of a bill that would expand health care for undocumented immigrants. Medicaid coverage for thousands of immigrants will go away after Oct. 1 under provisions of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. (Photo by Bryan P. Sears/Maryland Matters)Treatments for cancer, diabetes and other conditions could be disrupted for up to 4,500 Maryland residents who will no longer qualify for Medicaid under a federal rule that takes effect Thursday that will disqualify people for Medicaid based on immigration status.
It’s just one of the provisions that kick in Thursday under the federal “One Big Beautiful Bill Act,” including a change to the way states are charged for operation of the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, the food assistance program known as SNAP. That change could end up costing Maryland up to $57 million.
The changes under H.R.1 have been phased in since the budget reconciliation bill was passed by Congress in July 2025,  and more will come in 2027.
One of the biggest current changes will bar certain noncitizen immigrants from federal assistance programs. Leidi Garcia, director of health and human services at the immigrant advocacy group We Are CASA, worries about a woman diagnosed with colon cancer who recently contacted the organization. Garcia is concerned that the woman will not be able continue treatment when she loses coverage Thursday.
“That’s my biggest concern,” Garcia said. “Where are we going to be sending these individuals where they are actually going to be seen and provided with the care that they need in that moment? Especially when we see someone with a chronic disease diagnosed.”
Undocumented residents’ access to state health insurance marketplace delayed from 2026 to 2028

She expects more families to reach out to We Are CASA in the coming weeks, as an estimated 4,500 Maryland residents face the loss of Medicaid under H.R.1.
Under the new Medicaid restrictions, lawful permanent residents, also known as green-card holders, can still qualify for Medicaid along with Cuban and Haitian immigrants and migrants from the Compact of Free Association — Micronesia, Palau and the Marshall Islands. But starting Thursday, other noncitizens will get kicked from Medicaid, including those who came to the United States as refugees, asylum seekers, humanitarian parolees or victims of trafficking.
Options for immigrants who’ve lost Medicaid coverage could be limited. Those who had been receiving Medicaid coverage are likely low-income households, so the ability to purchase a private plan will be limited based on their income.
State officials suggest that those who no longer qualify for Medicaid get in contact with local community clinics, which can help those without insurance receive certain preventive care offered on a sliding fee scale. But in situations needing attentive and comprehensive care, community clinics may be limited in what services they can provide.
“There might be some resources to cover specific treatments,” Garcia said. “But when we’re talking about the comprehensive care of someone that is going through cancer, it’s not so much about just the treatment of the cancer, but the other issues that might come from that. Full coverage is needed in these cases.”
Otherwise, those who are booted from Medicaid and cannot afford other healthcare options will likely go without coverage until a medical emergency places them in the emergency room.
For those families who might be able to afford it, coverage on a subsidized health plan on Maryland’s insurance marketplace under the Affordable Care Act might be a solution. But it would be a temporary one, as those same immigrant populations will be barred from receiving subsidies after January 2027 due to H.R. 1.
Maryland may be steeply penalized after reducing SNAP payment error rates

Thursday also launches provisions under H.R. 1 that require state governments to contribute more to food assistance programs, increasing the state’s share of administrative costs to 75% while the federal government covers 25%. Previously, state and federal funds split administrative costs down the middle.
That means Maryland will now contribute around $57 million more to administer SNAP, on top of the $115 million it already pays for administrative costs.
Those increased administrative costs to the state, potentially growing by another $240 million in 2027, will strain an already constricted fiscal situation for Maryland, risking the resources and funds available to support state programs – some that could help the struggling immigrant populations.
Other federal policies increasing deportation efforts stoke fear in Maryland immigrant communities. Garcia says that more families are reaching out to groups like CASA for help in navigating those changes.
“We’re seeing the impact of these policies and how it has increased the fear,” Garcia said.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Congress tries end-run around Florida court decision protecting wetlands
description: When naturalist John James Audubon visited Florida in the 1830s, he marveled at our vast flocks of birds but complained about all the wetlands covering the landscape. “The general wildness, the eternal labyrinth of waters and marshes, interlocked and apparently never ending, the whole surrounded by interminable swamps — all these things had a tendency […]
text:
A Florida wetland cypress dome, via Everglades National Park. Developers have tried tor years get DEP put in charge of issuing federal wetlands permits, but judges have ruled that that system violates the Endangered Species Act.When naturalist John James Audubon visited Florida in the 1830s, he marveled at our vast flocks of birds but complained about all the wetlands covering the landscape.
“The general wildness, the eternal labyrinth of waters and marshes, interlocked and apparently never ending, the whole surrounded by interminable swamps — all these things had a tendency to depress my spirits,” he wrote in a poor-me note to his editor.
Hey, Mr. Audubon, cheer up! Congress is jumping in to help wipe out what’s left of Florida’s depressing swamps, marshes, and bogs! Isn’t that great news?
Here’s the situation: In 2020, at the tail end of the first Trump Administration, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency’s administrator — a former coal industry lobbyist —granted Florida’s request to take over issuing federal wetland destruction permits. We became the third state in the nation to do that.
Environmental groups sued, accusing the state of doing an illegal end-run around the Endangered Species Act to make its processing of the permits go faster.
When the state officials involved had to defend their actions in court, said attorney Tania Galloni of Earthjustice, their excuse was that the Endangered Species Act is just sooooooo doggone difficult to obey!
“’It’s hard’ is NOT a reason to not comply with federal law,” she told me four years ago.
In 2022, a federal judge agreed with the environmental groups. He ruled that the Florida Department of Environmental Protection had to stop handing out federal wetlands permits the same way wedding guests hurl rice at newlyweds.
The DEP appealed the judge’s ruling. In March of this year, a federal appeals court said the judge was right.
Rachel Silverstein via Miami Waterkeeper
Gil Smart via Vote Water
“Today’s decision restores critical protections for wetlands, endangered species, and the people who depend on clean water,” one of the environmental group leaders, Rachel Silverstein of Miami Waterkeeper, said.
So, naturally, the homebuilders who have spent years pushing this sped-up wetlands permitting program turned to Congress for help, crafting HR 9017, the “Restore Florida Water Independence Act.” The goal: Make what the court called illegal into something that’s officially legal, so they can get back to wiping out wetlands.
I’m sure Mr. Audubon would approve! But a lot of environmental groups do not.
“It seems to be in the service of making it easier and quicker for developers to develop,” said Gil Smart, executive director of Vote Water. “Look around you. Does it appear that Florida’s problem is that it’s developing too slowly?”
 Land by the gallon
Unlike Mr. Audubon, I like Florida wetlands. I’ve tromped through quite a few swamps, all of them wild and beautiful and full of life.
One of my favorite soggy-shoe excursions was a tour through the Big Cypress National Preserve organized by acclaimed photographer Clyde Butcher and his wife Niki.
The water was remarkably clear and, because this was late fall, a bit chilly. My group started off with the water level up to our knees. Then, suddenly, it was up to our waists. All the men’s voices, mine included, abruptly jumped an octave higher.
Despite occasionally being uncomfortable for us humans, wetlands are absolutely essential to our continued existence. They replenish our drinking water. They filter out pollutants. They protect us from flooding. They provide important habitat for wildlife. They combat climate change by soaking up excess carbon dioxide.
And, of course, they’ve long been used by scam artists trying to sell unsuspecting customers land not suitable for building. As one such sucker said after inspecting his bought-and-paid-for Florida swamp, “I have bought land by the acre, and I have bought land by the foot, but, by God, I have never before bought land by the gallon.”
But then the builders got the last laugh by filling in those swamps and paving over them.
Wetlands are supposed to be protected by the Clean Water Act, passed by Congress in 1972. Under that law, the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers was put in charge of issuing permits to limit the damage to wetlands.
That same law grants EPA veto power over any permits that should not have slipped by the Corps. In all this time, the EPA has vetoed only 14 permits — two in Florida.
In 2005, I was interviewing a well-connected lobbyist for Florida’s powerful development industry about federal wetland permits. He didn’t like them. The Corps said yes to nearly everything but took a looooong time to do so.
The state DEP would be SO much faster with those permits, he told me. Getting the feds to defer to the state on wetlands permits was, he said, “the Holy Grail” for developers.
It took them a while to make it happen, but finally they did. And then it blew up in their faces.
 Streamlining destruction 
Two states, Michigan and New Jersey, had already jumped through all the legal hoops of the Clean Water Act to take over handing out federal wetland permits. But none of the other 48 followed suit. They knew doing so would be expensive and labor-intensive.
In 2006, the Florida DEP looked into becoming the third state but quickly dropped the idea. The agency’s leaders realized it would require a lot more employees and money to do what the Corps was doing.
But by 2018, the builders had persuaded enough Florida legislators to join their cause. The Legislature passed a law calling for the DEP to take over federal permitting. They called it “streamlining,” as if you’d get the same product, but faster.
Ignoring the objections of every environmental group in the state, the DEP announced in 2020 that it would actively pursue the takeover. The state got a quick yes from the EPA boss, who claimed Florida had “beyond question one of the greatest environmental records of any state.” I’m assuming he then went and got his eyes checked.
But here’s where the DEP and homebuilders made their big mistake.
 It’s all good bro 
In designing the new state-run federal wetlands program, the DEP’s goal was the same as Sonic the Hedgehog’s: Gotta go fast!
One of the things that’s always slooooowed down the Corps from issuing wetlands permits was consulting with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service or the National Marine Fisheries Service.
The Corps permit reviewers would have to do this when the development project might affect an endangered species — say, by paving over Florida panther habitat or destroying a coastal marsh used by manatees.
Those agencies would be asked to provide an analysis for each project, called a “biological opinion,” about whether it would imperil the existence of the remaining population of the species.
They never said, “No, don’t do it!” Instead, they’d set a limit on how many of that species could legally be “taken” — in other words, harmed or even killed.
But the DEP was trying to speed everything up like in a Benny Hill chase scene. To that end, the agency obtained a blanket statement from the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service that said the state’s permits would never threaten the future existence of ANY of Florida’s more than 100 imperiled species.
The feds didn’t write, “It’s all good, bro! No worries!” but that was the intent.
That blanket biological opinion named just a handful of species “and, even for those, offers little analysis,” wrote the federal judge who found it illegal.
 Five tries, four failures 
The developers’ attempt to turn DEP into something like The Flash backfired in more ways than one.
According to a Bloomberg Law story from 2023, the developers didn’t get the speed-up they wanted. It was their own fault.
They filed triple the number of applications and DEP couldn’t handle it.
“Faced with the onslaught of permit applications, early staffing challenges, and the steep learning curve involved in taking over permitting from federal agencies,” Bloomberg reported, “Florida officials have approved wetlands permits at roughly the same rate as the Army Corps did in the eight years prior to 2021.”
And then the judges said stop.
You’d think the developers would have tallied their losses and dropped their pursuit, but no. Instead, they sought help from Congress to override what the judges said.
Bonnie Malloy via Earthjustice
“There have been five attempts so far,” said Bonnie Malloy, senior attorney in the Florida office of Earthjustice.
Some have been ham-handed efforts to slip language allowing the Florida DEP wetlands program into the federal budget.
“A lot of it was complete nonsense,” Malloy told me.
There have been actual bills, too.
Aaron Bean via U.S. House
Take, for instance, a bill filed by Rep. Aaron Bean in March 2025. Bean, R-Fernandina Beach, called it the “Maintaining Cooperative Permitting Act of 2025.”
The key word there is “cooperative,” as in “cooperating with everything the developers demand.”
Bean tried to spin it as something GOOD for the Florida environment.
Florida’s illegal wetlands permitting “remains essential for protecting our iconic wildlife and valued wetlands, while reducing wasteful duplication and improving responsiveness to applicants and the communities’ projects they serve,” Bean said.
When that bill went nowhere, the language was slipped into a bill modifying the Endangered Species Act, according to Casey Darling Kniffin of Friends of the Everglades, who’s been tracking all of this.
But that bill had so many problems that House leaders wound up pulling it from consideration.
Which brings us to the latest attempt, HR 9017. This bill was the subject of a hearing two weeks ago by the House Subcommittee on Water, Wildlife, and Fisheries.
The bottom line for this bill is the same as the rest: Speed things up and don’t worry about what gets flattened like so much roadkill.
Elizabeth Neville via Save the Manatee Club
“The consequences of getting this wrong will be disastrous,” warned Elizabeth Neville of the Save the Manatee Club.
 A free pass 
The three-page bill is sponsored by five Florida congressmen — four Republicans and one Democrat. So, it’s sort of bipartisan! How often do you see that these days?
U.S. Rep. Byron Donalds via U.S. House
The four Republicans are Mike Haridopolous, Vern Buchanan, Brian Mast, and Byron Donalds. The lone Democrat is Jared Moskowitz.
Within its tangled legalese, the gist of the bill is, “Those judges are wrong. We hereby declare Florida to be in compliance with the Endangered Species Act. The DEP can rubber-stamp all the federal wetlands permits anyone wants.”
During the subcommittee meeting, the members heard testimony from a U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service official, who said, “We’re working in alignment with the administration’s priorities, to … reduce environmental review.”
So, you can see what their priority is. This administration has been hard at work peeling back thick slices of wetlands protections and gutting endangered species language and the heck with the consequences.
George Roberts via screen grab
Another witness speaking in favor of the bill was George Roberts, chairman of the Northwest Florida Water Management District board — and oh, by the way, co-owner of Roberts & Roberts, a Panhandle construction company.
Roberts seemed particularly interested in what he called “efficiency” in permitting. I’m sure that wasn’t just the construction contractor in him talking.
Amber Crooks via Linkedin
The one witness most familiar with the bill’s origin and consequences: Amber Crooks of the Conservancy of Southwest Florida.
She warned the subcommittee that by approving the bill, they would be approving a permitting program “with no guardrails or backstops” to save Florida panthers, manatees, Key deer, and other endangered wildlife.
“This is essentially a free pass for development,” Crooks said.
But that’s not the way one of the bill’s sponsors saw it.
Congressman Donalds testified that the court rulings that stopped the DEP program involved “procedural paperwork, not an environmental failure.” He insisted that putting the DEP back in charge would cut “unnecessary red tape imposed by Washington.”
And then the gubernatorial candidate said one absolutely true thing.
“If we don’t take care of our environment, our state is finished.”
Who could disagree with that? Certainly not Mr. Audubon.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: An unsentimental obituary for the CCSU polytechnic vanity project
description: Nothing says student-centered public education like fastening the university’s future to a possible extinction machine.
text:
We gather today —not in sorrow, but with cautious relief— to mark the passing of the CCSU Polytechnic Vanity Project, a costly administrative hallucination that briefly mistook itself for the future of public higher education.
The exact time of death remains uncertain. For months, the project was kept alive by PowerPoint, executive fiat, and repeated infusions of the word innovation. But when a long-deferred accounting of numerous allegations of misconduct and institutional intimidation finally caught up with the mastermind who championed it —former CCSU President Zulma Toro— the patient’s condition deteriorated rapidly. Her sudden retreat from public scrutiny coincided with the collapse of her signature rebrand.
The official cause of death: prolonged exposure to reality, complicated by an unexpected outbreak of democratic resistance.
The polytechnic project was conceived in executive isolation and unveiled as a miraculous institutional upgrade. No one had asked for it, but that was apparently further proof of its visionary character. Shared governance, we were assured, would only slow the installation.
From the beginning, the project displayed the classic symptoms of administrative grandiosity: acute slogan production, chronic consultant dependence, compulsive rebranding, and a stubborn inability to distinguish a public university from a defense-industry trade show. Its architects promised to prepare students for “the jobs of tomorrow,” apparently by redesigning the university around whichever Big Tech companies, law-enforcement agencies, and military contractors already controlled today.
Every institutional problem came with the same prescription: more technology. Declining morale? Add artificial intelligence. Faculty dissent? Apply predictive analytics. Workplace-bullying allegations? Reboot the logo. A university community demanding a voice in its own future? Clearly a legacy-system compatibility issue.
The project’s “ethical AI” campaign was especially touching. Students would be taught to use powerful technologies responsibly while administrators placed no meaningful ethical limits on their own authority, partnerships, surveillance ambitions, or conduct. Ethics, under this arrangement, was something management uploaded to the curriculum and deleted from the executive suite.
Behind the polished language sat a much uglier machine. This promised digital future depended on industries built through mass data extraction, environmental destruction, labor automation, military contracting, racialized surveillance, deportation systems, and increasingly autonomous forms of state violence. Technologies already used to classify, track, target, and control human beings were repackaged as an educational identity.
And this was more than an uncritical alliance with a rogue technology. Even some of artificial intelligence’s leading architects are openly warning that the gleaming machine being sold as humanity’s inevitable future may already be drafting humanity’s obituary. Apparently, nothing says student-centered public education like fastening the university’s future to a possible extinction machine.
This was called transformation.
By transformation, management appeared to mean transforming students into workforce inputs, faculty into compliance problems, scholarship into product development, and the campus into a demonstration site for corporate technology. The university’s human beings would remain temporarily, one assumed, until a future system update eliminated the inefficiency.
Unfortunately for the project, the humans noticed.
They noticed that inevitable often means already decided without you. They noticed that innovation had become a password granting administrators access to decisions they could not defend democratically. And they noticed that a proposal supposedly devoted to the future relied on one of the oldest management systems in existence: command, intimidate, marginalize, repeat.
The calculations had omitted one troublesome variable. A university is not programmable software. Its intellectual life cannot be generated by executive prompt. Its consent cannot be simulated. And its people could not be dragged into the recycle bin when they rejected Toro’s preferred brand identity.
We offer no tears for the machine.
In lieu of flowers, mourners may send unanswered governance questions, expired consulting contracts, or lightly used copies of Ethics for Everyone Else. A memorial slideshow will not be shown. The campus has endured enough slides.
The project’s fatal defect was never poor messaging. It was not rolled out badly, misunderstood by faculty, or sabotaged by people insufficiently excited about tomorrow. Its central logic was defective. It treated democratic participation as an obstacle, public education as an underperforming asset, and corporate-military alignment as historical progress.
Ethical bankruptcy cannot be debugged with cleaner code. Institutional bullying cannot be concealed beneath a technological upgrade. No amount of technological glitter can turn executive vanity into a public mission.
Good riddance to the Polytechnic AI Vanity Project—undone by the messy human reality it tried to automate away.
But an obituary alone will not do. The collapse of this digital smoke screen must clear the way for genuine institutional change. A public university belongs to its students, educators, staff, and surrounding communities—not to an isolated executive, a fleet of consultants, or defense contractors shopping for publicly subsidized laboratories and workers.
Progress cannot be calculated by an algorithm. Institutional virtue cannot be manufactured through branding. Innovation imposed without democratic consent is simply coercion wearing a lanyard.
Now comes the harder work: dismantling the culture of fear, restoring meaningful shared governance, rejecting the corporate-military capture of public education, and rebuilding the university around the people whose labor, knowledge, relationships, and collective struggle actually keep it alive.
The machine is dead.
Long live the truly public university.
Timothy Scott is an Associate Professor of Social Work at Central Connecticut State University, a tech industry researcher, and the author of the book, Schooling for Silicon Valley.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: The numbers are in: EVs keep picking up steam in CT
description: The used electric vehicle market is actually hot, with sales of used EVs in July 10% higher than a year ago.
text:
There are so many good reasons to drive an electric vehicle, even Trump can’t stop them.
Since 2022, I’ve been driving a Chevy Bolt EUV. It’s been a great ride — pun intended! My car doesn’t cost much to run and maintain. It is fun to drive. It has no tailpipe, so there are no smelly fumes, and no pollution to choke on. I haven’t been to a gas station in four years, and I’m never going back. New statewide data shows that I’m not the only one.
It’s no secret the Trump administration has made the fossil fuel industry’s wish list its highest priority. They’ve done all they can to kill consumer appetite and access to electric vehicles by cancelling electric vehicle tax credits, trying to claw back funds for charging stations, and rolling back protections against tailpipe pollution. Yet, despite all this, electric vehicles are maintaining their momentum.
Worldwide, where these political headwinds don’t exist, one in four cars sold in 2025 was electric. The energy crisis caused by Trump’s war in Iran catalyzed record sales in global markets. In the United States, a slump in sales followed the repeal of federal tax credits, but signs of recovery are starting to appear. The used EV market is actually hot, with sales of used EVs in July 10.1% higher than a year ago. And here in Connecticut, the latest figures from the Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles show there are 75,210 electric vehicles registered in Connecticut as of July 2026.
The price of gas is one of the best reasons to choose an electric vehicle. We just experienced the most expensive August ever for Americans at the pump. The war in Iran is just the latest cause of oil volatility, but oil prices have spiked numerous times in the last few years, sending shockwaves through the American economy and household budgets. Fossil fuel dependence puts American families and businesses on a never-ending rollercoaster of price spikes. Even with Connecticut’s high electricity costs, it is still less expensive to drive an electric vehicle here than a conventional gas car. I am happy to be off that harrowing ride, and into an electric vehicle. 
With lower costs, and a better driving experience, EV owners are happier with their vehicles than those driving other cars — gas, diesel, and even hybrid — according to a new study by JD Power.
If you are considering ditching your gas powered vehicle for any of these reasons, you probably have some questions. Given the increase in electric vehicle registrations in Connecticut, I would guess you know someone who has one and wants to tell you more. If you don’t know someone who has an EV, check out a National Drive Electric Month event happening through October 12 in Connecticut and beyond. These EV events are a great way to meet EV drivers, check out their vehicles and learn how actual EV owners get from point A to point B. 
Samantha Dynowski is the state director of Sierra Club CT.

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: Idaho US Senate candidates weigh in on tariffs, Iran War, federal spending and more
description: Three out of four candidates running to represent Idaho in the U.S. Senate discussed their differing approaches on tariffs, military actions, immigration, and more Wednesday night in Caldwell. The race’s incumbent, Republican U.S. Sen. Jim Risch, declined to participate.  Independents Todd Achilles and Natalie Fleming, and Libertarian Matt Loesby, spoke at t[...]
text:
From left, League of Women Voters of Idaho President Jean Henscheid, independent U.S. Senate candidate Todd Achilles, College of Idaho moderatorsLatonia Haney Keith and McKay Cunningham, Libertarian Matt Loesby, center, independent Natalie Fleming, and Caldwell Chamber of Commerce Executive Director Travis Palmer. The League of Women Voters and Caldwell chamber hosted a U.S. Senate candidate forum Sept. 30 at Caldwell City Hall. (Photo by Laura Guido/Idaho Capital Sun) Three out of four candidates running to represent Idaho in the U.S. Senate discussed their differing approaches on tariffs, military actions, immigration, and more Wednesday night in Caldwell. The race’s incumbent, Republican U.S. Sen. Jim Risch, declined to participate. 
Independents Todd Achilles and Natalie Fleming, and Libertarian Matt Loesby, spoke at the forum hosted by the League of Women Voters, Caldwell Chamber of Commerce and the local American Association of University Women at Caldwell City Hall. 
[Voter Guide: 2026 primary election Voter Guide: The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
The three candidates differed in their proposals to address the federal budget deficit, reform immigration, and rein in military action abroad. 
Risch’s campaign manager Marc Kilmer told the Idaho Capital Sun in an email that Risch didn’t participate because, “It was organized by someone who has publicly endorsed our opponent, and therefore we felt it would not be an impartial debate.” 
Kilmer said the endorsement came from former Idaho Republican state Rep. Julie Yamamoto of Caldwell, but it wasn’t clear how she was connected to the organizers. He couldn’t immediately be reached to clarify. 
League of Women Voters of Idaho President Jean Henscheid told the Sun she didn’t know of any organizers that endorsed a candidate in the race. 
To watch the entire forum, visit the City of Caldwell Youtube page. 
 How would the candidates address the high cost of living and tariffs? 

All of the candidates agreed that the existing 50% tariff on a range of Canadian goods, should be rolled back and implemented more strategically. 
Achilles argued that Congress needed to “take back control” of tariff policy from the White House, and manage them in a “more strategic way” to protect domestic industries. 
“Congress needs to stand up and be an independent branch of government, and execute their constitutional duties, which is to be in control of tariffs,” he said. 
Loesby argued that tariffs were a small part of the problem when it came to addressing high costs of living for Americans. He agreed that the existing high tariffs should be rolled back and the taxes on imported products should be used to address trade imbalances with China. 
To address cost of living challenges, he said the U.S. needed to “end all these horrific foreign wars,” and “deport the millions of people who should not be in our country” to address housing costs. 
Fleming called the trade war with Canada, who imposed retaliatory tariffs against the U.S., “mind-boggling,” and said the import taxes should be rolled back. To address the high cost of living, she argued that the immigration systems should be reformed so immigrant workers can more easily work in the U.S. legally. 
“We all know that we have some wonderful immigrants who are building our homes and are providing food for us,” Fleming said. “And so we need to streamline the immigration process for them.” 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
 Candidates agreed Congress needed to intervene in foreign conflicts, such Iran War

Fleming criticized the U.S. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth for “embracing conflict and violence.” She cited American military support for Israel against Iran and Palestine.  
“We have become the aggressors overseas,” Fleming said. “So it is Congress’s role to stop this, and they’re just kind of a lame duck Congress not doing anything to stop any of this.” 
Achilles, who served overseas in the military, also criticized Hegseth as well as Risch, who is chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee. 
“He’s held zero hearings on Venezuela, zero hearings on the illegal destruction of boats in the Caribbean, and zero hearings on the Iran War,” Achilles said.
Loesby said the U.S. should defund all U.S. military bases abroad and call back American military members. 
“Congress needs to say, all right, if you want to keep sending our troops to die overseas for foreign governments, you’re not getting any money,” Loesby said, “and in fact, we need to impeach the president and remove him for treason for sending American troops to die for other countries.” 
 How would the candidates address the nation’s growing federal debt? 

The federal government’s debt in 2025 reached $37.64 trillion, according to the U.S. Treasury. 
Loesby proposed eliminating the government safety net programs Medicaid, Medicare and Social Security to reduce spending and address the debt, as well as ending overseas wars. 
“We have a spending problem, and it will not be addressed by just reducing things around to the edges,” Loesby said. “It will not be addressed by finding some fraud. It will only be addressed by aggressively cutting the government-run charity schemes that have replaced the actual generosity of the American people.” 
Fleming cited a study by the think tank, the Cato Institute, that found immigrants’ tax input into the economy have “reduced deficits by $14.5 trillion” since 1994.  
She argued that streamlining legal immigration processes would allow more people to “work legally and fully participate in the economy,” and would help boost the revenue and balance the federal budget. To cut spending, she said, “I think we should cut back spending on paying AIs to calculate which schools to bomb in Iran.” 
Achilles argued that Congress should reject a proposed $500 billion increase to the Department of Defense budget, and to increase federal revenue by closing tax loopholes for corporations and high-earning individuals. 
“We’ve got a tax system that’s nothing but a bunch of it’s a Swiss cheese of loopholes and carveouts,” Achilles said. 
 What are the candidates’ paths to victory in ruby red Idaho?

After the Democrat David Roth officially withdrew from the race earlier this month, the remaining challengers to Risch are not members of the two major parties in the U.S. 
Republicans in Idaho haven’t lost a U.S. Senate race in the state since 1974. 
Achilles said his campaign has “the best shot in 50 years” of beating the incumbent Republican. He said Idahoans are frustrated with Congress’s inaction against a “rigged economy that’s not working for them.” 
“They want change,” he said. “Now, what’s clear is that neither political party is delivering any of that change that Idahoans are looking for.” 
Fleming said that as she’s been talking to Idahoans, and they “are very stressed, and they are doing their homework.” 
“I really believe in the people of Idaho,” Fleming said. “That they’re taking their time to look people up, and to do their research. And that’s what I’m counting on.” 
Loesby said he believes Risch will win his reelection, but that he thought people should vote for him as a way to “send a message to the Republican Party,” for prioritizing foreign conflicts and “spending trillions of our dollars on ridiculous projects.” 
“These are things that need to be punished, so that’s why you shouldn’t vote for Republicans,” Loesby said. “But also, all of us on this stage should be realistic about what our odds actually are.”

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Sand completes second 99-county town hall tour of gubernatorial campaign
description: As Iowa Auditor of State Rob Sand completed a 99-county tour for the second time in his gubernatorial campaign, he called for supporters to keep momentum up and bring “divided government once again” to Iowa. Sand held the final stop of his 2026 town hall tour Wednesday at the Val Air Ballroom in West Des […]
text:
Iowa Auditor Rob Sand, the Democratic nominee for Iowa governor, asked the crowd to raise their hand if it was their first time attending a town hall event as he hosted his final stop on his 99-county town hall tour at the Val Air Ballroom in West Des Moines Sep. 30, 2026. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)As Iowa Auditor of State Rob Sand completed a 99-county tour for the second time in his gubernatorial campaign, he called for supporters to keep momentum up and bring “divided government once again” to Iowa.
Sand held the final stop of his 2026 town hall tour Wednesday at the Val Air Ballroom in West Des Moines.  More than 1,800 people attended the Democratic candidate’s event, braving the rain and congested parking lots to attend.
Polls and political forecasters show Sand leading Republican gubernatorial candidate Zach Lahn in the weeks ahead of the Nov. 3, 2026 election. While Sand told the crowd not to be complacent or assume he will win, he also said he was hopeful about the election outcome.
“I think we can win this campaign,” Sand said. “I don’t think it because the polls show that we’re leading. They do. That’s nice. I think it because I know Iowans, and I know people are looking around the state, going, ‘What happened to our state?'”
As he has at each preceding town hall, Sand began Wednesday’s event with the crowd singing the first verse of “America the Beautiful” together. After sharing some of his family history and political beliefs — speaking extensively about his opposition to the two-party political system — Sand took questions from the audience on topics from cannabis legalization to Flock cameras.
Iowa Auditor Rob Sand, the Democratic nominee for Iowa governor, addressed a crowd of more than 1,800 gathered for his campaign town hall at Val Air Ballroom in West Des Moines Sep. 30, 2026. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)
The Democratic candidate specifically called on two people who had identified themselves as registered Republicans earlier in the event to ask him questions. One of the Republicans spoke in opposition to the state’s Education Savings Account program, the law providing public funding for private school tuition and associated costs — a program Sand has also been critical of as he calls for oversight measures and income limits.
The other Republican who spoke at the event criticized Iowa’s public school system, saying more families were turning to private schools because they did not feel the public schools were adequately teaching kids about math, science, history and English — a comment that received a colder reception from the crowd.
“Let’s be nice, everybody,” Sand said. “Larry’s here to share his opinion in a room that he knew might not have a lot of people who shared it. That takes some courage … Larry’s concern was he thinks that the quality of Iowa’s public schools has gone down — and what are we doing to fix that? That’s a good question. Because whether or not we have an agreement or a disagreement about the quality of them, don’t we always want them to be better?”
Sand said he would advocate for a 5% increase to K-12 funding in his first term as governor if elected, but added that he would not make further commitments.
“A lot of people might say, ‘Well, Rob, what about the next year?’ Well, we have a $1.4 billion budget deficit, a 5% increase moves that in a different direction,” Sand said. “We’ve got specific plans for how to bring the deficit down. We should treat cannabis the way we treat alcohol, we should make data centers pay all their taxes, and we should put income limits back on the school vouchers program. Those three things alone would cover about half of the deficit, once we get the program up and running, but we’ve got room to grow from there.”
While Sand said he aims to bring “balance” to the Iowa statehouse, the body currently has a Republican trifecta – alongside GOP Gov. Kim Reynolds, Republicans hold a majority in both the Iowa House and Senate.
While this dynamic could change in the 2026 election, the Legislature is reconvening Friday, one month before the Nov. 3 election, to pass a measure providing tax incentives for a $15 billion steel mill project planned for Lee County. Trump, joined by several Iowa Republicans, announced the Mesabi Metallics project in the Oval Office on Monday.
While Reynolds has said state lawmakers will be considering changes to the state’s Major Economic Growth Attraction (MEGA) program, which provides incentives for large-scale development projects representing more than $1 billion in capital investment, the details of the legislation are not yet public.
Sand told reporters he wants to learn about the specifics of the potential tax breaks before giving a “hard answer,” adding that he wants to make sure the incentive package and steel mill project is something that serves Iowans.
“Certainly, you’d want to make sure that we are not paying out up front,” Sand said. “These folks had some real problems in Minnesota, and so we want to make sure that they’re actually making their investments of whatever money they’re bringing to Iowa before we would release — in, like, a stair-step fashion — any public benefits from the state side. And we want to make sure that we’re not overpaying.”
Some Democrats have expressed concerns about the bill’s scope expanding to include amendments restricting gubernatorial powers. One of the powers some Republicans have expressed concerns about is the ability for a governor to appoint a successor to longtime U.S. Sen. Chuck Grassley’s seat if he were to pass away while serving in office.
Grassley, who is 93 years old, told a group of Iowa Republicans last week, “I don’t plan on dying in office, but if I did, I don’t want a Democratic governor choosing my successor.”
Sand said he does not believe the special session will include a discussion on the governor’s powers, referencing Reynolds’ proclamation that the “sole and singular purpose” of the special session will be to amend the MEGA program.
“I would assume that they would be faithful to that,” Sand said.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Zach Lahn expects Iowans to reap benefits of proposed steel mill for decades
description: GRIMES — Zach Lahn called a $15 billion steel mill project planned for Iowa a “once-in-a-lifetime project,” saying it will make a positive impact for generations to come, as he campaigned Wednesday on keeping young people in Iowa and securing the state’s future. The Republican gubernatorial candidate held a rally in Grimes where he reiterated […]
text:
Iowa gubernatorial candidate Zach Lahn speaks to supporters at Destination Grille in Grimes on Sept. 30, 2026. (Photo by Brooklyn Draisey/Iowa Capital Dispatch)GRIMES — Zach Lahn called a $15 billion steel mill project planned for Iowa a “once-in-a-lifetime project,” saying it will make a positive impact for generations to come, as he campaigned Wednesday on keeping young people in Iowa and securing the state’s future.
The Republican gubernatorial candidate held a rally in Grimes where he reiterated the focal points of his campaign, including bringing Iowa agriculture into schools, raising Iowa’s education ranking, cleaning up waterways and keeping “the enemy” — Democrats — from the gate.
During his remarks, he didn’t mention during the plans by Mesabi Metallics to build a steel mill in Lee County, the subject of a special legislative session set for Friday, but told reporters later the project is “a very good deal for Iowans.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“This is a tremendous opportunity for the people of Iowa, for southeast Iowa, for an economically depressed place, and so this is something that’s going to affect people’s kids and grandkids down the road by getting it in the state,” Lahn said. “I think that the governor has done a great job in getting it to the state and getting it to the point it’s at, and I’m very thankful for that.”
The special session will focus on amending Iowa’s Major Economic Growth Attraction (MEGA) program, which provides incentives for large-scale development projects. Lahn said that while he hasn’t looked at any incentive packages for the project, he wants to ensure “we stair-step any incentive that we give” and that that Iowans and U.S. citizens are hired for the jobs the project will generate.
According to Trump’s announcement, the steel plant will be the largest in the U.S. and will create 1,750 permanent jobs and 6,000 temporary construction jobs.
Lahn states on his campaign website that he wants to “end tax credits and economic development funds for out-of-state and foreign corporations and prioritize Iowa-based companies with deep community roots,” but said Wednesday he’s referring to corporations like Chinese-owned company Syngenta with that line of thinking, not large projects like the steel mill.
Mesabi Metallics is an Essar Group company, according to its website, described as “a major Indian industrial conglomerate.” While Syngenta competes against Iowa companies, Lahn said there is no competition for the Mesabi Metallics project.
“This is going to go in some state, and we have to do what we can to bring it to the state of Iowa,” Lahn said.
When asked his thoughts on comparing tax incentives for data centers to tax incentives for the steel mill, Lahn said the two are “completely opposite.” While data center companies are trying to come into the state, wanting tax breaks but not offering much in return, the steel mill project is “one of one.”
According to an economic impact study from the Technology Association of Iowa, the state has more than 100 data centers being planned, built or already in operation.
There can be a return from corporations hoping to build data centers in Iowa, Lahn said, in the form of property taxes and help in lowering community costs and cleaning up Iowa’s water, but the benefits that will come with the steel mill are already apparent.
Lahn said while it’s hard to say what the mill’s impact on the state will be over the next 50 years he knows southeast Iowans will see benefits, and that companies — both new and returning — could want to set up shop close to where the steel is.
“What an opportunity to have Iowa become the state that builds again in a major way and start to get some of our manufacturing reshored here,” Lahn said. “Maybe we can get some of the plants that we used to have to see the opportunity to come back.”
