name: WyoFile
title: Billionaire Joe Ricketts resurrects plans for luxury Bondurant resort after ‘Saving Yellowstone’ accolades
description:
New effort to develop “The Confluence" is one of several recent business moves by the TD Ameritrade founder, who also bought the Rim Station and Timberline Ranch near Merna. 
The post Billionaire Joe Ricketts resurrects plans for luxury Bondurant resort after ‘Saving Yellowstone’ accolades appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Fresh off a spate of positive publicity for his conservation-oriented work under the banner Saving Yellowstone, billionaire Joe Ricketts has renewed his efforts to develop a luxury resort on ranchland that runs along the rural, remote Upper Hoback River. 
In 2024, the TD Ameritrade founder and patriarch of the family that owns the Chicago Cubs halted an underway upscale resort after Sublette County commissioners declined to waive stipulations that prohibited construction from Nov. 15 to April 30 to protect wintering elk and moose. Ricketts contended the abridged building season would add $60 million in construction costs when he pulled the project.  
Two years later, the 85-year-old financier is trying again. In July, his agents submitted a permit application to the Sublette County Planning and Zoning Department for a resort called The Confluence. The effort escaped media attention until Tuesday, when it was reported by the Cowboy State Daily. 
The modified project proposal calls for a recreational lodge, restaurant and bar, a wellness/spa center and 20 guest suites. But that’s just the first phase. More phases are expected, according to the application, and will be pursued with future applications. Construction is anticipated to begin this fall and wrap up by 2031. 




Click to enlarge: A detail of the main 20-room guest lodge from a landscape plan submitted July 20, 2026, to Sublette County Planning and Zoning for a new development on Joe Ricketts’ property along the Upper Hoback River Road in Bondurant. (Courtesy)
Ricketts has repeatedly espoused the idea that developing resorts and getting wealthy tourists to understand conservation are needed to protect the Greater Yellowstone Ecosystem. He made that case to a Pinedale audience in 2023, pitching his own luxury resort as a form of conservation, and echoed those views in August at a conference he hosted at his ranch under his new nonprofit, Saving Yellowstone.
“We need to accommodate growth in a way that [protects] the places that you see,” Ricketts told conference attendees in his opening remarks.
Ricketts’ earlier attempt at a resort, which had been dubbed the Homestead, went over very poorly in the small Bondurant community. The ranchland being developed by the billionaire Nebraskan is crossed by the longest known mule deer migration route in the world, which connects the Red Desert to Hoback Basin and beyond. It also contains crucial winter ranges for elk and moose. 
The first attempt in 2020 to rezone the ranchland from its former agricultural status failed, but he tried again the next fall and was given the OK by county commissioners in December 2021.
TD Ameritrade founder Joe Ricketts welcomes guests at the August 2026 Saving Yellowstone conference hosted at his ranch. (Mike Koshmrl/WyoFile)
At public meetings about the resort plans, oftentimes the only person speaking in support of Ricketts was Morgan Fischer, his former agent, who Ricketts is now suing alleging he was defrauded. 
In written responses to WyoFile’s questions on Wednesday, spokesperson Jessica Jaubert said that Ricketts is committed to being a good neighbor.
“[That] includes keeping people informed, answering questions directly, following County requirements and paying attention to how construction affects those who live and work nearby,” she said. 
A resolution appended to the resort application shows that Ricketts has agreed to not build from Nov. 15 through April 30 this time around.
Jaubert highlighted other wildlife-friendly measures in the plans. He’s committing to wildlife-friendly fencing, bear-resistant trashcans and dark sky-friendly lighting, she said. Guests will be given “toolkits” with instructions on being a good ecosystem tourists.  
“Mr. Ricketts is committed to these added measures to help wildlife move safely through the property, reduce conflicts between people and animals, and help guests understand their responsibility to care for the place they’ve come to enjoy,” Jaubert said. 
Some neighbors aren’t buying it, like Upper Hoback Road residents Lisi Krall.
“I am more skeptical than I’ve ever been,” Krall said. 
Krall, who’s a retired environmental economics professor, is especially critical of Ricketts’ theory that conservation and development are intertwined. 
“He frames it like this is an eco lodge, where he’s going to teach people about the Hoback region, blah blah blah,” Krall said. “This is not conservation. Building eco lodges for the very wealthy that have huge footprints up small river valleys is not conservation, and it negates his good conservation work.” 






Earth-moving equipment shaped out this construction site along Upper Hoback Road in 2024 in anticipation of a later-canceled luxury resort sought by billionaire Joe Ricketts. (Mike Koshmrl/WyoFile)






Construction crew barracks and stockpiles are leftover from a luxury resort that billionaire Joe Ricketts began building but canceled in July 2024. This photograph was taken from a public Bridger-Teton National Forest road. (Mike Koshmrl/WyoFile)


In Krall’s judgement, the nonprofits Saving Yellowstone and Ricketts Conservation Foundation are little more than public relations tools — and effective ones. 
“Based on the number of conservationists that he’s brought into his fold,” she said, “I’d say he’s doing a pretty good job of making conservationists believe this is the way to conservation.” 
Jaubert disavowed any connection between Ricketts’ resort and environmental initiatives. The Confluence application and Saving Yellowstone conference happening within a month of each other was “entirely coincidental,” she said. 
Fellow Upper Hoback Road resident Pat Burroughs attended the conference, and has tried to give Ricketts the benefit of the doubt. But she’s simultaneously skeptical.
“At the summit, Joe said that the thing that causes the most problems for the ecology of the ecosystem is Starlink,” she said. “Baloney. It’s commercialism.”
The on-again, off-again resort is “making me crazy,” Burroughs said. “I want to believe that our little valley is going to be safe,” she said. 
In the two years since Ricketts halted construction, he’s stayed busy with land dealings in Sublette and Teton counties. He purchased a Bridger-Teton National Forest inholding up Granite Creek, northwest of Bondurant, and this summer construction crews have been working to renovate and expand a guest ranch he’s dubbed The Hawken.
Ricketts also bought the Rim Station, a small market and RV Park located along U.S. Highway 191 at the divide between the Hoback and Green rivers. It’s now registered to Rim Station LLC, an entity that was organized in June by Ricketts agent Steve Christensen. 
And the billionaire also purchased the Timberline Ranch near Merna, formerly occupied by hunting influencers brought down for poaching. That property is now owned by Moose Lake Acquisition LLC, which was organized in March by Christensen. 
Some debate remains on whether Ricketts is on sound legal footing to develop The Confluence resort without again having to rezone the property. Neighbors are pointing to Sublette County zoning regulations, which stipulate that property rezoned to accommodate resorts must see “substantial development” within two years or the zoning change “shall” revert.
Ricketts’ ranchland was rezoned nearly five years ago. 
Sublette County Attorney Clayton Melinkovich declined to comment on the matter, citing the potential for litigation.

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Arkansas lawmakers told helping inmates return to society will ease prison overcrowding
description: Arkansas lawmakers and criminal justice reform advocates agreed Wednesday that improving the systems that help inmates return to society after incarceration will alleviate the state’s prison overcrowding problem. State correctional facilities have 15,362 beds and 16,804 inmates as of Sept. 1, and county jails are often tasked with holding inmates waiting for[...]
text:
Former Arkansas lawmaker Jeremy Hutchinson, who served two years in prison on federal bribery and tax charges, presents the House and Senate Judiciary committees with suggestions to reduce prison overcrowding on Sept. 30, 2026. (Photo by Tess Vrbin/Arkansas Advocate)Arkansas lawmakers and criminal justice reform advocates agreed Wednesday that improving the systems that help inmates return to society after incarceration will alleviate the state’s prison overcrowding problem.
State correctional facilities have 15,362 beds and 16,804 inmates as of Sept. 1, and county jails are often tasked with holding inmates waiting for state prison beds. 
“We also need to examine what happens before someone reaches those prison beds,” said Marybeth Hill, event coordinator with the ARCHway Institute, a Florida-based substance use treatment organization. “We cannot incarcerate ourselves out of a public health crisis.”
Hill, one of 19 advocates who testified during a daylong hearing on prisons before the House and Senate judiciary committees, said a combination of support, accountability and substance use treatment helped her move on after serving time for drug charges.
Arkansas’ 3,000-bed prison site is on hold. What are the other options?

One obstacle to reentry to society is the presence of drugs in prison, said Jarad Harper, executive director of the faith-based Shackle Free Ministries, based in Clarksville. Committee members said this needs to be addressed legislatively, especially if corrections employees are supplying inmates with drugs.
“I’m asking if we should be throwing the book not at the first-time criminals…but maybe throw the book at people who are government employees making a very good living and eventually getting a huge pension for being part of the problem,” Ferndale Republican Sen. Mark Johnson said.
Wednesday’s hearing was the latest in series of meetings the panel is holding on prisons and overcrowding. The meetings are being held as the state is looking at alternatives after Republican Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders’ plan to build a 3,000-bed prison in Franklin County was put on hold because of legislative resistance. 
Former Republican lawmaker Jeremy Hutchinson, son of former U.S. Sen. Tim Hutchinson and nephew of former Gov. Asa Hutchinson, also shared his criminal justice reform ideas with the committee.
Jeremy Hutchinson resigned from the Legislature in 2018 after he was indicted in federal courts in Missouri and Arkansas on federal bribery and tax charges. The corruption scandal involved several other lawmakers, as well as lobbyists and healthcare executives.
Hutchinson served two years of an eight-year prison sentence before President Donald Trump pardoned him last year. He then became director of strategic initiatives for Unify.US, a Washington D.C.-based criminal justice reform organization that works primarily with Republican-led states.

Overcrowded: Protect Arkansas Act to drive continued prison population growth for at least a decade


Sanders and the majority-GOP Legislature passed the Protect Arkansas Act into law in 2023. The law is expected to increase the demand for prison beds, likely adding 2,902 offenders by 2040, because it requires longer criminal sentences and reduces parole eligibility.
One policy change Hutchinson suggested was to allow nonviolent offenders over 60 years of age to serve their sentences in home confinement instead of in prison. This would save the Department of Corrections “a fortune” in inmates’ healthcare costs, since those individuals could be eligible for Medicaid, Hutchinson said.
“Their sentence isn’t being relieved, and if they screw up, they can be hauled right back into the prison environment, but they’re still in custody,” he said.
Hutchinson also suggested that Arkansas’ court system automatically expunge nonviolent crimes after inmates complete their sentences, since having a criminal record makes it difficult to obtain housing and employment and increases the likelihood of reoffending.
One of the contributors to Arkansas’ rising prison population is recidivism, a term applied when inmates violate the terms of their release or are convicted of new crimes within three years of leaving prison. Corrections staff turnover and high caseloads can reinforce the problem, according to experts.
Another policy change that could reduce recidivism and strengthen inmates’ reintegration into society would be to hold inmates financially responsible for it, said Sharon Garrett, executive director of Safe Haven Ministries, a Clarksville-based nonprofit that assists formerly incarcerated women.
Overcrowded: Arkansas’ prison system costs inmates, taxpayers

If the state paid reentry programs only $50 per day for 45 days, it would save $1,870 per inmate that uses the program, Garrett said. She added that many reentry programs are only 90 days, but many inmates need at least a year to make the changes that prevent them from reoffending.
“I propose that we treat them with dignity, we make them stay longer, we inspire their vision and we let them share in the cost of their journey,” Garrett said.
Arkansans can already rack up a variety of expenses while incarcerated, such as payments for court proceedings and commissary products, and they often continue to owe the corrections system after being released.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Crackdown on out-of-state vehicle registrations to start this month
description: Under a law that takes effect Thursday, Marylanders who register their cars in other states will have 60 days to register them in Maryland or face fines and other possible penalties, although state officials said they hope drivers will take advantage of the grace period.
text:
Maryland residents with vehicles registered in other states will have 60 days to register in Maryland or face fines and other penalties. Notices are expected to go out later this month. (File photo by Bruce DePuyt/Maryland Matters)State officials say they are ready to crack down on Maryland residents who register their vehicles in other states.
Under a law that takes effect Thursday, Marylanders who register their cars in other states will have 60 days to register them in Maryland. Those who do not could face fines and other penalties, but Maryland Motor Vehicle Administrator Chrissy Nizer said her agency hopes most will make use of the grace period.
“That’s the end goal of this. It really is not to fine people,” Nizer said. “We don’t want to have to do that. We want people to come in compliance prior to that.”
The number of vehicles registered in Virginia to Maryland drivers is a growing problem.
In November 2023, more than 101,000 vehicles registered in Virginia were associated with Maryland addresses. That number jumped to more than 111,000 by the following June, according to an analysis presented to lawmakers in January.
Motor Vehicle Administration Administrator Christine Nizer. (File photo by Bryan P. Sears/Maryland Matters)
In Baltimore City, 10% of fatal accidents from 2023 to 2024 involved vehicles registered in Virginia. Over 7,000 nonfatal crashes — about 47% of all non-fatal accidents during that same period — involved vehicles registered in Virginia.
Baltimore City Police Lt. Col. Derek Loeffler told lawmakers in January that out-of-state registrations account for 11% of all unpaid parking, speed camera and other citations.
In July, the Office of Program Evaluation and Government Accountability reported that 25% of all speed camera citations issued over a three-year period were issued to vehicles registered out of state. Topping the list were vehicles registered in Virginia.
Of primary concern is safety, Nizer said.
“It really all starts with safety, and we know what the requirements are in Maryland,” she said. “You have to have that safety inspection when you title and register a new vehicle. You have to comply with insurance requirements.”
Virginia has different insurance requirements. Additionally, Nizer said data shows that Maryland vehicles registered in Virginia are not in compliance with Virginia inspection requirements.
“Over 90% of them either were not completed or were not in compliance,” Nizer said. “That’s a real concern because if those vehicles are out there driving on the roads but don’t meet basic safety standards, and they are in a crash — obviously, that means that the risk of injury or even death is much higher.”
There are also budgetary concerns.
Registering in Virginia allows the vehicle to avoid Maryland registration fees. Those fees, based on weight class, make up 17% of the state’s Transportation Trust Fund, which pays for highway and transit projects. Some of the registration fees also help pay for emergency medical services and Shock Trauma.
Additionally, those vehicles avoid Maryland vehicle emissions testing.
A recent audit found that out-of-state vehicles owed more than $818 million in unpaid tolls and fees. Vehicles registered in Virginia owe nearly $235 million — more than any other state
Over the summer, officials started promoting the “Plate where you live” program. The goal was to give owners as much notice as possible.
The MVA and its counterpart in Virginia identified nearly 80,000 individuals who live in Maryland but register vehicles in Virginia. Seventy percent of the notices went to drivers in three jurisdictions — Prince George’s County, Baltimore City and Baltimore County. More than a third went to residents in Prince George’s County, according to the MVA.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
In July, those owners received “courtesy letters” announcing the new law. About 3,400 registered their vehicles in Maryland, Nizer said.
The agency expects an updated file from Virginia in October. The new data will be used to send official compliance notices.
“Most of our compliance periods start when we send that first notice out,” Nizer said.
Motorists who get their vehicle titled in Maryland within that 60-day window will face no fines or penalties. After that, owners of vehicles face a fine of $7 per day for the next 60 days. The maximum fine is $420.
After that first 120-day period, owners of vehicles not registered in the state are subject to other penalties that could include seizing license or immobilizing those vehicles.
For now, most of the discussion about enforcement has centered around vehicles registered in Virginia, but supporters of the program insist that the out-of-state tag bill is not meant to focus on one state.
“We try to call it the out of state tag enforcement bill,” Nizer said. “To be clear that it’s not about Virginia specifically.
Virginia law — unlike Maryland — allows non-residents to title their vehicles in the state.
“There are some other states who also have that kind of law,” Nizer said, adding that her agency is looking at other states with similar laws. Her agency also takes “complaints from individuals,” a process that has been “in place for many years.”

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: North Dakota to use ‘anchor partners’ to manage Rural Health grants
description: North Dakota’s Health and Human Services Department is turning to outside “anchor partners” to manage a federal grant program for millions of dollars meant to boost rural health care initiatives. Lawmakers wondered what an “anchor partner” actually is, how they are chosen and how the change will affect the timing to get more than $160 […]
text:
North Dakota Department of Health and Human Services Chief Financial Officer Donna Aukland addresses a legislative panel on Sept. 30, 2026. (Photo by Jack Dura/North Dakota Monitor)North Dakota’s Health and Human Services Department is turning to outside “anchor partners” to manage a federal grant program for millions of dollars meant to boost rural health care initiatives.
Lawmakers wondered what an “anchor partner” actually is, how they are chosen and how the change will affect the timing to get more than $160 million of awarded funding out the door by a looming deadline.
Earlier this year, the Republican-led Legislature accepted $199 million in federal Rural Health Transformation Program funding. The money is meant to improve technology, increase health care access in rural areas, boost workforce and promote healthy lifestyles.
All 50 states received a portion of the money under the five-year, $50 billion program.
North Dakota rural health plan approved, ‘now we’ve got to implement it’

North Dakota is the only state managing every single grant included in the Rural Health Transformation Program, estimated at 500 to 700 grants, HHS Chief Financial Officer Donna Aukland told a panel of House and Senate budget writers on Wednesday. The other states have “anchor partners,” she said.
“Anchor partners” are in-state organizations that directly handle grant applications and funding opportunities and individually manage the grants, Aukland said. HHS would still manage the grants but “from a higher level to ensure that the work was getting done,” she said. 
HHS will use three anchor partners, including the University of North Dakota Center for Rural Health. The two others are not finalized.
HHS chose partners it was already working closely with, but plans to work with more in the future four years of funding and figure out whether there will be an application process for anchor partners, Aukland said. 
Rep. Eric Murphy, R-Grand Forks, said details are lacking on the department’s change, a move Aukland called a “slight pivot.”
Rep. Jon Nelson, R-Rugby, said he doesn’t see the change helping the timeline for dispersing funds and wondered about a decision-making lag. More than $161 million remains to be awarded to grantees, awaiting final reviews, Aukland said. The deadline to do so is Oct. 30.
“There’s a lot of angst out there that the awards haven’t been granted yet,” Nelson said. 
More than $50 million available in new rural health grants

In the next week, HHS will look at all of the awards going out to anchor partners and will notify grant recipients that money is coming, “but we don’t know the total amount yet” because HHS needs to verify the amount in their grant application is allowable, Aukland said.
So far, HHS has obligated about $37.3 million of the funding.
HHS still has to have staff for the program to ensure the money is used according to plan, Aukland said. The change to anchor partners allows the department to focus on strategy and more follow-up “to ensure that we are actually getting the things out of the plan that we wanted to get.”
Earlier, she told another panel of lawmakers that HHS has had to hire about 20 positions to administer the Rural Health Transformation Program. Even with anchor partners, the department will still have administrative costs as it monitors the work for compliance with federal rules, Aukland said.
Anchor partners are allowed up to 10% of grants for administrative costs, she said. HHS requires information on administrative costs, she said.
The U.S. Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services will announce North Dakota’s second-year funding amount in October. HHS has estimated it will be around $200 million.
Evaluations for the next four years of Rural Health funding will be under HHS guidance with the anchor partners, Aukland said.
Deputy Editor Jeff Beach contributed to this report.
Reach North Dakota Monitor reporter Jack Dura at jdura@northdakotamonitor.com.

name: VTDigger
title: Texas company presents ideas for future Vermont Yankee property use
description:
PowerTransitions seeks community reactions and ideas about potential battery storage at the longtime nuclear reactor site. The company says it decided not to pursue solar or data center projects there, based on earlier feedback.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Texas company presents ideas for future Vermont Yankee property use.
text:
A worker cuts apart a beam during the deconstruction of the former Vermont Yankee nuclear power plant in Vernon in October 2023. The salvaged metal from the plant, which is not radioactive, is being recycled. File photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

This story by Olga Peters was first published in The Commons on Sept. 29, 2026. 
VERNON — PowerTransitions officials who held another community meeting on Sept. 23 faced community members who filled a meeting room, expressing skepticism and concern that Vernon could become home to an expensive, potentially hazardous energy installation.
Employees at the Texas-based company, which recently signed an option lease agreement with NorthStar to install an energy project on the 140-acre site of the former Vermont Yankee nuclear plant, arrived at the Governor Hunt House prepared to take feedback on a potential battery storage project.
PowerTransitions is considering using the Vermont Yankee property for a 110 MW to 440 MW battery energy storage system.
The company would negotiate an annual payment to the town, in addition to local and state taxes.
It operates multiple projects, including natural gas, and has redeveloped former energy facilities, such as the Quindaro Power Station in Kansas City, Kansas.
NorthStar is decommissioning the Vermont Yankee nuclear plant and preparing the property for redevelopment. Fifty-eight canisters of nuclear waste will remain on site.
“You have a very unique site here,” said PowerTransitions’ head of external affairs, Carrie Hitt. “It is electrically very interesting to people.”
“It housed one of the only large nuclear facilities in New England until very not too long ago, right?” she continued. “It’s very complicated. It’s very complex. It’s very interesting. I’m just going to say it’s very challenging.”

Zon Eastes and Laura Sibilia (standing behind those seated, from left), both state representatives, were among the attendees at a community meeting called by PowerTransitions to discuss uses for the former Vermont Yankee property. Eastes represents Vernon, while Sibilia, from Dover, is the Brattleboro Development Credit Corporation’s director of regional economic development strategies and programs. Photo by Olga Peters/The Commons

At times, the audience and PowerTransitions staff seemed as disconnected as the computer presentation that refused to open.
Several attendees expected to learn details about a specific project, but Hitt said that, with the company still exploring options for the site, nothing has been finalized.
Hitt said the company wants community support for any energy project it pursues before beginning the state permitting process that requires energy projects to earn a certificate of public good from the Vermont Public Utility Commission under Section 248 of the state’s statutes.
“We do want to work closely with the town and community before filing anything official,” she said.
“We view community engagement as essential and want to be fully engaged with the town long before we file for 248 — because we’re not going to file for 248, which is the statewide regulations for siting, if the town’s not in agreement with what we’re doing,” Hitt added.
Audience members raised concerns about the project’s potential use of river water for cooling, the risk of airborne toxins during a fire, and possible costs to the town if increased staffing, such as for the fire department, would become necessary.
Engineer and consultant Derek Porter explained that the battery energy storage system cooling uses a closed-loop system and therefore would not require water from the nearby Connecticut River.
Fire and battery safety expert Rocky Edwards told the audience that battery storage and fire-suppression technology have improved and that they have more safety features than current facilities do.
Recent fires at battery storage installations include two facilities in California: Moss Landing in 2025, a three-day blaze that caused $400 million of damage, and this year in La Verne, where a lithium-ion battery fire caused more than 500 residents to evacuate their homes, schools and businesses for days.
Community gives more feedback
Hitt said PowerTransitions decided not to pursue solar or data center projects after evaluating feedback from town officials and from those who attended an August community meeting.
Several audience members said they would prefer solar over a battery installation.
Hitt said the company is still investigating and will continue to seek community input before deciding the nature of the project and finalizing a design.
If a project moves forward, construction would begin in three to five years, she said.
The battery project would likely serve as an initial phase while the company develops a larger energy generation project for the site, Hitt said.
Hitt told the audience that PowerTransitions plans to hold additional community meetings. She emphasized that Vernon residents know the area best and understand what they want to protect — such as the Connecticut River.
“We’re just here sharing information because we’re trying to move through the process and see what the questions are, where the concerns are,” she said. “We’re trying to get that feedback from all of you so that we can put a plan together.”

name: WyoFile
title: Fremont County avoids EMT strike after extending contract
description:
The new two-year deal buys time to shift first-responder services under local government control while addressing employee needs, parties say.
The post Fremont County avoids EMT strike after extending contract appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
The union representing 30 emergency medical technicians and paramedics serving Fremont County cancelled plans to strike later this week after the county extended its contract with their employer as a stop-gap measure.
Organized under United Steel Workers Local 9012, the first-responders originally planned to walk out Monday and then postponed the strike to Thursday. The union officially stood down Wednesday, however, a day after Fremont County commissioners inked a new two-year contract with the bargaining group’s employer, Tennessee-based Priority Ambulance, which operates as Frontier Ambulance in the county.
Although the new contract includes a series of raises for the workers and an increase to their health savings account, “It was never about money,” United Steel Workers Staff Representative William Wilkinson told WyoFile. “It was about the safety of this community.”
Fremont County was paying Priority $1.9 million annually. Under the new contract, the county will pay about $2.3 million the first year and $2.4 million the second year, according to Fremont County Commissioner Mike Jones, who helped negotiate the contract. Those totals include a 5% salary increase for EMTs the first year and 4% the second year.
Nobody is 100% satisfied with the deal, Jones told WyoFile, “But at the end of the day, I think you hold to the faith that everybody wants ambulance service to continue on Oct. 1.” 
Messy negotiations
Normally, the union negotiates directly with the employer, Priority, and the county negotiates separately with Priority on its contract. But those independent negotiations became complicated because the county and the first responders share a common goal to eventually end their relationships with Priority and move the service under local government control.
The commission earlier this year signed a memorandum of understanding with towns in the county to shift EMT services under the Fremont County Association of Governments — a move that would better serve everyone, including tribal governments and the first responders, according to both county and union representatives who spoke with WyoFile. To help pay for it, Fremont County voters passed a ¾-cent sales tax in August.
Revenue from the new tax won’t begin arriving until the spring, however, and the county’s contract with Priority was set to expire Oct. 1. The separate negotiations both went sideways. The county wanted a short-term contract with Priority to fill the gap until the association can take over, and the union workers, Wilkinson said, found it difficult to gain traction on their interests.
A paramedic loads a gurney into an ambulance at Cody Regional Health. (Madelyn Beck/WyoFile) 
In the maw of fraught bargaining and positioning, commissioners flirted with an offer from Cody Regional Health to fill the gap. That angered first responders because, among other things, the proposed arrangement would not allow them to continue with union representation. Local 9012 promised to strike. 
But with the contract set to expire and the threat of a strike looming, all three parties found themselves at the negotiating table.
“Since it was down to the wire, it was really a three-party deal,” Wilkinson said.
The union is generally pleased with the outcome, he added, because it’s a nod from the county that the EMTs can maintain union bargaining power — a necessity given that first responders in Fremont County have continuously had to work long hours due to insufficient staffing. Plus, both Wilkinson and Jones agreed, the new two-year contract buys time for the Fremont County Association of Governments to prepare to take on the service. Doing so requires obtaining multiple certifications, as well as training and infrastructure for the nuts-and-bolts of managing the business side of EMT services — from scheduling shifts to bidding for equipment and supplies.
“You need administration — you need all kinds of stuff that you just can’t do overnight,” Wilkinson said.
The higher dollar figures under the new Priority contract have already raised some eyebrows, Jones said. Some of it can be chalked up to folding in some costs that were already coming back to the county and other entities under the old contract, he said. Other factors are simply the rising cost of providing the service.
“Yes, it’s an increase,” Jones said. “But, you know, fuel costs have gone up. Everything’s gone up. It’s inflationary.”

name: Georgia Recorder
title: DOJ lawsuit seeking Georgia voters’ unredacted data dismissed, again
description: For the second time, a federal judge in Georgia has dismissed a lawsuit from U.S. Department of Justice officials seeking access to sensitive voter data. Federal judge tosses out DOJ lawsuit seeking sensitive voter data in Georgia Federal officials have been demanding that state officials turn over Georgia voters’ personal data — including the Social […]
text:
Northern District Judge Victoria M. Calvert tossed the U.S. Department of Justice's second lawsuit seeking access to sensitive voter data. Jill Nolin/Georgia RecorderFor the second time, a federal judge in Georgia has dismissed a lawsuit from U.S. Department of Justice officials seeking access to sensitive voter data.
Federal judge tosses out DOJ lawsuit seeking sensitive voter data in Georgia

Federal officials have been demanding that state officials turn over Georgia voters’ personal data — including the Social Security numbers, full dates of birth and driver’s license numbers — since 2025, arguing the information was needed as part of an ongoing investigation into “Georgia’s compliance with federal election law.” 
But in a Wednesday ruling, Northern District Judge Victoria M. Calvert said neither law cited in the Justice Department’s lawsuit required states to disclose sensitive information to the federal government and that Georgia Secretary of State Brad Raffensperger had proven he was able to comply with federal voter maintenance laws without providing the unredacted information.
“The Court is not persuaded by any of Plaintiff’s arguments,” she wrote.
Secretary of State Brad Raffensperger. Maya Homan/Georgia Recorder
Raffensperger celebrated Calvert’s dismissal of the case.
“Georgia has worked with our federal partners and will continue to do so, but cooperation does not mean ignoring the law or surrendering the privacy rights of Georgia voters,” he said in a statement. “We stood our ground because the law was clear, and we are thankful the Court agreed.”
Justice Department officials have also lost in 25 other cases seeking states’ unredacted voter roll data across the country. Kiersten Pels, a press secretary for the Department of Justice, said the department is reviewing the decision and will most likely file an appeal.
Since last year, federal officials have been seeking access to the unredacted data of all registered voters in Georgia. In January, Judge C. Ashley Royal dismissed the Justice Department’s first lawsuit against Raffensperger because the case was filed in Georgia’s Macon-based Middle District court, which is not where the records were located. Less than a week later, federal officials re-filed their suit in Georgia’s Northern District, which covers the secretary of state’s Atlanta office.
Raffensperger, a Republican, had previously sent redacted voter registration data to Justice Department officials, but he argued that state law prohibited his office from divulging all the data requested. He also rebuffed a pressure campaign from some state lawmakers and members of Georgia’s State Election Board urging him to turn over the data.

name: Washington State Standard
title: Legislative staff in WA state Senate reject new contract
description: The union representing staff of Democratic state senators in Washington has overwhelmingly rejected a new two-year contract, citing its lack of adequate protections for workers facing termination. Legislative assistants, policy analysts and communications specialists for the Senate Democratic Caucus on Monday voted down the final offer from negotiators for t[...]
text:
The Senate chambers at the Washington state Capitol. (Photo courtesy of Legislative Support Services)The union representing staff of Democratic state senators in Washington has overwhelmingly rejected a new two-year contract, citing its lack of adequate protections for workers facing termination.
Legislative assistants, policy analysts and communications specialists for the Senate Democratic Caucus on Monday voted down the final offer from negotiators for the Senate Administration. The employees are represented by the Washington Public Employees Association.
The rejected deal contained no pay hike, only a provision to renew talks on wages next August, mirroring language in collective bargaining agreements with most other public sector unions amid state budget struggles.
But the lack of a raise wasn’t the sticking point for those who work for the Senate’s majority party.
Their concern centered on job security. Legislative staff are at-will employees, meaning they can be fired at any time. The union sought language to ensure there is a just cause for a dismissal. Negotiators for the administration wouldn’t budge on various proposals employees put forth, union officials said.
“Our fight is not with the electeds, it is with the administration,” stressed Sam Hines-Tinsley, legislative specialist for the union. “Members of our bargaining team made it clear that they were looking for fundamental change and for fair, reasonable and predictable treatment when it comes to discipline.”	


Need to get in touch?
Have a news tip?


CONTACT US




Jeremy Knapp, a Senate legislative assistant, said in a statement that his colleagues know “we can be let go for no reason, and while we know we may not get economic security, we need more job security. All we’re asking for is the same due process that almost every represented public sector worker in Washington has.”
Officials from the Senate Administration did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
State law sets an Oct. 1 deadline for public worker unions to submit ratified agreements to the Office of Financial Management to be considered for funding in the next two-year budget.
For Senate employees, their decision Monday means that when the current contract expires next July, most of its provisions will be extended until a new collective bargaining agreement is ratified.
Their counterparts working for the House Democratic Caucus could be in a similar situation within hours as they were still locked in contract talks Wednesday afternoon.
In contrast, the legislative assistants in the House and Senate Republican caucuses have approved their respective two-year agreements.
“Under the circumstances, given the position the state is in, we were OK with what was presented,” said Rob Barnes, president of the Legislative Professionals Association that represents the aides to Republican lawmakers in each chamber.
Last Friday, members of the Washington Federation of State Employees, the largest union of state government workers, ratified their two-year contract after months of tense talks and informational picketing. 
Federation units representing workers in community colleges, universities and administrative law judges also approved their contracts.
Earlier this week, the Washington Public Employees Association reported its units representing around 5,300 general government and community college employees had narrowly voted to approve new collective bargaining agreements. These cover workers at 14 community colleges and nine state agencies, including the Department of Natural Resources, Department of Revenue, the Liquor and Cannabis Board and Department of Agriculture.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.

title: Former US Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice says humility key to democracy
description: Humility, listening and serving others are important pieces of democracy, former U.S. Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice said Wednesday during a lecture at Bentonville’s Crystal Bridges Museum of American Art.  “The American spirit means to me that we don’t wait on our government to deliver for us, that we deliver for one another,” Rice said. […]
text:
Former U.S. Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice spoke with  Olivia Walton, Crystal Bridges Museum of American Art board chair, during a lecture at the Bentonville museum on Sept. 30, 2026. (Photo by Antoinette Grajeda/Arkansas Advocate)Humility, listening and serving others are important pieces of democracy, former U.S. Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice said Wednesday during a lecture at Bentonville’s Crystal Bridges Museum of American Art. 
“The American spirit means to me that we don’t wait on our government to deliver for us, that we deliver for one another,” Rice said. “I think the highest form of democracy is actually individual citizens delivering for individual citizens.”
Museum board chair Olivia Walton led the conversation, which was part of the museum’s Building Bridges lecture series that “brings together thought leaders, thinkers, and artists to model civic dialogue,” according to a press release. 
Past speakers have included President Barack Obama, Supreme Court Justice Amy Coney Barrett and documentary filmmaker Ken Burns.
Obama tells Arkansas audience young people give him hope for US democracy

During her nearly hourlong speech, Rice didn’t mention President Donald Trump or his foreign policy. The president has faced criticism that his policies, including tariffs and the war against Iran, have alienated U.S. allies. 
As a member of President George H.W. Bush’s National Security Council staff, Rice witnessed the fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989 and said the president’s reaction to the event was a lesson in humility. When advised to go to Germany to mark the occasion, Bush responded that it was a German moment, not an American one.
At Bush’s funeral in 2018, Rice said German Chancellor Angela Merkel said her country would have never unified without him. 
“I learned a lot at the time, that moment about grace,” Rice said.
From 2005 to 2009, Rice negotiated with world leaders as President George W. Bush’s secretary of state. She was the second woman and first Black woman to hold the position. She was also Bush’s national security adviser from 2001 to 2005, the first woman to serve in the role.
The ability to listen instead of always speaking first makes a good diplomat, Rice said. That lesson, which Rice learned from her father, was particularly important as a representative of a powerful country like the United States, she said.
“If you speak first, you can shut that room down in no time…I think it’s a really important thing to practice in diplomacy,” she said. “It’s also kind of an important thing to practice in life.” 
The Sept. 11 terrorist attacks occurred during Rice’s time as secretary of state and how Americans worked together in response showed “what the soul of America could be,” she said. 
Rice doesn’t blame social media for creating a more divisive country in the years since the attacks, but she said it has created a world where people can choose to only consume information that reinforces their beliefs.
“We’ve stopped listening to each other, we’ve stopped talking across differences,” she said. 
As a political science professor, Rice has served on the faculty of Stanford University since 1981 and said her students give her hope about the nation’s democracy because they’re “the most public-minded generation” she’s ever taught. 
For people looking to take action, Rice said they should do just one thing for somebody else because they’ll never be aggrieved and they’ll never be entitled. 
“And democracy’s best when its citizens are neither aggrieved nor entitled,” she said.

title: A power boom in eastern South Dakota raises questions about what comes next

text:
An image from the PowerOn Midwest website illustrates the dimensions of structures that would support a proposed 765-kilovot transmission line. (Photo by South Dakota Searchlight)Eastern South Dakota could soon host the largest transmission project in the state’s history. South Dakota’s first 765-kilovolt line would run through Grant, Deuel and Brookings counties.
The larger story is what could follow it.
South Dakota’s largest existing transmission lines operate at 345 kilovolts. The proposed 765-kilovolt line is the electrical equivalent of replacing a rural highway with a six-lane interstate.
One line this large can move more electricity in either direction with lower losses and less land than several smaller corridors.
160 miles of transmission lines planned for eastern SD, costing upward of $2 billion

The line would begin at Big Stone South near Big Stone City, travel south to a substation near White and turn east toward Lakefield, Minnesota. From there, the regional network reaches toward Iowa, Rochester and the Twin Cities.
Big Stone South already connects to Ellendale, North Dakota. Approved and proposed projects would extend that network toward Jamestown and Fargo and toward Alexandria, Minnesota.
The northbound Big Stone South-Hankinson-Bison line is part of a joint effort by the Midcontinent Independent System Operator, known as MISO, and the Southwest Power Pool, the neighboring grid operator.
Essentially, eastern South Dakota is becoming a bridge between two enormous regional power systems.
The focal point is Big Stone South, a switching station near the Big Stone coal plant. The station could remain important whether the plant operates for decades or eventually closes. The grid is being built around a hub, not one generator.
Utilities say the network is needed as older plants retire, electricity comes from more scattered sources, and extreme weather increases the value of alternative routes.
MISO is overseeing a $21.8 billion rebuilding of the Upper Midwest transmission system.
MISO says utilities are experiencing an unprecedented surge of requests from data centers, advanced manufacturing and other electricity-hungry industries. Many want power within 18 to 36 months.
South Dakota’s 765-kilovolt line isn’t expected to enter service until 2034 but could influence where power generation and industry locate for decades.
At Ellendale, Applied Digital is developing an artificial-intelligence campus whose initial 400-megawatt demand and potential 1,000-megawatt expansion would approach three times the generating capacity of the 475-megawatt Big Stone coal plant.
Producing that much electricity from wind over a year would require the output of roughly 875 turbines — more than the roughly 720 now operating or approved across northeastern South Dakota’s wind corridor.
Wind couldn’t provide that electricity every hour. Storage, natural gas or other dependable generation would also be needed.
Other large data centers are proposed near Fargo, Sioux Falls and across Minnesota, including Google’s Project Skyway near Rochester.
Neither Ellendale nor the Minnesota project caused the 765-kilovolt line, according to the utilities. That’s one of the most interesting parts of the story.
Engineers concluded this exceptionally large transmission network was needed before much of the data-center boom entered their forecasts.
Now those customers are arriving.
Google and Xcel Energy, for example, have proposed wind, solar and battery storage to help serve the Minnesota development.
The Northern Border natural-gas pipeline also crosses northeastern South Dakota. The Astoria gas plant in Deuel County was built where that pipeline intersects the Big Stone South-to-Brookings transmission corridor.


Let us know what you think...


 

Eastern South Dakota has wind, a major natural-gas pipeline, increasingly powerful transmission lines and access to two regional grids. Now some of the largest electricity customers ever contemplated on the Northern Plains are looking for places to plug in.
None of that guarantees another gas plant, more wind farms, batteries, data centers or factories.
But anyone who has watched development follow a highway interchange understands the principle. Once an interstate arrives in the neighborhood, the neighborhood seldom remains the same.
Electricity works much the same way.
Natural-gas developers need fuel and transmission. Wind, solar and battery developers need the grid. Large industries need enormous quantities of dependable electricity. A 765-kilovolt electrical interstate changes what is possible.
That could mean landowner income, construction activity, investment and additional tax base. It could also sharpen conflicts over agricultural land, rural housing, lighting, traffic and demands on local government.
For most of our history, South Dakota’s place in the power system has been defined by what we produced: Missouri River hydropower, coal-generated electricity, wind and some solar.
Something different is taking shape now.
An electrical interstate, a natural-gas pipeline, immense new customers and several forms of power generation are converging in the same rural corridor.
The new transmission line won’t determine what comes next. Farmers will still own much of the land. Counties will still make land-use decisions. Developers will still have to decide whether projects make economic sense.
But like a new highway interchange, the line creates opportunities that didn’t exist before — and intensifies competition over how the surrounding land should be used.
The towers may be only the first visible sign.

title: Court orders Dairy Farmers of America to keep paying its share of union employees’ health insurance after shuttering the St. Albans Creamery
description:
The Monday decision requires payments to continue as a dispute between the union and the co-op over the reasons for the plant's closure plays out.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Court orders Dairy Farmers of America to keep paying its share of union employees’ health insurance after shuttering the St. Albans Creamery.
text:
Members of the Teamsters local 597 union picket outside the Dairy Farmers of America plant in St. Albans on Tuesday, September 30, 2025. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

A U.S. District Court judge has mandated that Dairy Farmers of America keep contributing its portion of the union workers’ health insurance after idling the St. Albans Creamery plant in August.
The employees at the plant, which is a subsidiary of the Dairy Farmers of America co-operative, have been out of work since the plant closed on Aug. 17, and the portion of their health insurance covered by DFA was set to expire at the end of this month.
“That takes a big load off a lot of their minds,” said Curtis Clough, president of the union representing about 80 workers, Teamsters Local 597.
The union claimed DFA closed the St. Albans dairy plant in retaliation for union activity, including a strike which took place late last year. The co-op denied that assertion, describing the plant as unviable, and labeling the closure a private-sector business decision. 
DFA intended to stop paying its portion of the workers’ health insurance plans, which was about 85%, according to court documents. Nearly all the employees and many of their families are covered by the plan, according to the court filing.
Workers said they were paying about $80 per week for their insurance, and many said they would not be able to afford insurance without DFA’s contribution, according to court documents.
Several workers also have pressing medical issues and prescriptions that would cost thousands of dollars, according to the union.
Lawyers representing the union filed for an injunction with the court last week, asking the court to require DFA to continue paying its portion.
Teamsters attorney Jason Vazquez called U.S. District Court Judge William K. Sessions III’s decision on Monday a big win for the union.
“It’s very exciting and, most importantly, we’re very happy that the group’s insurance will be protected… for the next few months, or however long it takes for us to resolve this dispute with the company,” he said.
In his decision, Sessions cited the potential for irreparable harm to the workers.
“The declarations submitted by Plaintiff, including those employees who have secured new employment but whose access to new coverage will be delayed, illustrate the hardships employees will suffer,” he wrote. “For those employees, the emotional and physical harms resulting from a lack of insurance would be beyond the arbitrator’s ability to remedy.”
This latest filing comes in a series of legal actions taken by the union, which alleges DFA illegally retaliated by closing the plant after the union went on strike late last year. The union secured a temporary restraining order to stop DFA from making irreversible changes to the plant, like selling it. The union argues that, because the parties haven’t gone through arbitration, the plant should remain in a condition that would allow it to reopen.
The court vacated the restraining order once DFA agreed it would not take any more steps to further close the plant and would expedite arbitration proceedings to determine if DFA indeed closed the plant in retaliation for union activities.
The two sides have not set a date for arbitration, which is a separate process from the court’s proceedings. The union’s request to expedite the arbitration process was denied by the courts, but both parties have agreed on an arbitrator, according to Vazquez. He said they will start working to schedule arbitration as early as this week.
“We are ready to arbitrate,” Clough said. “We can arbitrate tomorrow.”
Vazquez said members of the union and their lawyers will meet with DFA Thursday to continue bargaining over a potential severance package for the workers.
DFA officials had not responded to VTDigger’s request for comment as of Wednesday afternoon.

title: US Senate Dems block bill curbing congressional stock trading, calling it too weak
text: WASHINGTON — U.S. Senate Republicans did not gain any support Wednesday from Democrats as they attempted to advance a bill that mashed together two hot-button midterm issues: requiring voter ID in federal elections and limiting stock trading for members of Congress.The Republican-led bill, titled the Stop Insider Trading Act, failed 53-47 when lawmakers stayed solidly within party lines for the procedural vote. Most legislation requires 60 votes, or three-fifths of the Senate, to advance.The House-passed measure attached a voter ID requirement onto a base bill prohibiting members of Congress and their spouses and close family members from purchasing certain stocks, and requiring a public notice and waiting period prior to selling stocks. House lawmakers approved the legislative package by a 232-192 margin.While 13 House Democrats supported the bill, sponsored by Rep. Bryan Steil, R-Wis., despite plenty of criticism, Senate Democrats did not bite.“The Senate GOP let their counterparts in the House take out all of the ban’s teeth and fill it with poison pills so it could never pass. This bill has no reform, no accountability, no substance,” Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., said on the Senate floor prior to the vote Wednesday.House and Senate Democrats panned the legislation for being a weaker version of other bipartisan bills aimed at stopping members of Congress from potentially profiting off insider knowledge while trading stocks. The issue has drawn support from both parties over the past several years.“Under (the) Republican bill, members would still get to own and sell stocks. And most importantly, this bill doesn’t do anything – anything – to stop Donald Trump from trading stocks. I guess Republicans forgot that Trump has made nearly 30,000 stock trades in the past year and raked in billions – more than all of Congress combined,” Schumer continued.The New York Democrat also said the measure “would make voting more difficult in every state than it is now” and described it as “some of the most twisted, radical schemes Trump has ever dreamed up to rig our election.”ID for votingUnder the measure, a voter would be required to present a current state-issued driver’s license or identification card, passport, valid military or veteran ID, or tribal government-issued ID card to be able to vote. If a voter doesn’t have one of the listed physical forms of identification, state election officials could issue a provisional ballot. The voter would then have three days to provide the accepted ID or an affidavit that the voter doesn’t have one because of religious objections to being photographed.Additionally, state officials would be prohibited from accepting absentee ballots unless the voter attaches a copy of a valid ID, the last four digits of their Social Security number with an affidavit that they cannot obtain a photo ID, or a notarized statement that the voter personally completed their ballot.‘Commonsense legislation’Senate Republicans pushed for the bill ahead of the vote, including Nebraska Republican Sen. Pete Ricketts, who posted Monday on X, “This bill would ban congressional insider trading. We need to pass this commonsense legislation and restore integrity to Congress.” Sen. Mike Lee, R-Utah, pointed to a Department of Justice indictment announced Wednesday to argue in support of the legislation.Quoting a post on social media about DOJ allegations that 10 noncitizens voted in a previous election, Lee wrote: “Every Senate Democrat just voted against legislation that would stop this.”While the DOJ has alleged instances of isolated election-related crimes, widespread voter fraud has never been credibly proven. A database published in 2024 by the right-leaning Heritage Foundation surveying millions of votes cast in seven states over decades found reported cases of fraud to be less than 1%, according to an analysis of the results by the progressive Brookings Institution.A comprehensive body of research has found the practice to be exceedingly rare.

name: VTDigger
title: Putney affordable housing project opens after clearing court battles
description:
The price tag for the apartment complex ballooned by nearly 50% over the course of its development, including two years of legal disputes involving neighbors.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Putney affordable housing project opens after clearing court battles.
text:
Developers held a ribbon cutting event for a new affordable housing project in Putney on September 30, 2026. Photo by Carly Berlin/Vermont Public

Carly Berlin covers housing and infrastructure for Vermont Public, in partnership with VTDigger. 
When Stormy Gammon got the call that she and her family had been approved for an apartment at a new affordable housing complex in Putney, she cried. 
Gammon, her husband, and their son had been homeless, living in a shelter unit in Springfield, she said. For a long time, she had felt drawn to Putney: The natural beauty of the small town near Vermont’s southeastern corner had a sort of magic. They moved into their new home over the summer, right next door to a community garden lined by sunflowers. 
“Every day when I pick my son up from school, I go out there, I touch the grass,” Gammon said. “I’m just so happy, so happy to be here.”
Gammon and her family are one of 25 households now residing at the Alice Holway Drive Apartments, a project that was delayed by years of legal opposition from neighbors and became something of a poster-child for how a few people can hold up widely-supported new housing projects in Vermont.

Stormy Gammon, a new resident of the Alice Holway Drive Apartments in Putney, poses for a portrait on September 30, 2026. Photo by Carly Berlin/Vermont Public

Regional and local plans had long identified the site as a good spot for new housing. It’s near the town’s co-op and library and was once part of famed Vermont politician George Aiken’s wildflower nursery. Windham and Windsor Housing Trust began envisioning plans for apartments on Alice Holway Drive seven years ago. 
But soon after the housing trust and co-developer Evernorth secured their first permit, a single neighbor appealed. That became the first of four legal challenges over the course of two years.
Neighbors’ concerns included impacts on traffic, the town’s shortage of social services, and a perceived lack of public engagement by the developers and the town as the project came together. Some nearby residents wanted to see the site preserved as a park and worried about disruptions from new neighbors. Courts sided with the developers in each case, and cleared the way for the project to proceed in late 2024.
The project’s price tag ballooned by nearly 50% since its outset, from $10.3 million to $15.3 million, said Elizabeth Bridgewater, executive director of Windham and Windsor Housing Trust.
The Putney Community Garden next to the new Alice Holway Drive Apartments on September 30, 2026. Photo by Carly Berlin/Vermont Public
Even as the housing trust tweaked its designs to save money, interest rates and construction costs escalated while the project stalled. The developers spent $85,000 on legal fees to fight the appeals, she said.
“It’s not right that one person can derail the sentiment of the whole community,” Bridgewater said.
For years, legislators and housing officials have eyed policies to rein in when and how neighbors can challenge new housing, from moving appeals out of the courtroom to attempts to limit who can launch an appeal. But they’ve yet to agree on the best approach. Heading into a new legislative session, lawmakers are considering the concept of “model codes” or “by-right zoning” that attempts to streamline the permitting process and get around project-by-project fights.
The new Alice Holway Drive Apartments are highly energy-efficient, using ground-source heat pumps and solar panels. Five of the apartments were set aside for households experiencing or at risk of homelessness, and Southeast Vermont Community Action provides services on-site. 
Funding came from federal Low Income Housing Tax Credits administered by the Vermont Housing Finance Agency, pandemic-era federal relief funds awarded by the Vermont Housing and Conservation Board, and a low-interest loan from the Vermont Treasurer’s Office, among other sources.
A 2025 town housing assessment found that Putney needed to add 80 new housing units — 44 homeowner and 36 rental units — by the end of the decade to meet the community’s needs.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico governor’s office releases up to $3.75M in emergency response to flooding
description: Flooding across New Mexico prompted state officials Wednesday to release up to $3.75 million in emergency funds aimed at helping communities respond to and prevent damage.
text:
Widespread flooding in New Mexico prompted state officials on Sept. 30, 2026, to authorize $3.75 million in emergency spending. Above: Flooding in Hondo in Lincoln County on Sept. 25, 2026. (Photo courtesy New Mexico National Guard)
Flooding across New Mexico prompted state officials Wednesday to release up to $3.75 million in emergency funds aimed at helping communities respond to and prevent damage. 
Lt. Gov. Howie Morales, who is serving as acting governor while Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham is out of state, issued five executive orders, each authorizing $750,000, for the state Department of Homeland Security and Emergency Management. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“Communities across New Mexico need help staving off these torrential floodwaters, and they need it now,” Morales said in a statement Wednesday. 
Above average late-monsoon moisture has caused widespread floods. Over the last week, a National Weather Service database shows more than 80 reports of flood events in 14 counties, particularly those in southern New Mexico. 
Flooding made numerous roads across the region impassable and even temporarily stranded a school bus in Lincoln County, according to the NWS database. Tuesday evening, Doña Ana County temporarily evacuated Rincon, Salem & Garfield in response to flooding and concerns about McLeod Dam. In Santa Fe County, officials set up a phone number for residents stranded due to closed roads.
Water also apparently breached the main gas line in Hatch, prompting the local police department to issue a warning on social media Wednesday afternoon not to “put gas” at pumps in the southern New Mexico town. 
“The main gasoline line has been breached by water,” the police department wrote. “The gasoline is now mostly water and will damage your vehicle.” 
A spokesperson for the Hatch Police Department did not immediately respond to Source NM’s request for further comment Wednesday.
Elsewhere, drainage pumps in Luna County were overwhelmed. Up to two feet of flowing water was reported in Socorro County; and “curb-to-curb” street flooding was reported in Artesia, according to the NWS database. 
The governor’s office said the floods have damaged public infrastructure, disrupted transportation routes and threatened homes and businesses. 
Officials noted that, with more rain in the forecast, local emergency response agencies might become overwhelmed, which is why the state funds are necessary. 
As of publication Wednesday afternoon, NWS forecasters had issued a “flood watch” for most of northern New Mexico, warning that risks of additional flooding persist through midnight Wednesday due to a surge of moisture that will fall on “already rain-soaked soil” and potentially cause additional floods.
The NWS also issued flood warnings through 6 p.m. Wednesday for parts of San Miguel, Santa Fe and Lincoln counties. 
The executive orders do not specify exactly what the funding will be used for but notes that it “may” be used to provide people with shelter, healthcare, food and transportation. 
“The State of New Mexico stands with every county, city and village working around the clock to keep their neighbors safe, and we are bringing every resource to the effort,” Morales said. 
Leah March, a spokesperson for the governor’s office, did not immediately respond to Source NM’s question about Lujan Grisham’s whereabouts, but she was scheduled to speak in Washington, D.C., on Thursday alongside Center For American Progress CEO Neera Tanden in a conversation about tackling the “biggest challenges facing America today, like healthcare, childcare, and housing access,” according to a news release.

title: Public hearings scheduled for Nebraska’s three 2026 voter-led ballot measures
description: LINCOLN — The Nebraska Secretary of State’s Office has scheduled a series of hearings in each of Nebraska’s three congressional districts to let the public weigh in on three ballot measures before the Nov. 3 general election. State law requires the office to host public hearings in each of Nebraska’s three congressional districts on all […]
text:
Nebraskans fill a hearing room in September 2025 to weigh in on a state-federal plan to convert a Nebraska prison into an immigration detention facility. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — The Nebraska Secretary of State’s Office has scheduled a series of hearings in each of Nebraska’s three congressional districts to let the public weigh in on three ballot measures before the Nov. 3 general election.
State law requires the office to host public hearings in each of Nebraska’s three congressional districts on all voter-led ballot initiatives on the November ballot. One measure this year seeks a constitutional amendment for sex-based requirements for K-12 and collegiate sports. Two more proposals would together legalize and regulate online sports betting.
The two sports betting measures will be part of a combined hearing. 
Secretary of State Bob Evnen’s office has prepared information pamphlets with the specific ballot language for each ballot measure and common arguments for and against. The information is available online in English and Spanish.
A separate constitutional amendment related to legislative term limits, Constitutional Amendment 1, will not be part of the hearing schedule.
Lawmakers in 2025 advanced the issue to voters to ask whether lawmakers should be able to serve up to three consecutive four-year terms, instead of two terms. The measure received a hearing during the legislative process in Lincoln. State law does not require separate hearings in other parts of the state for legislative-led ballot questions.
The hearing schedule:
1st Congressional District
Location: Nebraska State Capitol Room 1525, 1445 K St., Lincoln
Wednesday, Oct. 14

6-9 p.m. CDT, sex-based K-12 and collegiate sports constitutional requirements (Initiative Measure 442)

Thursday, Oct. 15

6-9 p.m. CDT, online sports wagering legalization and authorization measure (Initiative Measures 440 and 441)

2nd Congressional District
Location: Omaha Public Library’s Millard Branch Meeting Room 1, 13214 Westwood Lane, Omaha
Saturday, Oct. 24

10 a.m.-1 p.m. CDT, sex-based K-12 and collegiate sports constitutional requirements
1:30-4:30 p.m. CDT, online sports wagering legalization and authorization measure

3rd Congressional District
Location: Buffalo County Extension Building Bison Room, 1400 E. 34th St., Kearney
Thursday, Oct. 22

2-5 p.m. CDT, online sports wagering legalization and authorization measure
6-9 p.m. CDT, sex-based K-12 and collegiate sports constitutional requirements

2026 ballot measures
Three voter-initiated measures will appear on the Nov. 3 ballot:

Legalize online sports betting — Legalize online sports betting if conducted through vendors at Nebraska’s six licensed racetracks, in Grand Island, Ogallala, Lincoln, Omaha, Columbus and South Sioux City. (Initiative Measure 440)
Regulate online sports betting — Define online sports betting and require the Nebraska Racing and Gaming Commission to adopt any needed regulations, no later than June 1, 2027. (Initiative Measure 441)
Sex-separate requirements for K-12, collegiate sports — Make permanent part of a 2025 state law requiring public K-12 schools, colleges and universities, and any private schools or colleges in the state playing against those schools, to designate sports and athletic teams as male, female or coed. The ballot measure itself would not additionally define “sex,” instead relying on the 2025 law. (Initiative Measure 442)

More information on each ballot question for the 2026 election is available through the Nebraska Examiner’s 2026 General Election Voter Guide.
The general election is Nov. 3.

title: Slotkin, bipartisan group of lawmakers introduce bill to improve ovarian cancer prevention and care
description: U.S. Sen. Elissa Slotkin introduced legislation in Congress to expand access to ovarian cancer prevention and care, including expanding access to genetic counseling and testing, improving hereditary cancer risk assessment, strengthening cancer education, and helping patients connect with specialized gynecologic oncology care. The bill, cosponsored by Republi[...]
text:
U.S. Sen. Elissa Slotkin speaks during the Michigan Democratic Party Legacy Dinner in Detroit, Mich., on April 18, 2026. (Photo by Andrew Roth/Michigan Advance)U.S. Sen. Elissa Slotkin introduced legislation in Congress to expand access to ovarian cancer prevention and care, including expanding access to genetic counseling and testing, improving hereditary cancer risk assessment, strengthening cancer education, and helping patients connect with specialized gynecologic oncology care.
The bill, cosponsored by Republican Sen. Katie Britt of Alabama, was introduced on Sept. 24 and referred to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions. A counterpart bill in the House was introduced by Connecticut Democratic Rep. Rosa DeLauro and Nebraska Republican Rep. Don Bacon. 
“No family should have to fight both a cancer diagnosis and their insurance company at the same time,” Slotkin said in a press release. “Women, especially in rural communities like Michigan, should be able to get the genetic testing and specialty care they need to catch this disease early or prevent it altogether. Our bill tackles this issue from every angle — awareness, outreach and access to care and testing — and I thank my colleagues from across the aisle as we all work to save lives.” 
The bill, known as the “Ovarian Cancer Improving and Modernizing Prevention, Access, Care, and Testing Act,” would expand access to gynecologic oncology specialists in rural and medically underserved communities, including through telehealth, as well as prioritizing grants focused on rural, underserved and high-risk communities.
Slotkin also noted her own personal connection to the legislation, having lost her mother to ovarian cancer at 64 and her grandmother to the disease at just 39
A press release from Slotkin’s office notes that ovarian cancer is the fifth-leading cause of cancer deaths among women in the United States. When caught early, the five-year survival rate for the disease is over 90%, but most cases are only detected after the disease has reached an advanced stage. 
“We have an evidence-based strategy to reduce ovarian cancer risk and save lives with salpingectomy but need solutions to remove barriers to this care,” said Dr. Sandra E. Brooks, CEO of the American College of Obstetricians & Gynecologists, referring to the procedure which removes the fallopian tubes. “ACOG is proud to endorse the Ovarian Cancer IMPACT Act, which would expand awareness of and access to evidence-based prevention strategies, helping spare more patients and families from the devastating burden of ovarian cancer.”
