name: Mississippi Today
title: $6B data center planned for Jefferson Davis, one of the poorest counties in the country
description: Rep. Jill Ford, a Republican from Madison, signs an Amazon beam during an announcement about an Amazon data center in Ridgeland on Thursday, April 9, 2026.
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
A $6 billion data center is being planned for Jefferson Davis County. 
The developer, Eagle Rock Partners, hosted an informational meeting on Tuesday to talk with people about their concerns and answer questions about the project, which is called the Big Woods Technology Park. Construction could begin as early as 2027.
“Get informed. Get answers – straight from the people who know,” read a flyer for the meeting in Bassfield.
READ MORE: Your questions about Mississippi data centers, answered
Eagle Rock Partners told Mississippi Today that the company is in the design stage and is working on submissions. It is proposing a three-building complex that will be around 2 million square feet and said it will not request abatements or incentives. The company expects the project to create 200 permanent jobs and over 1,000 temporary construction jobs.
“Eagle Rock looks forward to creating new opportunities in Jefferson Davis County and creating resources for them to continue the ‘Mississippi miracle’ for their community,” the company said. 
Gary Russell Bass, director of the Jefferson Davis County Economic Development Association, said residents can go to a website the developer has set up to find answers about the project. Bass said he wants the project to be transparent to the public and be a model for how to develop a data center well. 
The website for the Big Woods Technology Park says the data center would use a closed loop cooling system to consume minimal water and use natural gas generation located on site that will need to be approved by the Mississippi Department of Environmental Quality before operation.
The site is on private property, and Jefferson Davis County does not have zoning, which means that the developer has more leeway to build what it wants. 
WDAM reported that some residents expressed concerns at Tuesday’s meeting over water usage, utility rate hikes, noise and opportunities for community feedback. 
Bass said that he did not seek out a data center, rather the developer approached him. When he first met with the developers, he said he shared many of residents’ apprehensions but, through conversations and due diligence, many of his concerns about water usage and electricity were addressed. 
He said the project is in an isolated part of the county, away from homes and that the Board of Supervisors is working on agreements between the county and the developer to make sure residents will have the best possible outcomes. 
Jefferson Davis is one of the poorest counties in the country with a population of about 11,000 that has declined in recent years. Bass said the jobs, investment and expected tax revenue from the data center “could completely transform this county.” 
Eagle Rock Partners is developing data centers in Georgia and South Carolina, and recently it canceled plans to build one in Illinois. The Southern Environmental Law Center is suing over the South Carolina data center. 
There are seven data center campuses under construction in Mississippi. Collectively, they represent over $55 billion of investment in the state. 
Local officials in other counties have said data centers present an opportunity to boost tax bases and make infrastructure upgrades. Amazon is expected to pay millions of dollars in taxes each year to the Canton Public School District that could go towards repairing buildings or raising teacher salaries. Compass Data Centers has partnered with Meridian Community College on a workforce development program.
However, many data centers have faced stiff community opposition in Mississippi and across the country over water, electricity rate hikes, environmental impact and concerns about artificial intelligence. In Southaven, Elon Musk’s SpacexAI has resulted in multiple lawsuits over the company’s use of mobile gas turbines. Residents can hear the turbines day and night and worry that the turbines are hurting the area’s air quality.

name: VTDigger
title: Vermont Medicaid braces for new rules coming for nearly 50,000 Vermonters
description:
It’s likely that most Vermonters on Medicaid will remain eligible for coverage once the rules start kicking in Oct. 1, but they will need to jump through more hoops to prove it.  
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont Medicaid braces for new rules coming for nearly 50,000 Vermonters.
text:
The People’s Health and Wellness Clinic in Barre in July 2020. File photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
The first of a series of changes to Medicaid is set to take effect Oct. 1, put in motion by the federal budget bill passed in July 2025. The next round of changes begins in January.
Combined, the changes to the state-federal health insurance program are expected to affect nearly 50,000 Vermonters, but that doesn’t mean that all will lose coverage, say healthcare advocates and Medicaid officials. Rather, it will be a major bureaucratic lift to keep those people insured.
“Everything we’ve been doing as far as implementation of (the federal changes) is built towards the mindset of ‘How do we maximize the amount of people who retain coverage through these changes, and how do we support them through what are ultimately very major changes to the Medicaid program?’” said Alex McCracken, the director of communications at the Department of Vermont Health Access, which oversees Medicaid in the state.
The Oct. 1 changes will prevent certain immigrants from receiving Medicaid. 
Most adult refugees and asylum seekers in Vermont will lose Medicaid; the state estimates that’s about 235 people. The exceptions are lawful permanent residents; immigrants from Cuba, Haiti, Micronesia and the Marshall Islands; pregnant people; and anyone under 21. 
Unless they’re able to get insurance through an employer or a spouse, the refugees and asylum seekers losing insurance will have few other options for coverage. 
“Honestly, it will be really devastating and hard for this small set of people,” said Mike Fisher, the state’s healthcare advocate. 
The second round of changes will begin at the start of 2027 and apply to a much broader group of Medicaid recipients ages 19 to 64.
This population will need to show that they make at least $580 a month while still earning under the Medicaid income threshold of 138% of the federal poverty level. If a person doesn’t make $580 monthly, they must attest to spending 80 hours a month on work, education or community service. They will also need to renew their Medicaid eligibility every six months instead of annually. 
The state estimates that 49,000 Vermonters will need to meet these requirements to retain coverage.
Fisher said that his office, which runs a healthcare help line and has guidance materials for those trying to navigate the changes, has fielded concerns about children or Medicare patients losing coverage. Those groups will not be affected, he said.
He added that many people are exempt from the January rule change and will not need to meet the new earnings, work and documentation requirements. 
Pregnant people, Indigenous people and those who are medically frail or eligible for federal food benefits are exempt. So are veterans with a disability and anyone who is otherwise eligible for Medicaid despite being incarcerated.
Parents of children under 13 and any family caregiver are also excluded from needing to meet the January requirements. 
“People shouldn’t lose their Medicaid due to failure to meet the work requirement, but they may and will lose their Medicaid because they don’t manage to get the right piece of paperwork,” Fisher said, adding that those without a home address may be most likely to struggle with the paperwork requirements. 
McCracken said the department is working to get information out to its beneficiaries in an array of languages, in videos and through community organizations. In the state’s 2026 budget, the department received funding for 12 new staffers meant to handle the new eligibility requirements. The Department of Vermont Health Access is also working to collect whatever state and federal data it has — information including wage data, work-requirement reporting for food assistance, data on incarcerated people and veterans — to keep people from needing to self-report. 
The Vermont Afghan Alliance, which works with Afghan immigrants in Vermont, has hosted a health insurance clinic with Vermont Legal Aid to try to prepare people for the changes. It has also connected people with Medicaid assisters and used its community WhatsApp channels to help people understand the changes and the options available to them. Many of the resources have been available in the Dari and Pashto languages, said Ellen Yount, the alliance’s director. 
Most of the Afghanis in the alliance are in Vermont on special permanent immigrant visas they received for working with the U.S. government during the war and military occupation of Afghanistan. Because of that permanent lawful status, those on Medicaid won’t lose their coverage Oct. 1 but they will still need to meet the work requirements.
Still, some Afghan asylum seekers without special permanent status will lose health insurance. 

READ MORE

The state is working with Vermont’s free clinic system to identify who can take newly uninsured patients at a low cost.
Melanie Clark, a Medicaid assister at the Open Door Clinic in Middlebury, said it’s likely many of the people losing Medicaid coverage will have low enough incomes to qualify for financial assistance in federally qualified healthcare clinics or with hospitals’ emergency rooms or urgent care facilities. 
“It’s not going to be a true health insurance plan,” she said. “It just won’t be through Medicaid. It’ll likely be through one of these other avenues.” 
Her clinic is ready for an influx of patients, but also prepared for patients to seek care elsewhere, she said. It’s a scenario the clinic saw play out with the expiration this year of the advanced premium tax credits that helped people afford coverage on the Affordable Care Act marketplace.
McCracken also worried about the strain that a surge in uncompensated care could have on a healthcare system unprepared to absorb the loss of income. In recent hospital budget hearings, many of Vermont’s hospitals raised concerns about an increase in uncompensated care as more Vermonters drop marketplace coverage.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont Medicaid braces for new rules coming for nearly 50,000 Vermonters.

text:
Photo of a single dose of the MMR vaccine. (Joshua Haiar/South Dakota Searchlight)A fifth measles-related death occurred in Pennsylvania, which remains one of the nation’s hot spots for outbreaks of the virus.
The state Health Department reported to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention that an unvaccinated person in Lancaster County died after testing positive for measles.
The number of confirmed measles cases stands at 943 across 39 counties this year. Less than 1% of the cases involved vaccinated people.
The department won’t release any details, in order to protect the privacy of the individual and their family. It’s providing up-to-date information on cases, hospitalizations, and deaths available on a measles dashboard.
Health leaders said the best protection against the highly contagious respiratory virus is to get fully vaccinated. The measles, mumps and rubella vaccine is available at each of the department’s 59 state health centers.
Measles can cause serious short- and long-term health problems including pneumonia and brain swelling. It spreads when a person who is infected breathes, coughs, or sneezes.
The death announced Wednesday is the third measles-related death in Lancaster County. Authorities said Aug. 25 that two Lancaster County infants died after exposure to the virus. The others were an 18-year-old from Mifflin County, according to the county coroner, and a 40-year-old Jefferson County woman. All were unvaccinated, the Health Department said.

title: Democrat for US House unveils proposals to lower tariffs, stabilize Social Security
description: South Dakota Democratic U.S. House nominee Nikki Gronli announced her top economic priorities Wednesday, including a return to tariff policies predating President Donald Trump, capping insulin costs, giving Medicare more drug-price bargaining power, and requiring higher-income people to contribute more toward Social Security. Social Security is the federal r[...]
text:
Nikki Gronli speaks in downtown Sioux Falls on Sept. 10, 2025, during the formal launch of her campaign for South Dakota's lone U.S. House seat. (Photo by Makenzie Huber/South Dakota Searchlight)South Dakota Democratic U.S. House nominee Nikki Gronli announced her top economic priorities Wednesday, including a return to tariff policies predating President Donald Trump, capping insulin costs, giving Medicare more drug-price bargaining power, and requiring higher-income people to contribute more toward Social Security.
Social Security is the federal retirement program funded through a payroll tax on individuals’ wages up to the taxable maximum, which is $184,500 per year. The trust fund that pays people benefits is projected to go into the red in 2032, requiring cuts to the program if Congress takes no action.
Gronli said she wants to eliminate the taxable maximum. 
“It will be made solvent by eliminating the income tax cap,” Gronli said. “That is long overdue.” 
[Voter Guide: 2026 general election Voter Guide: The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
Medicare is the federal health insurance program for people 65 and older. Gronli said the program’s ability to negotiate drug prices is too limited, driving up costs for taxpayers and patients. 
She also called for a $35 monthly insulin price cap for everyone.
Gronli criticized the Trump administration’s higher tariffs, saying they have increased costs for South Dakotans. Tariffs are a tax paid by those importing a foreign good.
“The next Congress must take action and end this added tax on South Dakota families,” she said. 
Gronli also said she would prioritize more funding for the Meat and Poultry Processing Expansion Program, which provides grants to help independent processors expand meat-processing capacity. Additionally, she proposed a heifer tax credit to expand the nation’s cattle herd, though she did not offer details of such a program. Cattle numbers have been low in recent years while beef imports have risen.
Gronli was the state director of the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s Rural Development program under former President Joe Biden, and she previously served as vice chair of the state Democratic Party. 
Gronli said her priorities differ from her opponent, Republican Marty Jackley. He is the state’s attorney general and formerly served as U.S. attorney for South Dakota.
“He’s made it clear that he supports the policies harming South Dakota,” Gronli said during a press conference on Wednesday in downtown Sioux Falls. “He’s made it clear he’s fine with the chaos and corruption in Washington, D.C., and Congress.”
Gronli told South Dakota Searchlight she was referring to things such as the non-Congress-approved war in Iran, Trump’s tariff policies and challenging of mail-in voting, and his administration sometimes ignoring court decisions.

Jackley for Congress campaign spokesperson Jason Glodt responded with a written statement. 
“Marty Jackley is the only candidate in this race who has a proven record fighting government corruption,” he wrote. “Marty has been prosecuting fraud for over a decade, passed government accountability legislation, and he will take that same fight to Washington to protect taxpayers.”
He agreed the two candidates differ. 
“Gronli served in the Biden administration and is advocating for Biden-era policies that will result in bigger government and higher taxes,” Glodt wrote. “Marty Jackley has a proven record fighting for less government, government accountability, and lower taxes.”
South Dakota’s lone U.S. House seat will be open because Republican U.S. Rep. Dusty Johnson ran for governor and lost in the June primary election.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Louisiana Tech president speaks on retirement decision: ‘I’ve got a lot more to do’
description: Louisiana Tech President Jim Henderson said he plans to relocate to Florida after he retires in December to continue his career as an educator by homeschooling his grandkids.  Henderson announced last week he intends to leave the leadership role at the Ruston campus at the end of the calendar year due to health concerns.  “I’m […]
text:
Louisiana Tech President Jim Henderson and his wife, Tonia, plan to move to Florida to be closer to their grandchildren (Louisiana Tech photo) Louisiana Tech President Jim Henderson said he plans to relocate to Florida after he retires in December to continue his career as an educator by homeschooling his grandkids. 
Henderson announced last week he intends to leave the leadership role at the Ruston campus at the end of the calendar year due to health concerns. 
“I’m not dying,” Henderson said in an interview this week. “I’ve been dealing with some blood pressure issues … I do need to look after some of the environmental things that might contribute to that.”
Henderson said his decision to leave at the end of this year was to give Louisiana Tech’s next president time to get caught up before the academic year begins next fall. 
Henderson became president of Louisiana Tech University in 2024 after leading the University of Louisiana System since 2017. Prior to that, he was the president at Northwestern State University and Bossier Parish Community College chancellor. 
Henderson is considered one of Louisiana’s most widely respected figures in higher education, but his departure fueled speculation he had been forced out for political reasons. Since Gov. Jeff Landry took office in January 2024, leadership has changed at LSU, Northwestern State, McNeese State, the University of Louisiana at Monroe, the University of Louisiana at Lafayette, LSU New Orleans (previously the University of New Orleans), LSU’s medical schools, the Southern University System and the Louisiana Community and Technical College System. 
Henderson said his decision to leave Louisiana Tech was totally his choice. 
“There’s always going to be, in a political environment, agreements, disagreements. Nothing like that forced me out at all,” Henderson said. “The governor has supported our work, and so that did not play a part in this.” 
Henderson said he plans to be totally retired for six months to a year and then consider whether he will pursue another job in Florida. He said he’s previously been approached to apply for university presidency jobs in the state, though he now says he is more likely to work as an instructor than an administrator. 
Before he returns to higher education, Henderson said he plans to help his daughter, Reagan, homeschool her four kids, ages 3, 5 (twins) and 6. 
“We’re gonna read the classics together,” Henderson said about his grandchildren. “We’re going to understand why journalism is important for sure. We’re also going to make sure that, like my dad did me, that they understand math at the deepest level an artistic, journalistic kind of person could.” 

Henderson studied journalism at Northwestern State University and worked in the profession before moving to academia. 
“I’ve got a lot more to do, but the main focus is being a grandparent to those four babies in Miami,” Henderson said. 
His wife, Tonia, will continue working in her media solutions company, which Henderson anticipates helping out with in his retirement. 
Henderson also said he plans to write, perhaps about character-based leadership or his many tales from years working in and around the State Capitol. 
A search committee for Henderson’s replacement will meet Oct. 8, though speculation is already swirling about who might replace him.
One name mentioned is state Education Superintendent Cade Brumley, a conservative ally of Landry. As in with other presidential openings, Landry is expected to influence the outcome. 
Brumley’s name has been mentioned as a contender for other university presidential jobs. 
“Dr. Henderson is a longtime friend of mine and a talented leader. Louisiana Tech is a dynamic institution with a strong faculty and invested community,” Brumley said in a statement. “Right now, however, my focus remains on our B-4 centers and PK-12 schools that have made historic progress.” 
Henderson said he doesn’t have any thoughts about who should replace him, as long as they have a compelling vision for the university. 
“This institution is remarkable … While it’s got such a sterling reputation and a great history, its future is even brighter, provided they have a leader that will embrace an audacious vision for the institution and work with the faculty, one, to articulate that vision and then to realize it,” Henderson said.

title: Vermont Conversation: ‘Gradually, then suddenly.’ Bestselling author Richard North Patterson on how American democracy was undermined.
description:
“If you look at authoritarians throughout time, they've always found an enemy. And for Trump, they were racial minorities,” said Patterson, who predicts that “2026 and 2028 are really democracy's last good shot at getting itself turned around.”
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont Conversation: ‘Gradually, then suddenly.’ Bestselling author Richard Nor[...]
text:
The Vermont Conversation with David Goodman is a VTDigger podcast that features in-depth interviews on local and national issues. Listen and subscribe for free on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, YouTube or wherever you get podcasts.

Author Richard North Patterson, left, and his new book “Tripwires: 15 Twenty-First-Century Events That Undermined American Democracy — and How to Reclaim It.” Courtesy photos
“Gradually, then suddenly, America reached the precipice of authoritarianism.”
That’s how author Richard North Patterson begins his exploration into key turning points in the last quarter century that have altered the course of American history. He breaks it down in his new book, “Tripwires: 15 Twenty-First-Century Events That Undermined American Democracy — and How to Reclaim It.”
“The fire hose of stuff around Trump has been so great that we can’t keep track of it,” Patterson told me. “If we don’t understand how we got here, then we can’t figure out how to get out of this place and restore and reinvigorate our democracy.”
Starting with the Supreme Court decision Bush v. Gore that awarded George W. Bush the 2000 presidential election, Patterson itemizes the fateful turns. There was the subprime mortgage crisis in 2008; the Citizens United decision by the Supreme Court in 2010 that unleashed unlimited campaign cash; future President Donald Trump’s demand for then-President Barack Obama’s birth certificate in 2011; and Sen. Mitch McConnell’s refusal to convict Trump for the Jan. 6 attempted coup by supporters in 2021.
The culmination of the events that undermined democracy was Chief Justice John Roberts’ Supreme Court ruling in 2024 that the American president had immunity for his actions, thus creating an unbounded presidency.
Patterson is internationally renowned as the author of 23 novels, 16 of which have been New York Times bestsellers, including “Protect and Defend” and “Degree of Guilt.” Patterson is a former trial attorney whose articles have been published in the New York Times, Wall Street Journal, London Times and elsewhere.
For the last decade, Patterson has devoted his energies to political commentary because, as he wrote in The Atlantic, “Trump rendered fiction redundant.”
As a fiction writer, Patterson recognized Trump’s gift for crafting a compelling story. “Trump creates a fantasy world in which we are beset by numerous forces, some real in themselves, some not real at all, like the great attack of communism and socialism he claims that we are suffering from,” he told me. “And then he creates the heroic narrative where Trump and Trump alone can save us from all of this.”
Patterson understands the allure of the story and its inherent danger.
“You had a meeting of the man and his megalomaniacal fantasies in a moment of extreme unease in the American polity, where people were willing to turn to someone who promised to be the all-purpose solution to their unease.”
“He claimed to make America great again. I would argue he made America hate again,” Patterson continued. “If you look at authoritarians throughout time, they’ve always found an enemy. And for Trump, they were racial minorities.”
Patterson predicted that “2026 and 2028 are really democracy’s last good shot at getting itself turned around.”
“If we have a JD Vance or somebody else who’s going to pick up on Trump’s proto fascism, then we are farther down the road to going from democracy to the authoritarianism in Hungary under (Viktor) Orban and beyond, where we simply can’t retrieve what we — what we once believed was secure.”

name: Maine Morning Star
title: Maine Senate confirms slew of nominees including new Superior Court justice
description: The Maine Senate returned for a one-day session Wednesday to confirm more than 40 nominees to assorted state positions.  Senators unanimously confirmed Gerald Reid as a Maine Superior Court justice. Reid previously served as the commissioner of the Maine Department of Environmental Protection, and before that served in the Maine Attorney General’s Office Nat[...]
text:
Senate President Mattie Daughtry looks on as Minority Leader Trey Stewart and Majority Leader Teresa Pierce converse before tabling the supplemental budget proposal on March 4, 2025. (Photo by Emma Davis/ Maine Morning Star)The Maine Senate returned for a one-day session Wednesday to confirm more than 40 nominees to assorted state positions. 
Senators unanimously confirmed Gerald Reid as a Maine Superior Court justice. Reid previously served as the commissioner of the Maine Department of Environmental Protection, and before that served in the Maine Attorney General’s Office Natural Resources Division. 
Sen. Anne Carney (D-Cumberland) praised his commitment to public service and the rule of law. 
“He’s a very thoughtful person,” Carney said. “He’s an objective decision maker, and most of all, he’s an extraordinarily careful listener. I am personally really excited that we’ll have someone with a strong environmental background on the bench in our state.” 
But not every confirmation was without debate. An earlier dispute from the Maine Legislature’s Environment and Natural Resources Committee spilled into the Senate Wednesday, over the nomination of Patrick Keliher to the Land for Maine’s Future Board. 
Keliher was the long-time commissioner of the Maine Department of Marine Resources, until he retired last year. He served under both Republican Gov. Paul LePage and Gov. Janet Mills, a Democrat, and was the longest-serving commissioner in the department’s history. 
But several Republican senators raised concerns about his post-retirement position on the board of trustees for the Nature Conservancy in Maine, because the organization last year announced it was purchasing four dams on the lower Kennebec River.
While Keliher was commissioner, the department proposed an amendment to the Kennebec River Management Plan aimed at improving fish passage and included the potential removal of the four dams. But after pushback, the department pulled the amendment due to a “process issue.” 
Sen. Brad Farrin (R-Somerset) said Marine Resources oversaw the river and the dams, and questioned when conversations about the sale began and what state officials knew.
“I’m not suggesting that those unanswered questions by themselves prove any wrongdoing, but I am being asked to decide whether Mr. Keliher should once again hold a position of significant public trust involving land conservation and public resources,” Farrin said. 
Farrin said he was particularly concerned because his district includes the Sappi Paper Mill in Skowhegan, which relies on water from the impoundment created by the Shawmut Dam.
He said several senators have asked the Government Oversight Committee to have the Legislature’s internal watchdog, the Office of Program Evaluation and Government Accountability, review the records and establish a timeline of conversations about the dams sale. 
Sen. Rachel Talbot Ross (D-Cumberland) countered that Keliher did not join the Nature Conservancy’s board of trustees until after he retired from state service, and that Keliher told the committee he had refused to work at the Kennebec River Restoration, the nonprofit that was formed to take ownership of the dams. 
Sen. Denise Tepler (D-Sagadahoc) said she did not understand how Keliher became the “bogeyman” of the Kennebec dam sale. 
“I do not understand how he has become the figure at the head of a conspiracy theory about what has happened with the Shawmut Dam, the Shawmut Dam still stands,” Tepler said. “It still has a reservoir that still feeds the Sappi Mill.”
Ultimately Keliher’s confirmation was approved in a 17-15 vote, much closer than the vast majority of Wednesday’s confirmations. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The most contentious confirmation of the day was about Dr. Patrick Connolly, who was nominated to the Advisory Council on Affordable Health Care. 
Senate Minority Leader Trey Stewart (R-Aroostook) said Connolly had appeared in a political ad making “disparaging statements” about Sen. Scott Cyrway (R-Kennebec). 
The ad features Connolly criticizing Cyrway’s votes on healthcare spending and praising the Democratic candidate in the race, Patric Moore. 
“Then Congress slashed funding for rural hospitals,” Connolly said in the video. “Cyrway could’ve helped save the ones we have left. He voted no.” 
Stewart said the ad was misleading about the timing of the legislative votes and the closing of Northern Light Inland Hospital in Cyrway’s district.
Stewart also said the video implied that Cyrway was solely responsible for the hospital’s closure and cast aspersions on the timing of the ad, which he said published weeks after Connolly’s confirmation hearing before a legislative committee. 
“I’m not going to impugn anybody’s motives in here,” Stewart said. “But I do, in fact, wonder with the timing of all of this, what might have happened? Could somebody have offered a tit for tat? We’ll put you on this board if you help out somebody else in a close race. I don’t know.”
“All I have is this evidence, which states that this individual has now lied publicly about what has transpired in an effort for political gain after receiving a bipartisan vote in committee,” Stewart continued. 
Sen. Dick Bradstreet (R-Kennebec) echoed Stewart’s points, and called the ad “demonstrably false” and said Connolly had “misled the Maine public.”
But Sen. Mike Tipping (D-Penobscot) said Connolly’s statement was not extreme commentary but rather the remarks were about helping save Maine’s rural hospitals.
“Obviously, the vote, the bill, and the roll call referenced were all relevant and clear,” Tipping said. “I’m disappointed to see my colleagues going after a doctor for speaking out on healthcare and issues of public concern, mischaracterizing his words on the Senate floor.”
Sen. Stacy Brenner (D-Sagadahoc) said she didn’t understand why the ad was relevant to Connolly’s nomination.
“​​I’m just nonplussed by the fact that we seem to be discussing and arguing about truth in campaign advertising, and that that is affecting the potential nomination of someone who has the right to political speech, and who has the right to be a member of a particular party,” Brenner said. “I’m kind of amazed that that political speech in campaign season has become an issue in a nomination.”
Despite attempts to table Connolly’s nomination or send it back to committee, the Senate ultimately confirmed him in an 18-12 vote.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: NJ bill would let out-of-state cops, judges shield their personal info
description: Daniel’s Law allows judges and cops in New Jersey to shield their personal information from public disclosure. A new bill would make out-of-state officials eligible.
text:
Sen. Parker Space, in glasses, is one of the lawmakers behind a bipartisan bill that would allow cops and judges in other states to shield their personal information from public disclosure. (Photo by Dana DiFilippo/New Jersey Monitor)Two New Jersey lawmakers want to expand Daniel’s Law to allow judges and law enforcement officials in other states to shield their personal information from public disclosure.
The bipartisan bill sponsored by Sens. Parker Space (R-Sussex) and Brian Stack (D-Hudson) would allow judges, police officers, and prosecutors from other states to request personal information like their addresses not be shared by governments or private firms.
The bill was spurred by a request from a constituent, a retired New York Police Department detective, who worried someone might seek vengeance over his time on the force, Space told the New Jersey Monitor.
“In today’s world, people are getting nuttier on certain folks, so safety is always a number one priority when it comes to somebody in that line of business,” said Space.
As written, Daniel’s Law references definitions in the state Open Public Records Act that narrowly refer to law enforcement personnel who administer New Jersey law. Existing provisions do not apply to individuals who held identical positions outside of New Jersey.
The law is named for Daniel Anderl, who was slain during a gunman’s assassination attempt on his mother, U.S. District Court Judge Esther Salas, at their home in 2020.
Individuals covered by the law can sign up for a state-maintained registry to have their information shielded in public documents, and they or their agents can request private data brokers remove their personal information or face a $1,000 fine for each violation.

Lawmakers have more than once amended Daniel’s Law to extend its coverage to new groups of workers or alter its enforcement provisions, and those efforts have generally won broad bipartisan support. Space expects his bill to follow that track.
“Obviously I’m on the Republican side, but I think this would be a nonpartisan issue. I think it should move along fairly swiftly,” Space said.
Though the law enjoys broad support in the Legislature, it has faced legal challenges from the press alleging it impermissibly chills speech, and dozens of data brokers have charged its enforcement mechanism unconstitutionally punishes speech without considering intent. The law has so far been upheld as constitutional.
Data brokers’ challenge returned to the U.S. 3rd Circuit Court of Appeals last month after New Jersey’s Supreme Court unanimously ruled the law’s fines do not require violations to be intentional, a decision seen as a win for firms facing penalties for thousands of individual breaches.

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Ohio lawmakers approve 90-day gas tax holiday just weeks ahead of election
description: Ohio state lawmakers have approved a 90-day gas tax holiday at the urging of Republican candidate for governor Vivek Ramaswamy. The House and Senate also cobbled together the two-thirds supermajority necessary for an emergency clause which ensures the measure takes effect immediately. The move comes as the rising cost of gas and diesel threaten Republicans’[...]
text:
Republican candidate for governor, Vivek Ramaswamy (speaking) flanked by his running mate and Senate President Rob McColley shortly after lawmakers approved a 90-day tax holiday. (Photo by Nick Evans, Ohio Capital Journal.)Ohio state lawmakers have approved a 90-day gas tax holiday at the urging of Republican candidate for governor Vivek Ramaswamy. The House and Senate also cobbled together the two-thirds supermajority necessary for an emergency clause which ensures the measure takes effect immediately.
The move comes as the rising cost of gas and diesel threaten Republicans’ chances at the polls this November. The bill now heads to Gov. Mike DeWine, who has said he intends to sign it.
Democratic candidate for governor Amy Acton proposed the tax break first, and Republican state leaders quickly co-opted the idea. What followed was a hastily arranged effort to call lawmakers back to Columbus to fast track legislation.
Ramaswamy joined Republican House Speaker Matt Huffman and his running mate Republican Senate President Rob McColley to announce the plan just a week ago. Senators got their chance to discuss the legislation Tuesday, and in the House, lawmakers held their first hearing the day of the vote.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Most lawmakers made it in for session — 31 of 33 senators and 96 of 99 representatives were on hand for Wednesday’s votes. That head count was particularly important in the Ohio House, where the partisan split is tight enough that Republicans needed to bring a handful of Democrats on board to pass the bill as an emergency measure. The GOP dominates the Senate thoroughly enough to clear the two-thirds requirement without any Democratic votes.
Last minute Senate changes
Gas tax holiday proposal gets first hearing in Ohio Senate

Wednesday morning a Senate committee abandoned the gas tax holiday proposal it discussed the previous day. Instead, members took up a House proposal explicitly criminalizing the use of unauthorized key fobs — a response to a rash of car thefts in Ohio, most notably by the “Kia Boys” in Columbus. Senators tweaked that bill, removing a requirement that youth offenders go to juvenile hall.
And then added back in the gas tax holiday.
In a nod to the earlier bill’s critics, Ohio state Sen. Jerry Cirino, R-Kirtland, explained Ohio House Bill 519’s new tax holiday wouldn’t require gas stations to provide an itemized receipt showing the state and federal tax rates, and includes changes to give retailers more flexibility in submitting tax filings.
H.B. 519 had already passed the House, and its sponsor, Ohio state Rep. Andrea White, R-Kettering, was also cosponsoring the House’s gas tax proposal, Ohio House Bill 1019. By switching gears to H.B. 519, lawmakers in the House would only need to concur with the Senate’s changes.
Ohio Senate Minority Leader Nickie Antonio. (Photo by Nick Evans, Ohio Capital Journal.)
Ahead of the Senate vote, Minority Leader Nickie Antonio sent McColley a letter asking him to recuse himself given his position on the Ramaswamy ticket. McColley turned her down.
On the Senate floor, Ohio state Sen. Michele Reynolds, R-Canal Winchester, described the measure as a way to show constituents that lawmakers are listening.
“No one state legislature alone can eliminate vehicle theft entirely and much less end a war,” she said. “But this body has an opportunity to respond to both crises by putting $725 million back into the hands of our taxpayers through this legislation.”
Immediately after Republican lawmakers finished introducing the measure, Ohio state Sen. Bill Reineke, R-Tiffin, made a motion to end debate — effectively cutting off Democrats’ opportunity to offer amendments. That motion passed, and the Senate quickly voted to approve the bill.
After the vote, McColley defended the procedural move. Republicans were “committed to delivering $725 million of cost relief” he said, while Democrats were more concerned with “theatrics.”
“Our caucus thought it was important to get in, get the job done on behalf of Ohioans across the state who desperately need this relief,” he said.
Antonio said her caucus was “disappointed” with the GOP’s tactics, and accused McColley of using the Senate “as a campaign ad.”
“There was a bill introduced in the House in May. If this had been so important, we would have acted then, but we didn’t,” she said. “Three weeks ago, all of our Senate sessions were canceled. They said we have nothing more to take up until after the election, and then suddenly they got polling numbers, and the polling numbers told them they were behind.”
Ohio state Rep. Andrea White, R-Kettering. (Photo by Nick Evans, Ohio Capital Journal.)
House concurrence
On the House floor, White said constituents keep asking what she can do to lower the cost of gas and groceries. Cutting state taxes on gas and diesel, she said, would flow through the economy lowering prices at the pump and many other retailers, too.
“The bottom line is three things: immediate relief, fully funding our roads at the local and state level, and making sure transparency is there so it’s consumers that are pocketing the money,” White said.
Even before the House session began, Democratic leaders explained they’d set aside their misgivings and support the measure. All told, 15 House Democrats voted in favor of the proposal.
House Minority Leader Dani Isaacsohn. (Photo by Nick Evans, Ohio Capital Journal.)
Still, the caucus didn’t go quietly.
Ohio state Rep. Bride Rose Sweeney, D-Westlake, dismissed the savings Republicans touted.
“We’re talking about $3 a week,” she said. “And if the options are nothing or $3 a week, if that’s all this body can do, then yes, I will vote for it. But I don’t think anybody should be proud of that.”
She also criticized the majority for posing the issue as a concurrence with changes made in the Senate, which again, closed off Democrats’ opportunity to offer amendments to the bill.
Minority Leader Dani Isaacsohn called it “embarrassing” for Republican lawmakers, only now, to declare an emergency.
“Was it not an emergency in April when gas prices spiked over $4?” Isaacsohn asked, “I don’t remember an emergency clause then. Was it not an emergency this summer when utility bills went to $800 for the first time for Ohio? Was that not an emergency that demanded that we come back and take action?”
“No, it’s an emergency on Sept. 30th — that’s the date today — less than five weeks before Nov. 3rd,” he added. “Now it’s an emergency.”
After the vote, House Speaker Matt Huffman acknowledged Isaacsohn had a point but explained he was optimistic things might improve on their own a few months ago.
“At some point you have to make a decision,” Huffman said. “If we said, well, we’re not going to do it because it will look too political, that’s a terrible reason not to do it.”
House Speaker Matt Huffman signing the concurrence shortly after Wednesday’s vote. (Photo by Nick Evans, Ohio Capital Journal.)
Victory laps
In a press release after the vote, Acton’s campaign took credit for forcing the issue.
“As the first candidate in this race to propose a gas tax holiday, Dr. Acton is glad the Statehouse has voted with bipartisan support to establish a gas tax holiday and provide Ohioans much needed relief at the pump,” said spokesperson Virginia Schaus.
Schaus went on to criticize Ramaswamy for not embracing her other proposal for a “conditional moratorium” on data centers.
“Ohioans know they can’t trust Ramaswamy to take their concerns seriously or make life more affordable,” she added.
Ohio GOP lawmakers tee up votes for gas tax holiday after Acton, then Ramaswamy, back idea

But for Ramaswamy, the episode must’ve felt like a tidy little victory. One week later, he was standing on the same stage with the same legislative leaders, congratulating them on getting a bipartisan tax cut across the finish line.
“You can consider this a preview of the way my administration, beginning in January, will work — a constructive partnership with leaders in both chambers, working together to solve problems for Ohioans.”
Pressed on Democrats’ complaints about being left out of the process, Ramaswamy said “we’re starting with a clean slate in January,” and promised to work with anyone regardless of party.
While Democrats downplayed the scope of tax relief, Ramaswamy insisted a few bucks might make a big difference for some households.
“That may be the difference between being able to afford a Christmas gift for your kids or not,” he said. “It may be the difference between being able to take a weekend trip in the holiday season versus not. That’s a big deal.”

title: Schumer: Democratic US Senate may block Trump nominees for Supreme Court, lower courts
text: WASHINGTON — U.S. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer indicated Wednesday that should Democrats regain control of the chamber following the elections, they plan to block judicial nominees sent up by President Donald Trump, including for any possible vacancies on the Supreme Court. "Look, the bottom line is, one of the reasons that we want to do everything we can to take back the Senate is not let Trump put such horrible justices, MAGA justices, on the Supreme Court and the lower courts," he said.  Trump nominated Justices Neil Gorsuch, Brett Kavanaugh and Amy Coney Barrett during his first term but has yet to nominate anyone to the country’s highest court during his second term. Schumer’s comments signal that even if one of the nine Supreme Court justices retires or potentially passes away, Democrats would hold the vacancy open until after the next presidential election. That would be somewhat similar to Kentucky Republican Sen. Mitch McConnell’s decision to block Merrick Garland from a Senate confirmation vote in 2016 after President Barack Obama nominated Garland to fill the vacancy created by the death of Justice Antonin Scalia. McConnell, then majority leader in a GOP-controlled chamber, said on March 16, 2016, “the next justice could fundamentally alter the direction of the Supreme Court and have a profound impact on our country, so of course — of course — the American people should have a say in the Court’s direction.”“It is a president’s constitutional right to nominate a Supreme Court justice, and it is the Senate’s constitutional right to act as a check on a president and withhold its consent,” he added.  Democrats, including Schumer, rebuked McConnell for the decision. Schumer predicts close electionTo make the choice about whether to approve any nominees during the next session of Congress, Democrats will need to regain the Senate majority. They now have 47 seats.Schumer said during the press conference he expects it to be a close election, declining to say how many seats he expects Democrats to pick up. “We do not want to be overconfident, but what we're seeing in state after state after state is that people are sick of Trump,” he said. “They're sick of the Republican Senate going along with him. And they see the clear divisions we have drawn between what we stand for and what they stand for. That has put us on the edge of victory. But we still got a ways to go.”Democrats need a net gain of at least four Senate seats to regain the majority.The Cook Political Report with Amy Walter rates North Carolina as leaning in Democrats’ direction, with Alaska, Iowa, Maine, Ohio and Texas, all currently held by a Republican, rated as toss-ups. The open races in Michigan and New Hampshire, which were won by a Democratic candidate last time, are also rated as toss-ups. Democratic priority to ‘lower people’s costs’Aside from blocking Trump nominees, Schumer didn’t detail what types of bills Democrats may put on the Senate floor, should voters give them the majority in the upper chamber. “We're going to do everything we can to lower people's costs. You've seen some of the things Trump's done that's raised costs,” he said. “We're going to do everything we can to clamp down on this horrible corruption and to end the chaos and end the war.”Schumer declined to answer a question about whether he believes he would get the support needed from other Democrats to remain their leader, given critical comments from some of the more left-leaning candidates who could be elected this November.“Our caucus is totally unified. We're in great shape. Everyone is really very, very pleased with where we are today compared to where we were 20 months ago, under our leadership,” he said. “And we're fighting hard. And we're on the edge of taking back the Senate.”

name: WyoFile
title: Lummis blocks Senate resolution criticizing Trump’s taxpayer-funded TV ads
authors: by Ali Swenson, The Associated Press, and Maggie Mullen, WyoFile
description:
The retiring senator from Wyoming argued the campaign-style ads are no different than PSAs from past administrations. 
The post Lummis blocks Senate resolution criticizing Trump’s taxpayer-funded TV ads appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
U.S. Sen. Cynthia Lummis of Wyoming blocked a bipartisan-backed resolution Tuesday denouncing President Donald Trump for using tax dollars to pay for campaign-style television ads. 
The series of ads, which began airing last week, have drawn fierce criticism by Democratic lawmakers as well as some GOP members, who say they break federal law. The White House, meanwhile, has defended the advertisements, including one that’s largely repurposed from Trump’s 2024 campaign. 
With three months left in office, Lummis, who is not running for reelection, stood in support of the ads Tuesday on the Senate floor when she objected to a resolution brought by New Hampshire Sen. Maggie Hassan, a Democrat. 
Hassan tried to pass a resolution by unanimous consent that stated it is the “sense of the Senate” that the campaign-style ads promoting Trump should not be funded by taxpayers. 
“The American people want their tax dollars to go towards helping them and keeping them safe, not propaganda campaigns for a president,” Hassan said. “He’s welcome to run whatever ads he wants with his own riches. But with taxpayer dollars, money that people have worked hard to earn, he needs to follow the law.” 
Lummis objected, asserting that past administrations of both parties “have used public service announcements to speak directly to the American people for decades.” 
“When a Democratic president tells Americans what to do, it’s a public service,” Lummis said. “When this president tells Americans that liberty is worth defending, it’s suddenly a problem.” 
Hassan pushed back, arguing that “people know the difference between a PSA and a political ad.” 

.@SenatorHassan (D-NH) and @SenLummis (R-WY) debate taxpayer-funded ad promoting Trump:Lummis: "A reminder that freedom beats communism and socialism…"Hassan: "If we're gonna talk about which side of the aisle is supporting communism and socialism, it is this president." pic.twitter.com/RKqGC4p91L— CSPAN (@cspan) September 29, 2026

Democrats haven’t been the only critics of the ads. U.S. Sen. John Kennedy, a Louisiana Republican, told CBS News: “You can’t spend public money to promote yourself.”
The initial advertisement, which began airing last Wednesday, features clips of Trump talking about defeating communism interspersed with onscreen text promoting the “largest tax cuts in history,” “reigniting American manufacturing” and a call to “defend law and order and police.”
Later in the week, a second ad began running, showing scenic videos of Mount Rushmore at night with quotes and clips from Trump’s Fourth of July weekend speech there honoring the country’s 250th anniversary. 
The latest of the ads, a spot first aired over the weekend, is virtually identical to an ad for Trump’s Republican reelection campaign in 2024. It shows him walking down a hallway as his voice can be heard warning of a “final battle” against “globalists” and “warmongers.” 
All three ads end with a message that says: “Paid for by the U.S. Government.” 
According to AdImpact, which tracks media spending, the spots have so far cost more than $1.4 million and run across a wide range of TV networks around the country. The actual amount spent could be significantly more, depending on whether networks classified the ad as a political ad. 
Multiple legal experts consulted by The Associated Press said the ads appear to run afoul of federal statutes, including a law against congressionally appropriated funds being used for “publicity or propaganda” and a law that limits the partisan political activities of government employees. 
They said the new ads, which are airing on network and cable TV and streaming, differ from other administrations’ PSAs because they aren’t designed to help Americans access any specific program. 
In defending the campaign, the White House published a list of PSAs from recent Democratic and Republican administrations. 
Among the examples it cited were Bush’s Republican administration touting a Medicare law, Barack Obama’s Democratic administration promoting Affordable Care Act subsidies and Joe Biden’s Democratic administration running ads promoting COVID-19 vaccinations. 
Associated Press writers Mary Clare Jalonick and Steven Sloan contributed to this report.

name: VTDigger
title: UVM awarded record $38M to create ‘AI twin’ of sick patients
description:
Researchers received the federal award to hone an artificial intelligence model designed to shorten patient stays in intensive care. The AI is designed to mimic patients and recommend treatments.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  UVM awarded record $38M to create ‘AI twin’ of sick patients.
text:
Dr. Gary An received a record breaking award for his research on AI “twins.” Courtesy photo by Jeff Paxton

BURLINGTON — For doctors struggling to treat patients with severe burns or infections, researchers at the University of Vermont are developing a not-so-human solution. 
They’re working to create an artificial intelligence “twin” of a patient, allowing doctors to test individualized treatments before they’re used on humans. The university received its largest research award ever— up to $38 million — to fund the development of the AI model for clinical trials. 
“It reinforces UVM’s role as a leading research university dedicated to improving lives,” university President Marlene Tromp said at the school’s event announcing the federal grant Wednesday. 
The work is important because patients with severe infections, burns or injuries can have very disordered immune systems, according to trauma surgeon and researcher Dr. Gary An, who is leading the project. Patients can fall “into a pit” in which their immune system can’t recover, and doctors have an incredibly difficult time treating them, he said. 
“This is extraordinarily frustrating to me,” An said. 
Enter the AI “twin.” 
The twin is a computer model that mimics the brain’s neural networks, representing a human body responding to an illness or injury, An said. Researchers are training an AI program that treats those conditions like a game, with the AI working to win the game and cure the patient. 
A doctor would take a sample of a patient’s blood, give it to the AI, then receive a recommendation from the AI about how to treat that patient, An said. That way, doctors might use more effective treatments and shorten patient stays in intensive care. 
An’s research will develop the model before it goes through clinical trials. It could take seven to 10 years before the model might be approved for widespread use on patients, said Kirk Dombrowski, vice president of research at UVM, during an interview Wednesday. Six researchers currently work alongside An in the lab researching the AI twins, according to the lab’s website. 
The grant comes via the Advanced Research Projects Agency for Health, an agency within the national Department of Health and Human Services that invests in medical technology research. The funds are expected to last across the project’s planned five years of work.
UVM’s announcement of the award comes just a week after it received a $19 million grant to build a national neuroscience observatory. And it comes nearly two years after the university earned R1 status in 2025, the highest designation a research university can receive. 
“I think we’ve just shown federal agencies and colleagues and partners that we’re capable of working at a different scale,” said Dombrowski, referring to the record award.  
While researchers at UVM will be leading work on building computational models and training the AI program, the research effort is coordinated among multiple hospitals and companies across the country. 
UVM researchers are collecting data from patients who opt in at three sites: Wake Forest University School of Medicine in North Carolina, WashU Medicine in Missouri, and University of Alabama at Birmingham Heerskink School of Medicine. 
The universities were chosen because UVM has existing research relationships with the institutions, according to Dombrowski. UVM’s hospital isn’t included in the data collection because it doesn’t treat a large enough number of intensive care patients. 
Dombrowski said that funding for An’s project comes as the federal government has signaled that it’s willing to invest in AI development. 
“I think that the scale of what we’re capable of in research has just grown so dramatically,” Dombrowski said.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Rhode Island road and bridge repairs only scratched the surface, RIPEC report finds
description: Rhode Island spent billions of dollars over the last several years to repair the state’s highways and bridges, once ranked among the worst in the nation. They’re better, just not good.  A new analysis by the Rhode Island Public Expenditure Council (RIPEC) found overall infrastructure improvements were largely from bridges moving out of the poor […]
text:
A section of the the ramp connecting Route 10 to Interstate 95 North was closed for over a week after a concrete barrier collapsed on to the train tracks below on the evening of April 24, 2026. (Photo by Christopher Shea/Rhode Island Current)Rhode Island spent billions of dollars over the last several years to repair the state’s highways and bridges, once ranked among the worst in the nation.
They’re better, just not good. 
A new analysis by the Rhode Island Public Expenditure Council (RIPEC) found overall infrastructure improvements were largely from bridges moving out of the poor category and into fair condition, meaning their primary structural elements remain sound despite some wear and tear to the road’s surface. 
In 2024, 66% of Rhode Island’s bridge deck was rated fair, the highest share in the country. Just 19% were rated good.
But other state roads maintained by the Rhode Island Department of Transportation (RIDOT) are still the worst in the nation, according to the 44-page report released Wednesday by the business-backed research group. RIPEC found that the state had the nation’s largest gap between spending on major capital projects and routine maintenance, putting an additional $8.40 toward capital projects for every $1 spent on maintenance.
“Routine maintenance has to become a much higher priority,” RIPEC President and CEO Michael DiBiase said in a statement. “While the state has focused heavily on major capital construction, it needs to do a far better job of preserving and maintaining these assets once built.”
RIPEC’s findings follow the commissioning of a third-party audit of the state’s transportation department by global accounting firm Baker Tilly as part of the state’s fiscal year 2027 budget. The London-based company was awarded a $108,800 contract by the state on July 20, with the audit due March 1, 2027.
RIDOT spokesperson Heidi Gudmundson said Rhode Island has made significant progress in reducing poor-rated bridges. 
“In fact, just two weeks ago, the state received official notification that for the first time in more than a decade, the percentage of Rhode Island’s bridges in poor condition was less than 10%,” she wrote in an email to Rhode Island Current, with an attached letter from the Federal Highway Administration.
Gudmundson added that RIPEC’s analysis does not reflect more recent road improvements including 80 pavement projects totaling $297 million since 2024 and 860 local road projects funded through RhodeRestore, the state’s municipal road grant program.
Rhode Island’s transportation spending over the past decade has been shaped by RhodeWorks, the multibillion-dollar program to repair highways and bridges signed into law by then-Gov. Gina Raimondo in 2016.
RhodeWorks was financed through a combination of state transportation revenues, federal funding and borrowing backed by future federal aid. The program also relied on tolls on large commercial tractor-trailers traveling through 13 highway gantries, which charged an average toll of $3.
Trucking companies challenged the toll program in federal court in 2018. A Rhode Island federal judge halted the tolls in 2022, cutting off an estimated $40 million in yearly revenue. The First Circuit Court of Appeals in Boston partially overturned the district court’s ruling in 2024, allowing the state to resume tolling under a revised structure.
RIDOT selected a company in June to restart the tolling system, with transportation officials targeting July 2027 to begin collecting revenue again. 
RIDOT picks the company that will restart Rhode Island’s truck tolls

Losing toll revenue added to RhodeWorks’ financial pressure, according to RIPEC’s report. The state ultimately used $70 million in general revenue to replace the lost toll money in fiscal years 2023 and 2024, while also directing gas tax revenue and other funds toward highway projects.
Rhode Island also faces a projected $278.9 million shortfall in matching funds needed to secure federal transportation dollars between fiscal years 2027 and 2031, according to the report. That comes as RIPEC estimates demolition and reconstruction of the westbound Washington Bridge will cost $572.1 million.
Financing includes $221 million in competitive federal grants, up to $334.6 million in Grant Anticipation Revenue Vehicles (GARVEE) borrowing approved by the state in 2024, along with other state funds including $67 million from the Rhode Island Capital Plan Fund and $35 million in unspent federal pandemic relief money.
“Rhode Island should pursue a more balanced approach to its transportation investments going forward: less reliance on debt, more dedicated state revenues, and more investments in roads,” DiBiase said.
A spokesperson for RIDOT acknowledged a request for comment, but did not have a response as of Wednesday afternoon.
Senate President Valarie Lawson and House Speaker Christopher R. Blazejewski said in a joint statement to Rhode Island Current that they are reviewing RIPEC’s report and its findings on the state’s transportation spending.
“We share their concerns, which, in addition to our committee hearings, is why we passed a requirement for an efficiency and performance audit of RIDOT as part of the state budget,” they said.

description: The deadline to update your voter record or register to vote before Rhode Island’s general election on Nov. 3 is fast approaching. text:
Rhode Island residents have through Oct. 4 to register to vote for the November general election. (Photo by Christopher Shea/Rhode Island Current)The deadline to update your voter record or register to vote before Rhode Island’s general election on Nov. 3 is fast approaching. Rhode Islanders must be registered to vote 30 days before an election to participate. That means eligible Rhode Island residents have until 4 p.m. Sunday, Oct. 4, to act in time to participate in the upcoming local, state and federal elections.
Registration can be completed online at vote.ri.gov, or by mailing or dropping off a paper form in person at your local board of canvassers office. 
As of September, over 695,021 eligible voters were registered, according to the Rhode Island Department of State’s online database. About 52% were registered independents, while Democrats comprised 34% of those registered, and Republicans made up 14%.
Close behind the registration deadline is a second key date: the deadline to apply for a mail ballot. Applications are already available online, due back no later than 4 p.m. Tuesday, Oct. 13. Applications sent by mail must be postmarked by the Oct. 13 deadline. 
Early voting begins Oct. 14 and runs through 4 p.m. Monday, Nov. 2.
For more information about upcoming elections and key deadlines, visit the Department of State website.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: House Democrats ask IRS to eye tax implications of $10M transfer to Hope Florida
description: Top Democrats in the Florida House are demanding the Internal Revenue Service open an investigation into whether the Hope Florida Foundation and two social welfare organizations that received money from it properly reported the funds to the IRS and, moreover, whether any of the organizations have to pay taxes on the funds. House Democratic Leader […]
text:
First Lady Casey DeSantis and Gov Ron DeSantis at a May 20, 2025, Hope Florida press conference in Tampa. (Photo by Mitch Perry/Florida Phoenix)Top Democrats in the Florida House are demanding the Internal Revenue Service open an investigation into whether the Hope Florida Foundation and two social welfare organizations that received money from it properly reported the funds to the IRS and, moreover, whether any of the organizations have to pay taxes on the funds.
House Democratic Leader Fentrice Driskell of Tampa and state Rep. Kelly Skidmore of Boca Raton sent a letter to IRS Chief Executive Officer Frank J. Bisignano this week detailing the findings of the Hope Florida grand jury report that was leaked to CBS News in August.
Although the grand jury found that $10 million in Medicaid was “misappropriated” by top Florida Republicans and wound up being used for “political activities,” it concluded there was not enough evidence to criminally charge anyone involved.
Democrats maintain the 19-page grand jury report shows that top Republicans flouted Florida law by diverting money that should have been returned to the state coffers and say they want accountability.
House Democratic Leader Fentrice Driskell speaks to reporters in the Capitol rotunda on May 26, 2026, while representatives debate the 2026 budget. (Photo by Christine Sexton/Florida Phoenix)
“We refuse to lift our foot off the gas when it comes to Hope Florida and the abuses of our taxpayer dollars from state officials at the highest levels.  There must be accountability to the people of Florida,” Driskell, from Tampa, said in a prepared statement. 
“The IRS has the authority to review any potential abuses that may have occurred in this case. We are willing and eager to assist them as we seek justice for Floridians.”
A Leon County grand jury examined the $10 million transfer from an overbilling settlement the state reached with a Medicaid managed care plan to the Hope Florida Foundation, a 501(c)(3) organization set up to assist an initiative championed by First Lady Casey DeSantis that aims to remove people from social service programs by helping them make private-sector connections.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
A 501(c)(3) is an organization with a focus on charitable, religious, educational, or scientific work. They are prohibited from participating in political campaigning and rules limit their lobbying. Contributions to a 501(c)(3) are tax deductible and must be disclosed.
The Hope Florida Foundation granted $5 million each to Secure Florida’s Future Inc. and Save Our Society From Drugs Inc. Those social welfare agencies, both 501(c)(4) corporations, then transferred most of the funds to Keep Florida Clean, a political committee once chaired by now-Attorney General James Uthmeier.
Keep Florida Clean transferred funds directly to the Republican Party of Florida, which spent it to campaign against 2024’s proposed state constitutional Amendment 3, the grand jury found.
A 501(c)(4) is a social welfare organization with the main purpose of promoting what’s best for the general welfare of a community. It has no lobbying limits. Contributions to a 501(c)(4) are not tax deductible and donors are not generally required to disclose their contributions to the IRS.
The amendment would have made recreational marijuana legal in Florida for adults over the age of 21 had it drawn approval by 60% of the voters. Gov. Ron DeSantis adamantly opposed it.
The Democrats’ letter notes that the IRS grants tax exempt-organizations significant benefits on the condition they operate for charitable or social welfare purposes. A 501(c)(3) organization cannot intervene, directly or indirectly, in any political campaign, and its lobbying must be insubstantial. 
A 501(c)(3) organization’s “political and excess lobbying expenditures are subject to excise taxes on both the organization and its managers,” the letter says.
It continues: “Although we recognize that [federal law] limits what the Service can share with us, we ask that you examine whether the three charitable organizations complied with these requirements and accurately reported the funds at issue, and that you assess any taxes owed as a result of the ultimate use of the funds.”

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: NC-11 candidates offer competing ‘mountain values’ in unique ads
description: 'These are two ads that only would have been run in NC-11,' said political scientist Chris Cooper.
text:
Image from Balkcom's "Mom" ad, one of two unique spots currently running in North Carolina's 11th Congressional District. (Photo: YouTube)Both major party candidates for North Carolina’s 11th Congressional District debuted new ads in the Asheville media market this week. The political commercials couldn’t be much more different, yet they’re competing to appeal to the same rural community.  
Democrat Jamie Ager, a fourth-generation farmer who owns Hickory Nut Gap, put out a spot titled “Barn Dance.” It’s the first ad to run in NC-11 this cycle in partnership with the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee. 
The ad opens with Ager wearing a collared shirt, jeans, and a baseball cap. He’s on a stage, rallying supporters in a wooden structure decorated with twinkling fairy lights. 
“Do you know what we need more of in Washington, D.C.?” Ager asks, speaking into a microphone. “Barn dances!”
The shot cuts to Ager dancing with his wife, Amy. In the background, musicians play violin, banjo, guitar, and upright bass. 
Ager explains that he and Amy host barn dances every month.
“Politicians just dance with lobbyists, but I’ll take a good mountain hoedown any day,” he said. “In Congress, I’ll invest in Western North Carolina again by taking on corporate greed that raises our costs, and I’ll fight for our Helene recovery funds.”
“Jamie and Amy host these barn dances at the farm where their focus for the past 25 years has been building community through agriculture,” Ager campaign manager Grayson Barnette told NC Newsline in a statement. “We operate with that same mindset, where we work to bring the community together through our campaign.”
Republicans, Democrats agree Rep. Edwards made right call withdrawing from NC-11 race

Republican Jennifer Balkcom, a state representative from Henderson County and eighth-generation Western North Carolinian, took a different approach to get voters’ attention. Her YouTube channel titles the spot, paid for by the National Republican Congressional Committee, as “Mom.”
As Balkcom says she comes from a long line of “tough mountain women,” the camera pans to Balkcom and her mother chatting in a field of cows. There’s mooing in the background. 
“Mom raised us on her own. She taught us to be strong,” Balkcom said, the two women holding mugs at a wooden table. “And when someone broke into her house, she shot them.”
“You break into my house, you’re going to get shot,” Balkcom’s mother said as the background music pauses.
“Mom’s a fighter,” Balkcom said.
“She is too,” her mother responded. “She’ll fight for lower cost, Helene funding, and better healthcare.”
The Balkcom campaign did not respond to NC Newsline’s requests for comment, but NRCC spokesman Reilly Richardson said, “While liberal Jamie Ager is running on Democrats’ far-left, high-tax, big-government agenda, Jennifer is focused on providing Western North Carolina families with independent leadership and real results.” 
DCCC spokesperson Madison Andrus criticized a quote from Balkcom’s ad, saying it didn’t reflect when a reporter asked Balkcom if Edwards should resign from Congress.
“‘Tough mountain leadership’ isn’t sitting in pained silence for 15 seconds after being asked if a serial sexual harasser deserves to keep receiving a taxpayer funded salary,” Andrus told NC Newsline.
‘Driving a conversation’
Western North Carolina political science professor Chris Cooper said he thinks the NC-11 race is more interesting than the other 434 congressional districts combined, and these two ads illustrate it.
“We spend so much time talking about nationalized politics and how very few campaigns really represent the place where they’re conducted, and then NC-11 is a big, bright exception to that rule,” Cooper told NC Newsline. “These are two ads that only would have been run in NC-11.”
He estimated Balkcom’s ad has received more attention and criticism than Ager’s, but said that isn’t necessarily a negative. 
Balkcom entered the race on Aug. 10, replacing GOP U.S. Rep. Chuck Edwards after his withdrawal earlier in the month. That left her with roughly four months to campaign before the November election. 
“The biggest problem with the Balkcom campaign to this point has been that she has low name recognition, that people just aren’t aware of who she is, or that she’s running for office,” Cooper said. “Now, because of this ad, she’s being talked about on television and print media and on the radio.”
Without explicitly saying it, the ad tells voters that Balkcom supports the Second Amendment and has the grit to run for office, Cooper said.
“It is driving a conversation around Jennifer Balkcom,” he said. “In today’s environment where we’re being inundated with ads and we’re being inundated with messages, it’s rare that a message gets through and forces you to have a conversation about that person.”

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Peltola’s words create a teachable moment, but an apology is required.
description: This commentary was originally published in the Anchorage Press. Subscribe here.  Mary Peltola’s use of hateful speech, including the R-slur and the F-slur, is more than a political matter. It cuts to the core of who we choose to be: Will we be a people that allows for words like this to be wielded without […]
text:
Mary Peltola speaks at a campaign event in Juneau on May 14, 2026. (Photo by Corinne Smith/Alaska Beacon)This commentary was originally published in the Anchorage Press. Subscribe here. 
Mary Peltola’s use of hateful speech, including the R-slur and the F-slur, is more than a political matter. It cuts to the core of who we choose to be: Will we be a people that allows for words like this to be wielded without consequence? Or do we decide what is acceptable for ourselves, our candidates, our party, and our nation by demanding accountability and apology?
Had anyone else used these terms, the response from the Democratic Party would be swift and unified, so there’s no need to make the case that the hate speech of slurs is abusive. And the Peltola campaign has acknowledged the veracity of many of the worst statements, so the cries of “fake news” are foolish.
The only question that remains is, since these hateful words were used: What should happen next? The way we answer defines who we are and what we choose to allow politics to be. My answer is this: It’s not enough to win an election; we have to be people who deserve to win.



That means that we have to expect and demand compassion from our leaders. Politics is getting uglier and uglier, and the way to work against that is not by following other candidates into their ways of cruelty. It’s by leading the way to something better by acknowledging and apologizing for the times when we fall short.
Mary’s campaign referred to her very real and enormous burden of grief as a factor in her making those statements. That’s fair; grief makes us do and say things we might otherwise not. That still requires a sincere apology. That’s how we can rebuild trust in our democracy, and trust that good and ethical candidates can get elected.
One of the gifts of living in Alaska is that we truly do know our elected officials. We see them at events and we build relationships with them. So this is the time for our candidates to lean in and build trust by acknowledging when harm has occurred, and naming what will be done to protect every constituent going forward. Expecting compassion and apologies for wrongdoing isn’t naive; it’s the foundation of every ethical system on earth. It defines who we are, it builds trust, and it differentiates the Democratic Party from the cruelty of MAGA. It’s how we demonstrate that we deserve to win.
Political machines will tell us to ignore these slurs and downplay the harm that they do to members of our community. But that cannot be who we become. It would be a betrayal of the people in our communities who are targeted by these slurs.
We should instead require basic human decency from all candidates, and apologies for when they fall short of it. If a candidate is unable to reach that very low bar, can we truly say that they deserve to win?
It’s absolutely appropriate to require an unequivocal apology from Mary herself, not a half-apology through a spokesperson. Responses from the Alaska Democratic Party and the candidates that they endorse should also be a bare minimum of thoughtfulness, because silence is also betrayal. I truly believe in grace and forgiveness, but they require an acknowledgment of the harm that has been done.
This is a teachable moment. We can show Alaska and the nation that apologies are a sign of wisdom and strength, that choosing words of compassion matters, and that people of good character can win elections. But if we follow the MAGA playbook of cruelty without apology, then we have forsaken our foundational ethical mandate to love our neighbor. And if we do that, we no longer deserve to win.
