name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Nebraska Supreme Court hears arguments over validity of ‘fairness for girls’ ballot measure
description: Nebraska Supreme Court heard arguments in a lawsuit attempting to disqualify a ballot measure that would cement sex-separate school sports requirements in the state Constitution
text:
The seal of the Nebraska Supreme Court. May 4, 2026. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — The Nebraska Supreme Court heard arguments Wednesday in a lawsuit attempting to disqualify a ballot measure that would cement sex-separate school sports requirements in the state Constitution.
Plaintiff Cara Ullman’s lawyer argued that the ballot measure’s sponsors failed to “adequately inform the public of what they are trying to accomplish.” Lawyers for Nebraska Secretary of State Bob Evnen and the ballot sponsors said the sponsors followed the steps needed to be on the ballot. 
Ullman originally had asked the Nebraska Supreme Court to weigh in earlier in September, but the high court declined. Ullman then went through Lancaster County District Court, where a district court judge dismissed all objections to the case. The Supreme Court decided to hear the appeal. 
The main argument from Ullman’s lawyer, Sydney Hayes, is that the measure’s object statement lacks specificity about what it aims to do, so it doesn’t comply with state law. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“The purpose is essentially to inform the public the gist or the key points of a measure on the very front of the petition page, and while talking to voters and soliciting their signatures,” Hayes said. 
Zachary Pullman, the lawyer for Evnen, said the object statement follows state law because it identifies the legal effect of filing the petition, states the object or goal of the proposed measure, and does so concisely. 
“The best evidence of legislative intent is to look at the text of the statute, and so in deciding, does the object statement accurately capture the proposed measure. We look at the text of the proposed measure itself, and this one again plainly satisfies that test,” Pullman said. 
The ballot is already certified, but the measure will appear on the ballot regardless. However, a successful appeal could invalidate the vote in November. Pullman said that if the court wants to overturn the lower ruling, it would need to do so by Oct. 27, giving state election officials enough time to work out how to withhold the results from the public since the ballot measure would be invalid.  
Former state Sen. Andrew La Grone of Dunbar, on behalf of the three sponsors behind Fairness for Girls, agreed with Pullman’s argument. 
The Fairness for Girls proposal would make permanent part of a 2025 state law that requires public K-12 schools, colleges and universities, and any private schools or colleges in the state that play against those schools, to designate sports and athletic teams as male, female or coed. Male students couldn’t play on female-only teams.
The ballot language wouldn’t define “sex” in the state constitution itself, relying on the definition in state law that was passed last year that defines sex as whether someone “naturally has, had, will or would have, but for a congenital anomaly or intentional or unintentional disruption, the reproductive system that at some point produces, transports and utilizes” either eggs (female) or sperm (male) for fertilization.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Whitmer, reproductive rights advocates urge no vote on ‘devastating’ constitutional convention
description: Gov. Gretchen Whitmer joined reproductive freedom leaders in advocating against a ballot measure that would launch a constitutional convention in Michigan, arguing that it would open the door to removing constitutional protections for abortion access and reproductive rights, which were enshrined in the state constitution through a ballot measure in 2022.  “T[...]
text:
A sign at the Michigan Pride rally in Lansing on June 26, 2022. | Photo by Laina G. StebbinsGov. Gretchen Whitmer joined reproductive freedom leaders in advocating against a ballot measure that would launch a constitutional convention in Michigan, arguing that it would open the door to removing constitutional protections for abortion access and reproductive rights, which were enshrined in the state constitution through a ballot measure in 2022. 
“This is not an attempt to work around the will of the people,” Whitmer said in a virtual press conference Wednesday. “It is an attempt to undo the will of the people, and we can’t let that happen.”
Loren Khogali, executive director of the ACLU of Michigan, emphasized that in opposing this ballot measure, she is not saying that the Michigan Constitution is perfect. 
“What I am saying is that a broad, open-ended constitutional convention poses serious risks to the civil rights and the civil liberties of every person in Michigan. The kind of legal uncertainty and risk that would be opened by a constitutional convention are simply unnecessary,” she said. “Now more than ever, we can’t risk opening up our state constitution to a complete rewrite. Voting no on proposal one will help Michigan avoid the long-lasting consequences and, quite frankly, devastating consequences for our state.”
Paula Thornton Greear, president and CEO of Planned Parenthood Advocates of Michigan, said that passing the ballot measure and convening a constitutional convention would be “gambling with our reproductive freedom.”
Gov. Gretchen Whitmer joins reproductive rights advocates in opposition to a ballot measure that would trigger a constitutional convention in Michigan. Screenshot.
She also focused on the lack of clear guidelines for public oversight of the constitutional convention process — a contrast to the ballot measure that enshrined abortion access in 2022, which happened through a public process of signature gathering and voting. 
“A constitutional convention would look very different,” she said. “It would mean certain people locked away in a Lansing room drafting a constitution on their own terms to serve their own selfish interest. Politicians shouldn’t have the power to make decisions over our lives and bodies. That power belongs to us, the people, and the people have overwhelmingly spoken in support of abortion rights.”
A large coalition of organizations has come out in opposition to the proposal to launch a constitutional convention, including Right to Life of Michigan.
Many opposition groups cite the possibility for special interests to intervene in the process, a sentiment echoed by the reproductive rights advocates on Wednesday’s call. 
“Wealthy donors and anti-abortion extremists want to exploit a constitutional convention,” Sommer Foster, executive director at Michigan Voices, said. “They could use it as a backdoor to rewrite the Michigan Constitution to promote their narrow agenda instead of the will of everyday Michiganders. Constitutional protections and freedoms that Michiganders fought for and currently enjoy under our state constitution would be at risk.”SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Despite wide-ranging opposition, a poll conducted between late August and early September showed that 47% of voters — a plurality, but not a majority — would vote yes on the proposal to hold a constitutional convention. Thirty-one percent said they opposed the proposal, while about 22% remained undecided.
As for how to sway public opinion on the question, Foster noted that the vast majority of Michigan voters have never witnessed a constitutional convention — the last convention was held in the 1960s.
“They don’t know what a constitutional convention would mean for the state,” she said. “For us, we want to use this opportunity in the next 30-some days before the election to make sure we educate people on what a constitutional convention would mean, what’s at risk, and what it would mean for the next couple of years for our state, and how much money would be spent in the ecosystem on a constitutional convention. I think once people get that information, they would be more opposed to the convention.”
Shanay Watson-Whittaker, the director of Michigan campaigns at Reproductive Freedom for All, added that she understands the frustrations of voters with the current Trump administration and their desire for change, but she emphasized the need to make that change by electing candidates who support reproductive rights, rather than through a constitutional convention.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: CT GOP proposes 3-month holiday on state fuel taxes
description: CT Republicans called for suspension of retail taxes on gasoline, diesel fuel through Dec. 31, saving motorists a collective $54M a month.
text:
Connecticut Republicans called Wednesday for suspension of the state’s retail taxes on gasoline and diesel fuel through Dec. 31, a break that would save motorists a collective $54 million per month.
But Gov. Ned Lamont and Democratic legislators counter-challenged the GOP to acknowledge one of the chief factors driving prices at the pump, the U.S. war with Iran begun under President Donald Trump’s administration on Feb. 28.
“The governor saw this coming. Democrats saw this coming,” House Minority Leader Vincent Candelora, R-North Branford, wrote in a statement released midday. “They talked about it in March and then did nothing.”
State Sen. Ryan Fazio of Greenwich, the Republican gubernatorial nominee, said it’s not enough for Lamont to say he raised the prospect of a gasoline tax holiday with the legislature seven months ago.
“He is the governor of the state of Connecticut,” Fazio said. “He has the ability to lead and the responsibility to act. If I were governor and said I wanted to provide relief for Connecticut families, I would act on the things I said I wanted to do.”
The Republican plan would suspend the 25 cents-per-gallon retail tax consumers pay on regular gasoline, and the 49.9 cents-per-gallon levy placed on diesel fuel.
Based on current estimates from state fiscal analysts, those two taxes generate about $42 million and $12 million, respectively, each month.
The GOP plan would not eliminate a third fuel-related tax. Connecticut imposes an effective rate of 8.81% on wholesale transactions involving gasoline and certain other fuels, but not diesel. Based on recent wholesale prices and a capping mechanism, the tax adds another 26.4 cents-per-gallon to the cost of gasoline — an expense retail stations build into the price charged to motorists.
The AAA reported an average retail price Wednesday of $4.48 per gallon for regular gasoline, which is up 28 cents from one month ago. It also reported an average retail price of $6.48 per gallon for diesel, up 78 cents from late August. Diesel set a record high in Connecticut two days ago at just under $6.50.
Democrats said the GOP was noticeably quiet about what has caused higher fuel prices.
“If Republicans have a problem with the price of gas and diesel, they should march their way down to 1600 Pennsylvania Ave. and talk to the head of their party, who sits in the Oval Office, about why he started this pointless, illegal war that has raised gas prices by over 40%,” state Senate Majority Leader Bob Duff, D-Norwalk, said. “Voters know Donald Trump is to blame for high gas and diesel prices, and Republicans can’t hide from that.”
House Speaker Matt Ritter, D-Hartford, added, “We all need to face the reality that state action would minimally impact fuel prices — fuel costs are heavily driven by federal policies.”
Lamont noted fuel tax receipts are one of the chief revenue sources for Connecticut’s Special Transportation Fund which not only supports the state’s Department of Transportation operations, but pays the debt service on the more than $1 billion the state borrows annually to maintain its highways, bridges and rail lines.
“If they want to, you know, forgive the gas tax, just tell me how we keep up our roads and bridges,” the governor added.
But Republicans counter that the transportation fund is flush with cash — partly because of actions Lamont and Democratic lawmakers took last spring.
The $2.4 billion transportation fund is on pace for a 9% surplus, a cushion of nearly $210 million. A three-month holiday would cost about $162 million, still leaving the fund in the black.
One reason for that cushion is that the governor and legislators held onto $100 million from last fiscal year’s transportation fund surplus, rather than allowing the treasurer to use it to pay down bonded debt tied to infrastructure projects.
“Let’s get this [fuel tax holiday] done for middle-class families and job creators,” said Senate Minority Leader Stephen Harding, R-Brookfield. “And this shouldn’t be partisan: We invite Connecticut Democrats to join us in providing this relief for people.”
CT Mirror reporter Ginny Monk contributed to this story.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico U.S. Sen. Luján shares documents related to feds’ fentanyl operations in state
description: U.S. Sen. Ben Ray Luján (D-N.M.) on Sept. 30, 2026, shared four documents related to the U.S. Department of Justice’s reaction to whistleblower concerns about “fentanyl walking” in New Mexico.
text:
U.S. Sen. Ben Ray Luján (D-N.M.) on Sept. 30, 2026, shared four documents related to the U.S. Department of Justice’s reaction to whistleblower concerns about “fentanyl walking” in New Mexico. Pictured above: Cash and drugs seized in Santa Fe and Albuquerque that the U.S. DOJ described at the time as the country's largest-ever fentanyl bust in April, 2025. (Courtesy U.S. District Attorney's Office, District of New Mexico)U.S. Sen. Ben Ray Luján (D-N.M.) on Wednesday shared multiple documents regarding how the federal Drug Enforcement Administration and higher-ups handled a whistleblower’s recent allegations regarding un-seized fentanyl shipments in Albuquerque. 
The U.S. Department of Justice Office of the Inspector General on Aug. 17 announced it was investigating whistleblower complaints alleging that DEA agents monitoring fentanyl shipments in 2024 in New Mexico would routinely stop short of seizing them in hopes of catching bigger traffickers down the line.
The whistleblower’s existence and allegations, first revealed in articles by the Associated Press and Albuquerque Journal, prompted widespread criticism from New Mexico elected officials at the local, state and federal levels over the possibility that the DEA sanctioned the release of hundreds of thousands of fentanyl pills into communities that already have high opioid addiction and overdose rates. 
All five of New Mexico’s U.S. senators and representatives asked the DOJ in a letter earlier this month to extend and expand its probe further back than 2024. DEA whistleblower complaints make reference to these tactics, known as “fentanyl walking,” as far back as 2022, they wrote. 
And in late August, New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez sued federal law enforcement agencies over documents related to their fentanyl investigations in the state. That lawsuit against the DEA and DOJ remains pending. 
Luján’s office announced Wednesday that the senator had received a briefing from the DEA and DOJ and said he “continues to press the federal government for more information to be released to the public.”
The senator shared links to four documents with redactions that related to the whistleblower allegations. They show how the DOJ’s Office of Special Counsel ultimately determined no misconduct occurred nearly two years after the whistleblower filed his complaint. 
The documents include a determination by the U.S. Office of Special Counsel in December 2023 that the whistleblower’s allegations were serious enough to justify a separate USDOJ investigation, followed by the USDOJ’s determination in September 2024 that no misconduct had occurred. 
The documents Luján shared also show the whistleblower shortly afterward disputed the DOJ’s determination and, finally, the Office of Special Counsel agreeing in September 2025 its determination that the DEA committed no misconduct.
“Prosecutors and investigators need to have the flexibility to choose the operational approaches they have concluded are the most effective in combatting drug trafficking throughout the country,” Special Counsel Charlis Baldis wrote on Sept. 4, 2025. “I have concluded that the agency’s approach to these matters is correct.”
While news reports have previously referenced those documents, a Luján spokesperson said he hopes sharing them in full helps New Mexicans “read for themselves” regarding the DEA’s fentanyl investigations in the state. 
“The Senator wanted to bring awareness to these documents as he has been receiving briefings by DEA and DOJ,” Luján spokesperson Adán Serna told Source NM in an email Wednesday.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Oklahoma County killer to seek clemency ahead of November execution
description: OKLAHOMA CITY – A man convicted of gunning down a father of two will ask the Oklahoma Pardon and Parole Board for clemency, saying that he was wrongfully convicted. Oklahoma County killer James Pavatt, 72, faces a November execution for the 2001 shooting death of Robert D. Andrew, 39, an advertising executive. Andrew was fatally […]
text:
Barbed wire and fencing surrounding the Oklahoma State Penitentiary in McAlester is pictured on Sept. 5, 2025. (Photo by Emma Murphy/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY – A man convicted of gunning down a father of two will ask the Oklahoma Pardon and Parole Board for clemency, saying that he was wrongfully convicted.
Oklahoma County killer James Pavatt, 72, faces a November execution for the 2001 shooting death of Robert D. Andrew, 39, an advertising executive. Andrew was fatally shot as he attempted to pick up his two children for a holiday visit.
Andrew and his wife, Brenda, 62, were separated and going through a divorce. Brenda Andrew and Pavatt were having an affair, according to prosecutors, who also alleged a $800,000 life insurance policy was part of the motive. 
Brenda Andrew, who is appealing her own death sentence, is housed at Mabel Bassett Correctional Center in McLoud.
The state alleges Pavatt and Brenda Andrew spent weeks, if not months, planning the murder after an earlier failed attempt in which Robert Andrew’s brake lines were cut. 
After the murder, Pavatt and Brenda Andrew, with the Andrews’ two children, fled to Mexico, prosecutors say.
According to his clemency packet, Pavatt is expected to argue he is innocent, and prosecutors orchestrated his wrongful conviction.
“The reality is that Jim Pavatt has never killed anyone,” according to his clemency packet. “He had never been arrested before this case. He is a decorated, 21-year Air Force master sergeant, a Baptist church deacon and Sunday school teacher, and a University of Oklahoma graduate who the state has never credibly shown was even at the crime scene much less shot victim Rob Andrew.”
Pavatt’s attorneys blame his conviction on prosecutorial misconduct, flawed forensics and an inadequate defense.
The Oklahoma Attorney General’s office said Pavatt was a killer who wanted the life Rob Andrew was living. 
“Rob Andrew was gunned down in his own garage, feet from the children he loved, by the man he had trusted as a friend and insurance agent,” said Oklahoma attorney General Gentner Drummond. “Twenty-five years later, Pavatt still won’t tell the truth about what he did. There must be justice for Rob.”
Pavatt’s clemency hearing is set for 9 a.m. Oct. 14. 
If the Pardon and Parole Board recommends clemency, Gov. Kevin Stitt will have the final word.
In a letter to the Pardon and Parole Board, Rob Andrew’s brothers said their parents, who raised his children, are gone now.
They described the void of his absence in their lives.
“We would let the laws of the State of Oklahoma decide their fate,” they wrote. “Vengeance is not ours. Our brother is gone and we cannot change that.”
His execution by lethal injection is set for Nov. 12 at Oklahoma State Penitentiary in McAlester.

name: Georgia Recorder
title: Georgia voters see tough future for next generation ahead of midterm race, poll finds
description: Georgia’s preschoolers won’t be able to cast a vote this November, but the state’s youngest residents could play a role in deciding the state’s next governor, according to a new poll. Nearly 70% of Georgians say they are pessimistic about children today having a better life than the previous generation, and among parents, that number […]
text:
Amy M. Jacobs (left), commissioner of the Georgia Department of Early Care and Learning, visited pre-K summer transition program classes in northeast Georgia. New polling finds Georgia parents and non-parents are pessimistic about prospects for the next generation and think childcare is too expensive. Photo courtesy of the Georgia Department of Early Care and LearningGeorgia’s preschoolers won’t be able to cast a vote this November, but the state’s youngest residents could play a role in deciding the state’s next governor, according to a new poll.
Nearly 70% of Georgians say they are pessimistic about children today having a better life than the previous generation, and among parents, that number is 78%, according to a new poll released by the Georgia Early Education Alliance for Ready Students asking more than 600 likely voters about policies for families with young children.
Among the respondents, 68% said childcare is too expensive – including 67% of those who are not parents – and 63% of those polled said they would be more likely to vote for a candidate who supports policies that give more families access to quality childcare and preschool.
That includes majorities of Democrats and independent voters. Among Republicans, 38% said they would be more likely to support such a candidate, and 10% said they’d be less likely.
Former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms speaks to reporters at an early childhood education event in Atlanta Sept. 29. Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder.
During a candidate forum hosted by GEEARS in Atlanta this week, the candidates for Georgia governor offered different priorities for policies to improve the life trajectories for preschoolers in the state.
Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms said a top priority for her administration will be to expand access to the state’s universal pre-K program.
Georgia offers free state-funded pre-K classes for all 4-year-olds that have received high marks for quality, but classrooms are more available in some parts of the state than others, and not every child who wants a spot can get one.
“Part of the reason the lottery was approved by voters in Georgia was so that we could properly fund pre-K in this state,” Bottoms said. “Unfortunately, the state has still fallen short in doing that. We claim to have universal pre-K in Georgia. We absolutely do not. It should be a priority. It’s an economic issue as well as an educational issue.”
Bottoms said she wants to make pre-K available to every family that wants it and make 3-year-olds eligible, paying for it by drawing from the Georgia Lottery’s $2 billion unrestricted reserves and by putting it to voters whether to allow casinos to operate in Georgia. Bottoms said doing so could bring up to $500 million per year in revenue.
“We know that we’ve got neighboring states that do have casino gambling, but it would allow us to keep that revenue within the state and then plug any gaps where we can, whether it be with education or healthcare in this state,” Bottoms told reporters. “It could be a significant game changer for our budget, and it can be life-changing for so many people around the state.”
Bottoms said fully expanding Medicaid would help the finances of families with young children and proposed other policies including emphasizing third grade literacy, raising teachers’ starting pay in the state from $48,000 a year to $60,000 and eliminating income taxes for teachers.
Republican gubernatorial candidate Rick Jackson speaks at a Georgia Chamber event in Athens, Aug. 5, 2026. Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder
Republican candidate Rick Jackson did not attend the forum, but sent a short video message outlining his priorities without many details.
Jackson pledged to increase literacy rates for third graders, make healthcare more available, reduce maternal and infant mortality rates and modernize the state Division of Family and Children’s Services.
“I’m not running for a title,” Jackson said. “I’m running to make life better for all Georgians, especially our children who don’t have a voice at the Capitol. They’ll have a voice because I will be helping every child in this state.”

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: As economic damage from climate change grows, NC experts urge ‘pre-recovery’ planning
description: When a slow-moving nor’easter battered the Outer Banks last weekend, the North Carolina Department of Transportation worked around the clock to remove broken asphalt, rebuild the dunes and shore up the vulnerable stretch of NC 12 near Pea Island. It’s a scene that’s played out many times over the past few years. NCDOT engineers estimated […]
text:
NCDOT crews will once again replace sections of Highway 12 after an early season nor'easter in Sept.  2026 heavily damaged the scenic roadway. (Photo: NCDOT) When a slow-moving nor’easter battered the Outer Banks last weekend, the North Carolina Department of Transportation worked around the clock to remove broken asphalt, rebuild the dunes and shore up the vulnerable stretch of NC 12 near Pea Island.
It’s a scene that’s played out many times over the past few years.
NCDOT engineers estimated at a March hearing that over the last 15 years, the state agency has spent nearly $51 million to maintain the NC 12 “hot spots” in Dare County.  Emergency repairs for last week’s nor’easter alone have been pegged at $2.5 million.
The emergency repairs won’t last – they never do. But they’re the only solution when residents are clamoring for a return to normalcy.
Mark Borsuk, Victoria Salinas and Brian McAdoo (Photos: Duke University)
A trio of Duke University climate experts who met with journalists Tuesday said the early-season nor’easter, Hurricane Helene, and scorching summer temperatures all underscore the need for communities and governments to rethink their approach to the changing climate.
Brian McAdoo, a climate science professor, said last weekend’s events were especially unfortunate for the Outer Banks. The nor’easter coincided with a full moon that created extremely high tides.
“[The ocean] had no choice but to wipe out the road,” said McAdoo. “The road’s only a couple feet above sea level, so it’s going to get wiped out again.”
The road keeps getting rebuilt because it’s an economic engine, said McAdoo. While NC 12 is a frequent victim of ocean overwash, the scenic stretch is critical in bringing in an estimated $2.2 billion in annual tourism spending.
‘We’re dumping money into the ocean’: Outer Banks seeks state help for long-term NC 12 fix

But just because the roadway can be rebuilt over and over again doesn’t mean it should, McAdoo said. “I always wondered, why on Earth would somebody want to put a solid structure out on a mobile spit of sand that gets hit by hurricanes and nor’easter all the time?”
Duke’s Climate Leader in Residence is Victoria Salinas, a former FEMA administrator. She said many small and rural communities know where their problem areas are, but lack the resources to fix them.
“They don’t have engineers. They don’t have staff. They don’t have the capacity to do that,” said Salinas. “For others, it may be that they don’t have the revenue.”
That makes building resilience exceedingly hard in this country, Salinas said.
Mark Borsuk, a professor in civil and environmental engineering at Duke University, said the key is to recognize that communities do not need to predict the future perfectly to make good decisions.
“Rather than asking what exactly conditions will look like in 2075, we should really be asking which decisions are likely to work reasonably well across the range of possible futures that we might face,” said Borsuk.
Building back better
Salinas points to building codes as one area where state governments can increase safety from weather-related hazards.
For years North Carolina lawmakers have delayed efforts to strengthen building codes, reasoning that increased regulations would increase costs. They also pushed back on a statewide standard for steep slope construction.
Salinas said stronger building codes would have helped in the aftermath of Hurricane Helene, because FEMA rebuilds to meet existing local codes. “So the communities that have stronger codes actually will get additional resources.”
Torrential rainfall during Hurricane Helene in September 2024 caused significant property damage in Asheville. North Carolina lawmakers have delayed efforts to update building codes, reasoning that increased regulations would increase costs. (Photo: Courtesy of Carly Brown)
It may cost a little bit more to make a building safer, but it will be safer for the next several decades, she said.
“In a post-disaster setting like Helene in North Carolina, having an outdated code in place really reduces the collective leap forward to resilient recovery,” said Salinas.  “It’s a huge opportunity for communities post-disaster to rebuild not for yesterday’s storms, but for the ones they know are coming.”
Borsuk says elected officials face tremendous pressure to restore homes and roads quickly after a climate-related disaster, so that’s not the ideal time to start debating resiliency.
“The planning needs to start early,” said Borsuk. “Communities need to ask themselves in advance of a disaster: What do we need to restore quickly? What should we rebuild differently? What might we decide not to rebuild at all in the same place?”
Charting a new path 
McAdoo, the climate science professor, says poorer communities need more help with climate resiliency.
“We really need to start thinking about how we proactively invest in these smaller, rural, underfinanced communities and figure out clever ways of financing and getting resources to them and improving building codes from the ground up,” said McAdoo.
McAdoo said one community that’s getting it right is Enfield, North Carolina. The small Halifax County town, founded in 1740, has fewer than 2,000 residents, but its leaders have an ambitious vision to improve its aged energy grid.
When the U.S. Department of Energy terminated Enfield’s clean energy grant earlier in the year, Mayor Mondale Robinson and others secured nearly $300,000 in seed money from the nonprofit BuildUS foundation to pilot a geothermal energy system to reduce rising energy costs.
“The geothermal energy network will increase efficiency in the town using geothermal heat pumps,” said McAdoo on Tuesday. “There are insane capabilities to really reduce people’s electric bills here by up to 60% while also reducing carbon footprint.”
A weatherization hub will also offer residents do-it-yourself energy-efficiency workshops to reduce soaring utility costs.
McAdoo said Enfield is thinking proactively about the next climate crisis that isn’t on many people’s radar yet.
“After this year’s El Niño, there will be increased heating in the summer of 2027,” McAdoo said. “It’s really going to be the hottest summer on record.”

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Enrollment up 0.7% at Kansas public universities, totals slip at community and technical colleges
description: Financial and demographic trends diminish enrollment at universities, community colleges and technical colleges coordinated by the Kansas Board of Regents.
text:
Wichita State University suffers the largest enrollment decline — a reduction of 2.5% — among six state universities supervised by the Kansas Board of Regents. Overall, state university enrollment increased 0.7%, while community colleges lost 1.9% and technical colleges enrolled 6.8% fewer students. (Photo by Tim Carpenter/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — A modest enrollment reduction of 0.8% this fall among 32 higher education institutions coordinated by the Kansas Board of Regents obscured more significant declines at five technical colleges, a dozen community colleges and two universities.
The six public universities commonly associated with the state Board of Regents reported a 0.7% increase in headcount, while technical colleges shrank 6.8% and community colleges tumbled 1.9%. Washburn University, a municipal university and its technical college in Topeka, scrambled its enrollment statistics through an administrative adjustment but documented 0.6% growth.
Overall, the regents system enrolled 177,768 students, 1,356 fewer than one year ago. The higher education system chronicled enrollment growth in 2023, 2024 and 2025. The fall 2026 enrollment was 6.5% greater than five years ago amid the COVID-19 pandemic, but 2.7% less than a decade ago.
“After three years of growth, our system is experiencing flat enrollment this fall, with uneven results across sectors and institutions,” said Alysia Johnston, chair of the Board of Regents.
Here are 2026 enrollments at six state universities and the change from 2025: Emporia State University, 5,110, up 6%; Fort Hays State University, 13,359, up 4%; Kansas State University, 20,789, up 0.3%; Pittsburg State University, 5,766, down 0.6%; University of Kansas, 27,352, up 0.5%; and Wichita State University, 18,003, down 2.5%.
The K-State veterinary school’s enrollment didn’t increase from 494 students, and the KU Medical School expanded 3.9% to 4,112 students.
Competition for traditional college-age students has intensified in Kansas and across the United States because of declining birth rates and rising costs.
ESU, FHSU and PSU enrollment fell over the past five years — most significantly by 9% at ESU. In the past decade, ESU shed 13.2% of its students, FHSU dropped 8.9%, K-State fell 10.8% and PSU lost 18.8%. WSU says enrollment grew 24.4% greater over this 10-year period, a trend powered by aggressive recruitment of international students. KU’s enrollment is up over the decade by 9.9%.
“We’re proud that students continue to see the value of a KU education and that more of them are staying on track to earn their degrees,” said KU chancellor Doug Girod.
Girod said combined enrollment of KU’s main campus in Lawrence, a satellite campus in Johnson County and the medical center in Wyandotte County expanded this fall by 295 students to a record 31,464. The 4,834-student freshman class at KU was the fourth largest in university history, he said, despite a 4.1% decline from new freshman enrollment in 2025.
Enrollment at K-State on campuses in Manhattan, Salina and Olathe reached 21,283 this fall. That represented the highest total since 2020.
“These steady enrollment numbers are proof of the success we’ve had in articulating the value of a K-State degree and the long-term rate of return it has for those who choose to become Wildcats,” said Jesse Perez Mendez, the provost at K-State.

Wichita State enrolled 455 fewer students this fall in wake of the stunning $16.2% decline in graduate student enrollment. WSU’s international student enrollment in graduate school crashed 23.9%.
“This year’s enrollment reflects both the opportunities and challenges facing higher education,” said Richard Muma, the president of WSU.

Overall enrollment at Kansas’ technical colleges fell 6.8% to 11,412 this fall. The shift ranged from a reduction of 29% at Flint Hills Technical College to a drop of 0.8% at Wichita State’s technical college. The state’s technical school enrollment — driven in the past by the Legislature’s investment in tuition subsidies — remained 20% higher than five years ago and 47% greater than 10 years ago.
Kansas enrollment at 19 community colleges eroded this fall by 1.9% to 63,605 students — a loss of 1,246. While Highland Community College reported growth of 12.3%, Pratt Community College plummeted 12.9%. More than half of enrollment shifts at community colleges were plus or minus 5%.
In 2026, the Kansas Legislature made changes to a program allowing high school students to enroll in subsidizing career and technical courses offered at community and technical colleges. The new rules limited enrollment to high school juniors and seniors and restricted college-credit to those students with a minimum 2.0 grade-point average. The alterations were expected to drive down student enrollment.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Large upgrade planned at Calvert Cliffs after power deal signed with Amazon
description: Constellation is planning massive upgrades at the Calvert Cliffs nuclear plant after signing a 20-year power purchase deal with Amazon.
text:
The Calvert Cliffs Nuclear Power Plant Units 1 and 2 are located near Lusby. Photo by the Nuclear Regulatory Commission. Constellation, the owner of Maryland’s Calvert Cliffs nuclear plant, said Wednesday it plans to move forward with massive upgrades at the facility after signing a 20-year power purchase deal with data center operator Amazon.
While the financial specifics of the deal remain confidential, Constellation officials said that because of the funding pledge from Amazon the company now plans to spend $3 billion on “state-of-the-art improvements” for the facility, located in Southern Maryland’s Lusby.
The agreement with Amazon will also “help provide Constellation with the revenue certainty to relicense the plant for another 20 years,” according to a company news release. Licenses for the two reactors expire in 2034 and 2036, according to the Nuclear Regulatory Commission.
Beginning between 2030 and 2032, the plant will be able to provide approximately 190 megawatts of additional energy to the grid, enough to power about 147,000 American homes.
“That’s a home run for Maryland,” said David Dardis, Constellation’s senior executive vice president and chief external affairs and growth officer, in an interview with Maryland Matters. “We think it’s a great transaction for our customer — and for us.”
A large deal like this one is a “huge step” toward deciding to continue operating the facility for another two decades, Dardis said.
Joe Dominguez, CEO of Constellation Energy, at an October 2025 news conference at the Conowingo Dam (Photo by Christine Condon/Maryland Matters)
“Without an agreement like this, and the certainty it provides, you have to make projections about future power prices,” Dardis said. “And one thing we know about future power prices is: We’re always wrong.”
Under the power purchase deal, the energy from Calvert doesn’t flow directly to Amazon data centers elsewhere in the region. All of the power produced by the facility will still flow onto the regional grid for all customers to use, Dardis said.
“Nothing about this agreement changes that,” Dardis said.
But the power deal does give Amazon a degree of certainty about its power costs and supply in the region over the next few decades.
“Amazon is committed to investing in carbon-free energy to strengthen the grid and benefit the communities where we operate,” said a statement from Kerry Person, the Amazon Web Services vice president for global operations and data center delivery.
Less than two months ago, Amazon Web Services backed out of a plan to construct a hyperscale data center campus on the Calvert Cliffs site, amid strong pushback from the community. In June’s primary election, voters ousted all three county commission members who had opposed a data center moratorium.
Constellation is still willing to consider placing a data center or another large customer at Calvert Cliffs, Dardis said, but as of now, “nothing is in the works.”
“We’re open to considering those sorts of arrangements, but we would only do so in partnership with Calvert County and other important stakeholders,” Dardis said.
The Calvert Cliffs Clean Energy Center, located on the western shore of the Chesapeake Bay, accounted for 38% of Maryland’s energy generation in 2025, according to the Energy Information Administration. Still, the state uses five times more energy than it generates, and relies heavily on the regional grid, operated by PJM Interconnection.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
“This agreement demonstrates how private investment can strengthen critical energy infrastructure,” said Joe Dominguez, Constellation’s chairman, president and CEO, in a statement. “Amazon’s commitment supports the long-term operation of Calvert Cliffs for generations to come and creates a strong foundation for future investment in both the facility and in advanced nuclear technologies.”
Constellation, a Fortune 200 company headquartered in Baltimore, considers itself the largest private-sector power producer in the world, with power generating facilities that have the capacity to power the equivalent of 27 million homes. Constellation and Amazon have also entered into a related retail supply agreement to support Amazon operations in the 13-state PJM market, according to Wednesday’s news release.
The agreement with Amazon covers 690 megawatts worth of power from the 1,790-megawatt plant — which will expand to 1,980 megawatts after the upgrade.
Constellation will likely continue to seek other long-term contracts with other power users in Maryland, Dardis said. That could include Maryland’s power utilities, who could use power purchase agreements to “hedge” their power costs, he added.
“We think that would be a prudent thing for them to do, at least for a portion of them,” Dardis said. “That’s prudent risk management, and we welcome those conversations.”
Thanks to the funding from Amazon, Constellation also said Wednesday that it plans to evaluate the possibility of new small modular nuclear reactors on the Calvert Cliffs site.
The Constellation Energy building in Baltimore’s Harbor Point. (Photo by Christine Condon/Maryland Matters)
“The only way you can get that done is to have a big company like AWS leaned into those opportunities,” Dardis said.
These power purchase deals are not unfamiliar to Constellation, which plans to reopen the Three-Mile Island nuclear plant, now renamed the Crane Clean Energy Center, in Pennsylvania next year, thanks to a 20-year agreement with Microsoft.
In June 2025, Constellation inked a 20-year power purchase deal with Meta for the Clinton Clean Energy Center in Illinois, which was expected to support its relicensing and add an additional 30 megawatts of capacity to the plant.
That plant had been slated for premature closure in 2017 because of financial losses, before the Illinois legislature stepped in with a zero-emission credit program that was set to last through mid-2027.
And the power deals aren’t just with big tech companies. Earlier this year, Constellation also agreed to a 176-megawatt nuclear power purchase deal in Illinois with Walmart.
But the power purchase agreement with Amazon is “a little bit unique,” Dardis said, because of the large amount of energy involved.
“690 megawatts is a big contract for us — and generally speaking, in the industry,” Dardis said. “A huge value of competitive markets is that customers like Amazon or Walmart … are able to go out into the market and find solutions that work for them.”

name: Daily Montanan
title: Montana officials praise repeal of power plant emission regulations, watchdog groups pan decision
description: Montana officials cheered a move by the Trump administration to roll back greenhouse gas emissions requirements for U.S. power plants, while environmental groups decried the change, which has already drawn one legal challenge. Last week, the Environmental Protection Agency proposed the new rules, arguing they will save the country $310 billion. “For over 15[...]
text:
Colstrip Power Plant (Photo by Darrell Ehrlick of the Daily Montanan).Montana officials cheered a move by the Trump administration to roll back greenhouse gas emissions requirements for U.S. power plants, while environmental groups decried the change, which has already drawn one legal challenge.
Last week, the Environmental Protection Agency proposed the new rules, arguing they will save the country $310 billion.
“For over 15 years, the Obama and Biden administrations implemented a war on coal to destroy reliable and affordable energy. The Trump Administration has come in to protect American energy and to make sure you can afford to keep the lights on,” said EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin in a statement announcing the repeal. “Americans will see a decrease in electricity prices, but this is just the beginning. We are working to go even further so that American energy can be fully unleashed.”
The final rule repealing carbon pollution standards for fossil fuel-fired power plants was published in the Federal Register on Sept. 14, kicking off a 45-day public comment period before taking effect on Nov. 16. 
The rollback includes repealing most of the federal greenhouse gas requirements for fossil fuel-fired power plants adopted during the Biden Administration in 2024. The EPA also issued a companion proposal that will go further and rescind all greenhouse gas emission requirements from fossil fuel-fired electric generating plants. 
Documents supporting the new rule say that many of the technologies the requirements are based on — such as carbon capture and sequestration — have “not been adequately demonstrated, are unachievable, (and) threaten to impose massive costs on the power sector.”
Players in the energy sector praised the Trump administration for the move. 
That includes NorthWestern Energy, Montana’s monopoly utility which is majority owner in Colstrip — the state’s largest coal-fired power plant — and operates the natural gas-fired Laurel Generating Station.
In 2024, NorthWestern argued before the U.S. Supreme Court to halt Biden’s emission rules, claiming it would cost $350 million to upgrade Colstrip or lead to the plant shutting down, calling the rules “economically irrational.”
A spokesperson for the utility said that it “supports regulations that protect reliable, affordable energy, service reliability, and the environment.”
But advocacy groups and energy watchdogs say the move is a step backwards for the environment and public health. 
Anne Hedges, Executive Director of the Montana Environmental Information Center, told the Daily Montanan that Treasure State residents know the impacts of pollution-induced climate change, which include reduced snowpacks and increased wildfires. 
“These impacts are costly to people’s health, agricultural operations, wildlife, fisheries, and the state’s economy,” Hedges said in an email. “It’s irresponsible to roll back extremely modest regulations that provide a reasonable path to reduce the pollution that impacts our climate. Such an action goes against the will of the majority of Montanans and defies common sense.”
A group of public health and environmental groups, including the American Lung Association and Environmental Defense Fund, have filed a federal lawsuit seeking a review of the EPA’s actions. 
In Montana, state and federal elected officials, all Republicans, have echoed the Trump administration’s praise for the rollback. 
“The EPA has put an end to the weaponization of the federal government against coal-generated power which threatened coal mines across the nation,” Gov. Greg Gianforte said in a statement. Under the leadership of Trump and Zeldin, “America’s coal-fired and natural gas power plants can continue to support thousands of jobs and provide affordable, reliable baseload power while ensuring public health and the environment are protected.”
Outgoing U.S. Sen. Steve Daines also said he was “thrilled” at the EPA’s announcement, adding that he believes it will save millions of dollars and provide much-needed jobs for Americans. 
The EPA is holding a virtual public hearing on the proposed rollback on Oct. 1 from, 11 a.m., to 6 p.m. Individuals wishing to speak can sign up online. Public comments will be accepted until Nov. 2

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Deadline hits for law agencies to remove license plate readers from state roads
description: Local law enforcement agencies in Florida were required to remove Flock-style license plate readers on state-owned land and right-of-ways on Wednesday. Those actions were required after Gov. Ron DeSantis expressed concern about data privacy and misuse of that technology last month. That led the Florida Department of Transportation (FDOT) to issue a memorandu[...]
text:
Flock automated license reader as captured on Aug. 5, 2026. (Photo by Valentin Termite/Idaho Capital Sun)Local law enforcement agencies in Florida were required to remove Flock-style license plate readers on state-owned land and right-of-ways on Wednesday.
Those actions were required after Gov. Ron DeSantis expressed concern about data privacy and misuse of that technology last month. That led the Florida Department of Transportation (FDOT) to issue a memorandum revoking existing permits for automated license plate recognition (APLR) systems installed within the right of way within the state highway system, effective Sept. 30.
The decision has received pushback from some law enforcement officials and mayors, who say that the problem isn’t with the technology, but with rogue officers.
“Don’t throw the baby out with the bathwater,” Pinellas County Sheriff Bob Gualtieri said Wednesday during a press conference to announce that two deputies had been arrested following allegations of misusing license plate reading cameras.
“It solves homicides and rapes and returns people with dementia and Alzheimer’s to their loved ones. It is a very, very productive and beneficial public safety tool. But what we have to do is make sure our people use it properly and adhere when there’s consequences to misuse.”
Gualtieri reported that one of the deputies arrested searched the license plate of a woman he was interested in dating 300 times, 207 of them while off duty. The other officer ran the license plate number of a 17-year-old he was romantically interested in.
Law enforcement agencies have been using APLR cameras for years — Gualtieri said Wednesday that Pinellas has used them for 20 years — but concerns about privacy and abuse of the technology by law enforcement officers erupted this summer across the country, with more than 150 local governments choosing to deactivate or cancel their contracts with APLR vendors, according to DeFlock, an advocacy group that tracks the cameras.
While Flock Safety is the best-known and most used license plate reading company in the country with an approximately 82% market share with law enforcement agencies, there are other ALPR companies as well, as reported by NewsNation.
‘Where is this data going?’ 
“There’s obviously times when I think that it’s probably been useful, but where is this data going?” DeSantis said during a news conference in late August. “How much data are the companies doing? They claim that the companies are going to misuse it, but nobody’s watching that.”
The governor said that while he was certain that nearly every sheriff in Florida could point to a situation in which Flock-style license plate-reading cameras were used appropriately and “probably effectively,” he was concerned about how the data could be misused.
The two men running to succeed DeSantis in office, Byron Donalds and David Jolly, have said they support DeSantis’ action.
A number of Florida sheriffs immediately responded to DeSantis’ concerns, announcing they were discontinuing the cameras’ use in their counties, even though some didn’t appear happy to be doing so.
“Please know that the majority of the Board of County Commissioners’ lack of support for this agreement will impact the solvability of crimes and our ability to locate missing and endangered children and adults, including the victims of human trafficking,” wrote Pasco County Sheriff Chris Nocco in a letter to the commission announcing his agency would terminate their use.
Miami Beach Mayor Steven Meiner and six other South Florida mayors contacted Gov. DeSantis and FDOT Secretary Jared Perdue on Sept. 1 expressing opposition to the memo and requesting an immediate pause on the enforcement of the agency’s request “pending consultation with affected municipalities.”
Other high-profile Florida sheriffs such as Gualtieri and Polk County’s Grady Judd have said they will continue to use these cameras but would comply with the ban on state right-of-way.
Gualtieri said Wednesday that “misuse” of such systems by officers isn’t anything new, and that there invariably will be “people who just do bad things and stupid stuff” in any profession. But he said he understands the need for accountability.
“I wholeheartedly support having a discussion and having greater guardrails on this and making sure that there are harsher consequences for misuse, and that we do everything we can to make sure that the public has confidence in what we’re doing,” he said.
The arrest of the two sheriff’s deputies in Pinellas County now make 27 law enforcement officers who have been placed on leave, fired, or arrested regarding the cameras, according to an investigation by TCPalm. One Central Florida police officer was arrested last month after being accused of using the technology to track his estranged wife’s vehicle 717 times over a 21-month period.

title: Colorado awards $1M for projects to deter human-bear conflicts
description: Colorado is distributing $1 million across the state to fund projects designed to lower the number of run-ins between humans and hungry black bears seeking trashcan meals. The latest round of the Colorado Parks and Wildlife’s Human-Bear Conflict Reduction Grants will fund 17 projects, the state announced Tuesday. Since its creation in 2021, the grant […]
text:
A black bear. (Photo by Jason Clay/CPW)Colorado is distributing $1 million across the state to fund projects designed to lower the number of run-ins between humans and hungry black bears seeking trashcan meals.
The latest round of the Colorado Parks and Wildlife’s Human-Bear Conflict Reduction Grants will fund 17 projects, the state announced Tuesday. Since its creation in 2021, the grant program has doled out $3.9 million.
“Our quality of life, plentiful outdoor recreation opportunities, and jaw-dropping landscapes attract both families and animals to our state,” Gov. Jared Polis said in a statement. “That’s why these common-sense and data-driven strategies are so important to reduce human-bear conflicts and ensure that all Coloradans and wildlife are safe.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The funded projects include $100,000 for Manitou Springs to give residents bear-resistant trash bins, $35,000 for a dumpster enclosure system at a new preschool in Eagle, $33,000 for the YMCA of Northern Colorado to install permanent infrastructure like electric fencing and $100,000 for Minturn to build a secure trash system for its commercial district.
Bear sightings in Colorado’s mountain towns — and even urban centers — have made headlines this summer. CPW believes a bear is responsible for dozens of garage break-ins in Littleton. Just in September, bears scratched a man in his backyard in Steamboat Springs, bit a woman at a campground near South Fork and broke into a teenage girl’s bedroom in Durango. And in Denver, a bear climbed into a tree in the Platt Park neighborhood in late August.
There have been 10 confirmed bear attacks this year, according to CPW, the most on record.
Bears seek human food, such as discarded food in trash cans, when their natural diet is limited by events like late freezes or a prolonged drought, according to a 2015 report from CPW. From mid-August to late September, bears are hungrier than usual as they prepare for hibernation.
“Because black bears can quickly become conditioned to seek human-provided food when it is made available, bear conflicts frequently reoccur in given locations,” the report says. That also means bears will return to a location where they’ve found food before.
CPW advises Coloradans to not leave trash outside, keep bird feeders high off the ground and away from trees ,and store pet food inside.

name: National
title: Republican AGs sue abortion ‘shield law’ states in U.S. Supreme Court
description: BATON ROUGE, La. — Louisiana Attorney General Liz Murrill and the attorneys general in Arkansas and Alabama filed a lawsuit Tuesday in the U.S. Supreme Court, suing California, Massachusetts and New York to invalidate the so-called “shield laws” that have allowed providers in those states to send abortion medication to people in states with abortion […]
text:
Louisiana Attorney General Liz Murrill speaks at a news conference in Baton Rouge, Louisiana, on Wednesday, Sept. 30, 2026, announcing a lawsuit challenging abortion shield laws in Democratic-led states. Joining Murrill were Attorneys General Steve Marshall of Alabama, left, and Tim Griffin of Arkansas, whose states are also plaintiffs in the case. (Photo by Piper Hutchinson/Louisiana Illuminator)BATON ROUGE, La. — Louisiana Attorney General Liz Murrill and the attorneys general in Arkansas and Alabama filed a lawsuit Tuesday in the U.S. Supreme Court, suing California, Massachusetts and New York to invalidate the so-called “shield laws” that have allowed providers in those states to send abortion medication to people in states with abortion bans.
The state officials, all Republicans, also filed a lawsuit in federal district court against individual abortion providers in the same three states.
“We will not allow activist states, activist providers or distributors profiting from killing babies to threaten Louisiana’s sovereignty, violate Louisiana’s laws and endanger Louisiana women and Louisiana babies,” Murrill said at a news conference on Tuesday. Arkansas Attorney General Tim Griffin and Alabama Attorney General Steve Marshall of Alabama also were present.
The lawsuit filed in the Western District of Louisiana seeks to stop the individual providers named from being able to prescribe and send abortion medication to those states, while the Supreme Court complaint asks the justices to find the shield laws are a constitutional violation of state sovereignty..
“Today, plaintiff states filed a lawsuit against as many organizations and individuals as they have been able to identify notwithstanding the shield laws intended to thwart such litigation,” the Supreme Court complaint reads. “To fully obtain relief, however, they must also eliminate other contributing causes for the harm that they are suffering, including … the shield laws.”
The district court suit names 30 defendants, including the Massachusetts Medication Abortion Access Project and its founder, Angel Foster, Dr. Remy Coeytaux in California and other telehealth providers around the country.
The complaint compares the mailing of abortion medication to anthrax, mail bombs and chemical weapons, despite studies since 2000 showing that abortion medication  is safe and effective to use.
“(Defendants) think themselves invincible because their agents swear to never step foot in plaintiff states (thereby avoiding arrest), and their home states have enacted so-called ‘shield laws’ intended to thwart legal liability for individuals perpetrating this interstate abortion scheme,” the complaint says.
Following the U.S. Supreme Court’s decision in 2022 allowing states to ban abortion at any stage of pregnancy, 13 states now have near-total bans, while others have expanded abortion access. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration allowed the drug mifepristone, one of two commonly used to terminate a pregnancy in the first trimester or to treat miscarriages, to be dispensed without a visit to an in-person provider in 2023, after years of safety studies.
Providers in states with access can prescribe and mail the medication to states with bans, and Murrill, along with other state AGs, has tried to extradite those providers to Louisiana to face legal charges for violating the ban. One of the providers Murrill tried to extradite in January was Coeytaux in California. Governors in those states have refused to comply with the extradition requests.
To protect those providers, California, Massachusetts and New York were among the 22 states and the District of Columbia that passed shield laws to block out-of-state investigations and prosecutions against providers dispensing for abortion medications to patients in other states.
Murrill is also leading a lawsuit against the FDA to reverse the 2023 provision allowing telehealth access to mifepristone, and two other lawsuits of a similar nature are ongoing in Missouri and Texas. The 5th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals heard arguments in Louisiana’s case earlier this month and is expected to issue a decision in the coming weeks about the future of nationwide access to the drug.
Stateline reporter Kelcie Moseley-Morris can be reached at kmoseley@stateline.org.
Louisiana Illuminator reporter Piper Hutchinson contributed to this report.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Lexington brewery owner’s email prompts questions about Kentucky campaign finance laws
description: An email from a Lexington brewery owner about a Sept. 23 fundraiser for one of the Kentucky legislature’s top Republicans has sparked questions about campaign donation laws.  Last week, an email from Andrew Bishop, an owner of Ethereal Brewing, circulated online from a now-deleted Reddit post on the Lexington subreddit. Copies of the email can […]
text:
Ethereal Brewing Public House is in the middle of a controversy over campaign donations for a GOP fundraiser held there. (Kentucky Lantern photo by Linda Blackford)An email from a Lexington brewery owner about a Sept. 23 fundraiser for one of the Kentucky legislature’s top Republicans has sparked questions about campaign donation laws. 
Last week, an email from Andrew Bishop, an owner of Ethereal Brewing, circulated online from a now-deleted Reddit post on the Lexington subreddit. Copies of the email can still be found on other sites, like Facebook. The screenshot did not include recipients of the email, but Bishop referred to an upcoming fundraiser for Rep. Jason Petrie, an Elkton Republican who chairs the House’s budget committee. 
“We are doing an in-kind donation. I know how sensitive everyone is to donations to politicians, so we’ve made it easier for you. We are donating roughly $4,500 worth of food, beverage, and rental fee and are asking membership to help by reimbursing us. This way, no one will have to worry about campaign disclosures or names being associated with this donation,” Bishop wrote, before asking that those receiving the email make checks out to the company’s Public House or pay via Venmo or CashApp. 
When asked about the email by the Kentucky Lantern, Bishop said he had been in charge of the legislative affairs for the Kentucky Guild of Brewers for about a month “and had not been fully caught up to speed on the legal aspects of the job.”
Bishop said in an email Wednesday to the Lantern his initial email “was poorly worded and did not reflect the intent of sending it.” 
“I have to own my ignorance to what the email was implying and my mistake in sending it, but there was no intent to hide anything nor was anything hidden,” Bishop said. “I sent it to my peers to help offset the costs of highlighting the industry as well as Lexington.” 
In their criticism, social media users questioned if the reimbursement process described in the email followed state campaign finance laws. They also debated if Petrie’s politics matched those of liberal Lexington beer scene customers.
“The $4,500 was a rough max estimate for planning purposes since we did not know the crowd size. The actual in-kind donation (food and beverages) was $1,134.00,” Bishop continued. “All in-kind contributions were fully disclosed and reported in accordance with all applicable laws. Including providing the itemized invoice of all food and beverages. All in-kind contributions were in accordance with law in regard to being reimbursed by private individuals. As I understand, the financial disclosures will be available publicly to reflect this on the next reporting cycle.”
Bishop emphasized that the fundraiser was “not an Ethereal Brewing event.”
“We were invited to participate in an attempt to highlight the industry and the culture of Lexington,” he said. “The event was a candidate sponsored event in conjunction with the Kentucky Republican Party and as part of highlighting Fayette Co/Lexington. The private event was held at one of our brewery locations on September 23rd, at our ‘public House’ — we were the venue.”
Rep. Jason Petrie, R-Elkton (LRC Public Information)
Adam Hope, a spokesperson for the Republican Party of Kentucky said “the party didn’t host the event” and “it was on behalf of the campaign.” He added “the party was unaware” of Bishop’s initial email shared online and “did not have anything to do with it being sent out.” 
Campaign finance rules
John Steffen, the executive director of the Kentucky Registry of Election Finance, said the registry is “certainly aware” of the social media posts, but could not “confirm or deny at this time whether we have received any complaints about it or whether we are investigating the matter” in a Tuesday email to the Lantern. 
“Based on the social media post alone, there are certainly concerns about what really transpired, and what, if anything, the candidate himself actually knew about the plans laid out in the post,” Steffen said. “We don’t know whether Rep. Petrie had any involvement in the planning, we just know what the host posted about the event.” 
Steffen said without knowing more about what happened during the fundraiser “some of the concerns would be the fact that corporate contributions to candidates are strictly prohibited, and that the individual contribution limit to candidates is $3500 per election.” 
State law prohibits someone from making a contribution to a political candidate or committee on their behalf, Steffen noted. Another law says that candidates, committees or other political groups “shall not conspire with an individual or other entity to disguise an illegal contribution as an in-kind contribution.” 
“So yes, the reimbursement referred to in the email COULD be a violation of campaign finance laws IF they actually took place as described in the email,” he added. “But at this point we still have no idea how things were actually handled or how they will be reported to us.” 
Petrie did not return a phone call or emails from the Lantern seeking comment. 
Ethereal Brewing also shared a lengthy post about the situation online Saturday. 
“We have heard your concerns and we would like to apologize for the email that was sent out — it was very poorly worded and held a lot of negative implications,” the post said. “We did not do our due diligence in making sure what we’re saying was completely accurate. Our in-kind donation of food and beverage service was disclosed in accordance with the law, but we take full responsibility for the email and any repercussions from it. Period.” 
Ahead of the fundraiser, the Fayette County Republican Party posted a flier about the event online, with the words “Paid for by the Jason Petrie Campaign Fund” at the bottom, that included information about how to RSVP and make donations to the campaign.
Petrie is not facing an opponent this fall in the 16th House District, which includes Logan, Todd and part of Christian counties in Western Kentucky.

title: Justice Department indicts 10 noncitizens in quest to prove Trump claims of election fraud
text: A federal grand jury indicted 10 noncitizens for unlawfully voting in Minnesota, U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche said Wednesday, highlighting the administration’s effort to keep election security a top issue, in line with President Donald Trump’s longstanding unsubstantiated claims of voter fraud.The indictments, which include nine counts of unlawful voting and nine counts of falsely claiming citizenship to register to vote, bring the number of noncitizens charged nationwide with election-related crimes since Trump re-took office last year to 90. The census reports 154 million people voted in the 2024 election.Blanche said at a news conference at Justice Department headquarters in Washington, D.C., that the indictments show how seriously the administration takes election security.“We have talked repeatedly about the importance of election integrity, and we're certainly not going to stop talking about that now,” he said. “Voter fraud erodes the public's trust in our electoral system, and it's vital to our democratic process that we do everything that we can to restore that trust.”Blanche’s participation in a press conference, alongside fellow Cabinet member Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, underlined the administration’s continuing focus on noncitizen voting, though numerous studies have shown it to be rare. Trump has for years amplified debunked conspiracy theories centered on election fraud.Mullin made that connection explicit Wednesday, saying the indictments confirmed Trump’s accusations.“The president said it for a long time, and the Democrats were sitting there denying it and saying, ‘There's no fraud. That wasn't taking place. There's no fraud. There's nothing, nothing here. Don't look over here,’” he said. “We're realizing there's actually a lot. And we believe that some of these states probably even knew about it, chose not to look into it. Well, we are.”But the allegations of illegal voting in Minnesota in the 2022 and 2024 general elections and 2026 primaries made virtually no difference to election results. The seven alleged illegal votes in the 2024 presidential election, for example, would account for only .0002% of votes cast in that election in Minnesota.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Health department can’t change Oklahoma gender designations on birth certificate, court rules
description: OKLAHOMA CITY – State law has never allowed changes to the sex designation on Oklahoman’s birth certificates, the state’s high court ruled. The Oklahoma Supreme Court issued the 6-3 ruling on Tuesday following questions from a federal appellate court stemming from a lawsuit filed by three transgender individuals who sought to change the sex designation […]
text:
The Oklahoma Judicial Center is the headquarters of the Oklahoma Supreme Court and Court of Criminal Appeals. (Photo by Carmen Forman/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY – State law has never allowed changes to the sex designation on Oklahoman’s birth certificates, the state’s high court ruled.
The Oklahoma Supreme Court issued the 6-3 ruling on Tuesday following questions from a federal appellate court stemming from a lawsuit filed by three transgender individuals who sought to change the sex designation on their birth certificates.
The three requested the Oklahoma State Department of Health make changes to their sex designations after obtaining  state court orders requiring it.
The Oklahoma State Department of Health refused, saying a 2024 executive order issued by Gov. Kevin Stitt barred the changes.
The executive order said a 2021 settlement agreement entered into by the Oklahoma State Department of Health was not authorized by Stitt’s administration and required amending birth certificates in a manner not permitted under law.
Starting around 2007, some people had obtained court orders directing the health department to amend birth certificates to match their gender identity, the order said.
The court said that the practice was “largely non-adversarial and persisted with little notoriety” until 2021 when the health department entered into a settlement enabling someone to obtain an amended birth certificate with a gender neutral designation.
The settlement prompted Stitt’s executive order, the order said.
The court said Tuesday that birth certificates may be amended when a name change is needed, to demonstrate paternity of a child born to unmarried individuals or to change a child’s surname.
The court found that state law prohibits amending a birth certificate to change the male or female sex designation assigned at birth even if someone’s gender identity does not align.
State administrative code also allows a birth certificate to be amended if the registrant’s name needs to be added, to correct an erroneous name or other changes to correct a misstatement of fact, according to the order.
No provision of administrative code allows a sex change designation on a birth certificate, the court order said.

title: Eastern Kentucky county gets biggest investment in its history, officials say
description: Speed Kentucky plans to open a $1.47 million facility in Owsley County and employ 60 people who will work on “final assembly and distribution” of the company’s utility task vehicles, Gov. Andy Beshear said Wednesday.  This is the “largest investment and job creation announcement” in the county’s history, Beshear said. Owsley County, in Eastern Kentucky, […]
text:
Speed Kentucky, a new business in Owsley County, will hold a ribbon cutting on Oct. 2, 2026. (Photo courtesy City of Booneville)Speed Kentucky plans to open a $1.47 million facility in Owsley County and employ 60 people who will work on “final assembly and distribution” of the company’s utility task vehicles, Gov. Andy Beshear said Wednesday. 
This is the “largest investment and job creation announcement” in the county’s history, Beshear said. Owsley County, in Eastern Kentucky, is home to about 4,000 people. According to U.S. Census Bureau data, the median household income was $22,188 from 2020-2024 and about 40% of the population was in the labor force. 
Jimmy Lewis, cofounder of Speed Kentucky, said in a statement that the company is “proud to call Owsley County, Kentucky, home and look forward to growing alongside this incredible community.”
Robby Gordon, also a cofounder of Speed Kentucky, and a renowned motorsports champion from North Carolina, said the state’s “strong outdoor and industrial communities make it a great place to grow this part of our business, including opportunities connected to the region’s coal and natural resource industries.”  
It’s unclear when the facility will open. As long as the company creates and maintains 60 full time jobs for Kentucky residents over 15 years and pays them an hourly rate of $26 an hour, it can receive $1.3 million in tax incentives from the state, Beshear’s office said.  
The Kentucky Economic Development Finance Authority has also approved up to $30,000 in tax incentives through the Kentucky Enterprise Initiative Act (KEIA) for Speed Kentucky, according to Beshear’s office, and it may be able to keep part of its generated tax revenue. 
Senate President Robert Stivers, R-Manchester, whose district includes Owsley County, said the region “was built for this kind of partnership.” 
“This investment is about more than Owsley County,” Stivers said in a statement. “It strengthens a regional asset that will draw people from across Eastern Kentucky and neighboring states, bringing visitors, supporting local businesses and creating economic opportunities throughout this region.”
