name: Source New Mexico
title: Vast majority of New Mexicans want state legislators held to higher ethical standard, poll finds
description: A poll that a New Mexico think tank commissioned as part of a new push for legislative ethics reform found that only 43% of New Mexico residents trust state lawmakers to do what is right all or most of the time.
text:
More than three-quarters of New Mexicans say they support holding New Mexico lawmakers to a higher ethical standard, according to a new poll commissioned by think tank Think New Mexico. (Patrick Lohmann/Source NM)A poll that a New Mexico think tank commissioned as part of a new push for legislative ethics reform found that only 43% of New Mexico residents trust state lawmakers to do what is right all or most of the time. 
New Mexicans’ lack of trust in the state Legislature echoed multiple times in responses to different questions that BSP Research posed during survey interviews between late July and early August of 800 New Mexico registered voters. 
Gabe Sanchez, a University of New Mexico political science professor and director of research at the polling firm, described the survey during a presentation Wednesday morning as likely the largest-ever poll of New Mexicans’ views of legislative ethics reform.
The firm surveyed 345 men and 455 women. Of the respondents, 271 identified as Hispanic and 420 identified as white. The firm’s methodology notes that responses were weighted to ensure demographics of those surveyed match the U.S. Census’ New Mexico statistics, which describe the state as 49.4% Hispanic and 50.6% female. 
Think New Mexico, a nonpartisan think tank that has previously pushed for legislative reforms to healthcare, education and the state pension fund, commissioned the poll as it pushes for lawmaker ethics reforms at the upcoming legislative session next year. 
The think tank recently released a report that calls on the Legislature to strengthen lobbyist disclosure requirements; improve conflict-of-interest policies for lawmakers; and close loopholes that enable funders of out-of-state political action committees to avoid being identified.
Think New Mexico’s ethics reform effort comes as the Legislature undergoes several “modernization” pushes, including the hiring of paid district legislative aides and opening of district offices. 
And, on the Nov. 3 general election ballot, voters will decide whether lawmakers can collect a salary. 
The poll that Think New Mexico commissioned found that 64% of New Mexicans support salaries for lawmakers only if they are required to comply with mandatory ethics reforms. Tying ethics reforms to salaries was similarly popular regardless of whether respondents were Democrats, Republicans or independent, according to the survey. 
In total, 81% of New Mexicans surveyed said they supported holding lawmakers to a higher ethical standard. 
Think New Mexico’s lobbyist reform proposals were also very popular, with three-quarters or more of those surveyed supporting requirements that lobbyists publicly report how much clients pay them, which elected officials are benefiting from a specific lobbyist’s spending and which bill lobbyists are lobbying for or against.
New Mexico Election 2026: Constitutional Amendment 4

New Mexico currently does not require lobbyists to disclose that information, though the Legislature did pass a bill in 2025 containing those disclosure requirements. Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham later vetoed the bill. 
Finally, 84% of those surveyed supported requiring lawmakers to publicly report when they have a financial conflict of interest with a particular bill. The reform’s sheer popularity struck Sanchez, a longtime pollster. 
“When you’re a pollster like myself, and you see 84% of the population supporting a particular issue, that’s not common,” Sanchez said Wednesday. “It tells you strongly that the overwhelming public, regardless of their demographics and their partisanship, supports these issues.”

name: Michigan Advance
title: Sanders, El-Sayed vow to improve healthcare work environments if Democrats take back U.S Senate
description: U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders has big plans for the U.S. Senate’s healthcare and labor policy-making committee if Democrats take back chamber in the upcoming general election, and Michigan Democratic U.S. Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed would be tapped to help him if he is elected in the fall. Sanders, the independent Senator from Vermont, said as […]
text:
U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, right, speaks at a rally with U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders, left, U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and U.S. House candidate William Lawrence in Lansing, Mich., on July 19, 2026. (Photo by Andrew Roth/Michigan Advance)U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders has big plans for the U.S. Senate’s healthcare and labor policy-making committee if Democrats take back chamber in the upcoming general election, and Michigan Democratic U.S. Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed would be tapped to help him if he is elected in the fall.
Sanders, the independent Senator from Vermont, said as much Wednesday in a virtual address to a gathering of the California Nurses Association and National Nurses Organizing Committee, which hails itself as the most progressive and “most militant” union representing registered nurses in the nation.
El-Sayed also spoke to the group in person on Wednesday, touching on the United States’ troubles with affordable healthcare and the fight for better worker protections for nurses and others in the healthcare industry. El-Sayed faces a general election battle against Republican nominee and former U.S. Rep. Mike Rogers of White Lake, and the Michigan seat is seen as a key pathway to a Democratic majority in 2027.
Specifically, Sanders said that if Democrats can win that majority, he would likely be the next chair of the U.S. Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pension Committee. Sanders said that if El-Sayed wins, whether he likes it or not, Sanders will place him on that committee to serve alongside him.
“I’m going to put him on the … committee because we need his voice as a physician, as a doctor fighting for Medicare for All,” Sanders said. “I want you just to think for a moment; I know we’ve been in this fight for so long, and sometimes we forget what it means. Do you know how many tens of millions of people are out there in Vermont, in California, all over this country, who are worrying that their kid gets sick, and their moms can’t afford a prescription drug? Do you know what that does to people’s well-being? They live under enormous stress.”
U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vermont) speaks to a gathering of the California Nurses Association and National Nurses Organizing Committee on the afternoon of Wednesday, Sept. 30, 2026, in San Francisco, Calif. (Screenshot)
Although El-Sayed received a medical degree from Columbia University and earned a doctorate in public health from Oxford University, he is not a practicing physician.
Sanders said he and El-Sayed won’t let up the fight to ensure Medicare for All, which remains a key plank in his own political movement and a major pillar of El-Sayed’s current campaign, as the candidate co-wrote and published a user guide for his Medicare for All policy.
“But at the very least, a civilized, democratic, sane society can make sure that we take the financial burden of sickness off the backs of our people,” Sanders said. “I know that the nurses unions go out and say, ‘Oh, we believe in Medicare for All,’ and they say, ‘Well, that’s a fringe idea. You’re all communists. It’s a radical idea.’ Understand that poll after poll now shows the American people understand that our current system is broken, it’s dysfunctional, and that we must move to a Medicare for All, single-payer program.”
Sanders said those calling for the policy now represent “the mainstream” of Democratic politics.
“They are the fringe folks,” Sanders said of those who oppose the policy. “We’re taking on the oligarchs in general, taking on all of the folks who make huge amounts of money off of human illness, taking on the people who do not want to see us keep people healthy; who do not want to focus on primary care disease prevention, taking on the power of the drug companies. That ain’t easy. It really is not easy, but we’re going to win this because we are mobilizing.”
El-Sayed’s address touched on key planks of his Michigan campaign and reiterated Sanders’ call to reform not only the healthcare system, but to improve the working environment for doctors, nurses and other hospital staff.
“I wanted to be the kind of doctor who worked on the system, not just in the system, because too often the question of whether or not you get access to that system is a function of the choices that we make that are outside of our control,” El-Sayed said. “How often is it that you’re asked to take care of a patient who you know is going to feel the pinch of that, even after they leave your clinic or your hospital?”
Michigan Democratic U.S. Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed speaks to a gathering of the California Nurses Association and National Nurses Organizing Committee on the afternoon of Wednesday, Sept. 30, 2026, in San Francisco, Calif. (Screenshot)
El-Sayed railed against excessive premiums charged by insurance companies and prohibitive high deductibles, which he has argued leads to insurmountable medical debt if Americans decide they need important medical care.
The nominee also touted his work supporting various unions through the years, including those based in Michigan. El-Sayed also told the nurses union that standing up for their rights also meant standing up to large hospital corporations, “and their handmaidens in this work, Big Tech.”
“AI corporations are figuring out how to use their algorithms to inflict prior authorization on everybody in the system, trying to figure out how to automate the incredible work that you all do every day,” El-Sayed said. “And I think I speak for all of us when I say that algorithms can’t heal people; people heal people. And so we have an opportunity to stand together to take back our healthcare system for the people who matter most in that system.”
El-Sayed said that his concern was not for the CEO of a healthcare corporation or other so-called “C-suite” positions, nor the marketing people who promote those systems, “but the patients and the providers who make healthcare what it is.”
“Standing together, we have an opportunity to say loudly that every single person in these United States, in the richest, most powerful country in the world, deserves to know that they’re going to get their healthcare without having to worry about a premium or a copay or a deductible,” he added.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Done being silent: Pa. legislators push package to close gaps in menopause treatments
description: As Rep. Liz Hanbidge started promoting her bill to educate and promote health access for women experiencing perimenopause and menopause this week, one fellow lawmaker said he’d support the measure — but wished she’d stop talking about it.  “He asked me to stop talking about it because he thinks it’s gross,” Hanbidge (D-Montgomery) said. “To […]
text:
Sponsored bills include education about perimenopause and menopause as well as expanding insurance coverage for treatment options.As Rep. Liz Hanbidge started promoting her bill to educate and promote health access for women experiencing perimenopause and menopause this week, one fellow lawmaker said he’d support the measure — but wished she’d stop talking about it. 
“He asked me to stop talking about it because he thinks it’s gross,” Hanbidge (D-Montgomery) said. “To my colleague, if talking about menopause makes you uncomfortable, imagine going through it without anyone talking about it all.”
“For generations, women have been expected to quietly manage these changes, figure it out themselves and keep going. We are done with that,” Hanbidge continued. 
Rep. Liz Hanbidge (D-Montgomery) listens to a committee question on her bill on Sept. 29, 2026. (Photo by Whitney Downard/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)
Several female legislators shared similar stories about overcoming the social aversion to discussing perimenopause or menopause, which every woman will experience in her lifetime. 
As the body’s hormone production ramps down, women experience fatigue, hot flashes, mental fogs, anxiety, insomnia, headaches, sweating, mood swings and more — but “for decades, it has been under-discussed, under-researched and under-reported,” Hanbidge said.
She pointed to a Gallup study released last week, in which just over one-third of women said they had “a good understanding of the symptoms of menopause.” Even fewer, 25%, said the same about treatment options.
Rep. Maureen Madden (D-Monroe) said that when she experienced menopause, she was advised to buy cooling pillowcases and nightgowns, but wasn’t warned about how it impacted her bone density. 
“I didn’t know I had a bone density problem until I fell and broke my shoulder at 65 years old,” said the 66-year-old. “We should be doing screenings. We should be taking care of women’s health at every turn.”
Women can live one-third of their lives post-menopause, with most starting the process in their 50s — though perimenopause symptoms can start a decade earlier. 
“We don’t just have babies and then we go through menopauses, and then we’re done. We’re women who want to have lives, who want to have careers, who want to be healthy,” said Madden. “These treatments will help and women deserve it.” 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Madden, who chairs the House Aging & Older Adult Services Committee, spoke in favor of four bills to expand insurance coverage for menopause treatment options. All of those, including two authored by Hanbidge, are part of a multi-bill package advancing through the House this week. 
Support wasn’t unanimous, however. A handful of Republicans opposed the measures in various committees, with some voicing concerns about increased Medicaid costs. 
“I have a very large percentage of my constituents that are seniors … but I have never had one senior come into my office asking for policy on menopause,” said Rep Barbara Gleim (R-Cumberland), who voted no on four bills in Madden’s committee. “What I do hear from my seniors (is) scamming, which we have worked on in this committee, and abuse. I would really like to focus on those main issues.”
 The individual bills

As of Tuesday, seven proposals have advanced through various House committees, including three from Hanbidge. Her efforts include an education partnership between the Department of Health and medical providers; required insurance coverage for pelvic floor therapy; and required private insurance coverage for hormonal and non-hormonal therapy. 
“Your ability to get care and support through this transition shouldn’t depend on what insurance carrier you have or how much money you make,” Hanbidge said. 
At a rally, Rep. Morgan Cephas (D-Philadelphia) spoke on her two bills, one of which expands Medicaid coverage for hormonal and non-hormonal therapy to treat menopausal symptoms and another which provides workplace protections and accommodations. 
“These are not just health issues, these are issues that are happening at the height of women’s careers when they’re earning the most money, when they’re leading teams and when they’re contributing decades of knowledge and experience to their workplaces,” said Cephas. “Access to fans … flexible breaks, modified uniforms or temporary seating. These are common sense adjustments that cost very little, yet can make the difference between a woman staying in the workforce or being pushed out.”
Rep. Melissa Shusterman (D-Chester) wears pins claiming there’s “No Time for a Pause” on menopause legislation. (Photo by Whitney Downard/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)
Cephas told the Capital-Star that the Pennsylvania Human Relations Commission, which handles complaints about workplace discrimination, confirmed it had received submissions related to menopause, but was working on tallying the number.
The final two measures are from Rep. Melissa Shusterman (D-Chester), specifically addressing osteoporosis and urinary tract infections — the severity of both conditions increases with decreased estrogen production.
“Broken bones are the leading cause of nursing home admissions for those of us over the age of 50,” said Shusterman. “All of this is preventable as women age.” 
Shusterman shared that the symptoms of UTIs, in particular, change as women age and delayed treatments can lead to sepsis and death. Though vaginal estrogen can help, few know about the option and insurers might not cover it. 
And though upfront costs can be a concern, Shusterman said that the commonwealth already loses out when menopausal women leave the workforce or need more expensive treatment because of missed preventative care. 
“We’re not going to rest until we get this package passed,” Shusterman concluded. “This is important work for women and one-third of their life. We can’t stop caring for women.”

title: State commission limits outside groups from weighing in on Kentucky Power audit
description: This story first appeared on WEKU. It’s republished here as part of the Appalachian News Exchange reporting partnership to strength Kentucky journalism. The state Public Service Commission said Tuesday it will not allow a group of stakeholders to intervene in an audit of Kentucky Power’s operations and management. The PSC launched the investigation earlier t[...]
text:
Members of the Kentucky Public Service Commission listen to residents in Ashland on Jan. 8, 2026. Seen from left, Andrew Wood, Chair Angie Hatton and Mary Pat Regan. (Photo by Curtis Tate, WEKU
This story first appeared on WEKU. It’s republished here as part of the Appalachian News Exchange reporting partnership to strength Kentucky journalism.
The state Public Service Commission said Tuesday it will not allow a group of stakeholders to intervene in an audit of Kentucky Power’s operations and management.
The PSC launched the investigation earlier this year, though the audit has not begun.
A group of stakeholders, including the Appalachian Citizens Law Center, Kentuckians for the Commonwealth and the Mountain Association, had filed a motion to intervene, a request the PSC denied.
Byron Gary, an attorney representing the groups, says it’s unusual for the PSC to exclude them from filing testimony and offering evidence. However, he said the commission allowed them a more limited form of participation as part of its request for proposals.
“It puts us sort of on the outside rather than being an active participant,” he said.” But we do appreciate that the commission at least put that in the RFP.”
The PSC’s request says the investigator that’s chosen will interview the groups to determine the scope of the audit.
Gary said those stakeholder groups advocate for low-income and energy burdened residents, a high concentration of whom live in Kentucky Power’s territory.
“In the case of KFTC, they have many members who are struggling ratepayers of Kentucky Power Company themselves, or Mountain Association that works with volunteer fire departments and churches and small groceries in Kentucky Power Company’s territory,” he said.
Residents in utility’s 20-county service territory pay some of the highest bills in the state. According to Heatmap, the average Kentucky Power August residential bill was $238.42. Only Kenergy in Western Kentucky was higher.
Customers who pay 6% or more of their income for heating and cooling are considered energy burdened, Gary said.
The groups he represents participated jointly in Kentucky Power’s most recent rate case before the commission.
During three public comment hearings in Eastern Kentucky, residents and local officials pleaded with the PSC to deny the company’s request.
The commission ultimately approved an increase, but less than the utility asked to be granted.
The Kentucky attorney general’s office functions as an advocate for electricity customers. Gary said, though, the attorney general does not advocate for specific classes of customers, such as residents with low or fixed incomes.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Barrett pushes for international AI agreement as health professionals back Doctors Not AI Act
description: As the U.N. General Assembly concludes its High-Level Week meetings and discussions, U.S. Rep. Tom Barrett is calling on officials to work towards an agreement with other nations regarding AI development. In a letter to U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio and U.N. Ambassador Mike Waltz, the Charlotte Republican voiced his belief that the General […]
text:
U.S. Rep. Tom Barrett (R-Charlotte) introduces a panel at the Michigan State University Research Foundation's 2026 Mobility Summit centered on mobility technology in national defense. Aug. 11, 2026 | Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan AdvanceAs the U.N. General Assembly concludes its High-Level Week meetings and discussions, U.S. Rep. Tom Barrett is calling on officials to work towards an agreement with other nations regarding AI development.
In a letter to U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio and U.N. Ambassador Mike Waltz, the Charlotte Republican voiced his belief that the General Assembly should include artificial intelligence as part of its conversations. 
“The 81st Session of the UN General Assembly is uniquely positioned to begin these conversations with other countries,” Barrett wrote in the letter. “This should not only happen with our allies, but our adversaries as well. While we may have disagreements, we should all work towards the common goal of ensuring this technology is properly regulated for the common good and safety of all countries.”
Barrett said those discussions should include ideas for an international AI treaty, incident-report sharing, risk management techniques and human control of offensive and nuclear weapons.
“This next frontier in emerging technology has the ability to propel this world into a golden age or send us into collapse,” Barrett said. “I respectfully request that you both work to create regular and consistent multilateral dialogue on AI moving forward. It is critical that we begin these talks before it is too late.”
In addition to his calls for an international AI compact, Barrett has backed multiple pieces of legislation intended to regulate artificial intelligence. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
He is among the lawmakers who led the effort to introduce a bill to ensure AI-enabled weapon systems cannot carry out an intentionally lethal strike without a human decision-maker in the loop. 
Barrett also helped introduce a bill to ensure that artificial intelligence is not used in health insurance coverage decisions to determine whether a treatment, prescription or procedure is medically necessary. Known as the Doctors Not AI Act, this legislation has received support from a broad coalition of mental health and healthcare organizations, including the American College of Physicians, the American Psychiatric Association, the National Alliance on Mental Illness and The Trevor Project.
“When health coverage is denied, the consequences include delayed treatment, financial strain, worsening health conditions, and in some cases, life-threatening harm,” the groups wrote in their letter of support. “Americans expect that decisions about their care will be made by qualified professionals exercising independent medical judgment — not by automated systems designed primarily for cost containment.”
Barrett is up for reelection in Michigan’s 7th Congressional District against William Lawrence, a Lansing-area political organizer and co-founder of the Sunrise Movement, who has made opposition to big tech and data centers a major facet of his campaign. 
Lawrence has called for a pause on advanced artificial intelligence development and data center construction and proposed a National AI Compact, which would include a jobs program funded by a tax on AI industry profits. Lawrence also supports efforts to reach an international treaty on the safe development, management, regulation and enforcement of AI.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Former public defender sentenced to prison for healthcare fraud
description: A former public defender from western Iowa has been sentenced to five months in prison for defrauding Medicaid and cancer patients. In June, a federal grand jury in Nebraska charged Iowa-licensed attorney Cassi Wigington with healthcare fraud. Prosecutors alleged that beginning in 2012, Wigington fraudulently sold medical equipment such as custom-made breast[...]
text:
(Photo by Getty Images)A former public defender from western Iowa has been sentenced to five months in prison for defrauding Medicaid and cancer patients.
In June, a federal grand jury in Nebraska charged Iowa-licensed attorney Cassi Wigington with healthcare fraud. Prosecutors alleged that beginning in 2012, Wigington fraudulently sold medical equipment such as custom-made breast prosthetic devices for women who had undergone mastectomies.
In some cases, she allegedly had customers sign, in advance, receipts for the delivery of prostheses that had yet to be provided. In other cases, prosecutors alleged, she forged the customers’ signatures. She then sent bills for the undelivered devices to various insurers, including Medicaid, Blue Cross-Blue Shield, Aetna and United Healthcare.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“Twenty-five patients were identified wherein their respective healthcare benefit program was billed for products that were never received or provided,” prosecutors alleged. Losses incurred by individual patients and their insurers were alleged to be as much as $28,000.
Wigington pleaded guilty to the fraud charge, and a federal judge recently sentenced her to five months of incarceration, followed by three years of supervised release. Wigington has also agreed to pay $445,455 in restitution in the case.
Court records show Wigington was first licensed to practice law in Iowa in January 2020. Last year, she admitted in court filings that in August and September 2023, she committed the crime of theft by shoplifting from a Hy-Vee store in Gretna, Nebraska.
Court records show Wigington admitted that during 13 trips to the store she stole more than 300 items worth a total of $2,721. After being criminally charged with felony theft by shoplifting, Wigington entered into a diversion agreement with the Sarpy County Attorney’s Office in which she agreed to pay restitution and the theft charge was dismissed.
In court filings, Wigington acknowledged she initially claimed to have been falsely accused of shoplifting, stating that when she made those statements, she “did not have the surveillance footage of my actions.”
Prior to the Iowa Supreme Court’s June 2025 decision to suspend her license for six months due to the shoplifting case, Wigington had argued for a 30-day suspension, noting that northwest Iowa was in serious need of public defenders.
“Any lengthy suspension of me will result in considerable disruption in the Second Judicial District,” she told the court. “I currently have approximately 700 cases assigned to me — several cases are companion charges pending against one defendant. It is extremely difficult to get lawyers to take these cases.”
License reinstated last year with support of judges 
In October 2025, Wigington applied for reinstatement of her Iowa law license. Buena Vista County Attorney Paul Allen wrote a letter to the Iowa Supreme Court supporting her application, as did Patrick Tott, chief judge of Iowa’s Third Judicial District in northwest Iowa, and Iowa Rep. Megan Jones, a Republican from Clay County.
District Court Judge Adam Miller also wrote in support of Wigington, calling her an “attorney of exceptional character and competence” and arguing she was “indispensable” to the Third Judicial District.
In December 2025, the Iowa Supreme Court agreed to lift Wigington’s suspension, making her fully qualified to resume the practice of law in Iowa.
Six months after her license was reinstated, on June 18, 2026, Wigington pleaded guilty in the fraud case. In August, the Iowa Supreme Court suspended her license to practice law until she can show good cause for the court to set aside its order and reinstate her license.
In its request for that suspension, the Iowa Supreme Court Attorney Disciplinary Board had cited what it called “a troubling, years-long pattern of dishonesty and fraud, including repeated theft accomplished through deception.”
The Iowa Capital Dispatch was not able to Wigington for comment.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: AG Liz Murrill sues states with shield laws protecting abortion-pill providers
description: Louisiana Attorney General Liz Murrill and her counterparts in Arkansas and Alabama announced Wednesday they are suing three Democratic-led states over laws that grant immunity to doctors who prescribe abortion-inducing medication to people in states where it is illegal.  The lawsuit, filed directly with the U.S. Supreme Court, alleges laws in California, Ma[...]
text:
Louisiana Attorney General Liz Murrill speaks at a news conference Wednesday, Sept. 30, 2026, announcing a lawsuit challenging abortion shield laws in Democratic-led states. Joining Murrill were Attorneys General Steve Marshall of Alabama, left, and Tim Griffin of Arkansas, whose states are also plaintiffs in the case. (Photo by Piper Hutchinson/Louisiana Illuminator)Louisiana Attorney General Liz Murrill and her counterparts in Arkansas and Alabama announced Wednesday they are suing three Democratic-led states over laws that grant immunity to doctors who prescribe abortion-inducing medication to people in states where it is illegal. 
The lawsuit, filed directly with the U.S. Supreme Court, alleges laws in California, Massachusetts and New York violate the U.S. Constitution by circumventing its Full Faith and Credit Clause, which generally requires states to respect the laws and judicial proceedings of other states. 
Following the 2022 U.S. Supreme Court decision in Dobbs v. Jackson’s Women Health Organization, which eliminated the right to access an abortion, Democratic-controlled states enacted shield laws that prevent medical providers in their states from being punished for providing abortion care to people in states where abortion is illegal. Murrill’s lawsuit asks justices to invalidate the laws of the three defendant states. 
“We will not allow activist states, activist providers or distributors profiting from killing babies to threaten Louisiana’s sovereignty, violate Louisiana’s laws and endanger Louisiana women and Louisiana babies,” Murrill said at a news conference in Baton Rouge announcing the lawsuit. Joining her were fellow Republican Attorneys General Tim Griffin of Arkansas and Steve Marshall of Alabama. 
Murrill’s conflict with shield laws most notably flared in 2025 when New York Gov. Kathy Hochul, a Democrat, refused to comply with her extradition request for a New York doctor. Murrill, with Republican Gov. Jeff Landry’s backing, indicted Dr. Margaret Carpenter for criminal abortion, a felony in Louisiana, after she prescribed abortion pills to a teenager in Louisiana. 
“Louisiana has changed their laws, but that has no bearing on the laws here in the state of New York,” Hochul said at the time. “Doctors take an oath to protect their patients. I took an oath of office to protect all New Yorkers … I will not be signing an extradition order that came from the governor of Louisiana. Not now, not ever.”
Murrill and other attorneys general previously called on Congress to end shield laws. 
Louisiana, Arkansas and Alabama all have near-total abortion bans, under which abortion is illegal at all stages except in extremely limited circumstances in which the individual’s life is endangered by the pregnancy. Doctors have raised concerns that these exceptions are too narrow. 
On Wednesday, Murrill, Griffin and Marshall compared abortion-inducing medications to illegal drugs. 
“It is no different than if they were sending fentanyl in these boxes,” Murrill said. 
The trio also filed a separate federal lawsuit in Louisiana’s Western District Court naming 30 medical providers or medical care organizations as defendants. It alleges they provide abortion-inducing medication without a medical consultation to individuals in Louisiana and that they misrepresent the risks of the drugs. 
The attorneys general said approximately 800 medication-induced abortions occur monthly in Louisiana, as well as 300 in Arkansas and 500 in Alabama. 
“There’s nothing about these mail order abortions that even remotely look like healthcare,” Griffin said. “A healthcare provider would never, anonymously, without ever seeing the patient prescribe a medicine, without knowing anything about the individual.” 
“It doesn’t matter how many times you call it healthcare or maternal care or whatever. It’s not. You can call a crawfish a shrimp all you want, but it’s still a crawfish,” Griffin added. 
Murrill said that in the course of investigating the issue, her office participated in controlled buys of abortion-inducing medication and said they were able to order the medication without speaking to a doctor or providing any information that would verify the identity of the purchaser or whether the pregnancy meets the criteria for the medication. 
“That’s part of what makes them so dangerous because there’s no accountability in this system whatsoever,” Murrill said. “There’s no oversight. There’s no medical treatment. There’s no medical healthcare provider.” 

Murrill showed several bottles of the medication her office was able to obtain. The bottles did not include any information about the prescriber or information about the risks of the medication. 
New York and several other states have laws that allow doctors to remove their names from prescribed abortion pills. 
Mifepristone and misoprostol, the two medications commonly prescribed to end a pregnancy, are considered safe and effective when used as prescribed. Like any medication, they also come with a risk of side effects or complications.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Utah among 40 states to settle with auto loan company accused of predatory lending
description: Dozens of Utahns are set to have their debt cancelled after a national auto loan company agreed to settle claims that it exploited borrowers.
text:
The office of the Utah Attorney General at the Capitol in Salt Lake City is pictured on Tuesday, Jan. 16, 2024. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)Dozens of Utahns are set to have their debt cancelled and get a check in the mail after a national auto loan company agreed to settle claims that it exploited borrowers with low credit scores. 
Utah and 39 other states reached the roughly $700 million settlement earlier this month with the Michigan-based Credit Acceptance Corporation. The states accused the company of quietly piling on extra costs that buyers didn’t know were optional and issuing loans they couldn’t afford. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“No company should be able to profit by setting its own customers up to fail,” Utah Attorney General Derek Brown said in a prepared statement issued last week. “This settlement holds Credit Acceptance accountable and makes clear that lenders who cut corners will answer for it.” 
A total of 124 Utahns will receive a share of about $178,000 in restitution, Brown said. That’s in addition to more than $1 million in full debt relief for those whose cars were repossessed and nearly $527,000 for drivers who kept their vehicles.
The agreement also requires the company to give buyers an out when loans go bad quickly and take steps to prevent dealers from sneaking extras into a deal, among other safeguards, the attorney general’s office said. 
The states alleged the company gave each of its loans a score indicating how much money it expected to collect, saying many of the low-scoring borrowers defaulted and had their vehicles repossessed. 
“Exploiting vulnerable Utah consumers through high-pressure sales and deception will not be tolerated,” said Katherine Hass, director of the Utah Division of Consumer Protection.
The company, for its part, said in a news release on its website it did not admit fault or wrongdoing in the settlement. 
“This resolution provides certainty for our business, our dealer partners and the customers we serve,” said Vinayak Hegde, the company’s chief executive officer of credit acceptance. “We believe the provisions we agreed to are constructive, customer-focused and consistent with the direction of regulatory expectations in our industry.”

title: Alaska prepares to surrender some Statehood Act land claims as it nears 105 million-acre goal
description: Alaska’s decades-long quest to obtain millions of acres of land from the federal government under the Alaska Statehood Act is getting closer to an end. But because the state is getting closer to its goal, its requests now exceed a limit in federal law.  This week, the Alaska Department of Natural Resources announced that it […]
text:
Earlier this year, the federal government lifted restrictions that had paused the transfer of 1.4 million acres of federal land along the Dalton Highway and trans-Alaska oil pipeline, seen here in 2023. (Bureau of Land Management photo)Alaska’s decades-long quest to obtain millions of acres of land from the federal government under the Alaska Statehood Act is getting closer to an end.
But because the state is getting closer to its goal, its requests now exceed a limit in federal law. 
This week, the Alaska Department of Natural Resources announced that it is preparing to surrender the claims to as much as 5.7 million acres scattered across the state, an area collectively bigger than New Jersey.
The original 1958 Statehood Act gave Alaska permission to take over 105 million acres of federal land, but the state could — and did — target millions of acres more than that before the selection period closed in 1993. 
That’s partially because some of the state’s initial selections were being used for another purpose and weren’t immediately available for transfer.
The state’s selections have paid off in a big way: The vast state-owned Prudhoe Bay oil fields were originally controlled by the federal government before being selected by the state in 1964.
Transfers move extremely slow; the land must be surveyed, marked and processed through the federal bureaucracy. 
Year by year, decade by decade, the federal government has incrementally passed parcels to the state. 
Earlier this year, the federal government removed restrictions that had blocked the transfer of 1.4 million acres along the Dalton Highway and trans-Alaska oil pipeline. That leaves about 3.2 million acres left to be transferred. 
Under federal law, the state can select no more than 125% of the acreage left to be transferred, which means that as the balance shrinks, Alaska needs to surrender some claims.
By phone on Tuesday, DNR officials said they’re preparing to give up some low-priority selections, places that are unlikely to be transferred or are less valuable than other selections.
In this week’s public notice, DNR listed 18 targets for relinquishment — the land under Eielson Air Force Base, a bombing range near Fort Greely, land surrounded by other owners in western Alaska, land envisioned for a road near Unalakleet, and more.
Relinquishing each claim involves a separate public process, and more are likely to come. Even if all 18 claims are relinquished, the state will remain above the 125% claim limit.
Alaska also has millions of acres of “top filed” selections — claims that haven’t been formally processed because the land is being used for some other purpose, like mining. 
If a federal mine claim ends, for example, the top filing means the state gets priority afterward.
Top filed selections don’t count against the 125% limit, but the state may begin eliminating some of those as well.
DNR officials said that as the state gets closer and closer to the Statehood Act’s limit, the state will become more selective about the claims it keeps, and it may keep some particularly valuable top-filed picks even if they’re not immediately available.
As it gets closer and closer to the 105 million-acre limit, Alaska could hold the last selections in reserve for those top-filed parcels, the officials said. 
Any final decision would be up to future governors and future DNR commissioners.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: SC’s growth story is becoming the South’s growth story
description: As the United States celebrates its 250th anniversary, the country’s economic center of gravity continues to move south. My new report, Accelerating South, captures the scale of that shift: the American South is now a roughly $6 trillion regional economy, outpacing both the Northeast and the Pacific while attracting people, capital and industries at a […]
text:
BMW vehicles parked at the Port of Charleston await being loaded for export Dec. 3, 2020. (File photo courtesy of BMW)As the United States celebrates its 250th anniversary, the country’s economic center of gravity continues to move south.
My new report, Accelerating South, captures the scale of that shift: the American South is now a roughly $6 trillion regional economy, outpacing both the Northeast and the Pacific while attracting people, capital and industries at a historic pace.
Howard Franklin is the author of “Accelerating South,” an analysis of the nine-state region released in July 2026. (Photo courtesy of Ohio River South)
Few states illustrate that momentum more clearly than South Carolina.
Over the past three years, South Carolina has assembled one of the strongest economic runs in the country.
It led the nation in real, inflation-adjusted growth in gross domestic product in 2024, at 4.2%; tied for first place in 2025, at 3.1%; and ranked first in population growth in 2024-25.
No other Southern state can claim that same combination of sustained output and population growth.
Those numbers are not simply the result of favorable weather or lower costs. They reflect an economic model built around global manufacturing, logistics, aerospace, defense and a growing base of skilled workers and residents.
The state has become a case study in how the modern South is competing for — and winning — investment that once might have gone elsewhere.
At the heart of South Carolina’s growth is its unusual ability to attract foreign capital. Its manufacturing sector is globally connected in a way few states can match.
That concentration matters at a time when global companies are reassessing where and how they manufacture.
Tariffs, geopolitical uncertainty, supply-chain disruption and a renewed focus on domestic production have all made U.S. operations more strategically important. South Carolina is well positioned to benefit from that recalibration because it offers something companies increasingly need: an established manufacturing ecosystem, access to ports and transportation networks and proximity to fast-growing Southern markets.
BMW battery plant nears completion in Upstate SC

BMW’s recent $1.7 billion U.S. investment in Spartanburg County underscores that advantage.
While the 2025-26 tariff environment has created challenges, it has also strengthened incentives to build and invest closer to American consumers. South Carolina has emerged as a natural beneficiary of that trend.
But a state’s economic strength cannot rest on manufacturing alone.
South Carolina’s long-term success will depend on its ability to maintain the infrastructure, workforce and energy capacity needed to support continued growth. This is particularly clear in the competition for data centers and other energy-intensive projects.
The Southeast’s data center boom has created enormous opportunity — and real limits. Data centers require large amounts of reliable, affordable power, as well as water, transmission capacity and community support.
Legislators recognized as much this year.
Senators debated a pair of bills to set guardrails on data-center growth — including protections to keep ratepayers off the hook for the industry’s energy demands. Neither bill reached a floor vote.
In the absence of statewide rules, the question hasn’t gone away; it has simply moved to county councils, several of which have begun enacting their own moratoriums.
The next phase of economic development will require policymakers and business leaders to make difficult decisions about where growth makes sense, how infrastructure is funded and how to balance corporate demand with the needs of households and existing employers.
That challenge should not be viewed as a reason to retreat from growth. It is a reason to approach it more strategically. South Carolina’s advantage is that it already has a diverse economic foundation on which to build.
Boeing looks to build on momentum at SC Dreamliner plant

As national defense priorities increasingly focus on readiness, domestic production capacity and technological advantage, South Carolina’s aerospace and defense base is positioned for increased relevance.
Boeing’s 787 operation is not just a major employer; it is an anchor for a wider network of suppliers, engineers and advanced-manufacturing capabilities.
Population growth reinforces all of these trends. More residents mean a larger labor pool, greater consumer demand and a stronger case for business investment.
But growth also brings pressure: housing affordability, congestion, workforce shortages and the need for schools and public services that can keep up with expanding communities.
The lesson from Accelerating South is that the South’s rise is no longer a prediction. It is a fact.
South Carolina’s recent performance shows what happens when a state combines global industrial ambition with the fundamentals that companies and families seek.
The challenge now is to ensure that this extraordinary run becomes durable prosperity — sustained not only by the next factory announcement or population milestone, but by the infrastructure, talent and long-term planning necessary to keep South Carolina moving forward.

title: NC traffic safety experts call for tougher laws on speeding, impaired or distracted driving
description: In a crowded hotel conference room in Raleigh Tuesday, traffic safety researchers, industry experts and state government officials attended the final summit hosted by the North Carolina Alliance for Safe Transportation. On the agenda: how to improve North Carolina’s distracted driving, speeding and impaired driving laws to reduce traffic fatalities. “I read[...]
text:
Mark Ezzell, director of the governor’s Highway Safety Program, gives a presentation on North Carolina's road safety issues in Raleigh on Sept. 29, 2026. (Photo: Tre Spencer/NC Newsline)In a crowded hotel conference room in Raleigh Tuesday, traffic safety researchers, industry experts and state government officials attended the final summit hosted by the North Carolina Alliance for Safe Transportation.
On the agenda: how to improve North Carolina’s distracted driving, speeding and impaired driving laws to reduce traffic fatalities.
“I read every day about the number of crashes we have in North Carolina, because there’s a story behind each of those stats,” said Mark Ezzell, director of the governor’s Highway Safety Program.
Ezzell says state lawmakers should keep trying to strengthen laws for impaired driving, including passing a law requiring ignition interlocks for first-time offenders.
These breathalyzer devices are installed on a car’s computer system. Drivers must breathe into them before starting the engine. If the device detects alcohol, then the car won’t start.
Currently, North Carolina does not require ignition interlocks for first-time DWI offenders. Earlier this year, a bill known as the SEATBELT Act would have required ignition locks for all drivers convicted of driving while impaired regardless of prior offenses, but it died in committee.
NC House lawmakers seek breathalyzer ignition locks for all DWI offenders

Ezzell also said lawmakers should strengthen North Carolina’s distracted driving laws, including adopting a hands-free requirement for drivers. He said his organization has pushed for years for a hands-free law like those in neighboring states.
North Carolina currently prohibits drivers from reading or texting while driving, but doesn’t have a broader law that prevents drivers from holding or using any device behind the wheel.
Another recommendation was to expand the use of cameras in school speed zones. North Carolina is currently experimenting with speed cameras in pilot school zones, following legislation passed in 2025. Ezzell said lawmakers should implement it across the state.
The organization has hosted three other summits in the state in Wilmington, Statesville and Asheville, where officials heard directly from attendees about what changes they wanted to see to North Carolina’s traffic safety laws.
The meetings were intended to help identify priorities lawmakers could take up next year during the legislative session, according to the organization’s agenda.
NCAST Executive Director Joe Stewart said speeding was a recurring concern among participants at each summit.
“Speeding is a menace,” he said. “Traffic cameras can make a big difference in enforcement and free up officers for other duties.”
 E-bike concerns emerge

Sen. Vickie Sawyer, R-Iredell, co-hosted the events. She chairs the Senate Transportation Committee.
She said common themes she’s heard from audiences across the state have been concerns about electric bikes, distracted driving and road rage.
The General Assembly has already taken steps this year to give local governments more authority over e-bike use. The new law redefines e-bikes and allows them to be used on roads and bike lanes, while giving power to municipalities to set limits on where the bikes can be used.
But Sawyer said she sees a need for clear e-bike rules while avoiding unnecessary regulations. She said clearer distinctions based on factors such as an e-bike’s top speed or weight could further help communities determine how the bikes should be regulated.
“I love any technology, especially around mobility,” she said. “But you have to get in the space between regulation and stifling innovation, and how do you balance that?

name: VTDigger
title: More cops can’t help downtown
description:
Burlington doesn't have the officers to spare, and state and federal law already limit what police can do about drugs and disorder downtown.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  More cops can’t help downtown.
text:
This commentary is by Brian Clifford, an abolitionist mutual aid organizer working in and around Burlington.
We can’t police our way to making downtown Burlington feel safe. I do not mean we shouldn’t. I’m not saying we should choose a higher path rooted in care and healing. I mean we can’t, as in, it is literally not possible at this time.
The idea that increased police presence will deter scary behaviors downtown makes logical sense. It’s been Burlington Police Department policy since 2023. If you are plugged into city politics, you may have seen interim Police Chief Shawn Burke share charts showing that police incidents are at an all-time high. Since the department refers to incidents as “a measure of police activity,” it is accurate to say that police have been more active downtown over the last three years than during the pre-2020 glory days, when they had over 90 sworn officers.A closer look at the data shows that Burke has responded to public pressure to boost police presence downtown. Under Burke, downtown’s share of citywide incidents rose from 30% to 39%, while downtown’s share of foot patrols rose from 72% to 92%. When you consider that the department’s sworn officer count continues to fall — reported as 55 in a recent City Council Public Safety Committee meeting — you can see there are no more cops to place downtown. You may also wonder how responsible it is to allocate nearly all foot patrols downtown when over 60% of violent police incidents citywide have historically occurred outside of downtown.
And if you think seasonal deployments of Vermont state troopers are the answer, there is one big problem with this approach: The troopers rarely arrest or even cite anyone. According to the Burlington Free Press, troopers logged 680 patrol hours during their most recent stint downtown. They made two arrests and issued three citations. When you consider that a trooper with one year of service makes $91,916.20, a very conservative estimate is that taxpayers spent over $30,000 for two arrests and three citations. I’m not sure how this scales, but it seems as if we may run out of money before noticing any impact.
So we can’t have more cops downtown because more cops do not exist. But what if cops simply enforce the laws we have, as so many armchair legal experts suggest? 
Burke has said police cannot simply roll out tougher enforcement due to legal restrictions at the state and federal levels: Bail statutes don’t allow it, so nonviolent offenders are either issued a citation or arraigned, depending on their situation. He has admitted the police department is often criticized by members of the public, but points out that police do not have the authority to blanket search people for drugs on the street, and making arrests for open drug use is very difficult to do legally.
As if to provide everyone an example of these limitations, the police department arrested 11 people in an August crackdown on drug-related activity in City Hall Park. Following the arrests, Burke reported that most of the people arrested were cited and released. He acknowledged that the arrests were about the optics of cleaning up the park, adding that it was not the best use of the drug unit’s time and that the department would be better served focusing on “mid- to upper-level traffickers.”

READ MORE

So if you interpret Burlington Forward’s call to “Strengthen Accountability for Unlawful Conduct” as a demand to lock up more poor people you see downtown, you should know that doing so is not legal. And if it were legal, county judges and prosecutors probably wouldn’t want to lock more people up. And if they wanted to, the prisons are all full. And if the prisons were not all full, our police chief is telling you that arresting poor people you see downtown is not the way to stop drug trafficking.
The overlapping crises we are seeing in Burlington are complex. They will take a long time to impact. I think most people understand that it will take more than policing to get where we all want to be, but the reality is that much of what we need apart from policing is being defunded. The police are not being defunded. Police budgets grow steadily every year. I worry that giving police agencies larger shares of our shrinking budgets will simply accelerate our decline. None of the more life-affirming recommendations in Burlington Forward will ever happen.

name: Washington State Standard
title: PSE new rate hike proposal draws ire at public hearing
description: The room was packed with a line out the door during the public comment hearing for a Puget Sound Energy rate proposal Tuesday evening at the Utilities and Transportation Commission’s headquarters in Lacey.  “We’ve replaced just about everything to something more efficient for which I’ve gotten no incentives and no rebates for,” Becky Foster, a […]
text:
The entrance to the UTC's offices. (Bill Lucia/Washington State Standard)The room was packed with a line out the door during the public comment hearing for a Puget Sound Energy rate proposal Tuesday evening at the Utilities and Transportation Commission’s headquarters in Lacey. 
“We’ve replaced just about everything to something more efficient for which I’ve gotten no incentives and no rebates for,” Becky Foster, a PSE ratepayer in Thurston County, said during the four-hour hearing that drew about 100 commenters. “The last two years [the bill] has skyrocketed and we’re paying more than 50% over what we were paying before.” 
She said she’s already paying around $600 a month on energy during the winter months. From 2022 to 2023, Foster said she paid $2,800 on electricity. 
“That’s just the winter months for us now,” Foster said.
Washington’s largest utility is asking regulators to approve an increase in electricity rates by 29.3% and gas rates by 19.8% over the next three years. It’s also asking to increase its allowed return on equity, or profit that shareholders earn on their investment, from 9.9% to 10.8%. 
In contrast with the state’s ambitious climate laws, the utility is also planning to use nearly $1 billion to maintain and build out its gas distribution system. 
Puget Sound Energy’s electricity rates have already increased this year by 18.85%. One after another, members of the public voiced their concerns of affordability. Retired people on fixed incomes, low-income households and those dependent on electronic medical devices are among the most vulnerable to another rate increase. 
“I’m here because my constituents are struggling to pay their energy bills, “ Rep. Beth Doglio, D-Olympia, told the three commissioners. 
“Washington residents should not have to choose between keeping the lights on and protecting our climate. We can and must do both,” Doglio added. 
In 2024, Doglio sponsored a bill that directs utilities that use both fossil fuels and renewable energy to phase out natural gas. The law, House Bill 1589, gives utilities new tools to make the energy transition affordable. 
Though Puget Sound Energy is using two of those tools in the rate proposal, the law was not intended to be used while a utility increases investments in natural gas, Doglio said. 
“Are these investments necessary? Cost-effective? And, consistent with Washington’s clean energy goals?” Doglio said. “I am deeply concerned that many of them are not.”
Puget Sound Energy says its power supply costs have tripled since 2019, when Washington passed the Clean Energy Transformation Act, a law that mandates utilities make all electricity sales greenhouse gas neutral. 
“We recognize that higher bills are difficult for our customers and that more rate increases are not what anyone wants to hear,” reads a Puget Sound Energy statement. “At the same time, the cost of providing safe and reliable energy has increased significantly.”
A glaring criticism of PSE’s proposal is its intention to convert the shut-down Centralia Power Plant into a gas-fired power plant, with operations projected to begin in late 2028.
“This is a very bad use of ratepayer dollars to put all this money into a project that isn’t necessary and that will interfere with our pollution and climate goals,” said Jan Hasselman, Earthjustice attorney. 
The utility is also seeking ratepayer recovery for two planned gas-turbine projects. 
“There’s this horribly ironic feedback loop where we’re spending more and more money on fossil fuel projects … and spending ratepayer money to make our system more resilient [to] climate change,” said Hasselman. 
The three commissioners will accept, reject or modify the proposal in early January. The next opportunity for public comment is Oct. 7.

name: Delaware
title: When Mom Doesn’t Seem Quite Right: Recognizing When a Parent May Need More Help
description: The first signs that an aging parent is struggling can be easy to miss. Knowing what to watch for can help families find support before a crisis forces the decision.   By George D. Rotsch, Delaware LIVE News HOCKESSIN Del. – For many adult children, there isn’t a single moment when they realize Mom may need more help. Instead, it ... Read More
text:
The first signs that an aging parent is struggling can be easy to miss. Knowing what to watch for can help families find support before a crisis forces the decision.
 
By George D. Rotsch, Delaware LIVE News
HOCKESSIN Del. – For many adult children, there isn’t a single moment when they realize Mom may need more help.
Instead, it happens slowly.
She asks the same question again. The refrigerator seems a little emptier. A bill gets paid late. She stops going to an activity she once enjoyed. Maybe she hesitates on the stairs or seems less comfortable driving at night.
Individually, those changes may not seem alarming. Together, however, they can signal that an aging parent is beginning to have difficulty managing life independently.
Recognizing those changes early can give families something particularly valuable: time and choices.
That is the focus of the first installment of Delaware LIVE’s series for adult caregivers — helping families recognize when a parent may need additional support and understand where to turn before an emergency makes the decision for them.
Why the person closest to Mom may miss it
One of the challenges is that aging usually happens gradually.
An adult child who sees a parent every day or every week naturally adjusts to small changes. A little more forgetfulness becomes familiar. Someone begins bringing Mom dinner more often. Another family member quietly starts paying a bill, driving her to appointments or handling something on the computer.
Without realizing it, the family may gradually be doing more and more.
Meanwhile, a sibling, grandchild or friend who has not seen Mom for several months may walk through the door and immediately notice something different.
“She seems slower.”
“She repeated that story three times.”
“The house doesn’t look like it used to.”
“That’s just not like Mom.”
Those observations shouldn’t automatically be treated as proof that something is wrong. Someone visiting for a few hours may see only a snapshot.
But they shouldn’t be dismissed either.
A useful question is: “What specifically did you notice?”
Specific observations — rather than general impressions — can help families determine whether a pattern is developing.
Watch for changes in everyday life
Memory loss is one possible warning sign, but it isn’t the only one.
Caregivers should pay attention to whether Mom is still managing the everyday activities she handled six months or a year ago.
Possible signs include:

Repeating questions or stories frequently.
Missing appointments or forgetting medications.
Unopened mail or unpaid bills piling up.
Difficulty preparing meals or forgetting to eat.
Expired food accumulating in the refrigerator.
Wearing the same clothes repeatedly or declining personal hygiene.
Increased clutter or an unusually messy home.
Trouble using appliances that were once familiar.
More falls, near-falls or difficulty getting out of a chair.
Unexplained weight loss or increased fatigue.
Withdrawing from friends, church, hobbies or social activities.
Becoming unusually anxious, irritable or suspicious.
Getting confused while driving or walking familiar routes.

Financial changes can be particularly important.
Late bills, duplicate payments, confusion about accounts or falling for scams may indicate that Mom is having more difficulty with judgment or organization even when casual conversation and memory still seem relatively normal.
The central question may be less about whether Mom occasionally forgets something and more about this:
Can she still function independently the way she did a year ago?
Listen to the people around her
Caregiving works best when one person doesn’t have to make every judgment alone.
Brothers and sisters, grandchildren, longtime friends, neighbors and others who know Mom well may notice changes the primary caregiver has gradually become accustomed to.
Families can periodically ask:
“Have you noticed anything different about Mom during the past six months?”
Then listen for examples.
If several people independently notice similar changes — problems with memory, mobility, organization, judgment or social engagement — it may be worth taking a closer look.
Writing down specific examples and approximate dates can also be useful when talking with Mom’s physician.
Why waiting can make things harder
Avoiding the conversation can feel easier, particularly when Mom values her independence and family members don’t want her to feel that decisions are being made for her.
But waiting until something happens can dramatically reduce the family’s choices.
Small problems can become larger ones: missed medications, poor nutrition, unpaid bills, falls, scams, driving problems or worsening health conditions.
And instead of making decisions gradually, the family may suddenly be making them in a hospital room after a fall or medical emergency.
Addressing concerns early doesn’t necessarily mean moving Mom into assisted living.
In fact, modest support may help her remain at home longer.
That support could include meal delivery, transportation, medication reminders, homemaker services, companion visits, an adult day program or a few hours of in-home care each week.
The better question may not be, “Does Mom need assisted living?”
It may be:
“What support would help Mom remain safe and independent?”
Start with a medical conversation
When noticeable changes begin occurring, Mom’s primary care physician or a geriatric specialist can be an important first stop.
Changes in memory, mood, balance or behavior can have many potential causes, including medications, hearing or vision problems, depression, illness, cognitive impairment or other medical conditions.
A medical evaluation can help families better understand what may be occurring and establish a baseline to compare against future changes.
Going into the appointment with specific examples is more useful than simply saying, “Mom seems different.”
Delaware caregivers don’t have to figure it out alone
Families also have Delaware organizations that can help them understand what assistance may be available.

Delaware Aging and Disability Resource Center:  The state’s Aging and Disability Resource Center can help families learn about in-home care, transportation, meal programs, respite care, adult day programs, benefits and long-term care options.  Phone: 800-223-9074
Easterseals Delaware Caregiver Resource Center:  Easterseals provides caregiver education, support and guidance for families trying to understand aging and caregiving options. Its resources can also help caregivers develop plans and address the stress that often accompanies caring for a parent.
Alzheimer’s Association Delaware Valley Chapter:  When memory or cognitive changes are part of the concern, the Alzheimer’s Association offers education, support groups, care consultations and guidance about evaluation and safety.  Its 24-hour helpline is 800-272-3900.

Pay attention before the crisis
There is an important middle ground between doing nothing and moving a parent into assisted living.
For some families, the answer may simply be additional help around the house. For others, it may eventually involve home care, an adult day program, assisted living or another level of support.
The advantage of noticing changes early is that Mom can be part of those decisions.
Families have time to ask what she wants, understand the options, review finances and determine what level of assistance makes sense.
Sometimes the first indication is nothing more specific than a feeling shared by adult children everywhere:
Mom just doesn’t seem quite like herself anymore.
That feeling shouldn’t automatically lead to a conclusion.
But it may be a good reason to start paying closer attention.



CAREGIVER CHECK: THREE QUESTIONS TO ASK
 

Is Mom safe?
Look at falls, driving, medications, cooking and whether she can respond appropriately in an emergency.
Is Mom managing?
Look at bills, meals, housekeeping, appointments and other everyday responsibilities.
Is Mom different than she was a year ago?
Consider memory, judgment, personality, mobility, and social engagement.
If the answer to one of those questions is “I’m not sure,” it may be time to gather more information rather than wait for a crisis.
