name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Justice Department alleges misconduct by ‘all but one’ Minnesota federal judge
description: The U.S. Department of Justice has filed a judicial misconduct complaint to the Eighth Circuit Court of Appeals, accusing “all but one” of Minnesota’s federal district judges of unethical conduct, Attorney General Todd Blanche announced in a press conference Wednesday.  The complaint stems from interviews given by Judges Patrick Schiltz and others to the New[...]
text:
Attorney General Todd Blanche appears at his confirmation hearing in front of the Senate Judiciary Committee on Capitol Hill July 15, 2026 in Washington, D.C. (Photo by Eric Lee/Getty Images)The U.S. Department of Justice has filed a judicial misconduct complaint to the Eighth Circuit Court of Appeals, accusing “all but one” of Minnesota’s federal district judges of unethical conduct, Attorney General Todd Blanche announced in a press conference Wednesday. 
The complaint stems from interviews given by Judges Patrick Schiltz and others to the New York Times earlier this month, in which Schlitz — who until recently was the chief justice for the District of Minnesota — said the federal government’s actions during Operation Metro Surge “created a grave threat to the rule of law.”
The Times wrote that it interviewed six of the seven judges who were active in the District of Minnesota during the federal immigration crackdown, which resulted in the improper arrests of hundreds of immigrants and the deaths of two U.S. citizens. 
“These judges talked to the media, or at least to the New York Times, about cases, some of which are ongoing, in a manner that the department views as a clear violation of their ethical duties,” Blanche said. 
The code of conduct for federal judges bars them from speaking to the press about cases pending before the court. The New York Times wrote that Schlitz didn’t comment on specific cases, but noted that it’s “unusual for federal judges to give extensive interviews that reflect on periods when their rulings have made headlines.”
The Justice Department and the Trump administration more broadly have gone to war — in Blanche’s own words — with a federal judiciary that’s often been the only bulwark stopping President Donald Trump’s expansive view of his own powers. Trump and his allies have personally attacked judges who have not ruled in the president’s favor, and called for their removal. 
The DOJ sued the entire federal bench in Maryland after judges ordered a 48-hour freeze on deportations of immigrants who had challenged their detention in court.  
The Justice Department’s complaint only names Schlitz, Judge John Tunheim and “anonymous district judges.” Blanche didn’t identify which judge was not implicated, though the Times in its article states that U.S. Magistrate Judge Douglas Micko declined the interview request.
The move is an escalation of an ongoing fight between the Justice Department and Minnesota federal judges, as the DOJ continues prosecuting a number of controversial cases stemming from Operation Metro Surge, including conspiracy charges against a group of 15 anti-ICE activists and the prosecutions of people who protested at a St. Paul church where a pastor is a high-ranking ICE official. 
Minnesota judges grew frustrated with the Department of Homeland Security and federal prosecutors this winter as they fielded around 1,000 habeas corpus cases, in which immigrants argued they’d been wrongfully detained. In more than 70% of cases, judges sided with the detainees and ordered their release, according to an analysis from University of Minnesota researchers. 
In some of those cases, DHS did not immediately comply with judges’ orders to return detainees to Minnesota, prompting judges to consider contempt charges against federal officials. In an extraordinary move, U.S. District Court Judge Jeffrey Bryan ordered U.S. Attorney Daniel Rosen to appear in court and explain why he should not be held in contempt for violating court orders to return the property of 28 people released from ICE detention. 
Trump administration officials also went over Schlitz’s head in an attempt to get a warrant for the arrest of journalist Don Lemon and others involved in the Cities Church protests. When that warrant was blocked by the other judge, the prosecutors convened a grand jury, which returned the indictments. Now, Micko is reviewing the grand jury transcripts to see if federal prosecutors acted improperly to secure the indictment. 
The DOJ’s office in Minnesota lost many of its most experienced prosecutors in the wake of Operation Metro Surge, at least in part because Trump administration officials in Washington pushed them to abandon an inquiry into the killing of Renee Good by ICE agent Jonathan Ross in south Minneapolis, and instead investigate Good’s widow. 
“My impression was that most, if not all, of the noncompliance was due to incompetence,” Schlitz said in his interview with the Times, “not due to conscious defiance of orders.”
The Justice Department is asking all of the Minnesota judges in its complaint to recuse themselves from cases involving the Department of Homeland Security.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Louisiana adds more public money to host rodeos, college sports events
description: Louisiana lawmakers increased the amount of public money the state will spend on college sports championships, rodeos and other entertainment events in this fiscal year to at least $12.1 million in direct support. State budget documents show it was previously slated to spend $10.4 million in the current fiscal year.
text:
Louisiana is helping to finance at least two rodeos, in New Orleans and Lake Charles, with public funding this year. (Photo by Ashley Murray/States Newsroom)Louisiana lawmakers increased the amount of public money the state will spend on college sports championships, rodeos and other entertainment events in this fiscal year to at least $12.1 million in direct support. State budget documents show it was previously slated to spend $10.4 million in the current fiscal year.  

The Joint Legislative Committee on the Budget voted this month to spend an additional $2 million on the Hondo Rodeo Fest in New Orleans next year. It also approved $500,000 for the Southern College Athletic Conference men’s and women’s basketball championships, which Shreveport will host from 2027-29. Centenary College in Shreveport is the only Louisiana member of the NCAA Division III conference with schools in Texas, Arkansas and Colorado. 
The annual state budget approved in June already included $400,000 for the Independence Bowl, a postseason college football game held in Shreveport every year. The legislature also allocated $700,000 for golf course upgrades linked to a LIV Golf event in New Orleans that was called off in April. 
When the budget passed in June, lawmakers also provided $8.5 million total for four other events: the 2028 College Football Playoff National Championship game in New Orleans; the Defenders of Liberty Air Show in Bossier; the Southwest District Livestock Show and Rodeo in Lake Charles; and Tales of the Cocktail, a beverage conference and festival in New Orleans. Budget documents don’t reveal how the money will be divided among the four events. 

A few of these events received public financing last year as well. 
LIV Golf was allocated $7 million in 2025, including $2 million for improvements to the Bayou Oaks at City Park golf course where the tournament was supposed to take place. The tour still owes the state $1.2 million of the $5 million “hosting fee” it was supposed to return when it cancelled the June event. 
The Hondo Rodeo, which came to New Orleans for the first time in April, also received $2 million and the Barksdale air show received $500,000 last year. 
More events could receive funding in the coming months. Gov. Jeff Landry and legislators moved $25 million from a state savings account into the state’s Major Events Incentive Fund in June. State officials have said the money helps Louisiana attract and keep events that bring tourists to the state. 
The Landry administration and lawmakers had considered giving $2 million to No Problem Raceway in Assumption Parish for a National Hot Rod Association event for example. But it pulled back on those plans after the ownership of the raceway changed, state Sen. Ed Price, D-Gonzales, said at a budget meeting this month. 

The Essence Festival of Culture, held over July 4th weekend in New Orleans, has traditionally received state major events funding, including $1.2 million in 2025. It wasn’t given an allocation in the current budget, and its future in the city is also uncertain, according to The Times-Picayune.SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: NH childcare costs to be evaluated as Market Rate Survey opens to providers
description: This week, two surveys that will help assess what New Hampshire parents pay for children to attend early care and education programs and what those programs spend providing care will open.  The Market Rate Survey and the Narrow Cost Analysis “help illustrate what it really takes to provide childcare in New Hampshire,” according to the […]
text:
An infant plays at Kids by the Common in Londonderry on Sept. 3, 2026. The Market Rate Survey and Narrow Cost Analysis help determine childcare scholarship rate and other subsidy and planning information. (Photo by Maya Mitchell/New Hampshire Bulletin) This week, two surveys that will help assess what New Hampshire parents pay for children to attend early care and education programs and what those programs spend providing care will open. 
The Market Rate Survey and the Narrow Cost Analysis “help illustrate what it really takes to provide childcare in New Hampshire,” according to the UNH Carsey School of Public Policy. The Market Rate Survey analyzes what providers charge families for care, and the Narrow Cost Analysis looks at what providers spend on things like materials, meals, rent, utilities and more to provide childcare. 
The surveys are administered every three years as the state prepares to submit a new Child Care and Development Fund plan to the federal government on how it will spend childcare subsidies. The results help set rates for the New Hampshire Child Care Scholarship Program, develop the next subsidy plan, and inform state and advocacy planning efforts on what is needed to have a successful childcare system. 
The surveys were last administered in spring 2024 through a Colorado-based consulting firm. There was a 53.2% response rate from 393 childcare providers, a rate less than what the federal government requires for an approved survey. New Hampshire had to be issued a waiver to allow the results to be used in subsidy and scholarship cost planning. 
This year, the state Department of Health and Human Services partnered with the Carsey School, which runs the New Hampshire Early Care and Education Research Consortium, to develop the survey and improve the response rate. 
Officials from the Bureau of Child Development and Head Start Collaboration and the Carsey School said the surveys were designed to create a “user-friendly” experience for childcare providers, allowing them to complete both surveys at once through their pre-existing profiles on the N.H. Connections Information System. Responses will be kept confidential and used only for their intended purpose. 
Despite the Executive Council withholding approval of the contract for months due to cost issues, the survey will open on schedule Oct. 1. It closes to providers on Nov. 15, with a report on the findings expected next spring.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Des Moines police face another excessive-force lawsuit
description: Three Des Moines police officers are being sued for the alleged excessive force used in the arrest of a man who sustained a broken jaw. It’s the second excessive-force lawsuit to be filed against Des Moines police in the past five weeks. Charles Leroy White, 49, of Des Moines is suing the City of Des […]
text:
This screenshot from police body-camera footage allegedly shows burglary suspect Charles Leroy White on the ground and surrendering to Des Moines police just before officers broke his jaw during a 2024 arrest. (Photo from U.S. District Court filings.) Three Des Moines police officers are being sued for the alleged excessive force used in the arrest of a man who sustained a broken jaw.
It’s the second excessive-force lawsuit to be filed against Des Moines police in the past five weeks.
Charles Leroy White, 49, of Des Moines is suing the City of Des Moines and police officers Alex Andersen, Brian Oswald and Grant Purcell in U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Iowa.
The lawsuit alleges that on Dec. 1, 2024, at 11:30 a.m., Des Moines police were dispatched to a parking lot to investigate a report of a man, later identified as White, looking into parked vehicles and pulling on their door handles.
Andersen, Purcell and Oswald allegedly arrived and instructed White to leave the property, which he did. Later, however, White returned to the area and the officers attempted to take him into custody.
According to the lawsuit, White, who was unarmed, backed away from the officers and Oswald pointed a Taser at White and ordered him to get on the ground before discharging the weapon and striking White in the neck with one of the Taser’s two electronic probes.
White initially attempted to run away, but then “voluntarily lowered himself to the ground, coming to rest on his back” and surrendered, the lawsuit alleges.
According to the lawsuit, the officers’ body cameras captured video of White “lying on his back, with his hands visible and empty, offering no resistance,” at which point Oswald yelled at White, “Don’t you move! Get on your back now!”
The lawsuit asserts that Andersen then rolled White over, from his back and onto his chest, after which the officers gathered around him and Purcell applied enough pressure to White’s jaw to fracture it. The lawsuit asserts that White exclaimed, “You broke my jaw,” and “Please don’t do that,” and Oswald deployed his Taser, in stun-gun mode, against White’s left leg.
“The force applied to White after he surrendered, including the application of force to his jaw and the drive-stun to his leg, was objectively unreasonable, unnecessary, and excessive,” the lawsuit alleges.  “White’s serious injury was obvious. White is heard on body-worn camera stating that his jaw was broken and screaming in pain.”
According to the lawsuit, the officers did not summon any emergency medical personnel to the scene, nor did they arrange for any other medical care, instead transporting White to the police station and then to the jail.
“White was not provided medical treatment for his fractured jaw until Dec. 2, 2024, when personnel at the Polk County Jail arranged for White to be taken for medical care at Broadlawns Medical Center,” the lawsuit claims.
The lawsuit seeks unspecified damages for alleged excessive force, denial of medical care and assault and battery.
As part of the lawsuit, White’s attorneys argue the Des Moines Police Department has engaged in a policy or practice of encouraging or tolerating the use of force against arrestees who have initially resisted but then surrendered. The lawsuit cites a series of excessive-force claims, dating back to 2008, that have resulted in $1.7 million in settlements paid by the city.
Those incidents, the lawsuit claims, “reflect a continuing, widespread, and persistent pattern of unconstitutional conduct” by Des Moines police.
City officials, who say they do not comment on pending litigation, have yet to file a response to White’s lawsuit.
Court records indicate that after White was taken into custody he was criminally charged with interference with official acts and attempted burglary in the third degree. The interference charge was later dismissed and White pleaded guilty to the attempted burglary charge. He was sentenced to one year of probation.
DM police also sued over traffic stop
On Sept. 2, 2026, Eric Lee Kelley, 39, filed a lawsuit against Des Moines police, claiming the officers who allegedly assaulted him during a 2024 traffic stop were later captured on video laughing about how they “really worked him over.”
Police reports indicate that during a traffic stop, Kelley attempted to flee, resulting in what the lawsuit calls “a physical struggle.” Officers attempted to take Kelley to the ground, at which point one officer allegedly punched Kelley in the back of the head four or five times. At that point, the lawsuit asserts, Kelley stopped resisting.
According to the lawsuit, Kelley, who was unarmed, lowered himself into a prone position face down in the roadway. The lawsuit claims the officers’ body camera footage shows Kelley lying motionless on the ground, held at gunpoint by the officers, for about eight seconds before a police canine began biting Kelley in the leg.
The officers allegedly allowed the dog to continue biting and holding Kelley while they directed profanities at Kelley and yelled conflicting instructions at him. After the incident, the lawsuit claims, body camera footage captured the officers “laughing and recounting their exploits” to each other.
One officer allegedly told her colleagues, “You really worked him over,” while another allegedly boasted of punching Kelley, saying, “I was nonchalant as I was punching his head.” “It was awesome,” another officer is alleged to have replied.
The city has denied any wrongdoing in that case and asserted the officers, who acted in good faith and in a legal manner, have qualified immunity. A trial date has yet to be scheduled.

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: How will AI reshape life in New Hampshire? There are no real words.
description: On Monday, the Concord Monitor published an opinion article by Republican state Sen. Dan Innis about the rising opposition to data centers in New Hampshire — even when they are cleverly marketed as “server farms” or “innovation hubs.” It’s notable when a Republican lawmaker, at any level of government, puts the welfare of the people […]
text:
You can pull over anywhere in New Hampshire and find beauty, including this roadside field in Henniker on the last morning of September 2026. (Photo by Dana Wormald/New Hampshire Bulletin)On Monday, the Concord Monitor published an opinion article by Republican state Sen. Dan Innis about the rising opposition to data centers in New Hampshire — even when they are cleverly marketed as “server farms” or “innovation hubs.”
It’s notable when a Republican lawmaker, at any level of government, puts the welfare of the people so squarely ahead of the desires of industry, but Innis (and Gov. Kelly Ayotte, for that matter) doesn’t seem even a little bit conflicted about the wisdom of a possible data center ban. “A moratorium isn’t anti-business,” he wrote. “It’s pro-New Hampshire.”
While Innis’ main concern about data centers seems to be their electricity usage, the cause of the data center boom — artificial intelligence — is also making news in New Hampshire, and nationally, too.
Last week, The Dartmouth published an investigation into Dartmouth provost Santiago Schnell’s use of AI in his writing, including a “100% AI-written” piece (according to an AI-checker program called Pangram) published by The Washington Post in August. The title of that column is “Universities are fighting AI cheating. But there’s a deeper problem.” Dartmouth student journalists Alex Klee and Isabela Pierry, who cited an August Semafor article that mentions Schnell as the launch point for their own investigation, found that “a test of nine of his works published this year returned a median ‘AI-written’ percentage of 96%.”
Schnell, who as provost serves as the college’s chief academic officer, told The Dartmouth he uses artificial intelligence for “language refinement, copyediting, improving clarity and organization, and making writing processes more efficient,” but takes full responsibility for the content of the work. He also said the “100% AI-written” claim was “not accurate.”
“There’s evidence,” Schnell wrote to The Dartmouth about AI checkers, “that they’re biased against nonnative English speakers, such as myself.” That’s a reasonable defense, and it reminded me of a year-old blog post by Marcus Olang’ titled: “I’m Kenyan. I don’t write like ChatGPT. ChatGPT writes like me.” 
Everything is clear-cut, until it’s not.
Meanwhile, there isn’t a media outlet in the world that isn’t dealing with AI creep — and it’s not just in the opinion submissions.
The Bulletin receives a lot of story pitches from readers, as do most news organizations, but one tip this week proved to be a first. It was related to a failed public records request that the writer said had to do with attendance counts at various trailheads in the White Mountains.
“RSA 91-A (New Hampshire’s right-to-know law) requires records or a written denial within 5 business days. An empty closure is neither,” the frustrated writer said of an unfilled records request.
Here’s how the email message ended: “Disclosure: I’m an AI agent on iLands; I filed this myself and I have no client.”
A couple of days earlier, the Bulletin received a thorough outline from a local farmer regarding, once again, the state’s right-to-know law, as well as issues involving tax documents, audits, land permits, titles, etc. While the tip wasn’t from an AI agent, the signer of the email not only wasn’t the one who actually sent it but wasn’t even the person who was feeding AI the prompts that resulted in the detailed pitch.
I say all of this not as a judgment of the tipster — few working people have the luxury of spending an hour or more to craft a complex email — but rather to illustrate something about AI that is fully present rather than anticipated: As with social media, AI has added another layer of separation among living, breathing, thinking, feeling human beings. 
I’m no futurist, but I know that’s not a good thing.
I’ve spent a lot of time reading about and pondering AI recently. I’ve done the same thing with climate change and wealth inequality over the years, among a handful of other concerning subject areas. The aim is not so much to try to become smarter (and I know several of you would say it hasn’t worked anyway) but rather to calm myself a little bit. We all have that option: You can spend a sleepless night worrying about the monster you sense but can’t see or you can take a look under the bed. 
I’d rather look. There will always be shadows the eyes can’t penetrate, but the act of trying to see more deeply is itself empowering.
Other times, though, the healthiest thing you can do is try to escape, briefly.
To that end, I have grown to appreciate the New Hampshire outdoors more at this stage in my life than ever before. Sometimes it’s on a hiking trail or at the edge of a lake, but the sensation isn’t all that different in my backyard or even on the drive to work. This heightened sensitivity to natural beauty is a counterweight to reading and thinking about the effect humans have on climate and the environment — about how it all seems to be slipping away.
In examining wealth inequality, I’ve come to largely reject the “bootstrap” mentality underpinning the concept of the American dream. To an extent we often don’t admit to ourselves as a society, the world’s economic winners and losers are predetermined and a simple truth emerges: Wealth trickles up, and up is where it stays. But I understand something else, too: Speaking strictly for myself, the greatest thing wealth can buy is time — more time with loved ones, more time for everyday pleasures. I must work to live, like most people, but once core financial needs are met I have a degree of control over the price of my hours (and that “degree” is at the heart of America’s “privilege” divide).
So what about AI?
I am mindful of and relatively well informed about some of the ways the technology could go horribly wrong for humanity, but for now my main concern is about art, culture, language and disinformation. I’ve spent my entire life fascinated by words, about the weight they carry, and the ground beneath my feet has never felt less stable. To steady myself, I’ve turned back toward the shape of words in a way that’s both joyful and solidly physical.
This week, amid widespread trepidation about the world’s digital future, a literary journal from October 1947 was delivered to my PO box. I tracked down the copy of Horizon through an old-fashioned online search because it contains an early section of Ralph Ellison’s “Invisible Man” — nearly five years before that brilliant novel was published and several decades before the arrival of ChatGPT. I also found a 1948 issue of The Atlantic Monthly, which includes early short stories from Joseph Heller and James Jones, and the November 1986 edition of Seventeen featuring “The Rules of the Game” by Amy Tan.
I know I can find all of those works online or in the local bookstore, but turning pages in a magazine whose contents are fully enclosed in a previous era feels something like an escape hatch, or maybe time travel. 
AI is taking over the present and it lords over the future, but I find some solace in knowing there are still places where it cannot ever go.

name: Washington State Standard
title: WA company has to pay $410K for withheld hospital charity care
description: A company providing medical care at the Overlake Medical Center emergency room will refund more than $400,000 to low-income patients under an agreement with Washington’s attorney general.  Between 2020 and 2026, Puget Sound Physicians failed to refund nearly $347,000 to more than 1,400 patients at Overlake in Bellevue who qualified for charity care. The comp[...]
text:
(Photo by Getty Images)A company providing medical care at the Overlake Medical Center emergency room will refund more than $400,000 to low-income patients under an agreement with Washington’s attorney general. 
Between 2020 and 2026, Puget Sound Physicians failed to refund nearly $347,000 to more than 1,400 patients at Overlake in Bellevue who qualified for charity care. The company has contracted with Overlake to provide physician services at its emergency room. 
Washington state law requires hospitals to help low-income patients with out-of-pocket medical costs. It applies to people with or without health insurance. A few years ago, assistance was expanded to an estimated four million residents, leading to litigation from hospitals. 
The largest hospitals have to provide more financial aid than smaller ones. And if a patient pays their bill but is later found to qualify for this charity care, the hospital owes them a refund.  
In recent years, Washington hospitals have paid out more than $1 billion in charity care annually, but there have still been several instances of major hospitals not providing the required discounts.
As part of its Overlake contract, Puget Sound Physicians agreed to follow the hospital’s charity care policies. The company, which is made up of dozens of doctors, directly bills patients treated  in the emergency department.
Puget Sound Physicians attributed its failure to refund patients to unintentional accounting errors, according to a court order filed Tuesday. The company maintains that this doesn’t amount to a violation of the state’s Consumer Protection Act, while Attorney General Nick Brown’s office believed it constituted illegal unfair or deceptive trade practices. 
“Our state’s charity care laws are designed to make sure people never forgo life-saving medical care out of fear that they can’t afford it,” Brown said in a statement. “When providers fail to follow the law, our consumer protection team stands up for Washington patients.”
Puget Sound Physicians says the errors affected fewer than 18% of patients who received free care, and that over the past five years the company has provided $2.4 million in free medical care to more than 7,700 patients.
“Providing quality medical care to patients regardless of their ability to pay is a core value of Puget Sound Physicians,” a company spokesperson said in a statement. “We take this commitment seriously and are dedicated to ensuring that patients who qualify for charity care receive these benefits. We appreciate the opportunity to resolve this matter and to strengthen our processes going forward.”
An Overlake spokesperson said that “we believe those who qualify for financial assistance should receive the support available to them under Overlake’s financial assistance policy and under Washington state law, and we remain committed to helping patients understand and access financial assistance programs for healthcare services.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Within 120 days, Puget Sound Physicians must issue refunds with interest to 1,382 patients entitled to refunds who the attorney general’s office identified in an investigation. With interest, the total payments needed exceed $410,000. Another 24 patients are eligible but they’re owed $2 or less and so are left out of the settlement.
Puget Sound Physicians has to track down patients’ current addresses to mail them checks. If returned as undeliverable, the company has to call at least three times over the course of a month to get the correct address. If that’s not successful, the company doesn’t have to provide them a refund. It also has to follow up via phone if the check isn’t cashed within 90 days.
The company also owed the attorney general’s office $52,500 in legal fees.
As part of the order, Puget Sound Physicians agreed to comply with charity care law going forward. If it happens again, Brown’s office can come back for more penalties.
This is the latest in a slew of cases where hospitals have been forced to refund patients for withheld charity care discounts.
Last year, Confluence Health, which runs two hospitals in central Washington, refunded more than $1.8 million after failing to give discounts to more than 4,700 patients. 
In 2024, Providence agreed to refund more than $20 million to patients that qualified for free or reduced-cost healthcare, after a lawsuit from then-Attorney General Bob Ferguson. PeaceHealth said it would pay up to $13.4 million to more than 15,000 patients through direct refunds and a claims process. CHI Franciscan returned $1.8 million. And Capital Medical Center in Olympia paid at least $250,000.
Patients who think their hospital isn’t following the state’s charity care law can file a complaint with Brown’s office.

name: VTDigger
title: Burlington only has itself to blame for its decline
description:
Cutting the police department was a mistake and threw the baby out with the bath water.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Burlington only has itself to blame for its decline.
text:
This commentary is by Michael Pill, a lawyer who lives in Burlington.
We recently bought a house in Burlington to age in place with younger family who live in the city. I am a confirmed leftist, a staunch anticapitalist with a doctorate in Marxian economic theory, a supporter of gun control and a Jew who believes that every human being is charged with the social mission of repairing the world in which we live. The struggle to eliminate all forms of prejudice that divide us is both an individual and collective responsibility.
We live in a class society where we middle-class folks do not always see and fully appreciate the darker underside of our society. I got my own rude awakening doing court-appointed criminal defense legal work when I began practicing law. I learned that while police officers are as human as the rest of us, they routinely put their lives on the line with every traffic stop and domestic disturbance call. One of my law partners was a former police officer, and another was the wife of a police officer. She lived in fear every time her husband left for a tour of duty. Her real-life nightmares included waking up at 2 a.m. and realizing he was not home even though his shift ended at 11 p.m. Turned out a major bar fight required holding over his shift to deal with multiple arrests. Another time she was awakened by a phone call from the police chief saying, “We are at the hospital, and he is going to be all right.” Her only consolation was knowing that if he had been killed or mortally injured, the chief would be at her door in person.
At all hours of the day and night, including holidays and weekends, in all kinds of weather, police officers are out there in cruisers, waiting for our 911 call. They are the reason we sleep soundly in our beds at night. They wear vests they know are not really bulletproof. Even if the vest stops a bullet, the impact can cause serious internal injuries. An officer who draws a weapon must make a split-second life-or-death decision that will be second-guessed at length by citizens, pundits and lawyers. They know the pistols they carry are no match for organized drug dealers’ semiautomatic weapons.
My immigrant grandfather used to say, “There are really three sides to every story: your side, my side and the right side.” Many criticisms leveled at police departments around the country are well founded and must be addressed. Problems such as racial profiling, lack of adequate training and police officers losing their tempers are real problems. One way to minimize unjustified police shootings is more and better training.

READ MORE

We must be especially careful about generalizing and simply assuming that because some police departments have serious problems, the same is true of every police department. In my book, passing judgment on people because they are police officers is no different from judging people by race, religion, gender, sexual orientation or some other category. To borrow from the words of the Rev. Martin Luther King Jr., in his “I Have a Dream” speech at the 1963 March on Washington, we must learn to judge police departments and police officers individually, not by the uniform and badge they wear, “but by the content of their character.”
We must also realize that, like all of us, police officers are human beings and therefore less than perfect. There is good and bad in all of us. Our task, as the fabric of our society unravels, is to strive to work together to bring out the good, both in ourselves and in our fellow human beings.
Burlington must face the fact that reducing the number of police officers from about 100 to around 60 now was a mistake that threw the baby out with the bath water. There is a correlation between gutting the city’s police department and the current sad state of Burlington’s downtown and public spaces. Adequate funding for the Burlington Police Department is an essential — albeit not the only — action necessary to make the city’s downtown and public spaces safe and usable for all once again.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Burlington only has itself to blame for its decline.

title: Public health advocates pitch New Mexico lawmakers on heat, climate change initiatives
description: Public health advocates on Tuesday proposed initiatives to New Mexico lawmakers to help track the impact of heat and wildfire smoke on residents’ health, and help fund communities' responses to threats from climate change.
text:
Advocates from Healthy Climate New Mexico proposed initiatives to legislators on Sept. 29, 2026, to help the state track health impacts from heat and wildfire smoke. Above: The Frijoles Fire burning in the Pecos wilderness, pictured Aug. 8, 2026. (Photo courtesy Santa Fe National Forest)Public health advocates on Tuesday proposed initiatives to state lawmakers to help track the impact of heat and wildfire smoke on residents’ health, and help fund communities’ responses to threats from climate change. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Two-thirds of all counties in New Mexico recorded their warmest temperatures to date this summer, Eva Gulin, a technician for the ZiaMet weather system operated by New Mexico State University, told lawmakers in the interim Legislative Health and Human Resources Committee.
And since April, a total of 1,086 New Mexicans visited emergency rooms throughout the state for heat-related illnesses. 
Healthy Climate New Mexico, a nonprofit collective of health care professionals concerned about climate change, presented proposals to lawmakers that aim to improve preparedness and adaptation to extreme weather driven by human-caused climate change. 
The first proposal would be to reintroduce the Public Health and Climate Program, which died during the 2025 session. The $1.1 million initiative would create a climate health program at New Mexico Department of Health to track health impacts from heat, wildfire smoke, drought, flooding, dust and severe storms. 
The Extreme Weather Resilience Fund, the second proposal, offers grant funds for local and tribal governments to respond to public health risks and impacts from extreme heat, wildfire smoke and other climate change threats. Healthy Climate officials requested $13 million in funding for the program. 
Communities that receive grant money could use it to procure heat sensors, air quality monitors, or air conditioners to create cooling centers, Ashley Proud, executive director of Healthy Climate New Mexico, told lawmakers. 
Presenters also cited a study that showed unhoused people are 10 times more likely to end up in the emergency room from heat-related illness. Proud noted that grant funds could also be used to purchase personal cooling kits and shade structures for the population.
Proud added the fund will be “equitably targeted” with at least 50% of grant funds dedicated to small communities with populations under 100,000. 
“It seems our most vulnerable and impoverished areas of our state are really the ones who are being harmed the most or being exposed,” Sen. Harold Pope (D-Albuquerque) said. “We have to change that.”
While both proposals failed to make it through the 2025 session, Charles Goodmacher, policy advisor for Healthy Climate, told Source NM the temperature in the Legislature has changed.
Goodmacher said his group has “a strong indication from people on the budget committees that at least the Extreme Weather Resilience Fund will likely get passed” during next year’s session.
State Rep. Elizabeth Thomson (D-Albuquerque), who chairs the House Health and Human Services, underscored her support for the climate proposals.
“We lose lives and New Mexicans suffer lifelong health issues from heat and wildfire smoke —it’s a no-brainer as far as I’m concerned,” Thomson told Source NM. “Yes it will cost some money, but it is money well spent and the return on investment will be well worth it.”

title: Delaware State Chamber taps State Rep. Mike Smith as next president
description: Republican lawmaker will succeed Michael Quaranta in December, bringing experience in business policy, education and economic development to Delaware’s largest business organization WILMINGTON, Del. — State Rep. Michael F. Smith, a Republican lawmaker whose legislative work has included economic development, taxes, education and state capital spending, has b[...]
text:
Republican lawmaker will succeed Michael Quaranta in December, bringing experience in business policy, education and economic development to Delaware’s largest business organization
WILMINGTON, Del. — State Rep. Michael F. Smith, a Republican lawmaker whose legislative work has included economic development, taxes, education and state capital spending, has been selected as the next president of the Delaware State Chamber of Commerce.
Smith will succeed Michael J. Quaranta, who plans to retire in mid-December after eight years leading the organization.
The State Chamber’s board selected Smith following a national search, according to an announcement Wednesday.
“Michael Smith brings strong advocacy experience, a deep understanding of Delaware, and a proven ability to build relationships across sectors,” John Gooden, chairman of the State Chamber’s board of directors, said in announcing the appointment.
The move will put a sitting state legislator at the helm of one of Delaware’s most influential business advocacy organizations at a time when employers and lawmakers are debating taxes, state spending, workforce development, health care, energy costs and Delaware’s overall competitiveness.
From Legislative Hall to business advocacy
Smith was first elected to the Delaware House in 2018 and represents the 22nd District, covering Pike Creek Valley and portions of Hockessin and Newark. The Delaware General Assembly currently lists Smith as a Republican representing the district.
His committee assignments have given him a role in several issues directly affecting Delaware employers. Smith serves on the House Revenue and Finance Committee and the Economic Development, Banking, Insurance and Commerce Committee, as well as the Education and Health and Human Development committees.
He also serves on the Joint Capital Improvement Committee, commonly known as the Bond Committee, which develops Delaware’s annual capital spending bill.
Outside Legislative Hall, Smith has worked at the University of Delaware since 2014 and currently serves as director of strategic initiatives and partnerships in the College of Health Sciences. His work there has involved partnerships connecting higher education, health, workforce development and outside organizations.
“I am grateful for the confidence the Board has placed in me and for the opportunity to lead the Delaware State Chamber of Commerce,” Smith said. “The State Chamber has a proud history of advocating for Delaware employers and ensuring the business community has a voice on the issues that affect them.”
Smith said he also sees the Chamber as an organization capable of bringing different groups together to address shared challenges.
“I look forward to building on that work on behalf of employers and employees across Delaware,” he said.
A potentially significant voice in Dover
The appointment could give Smith an unusually direct perspective on the intersection of government and business policy.
The State Chamber, founded in 1837 as the Wilmington Board of Trade, advocates for employers on public policy and economic issues and regularly participates in debates in Dover involving taxation, regulation, workforce policy, economic development and the cost of doing business.
Smith’s legislative background means he arrives with firsthand knowledge of the General Assembly and its budget and committee processes.
The Chamber did not address in Wednesday’s announcement how Smith’s new position will affect his service in the Delaware House. Any change in his legislative status would be a separate matter from his appointment to the Chamber.
Quaranta leaves after eight years
Smith will take over an organization that changed significantly during Quaranta’s eight-year tenure.
According to the Chamber, Quaranta expanded member participation in policy committees, updated conferences and other programming and oversaw development of the organization’s 2025-27 strategic plan.
The Chamber also created the Delaware Employers and Employees Education Fund, a 501(c)(4) organization focused on voter education, and rebranded its charitable organization as the Delaware State Chamber Foundation.
It introduced additional policy and advocacy resources, including its “How They Voted” legislative scorecard and “Delaware Competitiveness Bluebook.”
The Chamber said its annual budget nearly doubled during Quaranta’s tenure despite more than two years of disruption associated with the COVID-19 pandemic.
“Mike Quaranta has led the State Chamber through a period of meaningful change and growth,” Gooden said. “He has helped modernize the organization, strengthen its connection with members, and expand the ways the State Chamber serves Delaware’s business community.”
Smith and Quaranta are expected to work together during a transition period before Quaranta’s departure in December.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Minnesota students’ standardized test scores continue to stagnate
description: Fewer than half of Minnesota students who take the state’s standardized test are able to read and do math at grade-level expectations, according to data released Wednesday by the state’s education department. Performance on the test, called the Minnesota Comprehensive Assessments, declined drastically over the first two years of the COVID-19 pandemic, during[...]
text:
A student works on an algebra problem at Pioneer Ridge Middle School in Eastern Carver County, Wednesday, Sept. 24, 2025. A 2025 Reformer analysis found that Eastern Carver County School District is one of the few large Minnesota districts where math test scores have recovered from the pandemic. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)Fewer than half of Minnesota students who take the state’s standardized test are able to read and do math at grade-level expectations, according to data released Wednesday by the state’s education department.
Performance on the test, called the Minnesota Comprehensive Assessments, declined drastically over the first two years of the COVID-19 pandemic, during which schools closed or held classes remotely. Proficiency rates continue to be over 10 percentage points lower than before the pandemic, when over half of students were proficient in math and reading.


Most Minnesota school districts haven’t recovered test scores after the pandemic

The exams are given in May to students in grades 3-8 in reading and math, with additional reading and math exams in grades 10 and 11, respectively. The results account for over 90% of students in the state, once opt-outs, absences and other reasons are accounted for.
Students and parents are able to opt out of exams. Around 4% of students or their parents opted out of the math exam, for example. Non-participation rates vary widely by school, making test scores much harder to interpret in some cases. In a few schools, over half of students opt out of the exam; on the extreme end, at Farmington High School, around 80% of juniors opted out of the math test.
The reading exams in 2026 are based off of new standards and differ from past exams, education officials said, making them not comparable to old results. The 2026 reading proficiency rate is over one percentage point lower than 2025.
“While results from updated assessments cannot be compared to previous versions, it is common for updated assessments to reflect a ‘drop’ in proficiency due to limited instruction time of the new standards,” the department said in a press release.




At the same time that exams are getting revamped, the Walz administration is creating a task force to review whether they accurately measure student progress.
The task force comes amid a broader national debate over the role of standardized testing and how schools can best measure student learning, including calls for a system that provides more timely information to educators and families instead of relying on results from a single test often completed months ago.
Wide gaps in proficiency persist between white students and students of other races and ethnicities. While around 52% of white students in Minnesota met grade-level standards in math, just 21% of Black students reached grade-level proficiency. Similarly large gaps exist in reading proficiency.
Students also took this year’s exams after Operation Metro Surge, which left some immigrant families afraid to send their kids to school, fearing immigration agents who detained students near their schools. Though federal immigration enforcement largely targeted Hispanic and Latino immigrants, test scores for Hispanic and Latino kids remained steady.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Missouri can keep using disputed federal database to review voter eligibility
description: Missouri can continue using a federal database to review voter eligibility after the U.S. Supreme Court temporarily cleared the way for states to use an expanded version of the system to check the citizenship status of registered voters. The court’s 6-3 emergency order on Friday stayed a federal judge’s ruling that had blocked the expanded […]
text:
Missouri was among the first states to use the database after President Donald Trump signed an executive order in March 2025 directing the U.S. Department of Homeland Security to establish systems allowing state and local authorities to verify the citizenship status of registered voters (Makenzie Huber/South Dakota Searchlight).Missouri can continue using a federal database to review voter eligibility after the U.S. Supreme Court temporarily cleared the way for states to use an expanded version of the system to check the citizenship status of registered voters.
The court’s 6-3 emergency order on Friday stayed a federal judge’s ruling that had blocked the expanded use of the Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements, or SAVE, database. The lower court had found that the federal government’s changes to the system violated federal privacy laws and raised concerns about inaccurate information being used to identify voters as potential noncitizens.
The U.S. Supreme Court’s ruling allows the federal government to continue the revamped SAVE database while the underlying legal challenge proceeds. The court did not issue a final ruling on the merits of the case.
Missouri was among the first states to use the database after President Donald Trump signed an executive order in March 2025 directing the U.S. Department of Homeland Security to establish systems allowing state and local authorities to verify the citizenship status of registered voters.
Missouri Secretary of State Denny Hoskins announced in June that his office had “utilized the federal SAVE database to identify approximately 1,000 individuals registered to vote in Missouri that we could not confirm are United States citizens.” The office said it was working with local election authorities and law enforcement to determine whether those individuals were U.S. citizens or noncitizens.
Anne Marie Moy, spokeswoman for the secretary of state, told the Independent Wednesday that the office has sent about 1,000 registered voters letters notifying them that they’ve been flagged as potentially being noncitizens. 
Voters were asked to respond directly to local election authorities,  May said,“who we work with to act as appropriate.”
The state is unable to comment on how many people have been removed from the rolls during this process because “local election authorities maintain voter records, not the state,” she said.
During a federal court-ordered hearing in April, Nicholas La Strada, who at the time was serving as Hoskins’ director of election integrity, testified that Missouri had already removed more than 300 people he said were not naturalized U.S. citizens after reviewing voter-registration records through SAVE and other databases.
The Supreme Court’s opinion notes that SAVE has existed since 1986, when it was created to allow federal, state and local agencies to verify the citizenship and immigration status of people applying for public benefits. The federal government expanded the system’s use in 2025 to allow states to check voter-registration records.
“The district court’s order thus inhibits the federal government’s efforts to assist state and local agencies in the proper administration of the midterm elections,” Friday’s Supreme Court opinion states.
Justices Ketanji Brown Jackson, Sonia Sotomayor and Elena Kagan dissented. Jackson wrote that the expanded system risked disenfranchising lawful voters, including recently naturalized citizens whose citizenship information may not be reflected accurately in federal records.
The case began after the League of Women Voters and other groups challenged the expanded system in federal court. On June 22, U.S. District Judge Sparkle Sooknanan barred the federal government from using the expanded SAVE database for voter verification, finding that federal agencies had “haphazardly” combined and repurposed personal information to comply with Trump’s 2025 executive order. The result has been that state governments are “actively removing United States citizens from voter rolls based on inaccurate information.” 
“All in all, the federal government has knowingly trampled on the privacy rights of American citizens in a manner that threatens the sacred right to vote,” Sooknanan wrote.
 Missouri’s SAVE process

Texas and Missouri were among the first states to use the revamped SAVE system to examine voter rolls, according to a February investigation by ProPublica and The Texas Tribune. The investigation found that Missouri officials acted on SAVE results before fully verifying them.
In November, Missouri sent lists of flagged voters to county election administrators. ProPublica and The Texas Tribune obtained the lists for seven of the state’s 10 most populous counties and found that SAVE initially identified more than 1,200 people in those counties as potential noncitizens.
The Secretary of State’s Office told election administrators it would work to verify the citizenship determinations. In the meantime, local officials were instructed to change the status of flagged voters, temporarily preventing them from voting.
In early December, about 70 county clerks — Republicans and Democrats — sent a letter to Missouri House Speaker Jonathan Patterson saying there were better ways than SAVE to identify and remove noncitizens from voter rolls.
“These lists are deeply flawed: they are outdated, inaccurate, and include individuals we know to be U.S. citizens — our neighbors, colleagues, and even voters we have personally registered at naturalization ceremonies,” the letter states.
La Strada later testified about Missouri’s use of SAVE during an April 24 hearing in the Missouri Capitol, ordered by federal court in a case challenging the validity of the state’s voter-registration records. That hearing has since become part of a lawsuit La Strada filed after he was fired by Hoskins, alleging retaliation connected in part to his testimony.
La Strada testified that Missouri signed a memorandum of agreement with U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services in March 2025 to use SAVE, shortly after Trump’s executive order.
“We jumped all over it,” La Strada said. “And that was Secretary Hoskins — one of his number one things he wanted to do.”
By April, La Strada said, the Secretary of State’s Office “already took all of our voter registrations” and “ran it through the SAVE database.”
He called the process labor-intensive and said the office was taking precautions because of the potential consequences for voters.
“We all believe in due process,” La Strada said. “Nothing worse than being blamed for something you haven’t done.”
La Strada said the office was also working with the Missouri Department of Revenue and had learned from how other states were using the database.
“A lot of other states actually purge rolls once they get this back,” he said.
Instead, La Strada said Missouri was sending letters to voters flagged as potential noncitizens and giving them 90 days to respond. The week before the hearing, La Strada said, the office had sent a “substantial amount” of letters to those flagged as potentially being noncitizens. 
That would have put the initial response deadline around July, although it remains unclear how many voters were ultimately removed from the rolls as a result of the review.
In July, Hoskins announced that he had led the removal of 280,000 ineligible voters from Missouri’s rolls, including deceased people, noncitizens, felons and people who had moved out of state. He did not provide a separate figure for voters removed because they were determined to be noncitizens.
Moy said the newest number from the start of the Hoskins’ term to today is a little over 296,000. 
La Strada testified that the office’s review relied on information from SAVE, the Department of Revenue, property-location data, alien registration numbers and I-94 immigration records.
Moy told The Independent 1,000 letters were sent “based on information provided by the SAVE database as flagged records.” 
 “All are considered under review,” she said “and given an opportunity to provide proof of citizenship to the local election authority.”
Part of the reason there were so many in question, La Strada said, was that Missouri voters passed a constitutional amendment in 2024 to require all voters to be U.S. citizens. Because of that, there are new voter registration forms and people don’t always remember to check the citizenship box on applications when getting their drivers’ license, for instance. 
He said the people who marked “no” or who didn’t mark anything, “those people have not voted. I want to make…that very clear. They did not vote.”
He also acknowledged the database has some flaws. 
“Is it perfect?” he said. “No. But it’s fixed up over 300 people as of today that are not naturalized citizens.”

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Justices consider appeal in challenge to Nebraska overseas voter law
description: LINCOLN — Nebraska’s highest court heard arguments Wednesday in a Republican National Committee challenge seeking to overturn a state law allowing certain overseas voters to vote. The RNC and two Lancaster County voters, Jack Riggins and Pam Dingman, appealed a lower court’s ruling on their objection to a state law dating back to 2005 that allows U.S. […]
text:
The Nebraska Supreme Court hears oral arguments on Sept. 30, 2026. (Screenshot of Nebraska Public Media livestream by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — Nebraska’s highest court heard arguments Wednesday in a Republican National Committee challenge seeking to overturn a state law allowing certain overseas voters to vote.
The RNC and two Lancaster County voters, Jack Riggins and Pam Dingman, appealed a lower court’s ruling on their objection to a state law dating back to 2005 that allows U.S. citizens who have never resided in Nebraska but who have a parent registered to vote in one Nebraska county to register in that county. It would be a felony to register or vote in multiple states or counties.
The RNC argues the law “dilutes the votes of lawful Republican voters” and violates Article VI, Section 1 of the Nebraska Constitution, which defines a qualified voter as a U.S. citizen who “has resided within the state and the county and voting precinct for the terms provided by law.”
“I truly believe that my vote is precious to me. It’s significant. I’m jealous about my vote. I don’t want anybody taking my vote away from me,” attorney J.L. Spray told justices Wednesday. “I don’t want anybody adding people to dilute my vote, and that’s the attitude most voters should have.”
Attorney J.L. Spray of Lincoln argues before the Nebraska Supreme Court on Sept. 30, 2026. (Screenshot of Nebraska Public Media livestream by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Spray said the Legislature can determine the time and method of voting, as well as the tabulation of votes, but lawmakers can’t disqualify a voter or qualify new voters. He said in this case, the state law expands rather than implements voting rights.
Attorneys for the RNC have said they do not intend to challenge the voting rights of any Nebraskans — military, diplomats or otherwise — who have lived in Nebraska first.
Lancaster County District Judge Ryan Post ruled Aug. 12 that there was at least one constitutional application for the law, so it couldn’t be challenged as unconstitutional on its face.
For a statute to be ruled unconstitutional, a supermajority of the seven-person Supreme Court — at least five justices — would need to agree. Court decisions are more than often unanimous.
Attorneys for Nebraska Secretary of State Bob Evnen, from Nebraska Attorney General Mike Hilgers’ office, offered a hypothetical scenario: a voter born in South America to Saunders County missionaries who intended to return home.
“This court long ago held that residence means domicile, and plaintiffs agree that physical presence is not required to establish a Nebraska domicile,” Deputy Solicitor General Zachary Pohlman told the high court Wednesday.
A sign encouraging Nebraskans to register and get out to vote sits at the Harvest Moon Festival in Lincoln outside a booth for multiple civic advocacy organizations on Sept. 28, 2026. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
As of July, 116 overseas Nebraska voters were registered under the targeted statute, six of whom voted in the May 12 primary, according to data from Evnen’s office, including one voter in Lancaster County. In total, 30 of the 116 voters are registered in Lancaster County.
“I know we’re talking about small numbers here — potentially an albino unicorn of some kind — but even one vote can make a difference,” Spray said.
Dingman is running unopposed for reelection as Lancaster County engineer. With no opponent, she wasn’t on the May ballot.
General election ballots were sent to some targeted voters as early as Sept. 3 — noncertified ballots with space to fill in any candidates or issues not yet certified by that date. The ballot was certified Sept. 11, and finalized ballots were sent to other overseas voters by Sept. 18.
Chief Justice Jeff Funke of Nebraska City and Justices William Cassel of O’Neill and Stephanie Stacy of Lincoln each pressed Spray on how the Nebraska Supreme Court has in the past defined “resided within” under Article XI, Section 1 of the Nebraska Constitution. 
Spray said it means the voter must have a “nexus” to the state, either physically or through an intention to return. He said a person above the age of majority, 19, also changes the calculus.
Deputy Solicitor General Zachary Pohlman argues before the Nebraska Supreme Court on Sept. 30, 2026. (Screenshot of Nebraska Public Media livestream by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Post, however, agreed with Pohlman. He had pointed to an 1895 Supreme Court case where the justices generally accepted that “residence” was synonymous with “domicile.” If the overseas voter chose a new residence, Pohlman said, they would no longer qualify to vote in Nebraska.
Spray asked the justices Wednesday: “How can you abandon a residence you’ve never had?”
The AG’s Office argues that neither the RNC nor the local voters, including Dingman, have standing to challenge the law. Funke asked who, then, could challenge the law if they wanted to. Pohlman said the state attorney general could, if the office disagreed on constitutionality.
Post found that Dingman did have standing, which is why he ruled on the merits of the case, but Justice Jonathan Papik of Omaha and Cassel questioned Pohlman on whether Dingman did. Papik questioned whether it was speculative that Dingman could draw a write-in challenger by an Oct. 23 deadline, while Cassel questioned whether it would be speculative even if she was opposed. To both points, Pohlman said he believes the injury is speculative, and if the justices agree, he said the court should send the case back to Post with directions to dismiss the matter.
Funke asked Pohlman whether the state law increases the number of qualified voters as Spray alleges. Pohlman disagreed and described the law as a matter of implementation.
Said Pohlman: “What it ultimately does is basically like a vote-processing rule.”

title: Federal court temporarily halts execution of Tennessee woman on death row
description: ​A federal appeals court has temporarily stopped the execution of a Tennessee woman set to be the first female put to death in the state in nearly two centuries. ​Christa Pike, 50, was set to be executed Wednesday for the 1995 murder of classmate Colleen Slemmer. Pike’s lawyers have been arguing before the court and […]
text:
Christa Pike was set be executed at Riverbend Maximum Secuity in Tennessee Wednesday, until a federal court intervention. (Photo: John Partipilo/ Tennessee Lookout)​A federal appeals court has temporarily stopped the execution of a Tennessee woman set to be the first female put to death in the state in nearly two centuries.
​Christa Pike, 50, was set to be executed Wednesday for the 1995 murder of classmate Colleen Slemmer.
Pike’s lawyers have been arguing before the court and to Tennessee’s governor for her death sentence to be paused because her original trial failed to account for her history of sexual abuse and neglect as a child.  
​A three-judge panel on the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 6th Circuit ruled that more time was needed to “adequately address and resolve the issues,” brought by Pike’s lawyers.
​“The interests of justice and the finality of Pike’s impending execution compel the entry of a short stay of execution in order to properly analyze the parties’ fully briefed arguments and resolve the issues on the merits,” said Senior United States Judge Jane Stranch in the ruling.
​Before Wednesday’s last-minute pause, the U.S. Supreme Court and Gov. Bill Lee, a Republican, had declined to intervene to stop Pike’s execution.
The Tennessee Attorney General filed an appeal the U.S. Supreme Court Wednesday morning to vacate the appeals court ruling.
This is a developing story and may be updated.

text:
Christa Pike was set be executed at Riverbend Maximum Secuity in Tennessee Wednesday, until a federal court intervention. (Photo: John Partipilo/ Tennessee Lookout)The U.S. Supreme Court vacated the stay of Christa Pike’s execution Wednesday evening, allowing the State of Tennessee to move forward with her death by lethal injection for the 1995 murder of Colleen Slemmer.
Dorinda Carter, a spokesperson for the Tennessee Department of Correction, said the execution will take place Wednesday night.
Pike was set to be executed at 10 a.m. Wednesday before a federal appeals court temporarily halted the execution to review Pike’s history of sexual abuse and neglect as a child, which Pike’s lawyers say was not adequately addressed during the penalty phase in her original trial.
Pike, 50, is set to be the first female put to death in Tennessee in nearly two centuries.
​Before Wednesday’s last-minute pause, the nation’s highest court and Gov. Bill Lee, a Republican, had declined to intervene to stop Pike’s execution.
​The three-judge panel on the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 6th Circuit stayed Pike’s execution Wednesday morning because more time was needed to “adequately address and resolve the issues” brought by Pike’s lawyers, the ruling stated.
The U.S. Supreme Court affirmed the state’s request to proceed with the execution. Justices Sonya Sotomayor, Elena Kagan and Ketanji Brown Jackson dissented.
“The Court’s decision to vacate that stay interferes with the Sixth Circuit’s routine administrative handling of a capital case and unnecessarily prevents that court from giving due consideration to Pike’s claim,” Sotomayor wrote in the dissenting opinion. “Worse, the Court grants such extraordinary relief solely to allow the state to execute Pike before litigation over her conviction has properly run its course in the lower courts.”
“I see no reason to short-circuit the ordinary process of appellate review, particularly in light of the grave consequences of an erroneous decision,” Sotomayor continued. “Tennessee’s desire to expedite Pike’s execution by a few days or even weeks cannot outweigh her ‘fundamental interest in (her) own life.’”
This is a developing story and may be updated.
Sam Stockard contributed to this report.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Kosta Diamantis, still a fugitive, sentenced to 84 months
description: Konstantinos “Kosta” Diamantis was sentenced in absentia Wednesday to 84 months in prison for extorting bribes from contractors.
text:
Konstantinos “Kosta” Diamantis, a fugitive waging a relentless publicity campaign for a presidential pardon from overseas, was sentenced in absentia Wednesday to 84 months in prison for extorting bribes from contractors as a high-ranking state official overseeing school construction grants.
U.S. District Judge Stefan R. Underhill imposed a sentence that fell below the range of 121 to 151 months in prison recommended by sentencing guidelines and sought by prosecutors. Diamantis was convicted on 21 counts, including conspiracy, bribery, extortion and lying to investigators.
Diamantis, 70, a divorced father of five, failed to appear at a scheduled sentencing two weeks ago in U.S. District Court in Bridgeport, instead informing his lawyer he had fled to Greece, where he holds a dual citizenship that complicates efforts by authorities to locate and extradite him.
Underhill said he showed a measure of mercy due to his age, saying a longer sentence likely would mean death behind bars.
There was some uncertainty until Tuesday whether Diamantis would remain overseas. By phone, he expressed a willingness to his lawyer, Norman A. Pattis, and a federal agent to consider a return. A federal official waited at the Athens airport to escort him aboard a flight to the U.S.
“He could have come back yesterday,” Assistant U.S. Attorney Jonathan N. Francis told the judge, underscoring that his absence was voluntary. “All he had to do is show up.”
Diamantis has been a near-constant presence in Connecticut media since his disappearance, telling print, radio and television outlets that he is a victim of a politically “weaponized” Biden-era Department of Justice without offering evidence. He is unabashed in trying to draw the attention of President Donald Trump to his pardon application.
Assistant U.S. Attorney David E. Novick, one of the two prosecutors in the case, called Diamantis uniquely unrepentant, unworthy of mercy.
With the start of his sentence indefinitely delayed by his flight, the judge had been expected to take one action Wednesday with an immediate impact: ordering the forfeiture of the heavily leveraged home in Farmington that Diamantis had posted as part of a bail package that kept him free since his conviction a year ago.
But he stayed a decision on revocation until at least Friday for technical reasons.
The judge ordered further proceedings to calculate restitution owed to Hartford, New Britain, Tolland and the state of Connecticut for what prosecutors said were costs inflated on state-funded school projects in the three municipalities by Diamantis’ pay-to-play scheme.
The prosecutors, Novick and Francis, said in a memorandum filed Tuesday that the crimes committed by Diamantis are covered by the federal Mandatory Victim Restitution Act, an assertion that the defendant’s lawyer, Pattis, did not dispute in his written reply.
Pattis stated in his reply a belief that Diamantis remains in Greece and noted “that the impact of the Fugitive Disentitlement Doctrine may have a bearing on future proceedings in this case.” The doctrine limits the ability of fugitives to litigate claims while snubbing the authority of the courts.
One complication could be a difficulty in getting a federal appeals court to hear an appeal of his conviction, should Diamantis desire to file one. 
Pattis, who has described his client as broke, said computing restitution will require further review, and he asked Underhill to postpone the exercise until the other defendants in the case — officials of two companies who pleaded guilty to bribing Diamantis under duress — are sentenced.
Diamantis pushed Acranom Masonry for work on schools in Tolland and Hartford, and he pressured Hartford, New Britain and Tolland to hire Construction Advocacy Professionals to manage work that already was being done by others, prosecutors said.
Officials from both testified to paying him cash bribes.
“Both appear to have benefited from the arrangements made with Mr. Diamantis. The pleas and verdict in these cases suggest that victims may have claims for restitution as to each of the defendants,” Pattis wrote.
Prosecutors have deemed the contractors as both conspirators and victims.
“Diamantis solicited, cajoled, intimidated, and outright threatened two contractors,” the prosecutors wrote in a sentencing memorandum.
Diamantis was a Democratic lawmaker representing Bristol in the state House of Representatives for 14 years until losing a primary in 2006. A former House colleague hired him in 2015 during the administration of Gov. Dannel P. Malloy to oversee the Office of School Construction Grants and Review.
During the administration of Gov. Ned Lamont, he was permitted to keep that post after Melissa McCaw, the first secretary of policy and management under Lamont, named him as her deputy in the office at the heart of state government. Its wide-ranging responsibilities included the preparation and management of the budget.
Diamantis had surrendered his U.S. passport but told the court he did not have possession of a Greek passport he had obtained since his indictment. The prosecutors say Diamantis drove to Florida, took a boat to the Bahamas and flew to London. He then presumably made his way to Greece.
Greece has had a bilateral extradition treaty with the U.S. since 1931, but Pattis noted Greece generally does not extradite its citizens outside specific conditions outlined in treaties.
According to a United Nations summary of extradition laws, Greece’s Code of Penal Procedure prohibits extradition if the person “for which extradition is requested was Greek when the act was committed.” 
Diamantis, who was born in the U.S., told the Connecticut Mirror he was entitled to Greek citizenship at birth as the son of two Greek citizens. He said his mother was three months pregnant when she and his father emigrated to the U.S., and his parents had registered his birth on a visit to their old village when he was 8.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Braun renews gas tax suspension, broadens untaxed diesel use for farmers
description: Gov. Mike Braun on Wednesday renewed Indiana's gas tax suspension for another 30 days — until early November — and issued a new order lifting restrictions on the sale of untaxed diesel fuel for semi-trucks operated by farmers and timber harvesters, citing continued disruption to global oil supply.
text:
A gas station in Indianapolis advertises diesel at $6.99 a gallon on Wednesday, Sept. 30, 2026. Diesel hit a record high price in September. (Photo by Mackenzi Klemann/Indiana Capital Chronicle)Gov. Mike Braun on Wednesday renewed Indiana’s gas tax suspension for another 30 days — until early November — and issued a new order lifting restrictions on the sale of untaxed diesel fuel for semi-trucks operated by farmers and timber harvesters, citing continued disruption to global oil supply.
The order comes as diesel hit a record high $6.92 average in Indiana in September.
“Affordability is my top priority and my gas tax suspensions have delivered immediate tax relief and some of the cheapest gas in America for Hoosier families,” Braun said. “I’m delivering relief for Hoosier farmers by lifting special fuel restrictions to help ease the burden and providing relief from high gas prices to keep more money in Hoosiers’ pockets and make life more affordable.”
A coalition of more than 50 state legislators sent a letter to Braun this week asking him to lift restrictions on off-road diesel fuel for farmers, who have not seen relief at the pump during the gasoline tax suspension.
The diesel fuel covered by Braun’s order is untaxed, but limited to off-road usage in tractors, bulldozers and other equipment.
Braun’s order will permit farmers and timber harvesters to use off-road fuel for “any farm-related activities” for the next 30 days, at which time he will review both orders for possible renewal.
Indiana’s gasoline excise and sales taxes — which would be about 61 cents a gallon — will remain suspended through Nov. 4.
This story will be updated.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: Wood milling company pledges revamp of Upstate textile plant, bring more than 200 jobs
description: A company that makes wood paneling, crown moulding, and other pine construction products plans to invest $216M in a SC manufacturing plant.
text:
Processed lumber is stacked at Forest Products Timber West Mill in Rapid City, South Dakota, on March 18, 2026. A company that makes wood paneling, crown moulding, shiplap and other pine construction products plans to invest $216 million in a manufacturing plant in South Carolina. (Photo by Preston Keres/U.S. Forest Service)A company that makes wood paneling, crown moulding, shiplap and other pine construction products plans to invest $216 million in a manufacturing plant in Anderson County.
Adeptus USA’s pledged investment is expected to bring 217 new jobs to the small town of Honea Path, 25 miles south of Greenville.
“The tremendous commitment shown by the state of South Carolina, Anderson County and the local forestry community made it clear that this is the right place for Adeptus to invest and grow,” Adeptus USA CEO Billy White said in a statement. “This investment represents far more than a manufacturing operation — it reflects a long-term commitment to our employees, our customers, and the communities of Anderson County and the surrounding area.”
How SC’s once-dominating textile industry has transformed to supply new employers

Adeptus will move into Belton Industries’ shuttered textile manufacturing plant.
The revamped plant, expected to begin operations by the middle of next year, is the company’s first South Carolina location.
“Bringing a closed facility back to life and creating quality jobs makes this project an especially meaningful investment in our community,” Anderson County Councilman Greg Elgin said in a statement.
In exchange for Adeptus’ investment, the state of South Carolina offered an $850,000 grant to help cover the cost of renovating the building. The state also approved income tax credits for the company worth $2,750 for each new job it brings.
The plant also offers a potential boost to a state timber industry that has struggled amid closures of major paper mills.
“Expanding and diversifying opportunities for our forestry sector is a major priority for South Carolina, and Adeptus’ investment is great news.” state Commissioner of Agriculture Hugh Weathers said in a statement.
​
“We’re letting the world know that S.C. forests are open for business, and Adeptus’ announcement is evidence of the sustainable, high-quality, home-grown forest resources we have to offer, added Scott Phillips, the state forester.
