name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Arkansas governor’s ad on Medicaid work requirements draws flak from NAACP, right-wing commentators
description: A campaign ad from Arkansas Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders portraying a Medicaid recipient playing video games and eating junk food instead of working has prompted backlash from the right and left, but for very different reasons. The Republican governor unveiled an ad this week touting the state’s Medicaid work requirements, which will take effect in […]
text:
Arkansas Governor Sarah Huckabee Sanders addresses the press after casting her vote in the primary election in Little Rock, Arkansas on Tuesday, March 3, 2026. (Photo by Katie Adkins/Arkansas Advocate)A campaign ad from Arkansas Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders portraying a Medicaid recipient playing video games and eating junk food instead of working has prompted backlash from the right and left, but for very different reasons.
The Republican governor unveiled an ad this week touting the state’s Medicaid work requirements, which will take effect in January. The 30-second spot features a white actor portrayed as “Brad,” a fictional Medicaid recipient.
“You actually work hard,” Sanders says in the spot, airing statewide as part of a six-figure ad buy. “You pay taxes to cover welfare for guys like Brad who just choose not to work.”
The NAACP Arkansas State Conference said it was “deeply concerned” about the ad, saying it unfairly stereotypes the poor as choosing not to work.
“Arkansas families deserve policies that address poverty — not advertisements that oversimplify it,” the group said in a statement. 
But Sanders’ faced even stronger pushback from conservative influencers and commentators who accused the governor of stereotyping white people.
“This Antiwhite ad should be taken down, the comms team fired, and the Governor’s Office issue an apology,” conservative activist Jack Posobiec wrote on X. 
Matt Walsh, another conservative activist, also criticized the spot.
“These idiotic cowards don’t even have the guts to criticize groups that will never vote for them anyway,” he posted on X.
Nearly 57% of people on Medicaid in Arkansas are white, according to 2024 figures compiled by KFF, a health research organization. About 20% of the state’s Medicaid population is Black according to the figures.
Sanders, who was White House press secretary for part of President Donald Trump’s first term, is running for reelection against Democratic state Sen. Fred Love and Libertarian Colt Shelby. She was first elected in 2022.
Arkansas has begun a ‘soft launch’ of Medicaid work requirements. What does that mean?

Arkansas’ work requirements for its Medicaid expansion program will take effect in January under the federal One Big Beautiful Bill Act that Trump signed into law last year.
The requirements mandate that recipients of the federal insurance program must complete 80 hours of work, community service, higher education, work programming or a combination of the four each month, unless they meet certain exemption criteria. 
The last time Arkansas implemented work requirements for Medicaid, more than 18,000 people lost coverage before a federal judge blocked the restriction. Experts who studied the requirements found a significant increase in uninsured adults, and no signs the requirement created workforce gains.
Sanders has brushed off criticism of her work requirement ad.
“Some critics online don’t like my welfare work requirement ad. Next thing you know they’ll say I should have used cookies instead of cheese balls,” she posted on X.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Exemption for moral, ethical beliefs zapped from DeSantis administration’s proposed vax rule
description: The DeSantis administration is backing off its push to make it easier for parents to opt out of vaccinating their children by eliminating from a proposed rule change “sincerely held moral or ethical belief(s)” from the reasons a parent could object to required vaccinations for children to enter school. The administration announced the change Wednesday, […]
text:
Measles begins with a blotchy red rash that typically appears on the face and then spreads to the body of the person infected. (Photo by Natalya Maisheva/Getty Images)The DeSantis administration is backing off its push to make it easier for parents to opt out of vaccinating their children by eliminating from a proposed rule change “sincerely held moral or ethical belief(s)” from the reasons a parent could object to required vaccinations for children to enter school.
The administration announced the change Wednesday, along with plans for a four-hour rule hearing on Oct. 8 in Lake Mary to discuss additional changes the governor wants to make to the state’s vaccine policies before he is term-limited out of office in January.
The rule hearing was requested by the Florida chapters of the American College of Physicians and the American Academy of Pediatrics.
Chris Nuland, a Jacksonville healthcare attorney and lobbyist for the Florida Chapter of the American College of Physicians, lauded the change but sees it as a tactical move by the administration.
“We applaud the removal of the phrase ‘sincerely held moral or ethical belief(s)’ as the governing statute did not authorize such an exemption,” Nuland told the Florida Phoenix. But he added, “Our fundamental objection to the proposed rule is the deletion of those four vaccinations — haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib), hepatitis B, varicella (chickenpox), and pneumococcal conjugate.)”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.Rule hearings allow affected people to weigh in about proposed regulations before the state adopts them. Following a rule hearing, an affected party can file a challenge to the proposal in the state Division of Administrative Hearings, according to the Pocket Guide to Florida’s Administrative Procedures Act.

The DOH, headed by state Surgeon General Joseph Ladapo, in August published proposed changes to DOH regulations implementing the state’s vaccine requirement laws.
Gov. Ron DeSantis, who has been eager to eliminate all vaccine mandates from Florida law, opted for the administrative route to change policy after the Florida Legislature repeatedly rejected his efforts to change the law.
DeSantis wanted to make it easier for parents to refuse vaccines for their children but still send them to school by adding an exemption for parents who oppose vaccines based on sincerely held moral or ethical beliefs. The Legislature also rejected DeSantis’ push to require pediatricians and other physicians to treat unvaccinated patients, an effort opposed by organized medicine.
DOH: 162 measles cases as of Sept. 19
DOH Secretary and State Surgeon General Joseph Ladapo (image via the Department of Health)
The move to alter the state’s vaccine requirements and eliminate from rules other vaccines comes as the number of measles cases in Florida climbed to 162 as of Aug. 19. That includes four new cases reported to the DOH in September, a review of DOH data shows, including three new cases in Collier County in September. Collier accounts for 113 of the measles cases.
According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, the best way to protect against measles is to get the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine. Herd immunity for the measles occurs when 95% of a population is vaccinated.  According to the CDC, Florida’s MMR vaccination rate for kindergarteners for school year 2025-26 was 88.9%. That’s down from a recent high of 94.1% in the 2017-18 school year, the CDC data show.
Florida law requires children at a minimum to be immunized for poliomyelitis, diphtheria, rubeola, rubella, pertussis, mumps, and tetanus to attend school but allows exemptions for valid medical and religious reasons.
The DOH holds authority under the statute to also require vaccinations for “other communicable diseases as determined.” Under that authority, the DOH has required children to also be immunized for haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib), hepatitis B, varicella (chickenpox), and pneumococcal conjugate.
The proposed amendments would alter existing regulations to eliminate vaccine mandates that aren’t required by law and to codify in rule a 2019 statute that allows parents to opt out of having their children’s vaccine history included in the state’s health online tracking system, commonly referred to as SHOTS.

The proposed changes also remove the combination vaccine, MMR, from the attestation form Florida healthcare providers are asked to sign.
That proposed change would bring the state in line with an executive order signed by President Donald Trump this summer calling on drug manufacturers to unbundle the MMR and MMRV (which provides added protection from chickenpox) vaccines and to produce individual vaccines for each of those illnesses instead.
There are no single vaccines for any of those illnesses and manufacturers would have to produce them. Trump’s order also called for increasing the amount of time between vaccine shots.

name: Mississippi Today
title: MDA chief Bill Cork resigns with little explanation. Reeves appoints Waldrop
description: Bill Cork, chief economic development officer with the Mississippi Development Authority, speaks about a $246 million economic development project during a special session of the Mississippi Legislature in Jackson, Wednesday, November 2, 2022.
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Mississippi Development Authority Director Bill Cork, the state’s head economic development officer, has resigned with little explanation. 
Cork is leaving after a more than two year stint as MDA director. Gov. Tate Reeves appointed Cork in 2023 and he was confirmed by the state Senate in April of 2024. 
Reeves called Cork’s resignation a “retirement,” and wished him “all the best in his future endeavors” in a statement.
“Serving Mississippi has been the honor of my career,” Cork said in a statement, although he declined further comment and for a couple of days he and the governor’s office did not respond to questions of whether he had resigned. “Nina and I arrived on the Gulf Coast more than a decade ago, and this state gave us far more than we could ever give back. I am grateful to Governor Reeves for his leadership, his trust and his friendship.”
Reeves announced that Paul Jerrod “P.J.” Waldrop, the current deputy director and chief operating officer of MDA, will lead the agency, as Reeves enters his final year-and-a-half in office. Reeves in his statement did not say whether he would be submitting Waldrop’s appointment to the state Senate for approval as director.
P.J. Waldrop Credit: Special to Mississippi Today
Reeves during his two terms as governor has struggled to keep a permanent, Senate-approved MDA director in place. Former director Glenn McCullough Jr. resigned as Reeves took office. Reeves appointed John Rounsaville to the post, but he resigned after 15 months after he faced allegations of sexual harassment of female MDA employees. After a state investigation, it was recommended to Reeves that he fire Rounsaville.
Reeves announced that Rounsaville was “stepping down to pursue new opportunity,” and initially praised his work before news broke of the misconduct allegations.” Reeves’ appointed his former communications director, Laura Hipp Mayer, who led MDA as interim director for more than two years after Rounsaville resigned.
Waldrop joined MDA in 2021 as the director of the governor’s military affairs office. He spent more than a decade working for various U.S. senators, including the late Sen. Thad Cochran. 
“The award-winning MDA team is in great hands with PJ Waldrop as executive director. I can’t wait to see the records they break next. It’s been an amazing run, and Mississippi’s best days are still ahead of her. Thank you, Mississippi,” Cork said in his statement. 
Cork has overseen a time of historic investment in Mississippi, largely due to the artificial-intelligence data center boom across the South. The state has seen more than $65 billion in investments and the creation of nearly 23,000 jobs from major corporations such as Amazon, SpacexAI and Hitachi under Cork’s tenure as MDA director.
Before leading MDA, Cork served as the agency’s deputy director and chief economic developer. He was previously CEO of the Hancock County Port and Harbor Commission from 2016-2020 and had worked in Texas at the Texarkana Chamber of Commerce, TexAmericas and Sempra Energy. He is a Marine Corps veteran and received his masters in Urban and Regional Planning from the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign.
During Cork’s confirmation in the Mississippi Senate, questions arose about a report from the Mississippi Personnel Board, which had investigated claims that Cork had created a hostile work environment and complaints about sexual harassment and age discrimination. The report cleared Cork of any legal wrongdoing but said “Cork’s management style has created a toxic workplace.” 
Cork told a Senate committee that he had not done anything wrong but that he was a tough and direct boss, which some employees interpreted as hostile. The Senate unanimously voted to appoint him.
“The invitation to lead this amazing group of professionals, as part of Gov. Tate Reeves’ leadership team, is truly humbling,” Cork said at the time of his appointment. “I look forward to serving the great state of Mississippi in this new role and building upon the amazing momentum we are achieving together.”

name: Mississippi Today
title: Delta Harvest market adjusts from weekly to monthly
description: Carolyn Thompson, left, is assisted by Peggy Jennings in selecting vegetables at the Delta Harvest Neighborhood Market inside the Jackson Medical Mall, Thursday, Sept. 24, 2026, in Jackson.
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
The Delta Harvest Neighborhood Market is changing its hours as it continues its mission to support Delta farmers and Mississippi shoppers with fresh, locally grown foods.
The market is now open monthly rather than weekly. It will open on Oct. 22, Nov. 24, Dec. 23 and Dec. 29 at the Jackson Medical Mall from noon until 6 p.m. Shoppers can visit shopdeltaharvest.com to keep up with the market’s hours.
Tracy Johnson, farming employee and consultant for Delta Harvest Neighborhood Market, talks about the market at the Jackson Medical Mall on Thursday, Sept. 24, 2026. Credit: Vickie D. King/Mississippi Today
Tracy Johnson, executive director of the Itta Bena Economic and Cultural Alliance, explained that the pilot phase, which lasted from June to August, proved that there was enough demand to make the market work. Now, they’ve entered a new phase focused on supporting the farmers.
“We’re working with the farmers in the Delta, giving them the technical assistance they need so they can grow quality, safe produce, and also growing more volume so that we’ll be able to supply the market,” he said.
Alcorn State University and Mississippi State University are providing the farmers with training and technical assistance. This includes soil testing, food safety, business skills and more. A demonstration farm in Itta Bena will be used as a training center.
The project is also partnering with the city of Itta Bena, the city of Greenwood and Leflore County in the Mississippi Delta.
“It’s really not just about a market, it’s about the complete regional value chain,” Johnson said.
The market has grown to include eight Delta farmers, and they supply about 50% of everything sold there. The hope is that farmers will eventually supply 90%, but for now the market relies on wholesale farmers throughout Mississippi and from Tennessee. 
Sisters Nellie Woodard, left, and Shirley Haynes Price, select baskets filled with vegetables and fruit at the Delta Harvest Neighborhood Market inside the Jackson Medical Mall, Thursday, Sept. 24, 2026, in Jackson.Tyvan Johnson, right, creates baskets of fresh vegetables and fruit for shoppers at the Delta Harvest Neighborhood Market inside the Jackson Medical Mall, Thursday, Sept. 24, 2026, in Jackson.Brianna Barbour shops the variety of vegetables and fruit at the Delta Harvest Neighborhood Market inside the Jackson Medical Mall on Thursday, Sept. 24, 2026, in Jackson.The Delta Harvest Neighborhood Market offers a variety of vegetables and fruit at the Jackson Medical Mall location, Thursday, Sept. 24, 2026, in Jackson.Tyvan Johnson selects vegetables he will use to create baskets for those shopping at the Delta Harvest Neighborhood Market inside the Jackson Medical Mall, Thursday, Sept. 24, 2026, in Jackson.The Delta Harvest Neighborhood Market offers a variety of vegetables, fruit and some meats at its Jackson Medical Mall location, Thursday, Sept. 24, 2026, in Jackson.The Delta Harvest Neighborhood Market offers a variety of vegetables, fruit and some meats at its Jackson Medical Mall location, Thursday, Sept. 24, 2026, in Jackson.Shoppers line up to browse the fruit, vegetable and meat selections at the Delta Harvest Neighborhood Market inside the Jackson Medical Mall, Thursday, Sept. 24, 2026, in Jackson.The Delta Harvest Neighborhood Market offers a variety of vegetables and fruit at the Jackson Medical Mall on Thursday, Sept. 24, 2026, in Jackson.
They’re working to build a regional food system that will connect Delta farmers with local consumers. The long-term goal is to have a stand-alone location open daily and multiple locations across the state.
Some customers at a recent market didn’t mind the new hours. 
“Being open once a month, I think it’s better because it gives the buyer an opportunity to prepare, and they’ll probably spend more,” said Shirley Haynes-Price. She came to the market with her sister, Nellie Haynes-Woodard, to buy squash.
“It really helps me because there’s no one but me really cooking or eating anything,” she Haynes-Woodard, who was excited about her fruit and turkey wings.
At their first market back in June, farmer Patricia Potter spoke about the market’s benefits.
“It (Delta Harvest Market) gets you out to other people to know that you’re growing healthy food and good stuff coming out of the garden,” she said.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Kansas Legislature’s leaders still awaiting delivery of new bill-writing software program
description: TOPEKA — The bill-writing software for the Kansas Legislature that was supposed to be operational months before start of the 2026 legislative session in January remains ill-equipped for implementation. House Speaker Dan Hawkins, R-Wichita, said the objective was to work with contractor Propylon to get the system functional by the launch of the 2027 session.[...]
text:
House Speaker Dan Hawkins, a Wichita Republican, appears less frustrated Tuesday than Senate Minority Leader Dinah Sykes, D-Lenexa, amid further delays in implementation of a software program to help lawmakers draft and revise bills. (Kansas Reflector screen capture of Legislature's YouTube channel)TOPEKA — The bill-writing software for the Kansas Legislature that was supposed to be operational months before start of the 2026 legislative session in January remains ill-equipped for implementation.
House Speaker Dan Hawkins, R-Wichita, said the objective was to work with contractor Propylon to get the system functional by the launch of the 2027 session.
“The goal is still to go live in the next legislative session,” Hawkins said. ‘They still have work to do. Hopefully, we’ll still get there.”
Senate Minority Leader Dinah Sykes, a Lenexa Democrat, said relying on antiquated technology to craft bills would be unacceptable and that the inability of Propylon to deliver was frustrating.
“I hope we’re not just pushing on ‘hopefully,’ ” Sykes said. “We need to have bills drafted. Last session was a nightmare, and for government to function we need that working. I feel like they have just been dragging us along.”
Altaf Uddin, who leads the Legislature’s technology office, said Propylon had been more responsive to the state’s IT demands than in the past.
The company signed a $3.9 million contract with the Legislature in October 2022, but failed to complete its work by June and October 2025 deadlines. Extending the project beyond the Oct. 1 target compelled the state to devote another $190,000 to the project.
Uddin said intensive testing revealed deficiencies in the Computer Assisted Legislative Information System, or CALIS, that had to be addressed. The system eventually would be a resource for individual legislators, but also by legislative staff responsible for conducting policy research and for writing bills.
In 2025, Hawkins had joined a group of legislators who echoed sentiment that Propylon “doesn’t seem to deliver on their promises.”
Hawkins and Sykes are both candidates for the job of state insurance commissioner. Joining them on the November ballot will be Libertarian nominee Ric Koehn of Cimarron.
Meanwhile, the Legislative Coordinating Council — comprised of the bipartisan leadership of the House and Senate — received confirmation Tuesday a failed contract authorized by the LCC in 2024 would be canceled. The LCC was responsible for choosing Indigov to produce a service intended to assist lawmakers in managing communications and relationships with their constituents.
The LCC voted unanimously in August to spike the $288,000 per-year contract because the system wasn’t popular with senators and representatives. Indigov was notified Sept. 16 and the company affirmed it had received the letter. The existing contract with Indigov will expire in December.

name: Delaware
title: Delaware broadens the story of John Dickinson with new $14.5M visitor center
description: New permanent exhibit expands the Plantation’s story to include enslaved people, Indigenous communities and others who lived on the property DOVER, Del. — Delaware is preparing to open a new permanent exhibit at the John Dickinson Plantation that broadens the story traditionally associated with one of the state’s most important Founding Fathers. The exhibit,[...]
text:
Photo: Images provided by the Delaware Historical & Cultural Affaires office. Graphic created with AI on 9/30.
New permanent exhibit expands the Plantation’s story to include enslaved people, Indigenous communities and others who lived on the property
DOVER, Del. — Delaware is preparing to open a new permanent exhibit at the John Dickinson Plantation that broadens the story traditionally associated with one of the state’s most important Founding Fathers.
The exhibit, “One Land Many Voices,” will debut Oct. 10 inside the plantation’s new 14,000-square-foot visitor center, part of a $14.5 million state capital project.
Gov. Matt Meyer has proclaimed Oct. 10 “One Land Many Voices Day,” saying the exhibit reflects an effort to tell the stories of all of the people who shaped the historic property.
“Delaware’s history belongs to all of us, and telling it honestly means telling the stories of everyone who shaped it,” Meyer said. “The only way we can learn from our past is by refusing to hide from it, including the chapters that are difficult to confront.”
A broader interpretation of Dickinson
John Dickinson remains central to the site.
Known as the “Penman of the Revolution,” Dickinson was one of Delaware’s most influential political figures of the founding era. His Letters from a Farmer in Pennsylvania made him nationally prominent in the years before the Revolution, and he later played important roles in the Continental Congress, the Articles of Confederation and the Constitutional Convention.
The new exhibit intentionally places that political legacy alongside the stories of Indigenous people, tenant farmers, indentured servants, free Black residents and enslaved men, women and children who lived and worked on the property.
Dickinson enslaved people for much of his adult life. According to the state, he ultimately unconditionally freed all 59 people enslaved on the property in 1786.
The result is an exhibit designed to put Dickinson’s life within the larger social and economic world surrounding the plantation.
Secretary of State Charuni Patibanda-Sanchez said the goal is to acknowledge that complexity.
“Delaware’s colonial history is a complex one,” she said. “By honoring all who once lived here, we give voice to those whose work and sacrifice contributed to the legacy of this historic site.”
What the announcement leaves largely unexplored
While the state’s announcement emphasizes slavery and the broader communities connected to the plantation, it gives less attention to several parts of Dickinson’s political and constitutional legacy.
Dickinson’s Letters from a Farmer in Pennsylvania were among the most influential colonial arguments against British taxation. The National Archives also identifies Dickinson as the principal writer of the first draft of the Articles of Confederation, the nation’s first governing framework.
His record during the Revolution was complicated.
Dickinson opposed declaring independence in 1776 because he believed the colonies were not yet sufficiently unified or prepared for separation from Britain. After independence was approved, however, he served in the Delaware militia and later returned to national public life.
He later served as president of Delaware and Pennsylvania, chaired the 1786 Annapolis Convention that helped lead to the Constitutional Convention and represented Delaware at the 1787 convention. Dickinson left Philadelphia because of illness before the Constitution was formally signed and authorized fellow Delaware delegate George Read to sign his name.
Dickinson also argued at the Constitutional Convention for ending the slave trade. His own relationship with slavery changed over time, creating one of the contradictions that continues to shape interpretations of his life.
Those facts do not diminish the significance of slavery at the plantation or the experiences of the people enslaved there. They do illustrate why Dickinson remains a difficult figure to summarize neatly: He argued for colonial liberty while enslaving people himself, opposed independence before later serving the new nation and eventually freed the people he held in bondage.
The press release does not indicate how much of the permanent exhibit is devoted to Dickinson’s political writings, constitutional ideas and role in establishing the new American government compared with its treatment of slavery and other communities associated with the property.
That does not necessarily mean those subjects are absent from the exhibit. Visitors will be able to judge that balance once One Land Many Voices opens.
Broader approach predates Meyer administration
The broader interpretation of the plantation is not solely an initiative of the current administration.
The project and its emphasis on presenting the lives of people beyond the Dickinson family were developed before Meyer became governor.
That distinction is important because the exhibit arrives during a continuing national debate about how museums, schools and public institutions should interpret the founding era.
Supporters of broader historical interpretation argue that understanding the period requires examining not only prominent political leaders but also slavery, labor and the experiences of people who historically received less attention.
Others have argued that an increased focus on slavery and social history can sometimes come at the expense of explaining the political philosophy, institutions and achievements of the founding generation.
The state describes One Land Many Voices as an effort to provide a more comprehensive account of the property through artifacts, historical documents, photographs, narrative text and visual media.
$14.5 million investment
Beyond the historical interpretation, the visitor center represents a significant state investment in the plantation as an educational and cultural destination.
The new 14,000-square-foot building includes exhibition, educational and meeting space, along with a 1,400-square-foot screened pavilion designed for school groups, community meetings and other programs.
HCA Director Suzanne Savery said the expanded facility provides an opportunity to offer greater context to visitors.
“This expanded Visitor Center represents an important step forward in how we share Delaware’s history, allowing us to provide deeper context and a more meaningful experience for every visitor,” Savery said.
Visitors will continue to be able to tour the historic 18th-century mansion and reproduction structures elsewhere on the 450-acre property.
Admission, exhibits and programming will remain free. Fees will apply for some private uses of the multipurpose room and pavilion.
Opening Oct. 10
The permanent exhibit will be unveiled during a ribbon-cutting ceremony at 10 a.m. Saturday, Oct. 10, at the John Dickinson Plantation, 250 Kitts Hummock Road near Dover.
TO GO

Where: John Dickinson Plantation, 250 Kitts Hummock Road, Dover
When: Saturday, Oct. 10; ribbon-cutting at 10 a.m.
Cost: Free
About: The new visitor center is part of a $14.5 million state investment and expands exhibition, educational and meeting space at the historic property.

People line up outside of the downtown Anchorage Permanent Fund Dividend office on March 31, 2023, the last day to submit applications. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)The 2026 Permanent Fund dividend, worth $1,200 per recipient, will be direct-deposited into Alaskans’ bank accounts starting Oct. 1, according to a plan published by the Alaska Department of Revenue earlier this month.
This year’s dividend was set at $1,000 by the Alaska Legislature in the state budget signed by Gov. Mike Dunleavy. A $200 bonus was included because oil prices reached a threshold needed to trigger it. 
Both the Legislature and the Department of Revenue labeled the bonus an energy relief payment. 
Altogether, the state will spend more than $800 million on this year’s dividends.
The first round of dividends will go to people who applied for their dividend and requested direct deposit. A second round of payments is scheduled for Oct. 22 and includes people who filled out paper applications or requested physical checks for their dividend.

name: VTDigger
title: Nettie Morse focuses on a future in pediatric occupational therapy
description:
A founding member of VSAC GEAR UP Leads and a QuestBridge Junior College Prep Scholar, Nettie has been recognized for building opportunity for her peers. Now she's preparing her own college applications, with the goal of working with children.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Nettie Morse focuses on a future in pediatric occupational therapy.
text:
Aneta “Nettie” Morse is a senior at Oxbow High School in Bradford, Vermont. She’s a three-season athlete and is one of the founding members of VSAC GEAR UP Leads, the first-ever student-led leadership club in VSAC’s GEAR UP, a federally funded program that helps students access college and careers after high school. 
Recently, Nettie was named the national GEAR UP Student Leader of the Year at an award ceremony in Washington DC. This award recognizes a student who goes above and beyond for their GEAR UP program, encourages other students to get involved in college and career readiness, and embodies the change they want to see in the world. The award includes a $2,500 scholarship.
“I spent most of last year doing outreach and trying to build the program up to help more students,” Nettie said. “We started with SAT workshops and were able to tour a college in New York. This year I’m continuing outreach to make sure teachers and students get involved and that we’re able to help more Oxbow students.”
Working with her VSAC GEAR UP outreach counselor, Kassidy, to prepare her college applications 
Nettie herself has benefited from the GEAR UP program. She’s working with her VSAC GEAR UP outreach counselor, Kassidy Moore, on her college applications and financial aid paperwork. 
“Kassidy just knows everything,” Nettie laughed. “When I first started working with her, I was really not sure where I wanted to go. I knew I wanted to do pediatric occupational therapy (OT), but I didn’t have a sense of where I wanted to go to school. At that point, all I knew is that I needed financial aid to get there.” 
Kassidy stepped up to the plate for Nettie, introducing her to programs like QuestBridge, which helps connect high-achieving and modest-income students with admissions opportunities. Nettie was named a Junior College Prep Scholar by QuestBridge, one of only 4,000 students across the country to achieve that distinction. With that came additional help for her senior applications, including SAT review, more counseling, and more educational sessions. 
Nettie is submitting her final QuestBridge applications and is nervous but excited to get the college application process underway. QuestBridge features a mutual selection process, where students rank schools and schools rank students. If a student is “matched” for admission through the process, the partner school pays for tuition, housing, and more. Nettie’s hopeful that her odds are good. 
As she worked on her applications, Nettie leaned on Kassidy for help. “Sometimes I don’t know what to write for an essay or a prompt, so she will ask me a bunch of questions and we’ll look at the answers together and edit them and put them together into something comprehensive. She’s helping me figure out how to list my activities in the right order, so that I’m communicating what’s important about those activities to the colleges,” Nettie described. 
Pediatric occupational therapy is Nettie’s top interest
Nettie is prioritizing schools with good pediatric OT programs that are also close enough to home that she’s within driving distance. 
“I found pediatric OT scrolling one day,” she noted. “It seems to fit a lot of what I’m good at and what I want to do. I love kids, and childhood is one of the most important times of someone’s life and getting kids the help they need is so important.” 
She added, “I saw a collage of photos of someone playing with kids on mats, blocks, swings, and what the OT was doing with the kids working on sensory and motion and skills. I kept going, diving deeper and looking more and it was just so cool to me.”
Nettie shared that she would be both “honored and really excited and grateful to have that opportunity and to play that role in someone’s life.” 
Mentoring and making a difference
Given Nettie’s track record, it’s not surprising that she wants to make an impact on the lives of others, especially kids. 
In her free time, she volunteers for ENGin, a nonprofit that pairs volunteers like Nettie with Ukrainian citizens to help them learn English. Nettie enjoys it because her mentee is close to her age. She spends an hour each weekend with her, and she says it’s unlike anything else in her life.
Nettie is also involved in National Honor Society and student council at Oxbow. She plays soccer and does both indoor and outdoor track and field. She also works with the school’s IT department and interns at UP for Learning on their Vermont Student Advisory Council. With all of this on her plate, Nettie has meetings every day in addition to school. She wouldn’t have it any other way. 
She lives with her dad, grandparents, and two older brothers. One of her brothers did two years of community college online, and the other is a sophomore at Dartmouth College. Nettie is inspired by both of them, and the hard work of her dad. Soon she’ll finish up her applications and her financial aid paperwork. As her future unfolds, Nettie is sure to make an impact! 

The Vermont Student Assistance Corp. was created by the Vermont Legislature in 1965 as a public nonprofit agency. We advocate for Vermont students and their families to ensure that they have the tools they need to achieve their education and training goals. We create opportunities for all Vermont students, but particularly for those—of any age—who believe that the doors to education are closed to them. Growing families save for education with VT529, Vermont’s official 529 savings program. To help Vermonters plan and pay for college or job training, our counselors work with students in nearly every Vermont middle school and high school, and are also available to work with adults. Our grant, scholarship, and workforce development programs create opportunity, help students re-skill or learn new skills, and grow the economy. VSAC’s loan, loan refinance, and loan forgiveness programs provide competitive education financing to students and families. Find us at www.vsac.org or visit Facebook, Instagram, or LinkedIn.
