text:
A sign advertises that SNAP benefits are accepted at a grocery store in Fargo, North Dakota, on July 7, 2026. (Photo by Ceilidh Kern /North Dakota Monitor)Since the passage of President Trump’s signature legislation, the so-called “One Big Beautiful Bill” in July last year, enrollment in the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) has fallen by almost 23,000 in Maine, a decline of 13%. This includes almost 7,000 children who are no longer receiving food assistance.
The changes to SNAP eligibility in the bill were sold as tackling fraud and abuse and pushing people into employment through the expansion of work-reporting requirements. Yet since the bill’s passage, the number of Mainers working has remained unchanged, even as tens of thousands have lost SNAP. Meanwhile, true fraud in SNAP remains rare, and multiple pieces of academic research show work reporting requirements burden people with unnecessary paperwork that doesn’t increase work but does cause people to lose assistance.
The map below shows how many Mainers have lost food assistance by town, county, and legislative and congressional districts. The data shows losses are concentrated in the most rural parts of the state, where more people rely on SNAP for food assistance and where consistent year-round work is hardest to find.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Mass. voters hold Trump, utilities most responsible for high energy costs, new poll finds
description: Healey’s ability to evade the bulk of the blame with voters for high energy costs is notable as she seeks reelection this fall, given how energy issues have proven stubborn, dogging much of her first term.
text:
DURING AN ELECTION YEAR defined by affordability, voters aren’t directing their greatest outrage at Gov. Maura Healey for at least one of the central challenges confronting the state: spiraling energy costs.  
Instead, 32 percent of likely voters are pointing the finger at President Trump, and 28 percent say gas and electric utility companies are most to blame for the energy affordability crisis enveloping the state. Just 13 percent of respondents said the governor is most responsible for energy costs that have soared in recent years, according to a new CommonWealth Beacon/MassINC Polling Group survey (Toplines | Crosstabs). 
The findings, from 800 likely voters across Massachusetts surveyed earlier this month, aren’t necessarily surprising. Trump’s poll numbers have cratered in the Bay State — and he continues to flounder here. And the utility companies are the ones, after all, with their names on the monthly bills that customers receive.  
But Healey’s ability to evade the bulk of the blame with voters for high energy costs is notable as she seeks reelection this fall, given how energy issues have proven stubborn, dogging much of her first term.  
Massachusetts residents pay double the national average for electricity. And energy affordability is the top household concern in Massachusetts, business groups found in their own poll earlier this year — which was released just after the Iran war started. 
The numbers reflect the fact that much of the electorate understands that energy markets are global, said Dan Dolan, president of the New England Power Generators Association. Trump has directly impacted the landscape, Dolan added, noting that the president canceled offshore wind leases, to cut funding for solar projects, and launched hostilities with Iran, which has sent oil prices skyrocketing. 
“Massachusetts and New England have been uniquely impacted by the fact that this president, who holds himself out as energy dominance and energy abundance, has pointedly gone after some of the energy sources that this region is trying to expand, and so that dissonance, coupled with the run-up in global energy prices, points the focus on the president,” Dolan said. 
Massachusetts has adopted some of the country’s most ambitious climate commitments, aiming to reach net-zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050. Just 9 percent of respondents said, though, that clean energy programs bear the brunt of the blame for high energy costs, ticking up to 16 percent among Republican voters.  
That finding provides color to the larger backdrop, in which House Democrats advanced a measure earlier this year that would cut $1 billion from Mass Save, the state’s energy efficiency program funded by a charge on ratepayers’ bills, believing it to be an effective way to save customers money on energy costs. And it’s one of the few levers Beacon Hill can immediately pull to immediately lower energy bills.  
But if voters don’t see programs like Mass Save as the culprit for their high bills, according to the poll results, it could undermine the political appetite to enact such deep cuts. The Senate already rejected that proposal, and lawmakers will need to hash out their differences in conference committee. 
The polling “pinpoints the complexity of the issue,” said Barbara Kates-Garnick, a former state undersecretary of energy under Gov. Deval Patrick and a professor at Tufts’ Fletcher School. “There’s no one villain here.” 
Healey has tried in several ways to offer ratepayers relief in a bid to combat what could be a significant political vulnerability, though little has emerged yet in the form of tangible cost savings. She worked with the utilities to delay some charges last winter and has called on the Department of Public Utilities to open a wide-ranging investigation into customer bills. She has also urged legislators to reach agreement on a sprawling legislative package she first proposed close to 18 months ago and is now pitching lawmakers on suspending the state’s 24-cents-per-gallon gas tax for two months. 
Healey does pick up significantly more blame from voters who identify as Republican, more of whom – 26 percent — think the governor is most responsible for high energy costs than any other option in the poll. That’s compared with just 4 percent of Democratic voters who think Healey is most to blame on the issue.  
By contrast, 43 percent of Democratic voters call out Trump as most responsible for high energy costs, compared to 14 percent of Republican voters. Among independent voters, about 1 in 3 blamed Trump for high energy costs and 28 percent pointed to the utilities as most responsible.  
One reason why the utilities are receiving so much more blame than Healey overall is because “people can plug it into a progressive narrative about greedy corporations,” said Evan Horowitz, executive director at Tufts’ Center for State Policy Analysis, even though the companies’ profits and spending decisions largely need approval from state regulators. 
Still, Dolan said, “no one is immune” from voter backlash over rising energy costs.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: NC school finance officials call for more flexibility in funding rules
description: School finance officers told a state commission Monday that North Carolina’s complicated funding rules and delayed state budget decisions make it harder for districts to plan and spend money where they need it most.  The comments came during a panel before the Blue Ribbon Commission on Public Education. The panel included superintendents and finance officers[...]
text:
North Carolina public school educators, families, and allies demanded a budget that provides pay raises to teachers and funding to schools at a May 1, 2026 rally. (Photo: Brandon Kingdollar/NC Newsline)School finance officers told a state commission Monday that North Carolina’s complicated funding rules and delayed state budget decisions make it harder for districts to plan and spend money where they need it most. 
The comments came during a panel before the Blue Ribbon Commission on Public Education. The panel included superintendents and finance officers from Alamance-Burlington School System and Mooresville Graded School District, along with administrators from Lincoln Charter School. 
“Public school finance today has never been harder and more complex, ” said Tony Messer, chief finance officer for Alamance-Burlington. 
Messer said after Alamance-Burlington used all of its allotted classroom-teacher positions, the district had about $600,000 remaining in the allotment, but funding rules wouldn’t allow it to be used for other needs. He said the money could have helped cover costs such as exceptional children’s services. 
“If we could get a little more flexibility and maybe loosen up some of the restrictions around that, that will be beneficial for all parties involved,” Messer said. 
Angie Davis, chief financial officer for Mooresville Graded School District, said some reporting requirements ask districts for information state agencies already receive in another form. 
For example, she said, districts must report supplemental-pay data through an annual survey, even though the Department of Public Instruction already receives district accounting data each month. Davis said the State Treasurer’s Office also asks districts to report employee income for health-plan purposes, while the retirement system already receives employee salary information each month. 
“Just from a business standpoint, it’s very inefficient when you’re already supplying that information to different agencies,” Davis said. 
Jonathan Bryant, chief administrator of Lincoln Charter School, said having a state budget in place this year brought certainty after the strain of operating without one the previous fiscal year. 
Robert Taylor, the Wake County superintendent who moderated the panel, said the uncertainty becomes a problem when districts have to approve their own budgets before lawmakers finish theirs. A district could approve its budget and move forward, he said, only to learn months later that the General Assembly had added raises or other spending increases that the district would have to match. 
“The thing that scared us the most is the idea that the General Assembly could come back and decide that they were going to put raises in, but we’ve already punched the ticket on our budget and moved forward,” Taylor said. 
Bipartisan education panel unites NC Gov Stein, Republican leaders amid budget rift

Taylor said districts can absorb some delay, but not indefinitely. State lawmakers are supposed to complete the budget by June 30, he said, and districts can manage a delay into August. By December, he said, the uncertainty becomes much harder to manage. 
“If there’s one thing that I think this commission could lift up, it’s the fact that a late budget has a significant impact on how a school district makes decisions,” Taylor said. 
Rep. David Willis, R-Union, challenged the panel’s characterization of state budget delays, calling it “misinformation.”
“First of all, we always have a state budget, so let’s just clarify that,” Willis said. “Now, it may be last year’s budget, and you may not like that number, but you know what the number is.”
Willis said lawmakers regularly seek input from educators and school officials when writing the budget. He also agreed that the state’s education funding model needs to change.
“I think our model is broken,” Willis said. “Let’s go back to the drawing board and figure out what the funding model should look like.”

name: Mississippi Today
title: Who’s funding the Hinds DA candidates? Voters won’t know until a week before Nov. 3 election
description: Hinds County District Attorney special election candidates, from left, Wendy Wilson White, Marvin Sanders, Gwen Agho and Greta Mack Harris, listen to a moderator's question at a forum held by the Hinds County Democratic Executive Committee on Thursday, Sept. 24, 2026, in a church auditorium in Raymond.
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Hinds County voters will get their first comprehensive look at how the five candidates for district attorney are financing their campaigns just a week before the Nov. 3 special election.
Even some of the candidates aren’t sure exactly how much money is in their campaign coffers.
“You’d have to ask my wife,” said Marvin Sanders, a defense attorney who previously worked for the Mississippi attorney general’s office.
Sanders said he’s had one fundraiser so far, at the Continental Cigar Club in downtown Jackson. Off the top of his head, he said, he isn’t sure how much is in his campaign account.
“I’m not taking any money from anybody right now,” he said, adding that he’s contributed nearly $15,000 of his own cash to his campaign.
In a normal election year, voters would see multiple reports itemizing contributions of at least $200, according to a campaign finance guide produced by the Mississippi secretary of state’s office. But when the timeline for an election is truncated – such as in a special election – Mississippi law does not require candidates to file more than one report before Election Day, although last-minute contributions over $200 must be reported at least two days before balloting.
The limited financial disclosures take on additional significance for the Hinds DA special election, which was set after former DA Jody Owens pleaded guilty to a federal corruption charge and resigned three months ago.
Federal prosecutors say Owens took money from undercover FBI agents posing as real estate developers and wired the funds from his campaign account to help pay off a Jackson city councilmember’s campaign debt. He is set to be sentenced in early November. 
The deadline for candidates for Hinds DA to declare was Aug. 20. So far, many okf them told Mississippi Today the primary contributors to their campaigns have been themselves. 
“You mean how much I’ve loaned myself?” said Greta Mack Harris, an attorney practicing in Madison and Rankin counties, when asked how much she’s raised so far. The answer: More than $16,000. 
Mack Harris is the only candidate of the five who has filed paperwork with the secretary of state forming a political committee to solicit donations. 
In Mississippi, candidates for DA are not required to set up political committees. But doing so creates some separation between candidates and their day-to-day handling of campaign contributions, which is overseen by a treasurer.
Wendy Wilson White, a prosecutor in the Hinds DA office, said she is also self-financing her campaign. 
“At this stage of the game, I haven’t collected enough funds for anyone to be concerned about me mishandling any finances,” she said. 
“My campaign has been funded by me – 95% of it at this point has been handled by me,” she said, before revising her estimate. “Truly 100% of it.” 
Unlike her opponents, Gwen Agho, another prosecutor in the Hinds DA office, said most of her fundraising has come from donations. She has held two fundraisers so far: One at a bar in downtown Jackson in mid-September and another at her father’s restaurant in Clinton, Monte’s Steak and Seafood.
Agho said she’s raised tens of thousands of dollars, but she isn’t sure the exact amount because the donations have been deposited directly into an account that her campaign manager is responsible for checking. 
“It’s being aware of those laws and what’s required,” Agho said. “Even if you have someone else doing it for you, at the end of the day, it’s your name.” 
Darla Palmer, a defense attorney who is running for Hinds DA for a third time, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: States OK solar panels for balconies. Some safety guidelines haven’t caught up.
description: CT and other states have passed legislation allowing small, cheap, plug-in solar panels that can be hung from a balcony or porch.
text:
Over the past year and a half, a dozen states have embraced a new vision for solar power: small, cheap panels that can be hung from a balcony or porch, be plugged into a standard wall outlet and take a dent out of residents’ utility bills. 
These systems, known as balcony solar or plug-in solar, are attractive because they can be installed without permits, contractors or large investments. They can allow renters to tap into clean electricity. 
Lawmakers say the systems can help at a time when residents’ power bills are skyrocketing and utilities are struggling to keep pace with demand. They also can be paired with a battery, which can provide backup power during area outages. 
Backers see a future in which solar panels deployed across millions of balconies, porches and yards could ease strain on the electrical grid and save residents hundreds of dollars each year on their power bills. 
Twelve states — Republican and Democratic alike — have recently passed bills authorizing residents to install such systems. Nine have been signed into law, while three are awaiting signatures from a governor. 
But for most Americans, even some in states that have passed laws, the systems still sit in a legal gray area. That’s because the “plug and play” simplicity that creates balcony solar’s appeal might not yet work safely with most household electrical systems, experts and utilities say. Work is underway to develop industry standards for such products, and advocates agree that such guidelines are necessary to draw manufacturers to the U.S. market. 
Backers say that plug-in solar systems have a long track record of operating safely in Germany and other countries, and argue that it’s imperative for the standards to allow for products that do not require a permit, home upgrades or a certified electrician to install. 
Meanwhile, power utilities haven’t strongly opposed the bills, though some have expressed concerns that unregistered systems could affect power flows or endanger line workers. 
For all the legislative action to boost balcony solar, advocates say the market won’t take off until safety groups give the all-clear for systems that don’t require red tape or electrical upgrades. 
Solar bills
The recent burst of balcony solar bills kicked off in Utah. Republican state Rep. Ray Ward read an article about the balcony solar boom in Germany, where the devices have surged in popularity and are widely available in stores such as IKEA. 
In Germany, more than 1 million balcony solar systems have been installed across the country, providing more than 2 gigawatts of power — the equivalent of a large power plant. 
“I thought, ‘How come I cannot do that in Utah and in the U.S.?’” Ward said. 
In Utah, as in many states, putting any amount of power onto the grid requires a contract with a utility, an impossible barrier for the average homeowner. Ward’s bill removes that requirement for solar panels up to 1,200 watts, roughly the amount of power used by a hair dryer. 
The bill passed unanimously through both houses of the Utah legislature last year, and Ward has balcony solar at his home. But the law also requires systems to meet National Electrical Code and Underwriters Laboratories certification standards, guidelines that are still in development.
“The safety standards don’t exist, even though the products are plainly safe,” Ward said. “There is a way to make it safe, as Germany has shown, and we’ve just got to get safety standards in place here.”
Since Utah’s bill became law, state lawmakers across the country have drafted similar bills. 
Many of the bills also prevent landlords and homeowners associations from restricting balcony solar. And many also seek to establish safety guidelines for the technology. 
“These things are just easy, simple, affordable, permitless ways to generate your own electricity — in whatever your living arrangement is — that enables everyone to contribute to reducing energy consumption in our country,” said Virginia state Sen. Scott Surovell, a Democrat. 
His bill drew bipartisan support and was signed into law in April. 
In New York, a bill passed in May awaits action by Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul.
“These solar panels could help you save 10% of your electricity bill each month, which is significant considering how much costs are going up,” said New York state Sen. Liz Krueger, a Democrat who sponsored the balcony solar bill. “In New York city, a huge percentage of us are renters, and up until now there’s been no way for us to participate in green energy or energy lowering projects.”
Krueger said Hochul may ask for some small technical changes, which lawmakers are prepared to adopt.
Colorado enacted a new law in May. 
“With power prices going up, people are wanting to find a way to be able to participate and have some control over their own energy,” said Colorado state Sen. Cathy Kipp, a Democrat who sponsored the measure. “As more states adopt it, it will drive down costs, which will further increase adoption.” 
Connecticut, Maine, Maryland, New Hampshire, New Jersey and Vermont have also enacted balcony solar laws since 2025. Bills in California and Massachusetts have passed and sit on the governor’s desk. 
The state measures have been supported by Bright Saver, a nonprofit advocacy group that envisions 60 million balcony solar panels deployed across the country by 2035. Cora Stryker, the group’s co-founder, said several lawmakers told her they’d never seen a measure go from an idea to a law so quickly. 
But the success of those new laws, she said, hinges on the development of safety standards that allow balcony solar systems to be simple “plug and play” devices. 
“The widespread adoption we’re talking about will only happen when we get out of this legal gray area and every American can feel confident that they can plug it in without contacting their utility,” she said. 
Bright Saver sells balcony solar systems at cost, offering 180-watt panels for $285 and 360-watt panels for $414. But it cannot sell to customers in some states that have passed solar legislation, because products don’t yet exist that can meet their safety certifications. 
Other companies sell kits online, but experts say it’s hard for customers to know if those devices meet safety thresholds. While backers do not have estimates for nationwide adoption totals, they say the numbers will remain low until balcony solar systems are widely available at popular retailers. 
Safety standards
Underwriters Laboratories, a global safety science company, recently issued certification standards that would require residents to modify circuits before plugging in devices — a hurdle that advocates fear could slow the adoption of balcony solar. 
The main concern, experts say, is that power outlets in U.S. homes are not designed to carry power in two directions. Sending electricity back into the system could bypass circuit protection devices, overloading wires and creating fire or shock hazards. 
“Some of these (bills and laws) are a little ahead of their time,” said Nadav Enbar, program manager at the nonprofit Electric Power Research Institute. “There isn’t yet a product that can meet the letter of the law.”
Some of the state laws call for products to achieve certification from Underwriters Laboratories. The company issued its certification program, known as an outline of investigation, in January.
While those guidelines are still working through a committee process — which could take a year or more — to be finalized as a permanent standard, the company says they still count as official certification for manufacturers seeking to comply with state laws. 
The current certification requires residents to modify circuits in their home to safely receive electricity. Electrical experts said it’s possible that manufacturers will eventually be able to develop balcony solar systems that address the circuit overload concerns with onboard technology.
“Could there in the future be another way to address these problems? Sure,” said Joe Bablo, principal engineering manager with UL Solutions, one of the three organizations that makes up Underwriters Laboratories. “Will the standard adapt to that? Of course.”
The certification also requires the use of a proprietary connector that ensures the blades will not continue carrying electricity after being unplugged from the wall. 
The National Electric Code offers another possibility for a widely accepted standard that manufacturers could follow, but new revisions to the code will not be issued until 2029.
Some utilities have also raised concerns about large-scale adoption affecting local power flows, or solar systems feeding power into the grid during blackouts and putting line workers at risk. Utility leaders have called for a program that requires balcony solar users to register or notify utilities when installing their devices. 
“We just need people to let us know what they’re plugging in, so we can track anything that feeds back into the grid and can be a danger to line workers,” said David Eisenhauer, spokesperson for the California power utility Southern California Edison.
The utility initially opposed the California bill, but adopted a neutral position after language was added to allow utilities to require registration of balcony solar units. 
This story was first published Sept, 30, 2026 by Stateline.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Kansas Legislature’s budget cuts compel Fort Hays State University to close Sternberg Museum
description: Fort Hays State University, grappling with $2.4 million state-ordered spending cut, to close Sternberg Museum of Natural History.
text:
Fort Hays State University administrators are preparing for the December closure to the public of the Sternberg Museum of Natural History in Hays because of $2.4 million in budget cuts by the 2026 Kansas Legislature. (Photo by Morgan Chilson/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — Fort Hays State University president Tisa Mason says the Sternberg Museum of Natural History will close to the public in mid-December because of budget problems.
She said museum faculty and staff would remain this academic year to review collections, determine what must be retained for research and teaching, and collaborate with “appropriate organizations to ensure every specimen is handled responsibly and legally.”
“This is not a decision I make lightly,” the president said Monday. “The Sternberg Museum is woven into the identity of this university and this region.”
The Sternberg Museum contains more than three million paleontology, zoology and geology specimens documenting life and environments in the Great Plains region. The collection has roots in the early 1900s, but the museum moved in a quarter-century ago to the concrete dome-shaped building in Hays adjacent to Interstate 70.
Last week, FHSU faculty, Sternberg Museum staff and community members shared disappointment with speculation the museum could be shuttered.
“I want to be clear about what closing Sternberg is and is not. It is not the cause of our budget problem,” Mason said. “When you cut into your leanest, most efficient state university, you are not trimming excess. You are cutting into muscle.”
Mason said in a 1,500-word statement that Fort Hays State received a $2.4 million reduction in state funding during the 2026 session. In addition, the Legislature requested FHSU assess how it would slash administrative costs by 10%. The university has relied for decades on revenue from higher education programs in China, but restrictions by the state could jeopardize as much as $6 million in funding.
She said closing the museum would lower Fort Hays State expenditures by $850,000 annually. That savings would be combined with $1 million in cuts across the university to compress the known budget gap to $550,000.
The museum has proven to be financially unstable with revenue annual revenue of $470,000 and average expenditures of $1.3 million per year. Complicating the issue was the $20 million in deferred maintenance at the museum.
Mason said options for Fort Hays State were limited. Unlike some higher education institutions in Kansas, FHSU doesn’t have access to local property or sales tax revenue. No individual, foundation or government entity stepped forward to underwrite the museum’s costs.
“I am open to solutions and welcome conversations and ideas,” Mason said. “But let me be direct about what any solution requires. The university would need about $1 million in new revenue every year. Not once, but annually, in perpetuity. This is a recurring cost, and it will not be solved by a one-time gift, a single fundraiser or any single event.”
In response to the $2.4 million cut imposed by the Legislature, in addition to closure of the museum, Mason said the FHSU president’s office was reorganized and staffing reduced. The university stopped hosting the Small Business Development Center and the FHSU men’s and women’s golf programs were paused in June. A new entrepreneurship director position was frozen, she said.
Mason said questions had arisen about the potential of using student tuition revenue to backfill the museum’s budget. Increases in tuition dollars have been earmarked to keep academic programs whole, she said.
“The frustration in our community right now is real, and it is understandable,” Mason said. “However, its true source is not a disagreement about whether Sternberg belongs in our academic mission. It does. That was never in question. The real source is a funding model that has asked more of FHSU than it asks of its peers.”
During fiscal year 2025, the level of state funding per full-time equivalent student ranged from a low of $6,713 at Fort Hays State to a high of $19,379 at Emporia State University.
Other full-time equivalent student funding levels in fiscal 2025: University of Kansas, $8,423; Wichita State University, $10,421; Pittsburg State University, $11,540; and Kansas State University, $11,664.
“We cannot absorb repeated, deep legislative reductions and simultaneously preserve everything our community values. Those are choices with real consequences, and those consequences fall first on the people who had no part in making them,” Mason said.

name: Delaware
title: CRI urges Delaware to consider wood as part of ‘all-of-the-above’ energy strategy
description: Caesar Rodney Institute says biomass could provide a local energy source while supporting Delaware forests and forestry businesses, but regulatory and environmental questions remain DOVER, Del. — As Delaware looks for ways to produce more of its own electricity and reduce dependence on energy imported from outside the state, the Caesar Rodney Institute is ur[...]
text:
Photo: A biomass power plant surrounded by piles of low-quality wood used to efficiently generate electricity without CO2.
Caesar Rodney Institute says biomass could provide a local energy source while supporting Delaware forests and forestry businesses, but regulatory and environmental questions remain
DOVER, Del. — As Delaware looks for ways to produce more of its own electricity and reduce dependence on energy imported from outside the state, the Caesar Rodney Institute is urging policymakers to consider a resource already growing across roughly a quarter of Delaware: wood.
The free-market policy organization says sustainably harvested wood and other forms of biomass should be considered alongside solar, offshore wind, nuclear power and battery storage as Delaware develops what Gov. Matt Meyer has described as an “all-of-the-above” energy strategy.
Michelle Parsons, a physician and chair of the Caesar Rodney Institute board, made the case in a recent article arguing that wood energy could create a market for lower-value timber, support Delaware’s declining forest-products industry and provide another source of locally produced energy.
The idea is not entirely new to state policymakers.
Delaware’s own Statewide Forest Strategy calls for developing markets for low-quality wood for biofuels and specifically recommends examining restrictions imposed by Delaware’s incinerator law. The strategy also suggests exploring wood-energy systems at schools or other state-owned buildings.
Delaware looks for more homegrown energy
Meyer has made increasing electricity generation inside Delaware a significant part of his energy policy.
In his State of the State address, Meyer called for Delaware to generate more power “of multiple types,” and he has since described his broader strategy as “all of the above,” including solar, offshore wind, nuclear energy, battery storage and other technologies.
Delaware currently produces substantially less electricity than its residents and businesses consume, with natural gas serving as the state’s primary fuel for electricity generation.
CRI argues wood could provide another locally available resource.
“There is another energy resource Delaware already has in abundance,” Parsons wrote. “Wood.”
Forests cover about a quarter of Delaware
The Delaware Forest Service estimates forests cover roughly 352,000 acres, or about one-fourth of Delaware, with approximately 78% of that forestland privately owned.
State forestry documents describe those forests as renewable resources that can produce wood products while continuing to grow another generation of trees when managed sustainably.
Delaware forestry officials also have identified an opportunity involving lower-value hardwood trees.
The state’s forest strategy notes that Delmarva has significantly fewer sawmills than it did several decades ago, reducing the number of markets available for locally harvested timber. It identifies bioenergy as one potential market for lower-value wood.
A 2012 U.S. Forest Service analysis estimated that approximately 125,000 green tons of woody biomass could be available annually in the greater Delaware area without depleting the resource, including about 50,000 tons from Sussex County, 47,000 from Kent County and 28,000 from New Castle County.
Could schools be an option?
Other states have used wood for institutional heating. Vermont has used wood heating in public schools for decades, with modern systems designed to operate more efficiently and with greater emissions controls than traditional wood-burning systems.
Delaware’s own forest strategy includes a recommendation to explore a “Fuels for Schools” concept and consider converting a school or other state-owned facility to wood-based heating or cooling.
PJM also recognizes biomass, including wood, as a fuel that can be used to generate electricity within the regional grid.
State law presents a complication
One of the more significant questions involves Delaware law.
The state’s Renewable Energy Portfolio Standards Act recognizes sustainably harvested biomass as a renewable energy source.
But Delaware’s incinerator law imposes strict siting restrictions on facilities classified as incinerators, including requirements that generally keep them at least three miles from residences, residential communities, churches, schools, parks and hospitals.
CRI argues those restrictions could unintentionally block modern wood-energy projects, particularly smaller institutional systems that burn clean wood rather than municipal solid waste.
The organization is calling on lawmakers to determine whether clean wood-energy systems fall under those restrictions and, if so, amend or repeal the provisions that prevent them from being developed.
Delaware’s own forest strategy has previously called for examining those legal barriers.
Environmental questions remain
Using wood as an energy source also raises broader questions involving emissions, forest management and carbon impacts.
Modern biomass equipment can use advanced combustion systems and pollution controls that are substantially different from older wood-burning systems.
Still, the environmental impact of biomass depends on several factors, including what type of wood is burned, how forests are managed, how quickly harvested trees are replaced and what fuel source the wood displaces.
Delaware forestry officials have previously supported exploring the concept. The Delaware Forest Service’s 2020 forest strategy said the state has ample low-value wood available for bioenergy projects and said such projects could improve forest health. At the same time, PJM executive Michael Bryson recently cautioned that constructing a new biomass power plant can be costly and may make the most economic sense where wood waste is already generated as part of another business.
Air-quality concerns would also be part of any debate over expanded wood energy. DNREC has previously identified wood and biomass burning as sources of fine-particle pollution in Delaware. In regional haze planning documents, the agency said residential wood combustion represented about 23% of Delaware’s PM2.5 emissions in the 2011 emissions inventory used for that analysis. Modern commercial biomass systems can use substantially different combustion technology and emissions controls than residential wood stoves, but any Delaware proposal would still be subject to air-quality permitting and emissions standards.
Those questions would likely become part of any future Delaware regulatory or legislative debate.
Could markets help preserve forests?
CRI also connects the energy issue to Delaware’s continuing loss of forestland.
State environmental officials estimate Delaware is losing more than 1,000 acres of forest each year, largely because of development.
CRI argues that creating additional markets for sustainably harvested wood could give private landowners another financial reason to retain working forests rather than sell the property for development.
That argument also appears in state forestry policy, which calls for developing stronger markets for lower-quality timber while maintaining sustainable forest management.
No specific Delaware wood-energy facility has been proposed as part of CRI’s initiative.
Instead, the organization is asking lawmakers and state officials to include biomass in the broader discussion over how Delaware generates more electricity and thermal energy within its borders.
“If Delaware really means ‘all of the above,’ wood belongs in the conversation,” Parsons wrote.
Whether wood ultimately becomes a larger part of Delaware’s energy portfolio would depend on economics, emissions standards, sustainable forestry requirements and whether state law allows modern wood-energy projects to move forward.
To Go Box

What: Caesar Rodney Institute is urging Delaware policymakers to include sustainably harvested wood and biomass in the state’s “all-of-the-above” energy discussion.
Why it matters: Delaware’s Statewide Forest Strategy already identifies bioenergy as a potential market for lower-value timber and calls for examining legal restrictions on wood-energy facilities.
Read the full proposal: Caesar Rodney Institute, “All-of-the-Above Energy Means Wood, Too”
https://www.caesarrodney.org/post/all-of-the-above-energy-means-wood-too
Petition: CRI is asking Delaware residents to sign its Affordable Energy Petition.
https://www.caesarrodney.org/affordable-energy-petition
Learn more: Delaware residents can review the Delaware Forest Service’s Forest Action Plan and Statewide Forest Strategy through the Delaware Department of Agriculture.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: New poll finds strong voter support for auditing the Legislature holding steady
description: For all of the sound and fury legislative leaders have raised, voter support for the audit law has not budged in two years.
text:
THERE’S BEEN an awful lot of sound and fury from top Democrats when it comes to the long-stalled, voter-approved law empowering the state auditor to give the Legislature a closer look.
They say allowing the auditor to probe the House and Senate would violate the sanctity of the state Constitution, which requires a separation of powers between the legislative and executive branches. They say both chambers already undergo financial audits by outside firms and post the results online. And they say Auditor Diana DiZoglio, a former representative and senator herself, is motivated by personal animus toward her former bosses, rendering her a walking conflict of interest.
Yet all of the headlines and handwringing over the past two years have not moved the needle among voters, not even by a single point.
A new CommonWealth Beacon/MassINC Polling Group survey (Toplines | Crosstabs) found that 72 percent of likely voters support explicitly allowing the state auditor to audit the Legislature — exactly the same share that voted in support of a 2024 ballot question writing that power into state law. Only 7 percent of respondents oppose the law, and 21 percent said they are unsure.
Informed that the support margin in the poll mirrored the 2024 vote, DiZoglio’s first response was to chuckle.
“It’s certainly on theme,” she told CommonWealth Beacon. “We continue to push for the voter-mandated audit that 72 percent voted for, and as the poll demonstrates, that push is not waning. People are just as motivated as they were in 2024.”
Consensus among the electorate has not extended to the House and Senate. For more than a year following the question’s approval, top Democrats in each chamber refused to comply with DiZoglio’s newly empowered outreach, prompting the auditor to sue them earlier this year.
An initial skirmish before the state’s highest court brought little resolution. A case focused on the constitutionality of DiZoglio’s initial request for a limited batch of documents — official legislative budgets, financial audits of the House and Senate, information about the “balance forward” line items used to carry funds into another year, and monetary settlements between the branches and current or former employees — is now pending in Suffolk Superior Court.
In a brief filed in that case, the House’s legal counsel argued that DiZoglio’s January 2025 request infringes on the separation of powers between the branches and violates a section of the state constitution declaring that legislative speech cannot be the target of any legal action. Furthermore, the House’s top attorney contended, the court is not empowered to order the chamber to make any changes.
Meanwhile, the Senate argues that it should not be subject to the lawsuit because its leaders already voted to provide the documents in question to DiZoglio — even while insisting they had no legal obligation to fulfill other audit requests. The House followed up that vote with its own legislation that would limit the scope of any probe by the state auditor’s office, in perpetuity, only to the subset of documents DiZoglio outlined in her very first request.
“The House has long believed that the audit ballot question violates the state constitution – a position that we have held since before the question passed in 2024,” House Speaker Ron Mariano said in a statement to CommonWealth Beacon. “While the House remains opposed to a politically motivated audit conducted in violation of the Constitution, we did pass legislation earlier this year providing the Auditor with the authority to conduct a financial audit of the House, and we continue to undergo an audit conducted by an independent auditing firm every year.”
Gray Milkowski, a spokesperson for Senate President Karen Spilka, noted that the chamber’s latest legislative rules made more information about committee votes available because the Senate “understands that transparency is important to voters.”
“In addition, the Senate continues to put all of its expenditures—including payroll and payments to vendors—online for every resident of the Commonwealth to see and review,” he said.
With implementation in limbo, the law has morphed into a political utility tool. “Where the hell is our audit” or references to “the 72 percent” have become stand-in responses to a whole host of complaints about Beacon Hill, even if addressing such a grievance is not within the scope of a routine audit of one government entity by another.
Republicans, who are outnumbered in the Legislature seven to one, made a point to visibly embrace both the audit law and also DiZoglio herself, the only statewide Democrat who did not draw a GOP challenger this fall.
But among voters, support is massive across different ideologies. For all the complaints top House and Senate Democrats make, 70 percent of Democratic likely voters back the audit law, according to the new CommonWealth Beacon survey. Seventy-nine percent of Republicans support it, as do 72 percent of those not enrolled in either major party.
The poll involved 800 likely voters surveyed between September 14 and September 22. It has a credibility interval of plus or minus 4 percentage points.
Voters have another legislative transparency decision to make this fall. DiZoglio and her allies are pushing a new ballot question that would subject the House, Senate, and governor’s office to the state’s public records law, with the auditor pitching it as a natural follow-up to her winning campaign two years ago.
Already, that idea has been caught up in the gears of Beacon Hill.  Over the summer, while the ballot question was already well on track to land on the November ballot,  both branches approved legislation creating a new public records framework for themselves. Depending on where the final compromise bill lands, it could supersede whatever voters decide at the polls.
DiZoglio suggested she could take legal action if that comes to pass.
“The Legislature, in doing this, is signaling to the voters of this Commonwealth that they do not respect the will of the electorate and that election results don’t matter to them,” she said.
