title: A Familiar Voice, a Helping Hand: Delaware Hospice’s Care Goes Beyond the Bedside
description: A Familiar Voice, a Helping Hand: Delaware Hospice’s Care Goes Beyond the Bedside By John Riddle, Contributing Journalist, Delaware LIVE A favorite story read aloud. A quiet conversation. Someone willing to sit beside a patient and simply be present. At Delaware Hospice, those gestures are part of a broader effort to support people facing serious illness and[...]
text:
A Familiar Voice, a Helping Hand: Delaware Hospice’s Care Goes Beyond the Bedside
By John Riddle, Contributing Journalist, Delaware LIVE
A favorite story read aloud. A quiet conversation. Someone willing to sit beside a patient and simply be present.
At Delaware Hospice, those gestures are part of a broader effort to support people facing serious illness and the families walking through that experience with them. Medical care is central to the organization’s work, but its services also address the emotional, spiritual and practical needs that can accompany a difficult diagnosis.
Founded in 1982, the nonprofit, community-based healthcare organization serves people throughout Delaware and in southern Chester and Delaware counties in Pennsylvania. According to its website, more than 175,000 patients and families have turned to Delaware Hospice over the years.
Its mission reflects a commitment to caring for people as well as treating illness.
“Our mission is to support every individual, family, and community with compassionate and expert care for serious illness,” the Delaware Hospice website states.
For families, serious illness can bring questions that extend well beyond medical treatment. Daily responsibilities continue, caregivers need support, and children may need help understanding what is happening to someone they love.
Delaware Hospice’s services include grief support, community education, and assistance for children and caregivers. The organization describes its approach as one that recognizes the needs of the whole family, including help coping with loss and navigating everyday challenges.
Financial circumstances are also part of that picture. Delaware Hospice says it provides care and support regardless of the person’s ability to pay. Donor contributions help sustain services when insurance does not cover all costs.
The organization also outlines several measures intended to maintain and improve the quality of its care. These include a dedicated quality and compliance team, patient and family satisfaction surveys, and an in-house Education and Learning department.
Feedback from patients and relatives helps inform that work, while staff education supports continued learning about care practices. Delaware Hospice also identifies a partnership with Healthcentric Advisors as a source of outside oversight.
According to its website, the organization is licensed in Delaware and southern Pennsylvania, approved by the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, and accredited by the Joint Commission.
Its recognition as a We Honor Veterans Level 4 Partner reflects attention to the needs of veterans at the end of life. Delaware Hospice also reports receiving Four Rings in the National Alliance for Care at Home’s Quality Connections Program for four consecutive years across its four locations.
Alongside its professional care team, volunteers contribute time, companionship and practical assistance.
“Your time and talents also fuel vital behind-the-scenes roles in administrative support and community outreach,” the organization’s website states.
For someone interested in volunteering, there are several ways to participate. Direct patient support can include providing companionship, reading aloud or helping with daily activities. These roles offer opportunities to bring personal attention and human connection to patients and their families.
Other volunteers assist with administrative work, community outreach and special events. Those assignments allow people to contribute different skills while supporting the organization’s services.
The range of opportunities means participation can take different forms. A volunteer who enjoys conversation might provide companionship. Someone drawn to organizational tasks might find a role helping behind the scenes.
Together, those contributions support an organization whose work has reached Delaware families for more than four decades.
For residents seeking assistance or considering volunteering, Delaware Hospice’s website provides information about its services and opportunities to get involved. Whether through professional care, caregiver support or a volunteer’s visit, the organization’s approach emphasizes the people experiencing serious illness and the loved ones beside them. Sometimes, that support begins with a helping hand. Sometimes, it begins with someone willing to listen and stay awhile.

name: Nevada Current
title: State treasurer race pits office’s current deputy against think tank analyst
description: The state of Nevada collects a lot of money from taxes, fees and investments — and while the state Legislature directs how that money is spent, it’s the state treasurer who acts as steward of the state coffers. The current treasurer, Zach Conine, has served for two terms and cannot run for office again. That […]
text:
Tya Mathis-Coleman, Drew Johnson. (Candidate photos)The state of Nevada collects a lot of money from taxes, fees and investments — and while the state Legislature directs how that money is spent, it’s the state treasurer who acts as steward of the state coffers.
The current treasurer, Zach Conine, has served for two terms and cannot run for office again. That has opened the door for two candidates — Republican Drew Johnson and Democrat Tya Mathis-Coleman — to replace him as treasurer in November’s general election. 
Nevada’s treasurer is essentially the state banker, whose responsibilities include managing investments, administering the sale of bonds and securities, and cutting checks when money is spent by the state controller or state agencies.
While the treasurer’s office is best known for overseeing the state’s Millennium Scholarship and unclaimed property programs, they also play a critical role in financing various public works projects and affordable housing efforts through the Nevada State Infrastructure Bank.
The state treasurer is also responsible for overseeing the state’s credit rating, which helps to determine how much Nevadan taxpayers will end up paying when the state issues bonds. 
 Tya Mathis-Coleman

Mathis-Coleman has served as the Deputy Treasurer for College Savings and the Millennium Scholarship for more than six years. Prior to her role in the treasurer’s office, she worked in recruitment at her alma mater, the University of Nevada Reno, then moved to Clark County School District, where she would become the director of recruitment and oversee the team responsible for hiring approximately 2,600 teachers each year. 
If elected, she said her top priorities would be to protect taxpayer money and ensure the stability of state finances. 
“I know that I will be the only person that can hit the ground running on day one,” Mathis-Coleman said. 
Mathis-Coleman said she would leverage her long-time experience at the treasurer’s office to make housing more affordable, healthcare more accessible, and education more attainable.   
She highlighted her role in securing three credit rating increases for Nevada, bringing in over $1.6 billion in investment returns, and returning $400 million in unclaimed property.  
As part of the treasury leadership team, Mathis-Coleman said she helped leverage the State Infrastructure Bank to finance more than 10,000 affordable housing units across Nevada. She pointed to the Carville Park Apartments in Reno, which provided affordable housing to seniors for as little as $1 per month. If elected, she said she would continue working on expanding affordable housing. 
“We’ve made great gains when it comes to using the infrastructure bank for affordable housing,” Mathis-Coleman said. “I’m very proud of that work.”
Mathis-Coleman said she would also prioritize mortgage down payment assistance to first time homebuyers, especially for veterans. 
Managing the state’s Millennium Scholarship is a major responsibility of the office, however, the scholarship has faced financial troubles in recent years. Mathis-Coleman said she would work with the Legislature to fully fund the program for at least the next two years, and ensure students who are relying on the scholarship receive their expected funds.   
“My goal is to continue to work with the Legislature to make sure that the program is adequately funded,” Mathis-Coleman said. “I want to make the scholarship more effective and make it more competitive so that it actually keeps our best students in Nevada.”
Mathis-Coleman said she would also like to expand Nevada’s  529 college savings plans, which offer prepaid tuition programs.
While the state treasurer’s office does not directly fund healthcare, Mathis-Coleman said the office could expand the state’s Health Equity and Loan Assistance (HEAL) Program, which provides loan forgiveness to healthcare professionals who commit to providing healthcare services in rural or urban underserved communities. 
She also said the Nevada State Infrastructure Bank could be leveraged to help finance the construction of new health care facilities in rural communities. 
“I think it is such a disgrace that we have many rural communities that do not have access to emergency healthcare within an hour,” Mathis-Coleman said.
Mathis-Coleman said the main difference between her and her Republican opponent is experience and a proven track record managing the state’s finances. 
“I’ve spent years, decades in other public institutions here in Nevada serving Nevadans. Drew to my knowledge has never held an office and has no experience overseeing Nevada public funds in any capacity,” Mathis-Coleman said.
Drew Johnson
Johnson did not respond to Nevada Current’s request for an interview.
Johnson founded the Beacon Center of Tennessee, a conservative think tank, which expanded charter school vouchers, loosened regulatory rules on entrepreneurs and ended regressive taxes that harmed lower-income individuals, his website says.  The site also says he and his wife now have a consultant service that works with “free market think tanks and pro-liberty grassroots organizations.”
Johnson unsuccessfully ran against U.S. Rep. Susie Lee for U.S. Nevada House District 3 in 2024, losing by 2.8 points. In 2022, he unsuccessfully ran for Clark County commissioner, losing to incumbent Justin Jones by 336 votes.
On his campaign website, Johnson said his priorities for state treasurer are cutting waste, slashing fees, increasing financial literacy, modernizing the state financial systems, boosting Nevada’s credit rating, lowering borrowing costs, maximizing investment returns, and returning unclaimed property. 
Johnson describes himself as a “well-known government waste expert” and “budget watchdog” on his campaign website. Johnson said on social media that he was proud to serve on the board of DOGE Nevada, a nonprofit with no ties to the former federal government program. 
If elected, Johnson noted he would focus on reviewing state accounts, vendor contracts, and fee structures to push for leaner operations and greater accountability in the treasurer’s office. 
Administrative costs in the treasures office could also be trimmed by modernizing the state’s financial systems, Johnson’s website says.

name: Nevada Current
title: Compared to NV’s other U.S. House races, CD4 flies under the radar
description: “Although former Vice President Kamala Harris carried this seat by just two points in 2024, the 4th District isn’t a particularly high priority for either party,” reads the Cook Political Report’s thumbnail analysis of the race between incumbent Nevada Democratic Rep. Steven Horsford and Republican challenger Cody Whipple. Democrats held a nearly 6 percentag[...]
text:
Cody Whipple, Steven Horsford. (Photos: Whipple campaign website; Hugh Jackson/Nevada Current)“Although former Vice President Kamala Harris carried this seat by just two points in 2024, the 4th District isn’t a particularly high priority for either party,” reads the Cook Political Report’s thumbnail analysis of the race between incumbent Nevada Democratic Rep. Steven Horsford and Republican challenger Cody Whipple.
Democrats held a nearly 6 percentage point advantage in registered active voters over Republicans as of August, according to the secretary of state’s office. 
That might not sound like a lot, but it’s enough to make it the most Democratic-heavy of Nevada’s four congressional districts. Since CD4 was created after the 2010 census, a Republican has only won it once, in 2014. 
The lion’s share of registered voters in the district live in northern portions of Clark County, including Mesquite. The district also covers Nye, Esmaralda, and Mineral counties, along with portions of Churchill, Lyon, and Lincoln counties.
Whipple is a rancher and businessman in the latter.
In two of the three U.S. House seats currently held by Nevada Democrats, Donald Trump endorsed Republican challengers during the primary, and they each won, as Trump-endorsed Republican primary candidates almost always do.
Those two nominees — Carrie Buck in Nevada’s 1st Congressional District, held by Dina Titus, and Marty O’Donnell in the 3rd, where he’s challenging incumbent Susie Lee —  have since been named to the National Republican Congressional Committee “MAGA Majority” list, which means the NRCC has used its national organizing capacity to provide or encourage financial support to Buck and O’Donnell.
Trump didn’t endorse Whipple or any other Republican in CD4. And the NRCC did not put Whipple on the MAGA Majority list.
When in Las Vegas in August, Trump gave a shoutout to multiple Republicans, including Buck, O’Donnell, and a third Republican Trump endorsed during the primary, David Flippo in CD2. 
Whipple was at the event, but Trump didn’t namecheck him.
Flippo had started the 2026 campaign cycle in the primary with Whipple for Nevada’s 4th Congressional District, but relocated his hopes for a political future to CD2 after incumbent Republican Mark Amodei announced he was retiring from the House.
During Flippo’s momentary stint as a 2026 CD4 candidate, he and Whipple mixed it up a little. The Nye County Republican Party, which had endorsed Flippo, called on Whipple to drop out of the race, charging Whipple changed his primary residence from a Las Vegas metro area address to one in Lincoln County shortly before launching his candidacy.
Whipple dismissed the residency issue as “an attack by David Flippo and his team, nothing more.”
(Ironically, similar complaints would fly Flippo’s way over his rushed relocation to Reno to run in CD4.) 
On the day of the Trump Las Vegas visit, Whipple issued a statement saying Horsford “voted against his own constituents on essential tax relief — including keeping taxes off tips, overtime pay, and senior benefits.” 
Each of the items Whipple mentioned were references to measures in Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill that was passed by Republicans in Congress in 2025. 
“He didn’t vote that way because it helps Nevadans,” Whipple said, but because Horsford’s “D.C. party bosses demanded it.”
Horsford and other Democrats voted against Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill for multiple reasons, including cuts to Medicaid funding that now threaten the viability of rural hospitals.
 “While the ultra-wealthy locked in permanent tax relief under Republicans’ so-called ‘one big beautiful bill,’ working people were offered temporary and inadequate relief,” Horsford said in one of many broadsides launched at the Trump-backed legislation since its enactment. 
In February, Horsford introduced legislation that would, among other things, make “no tax on tips,” currently scheduled to expire after the 2028 tax year, permanent. Horsford’s bill would also eliminate the Trump bill’s so-called “marriage penalty,” by raising the tips tax deduction cap from $25,000 to $50,000 for joint filers.
Though Whipple attended the Trump event in Las Vegas, the rancher has also disagreed with Trump publicly. After Trump’s attempt to end birthright citizenship was rejected by the U.S. Supreme Court in June, Trump was touting the idea that Congress could enact legislation restricting birthright citizenship.
“The courts have made it clear that birthright citizenship is settled law under the 14th Amendment,” Whipple said in a statement to the Current in July, adding “our time is better spent securing our borders to prevent human trafficking and smuggling after years of neglect.”
Horsford’s campaign had raised more than $3 million in the 2026 cycle as of June 30 and had $1.5 million on hand. 
Whipple’s campaign had reported almost $900,000 as of June 30, including $300,000 he loaned to it, with $285,000 on hand.
Of the three Nevada U.S. House seats held by incumbents, two are listed by Cook Political Report and other ratings organizations as “leaning” Democratic, while only one is ranked “likely” Democratic — Horsford’s.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Equipment failure at Oxford compressor station sounded like jet engine, residents say
description: On the night of July 12, the Oxford compressor station had 2 equipment failures, according to incident data collected by federal regulators.
text:
The noise was so loud, ShawnaLee Kwashnak thought a jet engine had landed in her driveway.
“I remember being woken up from a sound sleep that, in that moment, I could only describe as a tornado or freight train smashing into my house, except there was no storm,” Kwashnak said.
“Then the next thought is, ‘What the heck is a jet engine doing in my driveway?’ It was that loud. It vibrated the house,” she said.
The sound started after midnight on July 12. It woke up residents in Oxford, Middlebury and Naugatuck and lasted for approximately 45 minutes.
“By the time it stops, it’s such a relief. But then you’re lying there wondering, ‘What happened and is it going to happen again?’” she said. “Nothing you could think of made any sense.”
Kwashnak lives in Middlebury, about two miles away from a compressor station in Oxford. The facility increases the pressure of natural gas, helping it move long distances along the Algonquin Gas Transmission pipeline – a 1,131-mile system that transports natural gas through New England, New York and New Jersey.
On the night of July 12, the Oxford compressor station had two equipment failures, according to incident data collected by the U.S. Department of Transportation, Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration.
The data shows malfunctions caused the release of more than 35 million cubic feet of natural gas in less than an hour. That’s roughly the same amount of natural gas used by 450 Connecticut homes in an entire year, according to 2024 data from the U.S. Energy Information Administration.
“That’s a huge amount of a gas that we ought not to be breathing in,” said Kirsten Ek, a hospitalist physician with Connecticut Health Professionals for Climate Action.
The incident is the largest release of natural gas in Connecticut reported to the federal government in the last 10 years and in the top 10 percent of all nationwide releases reported in the last decade.
Residents near the Oxford plant are raising concerns about a lack of communication after the incident.
The Oxford release happened as another compressor station in Connecticut, located in Brookfield and operated by Iroquois Pipeline Operating Company, has been making headlines as local residents fight a proposal to expand that facility.
Oxford station experienced two equipment failures on July 12
Both equipment failures involved the Oxford station’s emergency shutdown system, according to the federal government’s incident data. The system is designed to respond to abnormalities like unintentional pressure drops or natural gas leaks.
The first malfunction was a loose connection on a newly installed emergency pull switch that triggered the station to go into emergency shutdown mode at approximately 12:47am.
When an emergency shutdown system works properly, it automatically stops the compressor units, isolates the station away from the pipeline, and vents the remaining natural gas through the station’s discharge pipes.
But a valve meant to seal the station off from the pipeline failed to close completely, causing natural gas to flow from the pipeline, through the station’s discharge pipes, and out into the atmosphere for approximately 53 minutes.
The loud jet engine-like sound that woke up residents was likely caused by the rapid release of natural gas moving from high to low pressure as it left the pipeline and entered the atmosphere, according to Talor Musil, field manager at the Environmental Health Project, a nonprofit organization that helps residents whose health has been impacted by oil and gas development.
The valve remained open until approximately 1:40am, when personnel were able to manually close it.
Enbridge, the company that owns the natural gas pipeline, told Connecticut Public in an email that the station “experienced an unplanned outage” and that “at no time was there a threat to public safety.”
The Oxford Compression Station, a natural gas facility on Woodruff Hill Road in Oxford, Connecticut on September 21, 2026. It’s not immediately clear if the blowdown violated the Clean Air Act, which regulates air emissions and allows the Environmental Protection Agency to establish air quality standards. Credit: Ryan Caron King / Connecticut Public
Residents and activists say they were never told how much natural gas was released or what steps have been taken to ensure this doesn’t happen again.
“It should be transparent and there should actually be an apology,” Kwashnak said.
“You’re in your home, in your yard, and you’re supposed to feel safe. Something like that goes on, it changes things,” she said.
How natural gas affects the environment and your body
Natural gas is a fossil fuel that’s mostly made up of methane, a powerful greenhouse gas that contributes to global warming by trapping heat in the earth’s atmosphere.
It’s also highly combustible.
“It is known to cause violent explosions when it’s in high concentration and catches fire,” said hospitalist physician, Kirsten Ek.
When it comes to health impacts, methane is known to displace oxygen in the body. Low or moderate concentrations of methane can cause dizziness and nausea. High concentrations can worsen headaches, cause confusion, loss of coordination, faster breathing, heart stress and eventually a loss of consciousness, according to Ek.
“The people around that release may have experienced a lot of those early symptoms, and if they were close enough into the high concentration, they may have experienced more intense headaches, nausea, confusion, things like that,” Ek said.
Methane can also cause reactions that create ground-level ozone, another greenhouse gas that causes respiratory issues.
“When you breathe it in, [it’s] toxic to the lungs. It’s like getting a sunburn inside your lungs,” Ek said.
Connecticut already has some of the highest levels of ozone pollution in the United States, with over half a million children breathing in unhealthy air, according to a new report by the American Lung Association.
Middlebury resident Kwashnawk said her throat was burning the day after the release, a possible symptom of being exposed to another pollutant in natural gas – volatile organic compounds, also known as VOCs.
“Short-term effects that could occur include, eye, nose, throat irritation, headaches or nausea, even loss of coordination or dizziness,” said Musil at the Environmental Health Project.
“There absolutely is risk involved,” she said.
Who’s accountable and what happens next? 
When natural gas is released from a compressor station during an emergency shutdown, it’s referred to as a ‘blowdown’ rather than a ‘leak’ or ‘spill’.
That’s because the natural gas is intentionally released as part of the emergency shutdown process.
Blowdowns are not directly regulated by Connecticut’s Department of Energy and Environmental Protection, according to an agency spokesperson, who stated that blowdowns fall under the jurisdiction of the U.S. Department of Transportation.
A federal agency under that department, PHMSA, is responsible for setting and enforcing standards related to the safe transportation of energy. It also collects data on unintentional gas releases that exceed 3 million cubic feet.
But the agency declined to comment for this story, referring Connecticut Public to the Public Utility Regulatory Authority (PURA).
PURA also declined to comment, stating the issue might come before them for adjudication.
Although PURA is known for regulating utilities in Connecticut, it’s also responsible for pipeline safety in the state.
It’s not immediately clear if the blowdown violated the Clean Air Act, which regulates air emissions and allows the Environmental Protection Agency to establish air quality standards.
Any deviation from the act is required to be reported to DEEP within 24 hours or 10 days.
“At this time, the operator has not submitted a Clean Air Act deviation report to DEEP in relation to this matter,” a DEEP spokesperson said.
Environmental activists from the the Sierra Club’s Connecticut chapter say they’d like to see more transparency around blowdowns, including publicly available information on how much methane gas is released and notifying nearby residents.
“These events can be frightening to those who live nearby,” said Samantha Dynowski, state director of Sierra Club Connecticut, in a statement.
“They can also have dangerous impacts on those with pre-existing conditions who are especially vulnerable to poor air quality,” she said.
This story was first published Sept. 29, 2026 by Connecticut Public.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Missouri doesn’t require asking pregnant patients about their mental health. New moms keep dying
description: When a doctor starts asking a new mother about feelings of depression, therapist Haley Walker said the patient may be thinking about more than her actual symptoms. “[It] can feel scary as a new mom,” Walker said. “You’re like, ‘Is this person going to try and take my baby if I’m honest?’” Walker specializes in […]
text:
Of the 108 pregnancy-related deaths that the state of Missouri reviewed, 17 were due to mental health conditions, while another seven were due to substance use disorder.(Photo illustration/Naomi O'Donnell).When a doctor starts asking a new mother about feelings of depression, therapist Haley Walker said the patient may be thinking about more than her actual symptoms.
“[It] can feel scary as a new mom,” Walker said. “You’re like, ‘Is this person going to try and take my baby if I’m honest?’”
Walker specializes in mental health during pregnancy and postpartum at her private practice in Mexico, Missouri, about 40 miles northeast of Columbia. She said patients may not feel comfortable answering certain personal questions honestly unless providers explain why they are asking and normalize the fact that new mothers often struggle with their mental health.
But the stakes of detecting mental health struggles in new mothers couldn’t be higher.
In Missouri, mental health conditions are among the leading causes of death during pregnancy and in the year after giving birth.
The state’s latest Pregnancy-Associated Mortality Review (PAMR) report found that conditions including depression, anxiety and substance use disorders contributed to nearly a quarter of pregnancy-related deaths from 2019 to 2023.
And the risk is even higher for women in rural areas, who are 21% more likely to experience perinatal depression than women in urban areas, according to a 2020 study.
Compared to how other states address mental health during and after pregnancy, Missouri falls somewhere in the middle, according to the Policy Center for Maternal Mental Health, a national think tank that doles out annual report cards for states.
Missouri received a C in 2026, up from its D-minus in 2023.
That’s in part because the state has tried to boost screenings for mental health conditions among pregnant and postpartum patients, creating programs to help doctors and social service providers more easily identify patients who may need help.
But those kinds of screenings aren’t mandatory in Missouri.
And the screening, which only takes a few minutes, is just the first step to getting someone the care they need.
Finding providers to treat patients can take weeks, could require a long drive, or could end with no appointment at all.
 Too many preventable maternal mental health deaths 

Of the 108 pregnancy-related deaths that the state of Missouri reviewed, 17 were due to mental health conditions, while another seven were due to substance use disorder.
The numbers have stayed relatively steady, aside from an uptick during COVID-19. From 2017 to 2019, 17 women died from mental health conditions, including substance use disorder, the top cause of death during that time span.
Overall, the pregnancy-related mortality rate was 2.9 times higher for women on Medicaid than for those on private insurance, and the rate for Black women was 2.5 times the rate for white women, the report found.
Nearly 80% of the deaths were preventable, the review board determined, including every death related to mental health or substance use.
Dr. Kimberly Brandt, the incoming chair of Missouri’s PAMR board, said the reviews look across a patient’s care for places providers could have intervened.
“Can we see in their care — was there a point where somebody offered to help?” Brandt said.
One of the biggest opportunities? Asking patients the right questions.
Missouri’s report found that in 38 of the deaths, providers failed to complete screenings for mental health conditions or other top causes of death, like cardiovascular problems.
The findings don’t mean a questionnaire or screening alone would have prevented someone from dying. But they do show how often the healthcare system missed a chance to identify a potentially fatal condition and respond.
Limited resources create additional barriers for women in rural Missouri.
Northeast Missouri had the state’s highest pregnancy-related mortality rate, followed by the St. Louis region and southwest Missouri.
 Early screening

The PAMR board recommends that all providers who come into contact with new families try to complete a screening.
A screening detects possible symptoms, and an assessment then should determine what a mental health condition may be and its severity.
And those screenings should begin during pregnancy, said Nancy Byatt, a perinatal psychiatrist at University of Massachusetts Chan Medical School. She cited research that found among patients with postpartum depression, about two-thirds experienced the onset of depression before they gave birth.
“If we wait to start screening until somebody’s postpartum,” Byatt said, “we’ve missed a window.”
Parents may not recognize their own symptoms as depression or anxiety, said Alison Williams, the director of the Missouri Perinatal Quality Collaborative.
She recalled her own experience with mental health postpartum.
“I couldn’t have told you that I was depressed or that I had major anxiety,” Williams said. “I just knew I felt out of control.”
“I wish we would take the term ‘baby blues’ out of our nomenclature,” Williams said, “because it’s so much more than that.”
 Screenings don’t equal treatment for maternal mental health conditions

Following a screening, providers should connect patients with treatment options, including therapy, medications or social support.
But that’s where things can get tricky.
Byatt compared mental health screenings to checking someone’s blood pressure.
A doctor wouldn’t identify high blood pressure, tell the patient to find someone to treat it and consider the work finished, she said.
“The challenge with mental health is sometimes that’s what happens,” Byatt said.
Williams recalled hearing about a mother who scored high on a depression screening during a pediatric visit. The mom explained her history of mental health problems and was addressing them. Their provider responded that depression was common, and moved to the next topic.
“That’s a checkbox,” Williams said. “‘We said we were going to do a screening, and we did a screening.’”
Michigan illustrates the gap between boosting screenings and boosting treatment. In 2018, the state began allowing pediatric providers to bill Medicaid for screening mothers during well-child visits. Screening increased but was still below 10%.
Researchers found little overall increase in treatment, although ZIP codes with the highest screening rates were associated with a 10% higher probability of getting treatment.
Paying providers for the screening helped, but it did not guarantee people got the care they needed.
 Far from care

In Mexico, Missouri, Walker’s patients are frequently frustrated by the travel required to get care.
“The majority of the trend I notice is frustration with the fact that we don’t have anybody in Mexico that delivers babies,” Walker said. “We used to have a hospital, and now we don’t.”
Traveling to Columbia can mean taking time away from work and finding transportation, Walker said.
Nearly every county in the state is designated as a mental health professional shortage area, data shows. 
And the providers that Walker’s patients have easier access to aren’t always equipped to handle what’s going on, she said. Local urgent care and primary care providers often respond to immediate concerns, she said, but most don’t have the training to see how depression, anxiety or trauma appear during pregnancy and postpartum.
“It can be very disappointing and disheartening when (patients) finally ask for help,” Walker said, “and then they go there and they’re let down or made to feel inadequate.”
 Bringing maternal mental health expertise closer

Missouri’s solution can’t be to send every patient with depression or anxiety to a psychiatrist, Byatt said. There simply aren’t enough specialists, especially in rural communities.
“We can’t be referring everyone to a mental health specialist,” Byatt said. “It’s not realistic.”
Byatt developed a program in Massachusetts to help fill that gap. Now, similar programs operate in 31 states.
Missouri’s version, the Maternal Health Access Project, allows providers to consult with psychiatrists about how to respond to a positive screening and begin treatment or whether specialty care is needed.
The goal is to bring psychiatric experts to the patient’s providers, rather than asking patients to find new providers themselves.
Byatt acknowledged her programs aren’t a “build it and they will come” solution. Clinicians must first know the help exists, then know how to use it.
But patients still need someone to carry out the care plan and follow their progress.
That coordination can be difficult in rural communities when a patient’s therapist, primary care doctor and obstetrician often work in separate health systems.
Walker said that she has sent emails and faxes to doctors without receiving a response. Meanwhile, private psychiatric care exists but is out of reach for patients who need continuing treatment.
Clinical care is only part of what mothers need after delivery, Williams said. Family and community support matter too, and can often disappear when attention shifts to the baby.
“Everybody comes around the mom so much until she delivers,” Williams said. “They’re there for the week afterward, then people start to scatter to the four winds. It’s like, no, no, no — that’s when she really needs you.”
This article first appeared on Beacon: Kansas City and is republished here under a Creative Commons Attribution-NoDerivatives 4.0 International License.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Utah 1st Congressional District debate found middle ground among two moderates
description: In the race for Utah’s 1st Congressional District, two candidates from opposing political parties found themselves meeting in the middle, a shift from the scenes playing out in campaigns across the country seeking a spot in a profoundly divided U.S. Congress.  Ben McAdams, who won a crowded primary for the Democratic nomination by far, is […]
text:
Candidates for Utah’s 1st Congressional District Republican Riley Owen, left, and Democrat Ben McAdams participate in a debate at Salt Lake Community College, Tuesday, Sept. 29, 2026, in Salt Lake City. (Pool photo by Erin Hooley/Deseret News)In the race for Utah’s 1st Congressional District, two candidates from opposing political parties found themselves meeting in the middle, a shift from the scenes playing out in campaigns across the country seeking a spot in a profoundly divided U.S. Congress. 
Ben McAdams, who won a crowded primary for the Democratic nomination by far, is facing Riley Owen, a Republican, naval officer and former White House staffer, to represent a new blue-leaning district in Utah. The two met onstage Tuesday for a debate put on by the Utah Debate Commission.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Jesse West, a Libertarian, and Elias Montgomery, an unaffiliated candidate, are also running for the seat. They, however, didn’t meet the commission’s minimum 10% support threshold to participate in the debate.  
The race’s major contenders may be perceived as moderates by members of their own party, even partially agreeing on some issues, like the gerrymandering lawsuit that created the district they are competing for.
“I think there are numerous things that are the root of the corruption of Congress and the frustration with its inability to actually rise to the challenges and to solve problems, and we have incredible challenges today that we need them to rise to,” McAdams said. “At the crux of it, I would put gerrymandering, where politicians win or lose their election by catering to extremes, and we now live in a climate that, if you work across the aisle, it is to your own peril.” 
Candidate for Utah’s 1st Congressional District Democrat Ben McAdams participates in a debate at Salt Lake Community College, Tuesday, Sept. 29, 2026, in Salt Lake City. (Pool photo by Erin Hooley/Deseret News)
Owen views the issue differently. Unlike McAdams, he did not thank Better Boundaries, the group that filed the anti-gerrymandering lawsuit from where the state’s new congressional maps were born. He said he was frustrated by the new maps. But, he still reached a similar conclusion to McAdams’. 
“It doesn’t frustrate me that, statistically speaking, this is a blue-leaning district right now. What frustrates me is that the maps that we landed with created three of the most red districts in America and one of the most blue, ostensibly, districts in America,” Owen said. “That creates a breeding ground for extremism, and I don’t think any Utahn, whether you’re a Republican or Democrat, wants that on either side.” 
During the debate broadcast by PBS Utah and moderated by Natalie Gochnour, director of the Kem C. Gardner Policy Institute at Salt Lake Community College, the two candidates debated some of the hottest policy issues of the year with Owen often splitting from the Trump administration’s agenda. 
McAdams, the last Utah Democrat to serve in Congress, has also split from his caucus in the past. However, he has little faith in a Republican candidate doing the same.
“I was so happy to hear a lot of what we agreed on. I’ve been around long enough to know. Last time I served in Congress, I remember the entire Utah delegation talking about support for the Dream Act, and then remember that I was the only one who voted for it,” McAdams told reporters after the debate.
Owen, however, emphasized what he believed to be the biggest distinction between him and his opponent, arguing that McAdams wants a “bigger government,” while he wants more market-based incentives, he told reporters. 
Candidate for Utah’s 1st Congressional District Republican Riley Owen participates in a debate at Salt Lake Community College, Tuesday, Sept. 29, 2026, in Salt Lake City. (Pool photo by Erin Hooley/Deseret News)
About his stance on President Donald Trump’s agenda, Owen said, “There are some things he gets right. There are some things that he gets wrong, and that’s the case with every president and both parties.”
McAdams and Owen agreed on many issues, including the need for federal regulations around artificial intelligence, as well as higher standards to conserve the ailing Great Salt Lake, especially with the surge of data centers. 



Let us know what you think...


 


But, the issue that separated the candidates the most on Tuesday night was new work requirements for recipients of Medicaid and the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, which prompted an unmoderated back and forth.
“What we’ve done with Medicaid is we’ve created a maze, and then we play ‘gotcha’ for people who get lost in the maze through complicated paperwork,” McAdams said. “This administration has cut Utah’s targeted adult Medicaid program that has been a lifeline for so many people to get stabilized and to get back into society.”
But Owen argued the policy didn’t differ much from what Democrats did in the past.
“Ben, can I just ask what happened to the party of Bill Clinton? Work requirements were a hallmark of the welfare programs there, and Democrats lined up to support that. I don’t think it’s unreasonable,” Owen said.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Xcel’s faulty billing has residents, businesses and cities fired up
description: Xcel Energy’s billing practices are causing financial and logistical headaches for Minnesota residents, businesses and even municipalities, according to complaints filed with the state utility regulator this year. A municipal facility in Roseville and a private printing business in St. Paul were owed months of bill credits for onsite solar production. More t[...]
text:
Xcel Energy headquarters in Minneapolis. (Photo by Getty Images)Xcel Energy’s billing practices are causing financial and logistical headaches for Minnesota residents, businesses and even municipalities, according to complaints filed with the state utility regulator this year.
A municipal facility in Roseville and a private printing business in St. Paul were owed months of bill credits for onsite solar production. More than $6,500 in late fees were incurred by the city of St. Louis Park due, it says, to billing errors.  Residential electric invoices cancelled due to billing issues rose more than 50% from 2023 to 2026, according to Attorney General Keith Ellison.
Those are just some of the issues clocked by the Minnesota Public Utilities Commission’s Consumer Affairs Office during a yearlong investigation into the billing practices of Xcel Energy’s Minnesota electric utility, which serves about 1.5 million customers across the state.
The five-member commission launched the investigation about a year ago following a sharp increase in customer complaints since 2022.
“This alarming trend indicates that urgent action is needed to identify the causes of this significant increase in billing errors and determine how to bring billing error complaints back to acceptable levels,” the commissioners wrote.
The commission asked Xcel to detail what was behind the rise in billing errors, what it was doing to correct those errors and what it would do to prevent similar errors in the future. It directed Xcel to provide monthly data on new and existing billing errors, along with its efforts to remediate them, until further notice.
Billing errors continued in the subsequent months.
Rebel Ink Printing owner Todd Turfler told the commission this month that his business had not received any production payments yet this year for the solar array they installed at their building on West 7th Street in St. Paul, despite being told by Xcel in December that they were eligible for the payments. An Xcel employee, he said, confirmed earlier this year that the solar system was producing more energy than the building consumed.
“The inaccuracies in billing have completely undermined the financial viability of (the) commercial solar investment since we are receiving no credit for any solar energy generated,” Turfler said.
A Roseville municipal property received no electric bill — nor any monthly credits for solar energy produced by onsite solar panels — for eight months in 2024 and 2025, followed by a $15,000 bill in April 2025, city manager Patrick Trudgeon said in a Sept. 24 complaint. The error, which occurred even as Xcel’s gas utility continued to bill the property as usual, “caused issues in annual reporting for city electricity usage,” Trudgeon said.
Roseville’s complaint also detailed more widespread billing issues that created dozens of hours of additional staff work. The city only avoided late fees thanks to “staff checking each week for new incoming bills,” Trudgeon said.
The city of St. Louis Park wasn’t so fortunate, according to a complaint this month cataloguing multiple billing irregularities.
Xcel told the city it had incurred more than $6,500 in late charges in a recent 12-month period, St. Louis Park Administrative Services Director Cheyenne Brodeen told the commission. And the city lost $16,000 in 2023 — and likely more in the years since — because Xcel failed to give notice that it was eligible to switch to a lower-priced renewable energy subscription program that later closed to new subscribers, Brodeen said.
Separately, St. Louis Park continued to receive bills for a city-owned property months after it had been demolished, and at one point received a bill for a private business at another property the city no longer owns, raising privacy concerns, Brodeen said. She asked the commission to authorize an independent audit into Xcel’s billing and remittance practices and require the utility to notify affected customers of significant rate or program changes.
Xcel Energy spokesperson Megan Boldt said the utility is moving in the right direction and disagrees that an independent audit is needed.
“We have taken these issues seriously and have made significant progress improving our billing processes, reducing backlogs and addressing the underlying issues that contributed to errors,” Boldt told the Reformer in an email. “We are not suggesting our work is done…but we do not see systemic issues warranting a third-party investigation.”
Invoice cancellations typically happen when a utility discovers a billing error, such as an overpayment or incorrect rate, and voids the affected bills. Earlier this month, Xcel said the number of residential customer invoices cancelled “due to controllable factors” fell from 7,098 in July to 4,812 in August, the lowest monthly level in more than two years. The drop bucked a seasonal trend that typically sees invoice cancellations rise during peak moving season, the company said. 
Xcel also said it’s working to reduce billing errors affecting participants in Solar*Rewards, a compensation program for customers with onsite solar energy systems, while suggesting the apparent pattern of errors is overstated. 
An internal review found most of the nearly 600 accounts affected by “non-payments” in 2025 were either ineligible to receive payments under the program, were vacant, or had other issues beyond the utility’s direct control, Xcel said this month.
Ellison’s office appears unconvinced. In a filing last week, the attorney general suggested Xcel is selectively defining — and thus undercounting — billing errors. It asked the commission to cast a wider net in its investigation.
“Xcel’s reporting of billing errors shows that problems persist in its billing system, even as it appears that Xcel is under-reporting the actual number of errors experienced by customers. Xcel should therefore provide further information about the errors that it has excluded from its reporting in this docket,” Ellison’s filing said.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Dozens more lawsuits filed over sex abuse in NJ youth jails
description: Thirty people sued the state for creating a "culture of abuse" in New Jersey's youth jails. The lawsuits are the latest of nearly 500 now filed.
text:
Thirty people sued the state for creating a "culture of abuse" in New Jersey's youth jails. The lawsuits are the latest of nearly 500 now filed. (Photo by New Jersey Monitor)Thirty people who say they endured sexual abuse while incarcerated as minors sued the state Tuesday for negligence, accusing officials of hiring, training, and supervision failures that created a decades-long “culture of abuse” in New Jersey’s youth prisons.
The new lawsuits accuse officers and others who worked in youth justice facilities from the 1980s through the 2010s of inappropriate strip searches, coercive sexual contact, and rape. Abusers sometimes bribed those in their custody with cigarettes, drugs, alcohol, or privileges in exchange for sexual favors, and staff who witnessed the abuse failed to intervene or report it, the lawsuits say.
Jerome Block is an attorney whose New York City-based firm filed the lawsuits.
Most arise from the New Jersey Training School in Monroe, a boys’ lockup that is the largest and oldest and that remains open today despite repeated promises by multiple administrations since 2018 to close it, Block noted. The gang assault of an incarcerated teen earlier this month — a beating that was recorded and posted online — proves problems persist there, he added. A handful of the lawsuits involve smaller, community-based residential lockups and the Female Secure Care & Intake Facility, a girls’ jail in Bordentown.
“These cases reflect a juvenile justice system in New Jersey that is broken,” Block said. “We’ve seen no evidence that the systemic problems that have resulted in the sexual and physical abuse of children in these facilities have been fixed, and therefore we are very concerned that children in these facilities today are still at risk of abuse.”
Tara Oliver is a spokeswoman for the Attorney General’s Office, which oversees the Youth Justice Commission. She said all commission staff, volunteers, interns, and contractors must pass background checks, and the system has policies and protocols in place designed to prevent abuse and respond to and investigate abuse allegations.
Protecting youth in the care of the Youth Justice Commission is “extremely important,” Oliver said.
The new complaints come seven years after state lawmakers expanded the statute of limitations for sex crimes to give victims a longer timeline to file civil lawsuits.
Since then, nearly 500 lawsuits alleging sex abuse of children in state custody have been filed, with more than 300 involving claims against the juvenile justice system and the rest stemming from youth placed in psychiatric and developmental centers. They do not include sexual abuse claims related to the foster care system.
State budget documents released last spring show the state already has paid millions to resolve such lawsuits, with the median cost of settlements at $975,000 as of March.
With almost 500 cases now in the courts, that means taxpayers could end up on the hook for a half-billion dollars or more, as new cases are filed.
Block expects that will happen.
He noted that the incidence of childhood sexual abuse tends to be far higher than reported, especially among youth in state custody whose fears of retaliation and distrust of staff keep them silent.
The New Jersey Training School already has been flagged for a history of abuse, Block added. Federal authorities identified the jail in 2010 as one of the nation’s 13 worst for sexual misconduct and use of force by staff, with as many as 35% of boys who were surveyed there reporting sexual victimization by staff. A follow-up study in 2012 found that abuse at the facility had declined but persisted, with up to 15% of boys surveyed reporting sexual victimization by staff.
Thousands of youth, though, have also spent time in county juvenile lockups, Block added. More than 100 of the pending lawsuits stem from those placements, he said.
“It’s a growing liability, not only for the state, but for various counties,” he said. “What we’re seeing here is a growing amount of awareness among victims of sexual abuse in New Jersey juvenile detention centers, and survivors are continuing to step forward.”

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: The biotech reckoning is here
description: Price controls do not eliminate costs. They change incentives, reducing the expected return from developing medicines.
text:
FOR YEARS, critics of the Inflation Reduction Act’s drug price controls warned that winter was coming for biopharma. Massachusetts’s 2025 numbers suggest the reckoning has arrived: The state’s biotech industry lost jobs for the first time in two decades, with R&D employment down 3.9 percent. 
The warning was based partly on what had already happened in Europe. For decades, European governments have used sweeping price controls on medicines to contain health care costs. The result has been a weakening of the financial incentives that sustain drug development. China has now surpassed Europe in the number of innovative medicines produced, and one industry estimate says 40 percent of the world’s oncology research is occurring in China. 
The United States is now conducting its own version of that experiment. And Massachusetts may be giving us an early warning of the consequences. 
MassBio, the Massachusetts biotechnology trade association, reported that the state’s biopharma industry lost a substantial number of jobs in 2025 — the first such decline in two decades. Most strikingly, research and development employment fell by 2,563 jobs, or 3.9 percent. 
That matters because Massachusetts is disproportionately an R&D center. And when expected revenues from future medicines fall, research is among the easiest expenditures to cut. A company can cancel a clinical trial or shelve a prospective drug more readily than it can close a manufacturing facility, with all the environmental, labor, and other obligations that entails. 
The Inflation Reduction Act is hardly the only force affecting biotech employment. Interest rates, capital markets, and the post-pandemic correction have all battered the industry. But it would be equally mistaken to pretend that Washington’s decision to remove billions of dollars in expected pharmaceutical revenue has nothing to do with investment decisions. 
Indeed, the consulting firm Vital Transformation estimated that the IRA could ultimately cost the biopharma industry 66,800 to 135,900 direct jobs and another 342,000 to 676,000 indirect jobs. Its analysis explicitly warned of a “nuclear winter” for biotech investment. 
Meanwhile, the competitive threat is accelerating. 
In 2019, Chinese biotech companies generated $1 billion from licensing deals. Last year, the figure reached $79 billion. Massachusetts remains far ahead, with more than $250 billion in biotech licensing revenue, but China’s trajectory should command attention. MassBio apparently agrees: Its latest industry snapshot now includes a “China Watch.” 
MassBio points to rising venture funding in 2026 as evidence that the sector may recover. One important consideration: Even though top-line dollars are up, the average seed round has more than halved since 2022 ($11.1 million then, $4.65 million in the first half of 2026). That’s the venture equivalent of cutting R&D. With that, the magnitude of the IRA’s eventual effect on employment is legitimately debatable. But whether federal price controls represent a major headwind for the industry should not be. 
Massachusetts political leaders overwhelmingly supported those controls. We hope the industry here — and especially MassBio, whose latest industry report features so many Massachusetts politicians — begins telling them that their policy choices are weakening the very industry they are celebrating. 
That is precisely the debate Massachusetts should be having. 
Europe offers the warning. Faced with rising health care costs, governments suppressed drug prices. Investment and innovation migrated elsewhere. China has been one of the principal beneficiaries. 
America is now reducing the returns available from developing successful medicines at the same moment China is aggressively building a competing biotechnology industry. If the United States continues down Europe’s path, it should not be surprised if investment eventually follows Europe’s path as well. 
For Massachusetts, the stakes are unusually high. Biopharma is not simply another industry here. The Commonwealth has built one of the world’s great concentrations of scientific talent, research institutions, venture capital, and drug development around it. Policies that reduce investment in new medicines therefore threaten not only future treatments but one of the foundations of the Massachusetts economy. 
Price controls do not eliminate costs. They change incentives. Reduce the expected return from developing medicines, and over time companies will develop fewer medicines, invest less in research, and put fewer people to work doing it. 
Winter was coming. Now it’s here. 
William Smith is senior fellow and director of the Life Sciences Initiative at Pioneer Institute.

title: Wyoming elections chief applauds Supreme Court’s ruling on controversial voter data system
description:
The Trump administration has used the SAVE system to identify noncitizens voters on rolls. 
The post Wyoming elections chief applauds Supreme Court’s ruling on controversial voter data system appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
The U.S. Supreme Court temporarily revived a controversial federal database that Wyoming and other states have uploaded their voter lists to, clearing the way for the Trump administration to use the information to verify voters’ citizenship ahead of November’s general election. 
“I applaud and fully support the Supreme Court’s common sense decision upholding the use of the SAVE system,” Wyoming Secretary of State Chuck Gray said in a statement to WyoFile. “Voter list maintenance has always been a key priority for my administration.” 
Known as SAVE, the Systemic Alien Verification for Entitlements database was created 40 years ago with the original purpose of allowing federal, state and local government agencies to verify the immigration status of noncitizens seeking public benefits.
However, in its pursuit of noncitizens on voter rolls, the Trump administration has overhauled the system. It’s done so by linking the database for the first time with Social Security Administration records and allowing state and local officials to cross-reference voter records and conduct bulk searches, some of which have mistakenly flagged U.S. citizens. 
A legal dispute has since unfolded in federal court with the League of Women Voters and the Electronic Privacy Information Center challenging the changes to the SAVE system. The groups argue that outdated records in the now-expanded database risk disenfranchising eligible voters, particularly newly naturalized citizens. 
Siding with the Trump administration Friday, the court’s majority wrote that a lower court order halting the modified database “inhibits the Federal Government’s efforts to assist state and local agencies in the proper administration of the midterm elections.” 
What impact the decision may have on the midterm elections remains to be seen, partly on account of a federal law that largely prohibits states from removing voters from rolls within 90 days of a federal election. 

Secretary of State Chuck Gray applauds Gov. Mark Gordon’s State of the State address on Monday, Feb. 9, 2026, at the Wyoming Capitol in Cheyenne. (Mike Vanata for WyoFile)

For Wyoming’s part, Gray entered a memorandum of agreement in July  2025 with the federal government to upload the state’s voter lists to SAVE, according to public records. 
“This will help to ensure that only citizens are on the voter registration list,” Gray said in a press release announcing the agreement.
Around that same time period, Gray complied with a request to give the driver’s license numbers and partial Social Security numbers of every registered Wyoming voter to the Department of Justice. 
Gray declined WyoFile’s request for an interview Tuesday, agreeing instead to respond to written questions. 
In his response, Gray pointed to a 2025 state law that, among other things, authorizes the secretary of state to utilize SAVE to verify that voters listed in the Wyoming voter registration system are U.S. citizens. 
“As called for in Wyoming law, our office utilized the SAVE system to refer potential non-citizens to both county and federal law enforcement,” Gray wrote. “We have also used the SAVE system to refer potential non-citizens to county clerks.” 
County clerks manage elections on the local level. 
Moving forward, Gray said his office will continue to work with the Wyoming Attorney General’s Office “to ensure the law is followed.” 
Gray did not address a question asking how many voters have been flagged using the SAVE system since the 2024 election and how many were removed from Wyoming’s voter rolls. 
Previous statements from his office suggest at least four voters were flagged using SAVE. In a November press release, Gray announced three voters had been removed from the state’s voter rolls after they were flagged using the SAVE system. An additional voter was flagged in Johnson County in March, according to a press release.

title: What my classical education actually taught me
description:
The Heritage Foundation touts classical curriculum as the cure for America’s future. But columnist Jessica Brauer, an alumna of the classical system, sees herself as far from the conservative think tank's ideal case study.
The post What my classical education actually taught me appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
“Feet flat.Hips back.Shoulders straight.Eyes forward.”
We’d drone in unison.
This was how we announced our readiness at the teacher’s command from the front of the classroom.

Opinion

Thirty years ago, I thought this was how all young minds engaged in education. The teachers checked our bodies for compliant tucked-in shirts and belts; our pencil cases for only allowable writing utensils — six-sided pencils, sharpened, unmarred by bored children’s chews. Our curriculum was classical, before The Heritage Foundation touted classical curriculum as the hope for America’s future. 
Thirty years ago, I was 7 years old. I was learning how the world worked. 
This summer, the Steamboat Legacy Scholarship Act began disbursing up to $7,000 per K-12 student to Wyoming private and homeschool families despite ongoing litigation regarding the law’s constitutionality. Supporters, like Superintendent of Public Instruction Megan Degenfelder, assert that this law justly provides due support for families called to root their children’s education in religion and moral order from the home. Critics, like the Wyoming Education Association, believe it siphons already limited tax dollars without oversight, creating immense risk for Wyoming’s public schools and the quality of education for the state’s youth.
Both my elementary school, Fort Caspar Academy, and its related middle school, Casper Classical Academy, were founded in the mid-90s, predating Wyoming law allowing charter schools. Both remain public schools. I can’t speak to their founders’ intentions beyond a desire to shape young minds thoughtfully. However, the parallels are undeniable, particularly around “the trivium,” a foundational pillar of my alma mater and a favored tool of the highly conservative think tank The Heritage Foundation. 
In Latin, the trivium means “where three roads meet.” Those three roads — grammar, logic and rhetoric — formed the foundation of my classical education.
My schools operated with “pillars of virtuous character development” and “purposeful high expectations.” In our elementary classrooms, we recited long-form poetry. We dissected grammar and math verbally at the overhead projector with daily exercises called “Daily Oral Language (D.O.L)” and “Daily Oral Math (D.O.M).” In middle school, we were required to take Latin and logic class, learning the roots of rhetoric. In short, my schools were strict about everything from your midriff to your penmanship. 
Aristotle’s philosophy on logic is regularly quoted as: “All men are mortal. Socrates was a man. Therefore, Socrates was mortal.”
If children with poor posture often disrupt class, and disruptions to class interrupt the classroom experience, then children with poor posture interrupt the classroom experience. Enter the mantra recited in unison between lessons. 
Follow the syllogism further: If America needs compliant, orderly adults and schools discipline children toward compliance and order, then America will soon have its desired population. Yet, I look at myself, a once classically educated youth, and question that truth. I hesitate to believe I am the picture of the Heritage Foundation’s ideal case study. One glance and I’d be quickly diagnosed as terminal with “woke mind virus.” 
Thirty years ago, I looked to my teachers to teach me how the world worked. I was beholden to their power through report cards and threats of dress code violations. I learned to thrive in their systems with their tools for better and for worse. 
I don’t believe the trivium was a formula for compliant citizens. Rather, it was a foundation for what’s next: thought, expression, conversation — Heritage Foundation nightmare fuel. Imagine if they found out I have a nose ring.
The discourse around the Steamboat Legacy Scholarship explores topics that could be excavated endlessly. How does the state’s budget reflect how we educate our children? Who gets to decide what that education should produce? I don’t have those answers.
Perhaps I am a product of an education designed to shape America’s youth. From the time I was 7 years old, I anxiously adjusted my body and belongings to be granted my teacher’s approval. Sometimes, I still do. I learned to crave my teachers’ praise for my obedience. That’s a lot of power to hand in for a letter grade. 
Yet my future was not predetermined by my education. Rather, it was honed by it in ways that no trendy ideology or curriculum ever could. 
I learned the rules and followed them. Then I questioned them.

title: The plight of the pronghorn: Part 1
description:
Herds typically experience a reproductive bounce after a difficult winter. But that trend might not always remain, writes guest columnist Chris Madson.
The post The plight of the pronghorn: Part 1 appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Opinion

The horrific winter of 2022-23 has recently crept back into the news. The people who went out into the sage country south of Pinedale when the snow finally released its grip that year were appalled at the sight of scores of pronghorn carcasses scattered across the landscape. Estimates of the winterkill ranged as high as 70%. The Wyoming Game and Fish Department set the loss at roughly 50%, which meant that the weather had claimed something like 20,000 pronghorns in the Sublette Herd.
Some have said that it was the worst winter in living memory in that part of the world. I guess that depends to a marked degree on how long your memory is. The winter of 1983-84 was a ring-tailed screamer with temperatures in Pinedale as low as 37 below and average snow cover well over a foot. I won’t argue that it was worse than 2022-23 because I wasn’t there, but I think it’s fair to say it was comparable in its intensity and effect on big game, especially the smallest of our big game animals, the pronghorn.
In its most recent analysis of the Sublette Pronghorn Herd’s condition, Game and Fish commented: “Now three years after that winter [2022-23], better than average fawn ratios have let this herd start to recover and regain some of the ground that it lost during that winter.” The “ratio” referred to here is the ratio of fawns per 100 doe pronghorns in the herd. In the 2025 report, that ratio was 70 youngsters per 100 does, which is, as the biologists report, a ratio that may well result in more pronghorns in the Sublette Herd, assuming there isn’t another killer winter in our immediate future.
But the description of this ratio as “better than average” bothered me a little. I spent 30 years looking over the shoulder of the biologists who literally risk their lives collecting data on Wyoming’s big game herds, and the idea that 70 fawns per 100 doe pronghorns was “better than average” strikes me as more than a little myopic. This would be nothing more than a quibble among professionals — except that the fawn-doe ratio reflects a lot of ecological, physiological, meteorological and geographic variables that are particularly critical to the well-being of pronghorns. When the ratio is low, it whispers of management problems that have little or nothing to do with the length of a hunting season or the number of permits issued.
The winter of 2022-2023 was a classic example of the effect weather can have on a pronghorn herd. It was exceptionally long, exceptionally cold and exceptionally snowy. Pronghorns lose weight during the winter, even a mild one. How many survive depends largely on the amount of fat they have when the first storm hits, how much forage they can find to augment their fat stores and the amount of energy they lose to the cold as they look for that forage. 
The colder it gets and the longer the cold lasts, the more energy they need. The more energy they burn finding forage, the less they have to keep warm. In 2022-2023, nearly half the adult pronghorns in the Sublette Herd lost more energy than the combination of forage and fat could furnish — those animals died.
There is a lingering side effect to the winter energy audit. Pronghorns mate in September and early October, which means that does are carrying the next generation through the winter. In the most extreme winters, some does will resorb their growing embryos in a desperate attempt to survive. The does that deliver their young the next spring may not be able to produce enough milk to support the newborns, and the newborns themselves may be unusually small and weak. The fawn-doe ratio drops after a bad winter, reflecting the loss of reproductive potential.
Historically, there has often been a tiny silver lining in the black cloud of a killer winter. Deep snow and extended cold often result in a wet spring, which brings a smorgasbord of forage for the pronghorns that have survived. In addition, there is less competition for that forage since a large part of the herd has been erased. The bountiful supply of groceries allows adult does to fatten up for the fall rut, and the stored fat helps them survive the winter with their fawns safe in the womb and well-nourished with milk after birth the following spring.
In such years, nearly every doe will bear twins. Biologists who have watched pronghorn populations recover after a bad winter call it “the bounce,” an increase in population almost as startling as the reproductive potential in a population of rabbits. 
The winter of 1983-1984 was one of the epic killers of the last century. The population estimate for the Sublette pronghorn herd dropped by more than 13,000 animals after that winter. The fawn-doe ratio in the fall of 1983 was 72:100. In the fall of 1984, it dropped to 52:100 because the does in the herd were in such poor condition coming out of the winter. A year later, the ratio rose to 72:100. In 1986, it climbed again to 84:100. In 1987, it hit 90:100. The bounce.
The veteran biologists who have followed the ups and downs of Wyoming’s pronghorn population for decades and documented these meteoric recoveries are expressing concern these days. 
“The bounce,” they say, is gone.
Editor’s note: This is the first in a two-part look at the Sublette Pronghorn Herd. Check back tomorrow for Part 2.
