title: Idaho treasurer candidates have differing state investment mindsets
description: Two candidates will vie for the position to manage Idaho’s cash flow and investments, and they offer differing views on how to do so.  Incumbent Republican Treasurer Julie Ellsworth will face Democratic challenger Kevin Jones in the Nov. 3 general election. Jones, although running as a Democrat, believes the position should be nonpartisan and has […]
text:
Idaho State Treasurer Julie Ellsworth, left, and Democratic challenger Kevin Jones. (Photos courtesy of candidates) Two candidates will vie for the position to manage Idaho’s cash flow and investments, and they offer differing views on how to do so. 
Incumbent Republican Treasurer Julie Ellsworth will face Democratic challenger Kevin Jones in the Nov. 3 general election. Jones, although running as a Democrat, believes the position should be nonpartisan and has announced he will unaffiliated the day after the election. 
[Voter Guide: 2026 primary election Voter Guide: Dates to know, how-to instructions and candidate surveys for Idaho’s top contested primaries.]
The treasurer’s office serves as the state’s chief financial officer — which includes overseeing the receipt of state money, accounting for disbursement of funds, investing idle state money, and administering the unclaimed property program, the 529 College Savings Fund, and the Idaho ABLE savings accounts. 
Each of the candidates are focused on the state’s investment strategy, but with different approaches and metrics for success. 
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
 Who are the candidates seeking office for Idaho treasurer? 

Jones, 63, said he is running to improve the state’s investment yields and said his background better suits him to the job. He previously ran Boise-based Harmonic Investment Advisors. He is a longtime institutional portfolio manager and a chartered financial analyst, which is an internationally recognized professional certification for advanced investment management and financial analysis, he said.
“I’m a very logical individual, and I’m also a former college golfer, so I’ve spent my entire life competing, where numbers matter more than how someone dresses, what party they’re in, and so forth,” Jones said. “… You either post the score on the golf course, or you don’t. You either do well at managing investment portfolios, or you don’t.”
Idaho’s 2026 election voter pamphlet is coming to a mailbox near you

Ellsworth, 64, was first elected as state treasurer in 2018 after serving 12 years non-consecutively as an Idaho state representative. She has been a public school teacher, and a mediator and business consultant. She said she wants to run again because her work has helped the state. 
“I think I’m doing a good job, and I can see that it elevates Idahoans,” Ellsworth said. “It’s very uplifting. The main focus of my job is to assure that money is safe in the state of Idaho, that it is collected in a uniform manner. … and then when money is going to be spent but is idle at the time, we invest it. And I love turning money back to Idaho taxpayers.”
 How would the candidates manage Idaho investments? 

When the state has funds that aren’t yet ready to be spent, the treasurer’s office can invest the money to try and grow the fund until it’s ready to be spent. The Treasurer Investment Advisory Board reviews policies and performance of funds, and private firms that contract with the state help oversee investments with the treasurer. 
Jones said the state’s portfolios have been underperforming. He highlighted recent reports from the investment advisory board showing state funds, such as the IDLE fund, producing total returns less than a comparable index fund. An index fund tracks performance of a certain index — or group of investments that often have something in common — and tries to mimic it through buying a representative sample of stocks and bonds in that index. 
The state’s IDLE fund is used to balance cash flow and is used to ensure there is adequate money for state appropriation. Money that isn’t being spent right away can be invested “at the best rate possible at the safest level of risk,” according to the treasurer’s website. 
That fund has returned .34% less than a comparable index fund since its inception, according to an Aug. 13 Treasurer’s Investment Advisory Board presentation. Jones argued the professionally managed funds should always outperform the index. 
“The performance of our investment portfolios has been, in my personal opinion, almost the worst I’ve seen in 38 years of managing institutional portfolios,” Jones said. 
He said he managed retirement accounts for the state Public Employees Retirement System of Idaho, known as PERSI; the LA County Employees Retirement Association; and the California power utility Pacific Gas & Electric Gas. He’s also managed stock mutual funds for large companies such as Merrill Lynch and J.P. Morgan. 
Jones said his experience would lend itself well to the job. 
“I’ve been managing investment portfolios my entire life. I love it,” Jones said. “It’s a passion of mine, and I don’t believe that the state of Idaho should have someone who’s unqualified in the position of treasurer.” 
Ellsworth said she became interested in the position after working on state laws regarding investments as a legislator in the late 1990s. She countered her opponent’s claims that the funds were underperforming by noting that state law only permits certain investments, and anything not expressly allowed is prohibited.
“We’re not out to make money,” Ellsworth said. “My first goal is safety … I have my investment division that is investing money that will roll off in time to make the school payment in August. So it’s really an art, and the fact that you can make money because of the timing of your investments is really amazing. So I disagree with his portrayal. He’s not aware of statutes that limit us, and all the funds.”
She noted that a report from the investment advisory board compared Idaho’s distribution yield and found it was comparable or outpaced other states that face similar restrictions. She said there is a governor-appointed adviser that provides quarterly reviews of portfolios and she has a personal adviser to her office to help oversee the funds. 
“I would never say that my knowledge would supplant this mechanism,” Ellsworth said. 
How will the candidates handle challenges with state financial software Luma?  
In 2023, the Idaho Controller’s Office launched Luma, a new financial and business management software, replacing old systems dating back to the late 1980s. The Legislature authorized the creation of the new system in 2018 through House Bill 493. 
The launch created a number of financial reporting errors and challenges, including the delaying interest payments to state agencies in 2024 because the treasurer’s office couldn’t verify fund balances with the software, the Idaho Capital Sun reported at the time. 
League of Women Voters of Idaho announces candidate forums for state’s governor, US Senate races

Ellsworth said her office is still verifying all the numbers from 2023, but has since implemented ways to ensure ongoing statements were verified. 
Luma did not provide a way to verify the accuracy of financial statements between the treasurer’s office, the controller’s office and the bank. She has hired outside auditors to manually perform that verification process.
Ellsworth said she’s been working closely with the Controller Brandon Woolf’s office, and said she feels confident a reconciliation process will be in place by November. 
Jones said he was unconcerned by the challenges with Luma. 
“It does not affect the decision-making process and in managing the portfolios,” he said. “It doesn’t influence the decision-making process as it relates to debt.” 
He said with any hurdle that came up with reporting, he could call the banks where the funds were held. 
 Jones says treasurer’s office should be nonpartisan 

Jones said he’s running as a Democrat because he saw it as his best chance at winning the race. He previously filed to run as a Republican for the 2018 election, but withdrew to focus on his health after a heart attack. 
At the time, he thought Ellsworth’s Republican primary opponent, Tom Kealey, was the more qualified person for the job. 
“I saw what had happened back in 2018 when Ms. Ellsworth had beat Mr. Kealey in that closed primary, I realized that there are probably some underpinnings to the Republican Party that I don’t understand that resulted in her being able to beat him,” he said. 
Jones filed to run as a Democrat this election cycle, but said that party affiliation “doesn’t construe anything about the individual.” 
On Nov. 4, he plans to disaffiliate from either party and become an independent. 
“In fact, it may happen at 12:01 (a.m.). I’m so disgusted with all this,” he said. 
Ellsworth noted in a text message that the treasurer position was established in the Idaho Constitution. Under Idaho Law, the statewide constitutional officers are partisan positions.
“I respect that structure and remain focused on carrying out the responsibilities Idaho voters elected me to perform,” Ellsworth said.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Beale Street businesses ride out Memphis law enforcement surge
description: A year after a coalition of law enforcement agencies converged on Memphis, conducting widespread traffic stops and roundups, Beale Street businesses are struggling to stay afloat as customers avoid the historic downtown area. Although several factors are believed to be involved in the slowdown, some local leaders say the Tennessee National Guard’s deployment[...]
text:
A September Friday afternoon on a deserted Beale Street in Memphis: business owners say traffic is down, in part due to the influence of the Memphis Safe Task Force. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)A year after a coalition of law enforcement agencies converged on Memphis, conducting widespread traffic stops and roundups, Beale Street businesses are struggling to stay afloat as customers avoid the historic downtown area.
Although several factors are believed to be involved in the slowdown, some local leaders say the Tennessee National Guard’s deployment is part of the problem, while others believe the military presence is helping quell crime. 
“Downtown is a different place,” Memphis City Councilman J. Smiley says, and businesses are “taking a beating” until Memphis leaders can figure out a survival strategy.
As part of the Memphis Safe Task Force ordered by President Donald Trump to suppress street crime, Gov. Bill Lee deployed the Tennessee National Guard to the city in September 2025. 
Troops have spent a good deal of their time patrolling Beale Street, and although supporters of the surge say it has cut crime dramatically, Memphis’ most popular spot for tourism and local activities has become a ghost town as a result.
Smiley, a member of the Downtown Neighborhood Association who joined a failed lawsuit to stop the National Guard deployment, says people are inclined to move to different locations such as Midtown Memphis instead of visiting Beale Street because they feel they’re being “occupied.”
A. Schwab Dry Goods Store and Soda Fountain, a Beale Street institution, sits empty on Friday, Sept. 11, 2026. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)Formerly busy tourist destination Beale Street in Memphis has taken a hit over the last year or so, business owners say. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)
“If you think the National Guard and task force is going to be there, you go somewhere else,” Smiley told the Lookout.
At least two business fronts have shut down since the task force entered the city, including Coyote Ugly and one Ghost Rivers brewery location that merged with another one. The old Daisy Theatre is undergoing renovation after a fire.
Withers Collection Museum and Gallery, which documents Memphis’ civil rights and music history, has been in a “slump” for a year after rebounding from the COVID pandemic, according to curator Joe Calhoun.
Shootings near Beale Street were already keeping locals away. But when the task force and National Guard troops showed up, things didn’t turn around, he says.
“When you have a convention that’s coming to a city and they hear the narrative about the National Guard, you’re reluctant to bring your people to a city where you can’t guarantee their safety,” Calhoun says.
Black residents and Hispanic immigrants are also afraid to visit the downtown area in the evenings because of fear of Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents who often station themselves near Memphis’ judicial buildings, he says. 
Joe Calhoun, who operates the Withers Collection Museum on Beale Street, says he is optimistic for a business turnaround in the Memphis downtown area. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)
Calhoun prefers to take an optimistic view, pointing out that even though everyday traffic is down, turnout for scheduled events is good. He hopes that completion of St. Jude Children’s Hospital towers will bring a downtown “turnaround.”
The FedEx Forum where the NBA’s Memphis Grizzlies play is set to undergo a $550 million improvements project, including upgrades to the surrounding neighborhood. New apartments are under construction as well, a block off Beale.
“There is some new life, but it’s just slow moving,” Calhoun says.
At least two Republican lawmakers who represent portions of Shelby County told the Lookout they were unaware Beale Street was going through hard times.



Quotation







I personally have not heard any negative comments about the safe task force, National Guard being there. My personal opinion is we’d be best served if they continue to be there.


– Sen. Paul Rose, R-Collierville


State Rep. Kevin Vaughan of Collierville says he’s not a “regular purveyor” of Beale and couldn’t tell whether traffic is down, but he says constituents tell him they feel safer going into downtown Memphis to dine out and go to shows at the Orpheum.
“They feel as if downtown has been restored to what it was before the crime wave hit,” Vaughan says.
Sen. Paul Rose of Covington, a strong supporter of the task force, says he’s “always concerned about any legitimate business surviving.” But he says the only comments he’s heard come from people who describe how “pleasant it is, how safe they feel.” 
Rose adds that he understands a move is under way to grow business and bring people back to the downtown area.
“I personally have not heard any negative comments about the safe task force, National Guard being there,” he said. “My personal opinion is we’d be best served if they continue to be there.”
Rose called the results of the task force “phenomenal” but could not speculate about how long he feels it should remain in Memphis. 
Task force members have been involved in at least four shooting deaths, as well, including one in which an autopsy showed the victim was shot in the back. The task force claimed the man pulled a gun and was moving toward a National Guard soldier when he was shot.

title: Alabama Public Television survey shows majority support for continuing PBS affiliation
description: HUNTSVILLE — After nearly a year of discussion among the governing body for Alabama Public Television to drop Public Broadcast Service programming, a survey released Tuesday showed majority support from the public to continue its affiliation with PBS. The survey — conducted by Cygnal, a Republican-aligned polling firm that has worked with U.S. Sen. Tommy […]
text:
Rep. Marilyn Lands, D-Huntsville, speaks before the Alabama Educational Television Foundation Authority in Huntsville on Sept. 29 in support of maintaining Alabama Public Television's affiliation with PBS. (Ben Sessoms for Alabama Reflector)HUNTSVILLE — After nearly a year of discussion among the governing body for Alabama Public Television to drop Public Broadcast Service programming, a survey released Tuesday showed majority support from the public to continue its affiliation with PBS.
The survey — conducted by Cygnal, a Republican-aligned polling firm that has worked with U.S. Sen. Tommy Tuberville’s gubernatorial campaign, at a cost of $39,500 through APT’s emergency fund — found that 54% support maintaining PBS programming; 18% were against, and 28% were unsure.
The results were released after a push from some members of the governing body, the Alabama Educational Television Foundation Authority, for disaffiliation. Last year, commissioners Les Barnett and Ferris Stephens floated the idea after congressional Republicans cut $1.1 billion from the Corporation for Public Broadcasting.
Previously, 330 PBS and 246 NPR affiliates across the country had relied on that funding. Those stations have turned to fund drives and other philanthropic efforts to continue operating.
At an AETFA meeting last October, Barnett said his opposition to PBS programming wasn’t necessarily a matter of funding, but due to the public network’s alleged political bias. 
“PBS has made themselves an atma to the president and a sizable chunk of the state legislature, and probably a sizable chunk of the 65% of people who voted for Trump, and I’m one of those people in both categories,” he said. “I just, I don’t want to fund it, PBS has made themselves the enemy of what I stand with, and so I do not like them. I don’t follow the philosophy of feeding the beast.”
But the survey found that 62% said they wanted officials to stay out of programming decisions, versus 16% who supported such conduct.
In addition, 48% said tying funding to whether or not politicians approved of the content gives them too much power; 23% were for elected officials restricting public dollars in this way.
At an AETFA meeting in Huntsville on Tuesday, commissioners announced the public release of the survey but took no action based on its results. The authority’s next meeting is scheduled for Feb. 2.
Public pushback
As with other AETFA meetings over the past year, dozens turned out on Tuesday to oppose Alabama Public Television disaffilating with PBS. In Huntsville, local public radio station WLRH ended its NPR affiliation last year following the congressional cuts to CPB.
Many in attendance criticized that decision being made without public input, including Rep. Marilyn Lands, D-Huntsville.
“In 2025, after federal funding through the Corporation for Public Broadcasting disappeared, this commission and its chosen management made a unilateral decision to disaffiliate from NPR and impose a new hyperlocal format,” Lands said during Tuesday’s public comment period. “That decision was made without input from the community, without input from long-term station staff, and without input from the donors who had sustained this station for decades.”
Stephens, the chair of the commission, attempted to only allow those in attendance to speak if they had not made comments during prior meetings. After pushback from the audience, all 24 who signed up for public comment on Tuesday were allowed to speak. The meeting lasted well over an hour.
“I urge this commission to remember who you serve, all of the people of Alabama,” said Pam Caruso, a Huntsville resident who spoke in support of PBS programming and reinstating NPR to the local radio station. “Protect WLRH, protect PBS and protect the principle that citizens in a democratic society should be trusted with information and trusted to think for themselves.”
For some on the commission, the issue taken with PBS and NPR was a perceived lack of balance and fair reporting among their coverage.
“Obviously there’s a quantum divide here fed by all the algorithms on the social media that have caused us to get to the point where it’s almost like the North and the South back in the Civil War. It’s like you can’t talk to each other,” said Commissioner Bebe Williams. “I love the PBS kids. I love so much of the programming, and I don’t want to get rid of it, nor have I ever wanted to get rid of it. I wanted a balance. And I know how many people say News Hour is balanced, but the conservatives I talked to, they can’t handle it.”
At times throughout the meeting, especially when commissioners suggested NPR and PBS programming lacked balance or illustrated bias, Stephens hit his gavel to control what he called “outbursts.”
Only two people among about the 40 in attendance when asked raised their hands to say they backed the decision to disaffiliate from NPR, both of whom echoed concerns over perceived anti-conservative bias.
Most others in attendance viewed the commission as acting to block off information, not create political balance.
“Sadly for some, facts are seen as having a liberal bias,” said Susan Stewart, a resident who spoke during public comment. “I want to support WLRH, but I just can’t at this time without supporting what amounts to censorship.”

title: Arkansas Explained: How to register to vote in the midterms
description: In just under five weeks, Arkansans will have the opportunity to cast their vote for municipal, state and federal offices during the midterm elections.  Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders and U.S. Sen. Tom Cotton are seeking reelection, as are all four of Arkansas’ congressmen. The six Republicans all have challengers for their seats. More than 1.8 […]
text:
"I Voted" stickers sit next to a voting tabulator at the Pulaski County Regional Building on Thursday, Feb. 26, 2026 (Photo by Andrew DeMillo/Arkansas Advocate)In just under five weeks, Arkansans will have the opportunity to cast their vote for municipal, state and federal offices during the midterm elections. 
Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders and U.S. Sen. Tom Cotton are seeking reelection, as are all four of Arkansas’ congressmen. The six Republicans all have challengers for their seats.
More than 1.8 million Arkansans are registered to vote, according to the secretary of state’s office, and there’s still time for more to register ahead of the Oct. 5 deadline. 
Here’s what you need to know about registering to vote in the Nov. 3 election:
How do I know if I’m already registered to vote?
You can check your voter registration, view sample ballots and find polling locations here. 
How do I register to vote?
Voter Guide: 2026 General Election

You must fill out and submit a paper voter registration application by Oct. 5. Arkansans cannot register to vote online.
You can obtain a form from your local county clerk, revenue office, Department of Motor Vehicles office, public library, disability agency, military recruitment office or the Arkansas secretary of state elections division.
You can also request a form through the mail or print a form here. Applications are available in English or Spanish.
How do I know if I’m eligible to vote?
To register to vote, you must be a U.S. citizen, an Arkansas resident and at least 18 years old or turn 18 on or before the next election.
You can’t be a convicted felon whose sentence has not been discharged or pardoned. You also can’t be deemed “mentally incompetent as to your ability to vote by a court of competent jurisdiction,” according to the secretary of state’s office.
What documentation do I need to register to vote?
You need to provide your driver’s license number or the last four digits of your Social Security number on your application. 
If you don’t possess either a driver’s license or Social Security number, you can select the option indicating that on your application.
Do I need to register with a political party to vote in the midterms?
No.
Democrats see rare signs of hope in solidly red Arkansas’ midterms

The majority of Arkansans are not registered with a political party. Approximately 1.6 million Arkansans are registered as “Party Optional,” according to the secretary of state’s office. 
Nearly 85,000 voters are registered Democrats and more than 154,000 are registered Republicans. As of Friday, there were 754 voters registered with the Libertarian Party and 124 voters registered with the Green Party.
How do I know when I’m registered to vote?
Your local county clerk will send you a personalized voter registration card once your application is processed, and it could take several weeks. 
Arkansans should not assume they’re registered until they’ve received their voter registration card, according to the secretary of state’s office. 
You can check on your application’s status by calling your local county clerk or visiting www.voterview.org.  
Once I’m registered, when can I vote?
Early voting runs Oct. 19 through Nov. 2. Election Day is Nov. 3.
During early voting, polls are open from  8 a.m. and 6 p.m. Monday through Friday and from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. on Saturday. Early voting ends at 5 p.m. on the Monday prior to the election. 
On Election Day, polls are open from 7:30 a.m. to 7:30 p.m. You will be allowed to vote as long as you are in line by 7:30 p.m. 
More information about the election is available on the Advocate’s 2026 Voter Guide.

description: A federal court ruled in favor of Metro Nashville and five other cities and counties, striking down the Trump administration’s effort to withhold anti-terrorism funds unless they adopted election-system policies targeting to check citizenship. The Monday ruling by U.S. District Court Judge Amir Ali in the District of Columbia vacated conditions placed on ele[...]
text:
A federal judge sided with Nashville in a case against the Trump administration for threatening to withhold counterterrorism funds. Pictured: Metro Nashville Courthouse. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)A federal court ruled in favor of Metro Nashville and five other cities and counties, striking down the Trump administration’s effort to withhold anti-terrorism funds unless they adopted election-system policies targeting to check citizenship.
The Monday ruling by U.S. District Court Judge Amir Ali in the District of Columbia vacated conditions placed on election offices requiring that they enact multiple voting requirements or face an order by the Federal Emergency Management Agency holding back 20% of grant funds to counter terrorism, a program enacted 25 years ago in the wake of 9/11.
The local governments, which are represented by Protect Democracy, sued the Trump administration, saying the Department of Homeland Security was “holding public safety funding hostage” to “coerce” states and local governments to adopt policies the administration has failed to impose in court.
Metro Nashville joins lawsuit claiming feds withheld millions

In the ruling, Amir wrote, “[T]he statute gives FEMA the authority to fund projects proposed by states and high-risk urban areas; it does not give FEMA authority to use the possibility of grants to induce states or high-risk urban areas to carry out the federal government’s preferred projects at their own expense.”
Metro Nashville and the five other local governments said states were to be required to use DHS’s “notoriously error-filled” Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements (SAVE) system to “verify” citizenship for all pollworkers and registered voters, putting higher and “impractical” costs on electronic voting systems, and charging a 5% manual paper-ballot audit.
Metro Nashville Law Director Tyler Yarbro said Nashville doesn’t need Washington “dictating” the terms for elections in exchange for public safety funding. The ruling “demonstrates the necessity of the checks and balances the Trump administration is actively trying to eliminate,” she said.
Metro Nashville was joined in the lawsuit by Columbus, Ohio and four Texas counties, El Paso, Harris, Dallas and Travis counties.

title: After weeks of limbo, federal government now distributing COVID vaccines to low-income kids
description: The federal government has begun supplying COVID-19 vaccines to states, including Tennessee, to be used as part of a free immunization program for low-income children, a spokesperson for the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services confirmed Tuesday. The question of when — and whether — the federal government would make the vaccines available through […]
text:
After weeks of uncertainty, the federal government has begun distributing COVID-19 vaccines to states for the Vaccines for Children program, which provides free immunizations for low-income and uninsured kids. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)The federal government has begun supplying COVID-19 vaccines to states, including Tennessee, to be used as part of a free immunization program for low-income children, a spokesperson for the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services confirmed Tuesday.
The question of when — and whether — the federal government would make the vaccines available through the free program had remained in limbo for weeks, raising alarm among Tennessee health providers who typically begin offering the vaccines in September ahead of the fall respiratory illness season. 
COVID vaccines for uninsured Tennessee kids in limbo amid federal delays

About half of all children in the United States receive all or most of their vaccines, including standard childhood immunizations, COVID and flu, through the Center for Disease Control and Prevention’s Vaccines for Children Program, which distributes vaccines to state health departments around the nation to immunize low-income and uninsured kids.
In Tennessee, more than 5,000 children received the COVID vaccine through the program last year, according to a Tennessee Department spokesperson. The vaccines are administered to children at public health clinics in all 95 counties and through participating clinics and doctors’ offices.
The U.S. Food and Drug Administration approved 2026-2027 COVID vaccines in August, and they became almost immediately available to those with commercial insurance. A lag time in between when the vaccines are made available to those with private insurance and when they are made available through the Vaccines for Children program is not uncomment, but public comments made earlier this month by federal health officials contributed to uncertainty about whether they would be available this year at all through the program.

 Catching Our Eye

• Ohio farmers. WOSU’s Allie Vugrincic reports, “Ohio farmers feel the squeeze of diesel, fertilizer prices. Will that affect how they vote?”
Diesel fuel prices have been climbing since February, when the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran, and hit a record high this month. Chemical fertilizer that comes from the Middle East has faced supply chain disruptions, leading to higher prices.
Meanwhile, the costs of many other products needed for farming have gone up because of President Donald Trump’s tariffs…
A national Associated Press–KFF poll released last week found rural voters are “deeply unhappy” about the economy. However, while Trump’s standing among those voters has slipped a little, he still has a 48% approval rating — noticeably higher than Trump’s 33% approval rating among all U.S. adults.
• Paying for the gas tax holiday? Cleveland.com’s Jeremy Pelzer reports, “Ohio lawmakers overhaul Ramaswamy’s plan to pay for a state gas-tax holiday.”
Ohio lawmakers introduced legislation Monday to suspend the state’s gas tax for 90 days, using $726 million from the state’s anticipated general revenue surplus to cover what would otherwise be a massive financial hit to state and local transportation projects.
Senate Bill 475, which Republican legislative leaders intend to pass Wednesday at the behest of GOP gubernatorial nominee Vivek Ramaswamy, abandons parts of Ramaswamy’s original plan that Gov. Mike DeWine criticized, including potentially paying for the gas-tax holiday by tapping the Ohio Department of Transportation’s cash reserves and, if needed, the state’s $4 billion rainy-day fund.
• Dwindling international students in Ohio. Signal Ohio’s Amy Morona reports, “Ohio colleges enroll fewer international students — again.”
Ohio’s universities are experiencing double-digit drops in international enrollment as these students – and the campuses enrolling them – continue to comply with changing policies from the Trump administration.
Case Western Reserve University, the University of Cincinnati, Cleveland State University, Kent State University and Ohio State University report drops in international student enrollment ranging from 11% to 32.5% this fall, according to publicly available data and information provided to Signal Statewide.
• Censoring criticism of anti-trans ads? The Buckeye Flame’s Ken Schneck reports, “Insiders say the Ohio Democratic Party is censoring criticism of anti-trans ads.”
Ohio Democrats are accusing their own party leadership of removing social media posts that pushed back on anti-trans ads released by Democratic Rep. Marcy Kaptur, who is running for re-election in the 9th Congressional District in Northwest Ohio.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: WV Drug Czar Loyd resigns from Morrisey administration after leading state’s opioid response
description: West Virginia Drug Czar Dr. Stephen Loyd has resigned from his role after about two years on the job, he confirmed to West Virginia Watch Tuesday. “I’m heartbroken,” Loyd said of leaving the role earlier this month.  Loyd, an internal medicine and addiction medicine physician from Tennessee, was appointed by former Gov. Jim Justice to […]
text:
Dr. Stephen Loyd speaks to lawmakers at the State Capitol in Charleston, West Virginia, in August 2026 while serving as the director of the state’s Office of Drug Control Policy. (Photo by Will Price/West Virginia Legislative Photography)West Virginia Drug Czar Dr. Stephen Loyd has resigned from his role after about two years on the job, he confirmed to West Virginia Watch Tuesday.
“I’m heartbroken,” Loyd said of leaving the role earlier this month. 
Loyd, an internal medicine and addiction medicine physician from Tennessee, was appointed by former Gov. Jim Justice to be director of the state’s Office of Drug Control Policy in August 2024. He was the eighth person in the role of state drug czar since the position was created in April 2017. 
His is the latest in a handful of high-profile departures for Gov. Patrick Morrisey’s administration. Tourism Secretary Chelsea Ruby resigned in July after five years in the role. Earlier this year, state Human Services Secretary Alex Mayer resigned from his position after about a year on the job.
Sen. Tom Takubo, R-Kanawha. (Photo by Will Price/West Virginia Legislative Photography)
Sen. Tom Takubo, R-Kanawha, who is a physician, told West Virginia Watch it’s “devastating” that Loyd is no longer in the role. He said Loyd is a national expert who loved and cared deeply about the work he was doing in the state. 
“I am concerned that this was a preventable exit,” Takubo said. “My concern is that there wasn’t enough focus from the administration as to how important the substance abuse and drug epidemic is in West Virginia and the incredible work that Dr. Loyd was performing.”
West Virginia continues to lead the nation in drug overdose deaths, though the number of fatalities has declined under Loyd’s tenure. 
Loyd said Tuesday that in the year and a half he worked for Morrisey, he did not speak to the governor aside from through a text message around the time he resigned. 
“I don’t have any idea what the policy of the administration was,” he said. “I tried to find out.”
Loyd said he was required to report to Human Services Secretary Carl Ayers after Ayers was appointed in July, despite that according to state code, the drug control policy director reports directly to the governor. 
“I would have never taken a job to come to report to somebody else,” Loyd said. “I’m 60 years old. I’m not at that point in my career, and that can sound like it wants to. I really don’t care. 
“I came to work for Gov. Justice, and then when Gov. Morrisey won, I came to work with Gov. Morrisey. I was ready to, you know, to (do) whatever, you know, what policy he wanted to pursue, I’m the guy, and I still don’t know what that is, even now.”
He added that he has no ill will toward Ayers. 
“I’m not trying to impugn anybody. That’s not my goal,” he said. “I’m not upset at any of that, I’m upset because of the people that I left that I love.”
Loyd said being the state’s director of drug control policy was his favorite job he’s ever had.
Last month, he highlighted to lawmakers a 41.6% decline in overdose deaths from pre-pandemic levels. Loyd credited improvement to a range of policies, including overdose response policies and widespread use of naloxone, a medicine used to reverse an opioid overdose.
In a statement through a spokesperson, Morrisey said Tuesday “We wish Dr. Loyd well and thank him for his service and many contributions to the Mountain State.”
Loyd said he’s now working with the Trump administration on the Great American Recovery Initiative, a program established by executive order earlier this year and led by U.S. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and Kathryn Burgum, the White House’s Senior Advisor for Addiction recovery. 
“There’s so much of what we’ve done in West Virginia by the folks that I just mentioned that I think are scalable, I think that other states can benefit from,” he said. “And, you know, to me, that’s the part I’m going to keep working on.
“I’m not leaving my folks behind,” he said. “I love them. I just wished I was still in the role I was in, and I wish, you know, I had had direction, and you know, and relationship with some of the funding mechanisms within the state, mainly the First Foundation.”
Loyd — who earned his medical degree from East Tennessee State University — was previously the chief medical officer at Cedar Recovery in Mount Juliet, Tennessee, and he was chair of the state’s Opioid Abatement Council. Before that, he served as Tennessee’s top drug policy expert, holding the position of opioid czar for the state’s Department of Mental Health and Substance Use for about two years. 
He previously worked as a voluntary co-chair of The Helios Alliance, an Alabama-based organization that is using “innovative, transformative (and) evidence-based technologies” to confront the opioid epidemic while educating the public on interventions.
Loyd also has lived experience with substance abuse. He has been in recovery from opioid and benzodiazepine addiction for more than 20 years and is the inspiration for Michael Keaton’s character in the Hulu limited series “Dopesick” (based on the 2018 book of the same name by journalist Beth Macy).
“So much of this is about leadership and direction, and Dr. Loyd is very revolutionary in that oftentimes the country will follow his lead, not just the state of West Virginia,” Takubo said. He added that he had personally attended meetings in D.C. with the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Agency and other states. 
“Many of these states are throughout Appalachia that have very similar issues with the epidemic, and I can say firsthand that all of those states would lean on Dr. Loyd for guidance and help,” Takubo said. “He brought an incredible amount of expertise, experience and leadership to the state of West Virginia, which is going to create a massive void in his absence. I only hope that we are as successful in finding a successor as we did in Stephen Loyd.”

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Arkansas governor hopefuls focus on health, education, prisons
description: Republican Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders, Democratic state Sen. Fred Love and Libertarian Colt Shelby said they would address affordability, healthcare, education and the state’s prison system if elected governor, but differ in their strategies.  Lowering taxes “at a time when people are struggling to make ends meet,” is a top priority for Sanders, the former[...]
text:
Republican Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders, Democratic state Sen. Fred Love and Libertarian Colt Shelby are running for Arkansas governor in the 2026 general election. (Photos courtesy of the Arkansas secretary of state's office)Republican Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders, Democratic state Sen. Fred Love and Libertarian Colt Shelby said they would address affordability, healthcare, education and the state’s prison system if elected governor, but differ in their strategies. 
Lowering taxes “at a time when people are struggling to make ends meet,” is a top priority for Sanders, the former White House press secretary for President Donald Trump who was first elected governor in 2022. 
“We don’t want people to have to decide between whether or not they can put gas in their car or groceries on their table,” she said.
Lawmakers approved four rounds of income tax cuts and eliminated the state’s grocery tax during the 44-year-old’s first term. Sanders said she wants to continue “responsibly” phasing out the state’s income tax so people can keep more of their money and spend it how they want. 
Shelby agreed with helping Arkansans save money, and said he would focus on initiatives to help the middle class, such as eliminating the used car sales tax and increasing Arkansas’ standard deduction rate to match the federal rate.
The 42-year-old drill site manager said he also supports proposed legislation that would have provided $2 million in additional turnback funds, state-collected revenue distributed to local governments, to each county. This would give counties more control over what infrastructure they invest in to build up their local economy, he said. 
“It’s not the big government’s job for economic development, that should be up to the lower governments,” Shelby said. “What Arkansas tries to do is control where we put all these things and giving tax abatements, and I’m not for that.”
Love said he would address affordability by ensuring companies recruited to the state through incentives offer affordable wages. 
The 51-year-old term-limited state lawmaker also said it’s important to focus on skilled trades by getting young people involved in these industries and retraining older Arkansans who’ve fallen out of the workforce. 
Love applauded Arkansas’ $11 minimum wage for exceeding several other states’ rates, but said it’s not enough.
“Families are still working twice as hard not to make ends meet, so we need to start investing in jobs that actually are high-paying jobs,” he said. 
Healthcare
Sanders expects healthcare to dominate next year’s legislative session, and said she wants to ensure access to quality affordable care. Conversations are underway about “the best path forward” for Arkansas’ Medicaid expansion program, said Sanders, who has not specified what approach she’d prefer regarding the program’s delivery. 
The state requested a two-year extension after the Trump administration rejected its request to renew the program this summer. Arkansas’ program doesn’t meet a provision in a new federal law that requires it to not cost the federal government more than would be projected without the program.  
Issue Spotlight: Gubernatorial candidates on future of Arkansas’ Medicaid expansion 

The state needs to invest in Medicaid by increasing enrollment, Love said. Arkansas depends heavily on Medicaid, and the state’s healthcare system doesn’t work without it, he said. 
Many rural hospitals have closed or cut back on services due to increasing labor, equipment and administrative costs, and low reimbursement rates. 
Supporting Medicaid helps keep Arkansans healthy and prevents them from going to the hospital when they’re sick, which can be expensive, Love said.
Shelby said he hopes the state’s Medicaid expansion request is granted. He also said it was a “no-brainer” to opt into a federal policy that allows states to extend Medicaid postpartum coverage to 12 months. 
Arkansas is the only state to end postpartum Medicaid coverage at 60 days instead of extending to a year. Sanders has said the coverage isn’t needed because the state has other insurance options for low-income Arkansans.  
Education
Sanders said she’s not walking away from education, a major focus of her first term.
The 2023 LEARNS Act made several changes to the state’s public school system, including raising the minimum teacher salary to $50,000 and creating a school voucher program that allows state funds to be used on certain educational expenses, such as private school tuition. 
The program is open to all K-12 students and has received bipartisan pushback from lawmakers over its growing cost and impact on public schools. 
Love said one of his first acts as governor would be signing an executive order to end the program. Sanders dismissed Love’s vow.
“It’s illegal and so it’s not going to happen,” she said. 
Love vows order halting school vouchers if elected Arkansas governor 

The governor cited improvements in students’ test scores, and questioned why someone would move away from a system that’s working. 
The Arkansas Constitution vests legislative power in the General Assembly.  But Love argued he would have the authority to bypass the Legislature and end the voucher program under Section 6 Article 2 of the Arkansas Constitution, which says the “supreme executive power” of the state is vested in the governor.  
“The Arkansas LEARNS Act is a long-term, detrimental piece of legislation that’s going to end up closing a lot of public school systems if we don’t stop it now,” he said. 
These closures can hurt communities where school districts are the area’s largest employer, Love said.
Shelby said he would scale the program back to have income requirements, noting it’s helped some students access education they couldn’t have afforded otherwise.
Additionally, Shelby wants to restructure the state’s education department to allow for more decisions to be made at the local level instead of the Capitol. He also wants the department to be led by an Arkansas native who knows the state’s public school system. 
“I want to put a lot of emphasis on our public education, and I’m not saying money, I’m saying attention because throwing money at it doesn’t always work,” he said. 
Prison system
Sanders said she still believes Franklin County is the best place to build a new prison to address the state’s overcrowding issues. The project has been put on hold after facing public pushback and challenges with infrastructure and funding. 
However, Sanders said she’s open to other alternatives such as expanding a Little Rock recidivism program and expanding existing prison capacity. The state has opened up 1,500 additional beds at existing facilities and will continue working with the Legislature to expand capacity, she said. 
Issue Spotlight: What Arkansas gubernatorial candidates say about legalizing recreational marijuana

Shelby, who lives in Franklin County, and Love both oppose the prison project.
“Building more prisons is not the answer,” Love said. “We are not going to jail our way to a safer society.”
Love said he would look at the whole system, which he said needs to include a comprehensive plan for helping incarcerated people transition to society after being released, fairly compensating county jails for holding state inmates and increasing bed capacity at the state’s mental health hospital. 
He also highlighted the correlation between literacy and incarceration, and said the state needs to invest in a better childcare system so kids can start learning reading skills early. 
Shelby said he would look at amending the Protect Arkansas Act, the 2023 law signed by Sanders that overhauled the state’s prison system. The law requires the most violent offenders to serve the majority of their sentences, leading to more people in prison.
“The Protect Act’s one of the poorest bills that’s costing us a whole lot of money,” he said. “It’s not keeping anybody safer.”
Shelby said he would support reentry programs, as well as expanding the Calico Rock prison and existing county facilities in areas with high crime.

text:
The Alabama State Board of Education votes to approve a recommendation for social studies textbooks on March 12, 2026.  Board members earlier this month expressed their concerns with virtual school performance. (Andrea Tinker/Alabama Reflector)Members of the Alabama State Board of Education expressed concerns with virtual school performance at a meeting earlier this month.
Under state law, local school systems must provide a pathway for students to graduate with an online education.
But Alabama State School Superintendent Eric Mackey said during a State Board of Education meeting on Sept. 10 that it can be hard to track where students are transferring from to the virtual schools.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“All of them (schools) enroll people statewide. Some of them enroll a lot more people statewide, but all of them enroll people who are, in the law, transfers from another district,” Mackey told board members. “A lot of them we don’t know where they transferred from.”
Board members received a packet during the meeting detailing enrollment numbers for virtual schools in the state. The packet was not made available to the public due to FERPA regulations.
Traci West, a board member representing District 2, said during the meeting that she was concerned about test scores at the virtual schools.
“I absolutely believe… that there are some students that will not be successful in a traditional classroom,” West said. “I am, however, disturbed by the performance of some, not all, particularly now more so.”
This month’s meeting isn’t the first time West mentioned virtual schools. During a July State Board of Education meeting, she raised concerns with test scores at online schools after hearing about a student in her district who moved back to traditional schooling from virtual.
West said in an interview Tuesday afternoon that performance at statewide virtual schools is lower because of the lack of oversight.
“The teachers are not employees of the district, the teachers are employees of the company, so we do not know truly what is being taught and to what standard,” West said. “We know what our standards are as a state board of education, but those teachers are not employed by the state of Alabama.”
There are three statewide virtual schools. Alabama Destinations Career Academy in the Chickasaw City district, Alabama Virtual Academy at Eufaula City Schools in the Eufaula City district and Alabama Connections Academy in the Limestone County district.
Of the schools, Alabama Destinations Career Academy and Alabama Virtual Academy at Eufaula City Schools both received a D on the state report card. Alabama Connections Academy received a C on the state report card.
Messages seeking comment were left with Alabama Destinations Career Academy, Alabama Virtual Academy at Eufaula City Schools and Alabama Connections Academy Tuesday afternoon.
Mackey said under state law “public schools have to teach the public school standards” but the responsibility to enforce those standards for online schools lies with the local boards.
Allen Long, who represents District 7, also had concerns about virtual school performance, noting that some of the lower-performing virtual schools were receiving funding similar to the higher-performing virtual schools.
“It seems to me like somebody needs to let the legislature know that some schools are doing great and some are not,” Long said during the meeting.
A message seeking comment was left with Long Tuesday afternoon.
Mackey said during the September meeting that the “performance is generally lower for virtual schools than non-virtual” and that the department is working to help online schools better prepare students.
“We actually this last year launched a special program to kind of help districts understand how to support their virtual schools because they’re not seeing those people day-to-day, so how do they support those students who are way behind? We’re trying to help them with that,” Mackey said.
West said in the interview that he believes that giving the State Department of Education jurisdiction over the statewide schools could improve performance.
“I think the law could be tightened up to allow for state department oversight,” West said. “I do believe that individual contracts with individual school districts from outside vendors could be tightened up to have some provisions that truly serve the students and not just the profits of the company.”

name: Michigan Advance
title: Michigan secretary of state hopefuls discuss election security, office priorities
description: The five Michigan Secretary of State nominees from across the political spectrum appeared together for a virtual forum Tuesday hosted by the League of Women Voters, parsing questions on election security, battling misinformation and the role of the office in the modern age. Lt. Gov. Garlin Gilchrist and Macomb County Clerk Anthony Forlini, the Democratic […]
text:
Candidates for Michigan Secretary of States participated in an online forum Tuesday, Sept. 29, 2026, conducted by the League of Women Voters of Michigan. (Screenshot)The five Michigan Secretary of State nominees from across the political spectrum appeared together for a virtual forum Tuesday hosted by the League of Women Voters, parsing questions on election security, battling misinformation and the role of the office in the modern age.
Lt. Gov. Garlin Gilchrist and Macomb County Clerk Anthony Forlini, the Democratic Party and Republican Party nominees, were joined by their counterparts nominated by the minor-party candidates, including the Green Party’s Eric Borregard, the Libertarian Party’s Christine Sloan and the U.S. Taxpayers Party’s Scott Aughney.
Questions included the nominees’ views on the secretary’s role, the steps they would take in their first year if elected and their philosophies on maintaining safe and secure elections. Questions about misinformation, and how to combat it, also cropped up, which detailed how the ideologically diverse panel would take the office in different directions.
Here’s how each of the nominees tackled those questions, with responses edited for clarity and space.
 
What would be your priorities as secretary and what specific steps would you take to enact them?
Gilchrist said he sees the role’s first and foremost goal as protecting voters and their data, and that means standing up to President Donald Trump and refusing to hand over election-related data to the federal government. He added that his administration would make it a policy and a practice not to provide voter data and information in cases of what he considers apparent federal government overreach.
Forlini said that election integrity would be top of mind for his administration, and that his first year would focus on making elections believable again. He said he would examine election processes that he deemed as archaic and shed light on local clerks’ Election Day protocols and make them viewable to the public.
Borregard said he would like to address voter apathy, and would push to reduce the state’s voting age to 17, or as low as 16. He said that would create a powerful new voting bloc that could stand up to corporate interests in politics and fight back against a new “social dystopia.”
Sloan said she would work to remove Michigan from its involvement with the Electronic Registration Information Center, or ERIC, a nonprofit organization composed of state election officials that helps states maintain accurate voter rolls and identify potential instances of illegal voting. She would also embark on an audit of the state’s voter rolls and look into chain of custody issues raised by election skeptics over the past decade.
Aughney said that, in his view, the practices and processes implemented by current Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson do not currently comply with state statute — an opinion he said he formed by investigating those processes over the last six years. Aughney was convinced that those processes need to be changed to comply with the U.S. and Michigan constitutions.
 
How would you maintain safe and secure elections?
Clerks do the hard work of election administration because they believe in it, Gilchrist said. The lieutenant governor said that he sees his role in securing elections as being a shield between clerks and attacks against them, as election-denier conspiracy theories have led to threats of violence toward public officials. He would also bolster communication lines so that threats can be relayed quickly and so the office can respond to those threats swiftly.
As one of those clerks, Forlini said he did his best to listen to election skeptics’ complaints and concerns, while also pushing back against unfounded claims. Forlini said he made sure those with concerns were heard while also maintaining the laws governing elections. The Macomb clerk added that he has had ongoing meetings with local sheriffs and residents alike to make sure that everyone knew their rights before the Nov. 3 election — whether they were law enforcement, voters or election observers.
For Borregard, concerns about election integrity and the need for tighter security were overblown, and he would advocate for processes or measures that further expand the freedom to vote — and against policies that would close it off. Borregard also said that he would lower the threshold of what counts as proper identification, including allowing student IDs or utility bills.
Sloan said she would also partner with local sheriffs’ offices as a way to fast-track reporting of threats and concerns, taking cues from both Gilchrist and Forlini. However, Sloan disagreed with Borregard by adding that the public has legitimate concerns about the integrity of the state’s elections, its processes and how the office verifies the results of elections big and small.
Aughney proposed taking the state away from electronic voting systems and ending the use of electronic pollbooks. He would, instead, return the state to a manual hand count of votes.
 
How would you make sure rural residents and those with difficulties getting online can access services?
As a computer systems expert, Gilchrist said that work was dear to him and that he’s seen firsthand the struggle of communities lacking internet connectivity. Gilchrist said it would be important for the Department of State to bring as many services to those individuals instead of having to drive out to distant Secretary of State offices.
Forlini said he’s held forums with rural clerks to hear their concerns, and those meetings have led him to believe that the current system for service deployment took a one-size-fits-all approach that needed to be tailored to individual community needs. He also advocated for reducing wait times even further than Benson had during her tenure. In Macomb, Forlini said he was able to get 20-minute wait times down to 10 minutes “out the door.”
The state needs more Secretary of State offices and workers, Borregard said, while advocating for the state to stop spending money on complex computer systems, software or on large corporations that contract out voting equipment. While the question focused on bringing services to rural and low-connectivity residents, he said that clerks should be given time to tally the state’s elections and that residents didn’t need to know the results right away. Borregard said they should be able to take until the next morning to report results, or a week or two if necessary.
Expanding services to rural areas was worth considering, Sloan said, as well as adding more self-service stations across the state that expanded during Benson’s tenure. As a Libertarian, Sloan also said she viewed annual vehicle registration renewals as a hidden tax, and she would partner with the Legislature to institute a one-time registration fee that did not have to be renewed annually.
Aughney said he prefers humans to computers even though he has a fascination with computer systems. He said he would look at the state’s budget in any given year to see if the department had the resources to reopen closed Secretary of State offices, noting that Jackson had seen a decrease in the number of available locations. Aughney also called on all of the department’s public-facing offices to not reject walk-in appointments in favor of pre-scheduled visits.
 
How would you balance data privacy with the government’s need for maintaining and reviewing vital records?
Gilchrist said he would only share voter data or sensitive vital records information as far as the law allows, or if there was a legitimate reason, like a law enforcement investigation. He would also review records requests as they came in to understand what is being requested, and who is asking for it. And if it appeared that it was the federal government making inappropriate or intrusive requests, Gilchrist again said he would act as the “people’s shield” against those potential abuses.
Forlini said one of his concerns was public voter registration drives run by political organizations or other non-profit groups, preferring that those public drives be run by the state. Forlini’s main issue was for voter information — including addresses and sometimes portions of Social Security numbers. Forlini said Benson’s office has been negligent in allowing those types of voter registration drives to flourish.
The people’s personal information was already everywhere and especially available in some sense on the internet, Borregard said, and it was already difficult to hide it from what he called the “surveillance state”. The government, in his view, wasn’t doing much to protect that information if it was already giving it away to companies and corporations.
Sloan, who has a background in hospital administration, said her background speaks to how she would make distinctions between voter data and things like driving records, putting an emphasis on protecting voter data. She also shared Forlini’s concerns about public, non-state-organized registration drives, adding that registration and voter recruitment should be a function of the state.
Aughney was concerned about the significant increase in voter registration and a parallel increase in driver’s license registrations, claiming that there was a “1 million”-person “discrepancy” between what the state reports to the Federal Highway Administration, but without detailing his reasoning behind the claim.

name: Colorado Newsline
title: Refugee Coloradans work, pay taxes and build communities. Why strip away their healthcare?
description: The Trump administration has upended decades of bipartisan consensus that welcoming refugees — people displaced by war or persecution — is a staple of American policy. It has not only dismantled the system for admitting new refugees, but also made catastrophic policy changes affecting those already resettled here as they strive to rebuild their lives […]
text:
Participants have an impromptu dance as the World Refugee Day celebration, put on by Colorado Refugee Connect, ends at Aurora City Center Park in Aurora in June 2021. (Photo by Eli Imadali for Colorado Newsline)The Trump administration has upended decades of bipartisan consensus that welcoming refugees — people displaced by war or persecution — is a staple of American policy. It has not only dismantled the system for admitting new refugees, but also made catastrophic policy changes affecting those already resettled here as they strive to rebuild their lives as new Americans.

Congress has been shamefully complicit. In July 2025, H.R.1 — the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act” — revoked federal Medicaid eligibility for refugees and other categories of lawfully present immigrants. The ugly result is that beginning Thursday, approximately 7,000 Coloradans — including refugees, asylees, humanitarian parolees, and trafficking survivors — are expected to lose healthcare coverage.
How has it come to this?
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
For decades, the U.S. was a global leader in refugee resettlement. Americans could take pride in offering some of the world’s most vulnerable displaced people an opportunity to safely start over. Long standing policy gave refugees access to modest benefits to help them succeed in integration, including immediate eligibility for Medicaid.
What changed? The first Trump administration justified deep cuts to refugee admissions partly by arguing the U.S. could help more displaced people through humanitarian assistance closer to home than by resettling them here. Yet it also proposed major foreign assistance cuts, even as the worldwide refugee population grew.
The current administration has gone further, gutting USAID while directing considerable taxpayer resources toward expanded immigration enforcement and sweeping deportations. This includes gratuitously re-vetting refugees already legally admitted to the U.S. and making costly agreements to deport immigrants to third countries with which they have no connection — a practice unacceptable to nearly two-thirds of surveyed Americans.
The contrast is stark: Federal resources are funding expanded enforcement and deportation while healthcare coverage and other humanitarian supports are being eviscerated.
The stakes of losing healthcare coverage are high for refugees and their communities. Some arrive with serious medical conditions requiring ongoing treatment. Many are recovering from trauma. CWS and other resettlement agencies help refugee Coloradans who are managing diabetes, heart disease and acute conditions requiring surgery and follow-up care. Losing Medicaid does not erase those needs. Instead, it will leave conditions untreated and shift greater pressure onto local hospitals, food banks, faith communities and nonprofits.
At the same time, refugees must support their families, and those of working age are expected to find employment and move toward self-sufficiency almost immediately upon resettlement. Medicaid access promotes the ability to enter and remain in the workforce, especially as refugees often face barriers to living-wage jobs with benefits when their education, experience or credentials are interrupted or unrecognized.
Reliable healthcare provides stability as resettlement agencies and organizations like Spring Institute for Intercultural Learning help newcomers develop skills, find jobs and advance careers. As refugees build livelihoods, their work supports their families while contributing substantially to our shared prosperity.
Those contributions are measurable: Refugee Coloradans paid $127.1 million in state and local taxes and $233.3 million in federal taxes in 2023. A U.S. Department of Health and Human Services analysis found that refugees and asylees generated tens of billions of dollars more in tax revenues over 15 years than they cost in government services. In Colorado, researchers estimate refugees generate $1.68 in economic activity for every $1 in assistance.
In short, refugees don’t simply receive public support. They work, pay taxes, care for their families and help fund public systems that we all rely on.
Whatever disagreements exist about U.S. immigration policy, these Medicaid changes starting Oct. 1 affect refugees who are already Coloradans raising families and striving for secure futures.
The urgent question is whether our country will honor the commitments made to them — or bear the ethical and practical consequences of increasing uninsurance, growing uncompensated care and destabilized families.
Congress should restore Medicaid eligibility for refugees and other affected humanitarian populations. Refugees have overcome enormous challenges and contribute tremendously when given the opportunity to start anew. Maintaining healthcare access supports the wellbeing, stability and economic self-sufficiency of refugee families — and the communities we all call home.
Kristy Beachy-Quick is the local director for Church World Service in Fort Collins, Colorado, which she opened in 2024. Paula Schriefer has served as President and CEO of Spring Institute for Intercultural Learning in Denver since 2014. Both organizations are members of the Refugee Action Coalition of Colorado.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Virginia Democrats warn more healthcare strains loom after November election
description: Christina Rivera kept her health insurance this year because she needed major back surgery. But maintaining coverage meant absorbing a monthly premium that rose from $235 in 2025 to $1,336 in 2026 — with a higher deductible.  “That’s just not reasonable for anybody who is relying on the ACA for healthcare,” said Riviera, a Charlottesville-area […]
text:
A bed in Lee County Community Hospital. (Photo by Charlotte Rene Woods/Virginia Mercury)Christina Rivera kept her health insurance this year because she needed major back surgery. But maintaining coverage meant absorbing a monthly premium that rose from $235 in 2025 to $1,336 in 2026 — with a higher deductible. 
“That’s just not reasonable for anybody who is relying on the ACA for healthcare,” said Riviera, a Charlottesville-area resident and founder of the nonprofit Called to Justice. “I don’t have that sitting around. It’s not in the cushions of the couch.” 
Small nonprofits often depend on the Affordable Care Act marketplace because reasonably priced group coverage is out of reach, Rivera said. After enhanced federal premium tax credits expired last December, her insurance bill became another financial burden alongside groceries, gasoline and utilities. 
She and others have already exhausted familiar ways of stretching their budgets, Rivera said, from delaying turning on the heat to cutting food purchases or carpooling. She estimated the higher premium will cost her an additional $14,000 this year, and her surgery left her little choice but to maintain coverage. 
“Something has to give, because people just can’t sustain these costs,” she said. 
Rivera shared her experience on Tuesday on a call with reporters organized by the Defend America Action PAC that also included Democratic federal and state lawmakers five weeks before the Nov. 3 midterm elections. 
They urged Virginians to vote, arguing that pressure on household budgets could deepen as additional provisions of H.R. 1, the tax-and-spending law President Donald Trump signed July 4 of last year, take effect in January. 
“Republicans in 2024 campaigned on lowering costs,” said U.S. Rep. Jennifer McClellan, R-Richmond.
McClellan blamed Trump’s tariffs, the war in Iran, federal workforce reductions and cuts to healthcare and food assistance for worsening Virginia’s affordability problems. House Democrats, she said, should reverse the benefit cuts, restore Congress’ tariff authority and protect federal employees. 
The congresswoman also argued that higher insurance costs could discourage families from seeking preventive care. 
Virginia’s 2018 Medicaid Expansion, which McClellan backed at the time as a member of the state Senate, helped connect more residents to regular care while supporting rural hospitals, she said, and recent policy puts some of those gains at risk.
The Democratic lawmakers made their case as Virginians report growing financial unease. 
A Roanoke College poll released earlier this month found consumer sentiment fell sharply in August as inflation and a cooling labor market weighed on household finances. 
Healthcare costs have been affected by two separate changes in Washington. 
Congress allowed enhanced ACA premium tax credits to expire at the end of 2025. Separately, H.R. 1 made changes to Medicaid eligibility and financing, as well as food assistance. 
Virginia’s ACA marketplace had 295,000 enrollees as of late August, down 94,000 from last year, according to state data reported Sept. 2. The decline has been attributed in part to the expired subsidies, although employment and income changes also affect enrollment. 
Another round of changes arrives on Jan. 1. 
Certain adults enrolled in Medicaid will have to meet new work or community engagement requirements, generally requiring 80 hours a month of qualifying activities. Exemptions include pregnancy, medical frailty and some caregiving responsibilities. 
Virginia officials have said more than 500,000  Medicaid enrollees will face new requirements and additional verification, raising concerns that eligible recipients could lose coverage because of paperwork problems. 
Gov. Abigail Spanberger directed state agencies in August to improve outreach and coordination. 
Republicans have defended the Medicaid changes as a way to strengthen eligibility oversight and preserve resources for vulnerable patients. The Trump administration says the work requirements will encourage employment and independence.
U.S. Rep. Rob Wittman, R-Westmoreland, who is seeking reelection in one of Virginia’s more vulnerable GOP strongholds, has also pointed to a $50 billion rural health transformation program included in the law. Virginia received about $189.5 million from the program, with $122 million allocated so far.
Wittman broke with most House Republicans in January, however, when he voted to restore the enhanced ACA tax credits that Congress had allowed to expire.  
State Sen. Barbara Favola, D-Arlington, who chairs Virginia’s Joint Commission on Healthcare, said Tuesday the commonwealth can cushion some federal losses but cannot replace them entirely. 
A commission report released in June identified 13 of the state’s 36 rural hospitals as facing distant or immediate closure risk. 
Lawmakers also approved a $150 million state premium assistance program for households earning between 138% and 250% of the federal poverty level, with enrollment beginning in November. 
Del. Nadarius Clark, D-Suffolk, said on Tuesday’s call that rural constituents face additional pressures from agricultural trade disruptions, energy costs and threatened hospital services. 
“Elections have consequences, and we are dealing with the consequences right now,” Clark said. 
Early voting in the midterms is underway and continues through Oct. 31. 
“If our constituents are hurting, they need to vote accordingly,” Favola said.

title: Dominion unveils route changes for Valley Link Transmission line
description: One of the proposed routes of the controversial Valley Link Transmission line, which will stretch 765 kilovolt lines 115-miles across Virginia from Lynchburg to Culpeper, has been altered by developers, as Dominion Energy, Transource and FirstEnergy narrow down which path they’d prefer to present to the State Corporation Commission. Dominion has been meeting[...]
text:
The proposed Valley Link Transmission Line's Route 2 option with variations, which Dominion Energy has shared with nine Virginia counties that the line could cross, if approved.  (Photo courtesy Valley Link Transmission)One of the proposed routes of the controversial Valley Link Transmission line, which will stretch 765 kilovolt lines 115-miles across Virginia from Lynchburg to Culpeper, has been altered by developers, as Dominion Energy, Transource and FirstEnergy narrow down which path they’d prefer to present to the State Corporation Commission.
Dominion has been meeting with communities in the nine counties the line could traverse: Campbell, Appomattox, Buckingham, Fluvanna, Louisa, Orange, Goochland, Spotsylvania, and Culpeper. Members of these communities confirmed that the utility shared the updated route options with them in recent days. 
Route 2’s changes are mainly centered in Buckingham and Louisa, and there are alterations near the Joshua and Yeat substations at the beginning and end of the line.
Route 2 with variations of the proposed Valley Link Transmission line. (Valley Link Transmission)
“Valley Link has developed a potential variation to Route 2 in Louisa County that avoids crossing land owned by the Louisa County Board of Supervisors just west of the Louisa County Schools Campus,” said Craig Carper, a Dominion spokesman. 
The updated route will parallel an existing transmission line through the county’s technology overlay district and avoids “areas of the district proposed for rezoning,” he added.
Carper emphasized that the routes that are displayed on the official Valley Link website are not complete and that when routing and variations are finalized, “Valley Link will host a virtual meeting with the community to explain route details and ways to remain engaged.”
New route changes near Louisa, VA for the Valley Link Transmission line. (Valley Link Transmission)
The Louisa board has adamantly opposed the transmission line that is slated to bring 6.6 gigawatts of energy from the Ohio Valley into Northern Virginia where power demands are greatest, in part due to the large concentration of data centers in the region. 
The board filed a resolution against the project with the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission back in March. Now, even with the altered route option, county leaders will only be satisfied if developers “abandoned the project,” Louisa Board of Supervisors Chairman Duane Adams said.
Adams explained that the county has put aside $250,000 for legal fees to fight the project at the SCC and “in court if we have to”. 
“I just think Dominion’s not listening at all to the counties and the citizens across these nine counties,” Adams said. ”There is no good path for Valley Link, and there’s no positive for Louisa County.”
If the power needs are greatest in Northern Virginia, Adams said, then the energy generation projects should be built there rather than constructing the transmission line to cut through thousands of acres in Central Virginia.
Residents who live near the potential routes or whose property would be bisected by the power line have also pushed back against Valley Link. Some landowners, concerned about the health impacts of living in close proximity to the line, are considering leaving.
Carper said that the routes will be finalized “this fall,” ahead of the project’s official filing with the SCC. 
PJM, the regional grid operator for most of the East Coast, identified the Valley Link Transmission line as critical to maintain grid reliability. 
It will cost about $1 billion to build the line and state and federal authorities must grant approvals. The expected competition date, if approved, is in 2029.
