name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Could MLK Corridor title help revitalize Bridgeport’s East End?
description: The East End is one of seven CT areas designated as a Martin Luther King, Jr. Corridor, a program intended to stimulate economic development.
text:
In the 1970s, Stratford Avenue, one of the main arteries running through Bridgeport’s East End, was designated as Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. Boulevard.
The name has honored King’s legacy, but a state designation could now give the neighborhood an opportunity to put that name to work in a more tangible way — bringing attention to economic development, investment and opportunities for the people who live and work along it.
The East End is one of seven areas in the state designated as a Martin Luther King, Jr. Corridor under a program intended to promote secured and unsecured lending and stimulate economic development. Other municipalities with these corridors include Middletown, New Britain and Norwalk. 
“The designation gives the East End an opportunity to focus attention and resources on the neighborhood,” said Kelvin Ayala, an urban planner and economic development strategist with LBU & Associates, which is serving as the lead local organization for the Bridgeport effort.
The designation can also give applicants additional weight when seeking future state grants and funding, according to the Connecticut Department of Banking.
A separate East End streets study is examining issues on Stratford and Connecticut avenues like pedestrian safety, transit, bicycle access and improvements that could also support future economic development.
Councilman Ernie Newton, who represents the East End, said he is open to development that strengthens the neighborhood. “If there’s a way to generate more revenue, improve on what we’re doing, I’m all in,” Newton said.
For Newton, part of that vision is bringing back the kind of neighborhood he remembers growing up in, where residents could find many of the services and businesses they needed close to home.

Businesses and vacant storefronts are seen on Stratford Avenue in the East End of Bridgeport on Wednesday, Sept. 23, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

The neighborhood has long sought basic services, including a grocery store and bank. Honey Locust Square, a long-delayed project on Stratford Avenue, now has an M&T Bank branch, while a Gala Foods supermarket and other businesses remain part of the planned development. The project has received nearly $4.5 million in city, state and federal support, but has faced years of delays and financial challenges.
Opportunities for growth
The stretch of Stratford Avenue that runs through the center of the East End is only open to eastbound traffic, while Connecticut Avenue to the north provides only westbound traffic access. Some residents and business owners have in the past complained about the one-way designation and the limits it places on access to the local businesses that make up the commercial corridor.
Bill Coleman, deputy director of Bridgeport’s Office of Planning & Economic Development, said the city’s work on Stratford Avenue is intended to complement the MLK Corridor effort. The city has been working with East End leaders and state lawmakers on a plan to convert Stratford Avenue to two-way traffic and redesign Connecticut Avenue to include a two-way protected bicycle track.
“The thought is to really try to recreate, particularly on Stratford Avenue, the MLK Boulevard, a neighborhood street that is supportive of a higher quality of life for residents and of a higher degree of neighborhood-based commerce,” Coleman said.
The avenue also connects the neighborhood to downtown Bridgeport on the west and continues east into the town of Stratford, where it opens to two-way traffic. Local planners and community leaders see the designation as an opportunity to build on what is already there and bring more investment, jobs and opportunities to the area.
For some East End business owners, the neighborhood already has something that can’t be created through a development plan: a strong sense of community. Syed Imran, who has operated ELA Discount on Stratford Avenue for 21 years, said neighbors regularly look out for one another.
“If you treat them better… they help you. They will look after you. Like I look after them,” Imran said. Despite what he sees as negative perceptions of the area, Imran said he remains invested in the neighborhood. “I love this neighborhood. I have no problem,” he said. “Just people got a wrong conception about this area.”
Ayala said the designation creates an opportunity to build on the East End’s existing strengths.
“The broader objective is to create a stronger local economy,” Ayala said.
Ayala said the goal is to support existing businesses and create opportunities for residents to build wealth. LBU has divided the Bridgeport effort into three areas: public art and beautification, small business and workforce development, and real estate investment and economic development.
Keith Williams, head of the East End Neighborhood Revitalization Zone, said they need investment in several areas, particularly housing and infrastructure. “We need more for housing… and more businesses in the neighborhood,” Williams said.

East End resident Cherie Oeea, left, and a friend talk outside a vacant building on Stratford Avenue in Bridgeport on Wednesday, Sept. 23, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

He said improvements to Stratford Avenue, including the proposal to convert part of the corridor to two-way traffic, could help bring more activity to the area and support local businesses. Unlike other more high-density neighborhoods in the city, there is also some vacant land along the avenue that can provide opportunities for further development.
Coleman said the city views the MLK Corridor as complementary to its existing work, including efforts to improve infrastructure and complete projects such as Honey Locust Square. He said the goal is for Stratford Avenue to become a place where people spend time and do business.
“You don’t want to see Stratford Avenue and the MLK Corridor as a place you go through, but rather see it as a place you go to or that you live alongside,” Coleman said.
LBU is exploring ideas that could include helping entrepreneurs start and expand businesses, identifying opportunities for vacant properties, connecting residents with jobs and creating new public spaces along the corridor.
The designation itself does not guarantee those projects will happen. Instead, Bridgeport will have to use the designation to pursue investment and funding from other sources. Ayala said the goal is to bring together state and local officials, community organizations, businesses and residents around a common economic development strategy while building on what residents have already said they want.
Pastor Carl McCluster, senior pastor at Shiloh Baptist Church and managing director of the Freedom Faith Collaborative, which helped establish Connecticut’s MLK Corridor program, said Bridgeport’s success will depend on making the process broad and collaborative.
“It shouldn’t be a political prize, and should be an adventure in collaborative work in the community instead,” McCluster said.
Norwalk’s efforts
The state created the MLK Corridor designation in 2016, but expanded it in 2024 to increase the number of corridors the banking commissioner could designate from three to seven. 

A sign marking local streets in the East End of Bridgeport on Wednesday, Sept. 23, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

Matt Smith, the banking department’s director of government affairs and public policy, said the department only adds the designation and other agencies and organizations can consider it when awarding grants or other funding.
“There is no money associated with it,” Smith said. “We do not administer any money.”
Smith said the Department of Banking does not track whether other agencies use the designation when making funding decisions, so the department does not have data showing how often the designation has helped communities secure additional funding.
Rep. Kadeem Roberts, D-Norwalk, who has been involved in that city’s MLK Corridor work, said the designation became part of a broader local planning and investment effort that included public art, trees, walkways and bike infrastructure. Roberts said artists were brought into the process to create murals and other artwork reflecting Black history and culture in the neighborhood.
Norwalk’s corridor includes about two miles of Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. Drive and surrounding streets near the South Norwalk train station.

A sign marking welcomes visitors and residents to the East End of Bridgeport on Wednesday, Sept. 23, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

Roberts also pointed to a $14 million federal RAISE grant that Norwalk received in 2024 for improvements along MLK Drive and six surrounding roadways near the South Norwalk train station. 
McCluster said the designation was created to bring residents together on economic development efforts and help leverage additional resources.
“I think you have to learn how to really bring the community together and to leverage a small amount that you have,” McCluster said. He pointed to Norwalk, where about $3 million in state funding helped leverage roughly $30 million for improvements, including facade work for longtime homeowners along the corridor.
Norwalk has used the broader MLK Corridor initiative to support other investments as well. Since 2019, the city says it has identified more than $7.6 million in priority investments in economic and community development, education, housing and safety, with funding from local, state and federal sources. Those efforts have included residential facade improvements, low-interest home improvement loans, streetscape projects and support for minority- and women-owned businesses.
Bridgeport’s vision
In Bridgeport, Ayala sees several ways the corridor could help the area grow and build on existing plans.
One idea being explored through the local effort is creating a pocket park near Stratford Avenue and Sixth Street on city-owned property. Ayala described it as a concept, not a project that has been approved by the city. The idea could create a small public gathering space while improving pedestrian safety. He also sees opportunities to connect East End residents with jobs and provide technical assistance to people interested in starting or expanding businesses.
A view of the East End of Bridgeport on Wednesday, Sept. 23, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror
Housing is another piece. Vacant and blighted properties could potentially be redeveloped, while existing housing and property-improvement programs could be pursued as part of broader investment efforts in the neighborhood.
“I’m hoping that we get more home ownership,” Newton said. “Because you need a middle class … in order to sustain any community.”

A cat inside the ELA Discount Store on Stratford Avenue in Bridgeport on Wednesday, Sept. 23, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

Longtime East End resident Cherie O’Dea said new investment alone will not be enough. She said residents also need better access to education, job opportunities and basic resources that can help them take advantage of that investment.
“I think it goes farther than just the East End,” she said. “It comes from putting systems in place that actually help people — more education systems, more systems to help people get their licenses. Because a lot of us, we didn’t have a chance from starting out.”
Ayala said the designation is one tool that can help bring people and potential resources to the same table, but the outcome will depend on whether the ideas developed locally can attract funding and move into implementation.
Ayala believes the opportunity is there for the neighborhood many residents have argued has been ignored by economic development officials and developers for years. 
“We still have time to salvage it,” he said.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Gargantuan feedlot telegraphs woes for cattle and the environment
description: I was just reading about a feedlot in Nebraska, near where that state meets Kansas and Colorado. It is set to become the largest in the country, holding in one square mile up to 150,000 head — as many cattle as were driven here in 1886 during the peak of the great drives. After reading […]
text:
Cattle crowd a Kansas feedlot in 2022. Plans call for an enormous new operation in the region. (Jill Hummels for Kansas Reflector)I was just reading about a feedlot in Nebraska, near where that state meets Kansas and Colorado. It is set to become the largest in the country, holding in one square mile up to 150,000 head — as many cattle as were driven here in 1886 during the peak of the great drives.
After reading that I did some math. One cow slaughtered yields about 550 pounds of beef, or about a quarter of a metric ton. According to a recent social media post from President Donald Trump, he will allow 300,000 metric tons of beef imported tariff-free from countries not mentioned (mostly not even shown on the JBS website, the mega packing firm controlled by Brazilian billionaire and Trump donor Joesley Batista).
Afterward, the August Feeder Board dropped several dollars per head. I figured that much beef would come from 1.2 million cows. (Likely more than that. Those Brazilian cows don’t look as heavy in spite of being raised on tropical grasses all year long, maybe due to the parasites.)
Instead of riding in boxcars to slaughterhouses in Omaha, Chicago or Kansas City, these cattle ride in aluminum double-decker semi-trucks called “cattle pots” for, you know, where the waste collects. Maybe they’re roomier than boxcars, but who can say, watching those faces through the slots as you pass one on the highway.
Before the feedlots, these cattle have only known rolling pastures, or the welcome sound of the rancher’s truck bringing hay or breaking ice on the water tank. One day comes the confusion of being rounded up and trucked to pens with crushed concrete floors and robotic waterers and feeders, packed alongside other terrified animals.
There isn’t even natural darkness there, as intense lights flood the area and can be seen from the next county. Residents of the nearby town of Haigler don’t get to see the night sky either.
The swill they are fed is mostly corn and distiller’s waste from ethanol plants — an industrial system. No selective grazing among native plants, no exercise, no respite from the flies and other tormenters. Their weight swells as their veins clog. The hormones reboot their physiology, the antibiotics disrupt their gut flora and they belch methane, the gas that disproportionately heats the planet.
Excuse me if I mentioned antibiotics. Or is it the growth hormone we like to say isn’t used in beef production (wink, wink, nudge, nudge).
Backers in Canada promise jobs and prosperity (wink, wink, nudge, nudge). But as the trucks roll in and out, damaging road surfaces and raising dust, few stop at local businesses. Few locals find employment.
Talk at the Country Café in Haigler is often about water woes of the region, where the Ogallala Aquifer has dropped out of reach and the nearby Republican River is reduced to a trickle of bathtub warmth, devoid of dissolved oxygen. It’s not just the drought (although recent summers have rivaled the Dust Bowl). Most of those planted windbreaks are gone. So is the Rockies snowpack.
The Bluestem Bison Ranch near Glade and pasture-finished cattle operations farther east offer sustainable alternatives, if only granted a level playing field with the big boys, those multinational conglomerates with deep pockets but shallow concern for local enterprises.
Wendell Berry passed from this earth in August. He was an eloquent voice in the 1970s warning against the corporatization of agriculture and emptying of small towns, which he called the “Unsettling of America.” He lived to watch it happen. His talks at the Land Institute in Salina were inspiring and hopeful, and his poetry warms the soul like the Chinook winds.
The company says it will compensate for the massive water use of the feedlot and its waste management system by buying irrigated crop fields that will be retired (as they would have been anyway). Supposedly they will be replanted to prairie.
Anyone who believes this is possible knows nothing of a prairie. True prairie develops over centuries or longer where soils are deep. They take much longer on the high plains, where competition with cheat grass and other invasives requires intensive management.
Once the banks of the Republican were home to vast herds of bison, although at least they moved about over an area stretching from Dakotas to the Pesos. The Pawnee called it the river of “much manure,” and how prescient they were!
Bill Beachly was a biology professor at Hastings College in Nebraska for 27 years before semi-retiring near Concordia, Kansas (where he still works at Cloud County Community College). Through its opinion section, Kansas Reflector works to amplify the voices of people who are affected by public policies or excluded from public debate. Find information, including how to submit your own commentary, here.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Pa. House panel advances bill to regulate kratom
description: Under the proposed law, retailers who register with the state would be allowed to sell natural leaf kratom products to people 21 and over, but those products would have to meet strict packaging requirements and be subject to the tobacco tax.
text:
A variety of kratom and 7-OH products — including capsules, cartridges and wellness shots — are on display at a smoke shop in Buffalo, N.Y. States have led the way in regulating kratom, and now federal officials want to ban 7-OH, a powerful compound found in some kratom products. (Photo by Amanda Hernández/Stateline)
A panel of Pennsylvania House members advanced a bill Tuesday that would allow the sale of some kratom products to continue in the state, while banning others and creating stricter regulations for sellers.
Under the proposed law, retailers who register with the state would be allowed to sell natural leaf kratom products to people 21 and over. But those products would have to meet strict packaging requirements and be subject to the tobacco tax.
Packages would have to include the manufacturer’s name and address, a warning that the products have not been evaluated by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and not contain any medical claims. They would also have to be child resistant and not designed to appeal to minors.
The bill would also ban the sale of so-called synthetic or adulterated kratom products, including those that contain more than .5% alkaloid composition of 7-hydroxymitraynine or 7-OH, a potent intoxicating compound found in only trace amounts in the kratom leaf. Violators would be subject to criminal penalties, though those would target sellers and not individual users.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Kratom is a substance that, in low doses, acts as a stimulant and, in higher doses, more as a sedative. It’s made from a plant native to southeast Asia, where it’s been ingested for medicinal, ceremonial and recreational purposes for hundreds of years.
But recently, its popularity in America has skyrocketed. 
Along with natural kratom leaf, more potent synthetic derivatives and products made by extracting intoxicating compounds from the plant have become readily available at many gas stations and smoke shops throughout the country. 
It has reportedly also been used by some who’ve struggled with addiction to more powerful opioids in an attempt to manage their withdrawal symptoms outside of the medical system.
Experts in public health and substance abuse treatment have warned kratom in any form can be addictive and research into the long-term effects of taking it and other issues like potential drug interactions are extremely limited. They also warn that using kratom in an attempt to mitigate opioid withdrawals has not been proven effective, and that those struggling should seek professional help.
“The goal is to continue to make products that some find therapeutic available, while eliminating the most dangerous products or forms that might be appealing to young people or consumers who simply don’t understand how dangerous kratom can be,” House Health Committee Chair Dan Frankel (D-Allegheny) said.
The measure received a unanimous committee vote, though Frankel said the bill’s sponsor, Rep. Bridget Kosierowski (D-Lackawanna) intends to offer a future amendment to address “potential loopholes in the bill, to tax the products in a simpler way, and to direct those tax dollars towards oversight amongst other changes.”
The amendment, he said, would be brought before the full House as the bill advances in an effort to pass the legislation before the end of the current legislative session in November. 
In recent years, a number of overdoses have been recorded where kratom was found in the victim’s body alone or in combination with other drugs. According to the state Department of Health, there have been 33 in Pennsylvania since 2025. 
Calls to poison control centers regarding kratom have also increased, with 106 this year through June 30, including 41 involving 7-OH.
A vape shop advertises kratom in Etters, York County. (Photo by Ian Karbal/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)
As it stands, kratom is marketed as a dietary supplement, a category of product that includes vitamins and minerals and receives limited scrutiny from federal regulators like the FDA.
Mac Haddow, a senior fellow on public policy with the American Kratom Association, a lobbying group that represents kratom product manufacturers and sellers, says the group broadly supports the aims of the bill, but would like to see some changes.
He said that he would like to see the proposal l allow the sale of products made from kratom using extraction methods that have been deemed safe for food by the FDA, even if it stipulates they can be no more potent than natural leaf products generally.
“As long as they are properly extracted using FDA-approved solvents that maintain the ratio of the plant material the same as it is in the natural plant, it should be fine because they’re safe,” he said. “Depending on when they were harvested in southeast Asia and how they’re transported, you can have variances [in potency] that are fairly significant in the powdered form. An extract standardizes that dose.”
Haddow said he would also like to see language that he believes could better preempt the sale of newly derived synthetic compounds based on those found in kratom. New ones, he says, often pop up faster than regulators can act.
Recently, the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) classified three synthetic compounds as Schedule I on an emergency basis, meaning the designation will last two years. Those include mitragynine pseudoindoxyl, MGM-15 and MGM-16, potent compounds that produce opioid-like effects.
The DEA has also opened a public comment period on a proposed Schedule I classification for 7-OH.
In Pennsylvania, district attorneys in Bucks and Chester counties have asked the state Department of Health to use emergency powers to classify 7-OH as a schedule I substance, similar to drugs like heroin and LSD.
“At this time, DOH is reviewing the situation and considering all options to ensure any decisions support the health and safety of Pennsylvanians,” a department spokesperson told the Capital-Star earlier this month. “DOH is working to raise awareness and educate the general public …. These products are often sold in retail stores, which can make people assume they are regulated and safe when they are not.”

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Good Samaritan Coalition says saving a life should take priority over punishment
description: In 2009, Jennifer Olson was on parole, out of prison and under community supervision for a felony conviction, when she stopped at a friend’s house on the way to the mall. When Olson arrived, the friend was overdosing, and the friend’s brother was panicking, unsure what to do. After attempting CPR and placing her friend […]
text:
Narcan was handed out by Andrew Garr during a meeting of the Good Samaritan Coalition in Eau Claire. Garr encourage all the participants to carry Narcan to save a life. (Frank Zufall/Wisconsin Examiner)The Wisconsin Examiner’s Criminal Justice Reporting Project shines a light on incarceration, law enforcement and criminal justice issues with support from the Public Welfare Foundation.
In 2009, Jennifer Olson was on parole, out of prison and under community supervision for a felony conviction, when she stopped at a friend’s house on the way to the mall. When Olson arrived, the friend was overdosing, and the friend’s brother was panicking, unsure what to do.
After attempting CPR and placing her friend in a cold shower to revive her, Olson called 911 to save her friend’s life.
The friend was placed in a medically induced coma for 37 days and lived, but during those 37 days, Olson was held in the Waukesha County Jail, incarcerated because, as a condition of her parole, she wasn’t supposed to be around criminal activity or drugs, and it didn’t matter that she had no drugs in her system, having been clean for two months after she went to rehab.
While in jail, Olson said, she lost custody of her children, and she lost her apartment and her job.
“Would I have gone to jail for calling 911 for someone having a heart attack? No.” she said. 
The Wisconsin Good Samaritan Coalition is advocating to change Wisconsin’s law to prioritize saving a life without fear of consequences for those seeking help.
Jennifer Olson recounted calling 911 to save a friend’s life who was overdosing and then later spending 37 days in jail for violating conditions of her parole. (Photo by Frank Zufall/Wisconsin Examiner)
Opioid overdose deaths in Wisconsin have dropped from a peak of 1459, or about four per day, in 2022, to 815 in 2024, according to state health department statistics.  “Many of those deaths could be prevented if people did not fear calling 911 to save a life,” the coalition says in a statement advocating for strengthening the state’s Good Samaritan law to offer protection from prosecution for people who survive an overdose and the people who help save their lives by calling for help on the scene. 
On Monday night, Sept. 28, the coalition met in Eau Claire at Hope United Methodist Church. A large contingent of University of Wisconsin-Eau Claire nursing students attended.
The Good Samaritan Coalition was the main organizer of the event, with support from ProSay, an advocacy organization for formerly incarcerated people  on community supervision, and WISDOM, a faith-based organization with 12 affiliates addressing systemic injustice, and WISDOM affiliates Free and Jonah, with Jonah hosting the event.
“Currently, Wisconsin law deters people from calling 911 in an overdose emergency and Good Samaritan Coalition feels everyone should feel safe to call 911,” said Lynn Buske, a representative of the coalition. Wisconsin has a Good Samaritan law, “but it offers very few protections, leaving people nervous,” she added.
Juli Bliefnick of ProSay said the issue was “deeply personal” to her because she had her supervision revoked and was sent to jail, losing her job and housing after she called 911 to save a life.
Several nursing students from the University of Wisconsin- Eau Claire attended the meeting. (Photo by Frank Zufall/Wisconsin Examiner)
“People should not be forced to choose between their freedom and someone else’s life,” she said.
Bliefnick recounted the history of  Wisconsin’s  Good Samaritan law.
The current law, passed in 2013, grants immunity from prosecution for possession of a controlled substance to a person who summons or provides emergency medical assistance to another person suffering from an overdose. A 2017 update of the law, which is no longer in effect, also granted immunity from having parole, probation, or extended supervision revoked. The protections for people on parole, probation or supervision expired under a sunset clause in 2020.
The No. 1 reason people cite for not calling 911 in overdose cases is fear of arrest.
Mark Rice of WISDOM talked about why his organization supports the goals of the Wisconsin Good Samaritan Coalition. (Frank Zufall/Wisconsin Examiner)
“I’ve experienced the grief of losing someone that I care about due to an overdose, an overdose death that could have been prevented if help had arrived in time,” said Mark Rice, the Transformational Justice Campaign Coordinator for WISDOM.
Rice said WISDOM’s goals of reducing the prison population and changing the culture and laws that result in “permanent punishment of people who have conviction records” align with the Coalition’s efforts.
“So many people fear calling 911 because of fear of arrest,” he said.  “…  the Good Samaritan Coalition is aiming to strip that fear away and to replace fear with health-centered care, and so definitely this is something that WISDOM strongly supports.”
Sarah Ferber, a regional organizer for Free, said she had several friends die of an overdose, and she had also been in situations where she had to call 911 to save a life, but she had not faced any repercussions for seeking help; however, she knew others who had called 911 and did face consequences.
Kelly Green said that when her partner overdosed, she applied six vials of Narcan to save his life, but she never called 911 out of fear of what might happen after first responders arrived.
Kelly Green said she was fearful of calling 911 when her partner overdosed and she saved him using six vials of Narcan. (Frank Zufall/Wisconsin Examiner)
“Calling 911 meant bringing police and emergency services to my house, and once they were there, I couldn’t control what happened next,” she said. “What would they see? What would they ask? What would Child Protective Services see or if they would get involved? What would happen to my kids? Could I lose them? Those thoughts were going through my head while someone I loved was overdosing in front of me, and I know how that sounds after the fact. Of course you call 911. Someone might die, but that’s not what fear looks like when you’re actually living it.”
Andrew Garr, executive director of Wisconsin Milkweed Alliance (a non-profit using the lived experience of members with mental health and substance abuse to “uplift and empower”) recounted his experiences of administering naloxone (Narcan is the brand name) to revive someone he knew who was overdosing and explained how to administer it. Following that, there were discussions about advocating for an update of Wisconsin’s Good Samaritan law.
Buske encouraged participants to sign a petition, talk to others about the subject and press legislators to change the law.
Bliefnick noted that other states, even some that are more conservative than Wisconsin, including Iowa, have broader, more protective Good Samaritan laws.
She also recounted recent attempts to change the law that stalled in the state Assembly, where Speaker Robin Vos didn’t allow it to come up for a vote.
More information on the Wisconsin Good Samaritan Coalition and its effort to change the law is available on the group’s website.

title: Bookman: Whatever came of that urgent FBI probe into the 2020 election in Fulton County?
description: Nine months ago this week, FBI agents raided the Fulton County elections office, seizing hundreds of boxes of ballots cast in the 2020 election. According to the subpoena authorizing that seizure, federal officials had “probable cause to believe” that Fulton officials had “knowingly and willfully deprived” the people of Georgia of a “fair and impartially […]
text:
FBI agents were spotted loading boxes of election documents onto trucks at the Fulton County Election Hub and Operation Center in Union City on Jan. 28, 2026. Ross Williams/Georgia RecorderNine months ago this week, FBI agents raided the Fulton County elections office, seizing hundreds of boxes of ballots cast in the 2020 election.
According to the subpoena authorizing that seizure, federal officials had “probable cause to believe” that Fulton officials had “knowingly and willfully deprived” the people of Georgia of a “fair and impartially conducted election process” in 2020, just as President Trump had claimed.
Conservatives celebrated the news, certain that the truth – their truth – would now be confirmed. “Georgians have waited years for real answers about what happened in 2020,” as Georgia GOP Chair Josh McKoon put it.
Then six months passed. Nothing.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
In early July, FBI leadership in Washington suddenly ordered “all FBI field offices to immediately surge support to an FBI Atlanta priority investigation,” ordering hundreds of analysts around the country to drop whatever they were doing to assist in the Atlanta vote-fraud investigation.
“Overtime (including weekends and holidays) has been authorized,” the FBI memo noted.  
Three months, and tens of thousands of man hours, have since passed since that massive surge. Early voting for the 2026 mid-term elections begins Oct. 13, but nothing more has been heard of the Fulton investigation. 
Nothing.
Ordinarily, it might be safe to assume that since nothing has been heard, nothing has been found. If actual evidence of fraud had been discovered, Trump would have demanded a prime-time speech before Congress to announce that he had been vindicated. Given his history, he might even do it without evidence of fraud.
But that hasn’t happened. At least not yet.
In other voting-related news, the U.S. Department of Justice last week claimed success in its campaign to demonstrate that non-citizens have illegally registered to vote in Georgia and elsewhere. Three people – that’s one plus one plus one – were charged with voting illegally in Georgia elections going back as far as 2008, a time frame in which tens of millions of ballots were cast.  
All three are isolated, individual cases, with no sign of collusion or an organized conspiracy.
Of course, some will still argue that three is three too many, and in a perfect world, maybe so. But we do not live in that perfect world, and three is far, far too few to alter the outcome of an election, as election conspiracy nuts like to claim. 
In fact, three is an absolute repudiation of such claims. After all this time, with all the rhetoric and all the investigatory resources committed to it by the Trump regime, three is all you’ve got?
It could be worse, though. In July, the Trump administration claimed to have found almost 16,000 non-citizens registered to vote in Nevada. 
“No way!” said Nevada officials, and after they demanded proof, the administration was forced to reduce its list to 185 supposed non-citizens registered to vote.
“No way!” Nevada officials said again, and once again the list was drastically reduced.  After investigation, this time the number went to zero.
Zero is not enough votes to alter the outcome of an election.
Again, these are the results of in-depth, well-resourced investigations by an administration that could not be more committed to finding mass voting fraud, yet time after time they are coming up empty. 
It’s time to end this nonsense. While we should always be vigilant in protecting the integrity of elections, we do considerable damage to our democracy by claiming mass fraud where none exists.
Such false claims helped to fuel the attempted coup on Jan. 6. They undermine faith in the legitimacy of our government. They give cover to those who want to destroy our democracy. They encourage people who lose elections to explain it away as cheating, because that’s easier to accept than the fact that they lost. 
Such claims also feed demands for complex solutions to problems that simply do not exist on any scale that matters. The additional paperwork, bureaucracy, hassle and expense that would be needed to drive the number of non-citizen voters from three to zero would be immense, and in the process would discourage or prevent thousands of actual citizens from casting ballots and participating in this great country.
It makes no sense. None of it.

title: South Lyon City Council votes to cover cameras, end contract with Flock
description: ﻿﻿﻿﻿ After instructing city officials to examine the legal implications of ending their contract for a pair of automated license plate reader cameras, members of the South Lyon City Council on Monday moved to terminate their relationship with Flock Safety. City Council members voted 5-2 in support of a resolution to notify Flock that the […]
text:
Flock license plate reader camera in South Lyon on Sept. 14, 2026. (Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance)﻿﻿﻿﻿
After instructing city officials to examine the legal implications of ending their contract for a pair of automated license plate reader cameras, members of the South Lyon City Council on Monday moved to terminate their relationship with Flock Safety.
City Council members voted 5-2 in support of a resolution to notify Flock that the city would not be renewing its contract. The resolution also requires the South Lyon Police Department to discontinue accessing, searching, or otherwise using data obtained through cameras, and to stop sharing data or providing access to any outside agency or third party, except as required by law. 
The motion also directs the South Lyon Police Department to cover the two cameras, located along 10 Mile Road. At 11:45, the department shared a post to Facebook noting the cameras had been covered and were no longer capturing data. 
The city council agreed to have the cameras installed in November 2025. After residents voiced data privacy and Fourth Amendment concerns, city council opted to reconsider the contract.

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Ohio job growth is slowing, analysis says
description: Unemployment rates in Ohio remained low in August but Ohio’s job growth has also slowed, a recent analysis by Policy Matters Ohio said. There are several reasons for low unemployment happening along with slow job growth, and none are encouraging. Ohio added an average of 3,100 jobs per month from January to August. But that […]
text:
A sign for a business hiring employees. (Photo by Joe Raedle/Getty Images)Unemployment rates in Ohio remained low in August but Ohio’s job growth has also slowed, a recent analysis by Policy Matters Ohio said.
There are several reasons for low unemployment happening along with slow job growth, and none are encouraging.
Ohio added an average of 3,100 jobs per month from January to August. But that number dropped to just 2,200 in August.
Meanwhile, the state unemployment rate actually fell slightly — from 3.4% in July to 3.3% in August.
Slowing job growth comes against a backdrop of bigger-than-expected gains nationally. U.S. employers added 162,000 jobs in August, more than double initial predictions, Policy Matters said.
The latest employment data might signal increasing caution among Ohio employers, said Policy Matters researcher Molly Bryden.
“Modest job gains in August could signal a hiring slowdown, after revisions to July’s estimates revealed overstated job growth,”she said in a written statement. “Revisions to both statewide and national indicators over the past several months make a departure from our recent observations – while downward revisions to Ohio’s jobs numbers show weaker growth than initially reported, substantial upward revisions to national estimates show accelerating growth nationwide, reversing job losses shown by preliminary estimates for July.” 
She added, however, that stronger-than-expected hiring nationally “signals a recovery from an earlier slowdown, rather than a continued upward trend.”
An important reason why job growth and unemployment rates are falling simultaneously is that the Ohio workforce shrank by another 10,000 people between July and August. 
Unemployment only measures the rate of people who have or are actively seeking work. It doesn’t count people who have aged out or have given up.
“Ohio has seen the nation’s largest decrease in statewide unemployment (-1.5 percentage points) since January of 2025,” Bryden said. “However, lower unemployment isn’t always a positive sign – over the same period, Ohio’s labor force level has shrunk by 1.9%: the 10th-largest decrease in the country.”
She added, “As of August 2026, there are 95,000 fewer Ohioans in the labor force than there were this time last year, despite a 39,000 increase in the working age population. While there are 100,000 fewer unemployed Ohioans in the labor force actively looking for work, employment is up by only 5,000 since August of 2025.”
That is part of a national trend. The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics reports that, in seasonably adjusted numbers, the U.S. labor force shrank by 1.3 million between July 2025 and July 2026.
And one cause of that is President Donald Trump’s mass deportations.
A report published early this month by Dayton-based data analyst Eric Pachman showed that 2.1 million foreign-born, working-age men left the country since the start of Trump’s second term in January 2025. Eighty-eight percent of them were working when they left, according to the analysis.
The loss was by far the biggest in the data Pachman analyzed. 
He also found declining workforce participation by native-born men. Fewer foreign-born male workers and fewer native-born counterparts seeking work could add up to necessary jobs going undone, Pachman said.

title: Will gas tax gimmick make Ohioans forget why we are in this mess and who got us here?
description: Over the last 20 months, Republican majorities in the U.S. House and U.S. Senate have subordinated themselves to the president of the United States. They abrogated their Article 1 responsibilities as a co-equal branch of the federal government to carry water for the convicted felon in the White House. History will note their slavish obedience […]
text:
File photo by Hugh Jackson, States Newsroom.Over the last 20 months, Republican majorities in the U.S. House and U.S. Senate have subordinated themselves to the president of the United States. They abrogated their Article 1 responsibilities as a co-equal branch of the federal government to carry water for the convicted felon in the White House. 
History will note their slavish obedience to Donald Trump, their willingness to cede core constitutional powers to the dear leader — power to declare war, power of the purse, power to levy tariffs, power to conduct government oversight as a critical check on abuses of power. 
Trump is lawlessly usurping Congress’s power now by cutting nearly $1 billion in funding it approved for programs the White House unilaterally decided were not worth “wasteful and harmful government spending.”
But under GOP leadership, the 119th Congress allowed itself to be diminished and bypassed by a megalomaniac chasing unlimited power.  
From the beginning, Trump set the agenda on Capitol Hill and Republican lawmakers fell in line. 
The partisan rubber-stamps enacted the largest-ever cuts to basic needs programs in the U.S. to fund Trump’s $1 trillion in tax cuts for the ultra wealthy, declined to oversee the illegal war Trump began without congressional authorization or public debate, ignored the brazen defiance of congressional statutes by the Trump regime, (from gutting federal agencies to renaming institutions) and refused to even superficially check the most corrupt president in American history. 
Party loyalty and protecting the party boss was/is the preferred default move among team players in the House and Senate. Principle and prudence in federal legislating and constitutional duties take a back seat to political allegiance.
The same rule of thumb applies to the Republican supermajorities in the Ohio House and Ohio Senate. Party trumps all. 
But under one party rule, power has always been zealously guarded and wielded in the legislature. Which makes it all the more astonishing that GOP leadership in the Statehouse jumped to give so much power to an unelected Republican candidate running for governor. 
Vivek Ramaswamy is a venture capitalist who made a fortune in biotech and notably moved a company he co-founded from Columbus to Dallas two years ago. 
The 41-year-old billionaire, who has never served in any public office, spent tens of millions of his own money on a brief presidential campaign before jumping on the Trump train in 2024. 
His reward was a five-minute stint as co-leader of an advisory cost-cutting initiative (the so-called Department of Government Efficiency, DOGE) that ended up costing the federal government billions of dollars in paid leave and related expenses to haphazardly shrink the workforce). 
When Republican Gov. Mike DeWine passed Ramaswamy over for a U.S. Senate appointment, the Ohioan settled for DeWine’s job in 2026 while he waits for another shot at the presidency. 
The Republican nominee eying the governor’s mansion has struggled to gain traction against Dr. Amy Acton, former head of the Ohio Department of Health under DeWine and the Democratic candidate campaigning for the same office. 
The latest polls show Acton with a slight edge over Ramaswamy. 
Twice the GOP-run General Assembly has rallied to kick-start his flagging momentum with hurried legislation the candidate pitched as a winning gambit with voters — directing policymaking as though he were governor already. 
Ramaswamy called on the legislature to make Ohio’s voter ID law, that polls favorably, a constitutional requirement to juice turnout and Republicans jammed through a resolution in three weeks that put a needless voter ID amendment on the November ballot. 
Last week, Acton called for an emergency state gas tax holiday to lessen the sticker shock at the pumps from Trump’s war of choice with Iran. 
In response to her proposal to temporarily suspend Ohio’s state motor fuel tax (38.5 cents per gallon of gasoline and 47 cents per gallon for diesel), Ramaswamy announced a similar 90-day gas tax suspension proposal about six hours later. 
Ohio Republicans spun into action at the behest of their boss (?) and scheduled an unprecedented special legislative session today (Wednesday) to vote on his plan — a week before early, in-person voting begins in Ohio. 
What extraordinary power state legislative leaders, like their federal counterparts in Washington, have ceded to one man who, unlike Trump, has not been elected to anything. 
Ohio Senate President Rob McColley, Ramaswamy’s running mate, and Ohio House Speaker Matt Huffman have stooped to carrying water for the former hedge fund manager/biotech baron in their respective chambers. 
It’s wild. A Republican candidate, in a toss-up race for governor, is calling the shots in the legislature on what extra amendment should go into the Ohio Constitution and what should be suspended in gas taxes that fund road and bridge work and will cost the state around $700 million in lost revenue. 
It’s unclear how that significant shortfall in road funding will be replaced and Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine is adamant that using money from the Ohio Department of Transportation to make up for a gas tax is a “very, very bad idea.” 
But it’s easy politics, right? Who doesn’t like discounted gas prices? 
This is a last-ditch effort by Ramaswamy — in league with compliant team players in the legislature — to change the trajectory of a political campaign many assumed would be a slam dunk. Trump pulled a similar maneuver to change midterm trends when he dangled a $5k giveaway to every citizen if voters returned Republican majorities to Congress. 
Whether either stunt works to sway the electorate as voting starts is anyone’s guess. But voters are smart. In 2026, they are razor focused. On course correction. Will gimmicks work?
