name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Bill to end Pennsylvania’s closed primary elections passes state House
description: Advocates for open primaries have argued that the current system disenfranchises groups including about 400,000 Pennsylvania veterans and nearly two-thirds of young adults who choose to join an alternative political party or remain independent. The commonwealth is one of just 10 states with closed primaries.
text:
Advocates for open primaries have argued that the current system disenfranchises groups including about 400,000 Pennsylvania veterans and nearly two-thirds of young adults who choose to join an alternative political party or remain independent. (Photo by Pat Sutphin/Idaho Capital Sun)A bill to allow independent and third-party voters to cast ballots in Pennsylvania primary elections passed Tuesday in the state House.
Despite the 115-88 vote, the legislation attracted opposition from both sides of the aisle from lawmakers who argued the primaries are the exclusive domain of the parties to nominate candidates for the general elections. 
State Rep. Jared Solomon (D-Philadelphia), who is the measure’s  prime sponsor, said opening the commonwealth’s primaries would correct an injustice for 1.5 million unaffiliated voters that has existed since the state Election Code was made law in 1937. 
“Our election system has all the gloss and feel of being open to voters throughout Pennsylvania, there are our community centers, our synagogues, our mosques, our churches, our civic institutions that welcome people,” Solomon said. “Yet these voters are counted out each and every election.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Solomon’s bill was introduced in 2025 but  not reported out of the House State Government Committee until Monday. It now heads to the Republican-controlled Senate for consideration.
Advocates for open primaries have argued that the current system disenfranchises groups including about 400,000 Pennsylvania veterans and nearly two-thirds of young adults who choose to join an alternative political party or remain independent. The commonwealth is one of just 10 states with closed primaries. 
“This year, we can bring in those veterans, those young people, and those that diverse coalition of voters into the civic fabric of Pennsylvania,” Solomon said.
But Rep. Wendy Fink (R-York) argued that the commonwealth’s general elections are open to every U.S. citizen who registers to vote and Solomon’s bill would actually alter the nomination process.
“The primary is not an election in the purest form,” Fink said, adding that allowing non-party voters to participate in primaries would add complexity to elections. 
A voter registration booth features a cardboard cutout of the late Charlie Kirk at the NRA’s Great American Outdoor Show at the Farm Show complex in Harrisburg, on Feb. 11, 2026. (Photo by Tim Lambert/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)
Although the measure passed with 16 Republicans voting “yea,” Democratic  support was not unanimous. 
Rep. Greg Vitali (D-Delaware) echoed Fink’s argument and added that independent voters choose to exclude themselves from the partisan process. Vitali said in conversations with some independent voters, they told him they find it distasteful to be affiliated with either party.
“I find it very inconsistent on the part of those people … who find it too distasteful to be affiliated with a party, yet at the same time want a voice in choosing its standard bearer,” he said. “That’s just inconsistent.”
One lawmaker compared the spring elections to football draft picks.
“It would be really bad if, when the NFL draft came along, that my Eagles would allow some person from the Steelers to make their draft picks,” Rep. Russ Diamond (R-Lebanon) said.
But Democratic Whip Mike Schlossberg (D-Lehigh) said every elected official should be working to make government participation easier for constituents. And he rejected the notion that voters who want to participate in primaries should just pick a party.
“Our job is to do everything we can to expand the franchise and to make sure that our citizens have an easier pathway to communicate with us, an easier pathway to influence our decisions, because that is a core tenet of democracy,” he said.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Byron Donalds says solar power is a ‘fad’ but Florida utilities are expanding its use
description: Despite the Trump administration’s hostility towards renewable energy, information released by the U.S. Energy Information Administration shows that utility solar capacity — large scale projects that provide electricity to power grids — has increased 33% since 2025. That’s according to the SUN DAY campaign, which tracks renewable energy nationally. The presi[...]
text:
Solar farm via Florida Power & Light, 2022.Despite the Trump administration’s hostility towards renewable energy, information released by the U.S. Energy Information Administration shows that utility solar capacity — large scale projects that provide electricity to power grids — has increased 33% since 2025.
That’s according to the SUN DAY campaign, which tracks renewable energy nationally.
The president’s signature One Big Beautiful Bill Act in 2025 removed solar power tax credits, which industry groups in Florida feared could devastate the solar industry in the Sunshine State.
Trump’s pick to lead Florida for the next four years, Republican Byron Donalds, said last week that he’s not a fan of solar power and was openly dismissive of its ability to power the state.
“We are in the middle of the solar fad, and I’m going to call it a fad,” he said during a campaign event in Daytona Beach Shores.
“Because we know how this works,” he added. “We’ve seen these solar arrays all over the state of Florida. They’re taking land out of production and taking land off the interstate. We’ve seen how this has worked time and again. What happens very clearly is you have some power in the day, no power at night, when most people are using electricity anyway. And so it’s not consistent power.”
His Democratic opponent, David Jolly, has a different take.
“Solar should be a part of Florida’s future,” he told the Phoenix last Friday, following his appearance in front of the Tampa Tiger Bay Club. “I think that the more people we can get off the traditional grid with solar panels, whether it’s through incentives or some soft mandates into our Public Services Commission, great.”
He went on to say that the state’s biggest investor-owned utilities are “going to widespread adoption of solar.”
Eight percent of the energy generated in Florida comes from renewable sources (mostly solar), according to a 2026 report from the Florida Public Service Commission (PSC). Nearly 75% of the energy generated in Florida comes from natural gas. Another 11% comes from nuclear power, 3% from coal, 2% from purchases and less than one percent from oil.
The Phoenix reached out to the three largest investor-owned utilities in Florida to learn how much solar power is in their plans.
Florida Power & Light (FPL) is the state’s largest energy provider. In 2025, FPL delivered 11% of its energy from solar generation. Its 10-year 2026 Ten-Year Power Plant Site Plan calls for that to increase to 26% by 2035.
However, that is 30% lower compared to its 2025 plan. The Southern Alliance for Clean Energy (SACE) attributes that reduction to expiring federal solar tax credits passed by Congress last year. (SACE notes that NextEra Energy, FPL’s parent company, “quietly” abandoned it goal of net-zero emissions by 2045).
Duke Energy Florida intends to add 12 solar sites to the electric grid, increasing capacity by 900 megawatts by 2027, according to spokesperson Ana Gibbs. The plan, she said, is to have Duke Energy generate approximately 30% of the electricity it sells from solar power by 2035.
Tampa Electric Co. generated 12% of its energy portfolio from solar power in the 12 months ending in June 2026, spokesperson Cherie Jacobs said. Next year, about 17% of its energy is expected to come from the sun.
For years, environmentalists in Florida complained that the investor-owned utilities were behind other states in adopting solar power. That’s changed dramatically in recent years, in large part to the enormous reduction in costs associated with it. Solar panels that sold for $5-$6 per watt around 2000 now cost about 12 cents per watt, according to Dave Ember, chief analyst and co-founder of a global energy think tank.
Small modular nuclear reactors
While playing down solar, Donalds is promoting another product he says could play a part in fueling Florida’s energy needs. “I believe that we need to be investing in small, modular nuclear reactors in Florida,” he said in Daytona Beach Shores. “We have to have a consistent power base.”
There has been a lot of interest in what are known as SMRs in Florida and around the country. Advocates say that they promise greater safety, quicker deployment, and cost less than traditional nuclear generation.
The Florida Legislature approved a bill in 2024 requiring the PSC to conduct a feasibility study on advanced nuclear reactors.That report, issued last year, recommended a more comprehensive study, perhaps by a major university, to help define the benefits of nuclear development. However, that momentum stalled when a bill (HB 1461) that would have authorized the PSC to regulate advanced nuclear reactors (and passed 108-0 in the House) stalled in the Senate.
But perhaps most important for now, anyway, is that the utilities say these reactors are not in their mix at all going forward.
“Regarding SMRs, at this point, they are not yet commercially available at scale or cost effective,” said Andrew Sutton, an FLP spokesperson. He added that the company has a “dedicated team” evaluating the technology so that it could be deployed quickly if it does become cost effective.
Duke Energy Florida plans no nuclear deployment — its Ten-Year Site Plan proposes new solar and upgrading existing generation units, Ana Gibbs said. “Advanced nuclear overall is still a longer-term option.”
Tampa Electric is looking into small modular nuclear reactors as a possible solution. However, right now, “the technology isn’t commercially viable,” spokesperson Cherie Jacobs said.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Regional cooperation is delivering real results for southeastern Connecticut
description: Not every school district needs to build and maintain every operational function on its own. Sometimes, the better answer is to share.
text:
As school districts across Connecticut confront rising costs, increasingly complex operational demands, and continued pressure to use public resources responsibly, the conversation often turns to what districts can cut, consolidate, or simply do without.
There is another option.
Across southeastern Connecticut, school districts are demonstrating that voluntary regional cooperation can help communities stretch resources further, access specialized expertise, and strengthen local schools without sacrificing local identity or local decision-making.
That distinction matters.
Regional cooperation does not have to mean consolidation. It does not require every district to operate the same way or give up control over decisions that belong to its community. It means recognizing that not every school district needs to build and maintain every operational function on its own.
Sometimes, the better answer is to share.
We are seeing that approach produce measurable results through LEARN’s Regional Shared Service Solutions Program.
More than a year ago, LEARN partnered with area superintendents to pursue a funding opportunity through Connecticut’s Office of Policy and Management’s Regional Performance Incentive Program, which supports voluntary regional shared-services projects designed to improve service delivery and reduce costs. The opportunity focused on improving efficiency and enhancing services in operational areas such as instructional technology, human resources, and business office functions.
The premise was straightforward: make it easier and more affordable for districts to share expertise and operational capacity.

Katherine Ericson

Through the grant, districts already using LEARN shared services received a 25 percent discount, while reduced rates over a three-year period provided an affordable entry point for districts new to the model.
The value of the initiative was never simply about lowering a bill, though.
School district operations have become increasingly specialized. Technology systems evolve quickly. Human resources requirements can be complex. Business operations demand certain expertise. Recruiting and retaining professionals with specialized skills can be difficult, particularly when an individual district may not need or be able to support a full-time position in every area.
Regional shared services allow districts to access that expertise collectively.
By the end of the program’s first year, 14 school districts across eastern Connecticut had participated in one or more shared service areas. Some needed support with human resources functions. Others partnered with LEARN around technology or business operations.
Their individual needs were different, but the question behind them was largely the same: Why duplicate infrastructure, expertise, and cost when collaboration can provide another way?
The financial results are significant. Based on first year projects, participating districts were expected to realize more than $325,000 in collective savings.
Those dollars matter. They are public resources that can remain in local school communities rather than being absorbed by duplicative administrative and operational costs.
However, savings tell only part of the story.
When a superintendent can rely on regional expertise to address a complicated operational need, that leader has greater capacity to focus on educational leadership. When a district can access an established system rather than create one independently, staff time and resources can be directed elsewhere. When several districts share specialized expertise, smaller communities can gain access to capacity that might otherwise be difficult or too costly to maintain.
Ultimately, stronger systems behind our schools provide stronger support for the educators and students those systems exist to serve.
This is precisely why Connecticut created Regional Educational Service Centers. RESCs give districts a mechanism for working together voluntarily-sharing expertise, building capacity, and creating efficiencies while preserving local governance.
That model may be even more relevant today than it was when LEARN was founded 60 years ago.
Connecticut’s school districts will continue to face difficult financial and operational decisions. There will be legitimate conversations about costs, efficiencies, and how public education should adapt to changing circumstances.
 Regional cooperation should be a larger part of those conversations.
The first year of this initiative offers a useful example of how state government, regional organizations, and local school districts can work together. The state created an incentive for collaboration. LEARN and area superintendents developed a regional approach. Individual districts then chose whether and where participation made sense for their communities. Fourteen districts participated. More than $325,000 was saved in the first year. Local decision-making remained intact.
That is not consolidation. It is cooperation with measurable results.
As LEARN celebrates 60 years of Supporting Students, Strengthening Systems, and Serving Communities, the principle on which much of our work was built remains remarkably current: school districts can achieve more together than they can alone.
Connecticut should continue investing in opportunities that make voluntary regional collaboration possible.
When collaboration preserves local choice, expands access to expertise, and makes public dollars work harder, regional cooperation is not simply a good idea.
It is good public policy.
Katherine Ericson is executive director at LEARN,  southeastern Connecticut’s Regional Educational Service Center.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: CT’s reckless drive for more nuclear power
description: We don’t need more nuclear power. What we do need is to stop rushing toward the climate cliff.
text:
Our governor will be joining other New England governors in a “summit” today to push for more nuclear power.  Supposedly there’s a crisis, a need for lots more electricity for data centers so they can embrace the wonders of AI.  
There’s a crisis, all right, but it’s not some desperate need for AI.  Instead, it’s the fires, droughts, glacier breakdowns and extreme weather all over the world –symptoms of collapsing climates.
Over the last year the CT Department of Energy and Environmental Protection held  four webinars to encourage building nuclear power plants in Connecticut.  Their pitch was that new “advanced” reactors are much safer, that smaller ones can be built rapidly and that nuclear waste is not an immediate problem.  The legislature set aside $5 million to foster sites all over Connecticut.
The supposed advance is the SMR, the “small modular reactor,” a uranium-power fission plant that is lots smaller than giants like Millstone or the closed Indian Point facility.  SMR boosters say assembly line construction of SMRs will save lots of money and that they are so fail-safe they need little or no safety areas around them.  
The problem is corporations planning to build SMRs are mostly start-up companies that have had no experience in nuclear power at all, which have no orders, no revenue, no profit, and no actual reactors.  Not a single SMR has been built in the U.S.  If fact, there are only three in the whole world.  Nuclear power has an impressive track record of being incredibly slow to bring online (17 years on average) and has a consistent record of being many times more expensive than initially planned.
Take the example of NuScale Energy.  It began as a university research project. In 2020 it was the first (and only) SMR to receive U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) design approval. It received $600 million from the U.S. Department of Energy.  NuScale planned to build reactors in Idaho and go online in 2030.  But costs started to skyrocket, partners pulled out and the whole project was cancelled.  Its stock price has gone down over 80% in the last year.
One huge and obvious problem with fission is radioactive waste.  In the nuclear power process, radioactive uranium is mined, then enriched and formed into rods, and the uranium goes through a process that splits its atoms and gives off energy. That’s done until the rods are no longer productive.  Then they are classified as “spent.” However, spent rods are incredibly radioactive and intensely hot.  So these rods are put in cooling ponds of the facility for years.  Then they have to be stored indefinitely because there’s no agreed upon way to dispose of them permanently.
Nuclear power waste has been around for more than 80 years, but in all that time there has been no way found to discard it. There was a plan to put 90,000 tons of high-level radioactive waste deep under Yucca Mountain in Nevada, but state leadership became vehemently against it. Nevada’s official position is that the area is “seismically and volcanically active, porous and incapable of geologically containing the waste.”  The Yucca Mountain “repository” was cancelled 15 years ago.  
The Trump Administration is trying to open “campuses” that would both create nuclear power and take in nuclear waste from all over the country and put it deep underground. Some legislatures support the idea but once the citizenry realizes what they’d be accepting expect tumultuous opposition.
At present the high-level and long-lasting radioactive waste produced by the nation’s civil nuclear power plants remains at the 75 sites — both operating and closed (like those at Indian Point) – where they were created and they’ll stay there forever.   They sit in the open air in steel/concrete casks.  That’s a risk because as we’ve found out by Russian attacks on Ukraine, regimes may be desperate or cruel enough to target those casks. 
Putin forces did just that in June of this year within the Chernobyl exclusionary zone, partially destroying a building used for receiving containers of radioactive waste.  There are ways to build facilities holding the casks to a HOSS standard (hardened on-site storage) similar to what is used in building nuclear missile silos, but they’ve never been required in the U.S.  So we’re just left with hope — hope that a foreign military or terrorist group won’t one day try to blow up a field of casks.
Another problem is that we’re finding that extreme heat can lead to nuclear reactor shutdowns.  During heat waves river water levels drop so the water level is too low to be  drawn upon for use in the plants.  Witness Hungary in August 2026.  It had to shut down its nuclear reactors due to low water levels for the first time in its history.  Romania shut down its nuclear plant, too.
We don’t need nuclear. What we do need is to stop rushing toward the climate cliff. We know how to do it.   Use solar, wind, water, batteries and conservation to meet our electrical needs and swiftly stop burning fossil fuels.
Stanley Heller is Administrator of Promoting Enduring Peace which was founded in New Haven in 1952. He’s also a member of Jewish Voice for Peace.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Cutting regulations should be more than an empty slogan
description: It’s election season, and therefore time for certain candidates for state office to trot out the well-worn campaign promise to “cut regulations.”
text:
It’s election season, and therefore time for certain candidates for state office to trot out the well-worn campaign promise to “cut regulations.” This sounds like a great idea — in general — but seldom if ever describes anything more specific. 
It’s not much different than promises to “cut taxes,” or “cut spending.” A goal so ill-defined is not a serious political or governing principle. It’s an empty slogan.
When I was a lawyer at the Massachusetts Turnpike Authority, I had a personal experience with this issue that is instructive. The Authority was a separate, quasi-public entity governed by a board of three members, with staggered terms, all appointed by the Governor. After I’d worked there for a short time, political control of the board turned over from Democrat to Republican – when one of the member’s terms expired and Gov. William Weld filled the vacancy with a Republican.
Soon thereafter, I was visited by a young staffer from the Governor’s office, who informed me that the Governor wanted the regulations that governed the use and policing of the Turnpike “reduced.” Now, the Turnpike was known for having more stringent requirements than applied to other roads state-wide. For instance, the transport of an over-sized load required a certain kind of state police escort, while these vehicles, as I recall, did not always require this extent of coverage on other interstate highways. There were other such regulations specific to the Turnpike that I don’t recall now, 30 years later.
Assuming the Turnpike Authority had good reason to adopt these regulations when they did, it would still have been a fine idea to compare the state DOT’s regulations with the Turnpike’s, and look for ways to reduce any regulatory burden imposed by the Turnpike Authority that could not be justified by, for instance, safety concerns.
However, that kind of review was not what they wanted. That would have required doing the hard, tedious, slow, work of government: reviewing and comparing the specific language and requirements of the regulations, gathering information from the state police, and the trucking industry and other stakeholders, to determine if the burden of the regulations outweighed the benefit of any safety benefits, for instance. Additionally, when public agencies propose revisions to their regulations, the law requires that the public be notified and provided an opportunity to comment, and that the agency respond to these comments on the record. 
Which is to say there’s a process, meant to ensure that government agencies do not act, in a term from Administrative Law, in ways that are “arbitrary and capricious.” To understand the gist of that legal standard, one need only observe what the Trump Administration does every day – that is what it means to govern in an arbitrary and capricious manner. The so-called DOGE effort is the most reckless example I have seen in my lifetime. (I am still waiting for my “DOGE check,” by the way.)
However, pressed into this task of “reducing regulations,” I questioned further how we were to measure this undefined “reduction” – by eliminating numbered provisions, number of pages, lines of text? Unsurprisingly, the staffer had no specific thoughts on this matter, other than to deliver the directive of “reducing” regulations. As I recall, I never heard another thing about it, and six months later I left the agency for a better opportunity. (Ironically, 20 years later I was a Deputy Secretary of Transportation in Massachusetts, when the state legislature and Democratic Gov. Deval Patrick implemented a transportation reform act. This comprehensive reorganization of the transportation agencies in Massachusetts eliminated the Turnpike as a separate entity entirely and absorbed it into the state DOT, ensuring that one set of state-wide regulations applied to all interstate highways in the state.)
So it’s all well and good to vow to cut regulations. And it certainly makes a great sound bite in a political ad. But it doesn’t really mean anything. Which regulations? And why?
Laws and regulations are adopted to insure our health, safety and welfare. Review of these regulations across all aspects of government should be a continuing effort, to identify ones that can be revised, simplified, or simply eliminated. And talking to the parties typically complaining of unnecessary burden, the businesses or individuals most affected, is the best place to start.
While candidates love to wield “cutting regulations” as a campaign slogan, the actual work of accomplishing this is more of an effort than they often seem willing to pursue once elected. All too often, it is simply an empty slogan, forgotten as soon as Election Day has passed.
Peter O’Connor, of Mystic, is a retired attorney and state and local government official.

name: Maryland Matters
title: 21% of poverty in Maryland driven by high housing costs, report says
description: Maryland is one of 10 states where high housing costs contribute the most to the state’s poverty level, according to a new report by the Pew Charitable Trusts, that attributes as much as 21% of Maryland's poverty to ita above-average housing costs.
text:
A new report says Maryland is among the states where high housing costs contribute most heavily to the state's poverty rate. (Photo Getty stock images)Maryland is one of 10 states where high housing costs contribute the most to the state’s poverty level, according to a new report by the Pew Charitable Trusts.
The report, released Tuesday, said approximately 21% of Maryland poverty is attributable to above-average housing costs, stretching the budgets of the state’s low-income families and offsetting positive impacts of anti-poverty measures such as federal food assistance.
The Pew report says that Maryland and other states face a severe housing shortage that drives up housing costs. It urges states to prioritize building new units, arguing that a 20% decline in rental costs could significantly reduce poverty rates.
“Not only does adding housing reduce rents, it reduces poverty as well because people have more wiggle room in their household budgets, and their limited incomes aren’t as strained,” said Alex Horowitz, project director on housing policy for Pew.
While Maryland officials have pushed some measures to speed up new housing, Horowitz said more could be done to chip away at the state’s nearly 100,000 housing unit shortage.
“Maryland’s taken a couple small steps to make it easier to build housing,” Horowitz said. “Clearly taken some steps in the right direction, but not to the degree that would be needed to dig out of a housing shortage.”


According to state data based on the U.S. Census Bureau’s Supplemental Poverty Measure in 2024, about 169,000 Maryland children fell below the poverty line that year, or 12.4% of that group. Approximately 400,000 Marylanders aged 18 to 64 fall below the threshold, or 10.6% of that age group, while 12% of those 65 and older, or about 131,000 people, fell below the threshold.


The report — “The Housing Shortage Is a Major Driver of Poverty” — is based on research by Zachary Parolin, a professor at the University of Oxford in England, who looked at 2023 housing costs and identified states where the greatest share of poverty was due to high rent.
Horowitz explained that the figures were calculated by looking at states with current affordability challenges and estimating how poverty may improve if rents were closer to the national average rental costs.
“Maryland’s median rent right now is over $1,800. In the U.S., the median rent is a little under $1,400. So if Maryland added enough housing so that its median rent was in line with the national average … how much of its poverty is caused by that gap?” Horowitz said. “The answer, 21% of Maryland’s poverty is attributable to that.”
Other states with the highest share of housing-driven poverty include Hawaii, California, New Jersey, Massachusetts, Colorado, Connecticut, New York and New Hampshire, as well as the District of Columbia.
Hawaii topped the list, with the highest percentage of poverty driven by housing costs, at 34%. High housing costs are responsible for up to 42% of Hawaii’s child poverty, the report said.
Meanwhile, Maryland had the seventh-highest percentage of housing=driven poverty, at 21%. The report shows that 17% of Maryland’s child poverty is driven by housing costs, lower than most of the other states.
But the report says that efforts to boost housing supply can reduce poverty, pointing to cities that built so much new housing that inflation-adjusted rents have fallen by 20% in cities like Austin, Texas, and Minneapolis.
If Maryland were similarly able to reduce inflation-adjusted rent by 20%, the state’s poverty rate could fall by 24% overall and for children, according to the analysis.
“Housing costs are the biggest line item in most families’ budgets and so each dollar that goes to higher rents isn’t available to cover food, transportation, clothing, healthcare needs and day-to-day spending,” Horowitz said. “That’s why the poverty threshold is so sensitive to housing costs. High housing costs crowd out essential spending.”
What type of housing to build is a question for research analysts and lawmakers. Horowitz says that while subsidized housing is still necessary, even building new housing for higher income households can create an “escalator effect” that helps the affordability challenge at large.
“When there’s a lot of housing getting built, the escalator moves up, and people trade into better options,” Horowitz said. “High-income residents tend to move into new homes, and that frees up the homes that they were living in before. Those tend to be occupied by people whose incomes are a little lower, and so on.”
Financing, permit challenges stand in the way of building new housing, officials say

But a significant housing shortage leads to the opposite effect, where lower-income households are frozen out of housing options and face increased risks of homelessness.
“When there’s not a lot of housing getting built, the escalator moves down, and people trade down to find something they can afford,” Horowitz said. “It’s important to build subsidized housing too and the lowest-income residents still need housing choice vouchers.”
The report suggests that lawmakers reform permitting and zoning laws to allow faster approval of new builds.
Removing red tape in permit approvals has been a legislative priority for Gov. Wes Moore during his term, though his efforts often run up against county officials who may be skeptical of policies that weaken local authority.
As lawmakers prepare for the 2027 legislative session, Horowitz suggests that they continue to push bills that encourage new housing options, such as  legislation that makes it easier to convert office spaces into residential units, increase production of smaller “starter homes” homes on smaller lots, or remove the limit on how many non-relatives can live in a residential unit.
“When not enough housing gets built, low-income residents get frozen out, and there’s not much to choose from,” he said. “Anti-poverty programs are crucial, but rising rents are consuming a lot of the dollars that we’re spending on those programs, and that’s money that households need in their pockets to cover day-to-day bills.”

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: South Dakota governor’s response to diesel prices may not help producers, ag leader says
description: South Dakota’s Republican governor issued an executive order to blunt the impact of high diesel prices for farmers during harvest season, but an agricultural leader in the state said the order “doesn’t do anything” to help. Gov. Larry Rhoden’s order allows producers to haul crops, livestock and other agricultural products at 10% above weight restrictions […]
text:
Andrew Streff drives his combine while harvesting soybeans on Sept. 29, 2025, near Salem, South Dakota. (Photo by Joshua Haiar/South Dakota Searchlight)South Dakota’s Republican governor issued an executive order to blunt the impact of high diesel prices for farmers during harvest season, but an agricultural leader in the state said the order “doesn’t do anything” to help.
Gov. Larry Rhoden’s order allows producers to haul crops, livestock and other agricultural products at 10% above weight restrictions and suspends a $25 overweight trip permit.
Agricultural producers are typically only allowed to haul crop loads that are 10% overweight when they’re going from harvesting in the fields to the grain bins. The order expands the 10% allowance beyond crops and covers more trips, according to Josie Harms, a Rhoden spokesperson.
“Farmers haul from their bins to elevators, feedlots, ethanol plants, or other facilities and haul other products back (like dried distillers’ grain from ethanol plants),” Harms said in a message to South Dakota Searchlight. “This also applies to more than just crops, as all agricultural commodities are covered, including livestock, milk, and other commodities not from a field.”
Doug Sombke, president of the South Dakota Farmers Union, said a neighboring state’s response to the nation’s skyrocketing diesel prices was “a step in the right direction” that could have a greater impact.
Last week, Nebraska Republican Gov. Jim Pillen announced a 90-day pause on diesel taxes for producers hauling during the harvest season. Producers can submit fuel receipts to be refunded for diesel taxes over the coming months. Pillen also issued a separate executive order allowing ag producers to haul at 25% above the weight limit.
Gov. Pillen announces 90-day pause on diesel taxes for Nebraska ag producers

“It’s way better than what we’re being offered,” Sombke said.
Most trucks hold about 250 gallons of fuel, but some can hold more, Sombke said. Filling up an empty tank at the state’s $6 average per-gallon diesel price, he said, won’t be counteracted by pausing a $25 permit on overweight hauls.
“Not even close,” he said.
But South Dakota’s governor doesn’t have the same power to suspend the diesel tax that Nebraska’s governor does during an emergency, according to Harms. In South Dakota, the governor can only suspend administrative rules, she said. State law sets the tax at 28 cents per gallon.
Rhoden’s legal and policy teams are “reviewing potential action by the Trump Administration, as well as actions taken by other states, to see if there is opportunity for South Dakota to take further steps to provide flexibility for farmers,” according to a Monday news release.
Charlie Johnson, a Lake County organic grain producer, is concerned about heavier loads damaging roadways. The plan to allow overweight trucks to haul on public roads could end up costing the state more in the long term when it comes to maintenance and repairs for those roadways, Johnson told Searchlight.
The ongoing war in Iran and a volatile tariff policy from the Trump administration have had long-lasting effects on producers’ bottom lines, he said.
In a social media post, Johnson criticized Rhoden’s directive as an effort to “win votes in the days before the general election.”
“What Rhoden really should be doing is speaking out for farmers by taking the president to task for what he’s done to this state and to our farmers economically,” Johnson said.
Democratic governor candidate reacts to changes
Rhoden, who became governor in 2025 after former Gov. Kristi Noem resigned, is running to keep the job. Democratic challenger Dan Ahlers, a former state lawmaker from Dell Rapids, said “there are other things that we could be doing that would in the long run” to ease the burden on ag producers in the state.
He wants to see South Dakota producers and policy leaders standing up against federal policies like the ongoing war in Iran, tariffs and importing beef from foreign countries. Those actions are creating economic strain for producers, Ahlers said.
“I think that’s where the governor of South Dakota, along with producers, show up and have those conversations,” Ahlers said. “Getting photo ops with the president just isn’t good enough. We need to actually be out there, speaking on their behalf and working with our members of Congress.”
In a debate with Ahlers at the start of the month, Rhoden said he disagrees with President Trump’s push to import beef from other countries.
Ian Fury, a spokesperson for Rhoden’s campaign, told Searchlight that Rhoden “has always said good policy makes good politics.” He said Rhoden understands that diesel prices have an impact on farmers, especially during harvest season, and that he’s already received calls from producers who support Monday’s executive order.
Fury did not immediately respond to request for comment on the Iran war or tariffs.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Rep. Mike Kennedy, a doctor, says the nation doesn’t need a surgeon general
description: Kennedy said states should have more authority over health matters and the U.S. does not need a surgeon general.
text:
Utah Rep. Mike Kennedy is pictured at a speaking event hosted by the Hinckley Institute of Politics at the University of Utah and the Sutherland Institute of Politics on Tuesday, Sept. 29, 2026. (Annie Knox/Utah News Dispatch)In a wide-ranging forum Tuesday, Utah Rep. Mike Kennedy said he sees promise for enhanced use of artificial intelligence in medicine and believes states, not the federal government, should have broad authority over matters of public health and disease control. 
Kennedy, a first-term Republican congressman representing Utah’s current 3rd Congressional District, made the comments in a Q&A session hosted by the University of Utah’s Hinckley Institute of Politics and the conservative Sutherland Institute. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
In response to a student’s question regarding the post of U.S. Surgeon General that has been unfilled for nearly two years, Kennedy said, “I’m warning you right now, that position shouldn’t be there. We don’t need a chief doctor. If anybody understands this, you young folks should understand this.” 
The surgeon general, a role established more than 150 years ago, can issue advisories warning about public health threats. Surgeons general have also advocated for vaccination, though they don’t set vaccine policies.  
President Donald Trump’s third and current pick for surgeon general this term, Nicole Saphier, spoke in favor of immunization earlier this month during a Senate confirmation hearing. The committee didn’t take a vote on her nomination, which also requires approval from the full Senate. 
The left-leaning Center for Science in the Public Interest has joined other groups in calling the post “a critical role as the nation’s chief health communicator” informing the nation about the best available science. 
Kennedy, a physician, said communities throughout the country experienced the COVID-19 pandemic in very different ways and he believes states are in a better position to tailor their own responses to such outbreaks. 
“New York City had significant problems, but Sanpete County in the state of Utah? Totally different world with COVID, even though it’s still the same virus,” he said. 
Kennedy said he sold his medical practice when he was elected to Congress, but still sees patients in Utah and uses notetaking and transcription software to make notes of their conditions. He sees artificial intelligence as a tool that could help people analyze aspects of their own health, he said, and could also assist doctors, physician assistants and nurse practitioners by making suggestions to them. 
Kennedy is sponsoring federal legislation seeking to limit gender-affirming care for teenagers and extending the timeline for patients to sue a healthcare provider if they later regret the treatment. 
He carried a similar Utah law while a state senator in 2023 and said Monday he sees the measures as helpful and a recognition of the long-term effects of some treatments, but said he does not support efforts to have doctors jailed for the care they provide. 
Critics of the bills have pointed out that about 1% of those who undergo gender-affirming surgeries later regretted the decision, according to the American Journal of Surgery. They have countered that surgeries for minors are exceedingly rare and that a study commissioned by Utah lawmakers found treatments effective in terms of improving mental health and other outcomes. 
Kennedy, who is running for election in Utah’s newly drawn 4th Congressional District, faces Democrat Jonny Larsen, libertarian Taylor Wright and unaffiliated candidate Steven Burt in the Nov. 3 general election.

name: Washington State Standard
title: WA state lawmaker to resign 3 days before the election
description: In a surprise announcement, Republican state Rep. Skyler Rude of Walla Walla, said Tuesday that he will resign from office days before the election to start a new job with Democratic Secretary of State Steve Hobbs. Rude, a moderate Republican, said he will step down Oct. 31 and begin work the next day as Hobbs’ […]
text:
Rep. Skyler Rude giving a speech on the House floor. (Photo by Jacquelyn Jimenez Romero/Washington State Standard)In a surprise announcement, Republican state Rep. Skyler Rude of Walla Walla, said Tuesday that he will resign from office days before the election to start a new job with Democratic Secretary of State Steve Hobbs.
Rude, a moderate Republican, said he will step down Oct. 31 and begin work the next day as Hobbs’ legislative director.
The timing means Rude’s name will be on the ballot for the Nov. 3 election. Until Tuesday, he had been expected to win a fifth term against a Democratic challenger, Derek Sarley.
Rude said in an interview that the job opportunity arose after ballots arrived for the August primary and the offer became final a few days ago. He said he considered and decided against waiting until after the election to tell constituents in the 16th Legislative District which encompasses parts of four counties, Walla Walla, Franklin, Benton and Grant.
“The timing is difficult given the proximity to the general election. The politically safer decision would be to announce after the election,” he said in a statement. “I entered office committed to acting honestly and transparently, and I’m not going to change that commitment now as I complete my elected service.”
If Rude wins, Republicans will have essentially two vacancies to fill — one to complete the lawmaker’s current term and one that would begin in January when the new two-year legislative term starts.
If Sarley wins, the GOP could appoint someone to serve the final weeks of Rude’s term until the Democrat is sworn in.
Sarley said late Tuesday that even though it had seemed like the incumbent had not been actively campaigning he was “quite surprised” by the news.
Sarley now hopes voters understand that if Rude wins, they will have no say in who is appointed to the job. That’s up to Republican precinct officers and elected officials in four counties.
“I don’t think this is the kind of decision that should be made by county commissioners,” he said.
Rude wants his party to retain control of the seat.
“Voters who want a Republican appointed to replace me should vote for me,” he said. House Republicans, he continued, are “fighting hard to make Washington a more affordable, safer place to live” even as Democrats outnumber them 59-39 in the chamber.
“An imbalance that large diminishes the voices of moderate Democrats and Republicans alike,” he said. “It gives the most extreme voices outsized influence and reduces the need to build consensus on public policy.”
Rude won his House seat in 2018. He is the assistant floor leader for his caucus and the ranking Republican on the House Education Committee. He also serves on the Appropriations and the Postsecondary Education and Workforce committees.
In addition to leaving office, he will be shutting down a stagecoach tour business he ran in the Walla Walla Valley.
“Serving our district for eight years has been the honor of my life,” he said. “Leaving is bittersweet, but I’m grateful that my next role brings together two things I care deeply about: Washington’s history and the integrity of our elections. The Secretary of State’s office safeguards our state’s historical records and helps administer the elections on which our democracy depends.”

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Alaska’s Bristol Bay salmon return about average this year, with higher prices paid to fishers
description: Alaska’s Bristol Bay region, site of the world’s biggest sockeye salmon runs, produced a total harvest this year that was a bit smaller than the 20-year average but fetched more dollars for fishers, according to a state summary. The 2026 sockeye salmon run totaled 45.7 million fish, making this the first year since 2014 that […]
text:
Sockeye salmon returning to spawning grounds in Katmai National Park and Preserve crowd together on Aug. 12, 2021. Katmai is part of the Bristol Bay watershed, which had a nearly average sockeye run this year after several years of massive runs. (Photo by Lian Law/National Park Service)Alaska’s Bristol Bay region, site of the world’s biggest sockeye salmon runs, produced a total harvest this year that was a bit smaller than the 20-year average but fetched more dollars for fishers, according to a state summary.
The 2026 sockeye salmon run totaled 45.7 million fish, making this the first year since 2014 that the run was below 50 million, according to the Alaska Department of Fish and Game preliminary summary, released last week. While the total run was 4% above the preseason forecast, the total catch of 30.1 million sockeye was 7% below the preseason forecast, according to Fish and Game.
“This is by no means a small run,” said Stacy Vega, a department biologist. Massive runs cannot continue forever, she said. “Eventually, it’s got to come down,” she said.
Additionally, Bristol Bay commercial fishers harvested 10,700 Chinook, 457,100 chum, 55,100 coho and 666,700 pink salmon.
The total price paid to harvesters for all salmon species harvests, an amount known as exvessel value, was $264 million, the department said. That was 21% above the 20-year average of $207.8 million, the department said in its preliminary summary.
The total sockeye run was 8% below the 20-year average of 49.6 million fish according to the department. The total harvest was 3% lower than the 20-year average, the department said.
But those 20-year averages reflect some years of huge runs, including the record run of 79 million sockeye in 2022, said Vega.
That puts the 2026 salmon season into perspective, said Vega, who focuses on the Egegik and Ugashik rivers, which are among several Bristol Bay salmon rivers.
In many ways, it was a very average year for Bristol Bay sockeye salmon.
The sockeye in that region generally range from 4 to 6 years in age, splitting their lives between freshwater and ocean habitats, and there was a fairly even distribution among age groups this year, Vega said. The most common age groups are those that spend two or three years in the ocean, she said.
The average sockeye size was 5 pounds, about equal to the average over the last five years and above the record-low average size of 4.53 pounds reported in 2024.
Salmon in Bristol Bay, other parts of Alaska and around the North Pacific have been declining in size over the past decades.
For Bristol Bay, the shrinking size has been correlated in part to big runs, Vega said.
“Usually, when we have a really big run, the fish are smaller,” she said. More fish in the ocean competing for food tends to result in smaller fish, she said.
The season’s run and harvest totals came very close to the department’s preseasons forecasts, a gratifying result for biologists who know that preseason predictions are difficult and always different from reality, Vega said.
Biologists say early indications are that next year’s Bristol Bay sockeye run will be similar in size to this year’s run. But the department has not yet released its official 2027 forecast.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Minneapolis council advances proposal to mandate human drivers in robotaxis
description: The Minneapolis City Council voted 7-4 to advance a proposal on Tuesday to require human “safety monitors” earning minimum pay rates in the drivers’ seats of autonomous robotaxis like Alphabet’s Waymo and Amazon’s Zoox. The proposal aims to protect the jobs of the state’s roughly 10,000 rideshare drivers, the majority of whom are Black and […]
text:
An autonomous vehicle operated by Waymo is displayed outside the Pennsylvania Capitol in Harrisburg on June 24, 2026. (Photo by Peter Hall/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)The Minneapolis City Council voted 7-4 to advance a proposal on Tuesday to require human “safety monitors” earning minimum pay rates in the drivers’ seats of autonomous robotaxis like Alphabet’s Waymo and Amazon’s Zoox.
The proposal aims to protect the jobs of the state’s roughly 10,000 rideshare drivers, the majority of whom are Black and immigrant men, according to a 2024 state study.
Its authors say the proposal is part of a larger fight against Big Tech rolling into cities in regulatory gray areas — as Uber and Lyft did a decade ago — and the widespread job losses many fear from artificial intelligence, from Uber drivers to coders to lawyers.
“(Tech companies) do displace. They do exploit. And without measures like what we’re taking up today, we will experience the collateral and negative impacts of technological advances,” said City Council Member Robin Wonsley, the chief author of the ordinance.
Minneapolis Mayor Jacob Frey is expected to veto the measure if it passes a final City Council vote, and it’s unlikely the 13-member council will be able to muster the nine votes necessary to override him.
A spokeswoman for the mayor said he considers it a “back-door ban, and a bait for the state to come in and preempt us.”
That’s what happened the last time the Minneapolis City Council took on Big Tech rideshare companies. In 2024, the council overrode a mayoral veto to pass minimum pay rates for Uber and Lyft drivers despite threats by the companies to cut service in the city. The Legislature then stripped cities of the power to enact minimum driver rates as part of a deal that raised driver pay while keeping Uber and Lyft operating in the state.
The robotaxi ordinance, even if passed, wouldn’t take effect until October 2027, which Wonsley said gives the Legislature more time to consider statewide regulations.
Supporters of autonomous vehicles say it simply doesn’t make sense to require a human to sit behind the wheel of a car that drives itself, pointing to cities that already have autonomous taxis such as San Francisco, Austin and Atlanta.
Waymo, which opposes the proposal, began testing its technology in Minnesota last fall. The company says it currently provides more than 500,000 fully autonomous rides every week in 15 major U.S. cities, none of which require human monitors.
Reducing accidents caused by distracted, sleepy, impaired and careless drivers is perhaps the greatest promise of robotaxi companies, though experts caution the safety risks of autonomous vehicles are not fully understood. Nor have the vehicles been widely tested across difficult driving conditions on icy city streets and congested highways.
Safety goes beyond car accidents. Proponents note that autonomous vehicles eliminate the risk of sexual assault and abuse. Uber, for instance, received more than 400,000 reports of sexual assault and misconduct over a five-year period from 2017 to 2022, according to court records reported by the New York Times. Uber said about 75% of reports were for “less serious” conduct, such as flirting or comments on appearance.
Alec Smith told the council he worries about his daughter’s safety because she has severe physical disabilities and cognitive impairments, and needs to be driven to medical appointments.
“There’s no reason to require some of the most vulnerable among us to be driven around by total strangers, and it really hurts their independence,” Smith said.
Drivers and their advocates say they abhor misconduct, and they note driverless cars present their own safety risks. Robotaxis have shown a propensity to get stranded and block emergency vehicles, as hundreds did last December when a blackout in San Francisco knocked out traffic signals.
Plus, drivers do more than turn the wheel and press the gas: They can help elderly riders with their bags and luggage, troubleshoot navigation during construction and inclement weather, and respond to emergencies and accidents.
They’re also local taxpayers and consumers, who spend their wages here in Minnesota.
“I think we impact the city, and for us not to be working, that would impact the city,” Mardice Washington, an Uber and Lyft driver, told the council.
Some disabled people say Uber and Lyft drivers don’t always live up to that ideal of community service, however. Jennifer Dunnam, president of the National Federation of the Blind of Minnesota, said people who use service dogs have to budget in extra time for trips to account for drivers canceling on them.
Ultimately, the decision to give consumers more choices or protect jobs became the dividing line for members.
“Job loss or options … It’s a no-brainer,” said Council Member Jamal Osman, a co-author of the ordinance.
Council Member Pearll Warren went the other way, using the kind of colorful — and in this case, flavorful — argument that’s become a trademark during her short time on the council.
“Just because I don’t like peanut butter and jelly sandwiches doesn’t mean that I’m going to put an ordinance out there that says no one should eat peanut butter and jelly sandwiches,” Warren said. “There’s way mo’ ways than the way that you got.”
Voting in favor of the ordinance were Council Members Wonsley, Osman, Aisha Chughtai, Jason Chavez, Elliott Payne, Aurin Chowdhury and Soren Stevenson. Voting against were Council Members Warren, LaTrisha Vetaw, Linea Palmisano and Michael Rainville. Council Member Elizabeth Shaffer, who voiced opposition to the ordinance, was absent for the vote as was Council Member Jamison Whiting.

name: Daily Montanan
title: Fish, Wildlife and Parks euthanizes 14 black bears after finding them ‘extremely food conditioned’
description: Montana Fish, Wildlife and Parks game wardens captured and euthanized 14 black bears near Bozeman after investigators found animals that were “extremely food conditioned” and unafraid of people at a property north of the city, the agency said Tuesday in a news release. FWP said wardens and staff responded to a report of “supplemental feeding” […]
text:
Black bear gathering huckleberries in the west boulder campground on the Yellowstone District of the Custer Gallatin National Forest during the fall of 2024. Photo taken September 9, 2024. (USDA Forest Service photo by Brandon Yoder.)Montana Fish, Wildlife and Parks game wardens captured and euthanized 14 black bears near Bozeman after investigators found animals that were “extremely food conditioned” and unafraid of people at a property north of the city, the agency said Tuesday in a news release.
FWP said wardens and staff responded to a report of “supplemental feeding” of wild black bears on the property. On Sept. 24 and 25, investigators found bears there that were used to getting fed and being around people.
FWP said it euthanized the bears due to safety concerns. It also took one cub to FWP’s Montana WILD facility in Helena for possible placement in a zoo.
The investigation into why the bears were on the property is ongoing, the agency said.
FWP region spokesperson Morgan Jacobsen said he could not confirm whether the agency had one or multiple suspects under investigation.
He said he doesn’t know of any other case where FWP has had to kill as many bears, although he didn’t have a historical record immediately available.
“But 14 bears at one property is not normal,” Jacobsen said.
State law prohibits providing supplemental feed to game animals, including bears, FWP said, citing Montana law.
“These bears were unafraid of humans and stopped relying on natural foods, which created a human safety risk. It’s very unfortunate they had to be euthanized,” said game warden Capt. Josh Leonard in a statement.
A person convicted of a violation may be fined as much as $1,000 or imprisoned for as much as six months, or both, state statute says. It also says the person may have to forfeit any hunting, fishing or trapping license for a period of time set by the court.
“When bears become accustomed to finding or receiving food from urban and residential areas, they lose the desire and ability to forage in natural, healthy ways,” the department said in the news release. “This behavior cannot be corrected through rehabilitation or relocation.”
The result puts humans at risk from bears that start looking for food near or inside homes, the news release said.
“Zoo placement is a very limited option that’s not always possible,” FWP said.
The agency said euthanizing the animals is a last resort.
FWP directed people to educational information, resources and events on bear safety on its website.
It said people can help prevent conflicts with bears by not feeding them, and by keeping garbage, bird feeders, pet food and other attractants secured.
The department also advised people to report bears attempting to access garbage or other food sources near homes to the agency as soon as possible. That way, FWP can undertake “corrective management” before problematic bear behavior becomes a habit.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Key lawmakers suggest income taxes cover homestead property tax credit
description: WARSAW, Ind. — About 300 Hoosiers showed up Tuesday night in Warsaw to hear a pitch headlined by three high-ranking legislators about ending “property taxes on the home you live in.” Another dozen lawmakers also attended, and the room also had local government officials worried about revenue cuts and homeowners worried about keeping their homes. […]
text:
A crowd of about 300 Hoosiers attended a meeting to hear a plan to eliminate property taxes for owner-occupied homes. The event was Sept. 29, 2026 in Warsaw. (Photo by Niki Kelly/Indiana Capital Chronicle)WARSAW, Ind. — About 300 Hoosiers showed up Tuesday night in Warsaw to hear a pitch headlined by three high-ranking legislators about ending “property taxes on the home you live in.”
Another dozen lawmakers also attended, and the room also had local government officials worried about revenue cuts and homeowners worried about keeping their homes.
A flyer for the event started circulating in August but those involved remained mum, until now.
Sen. Ryan Mishler, R-Mishawaka, started by explaining that proposals to completely eliminate property taxes simply aren’t realistic because of the $54 billion in local debt backed statewide by the revenue. He chairs the appropriations committee in the Indiana Senate and is a fiscal leader in the chamber.
Instead, Mishler introduced a solution he said already exists: local governments can increase their local income tax rate now and use that to give owner-occupied homes a full 100% credit on property taxes, phased in over a five-year period.
Mishler said all but 14 counties have capacity now to cover that full amount and those counties will reach that over time due to reforms the Legislature passed in 2025, also known as Senate Enrolled Act 1.
That new law means local units will see their property taxes grow at a smaller rate and many local officials and residents are concerned about cuts to services.
Sen. Ryan Mishler, left, and Sen. Chris Garten address a crowd of about 300 people in Warsaw on Sept. 29, 2026. (Photo by Niki Kelly/Indiana Capital Chronicle)
Mishler gave the example of Kosciusko County needing to cover $44 million in homestead property taxes.
“You still get a property tax bill because, again, remember you can’t eliminate it because of the bonds,” he said. “But if you have a 100% credit, the bill is zero.”
The only caveat would be if a community approved a referendum for additional property taxes for a school district or other entity.
Mishler said a credit avoids the shifting of the taxes to other classes of property, such as agriculture or business.
“This really gives the locals the ability to make that decision. You know, it’s their money. It’s their decision to make, and it’s already there. So, we don’t really do anything legislatively to allow them to raise bills,” he said. “So that’s it. The key thing here is to simplify. It would take it down to zero.”
Property taxes on owner-occupied homes amounted to nearly $4.1 billion, or 38%, of the $10.6 billion in statewide property taxes billed during 2025, according to a Legislative Services Agency report.
The trio of legislators took questions from the crowd, which included several people pushing back on the idea and others saying they aren’t doing enough.
“When the state has excess revenue why aren’t you kicking some of that revenue back to the counties?” asked Mike Felker. “It’s public money.”
Left to right: Sen. Ryan Mishler, Rep. Craig Snow and Sen. Chris Garten talk before a property tax event in Warsaw Indiana on Sept. 29, 2026. (Photo by Niki Kelly/Indiana Capital Chronicle)
Another person said, “you’re telling us locally take care of yourselves” and argued that a large part of local property tax use is for public safety.
Sen. Chris Garten, R-Charlestown, responded “if I’m a taxpayer I think anyone here who is a local elected official should have to justify why you need more money out of my pocket. That’s the case you make to your taxpayers.”
Garten is set to become the next Senate president pro tem after the November election.
Mishler ended the event by noting that he personally would likely pay more in income taxes than he would save on property taxes because he has downsized his home.
“All I’m doing is putting together something to answer those people who have reached out — something that can actually work … it’s good policy for everyone as a whole,” he said.
Another proposal from a Republican legislator would eliminate all property taxes and replace that revenue by extending the state’s 7% sales tax to include a vast array of currently untaxed services such as haircuts, construction labor costs and lawyer fees.
Rep. Craig Snow, R-Winona Lake, said lawmakers in 2025 began moving property taxes from a levy-based system to a rate-based system. And he hopes another step can be taken in the 2027 session. He is vice chair of the House Ways and Means Committee, which handles tax code legislation.
“We don’t have it all figured out, but we did take the right step to move forward in that fashion,” Snow said. “It’s going to take time to get us there. We’re going to land the plane at some point, but we’re looking at three or four years.”

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Minnesota Truth Council concludes public testimony on Operation Metro Surge
description: A council tasked with documenting the harms of — and resistance to — the federal government’s immigration crackdown held its final public meeting Tuesday in Rochester.  Gov. Tim Walz established the Minnesota Truth Council by executive order in March and selected former Hennepin County judge Peter Cahill — best known as the judge in the […]
text:
Minnesota Truth Council Chair Peter Cahill and Vice Chair Jennifer Prestholdt of The Advocates for Human Rights listen to testimony during the first full meeting of the Minnesota Truth Council on Wednesday, Aug. 26, 2026. (Photo by Madison McVan/Minnesota Reformer)A council tasked with documenting the harms of — and resistance to — the federal government’s immigration crackdown held its final public meeting Tuesday in Rochester. 
Gov. Tim Walz established the Minnesota Truth Council by executive order in March and selected former Hennepin County judge Peter Cahill — best known as the judge in the murder trial of former Minneapolis police officer Derek Chauvin — to lead the council. 
Truth commissions are a common practice in the aftermath of human rights abuses committed by governments — for example, in Argentina in the wake of a military dictatorship, and in South Africa following the end of apartheid.
Tuesday’s hearing, the first and only outside of the Twin Cities, focused on federal policies and systems contributing to harm, featuring testimony from former federal officials, legal experts, immigrant support groups and immigrants affected by the operation. 
A former high-ranking Immigration and Customs Enforcement official in the Biden administration, Claire Trickler-McNulty, called Operation Metro Surge “a travesty.”
Minnesota Truth Council begins process of documenting impact of federal immigration operations

“Too many systems failed at once, and they failed far too easily because the Department of Homeland Security was filled with structural flaws that have never been corrected, and because this administration was willing to exploit them,” Trickler-McNulty said. 
One flaw, Trickler-McNulty said, is that previous administrations prioritized the arrest of people who posed a public safety threat — but that was an executive choice and a result of budget constraints, rather than a law passed by Congress. So nothing is stopping the Trump administration from targeting people without criminal records, or those who have lived in the U.S. for a long time. 
(Congressional Republicans have accused Trickler-McNulty of “working to effectively abolish ICE from the inside.”)
Other speakers addressed the politicization of the Justice Department; the increase of racial profiling and Supreme Court decisions allowing it; the rollback of protections and services for unaccompanied immigrant children; and, the targeting of refugees for deportation, among other topics. 
Ryan Wood, a former assistant chief immigration judge who oversaw the immigration court at Fort Snelling, recounted his decision to retire in January 2025, just after President Donald Trump took office for his second term. 
“I saw the writing on the wall,” Wood said, as the top leadership of the immigration court system resigned and were replaced by people with little or no relevant experience. 
Immigration courts are part of the executive branch, and the Trump administration has engaged in a systematic purge of immigration judges who are likely to grant immigrants relief, such as freedom from detention while their cases work through the system. Those judges were replaced by people who back the president’s mass deportation efforts, and who order deportations at much higher rates. 
The truth council will include policy recommendations at the local, state and federal level to prevent another Operation Metro Surge in the future. 
“Independence is the first reform that I would recommend,” Wood said. 
The Advocates for Human Rights, a Minnesota-based nonprofit that consults on human rights issues worldwide, is staffing the commission and writing the council’s report. A preliminary report is due at the end of October, and a final report by Dec. 1. 
Cahill, the council chair, said he had invited Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and Attorney General Todd Blanche to appear but did not receive a response.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Report: Minnesota’s home insurance rate rose more than any other state in first half of 2026
description: Minnesota home insurance rates rose steeply in the first six months of 2026, up 13% from the end of 2025, according to a report from insurance comparison website Insurify. Minnesotans continue to see the biggest rate increase in the country, with some Minnesota counties seeing a spike of 20% in just six months. The increase […]
text:
Arcus roll cloud over farm land at the front of a storm in Luverne, Minnesota. Damage from storms is contributing to rising homeowner insurance costs in the state. (Photo by John Finney/Getty Images)Minnesota home insurance rates rose steeply in the first six months of 2026, up 13% from the end of 2025, according to a report from insurance comparison website Insurify.
Minnesotans continue to see the biggest rate increase in the country, with some Minnesota counties seeing a spike of 20% in just six months.
The increase of $457 brought the state’s average annual insurance premium to $3,987 as of June.
Report: Minnesota’s home insurance rates rose 34% in 2025, the highest increase in the nation

In 2023, the state had insurance rates below the national average; rates have surged since then, and now exceed the national average by over 30%, driven by hail and thunderstorms. Home insurance is more expensive in five states, including Florida, where rates are, on average, $8,486 a year.
The National Centers for Environmental Information estimates that Minnesota had $10.3 million in property damage from severe weather events from January to May. The vast majority took place on April 17, when five tornadoes struck southeastern Minnesota and caused over $9.7 million in property damage, according to NCEI estimates.
That’s still far less compared to the billions of dollars of damage in previous years, which led to losses for insurers and catapulted Minnesota’s home insurance premiums to some of the highest in the nation. In 2022, a hailstorm with golf ball-sized hail in some areas caused at least $2.6 billion in damages; a powerful 2023 thunderstorm resulted in at least $1.5 billion in damages from hail and wind.


Large hail could become more common as the climate warms: In 2024, Northern Illinois University researchers projected that warmer climates over the course of the century will melt smaller hailstones but also result in stronger updrafts producing larger hailstones.
Of the 10 counties in the nation with the highest premium increases in 2026 so far, five were in Minnesota: Le Sueur County, Watonwan County, Martin County, Hennepin County and Steele County, according to the Insurify data. Every county in Minnesota now has an average home insurance rate that’s higher than the national average.
At the same time that insurance premiums are rising, homeowners have found that insurance policies are covering less than expected — and roof repair costs are multiplying, CBS reported. The Better Business Bureau has also warned homeowners to beware of “storm chasers” —  scammy contractors knocking on doors after a storm damages homes and pressuring homeowners into contracts.
Insurify had projected Minnesota’s insurance rates to rise only 4% in 2026. The state’s rates have exceeded that in just the first six months of the year.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: North Dakota gives farmers a break on diesel as harvest ramps up
description: North Dakota farmers will get a break on surging diesel fuel prices as Gov. Kelly Armstrong on Tuesday issued an order allowing a lower-taxed version of diesel to be used on highways and not just in the field. North Dakota charges a tax of 23 cents per gallon on regular diesel fuel but only 4 […]
text:
Farm workers load beans into a grain truck Sept. 28, 2025, in Wells County, N.D. Diesel fuel used in trucks is usually taxed at a higher rate than diesel used in the tractor. A governor's executive order for the 2026 harvest means trucks can use lower-taxed diesel. (Photo by Lora Wobbema/For the North Dakota Monitor)North Dakota farmers will get a break on surging diesel fuel prices as Gov. Kelly Armstrong on Tuesday issued an order allowing a lower-taxed version of diesel to be used on highways and not just in the field.
North Dakota charges a tax of 23 cents per gallon on regular diesel fuel but only 4 cents per gallon on red-dyed diesel, which is normally only allowed for off-highway agricultural, industrial and railroad use.
Record diesel prices hit North Dakota farmers at the wrong time

Armstrong’s executive order temporarily expands the use of dyed diesel fuel to vehicles used in ag operations, such as hauling crops to a grain elevator or processing plant. It also can be used when hauling livestock, feed, seed, fertilizer and equipment.
The order is effective immediately and remains in place through Nov. 30, when fall harvest will be winding down. It does not affect the federal government’s 24.4-cent-per-gallon tax on diesel fuel.
The average price for diesel fuel in North Dakota was $6.17 on Tuesday, according to AAA. 
“Farmers burn more diesel during harvest than at any other time of year, and saving 19 cents per gallon can make a meaningful difference when margins are razor thin,” Agriculture Commissioner Doug Goehring said in a news release.
About 22% of North Dakota’s soybeans had been harvested as of Sunday, according to the National Agricultural Statistics Service. Corn harvest was 8% complete.
