name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Researchers say demographics, behavioral risks account for much of Iowa’s high cancer rates
description: After concluding year one of research into why Iowa has higher instances of cancer than other states, Iowa Department of Health and Human Services and the University of Iowa College of Public Health officials said their analysis found 76% of Iowa’s higher rates of five common types of cancer could be attributed to demographic and […]
text:
Jacob Oleson, an associate professor at the University of Iowa College of Public Health, shared details from a report compiled by UI researchers and the Iowa Department of Health and Human Services about the key factors driving Iowa's cancer rates at a news conference in Des Moines Sep. 29, 2026. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)After concluding year one of research into why Iowa has higher instances of cancer than other states, Iowa Department of Health and Human Services and the University of Iowa College of Public Health officials said their analysis found 76% of Iowa’s higher rates of five common types of cancer could be attributed to demographic and behavioral risk factors.
In 2025, Iowa lawmakers approved Gov. Kim Reynolds’ request to provide $1 million in funding for a year-long cancer research projected conducted by HHS and UI researchers to identify the key factors driving Iowa’s high cancer rates. Iowa has been one of the only states in the country where rates are rising for new instances of cancer. In 2026, the state had the second highest rate of cancer incidences in the country, and was one of only three states with a rising rate.
Preliminary data from the research project was first presented in February. Researchers concluded Iowa had higher rates of prostate, breast, lung cancer and melanoma, but found Iowa had a more comparable rate when compared to other states with similar rates of certain risk factors that increase instances of cancer — such as binge drinking, obesity and insurance rates, as well as certain demographic factors.
However, the research found Iowa had significantly higher instances of lung cancer and mortality rates when compared to the rates of other Midwestern states and nationally.
The updated report included more information about how demographic and behavioral risk factors might account for Iowa’s cancer rates. Edith Parker, Dean of the UI College of Public Health, said “selected risk factors explain approximately 76% of Iowa’s excess cancer burden across the five most common cancers.”
“The results suggest that prevention efforts targeting modifiable risk factors would reduce the number of excess cases of cancer in Iowa,” Parker said. “Counties and cancer groups with remaining excess cases may be influenced by additional factors not included in the current analysis.”
Even when accounting for expected excess cases based on behavioral risks like smoking, obesity and binge drinking, there were some specific groups that had higher than expected cancer rates. This included more cases of prostate cancer for men over age 50, higher rates of breast cancer for postmenopausal women, and more instances of melanoma amongst younger women.
For lung cancer, Jacob Oleson, an associate professor at the UI, said that when factoring in both smoking rates and potential radon exposure, all excess cases of cancer were explained for women, but that 13 counties have higher-than-expected lung cancer rates among men.
Researchers have not yet investigated the influence of genetic, environmental, or other factors and combinations on Iowa’s cancer rates. Parker said the next phase of the group’s research on environmental factors is expected to be more difficult.
“The data is not as readily available as it is for this, behavior risk factors,” Parker said. “For example, we don’t, in the state, monitor air quality in the community. So what we are looking at now is what data is available already. For example, most water systems, we do have data for that, and that comes with levels of monitoring.”
Researchers told lawmakers earlier in the year that Iowa does not collect information on state pesticide usage, which could contribute to cancer data, and said that although the state has robust systems for monitoring water quality and nitrate levels, unregulated private wells used by an estimated 300,000 Iowans could be the source of problems that would not be shown in the collected data.
Other researchers and public health experts have said a larger emphasis needs to be placed on mitigating dangers caused by environmental factors. The Harkin Institute for Public Policy and Citizen Engagement and the Iowa Environmental Council released a report in March — separate from the UI and HHS report — that found the five most common types of cancer in the state have connections to environmental risk factors like pesticides, per- or polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), nitrate and radon. The report also found a majority of cancer types associated with these factors are increasing in the state.
Robert Kruse, the Iowa State Medical Director, said while research will continue, the behavioral risk factor data shows areas where Iowans and state government can take action to decrease cancer rates in Iowa by limiting alcohol and tobacco consumption, protecting skin from UV exposure and testing homes for radon.
“Our responsibility is to act where the evidence is strong, while continuing to investigate where questions remain,” Kruse said. “And those two things are not in conflict. Good public health requires us to do both.”
Kruse also said $93 million of the $209 million in federal funding awarded to Iowa in year one of the Rural Health Transformation Program is going to cancer prevention, screening and treatment services. Iowa’s rural health care improvement plan, “Healthy Hometowns,” received funding through the federal program that was created to offset expected an estimated $137 billion decline in Medicaid spending due to the 2025 “One Big, Beautiful Bill” Act. He said over the next five years “we anticipate that investment approaching $240 million” for cancer-related services.
Kruse said the new investments will build on ongoing efforts to address and prevent cancer in the state.
“Iowa has longstanding cancer prevention control efforts across public health, across healthcare systems, local public health agencies, and community organizations throughout the state,” Kruse said. “That work ranges from tobacco prevention and cessation to breast, cervical, and colorectal cancer screening, to radon education, to strengthening systems that ensure an abnormal screening result leads to timely diagnostic follow-up.
“This work is also guided by the Iowa Cancer Plan, our statewide roadmap developed with partners from across public health, health systems, community organizations, researchers, and cancer survivors. The goal is to reduce cancer risk, improve early detection, strengthen treatment and survivorship, and reduce disparities in access and outcomes. Healthy Hometowns does not replace that work; it strengthens it.”

name: Rhode Island Current
title: URI to reconsider running its own payroll amid state’s Workday troubles
description: A colossal software overhaul of the University of Rhode Island’s (URI) administrative and payroll systems on track to launch next fall may need to change course after state officials asked university officials to possibly take over a big responsibility it previously told them not to pursue. URI began its transition to a more modern infrastructure […]
text:
The University of Rhode Island Board of Trustees meets in the Robert J. Higgins Welcome Center on Upper College Road on the Kingston campus. (URI photo)A colossal software overhaul of the University of Rhode Island’s (URI) administrative and payroll systems on track to launch next fall may need to change course after state officials asked university officials to possibly take over a big responsibility it previously told them not to pursue.
URI began its transition to a more modern infrastructure for its finance, human resources, payroll, budgeting, and faculty administration systems in January. Based around the Workday platform — the same software used by the state of Rhode Island to administer its payroll — the project is about halfway complete and is expected to launch in October 2027.
Abby Benson, URI’s vice president for administration and finance, told trustees during a Sept. 14 Finance and Facilities Committee meeting that the school has always managed its own administrative systems while still relying on the state for payroll.
But before the project began, URI had asked the state whether it should assume payroll processing duties for the university’s full-time employees — a decision URI needed to make early in the planning phase, so it would know whether to build around payroll or not.
“We had asked them that question explicitly a year ago, and they said no,” Benson told trustees.
After the trustees reviewed an outline of the Workday plans last November, URI embarked on its lengthy modernization process. It left payroll processing for its full-time employees to the state’s own Workday system, which experienced numerous problems after it debuted late last year.
The state’s Workday-based ERP rollout cost approximately $99 million and was completed late last year, with the firm Accenture responsible for the system’s implementation. The state’s transition from its older, often analog payroll system has led to paychecks with incorrect wages, overtime, holiday pay, benefits or deductions. There were also mislabeled W-2s which led to some state employees having to amend their tax filings multiple times during the height of tax season.
Earlier this month, the Department of Administration also attributed an almost yearlong lapse in updates to the state’s online payroll transparency portal to the ERP switchover. The portal, which provides easy lookup of any state employee’s wage and salary information, has not been updated since October 2025.
URI and state leaders meet once a month to discuss the school’s own Workday project. Recently, Benson told trustees, the university started talks with the state to determine whether the school should assume the payroll functions its system was not expecting to fulfill.
State officials have been “good partners,” Benson said. But the symbiotic relationship between the two payroll systems has generated some concern for the university, Benson suggested at the meeting: “I can’t say that there won’t be issues on the state side, just like there are issues on the state side now.”
‘Significant’ impact
This new set of potential demands on URI’s Workday timeline, Benson warned, could have “significant monetary and project schedule impacts” for the school. Benson told the trustees on Sept. 14 that the school was meeting with state officials later that week to continue discussing the two Workday systems.
On Tuesday, about two weeks after that trustees meeting, Benson wrote in an email to Rhode Island Current that URI and the state are still “closely collaborating” to determine the best ways for their newly-designed enterprise resource planning, or ERP, infrastructure to live in harmony. Both systems, Benson wrote, “involve dependencies required for successful implementation.” 
“We are actively exploring with the State the best approach to address these dependencies,” Benson wrote. Asked whether that includes the possibility of URI administering payroll in-house, she added, “We’re looking at several options, including that one.”
The Department of Administration, meanwhile, declined to comment on any discussions taking place. 
“While we don’t comment on internal discussions and defer any specific questions about URI’s project to the university, the State is fully supportive of URI’s Workday implementation project,” department spokesperson Karen Greco wrote in an email. “The State team’s specific role in this is to ensure the integration with the State system is secure, efficient and meeting the necessary requirements to achieve mutual success.”
Stephanie Cavanaugh, URI’s Workday program director, told trustees on Sept. 14 that the new platform will replace URI’s PeopleSoft-based human resources and finance systems, as well as the school’s current budgeting software. The school’s student information system is staying put and will integrate with Workday.
Currently, URI’s full-time employees, including those eligible for benefits, are paid via the state’s payroll system. URI’s internal systems handle the remainder of the university’s workforce, which includes several thousand part-time and non-benefit employees.
The new system is designed to track time for full-time employees while still sending payroll data to the state, which would continue processing paychecks. 
“Any problem that the state has with their payroll system impacts our employees, and we’ve been managing and mitigating that for the last six months,” Benson told the Finance Committee. She suggested the state had revived the possibility of URI handling payroll “based on some of the challenges on their end.”
Benson reiterated that the problem was not the Workday software per se, which she called “a great system,” but its configuration.
“It has to do with how the software was configured,” she said. “There’s a lot of factors that go into this. There’s the software itself, and there’s the group that you use to help you implement the software and how you design the software, and that’s the process we’re in right now.”
Cavanaugh said the university’s Workday project is “generally…in a good place,” and the project remains on schedule, but added, “We cannot vary too much from that schedule and from the scope we’re currently on to maintain the current budget status.”
Functional teams working on the school’s ERP effort continue to meet weekly, she said, and the university is planning a lengthy testing period, from December 2026 to August 2027, to prepare for launch next fall.

title: Weld County group collecting petition signatures to block Global AI data center
description: A citizens group wants Weld County voters to have the final say on county commissioners’ recent approval of a large data center project near Windsor — and to require voter approval of all such developments in the future. Two petitions backed by the group Protect Our Water and Energy Resources, or POWER, were approved for […]
text:
Global AI is set to create a data center at the former Carestream Health property at 2000 Howard Smith Avenue W in Weld County. (Screenshot from Google Maps) A citizens group wants Weld County voters to have the final say on county commissioners’ recent approval of a large data center project near Windsor — and to require voter approval of all such developments in the future.
Two petitions backed by the group Protect Our Water and Energy Resources, or POWER, were approved for circulation Monday by the Weld County Clerk and Recorder’s office, the group said.
One would force a referendum on the Weld County Board of Commissioners’ Sept. 9 approval of New York-based Global AI’s plans to construct a new 41-acre data center, which could become the largest such facility operating in Colorado, on the former Carestream Health site southeast of Windsor. The second measure is a citizen initiative that would prohibit the county from issuing an occupancy permit to any data center unless “approved by a majority of the registered electors of Weld County voting at a regular or special election.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Both measures need the support of at least 9,103 registered voters in the county — equal to 5% of the total number of ballots cast there in the previous general election — to go before voters.
“This referendum puts power back in the hands of the people of Weld County,” Patricia Garcia-Nelson, a longtime Weld County environmental activist, said in a press release announcing the campaign. “We have the right to decide what happens to our community, not just on this project, but on the ones that come next.”



Quotation







We have heard residents of Weld County speak out at meeting after meeting about their concerns with the Global AI data center ... Those concerns were not heard, so now we're taking this to the voters. The commissioners had their vote. Now it's the people's turn.


– Matt Cheroutes, campaign manager for POWER


Commissioners’ 5-0 vote in favor of the Global AI proposal came after a daylong hearing earlier this month that included hours of public comment, mostly in opposition to the project. Local opponents have organized against the proposal for months, citing concerns about its energy and water use, noise levels and other potential impacts, part of a statewide and national trend that has many local governments weighing moratoriums on data center development.
Global AI has said that the facility will use a closed-loop cooling system that minimizes water use, and its initial 27.5-megawatt capacity would be served by the Poudre Valley Rural Electric Association, though it has long-term plans to expand to a much larger capacity of up to one gigawatt. The company claims the project will bring about 1,500 construction jobs and 200 long-term jobs to Weld County.
Local governments in Colorado enact moratoriums on data center development

In granting the project a so-called Use by Special Review permit, Weld County commissioners deemed it “compatible with the surrounding land uses” and with “adequate provisions for the protection of the health, safety, and welfare of the neighborhood and County.”
Opponents have 45 days to collect enough valid petition signatures to trigger a veto referendum on the commissioners’ resolution, and to put their initiated ordinance to voters. If the measures receive sufficient signatures, the county commissioners board must call a special election to be held within 60 days, according to the county charter.
“We have heard residents of Weld County speak out at meeting after meeting about their concerns with the Global AI data center,” said Matt Cheroutes, campaign manager for POWER, in a statement. “Those concerns were not heard, so now we’re taking this to the voters. The commissioners had their vote. Now it’s the people’s turn.”

title: Gas tax holiday proposal gets first hearing in Ohio Senate
description: Ohio senators got their first chance Tuesday to discuss a gas tax holiday Republican leaders announced last week. The GOP is aiming to pass its plan with an emergency clause so the measure can take effect immediately. To do that, they’ll need to pick up Democratic votes in the House. If the reaction among state […]
text:
The Ohio Statehouse in Columbus. (Photo by David DeWitt, Ohio Capital Journal.)Ohio senators got their first chance Tuesday to discuss a gas tax holiday Republican leaders announced last week. The GOP is aiming to pass its plan with an emergency clause so the measure can take effect immediately. To do that, they’ll need to pick up Democratic votes in the House.
If the reaction among state Senators is any indication, they could be met with skepticism.
The plan
The 90-day tax break comes on the eve of November’s election. Midterms are historically challenging for the party in power, and with price of gas and diesel surging, state leaders are getting antsy.
Democratic candidate for governor Amy Acton first floated the idea of suspending the gas tax. Her Republican opponent Vivek Ramaswamy quickly took up the call and announced he had a plan to pay for it and the backing of statehouse leaders, one of whom is his running mate.
That running mate, Republican Ohio Senate President Rob McColley, praised Ramaswamy and called it “unprecedented” for a nominee to pitch in even before an election.
Ohio GOP lawmakers tee up votes for gas tax holiday after Acton, then Ramaswamy, back idea

Bringing lawmakers back to the capitol to pass emergency legislation weeks before an election is unusual.
The distinction McColley touted between the GOP proposal and what he called Acton’s “empty rhetoric,” however, crumbled between the plan’s announcement and the measure’s drafting.
Gas taxes fund work on the state’s roads and bridges. Initially, Ramaswamy’s proposal would’ve relied on the Ohio Department of Transportation’s surplus cash balance. But all the department’s cash is spoken for, and Gov. Mike DeWine shot down the idea of raiding ODOT’s coffers.
So instead, lawmakers are essentially looking to the state’s checking account — dipping into the general revenue fund for the $725 million needed to cover lost revenue.
The bill and the critiques
Ohio state Sens. Michele Reynolds, R-Canal Winchester, and Jane Timken, R-Jackson Twp., are sponsoring Ohio Senate Bill 475.
“Ohioans have made their voices loud and clear,” Timken said. “They want relief at the pump, and they want their hard-earned dollars to work for them. We owe it to the people of Ohio to provide relief during this time of financial hardship.”
The current tax rate is 38.5 cents for gas and 47 cents for diesel.
“For a 20 gallon fill up, this equals a savings of nearly $7.70,” Reynolds said.
Democrats on the committee questioned how impactful those savings would be. According to AAA, Ohio’s average gas price on Sept. 29 is $4.27.
Even filling up that 20 gallon tank weekly, a driver would see their gas bill of $1,026 gas over 12 weeks drop to $933.62. That’s not nothing, but the state is putting up significant money to get there, they noted.
Ohio state Sen. Willis Blackshear, D-Dayton also questioned the timing.
‘Very bad idea.’ Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine pumps brakes on proposal to suspend gas tax

“Gas spiked late February, early March,” Blackshear said. “Why are we just now starting? Why are we acting on this now?”
Reynolds pointed to diesel prices, which have risen sharply in recent weeks.
“The time is now,” she said. “Ohioans are suffering — we’re listening.”
“There are a number of things that we can’t control from the national environment,” she added, “But what we can do in Ohio, we should do, and that’s why we’re doing it.”
Ohio state Sen. Bill DeMora rejected he effort as a transparent bid to help Ramaswamy.
“It’s all a gimmick for your governor candidate who’s underwater,” he said. “That’s the only reason you’re doing this.”
Speaking after the hearing, DeMora said he wouldn’t vote for the bill even if lawmakers added an amendment “to make me the king of England,” and that Acton calling for a tax holiday first makes no difference to him.
“I’m not a sycophant,” DeMora said. “My governor candidate was wrong on this issue, and I told her she’s wrong.”
Senators expect to vote the measure out of committee Wednesday and have it on the floor in the afternoon. In the Ohio House, lawmakers are slated to introduce a companion measure Wednesday, with a floor session scheduled later in the day.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico Election 2026: US House of Representatives, District 2
description: The race for New Mexico’s 2nd Congressional District regularly constitutes one of the most competitive and closely watched in the country. This year has heightened stakes as Democrats seek to retain the seat in their push to regain control of the U.S. House of Representatives.
text:
U.S. Rep. Gabe Vasquez (D-N.M.) is running for re-election to a third term against Republican Greg Cunningham, right, a former Albuquerque Police Department detective, to represent New Mexico’s 2nd Congressional District. (Courtesy photos) 
The race for New Mexico’s 2nd Congressional District regularly constitutes one of the most competitive and closely watched in the country. This year has heightened stakes as Democrats seek to retain the seat in their push to regain control of the U.S. House of Representatives. 
Incumbent U.S. Rep. Gabe Vasquez (D-N.M.) is seeking re-election to his third term representing the district, which stretches across the southern third of New Mexico as well as into Albuquerque’s South Valley. He has narrowly defeated Republican opponent Yvette Herrell twice in previous elections in 2022 and 2024.
This Nov. 3, Vasquez will face Republican Greg Cunningham, a former U.S. Marine and Albuquerque police detective, who is eligible to run in the seat for the first time following redistricting that made his South Valley home part of CD2. 
In a sign of national interest in the race, political advertisements paid for by national political action committees are airing repeatedly on television sets across the state. Ads supporting Cunningham generally cast Vasquez as soft on crime. Those supporting Vasquez say the Republican is beholden to President Donald Trump. 
National political observers, including the Cook Political Report, have said the race leans toward Vasquez this cycle, in a year many have predicted could mark a “blue wave” benefiting Democrats up and down the ballot. 
The incumbent Democrat also has so far outraised his Republican opponent. Federal Election Commission filings show Vasquez raised nearly $3.8 million for his campaign; Cunningham has raised slightly more than $1.5 million. 
Still, recent polling has the candidates within the margin of error of each other. A KOB-TV poll earlier this month of likely voters showed Vasquez leading Cunningham 46% to 43%, with a 4.6% margin of error, and 11% of voters remaining undecided.
Source NM spoke to both Cunningham and Vasquez about the election and their fights to represent CD2 in a job that pays an annual salary of $174,000. Their answers below are edited for clarity and concision. 
Greg Cunningham 
Greg Cunningham, a retired Marine and Albuquerque detective, speaks alongside U.S. House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) at an Albuquerque campaign event on Aug. 26, 2026. (Joshua Bowling/Source NM)
Republican Greg Cunningham describes his first foray into politics after a career as a police detective as “unconventional,” but said he was motivated to jump into the race due to the same sense of public service that defined his life in the Marines and as a longtime police detective. 
“I would highlight my personal experience with keeping New Mexicans safe and allowing an environment where we can thrive and go to school and go to work and raise our families,” he said. “That’s my wheelhouse. That’s my area of expertise.”
President Donald Trump endorsed Cunningham in April, well before the June 2 primary election, and Cunningham defeated his primary opponent Jose Orozco by a wide margin. The moment Cunningham declared victory, national Republican organizations set their sights on unseating Vasquez.
Late last month, U.S. House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) visited an Albuquerque brewery to stump for Cunningham, calling him “straight out of central casting.” Cunningham, for his part, shouted over protesters in his speech alongside Johnson, in which he said he is “not a politician.” 
What is the most important issue facing this district?
Public safety and the safety of our families and communities is paramount. If we are not safe in our homes and in our schools and in our workplaces; if our families cannot go to the store without having to buy things that are locked up because things are being stolen at a high rate — all of those things tear at the fabric of who we are as a society. We have to get a handle on that. Until we are safe in those places, nothing else is going to matter.
What piece of legislation would you prioritize sponsoring in the next term?
I would love to see an updated and modernized version of the national crime bill that was signed in the ’90s. I’d like to address sanctuary cities. I’d like to address sentencing guidelines. I’d like to address the border and the ongoing conflict that we’re having with the cartels. And so, right off the bat, you know, putting my expertise and putting my experience to work on a national level, I think would be a priority for me.
How would you describe the impact of the Trump administration on New Mexico and what would your approach be to working with the Trump administration?
As a detective, I did big cases — federal cases, local cases — but I was able to bring local law enforcement, federal law enforcement, different agencies, different district attorneys, and the U.S. Attorney’s office together for a common goal, and that was to better our communities. And I would take the same approach. It’s people from different backgrounds, people from different beliefs and ideologies, working together for a common cause. 
If something is good for the people of New Mexico, why would anybody let their ideology or their political party stand in the way of what’s best for New Mexicans? This administration’s policies — no tax on tips, no tax on overtime, the Social Security deduction — those are working-class things that we need. Those are not things that billionaires are taking advantage of, or even millionaires. These are everyday, working New Mexicans that are benefiting.
And, man, we really need to do whatever we can to continue to help working New Mexicans, and that would be something that I would absolutely do, regardless of party or ideology.
What border-security policies would you support?
I’m someone that again worked the border, and so as a DEA (U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration) detective task force officer, I worked on border cases at all levels, from the undercover level on the street to the wiretap level, and so I know that it is vital that people that enter this country illegally, that come here and commit crimes, we have to identify those people.  And we have to make sure that when they’re arrested here in the United States, that we follow the law and that we don’t allow them to victimize our systems anymore. And so, right now, we’re shutting the border down. It’s absolutely the first step. But I can tell you, from a detective point of view, a lot of the same challenges that I faced 20 years ago at the border, we’re still facing as New Mexicans. Our fentanyl deaths — our percentages are rising, and that’s in contrast with the national trend. 
Project Jupiter, the controversial data center project in Doña Ana County, sits in CD2. If elected, what will you do, if anything, to change the trajectory of that project?
I was not there during its infancy phase, and so to speak on how I would change the arc of it now would be very difficult. I don’t know what those specifics are. But, you know, communities, we do have the right to ask questions. We do live in a desert. Water is central to us. We have power issues. We’ve got to make sure that whatever data center comes into our community, those contracts fit that community’s needs. And if it fits that community’s needs, then I think we should allow that community to move forward. 
As a congressman, I’m going to make sure that contracts are adhered to, that communities are taken care of, but (it’s) not my job to tell them what to do or what not to do. I don’t think that should be the government’s job.
The Otero County Processing Center, which houses most of the ICE detainees in the state, also sits in CD2. Do you support or oppose the Legislature’s efforts to ban public entities from contracting with ICE for immigrant detention?
I don’t support that. Again, I support every community’s right and opportunity to do what’s best for them. I’ve talked to folks in Otero County that are directly affected by that and involved in that, and they want that facility. They need that facility for their community, for jobs, for opportunity, for stability. And so, going back to the question of working with people and letting ideology get in the way of progress or community stability — that’s one instance where I think that’s what’s happening. I think there are legislators that are letting their ideology override their practicality, and that’s not something I would be in favor of.
CD2 is considered one of the closest races in the country. What will be the deciding factor this year?
Coming from a Marine, I would say hard work. That’s what it comes down to. When a person commits to a process like this, it comes down to meeting people. It comes down to hard work. It comes down to being who you say you are. Right now, there’s sort of a mistrust with our government and with our entities and agencies. My history shows that I am who I say I am.
CD2 is one of 13 congressional districts in which a majority of voters supported Donald Trump in 2024 but also elected a Democrat. How does that factor into your approach to unseating the Democratic incumbent?
It tells me that at a national level there is support for the president and his administration. It also tells me that I’m a different candidate than was there last time. I bring a different skill set. I bring different characteristics, and the choice that New Mexicans are going to have for CD2 is a very different one this time than it was in 2024. 
The choice is very stark in my mind as to who Gabe Vasquez is and who I am. Because it’s so clear, I firmly believe that New Mexicans are going to choose a different path.
U.S. Rep. Gabe Vasquez
U.S. Rep. Gabe Vasquez, the Democrat representing New Mexico’s 2nd Congressional District, held a news conference June 17, 2025 in Las Cruces to denounce new GOP efforts to sell off public lands. (Leah Romero for Source NM)
U.S. Rep. Gabe Vasquez (D-N.M.) is a former Las Cruces city councilor. He has spent much of his second term pushing legislation that aims to reduce prices, as well as championing legislation particular to the vast 2nd Congressional District, which sits along the United States-Mexico border. 
As congressman, Vasquez sits on the House Agriculture Committee, where he has decried cuts to the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program and other benefit programs on which many New Mexicans rely. 
While he opposed the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act” that President Donald Trump signed into law last July, he also criticized New Mexico leaders for allowing the state’s SNAP “error rate” — a measure of SNAP over- or underpayments to recipients — to become one of the highest in the country. 
What is the most important issue facing this district?
The economy. I think my opponent has made it clear that his loyalty is with President Trump and MAGA. My loyalty is to the people of the 2nd District of New Mexico, and what they’re telling me is that Trump’s economy right now is really hurting them. We have to bring down the costs that are continuing to rise. We have to end this reckless war in Iran that’s about to hit its seventh month, and it’s caused gas and diesel prices to soar. Honestly, it’s made life hell for my rural constituents with the prices of diesel and fertilizer prices that have gone through the roof. New Mexicans losing access to their health care. Over 80,000 are predicted to lose health care in the next year because of HR1, the Republican Trump bill, and we’re expected to see somewhere around 20,000 New Mexicans already losing access to food assistance and benefits; those are some of the basic things that New Mexicans need to raise healthy families and healthy kids. 
What piece of legislation would you prioritize sponsoring in the next term?
I do have a bill called the Keep Mobile Homes Affordable Act. One in six houses in New Mexico is a manufactured home, and right now, out-of-state wealthy investors, hedge fund managers, private equity are buying up our trailer parks all across the state, and they are raising lot fees for senior citizens, first-time homebuyers, starter homes for young families. It’s got to stop. I’ve heard this from Alamogordo to Albuquerque. It’s a bill that is much needed to bring the cost of housing down. 
How would you describe the impact of the Trump administration on New Mexico and what would your approach be to working with the Trump administration?
I think the impact’s been great. Seeing the incredible amount of corruption in Washington, New Mexicans have had enough of the pay-to-play politics in Washington from both parties, which has only gotten worse during this administration. So we have to pass a real stock trading ban that would prohibit the president, members of Congress and their families and trustees from owning and trading individual stocks or trading on the futures markets. That’s incredibly, incredibly important. 
Look, I will always work with the president in areas where you know it’s going to make the lives of New Mexicans better. The 21st Century Road to Housing Act is an example of Republicans and Democrats working together. And although the president didn’t sign that bill, he didn’t veto it either. I look forward to working with the president as well on border security investments. 
What border-security policies would you support?
I’ve actually developed what I call the New American Immigration Plan, and I believe it’s a set of policy recommendations that will turn into actual legislation that keeps our border secure, that makes sure that folks have a legal pathway to status in this country in specific sectors. We are seeing a shortage of field workers, of care workers, of construction workers, hospitality workers, health workers. It’s incredibly important that we fix this broken immigration system, and both parties have failed for far too long to come to terms with just about anything related to immigration. 
We really got to take stock of what ICE is doing and the damage that it’s causing to our families, to our communities in New Mexico, to our economy and small businesses. And we’ve got to bring forward solutions to the table. That does include investments in border security, specifically at our ports of entry. I think the Santa Teresa port of entry, in particular, is at the top of the list for improvements that I’m hoping to champion to expand commercial traffic and grow the economy in southern New Mexico, but also to keep us safer. 
Project Jupiter, the controversial data center project in Doña Ana County, sits in CD2. If elected, what will you do, if anything, to change the trajectory of that project?
I think, bottom line, my constituents should know that for any business that wants to do business in our state, that they need to do it the right way, and that New Mexicans get to make the choices in our state about who uses our most precious resources, which is our water, our air quality, our land and our natural resources. Look, I have called for a moratorium in Socorro for the proposed data center there, which was something the County Commission approved. I’ve also heard from community members in Grant and Hidalgo counties who have echoed their calls for a moratorium from the new data center proposal, and I’ve led legislation in Congress just recently to force data center developers to make sure that they’re paying for their own electricity. The truth is, water is too scarce. Electricity is already too expensive for New Mexicans.
As it pertains to Project Jupiter in particular, there’s some important actions that the state has to take that I’m looking forward to seeing in this next legislative session, and that the governor has to take as well. Of course, that includes the upcoming air quality permit. So, those permit decisions and where this project continues from there will really determine the opportunities for me to be engaged in this process. 
I think there hasn’t been transparency, and just like many New Mexicans, I’ve been mad as hell that there hasn’t been enough transparency about both water use and emissions, and truly what the scale of this data center is going to represent, and who’s actually working on the ground. Is it New Mexicans or is it out-of-state workers? We’ve got to get to the bottom of all those things.
The Otero County Processing Center, which houses most of the ICE detainees in the state, also sits in CD2. Do you support or oppose the Legislature’s efforts to ban public entities from contracting with ICE for immigrant detention?
I’ve supported HB9, which was the bill introduced in the Legislature in the last legislative session. Look, I think in general, private prison corporations that are making millions and millions of dollars of profit for their stockholders to keep nonviolent offenders, nonviolent immigrants in detention centers is not reflective of our American or New Mexican values. And I visited all of the detention centers in my district, as well as the one just outside my district in El Paso that also holds many New Mexicans. And I can tell you, the folks that are there for months at a time, many of them waiting to just be deported back to their home countries, are not being allowed to leave, see a judge, have access to legal counsel, all so that they could fill a bed for one more day to go to those private prison corporations. It’s got to stop. It’s not who we are. 
CD2 is considered one of the closest races in the country. What will be the deciding factor this year?
I think it’s the economy. I think people are pissed as hell that they go to the pump and they’re paying $120 to fill up their truck if they have a diesel truck if they are hauling horses or hauling hay. Life has gotten really, really tough for them. My opponent is in line with Trump’s damaging tariff agenda, which has also caused prices to skyrocket for consumers. Let me be clear: That’s a tax on New Mexicans that I don’t support. 
If Democrats secure a majority in the House this November, what will be your first order of business? 
Bringing down costs for the American people. We’ve got to do it as quickly as possible, and it has to be as impactful as possible. We can’t simply oppose the Trump agenda. We must actively provide solutions to help lower the cost for everyday New Mexicans. That’s got to be at the top of our list.

description: Two behavioral health professionals from Iowa are currently facing disciplinary charges related to their relationships with patients. The first of the two cases involves Chad M. text:
(Stock photo by Getty Images)Two behavioral health professionals from Iowa are currently facing disciplinary charges related to their relationships with patients.
The first of the two cases involves Chad M. Elbandagji of Cedar Falls, who does business as Chad Mohammad. The Iowa Board of Behavioral Health Professionals has charged Elbandagji, an independent social worker, with violating the regulations of his profession.
Those alleged violations include engaging in sexual activities or sexual contact with a client’s or former client’s relative when there is a risk of exploitation or potential harm, two counts of violating the National Association of Social Workers’ ethics rules related to dual relationships with clients or former clients and two counts of unethical conduct that may include the betrayal of professional confidence.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The board has not disclosed any information related to the alleged conduct that gave rise to those charges, except to say that it occurred while Elbandagji was practicing in Cedar Falls.
State and federal records indicate Elbandagji works at Chad Mohammad Therapy in Cedar Falls.
Although the board approved the charges in January and March of 2026, they were only recently made public by the Iowa Department of Inspections, Appeals and Licensing.
A board hearing on the matter is scheduled for Nov. 4, 2026.
Des Moines-area psychologist charged
In a separate and unrelated case, the Board of Behavioral Health Professionals has also charged Des Moines-area psychologist Susan M. Guenther with violating regulations that require psychologists to take “reasonable steps to avoid harming their clients/patients” and to “minimize harm where it is foreseeable and unavoidable.”
In addition, Guenther is charged by the board with failing to comply with regulations concerning multiple relationships that involve a psychologist acting in a professional role with a person while being engaged in “another role with the same person.”
The board has not disclosed any information related to the alleged conduct that gave rise to those charges, except to say that it occurred while Guenther was practicing in Des Moines.
Guenther has been an Iowa-licensed psychologist since November 1985. A board hearing on the charges is scheduled for Nov. 16, 2026.
The Iowa Capital Dispatch was not able to reach either Elbandagji or Guenther for comment.

title: Lee Enterprises brings Great Falls Tribune into portfolio
description: Lee Enterprises, which owns five of Montana’s largest circulation newspapers, is acquiring one more daily paper, the Great Falls Tribune, the company announced on Monday. In Montana, Lee Enterprises owns The Billings Gazette, the Missoulian, the Helena Independent-Record, the Montana Standard, and the Ravalli Republic. With Lee’s acquisition of the Tribune,[...]
text:
Photo illustration by Getty Images.Lee Enterprises, which owns five of Montana’s largest circulation newspapers, is acquiring one more daily paper, the Great Falls Tribune, the company announced on Monday.
In Montana, Lee Enterprises owns The Billings Gazette, the Missoulian, the Helena Independent-Record, the Montana Standard, and the Ravalli Republic.
With Lee’s acquisition of the Tribune, the company controls newspapers in most of the state’s major population centers. Only Bozeman, Livingston and the Kalispell area are served by daily news outlets owned by other parent companies.
In addition, Lee added three South Dakota papers to its nationwide portfolio of nearly 200 mastheads. The company already owned the Rapid City Journal and now will operate the Sioux Falls Argus Leader, the Aberdeen American News (including the Farm Forum), and the Watertown Public Opinion.
All four papers were acquired from the USA Today Company.
In a press release, Lee said the change would allow the company to “invest in growth, serve local audiences and support the future of community journalism.”
“We’re honored to deepen our commitment to the communities of Montana and South Dakota,” Nathan Bekke, Lee’s president and chief executive officer, said in a statement. “Across the 193 brands we serve in 28 states, our focus is the same: Providing trusted local news and information that helps people stay informed, connected and engaged in their communities.”
But the future of the Tribune — and Montana’s other print newspapers — remains in question, as consolidation of news outlets by corporate owners has shown to decrease staff and news coverage, according to a Nieman Labs report.
The Great Falls Tribune currently lists a single person in its staff directory, editor Grady Higgins, who did not respond to emailed questions about the transition by publication time.
The company has been cutting newsroom staff in the state for years. In spring 2023, Lee Enterprises eliminated at least 13 newsrooms positions in Montana representing one-third to one-half of existing editorial staff at its papers.
Earlier this year, Lee announced billionaire David Hoffman had acquired a controlling stake in the company and became chairperson. In a glowing profile that all Lee newspapers ran about Hoffman, he was announced as the “new hope for local news.”
But the company has continued to lay off editorial staff in recent weeks and implemented hiring freezes across its network.
Lee Enterprises declined to provide additional comments about plans to hire editorial staff at the Tribune or hiring practices in Montana newsrooms.
The Tribune opened in 1885 as a weekly newspaper and is the oldest continuously running business in Great Falls. At its peak last century, the paper had a staff of around 300 and in 2010 still had around 165 employees, a number which was cut in half over the next decade.
Editor’s note: Daily Montanan staff members Darrell Ehrlick, Keila Szpaller and Jordan Hansen are all former Lee Enterprises employees. Szpaller previously worked for the Tribune.

title: 2nd Fargo-area data center would use double the power of Harwood site
description: A data center planned in North Dakota’s Cass County would use nearly twice the power of a data center under construction in the Fargo area.  Minnesota-based Geronimo Power has filed for a conditional use permit for a data center in Harmony Township, near the Bison Substation north of Mapleton.  The company also has created a […]
text:
An electrical substation is adjacent to a solar farm north of Mapleton, North Dakota. The Bison Substation area could also become home to a battery storage site and a data center. (Photo by Jeff Beach/North Dakota Monitor)A data center planned in North Dakota’s Cass County would use nearly twice the power of a data center under construction in the Fargo area. 
Minnesota-based Geronimo Power has filed for a conditional use permit for a data center in Harmony Township, near the Bison Substation north of Mapleton. 
The company also has created a web page about its plans and invited people to discuss the Harmony Energy Park project at its Casselton office and Thursday morning at a cafe in Casselton.
Energy company eyes adding data center west of Fargo

The company describes its planned data center as similar in size to the Applied Digital project near Harwood, north of Fargo. Applied Digital’s Polaris Forge II campus would use up to 280 megawatts of power. 
Geronimo’s project would use 540 megawatts at peak demand, according to the website. 
The data center in Harmony Township would have a similar footprint to the Harwood site, built on 640 acres, according to Geronimo. Construction would take two to four years. 
“Filing the permit application starts the process of discovery to see if a data center makes sense for the community,” Geronimo says on its Harmony Energy Park web page. “What we ask is that the project is given a fair and transparent public review, where the community has the opportunity to hear the facts and participate in that process.” 
Geronimo says peak water demand would be 20,000 gallons per day. It would use a closed-loop system cooling system, similar to a car radiator. 
The company says the data center would be powered by new electricity generation. Existing power customers in the area would be protected from rate increases under a plan submitted by Otter Tail Power. The plan for what is called a large load tariff is under review by the North Dakota Public Service Commission.
The Harmony Energy Park site includes a 200-megawatt solar farm that Geronimo is building next to the Bison Substation. It also wants to add a 200-megawatt battery storage facility at the site. 
Dustin Burchill speaks Sept. 15, 2026, in Casselton, North Dakota, at a meeting to discuss data center development organized by the campaign of ag commissioner candidate Vern Thompson. (Photo by Jeff Beach/North Dakota Monitor)
Harmony Township resident Dustin Burchill spoke at a community meeting in Casselton on Sept. 15. He cited a second Geronimo solar project, which PSC documents show as being 4 miles northeast of Casselton. 
A proposal for a 500-megawatt wind farm northwest of Casselton also has been filed with the PSC, though Geronimo said it is not part of the data center project.
Other potential energy projects include a power line from the Bison Substation to Hankinson and the Bakken East natural gas pipeline.
“They’re setting up the Casselton-Mapleton area as a major energy hub,” Burchill said. 
Burchill on Sept. 22 became chair of the Harmony Township Board of Supervisors, which faces questions about zoning changes that were made.
Burchill says township officials are awaiting an opinion from the township’s attorney on whether a conflict of interest involving former township supervisor Tom Roden might nullify zoning changes. A phone number for Roden Farms gave a busy signal multiple times all afternoon Tuesday.  
Roden had agreed to sell land to Geronimo Power for the data center site but didn’t disclose that deal when voting on the ordinance changes, The Forum of Fargo-Moorhead reported. 
Burchill said zoning changes included changing allowable noise levels and removing some nonresidential buildings, such as farm shops, from within the 1-mile setback area, making it easier to site a data center. 
The Harmony board meets next on Oct. 20. 
That same week, on Oct. 23, the PSC is holding a hearing in Casselton on the Harmony battery storage project. 



Learn about Harmony Energy Park
Geronimo Power officials will be available to answer questions in the coming days:
Geronimo’s Casselton office at 26 6th Ave. N. from 5-6 p.m. Oct. 6; and 8-9 a.m. Wednesday and Oct. 7.
Bondegard Café, 730 Front St. Casselton, 7 to 9 a.m., Thursday.



Reach North Dakota Monitor deputy editor Jeff Beach at jbeach@northdakotamonitor.com

name: Maryland Matters
title: School officials celebrate drop in chronic absenteeism, but are still shy of goal
description: Maryland school officials Tuesday celebrated a sharp drop chronic absenteeism since the pandemic, despite uneven results across school districts and not reaching their goal of cutting post-pandemic rates in half.
text:
Maryland Board of Education members pose with T-shirts promoting the "Maryland Shows Up!" campaign, implemented to incentivize student attendance, at their meeting Tuesday. (Photo courtesy Maryland State Department of Education)Maryland school officials Tuesday celebrated a sharp drop chronic absenteeism since the pandemic, despite uneven results across school districts and not reaching their goal of cutting post-pandemic rates in half.
The Maryland Department of Education announced earlier this month that nearly 23% of students were chronically absent during the 2025-26 academic year, down from almost 32% in the 2021-22 academic year.
But data released during Tuesday’s Board of Education meeting showed rates ranging from 41.4% in Baltimore City to 15.4% in Harford and Howard counties. The state considers a student who misses 10% of the school year, or 18 days of the 180-day school calendar, as chronically absent, whether the absences were excused or unexcused.
On a school-by-school basis, most saw a decline in absenteeism since the pandemic, but 14% did not.
“The most foundational part of school is showing up to school,” Board President Joshua Michael said in an interview earlier this month. “When you’re not in school, there’s also a higher likelihood that you’re engaged in things that may not be productive.”
Michael said the sharp increase in absenteeism during and after the pandemic made state officials realize it was not just a national problem, but also a Maryland problem. Chronic absenteeism was just under 20% in 2019, before the pandemic.












View this post on Instagram






















 
A post shared by MSDE (@mdpublicschools)



The state is taking action in three different ways, Michael said: Expanding data collection on chronic absenteeism, working with staff and groups like Attendance Works, a national nonprofit, to provide resources to school districts, and running campaigns like “Maryland Shows Up!” to analyze progress and promote the cause.
“When we are able to put our eyes on children at school, we can check in with them and identify what supports they need,” Michael said. “It really makes a big difference in making sure that student is OK.”
State data from early February showed that chronic absence rates are highest in economically disadvantaged students, while those with disabilities and multilingual learners were close behind.
Attendance Works founder and CEO Hedy Chang said in an interview last week that the organization provides guidance to the education department based on their latest research findings.
The partnership is still working to improve chronic absenteeism in middle and high schools across the state. These grade groups can be tough for student attendance because of the transitions from elementary to middle school and middle to high school, Chang said.
Though chronic absenteeism in high schools across Maryland remains about 10%  to 15% higher than in elementary and middle schools, all grade groups have experienced a decline since the 2021-22 academic year, the state’s data shows.
Chang also noted that data collection has been expanding, especially in Maryland, to go beyond solely logging unexcused absences. This allows researchers to dive deeper into the root causes of absenteeism in schools at a district level.
Students are likely to reach chronic absence due to academic disengagement, social and peer challenges, anxiety and misconceptions about the effect of an absence, Chang said.
“Whether a kid shows up to school is a reflection of both what happens in the community and the school,” she said.
Kent County Superintendent Mary Boswell-McComas wrote in a statement last week that chronic absenteeism has fallen sharply in her county, to the lowest level in five years. The share of students in the county with perfect attendance also increased from 39% to 61%, or three in every five students, in the last academic year.
Boswell-McComas attributes the improvement to county board efforts to push the benefits of attending schools and the drawbacks of not doing so, while also providing more clarity to families on why even an excused absence can be harmful for a students’ learning.
State educators and Attendance Works officials on Tuesday highlighted Hall’s Cross Roads Elementary School in Aberdeen as a bright spot for declining chronic absenteeism. It went from nearly 44% absenteeism to just under 15% over a two-year period, according to data presented at Tuesday’s meeting by Principal Karen Jankowiak.
Hall’s Cross Roads is a Title I school, which receives federal funding because 90% of its 420 pre-K to fifth grade students live in poverty, Jankowiak said. Administrators and teachers have been incentivizing student attendance by holding schoolwide events and programs for those reaching a certain level of attendance.
K-12 spending, absenteeism programs at risk as feds end monitoring, watchdog says

Jankowiak and Amanda Coyne, teacher specialist at the elementary school, both discussed the baseline that proper attendance and academic prioritization provides for a student’s future.
“You want [parents] to really understand that when your kids come to school, you will help them not be dependent on you,” Jankowiak said. “You want them to get a driver’s license. You want them to have a job.”
Family engagement and student-teacher connectedness are two strategies that have shown the most improvement in chronic absentee rates, according to Chang. But she noted it’s important for school systems to recognize what is and isn’t working and develop an initiative that works for students based on their data results.
Coyne echoed this statement, saying schools should be creative with already existing incentives and loop attendance requirements within.
On a state level, Michael said he’s confident Maryland will continue to see improvements in absentee rates and eventually hit its 15% goal, even if cutting the post-pandemic rate in half  seems like a long shot.
“[The state’s efforts] are going to help emphasize the importance of school, and that we’re going to see positive impact reverberate,” Michael said. “Because fundamentally, what we’re saying to young people and their families is, ‘We value you. We want you to be here. You matter.’”

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Iowa caregivers are fired for alleged abuse and workplace misconduct
description: Several Iowa nursing home workers have been fired in recent months due to allegations of patient abuse and other forms of workplace misconduct. Among the cases is that of Amanda Hanrahan, who worked as a certified nursing assistant for the Lone Tree Health Care Center in Johnson County from 2024 until August of this year, […]
text:
Iowa Workforce Development manages unemployment claims filed on behalf of Iowans. (Photo by Getty Images, logo courtesy the State of Iowa)Several Iowa nursing home workers have been fired in recent months due to allegations of patient abuse and other forms of workplace misconduct.
Among the cases is that of Amanda Hanrahan, who worked as a certified nursing assistant for the Lone Tree Health Care Center in Johnson County from 2024 until August of this year, when she was discharged for allegedly verbally abusing a resident.
According to the findings of Administrative Law Judge Carly Smith, who recently presided over a state hearing on Hanrahan’s request for unemployment benefits, Hanrahan was working at the facility on July 28, 2026, when she had to respond to a resident’s call light on several occasions.
At one point, Hanrahan allegedly told the resident to “stop messing with the call button” because there were other residents who actually needed assistance, adding, “I’m done f—ing with you tonight.” Another CNA reported the incident to the charge nurse, and Hanrahan was fired.
Recently, Smith ruled Hanrahan was ineligible for unemployment benefits due to workplace misconduct. “Swearing at a resident due to them requesting repeated assistance is disqualifying misconduct, and benefits are denied,” Smith ruled, ordering Hanrahan to repay the $2,076 in benefits already collected.
The Iowa Capital Dispatch was not able to reach Hanrahan for comment.
Other Iowa caregivers whose unemployment cases were recently decided include:
— Haley Sly, who worked as a certified medication aide at Accura Health Care nursing facility in Cascade until her dismissal in April of this year. On April 23, 2026, Sly had allegedly asked a resident come to the dining area to eat dinner, and the resident refused. A certified nursing assistant at the home allegedly saw Sly grab the resident and pull them up out of their chair and then forcibly direct them to the dining table. The CNA reported the incident to a charge nurse, and the resident was then given a physical examination that indicated they had sustained “substantial bruising” in the incident. Sly was fired that same day.
Administrative Law Judge Elizabeth Johnson recently ruled Sly was ineligible for unemployment benefits, citing “credible testimony establishing that claimant tried to physically force a resident to attend a meal,” which Johnson called “abusive and in deliberate disregard of the duty of care that she owed to this particular individual.” Sly has been ordered to repay the $3,570 in benefits already collected.
The Iowa Capital Dispatch was not able to reach Sly for comment.
— Bobby Jo Eck, who worked as a certified nursing assistant for Parker Creek Healthcare’s Spencer Post Acute Rehabilitation Center until her dismissal in July of this year. According to the recent findings of the judge who presided over Eck’s unemployment-benefits hearing, Eck was fired by her superiors after they concluded she was sleeping on the job, did not complete her training, conducted an unauthorized procedure of some kind on a patient and changed one patient’s diet without authorization.
Administrative Law Judge Daniel Zeno recently ruled Eck was eligible for unemployment benefits due to her employer failing to provide fair warning that her job was in jeopardy.
The Iowa Capital Dispatch was not able to reach Eck for comment.
— Susan McMullen, who worked as a certified nursing assistant for the Tripoli Nursing & Rehabilitation Center of Bremer County until her dismissal in August of this year. According to the recent findings of the judge who presided over McMullen’s unemployment-benefits hearing, McMullen was accused of taking excessive breaks and was captured on video not beginning to work her shift until 49 minutes after she’d clocked in. In one shift, she allegedly remained on break for more than 100 minutes, had previously been warned for not answering call lights, for “hanging out at the nurses’ station” even when residents’ call lights were flashing and for ignoring call lights altogether.
Administrative Law Judge Blair Bennett recently ruled McMullen was eligible for unemployment benefits after finding that the final incident that brought about her discharge — taking excessive breaks — did not constitute disqualifying misconduct because she had not been previously warned about such behavior.
The Iowa Capital Dispatch was not able to reach McMullen for comment.
— Patricia Williams, who worked as a certified nursing assistant for Eagle Point Nursing and Rehabilitation until her dismissal in July of this year. She was fired for allegedly using foul language in speaking about a resident despite previous warnings for that same offense. Prior to her dismissal, a resident of the home had asked that Wiliams not provide any care for him as she was too rough in handling him. Shortly thereafter, Williams was overheard by the resident and several co-workers complaining that she was “sick of mother——s lying on me.”
Administrative Law Judge Blair Bennett recently ruled Williams was ineligible for unemployment benefits, finding that Williams “knew that foul language would not be allowed, and let her emotions get the better of her in front of residents and coworkers.”
The Iowa Capital Dispatch was not able to reach Williams for comment.
Fantasia Gaddy, who worked as a medication manager for Grand Meadows Senior Living & Health Care in Asbury from May 2024 until her dismissal in June of this year. According to the recent findings of the judge who presided over Gaddy’s unemployment-benefits hearing, Gaddy was issued a warning in November 2025 for a medication error and another warning in February 2026 for an altercation she had with a coworker. In April 2026, a coworker reported finding unadministered medications in two residents’ rooms, as well as unadministered medications by the computer at the nursing station.
During the home’s subsequent investigation of the matter, it was discovered that Gaddy had an outstanding warrant for her arrest and had been incarcerated. Court records indicate the warrant was tied to a charge of being a fugitive from justice, which was in turn tied to a Wisconsin charge of first-degree reckless injury. Gaddy was fired on June 3, 2026.
Administrative Law Judge Carly Smith ruled recently that Gaddy is eligible for unemployment benefits, finding that her employer did not inform her she was under investigation and didn’t take final action in the matter until several weeks had passed.
The Iowa Capital Dispatch was not able to reach Gaddy for comment.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: New Florida Department Law Enforcement commissioner is a familiar face
description: With just months before Florida gets a new chief executive, Gov. Ron DeSantis on Tuesday installed a familiar face to lead the state’s main law enforcement agency. DeSantis appointed Larry Keefe, a former top aide to the governor who helped carry out the plan to transport immigrants from Texas to Martha’s Vineyard in 2022, as […]
text:
Larry Keefe was appointed FDLE  Commissioner by Gov. Ron DeSantis and the CabinetTuesday (Photo of Keefe at Florida Capitol on Feb. 19, 2025 by Jackie Llanos/Florida Phoenix)With just months before Florida gets a new chief executive, Gov. Ron DeSantis on Tuesday installed a familiar face to lead the state’s main law enforcement agency.
DeSantis appointed Larry Keefe, a former top aide to the governor who helped carry out the plan to transport immigrants from Texas to Martha’s Vineyard in 2022, as commissioner of the Florida Department of Law Enforcement. 
The operation sparked outrage and eventually led to state legislators putting limits on immigration enforcement outside of the state of Florida.
The governor’s choice to hire Keefe was approved by the three members of the Florida Cabinet, as required by law. The appointment does require Senate confirmation.
Keefe’s service in the DeSantis administration has included time as public safety czar and eight months as executive director of the State Board of Immigration Enforcement; Keefe left that job a year ago.
During brief remarks before the vote, DeSantis praised Keefe.
“In every position he had he has performed at the highest possible level,” DeSantis said. “Larry will lead the agency with distinction, ensuring the rule of law and public safety remain a top priority.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Keefe takes the place of Mark Glass, who had been in charge of FDLE since 2022. Glass, a military veteran who had become director of Capitol Police before his promotion to FDLE commissioner, is taking a job in Miami-Dade County, where he will be the second-in-command in the sheriff’s office.
Keefe, who once worked in a Northwest Florida law firm with Matt Gaetz, was U.S. attorney for the Northern District of Florida during the first term of President Donald Trump. He was not retained by President Joe Biden and was then hired by DeSantis.
It was during his time as public safety czar that he played a key role in setting up the high-profile migrant transport to Martha’s Vineyard and was on the initial leg of the flight from Texas. Public records obtained by news organizations showed that Keefe had used private emails under the alias “Clarice Starling” — a character in “The Silence of the Lambs” novel — to help a former client win the contract to operate the migrant flights.
Keefe also was also involved in DeSantis’ 2022 removal of Andrew Warren as state attorney for Hillsborough County. The governor removed Warren on several grounds, including his pronouncement that he would not enforce laws limiting abortion. Warren unsuccessfully challenged his removal in federal court but during the trial Keefe testified about the research and work he did ahead of Warren’s suspension.
In early 2025, Keefe became the first executive director of the State Board of Immigration Enforcement. The Legislature in concert with DeSantis created the board to consolidate efforts against undocumented immigration and approve state grants to reimburse state and local law enforcement.
But Keefe left several months later, in October of last year, in what the governor’s office called a planned move at the time.

name: WyoFile
title: ‘Dire’ financial situation: Game and Fish interim director warns of future severe budget concerns
description:
The cost of diesel fuel, vehicles and salary increases to attract top employees has been driving up costs. 
The post ‘Dire’ financial situation: Game and Fish interim director warns of future severe budget concerns appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
POWELL—The Wyoming Game and Fish Department budget has jumped by its highest amount in years and the interim director is calling budget concerns “dire” as inflation, especially in transportation costs, dramatically increases costs to the department. 
The budget has increased by 8.3%, according to department Chief Financial Officer Meredith Wood, who presented during the July commission meeting in Sheridan. 
The commission voted unanimously to approve an annual budget for 2027 of more than $108 million and a one-time expenditures budget of just over $2 million for a grand total of $110,640,013. 
The final year of a five-year mule deer study accounts for $1.275 million of the one-time budget expenditures. 
The 2026 standard budget was just over $100 million. 
The department had been running a largely flat budget for about a decade, but the cost of diesel fuel, vehicles and the need to increase salaries to compete for top employees has been pushing the need for more revenue. 
During the commission’s September meeting last week in Evanston, Interim Director Eric Wiltanger called the budget situation of great concern.
“Our costs continue to rise, and without intervention, our financial outlook over the coming years will become increasingly difficult,” he told commissioners. “A few weeks ago, I described our projected financial situation as dire, and I stand by that statement. I use the word intentionally because I want to make sure there is a clear understanding of the importance of acting now.” 
Eric Wiltanger was named interim director of the Wyoming Game and Fish Department following the Aug. 7 resignation of the agency’s director, Angi Bruce. (Wyoming Game and Fish Department)
Wiltanger had first sounded the alarm during the Legislature’s Joint Travel, Recreation, Wildlife, and Cultural Resources Committee hearing Sept. 9. 
Yet in front of the commission, Wiltanger only had to mention the price of diesel fuel to get his point across. 
“I’m sure everybody that drives a diesel truck right now, when you drive by the gas station, you recognize it’s over six bucks a gallon. Well, those hit our divisions every day,” Wiltanger said. “I mean,we’re spending more money than we anticipated just this budget cycle, just in gas alone.” 
While the budget has increased for next year, Wiltanger said the real problem will rear its ugly head in the early 2030s. He might send the Wyoming Legislature a message to possibly increase fees for tags and licenses, something that hasn’t happened since the department was cut off from state general funding.
The foundational costs for standard hunting and fishing tags (such as resident and nonresident big game licenses) require an act of the  Wyoming Legislature to change or adjust. Other ideas, like a trust fund that could possibly increase revenue by a few million, have been discussed. Wage increases over 2026 account for about $4.8 million of the budget increase. Deferred maintenance and capital construction costs account for another $4.5 million.
Wood told the commission that a little over $68 million of the budget are fixed costs such as salaries, animal damage costs and utilities. The rest of the budget (about $40 million) pays for everything else the department does, she said, including all conservation efforts, vehicles and fuel, education, the Access Yes program, stocking programs and payable grants.
Salaries for the department’s more than 400 employees account for nearly $59 million of the budget, or about 54% of the total cost to run the department. Retaining employees has been a priority in recent years due to federal and state agencies offering higher pay and better benefits. 
Wiltanger is temporarily replacing former Director Angi Bruce, who left the department in July. Yet he hasn’t hesitated to warn of future financial struggles should solutions not be found soon. 
“We have time to navigate these challenges, but that time is an opportunity, not a reason to wait. Being proactive is … exactly what we are doing. Our responsibility is to understand the financial trajectory, identify the challenges ahead and work together on solutions before those challenges become a crisis,” he told the commission. 
His responsibilities as interim director are to lead the department toward continued success in every aspect of the mission, not just in managing the budget but in managing and conserving wildlife, supporting employees and partners, and maintaining the outstanding outdoor opportunities that Wyoming is known for, he said. 
A permanent hire for director is likely to occur after a new governor is elected. 
“Looking ahead, we will continue to focus on our wildlife and habitat conservation, landowner partnerships, public access and responsible management of Wyoming’s fish and wildlife resources,” Wiltanger said.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Local officials knock NIPSCO storm outage response
description: NIPSCO defends storm outage performance as lawmakers crowdsource ideas for fixes next session.
text:
NIPSCO President and Chief Operating Officer Vince Parisi speaks during an interim committee hearing focused on the utility's storm response, on Tuesday, Sept. 29, 2026. (Photo by Leslie Bonilla Muñiz/Indiana Capital Chronicle)Northwest Indiana residents and officials on Tuesday panned the Northern Indiana Public Service Co.’s response to devastating storms last month, calling for a slate of changes in the upcoming legislative session.
Strong winds from Aug. 11 storms inflicted the worst damage in NIPSCO’s history, knocking out power to 375,000 customers — largely in Lake and Porter counties. Some homes and businesses didn’t regain electricity for two weeks.
“There seemed to be a failure in communication,” Griffith Police Chief Albert Tharp told lawmakers during an interim legislative committee meeting repurposed into a storm hearing.
Tharp said town leaders “weren’t getting” regular meetings with NIPSCO for at least a week after the Aug. 11 storms and that the meetings ended before all customers were reconnected. Residents calling NIPSCO were repeatedly told their outages weren’t showing up on the logs.
And when the town convened state staff and prison labor to help clear alleyways of debris and access utility equipment, NIPSCO sent “different workers than were planned and the management there didn’t really have a game plan.”
“Let’s do better with our execution,” Tharp said.
