CONTACT US



NIPSCO President and Chief Operating Officer Vince Parisi said the utility was “prepared for what we understood was coming” but weather forecasts “consistently underestimated” the storms’ eventual severity. The first indication wind speeds would top 100 miles an hour came just 11 minutes before the storm crossed into the utility’s territory, Parisi said.
He said thousands of trees were downed — “primed” by heavy rains and saturated soils — with five transmission towers and 1,500 utility poles damaged. The wooden distribution poles that line the average street are typically rated for 55 mile-an-hour winds.
Wind speeds “exceed(ed) what the system was designed to withstand,” Parisi said.
NIPSCO has plenty of spare wooden poles in inventory with higher ratings than older ones, but the utility will also likely consider hardier steel poles in the future, according to Parisi.
He said the company is paying for an internal after-action review that will be provided to the legislative committee. An outside contractor will also review the response, with the results published publicly. It’s unclear if the costs will be passed to ratepayers; NIPSCO didn’t immediately respond to a request from the Capital Chronicle.
The Interim Study Committee on Energy, Utilities and Telecommunications met to hear statutorily required reports from state utility regulators and consumer advocates before turning to the storm response.
The bipartisan group unanimously approved recommendations for legislation that would require utilities to file written emergency response procedures with the Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission and update them annually.
The other recommendation was to require the IURC to inspect utility vegetation management every two years. Trees and other vegetation are a main cause of electricity outages.
Lawmakers and constituents provided more suggestions.
United Steelworkers Local 12775 President Ryan Baker, a station chemical technician at NIPSCO, said the utility now has 183 electrical line workers — down from 233 in 2020.
“Fifty extra line workers would have provided an extra 800 man hours per day of experts on our system efficiently and safely restoring power,” Baker said.
Ryan Baker, president of the NIPSCO employee union, speaks during an interim committee hearing focused on NIPSCO’s storm response, on Tuesday, Sept. 29, 2026. (Photo by Leslie Bonilla Muñiz/Indiana Capital Chronicle)
He suggested the Legislature ensure utilities have enough staff to meet baseline customer need and lower reliance on expensive out-of-state contract workers.
Others want NIPSCO to pay for lost food and medicine, skip charging customers for fixed costs over the time they had no service and improve its public communications.  Several communities weren’t listed on storm restoration communications, which Parisi said was because NIPSCO didn’t have information.
“Even if the answer is, ‘We don’t know yet, we haven’t worked out a timeline for your city yet,’ some sort of communication has to be in place,” said Rep. Earl Harris, D-East Chicago. “This way, people at least have an idea.”
Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission Chair Anthony Swinger said the agency’s investigation into the storm response would include field hearings in northwest Indiana. He also encouraged customers to submit written comments, which become part of the case record.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: NC has a list of nearly 1600 people flagged as noncitizens on its voter rolls. How will it be used?
description: The North Carolina elections board says it has the names of nearly 1,600 potential noncitizens on its voter rolls who were flagged by a federal database. But as of two weeks ago, it hadn’t tried to contact any of them.  The U. S. Supreme Court is allowing states to use a Homeland Security database called […]
text:
North Carolinians continue to express high confidence in the security, safety and integrity of their own elections, but that confidence drops substantially when they consider elections beyond their local communities, according to a new Catawba College-YouGov Survey. (Photo: Clayton Henkel/NC Newsline) The North Carolina elections board says it has the names of nearly 1,600 potential noncitizens on its voter rolls who were flagged by a federal database. But as of two weeks ago, it hadn’t tried to contact any of them. 
The U. S. Supreme Court is allowing states to use a Homeland Security database called SAVE to look for noncitizens on voter rolls. North Carolina opted into using the SAVE database last year, and in July the state board sent an email saying it had identified 1,599 potential noncitizen voters on the rolls. 
However, it’s still not clear how the North Carolina Board of Elections will use that information. 
The board had not yet shared the names with county boards, board spokesman Jason Tyson said in a Sept. 11 email. “Additionally, neither the state board nor county boards have attempted to contact any individuals identified by SAVE as possibly being noncitizens,” he wrote. 
After the Supreme Court decision on Sept. 25 to allow the use of the database, state Elections Director Sam Hayes sent an email applauding it, saying he intended to use “every legal means in my disposal” to conduct voter list maintenance. 
“The State Board welcomes today’s decision by the U.S. Supreme Court. Both the United States Constitution and the North Carolina Constitution are clear: you must be a citizen of the United States to register and vote in our elections,” Hayes’ statement said. 
However, Hayes also added that “no voters will be automatically removed as a result of any voter list maintenance we do utilizing the database.”
In an email after Hayes’ statement, Tyson wrote, “[T]he plan on this has always been to operate within the parameters of the law. The ruling does have a lot of stipulations on timing which we plan to follow. There will be no automatic removals, of course, and the use of it is limited until after the election.”
Federal law prohibits voter roll purges within 90 days of an election. 
The state board in a party-line vote endorsed a rule for handling information about potential noncitizen voters gleaned from SAVE, NC Newsline has reported. The Rules Review Commission unanimously approved the rule in May, but it cannot be enforced because at least 10 people or organizations opposed it. With that opposition, the rule is being held for legislative review.
NC election officials approve new rules for noncitizen voter challenges

Under the procedure, when people are flagged as potential noncitizen registrants, their county’s elections administrators will be notified and will search their own records for proof of citizenship. If they can’t find any, people flagged would be called in to preliminary hearings to show documentation. If there’s a question after the preliminary hearings, the county boards will hold challenge hearings. 
The SAVE list is known to be inaccurate for mistakenly including citizens.
Texas was one of the first states to use the SAVE database to look for noncitizens registered to vote. Two weeks ago, the Texas Secretary of State said in a press release that of the 2,724 people the database flagged as potential noncitizens, 578 were actually citizens.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: DOJ awards Louisiana $1 million to assist cybercrime victims
description: The effort will fund the creation of victim’s rights materials and other resources for police to distribute and expand access to services for people targeted through cybercrimes.
text:
(Photo credit: Wes Muller/Louisiana Illuminator) The Trump administration has provided Louisiana’s attorney general with a $1 million grant to support victims of cybercrime, the U.S. Department of Justice announced Tuesday.
The money will be used in “a statewide effort to identify, serve and empower victims of technology-facilitated abuse, including image-based sexual abuse, non-consensual dissemination of intimate images and sextortion,” according to a DOJ news release.
The effort will fund the creation of victim’s rights materials and other resources for police to distribute and expand access to services for people targeted through cybercrimes. State officials will also establish a protocol for multiple agencies to respond to such instances.
“The protocol will directly address rapidly evolving digital crimes …” Attorney General Liz Murrill said in the news release. “Initiatives like these strengthen real-time collaboration among prosecutors, law enforcement and victim services.”

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Civil liberties group clashes with GOP election chief over voter challenge
description: The American Civil Liberties Union of New Jersey says Ocean County GOP officials are trying illegally to purge Democratic and unaffiliated voters from voter rolls.
text:
The American Civil Liberties Union of New Jersey says Ocean County GOP officials are trying illegally to purge Democratic and unaffiliated voters from voter rolls. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)[2026 election Voter Guide: Who is running in this November’s midterm elections?]The American Civil Liberties Union of New Jersey has demanded the Republican chairman of Ocean County’s Board of Elections stop investigating the residency of Democratic and unaffiliated voters in Bay Head, warning the “unlawful mass voter challenge” violates multiple state and federal voting rights laws.
The challenge originated with Dennis Shaning, the chairman of Bay Head’s all-Republican borough council, who compiled a list in August of Bay Head voters whose tax bills get mailed to addresses outside the borough, according to the civil liberties group.
Shaning sent the list — omitting any similarly situated Republicans — to George Gilmore, the longtime chairman of both Ocean County’s election board and its Republican organization, saying he believed they “should not be voting in Bay Head” and urging Gilmore to consider removing them from the borough’s voter rolls, according to a letter the ACLU sent Gilmore and Shaning Tuesday.
Gilmore then sent letters on Sept. 15 to the voters on Shaning’s list, directing them to fill out a “domicile questionnaire” and warning they might be deemed ineligible to vote in the Nov. 3 general election, the ACLU’s letter says. He also asked for documentation proving their residency and said they could attend an Oct. 13 board meeting to provide further information for commissioners mulling their eligibility.
All of that was illegal and unconstitutional, according to the ACLU.
“The Board has targeted voters based on their constitutionally protected political association and chilled their participation on the eve of an election with total disregard for the laws that prohibit precisely this kind of interference,” said Liza Weisberg, the ACLU-NJ’s supervising attorney. “We will always protect New Jerseyans’ access to the ballot — we are urging Ocean County officials to do the same.”
In their letter to Gilmore, Weisberg and Jeanne LoCicero, the civil liberties group’s legal director, advised him to stop his challenge, alert the targeted voters that they can disregard his earlier correspondence, and cancel the Oct. 13 meeting.
If he doesn’t, the lawyers warned, they’ll take him to court.
But Gilmore told the New Jersey Monitor that the county’s elections board, which is comprised of two Republicans and two Democrats, unanimously agreed to investigate the voters Shaning reported — and any decision to reverse course would also have to be made by the full board.
“The only thing we’ve done is ask for information from certain voters in regard to a letter that was submitted to the board. This has been our practice for over 30 years, and it’ll continue to be our practice until a court tells us we cannot do it,” Gilmore told the New Jersey Monitor. “We don’t go out looking for people. We react to challenges that come into the board.”
Shaning did not respond to requests for comment the New Jersey Monitor made via phone and email.
Weisberg estimated 39 Bay Head voters received the letter, but Gilmore couldn’t confirm that, saying he couldn’t remember how many people the letter went to and he didn’t have a copy of it handy to share with the New Jersey Monitor.
One voter contacted has already notified the board asking to be removed from the rolls because they no longer live in New Jersey, Gilmore added. As for the others, he added, “if everybody’s information verifies their domiciles in Bay Head, they’ll all be permitted to vote. Period. End of story.”
Weisberg and LoCicero said the board’s voter-purge effort violated several state and federal laws protecting voting rights, including a state voter empowerment act Gov. Mikie Sherrill (D) signed in July prohibiting intimidation and deceptive practices that discourage voting.
It also violated the National Voter Registration Act, which prohibits both “non-uniform” efforts to target voters for list-maintenance purposes and systematic voter-removal efforts during a 90-day “quiet period” before a federal election, Weisberg and LoCicero wrote.
While New Jersey law requires citizens to vote where they reside, the mailing address on a tax bill doesn’t prove domicile, they wrote.
“It reflects the location where an individual has asked the tax collector to send correspondence (perhaps the address of a relative, a second home, or an accountant’s office), and it furnishes no basis to doubt or displace a voter’s sworn registration address,” they wrote.
The state Supreme Court in 1972 decreed that when someone has more than one residence, “he, and he alone, can decide” where his political “interests” are more important to him, and the state cannot “decide for any voter that he ought to vote from one abode rather than another,” Weisberg and LoCicero wrote.
“A comprehensive statutory scheme prescribes the methods for determining voter eligibility in New Jersey. The process that you have concocted here is not part of it,” they told Gilmore.
Gilmore told the New Jersey Monitor he didn’t know Shaning only submitted Democratic and unaffiliated voters for residency checks, although he called it unsurprising.
“I never reviewed the list. I did not see it. I was told it came in, that there was questions raised, and we authorized the questionnaire to be sent out,” Gilmore said. “I don’t know what Shaning did. He may have only looked for Democrats. Normally, the president of the Republican Club would look to challenge Democrats. The president of the Democrat club would look to challenge Republicans. That’s common sense.”
Weisberg told the New Jersey Monitor her group would give Ocean County time to respond, “but we are prepared to litigate if we need to.”
“The legal violations are so clear, I think it would really behoove Ocean County to work with us to resolve this,” Weisberg said.
Gilmore remained defiant, taking a swipe at the ACLU over Sherrill’s July revelation that thousands of noncitizens were erroneously registered to vote through the state Motor Vehicle Commission, and about 340 of them cast ballots.
“Some voted! But the ACLU would say: ‘Let them vote!'” Gilmore said.
Republicans have cited the motor vehicle goof, which Sherrill blamed on a software error, to argue that the voter rolls brim with ineligible voters. Such claims have been repeatedly debunked, but polling suggests the allegations work to erode public confidence in the electoral system.
Gilmore said the Bay Head challenge was the only one his board has received this election season, but he expected more could arise.
“A lot of times this comes up a couple weeks before the election,” he added.
Republicans comprise the biggest voting bloc of Ocean County voters, representing 42% of the county’s nearly 482,547 registered voters, according to state data. Democrats, in comparison, make up 21%, and unaffiliated voters, 35%, of voters in the county, the data shows. About 47% of Bay Head voters are Republican; 23%, Democrat; and 30%, unaffiliated. The town has voted for Donald Trump all three times he’s run for president.
LoCicero said the ACLU stands ready to protect the ability of voters statewide to cast their ballot.
“We will not let local, state, or federal officials infringe on New Jerseyans’ fundamental right to make their voices heard,” LoCicero said in a statement.

name: VTDigger
title: Woodstock police chief resigns after demotion overturned
description:
Woodstock police chief Joseph Swanson announces retirement after a judge overturned efforts to demote him from his role.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Woodstock police chief resigns after demotion overturned.
text:
Former Woodstock Village Police Chief Joe Swanson, stands and stretches during his appeal hearing in Vermont Superior Court on Tuesday, June 30, 2026 in Woodstock, Vt. On the left is Woodstock attorney John H. Klesch, representing the village. Photo by Jennifer Hauck/Valley News

This story by Sofia Langlois was first published in the Valley News on Sept. 29, 2026.
WOODSTOCK — A judge ruled Tuesday in favor of the Woodstock police chief who town officials have now failed twice to demote.
But he has decided to retire.
Judge Kerry McDonald-Cady ruled in favor of Joseph Swanson and ordered that any further demotion considerations go before an impartial board. But Swanson has instead decided to retire as chief, as confirmed by his attorney, Linda Fraas.
In her decision, McDonald-Cady focused on an email exchange between Swanson and his husband, Nicholas Seldon, that included footage of Trustee Jeffrey Kahn involved in a 2023 road rage incident.
Since it was discussed by Trustees as they considered demoting Swanson, Kahn should have recused himself, McDonald-Cady wrote in an eight-page decision.
“Kahn’s self-assessed lack of bias is not sufficient,” she stated.
Swanson spent over 20 years with the department and started as chief in 2023. He received a positive performance review after his first year, but Municipal Manager Eric Duffy placed him on administrative leave after a verbal altercation involving Swanson’s husband in a 2024 traffic incident, where Swanson was the passenger, court records indicate.
An investigation by Vermont State Police and the Vermont Criminal Justice Council cleared Swanson of wrongdoing, but Duffy hired an outside investigator to look into his conduct as chief.
The investigator, who interviewed department staff, alleged that Swanson worked inconsistent hours and was absent during the day, kept a messy office and sometimes reported for duty out of uniform. He also claimed that Swanson did not respond to investigatory matters in a timely or thorough way and was inconsistent or unresponsive in exercising discipline.
Swanson filed a multi-million-dollar discrimination lawsuit in April 2025 against Duffy, the Town of Woodstock, the Village of Woodstock, acting Chief Christopher O’Keeffe and Seton McIlroy, the former Village Board chair, over his demotion.
Duffy had proposed Swanson be demoted from chief to patrol officer, the lowest-ranking position. The Village Trustees held a 14-hour hearing on the matter in March 2024 and ultimately decided to uphold the decision in July, though they opted not to demonstrate the specific legal cause.
When Swanson appealed the decision in court, Judge H. Dickson Corbett ruled in his favor, noting that the Village Board was required to establish cause finding that Swanson became “negligent or derelict” in his official duties, “engaged in ‘conduct unbecoming an officer,’” or otherwise became “unable to perform the functions” of his job, the superior court judge wrote in an August 2025 decision.
As a result, the Trustees went back to the drawing board with a second hearing where they tried to establish cause for the demotion, in a 126-page decision.
Back in court on June 30, 2026, Fraas and Woodstock’s attorney, John Klesch, made their cases to Cady-McDonald.
Fraas noted that Swanson received no prior notification of failure to perform, or of policy violations prior to his demotion. She argued that the trustees acknowledged there was no “one particular act” that warranted dismissal, and that instead, Duffy based his decision on the totality of complaints.
Klesch argued that Swanson’s repeated lack of professionalism led to demotion, and the court needed to determine not if a reasonable person “would” make the same decision as the Trustees, but if they “could.”
On Sept. 22, nearly three months after the oral arguments, McDonald-Cady decided that Swanson had been robbed of due process in the second hearing, because Kahn, a Trustee, declined to recuse himself.
Part of the argument for demoting Swanson included the fact that, through his work email, he sent footage of a 2023 road rage incident involving Kahn and a member of the public to Seldon, who is a local attorney.
Despite Swanson’s request that Kahn recuse himself from the vote, he declined, McDonald-Cady noted in her decision.
The Trustees determined Swanson did not share the videos for a professional purpose, such as legal advice, but rather “because he was looking to share something with his husband that he found interesting,” the Trustees said.
As such, the decision to demote Swanson is officially reversed, said McDonald-Cady, who added in her order that further reconsiderations must be by an impartial board.
Swanson’s retirement makes that unnecessary, however. Duffy declined to comment on the retirement but said generally that when an employee resigns, their accrual time is paid out and their benefits end.
The appeal is now closed. Court records indicate the discrimination lawsuit is in mediation, with a status conference set for Oct. 5 at 3 p.m. in the Woodstock courthouse.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: $15 minimum wage is here, but it’s not a livable’ wage, group says
description: An estimated 1.29 million minimum-wage (nontip) Florida workers will start earning a $15 hourly wage Wednesday. For those in the service industry who earn tips, the minimum wage will be $11.98 an hour. But is the minimum wage a livable wage? “At its simplest, a living wage is what one full-time worker must earn on […]
text:
Sisters Kristine Ownley (left) and Leigh Anne Balzekas (right) are co-owners of The Disco Dolls Studio in Tampa  and helped champion a $15 minimum wage in 2020. (Photo credit: Scott Purks)An estimated 1.29 million minimum-wage (nontip) Florida workers will start earning a $15 hourly wage Wednesday.
For those in the service industry who earn tips, the minimum wage will be $11.98 an hour.
But is the minimum wage a livable wage?
“At its simplest, a living wage is what one full-time worker must earn on an hourly basis to help cover the cost of their family’s minimum basic needs where they live without depending on public or private assistanc[e],” the Massachusetts Institutte of Technology offers in its Living Wage Calculator.
The Florida Policy Institute (FPI) has tracked the implementation of the minimum wage and how it compares to a livable wage since 2020.
The  FPI estimates that, statewide, a living hourly wage ranges from $19.57 for a single person without children to $34.10 for two adults with one child.
FPI relies on the Economic Policy Institute (EPI) — which analyzed the 2015-2019 American Community Survey U.S. Census data, wage data from the 2025 U.S. Census Bureau, and the Bureau of Labor Statistics — for its workforce estimates of people earning less than $15 an hour.
“Far too many Floridians will continue to struggle to make ends meet at a $15 minimum wage — even those in households with more than one person working full time or with single people without kids,” said Alexis Tsoukalas, senior policy analyst at FPI.
“So while passage of Amendment 2 in 2020 was a historic and important step forward, ensuring the minimum wage is a living wage should be top of mind for state policymakers, along with actually enforcing the current wage to prevent wage theft.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
According to FPI, an estimated 1.29 million Floridians were earning less than $15 an hour before Sept. 30. Most, 696,100, were women.
Of the 1.29 million workers:

569,000 were between the ages of 18 and 24.
345,800 were between the ages of  25 and 39.
146,400 were between the ages of  40-54.
139,800 were 55-plus.
436,700 people were white.
422,700 people were Hispanic.
280,900 were Black.
28,400 were  Asian American or Pacific islander.




Quotation







I'm the owner, so its up to me to make the business profitable, it's not my employees responsibility to work for less.


– Kristine Ownley, co-owner of The Disco Dolls Studio




Florida voters approved the $15 minimum wage in 2020 in the form of Amendment 2 when the state’s minimum wage at the time was $8.46 an hour.
Amendment 2 required that the minimum wage be increased to $10 an hour on Sept. 30, 2021, and by $1 a year thereafter until Sept. 30, when it hit the $15 mark.
Thereafter, the minimum wage increases annually based on inflation.
It was adamantly opposed by Florida Restaurant and Lodging Association and other business that argued the increase would hurt small businessses struggling to recover from COVID-19 pandemic.
But not all business owners saw it as a bad thing.
Sisters Leigh Anne Balzekas and Kristine Ownley are co-owners of The Disco Dolls Studio, a clothing store, hair salon, and art gallery in Tampa. The business is celebrating its 16th anniversary this year.
The siblings worked with the group Business for a Fair Minimum Wage in 2020 to support passage of the  $15 minimum wage.
They say the shop doesn’t have high turnover and its customer service is great, which they attribute to happy, well-paid employees.
Ownley told the Phoenix costs at the retail shop are high. “But so are living expenses. I’m the owner, so it’s up to me to make the business profitable, it’s not my employees’ responsibility to work for less,” she said.

name: DC
outlet: News From The States - Fair. Fearless. Free.
title: Trump TV ads paid for with $20M in Homeland Security funds, Dems find
text: President Donald Trump is tapping $20 million in Homeland Security funding to pay for TV ads that heavily feature him ahead of the midterm elections, Democrats said Tuesday as the promos critics call propaganda come under bipartisan attack.The Trump administration recently moved the funds into a U.S. Customs and Border Protection budget line intended for “commemorative events” related to border security, according to federal records. Congressional Democrats said the dollars appear to be funding the ad campaign.The ads face mounting criticism as Republicans confront an angry electorate that, according to polling, appears likely to place Democrats in control of the House and possibly the Senate. Yet the messaging reflects Trump’s strategy of centering the election on himself and telling supporters to vote as if he was on the ballot, as he urged during the GOP midterm convention.The three ads released so far feature stylized imagery of Trump and include “Paid for by the U.S. Government” disclosures. One is nearly identical to a 2024 Trump campaign ad. Some $2 million in ads have aired on cable and broadcast stations over the past week. “This is the final battle,” Trump says in a voiceover in one black-and-white ad that shows him walking silently toward the camera. Another ad uses the song “Love Me” by the artist JMSN. Attorneys for the performer have sent a cease-and-desist letter to the administration demanding the ad be taken down.Both Dems and Republicans objectSenate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, a New York Democrat, slammed the ads as indistinguishable from Trump’s 2024 campaign ads, yet funded by taxpayers. “It’s an absolute violation of what democracy is supposed to look like. Americans sat down to watch football, not to be force fed Trump’s propaganda on their own dime,” Schumer said Monday on the Senate floor.Some GOP senators have also split with the Trump administration over the ads. Senate Majority Leader John Thune, a South Dakota Republican, told reporters that while he liked the ads’ message, tax dollars shouldn’t pay for them. Sen. John Kennedy of Louisiana and Sen. John Cornyn of Texas have also pushed back, among others."I don't think any public official, including President Trump or (former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi) Noem or John Kennedy, should spend public money on private ads for themselves,” Kennedy told “Face the Nation” on CBS.$20 million materializesOn Tuesday, Sens. Patty Murray of Washington, the top Democrat on the Senate Appropriations Committee, and Christopher Murphy of Connecticut, the ranking Democrat on the Senate Appropriations Homeland Security Subcommittee, in a letter to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said his department appeared to have dedicated $20 million to the ads that had been provided to Customs and Border Protection, a sub-agency of DHS, in the “One Big Beautiful Bill” Act last year.House Democratic Reps. Rosa DeLauro of Connecticut and Henry Cuellar of Texas in their own statement also cited federal apportionment changes by the Office of Management and Budget recorded by OpenOMB, a non-governmental database that tracks apportionments. OpenOMB shows that on Sept. 19, $20 million was moved into a fund that pays for border security commemorative events and that previously held just $500,000.Republican blocks resolution on adsSen. Maggie Hassan, a New Hampshire Democrat, sought unanimous consent in the Senate on Tuesday to pass a resolution stating that the federal government shouldn’t pay for the ads. “The Department of Homeland Security should be working to tackle the enormous national security threats we face like stopping fentanyl, not bankrolling a vanity project for the president,” Hassan said.Sen. Cynthia Lummis, a Wyoming Republican, objected, saying the heart of the ads is about defending American values from communism and socialism. Lummis said if that message has Hassan concerned, it says “more about her side of the aisle than it does about” the ads. The action by Lummis halted action on the resolution.Administration defends adsThe White House and Homeland Security didn’t deny that the government fund was being used to pay for the ads, in response to questions from States Newsroom.The White House said in an unsigned statement that the ads — which it calls public service announcements — are educational and intended to remind Americans “to love their country and understand what makes it worth defending, at home, at our borders, and abroad.” Homeland Security referred States Newsroom to a White House webpage that also defends the ads. The page says they aren’t campaign ads, noting that Trump isn’t on the ballot and that the messages include no call to action.Government ethics and legal experts say that explanation misses the point.“There’s a distinction between providing people with information about government programs and engaging in communication that merely aggrandizes government officials. And what we have here is purely aggrandizing Donald Trump,” Samuel Bagenstos, who served as general counsel to the Office of Management and Budget during the first year and a half of President Joe Biden’s administration, said in an interview.Bagenstos, who is now a professor at the University of Michigan Law School, said that if the issue was simply whether the ads violate the Hatch Act, a federal law that limits federal employees — but not the president – from engaging in partisan politics on the job, the question of the ads’ legality could be more complicated. But the most important legal issue with the ads, he said, isn’t the Hatch Act but whether the messages violate prohibitions on using government funds for propaganda. During his time in government service, which also included a stint as general counsel to the Department of Health and Human Services during the Biden administration, Bagenstos said agencies were constantly communicating with the public, and there’s always a question of how far officials can go. But he said these kind of issues were reviewed carefully, often in ways that annoyed communications staff who wanted to put out messages immediately.“But if something like this had crossed my desk, I would have said, ‘You can’t pay for this ad. It is clearly illegal,’” Bagenstos said, adding that the ads are the kind of thing he would have considered resigning over. “It’s that clear a violation of law and it’s really corrosive to democracy,” he said.Similarity to franking?Members of Congress and state-level officials regularly release slick official communications that sometimes echo campaign messaging. But that practice, known as “franking,” comes with clear restrictions, including a U.S. House prohibition on mass mailings 60 days before an election.In sending franked mail, members of Congress are barred from sending mail that “solicits political support” for the lawmaker or any person or political party, Margaret Dylus-Yukins, senior legal counsel for ethics at the Campaign Legal Center, wrote in an email.The Trump ads, by contrast, don’t pertain to any policymaking process or function of government, and while the White House has said the messages remind Americans to love their country, there’s no apparent connection to any federal program or service, Dylus-Yukins wrote. Instead, she wrote that their inflammatory language, widespread distribution and touting of Trump’s term in office, as well as their close proximity to the midterms, “all suggest that these advertisements were produced with the intent to solicit political support for President Trump’s political allies ahead of the midterm election.”“These advertisements therefore appear to be in violation of the Hatch Act and raise serious concerns about the use of taxpayer funds to possibly sway the upcoming election’s outcome,” Dylus-Yukins wrote.No lawsuit yetAs of Tuesday afternoon the ads didn’t appear to face a legal challenge. The watchdog group Democracy Forward said Monday it was launching an investigation into the ads and had filed records requests for communications regarding the ads and financial paperwork related to them.Bagenstos suggested the courts may not be the best avenue to fight the ads. Instead, he said, Congress needs to assert itself and retaliate against inappropriate spending.“In our separation of powers system, what our framers expected was that Congress would stand up for its power first,” Bagenstos said.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Refugees, asylum seekers to lose Medicaid coverage Oct. 1
description: A family arrives at the Immigrant Alliance for Justice and Equity Center (IAJE) to pick up free diapers during a giveaway, Thursday, Sept. 24, 2026, in Jackson.
text:
Multiple groups of lawfully present immigrants, including refugees and asylum seekers without a green card, will become ineligible for Medicaid and CHIP, the Children’s Health Insurance Program, starting Oct. 1. The changes take effect following the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act” that President Donald Trump signed into law last year. 
Health policy experts and organizations that work with immigrants in Mississippi warn the changes will worsen a culture of fear that could compel immigrants to delay seeking medical attention. Downstream, this can lead to costlier care of potentially preventable illnesses and create more strain for an already burdened healthcare system.
“These immigrants will be left with very few affordable coverage options,” said Drishti Pillai, director of Immigrant Health Policy at KFF, a national nonpartisan health policy organization. Pillai pointed to upcoming restrictions on subsidized Affordable Care Act Marketplace and Medicare plans. Starting in January, these options will be limited to only the three groups of immigrants that also retain Medicaid eligibility.  
Who is and isn’t eligible
Green card holders, also known as lawful permanent residents, will still be eligible for Medicaid, the joint federal and state program that provides free or low-cost health insurance to low-income individuals. Immigrants from Cuba, Haiti and Pacific Island nations in the Compact of Free Association, an international treaty with the United States, also will remain eligible for such benefits.
Several groups of immigrants with vulnerable backgrounds, however, will lose access to Medicaid coverage. Refugees and asylees, who fled their home countries for fear of persecution and have received humanitarian status in the U.S., will no longer be eligible. Neither will survivors of domestic violence with approved or in-progress applications for a green card under the Violence Against Women Act. The act created a pathway to lawful permanent resident status for women whose green card sponsors abused them. 
Refugees in the U.S. are fleeing terror and violence in their home countries, said Lorena Lewis-Quiroz, executive director of the Immigrant Alliance for Justice and Equity, a Jackson-based immigration advocacy group. 
“You’re already coming from that and then losing access to care. I just can’t believe that this is happening, you know?” she said. “This is chipping away at this system of healthcare for immigrants.”
Similarly, immigrants who will lose eligibility include victims of human trafficking, such as sex and labor trafficking, and those who have an approved or pending T visa. This temporary status allows immigrants to apply for permanent residency. Other groups losing Medicaid are: 

Immigrants granted humanitarian parole to stay in the U.S. for at least one year;
Immigrants who have been granted a withholding of deportation;
Canadian-born members of a federally recognized Indian tribe or American Indians;
Older individuals who were granted conditional entry before the Refugee Act of 1980 (including people who fled communist countries in the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe as well as some refugees from Southeast Asia).

In Mississippi, children and pregnant adults who have legal status will also lose Medicaid eligibility. Some states have opted to continue offering coverage for these groups under the 2009 Immigrant Children’s Health Improvement Act, which waives the five-year period many immigrants wait between gaining their green card and being able to enroll in Medicaid. Since January, 38 states have chosen to provide health coverage for legally present immigrant children, and 32 states have done so for people who are pregnant. Mississippi has not chosen to cover either group. 
“The changes to Medicaid are harsh and could prevent coverage for eligible children, if the parents can no longer file on their citizen children behalf due to the parent’s immigration status,” wrote El Pueblo Executive Director Kathy Sykes over email. The statewide organization provides free legal and social services to immigrants. 
“There are so many changes coming down from the federal government it gets quite confusing and may scare away those who are eligible from ever applying for needed services,” she said. 
Impacts beyond losing insurance
Pillai worries about the broader impact of losing eligibility and verification processes — even for immigrants who are still eligible for Medicaid.
States will need to verify the immigration status of people being disenrolled through the Department of Homeland Security’s database, Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements (SAVE) and social security databases. If the state Medicaid agency can verify eligible status, enrollees will maintain their Medicaid coverage. If officials are unable to verify status with that information, they must request additional information from the person affected, and give them 90 days to respond. 
Khaylah Scott, program manager at the Mississippi Health Advocacy Program, said the rules around Medicaid eligibility have been in place for 30 years, since the 1996 Welfare Reform Act.  
“When you’re facing few or little communication from the Division of Medicaid and the first time hearing about this may be receiving that letter, it is pretty sudden,” she said. “I’m just imagining the confusion, the fear that some could experience just receiving this letter in the mail and knowing at the heart of it is your immigration status.”
This verification process may be confusing for immigrants, especially those with low-English proficiency. Pillai said past research has shown that when disenrollment occurs, it can also affect people who changed their address or otherwise weren’t able to fill out the required paperwork. 
“All of these could lead to disenrollments, not due to eligibility, but for administrative reasons,” she said.
The Mississippi Division of Medicaid did not respond to Mississippi Today’s request for comment on how these changes will be implemented. A Sept. 14 public notice for a proposed Medicaid state plan change notes that the amendment “is anticipated to be budget neutral due to a low number of effected individuals” but does not provide an estimate on how many immigrants will be affected.  
Immigrants who no longer qualify for Medicaid or the Children’s Health Insurance Program can still receive coverage under Emergency Medicaid in specific circumstances, such as sudden onset of severe symptoms that, if left untreated, could result in serious harm. A pregnant person entering labor, for instance, is covered in all states. Because Mississippi has not expanded Medicaid, eligibility is limited to a narrower group of categories. A low-income undocumented adult who is not pregnant, not a qualifying parent, and does not qualify through a disability category cannot rely on Emergency Medicaid even if they have a qualifying event. 
In the long term, Pillai said, this loss of eligibility could lead to worse health outcomes as people wait until their conditions become unbearable. 
“If individuals don’t have coverage and they’re not getting routine care, it’s likely to increase reliance on emergency rooms,” she said. “It could further strain community health centers, since those treat patients regardless of immigration status, regardless of ability to pay.” 
Lewis-Quiroz sees a similar impact looming: “It’s just gonna be another case of, ‘Well, you know what? I will just wait until I have that stroke.’”
This story was produced with support from the Sarah Yelena Haselhorst Fund for Health Journalism.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: RI federal judge strikes down Trump grant restrictions for domestic violence groups
description: A Rhode Island federal judge on Tuesday struck down the Trump administration’s attempts to  restrict federal grants for organizations serving victims of domestic violence and sexual assault. U.S. District Court Judge Melissa R. DuBose ruled that the U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) failed to adequately explain its decision to condition grants on restrictions[...]
text:
The exterior of U.S. District Court for the District of Rhode Island at 1 Exchange Terrace, Providence. (Photo by Alexander Castro/Rhode Island Current)A Rhode Island federal judge on Tuesday struck down the Trump administration’s attempts to  restrict federal grants for organizations serving victims of domestic violence and sexual assault.
U.S. District Court Judge Melissa R. DuBose ruled that the U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) failed to adequately explain its decision to condition grants on restrictions involving immigration status and programs related to diversity, equity and inclusion, and gender identity.
The 10-page summary judgment order resolves a lawsuit brought by the Rhode Island Coalition Against Domestic Violence and other organizations challenging the conditions imposed on grants administered through DOJ’s Office on Violence Against Women and Office of Justice Programs.
“Defendants have failed to provide actual, substantive, and contemporaneous support for the idea that they considered the adverse impact of these conditions in a material manner,” DuBose, a Biden appointee, wrote.
Plaintiff organizations led by the Rhode Island Coalition Against Domestic Violence challenged the legality of withholding grants in order to advance Trump’s policies last June, arguing the eligibility requirements for Violence Against Women Act funds were in violation of the Administrative Procedure Act since the changes were made without any clear reasoning.
Judge blocks feds from restricting grants serving victims of domestic violence and sexual assault

The grants were created under the Violence Against Women Act, part of the Violent Crime Control and Law Enforcement Act of 1994, to help organizations that support victims through legal services, housing assistance and crisis counseling.
According to the lawsuit, the DOJ is now demanding that grant recipients certify they are complying with the conditions and could be subject to penalties. including the potential withholding of funds, contract termination or termination of awards. The federal government separately warned of potential criminal prosecution under the federal False Claims Act if they made false or fraudulent statements concerning their awards. 
The DOJ argued that administration officials had devoted sufficient time and effort to the changes.
DuBose did not see it that way.
“Defendants’ attempt to impose these conditions on Plaintiffs served as a sweeping and chaotic overhaul of the prior way in which Defendants required grantees to comply with these programs,” she wrote.
Plaintiff organizations in a joint statement said they were relieved to see DuBose’s final order on the case.
“These grants help sustain shelters, crisis response services, legal assistance, and coordinated community efforts that survivors rely on in moments of profound danger,” they said. “We are grateful that this ruling means that this critical funding will have lasting, permanent protection.” 
Plaintiff organizations numbered 25 in all and represented 22 states plus the District of Columbia. The organizations were based in California, Colorado, D.C., Wisconsin, Georgia, Hawaii, Idaho, Indiana, Iowa, Massachusetts, Kansas, Maine, Maryland, Montana, New Jersey, North Carolina, Oregon, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, Vermont, Minnesota, Virginia and Washington. 
The plaintiffs’ legal team included attorneys from Democracy Forward, the ACLU of Rhode Island, the National Women’s Law Center, the Lawyers’ Committee for Rhode Island, and Daniel Jacobson, a former counsel for the U.S. Office of Management and Budget during the Biden administration, and now head of Jacobson Lawyers Group.
A spokesperson for the U.S. Department of Justice did not immediately respond to request for comment.

name: VTDigger
title: A rising cohort of vets is giving Vermonters new ways to say goodbye to beloved pets
description:
At-home pet euthanasia and hospice services allow owners to give their animals greater comfort at the end of life. 
Read the story on VTDigger here:  A rising cohort of vets is giving Vermonters new ways to say goodbye to beloved pets.
text:
Finnegan and Duffy sit on a chair. Photo by Laura Cadmus
Laura Cadmus’ cat, Duffy, used to sit on the edge of her table and a CD rack with his front legs dangling off the side. 
Now, the same spots are decorated with photos of him in those odd positions, her way to hold onto his memory after he died of cancer earlier this year at age 8. 
“(It) was absolutely so devastating to me,” said the Barre native. “I mean, it’s probably just in the last couple months that I’ve stopped crying every day.”

Duffy the cat leans an arm over the side of an end table, showing off a shaved patch of fur. Photo by Laura Cadmus

There’s one thing that has brought Cadmus comfort through her grief. Duffy was able to avoid the veterinarian’s office, which was always a “nightmare” to get him to, and pass away in the comfort of his own home thanks to the work of Dr. Erika Bruner, a Washington County vet who specializes in at-home euthanasia. 
A small but growing contingent of Vermont veterinarians is offering at-home end-of-life care to pet owners, including hospice and palliative care along with euthanasia. In the process, they’re rethinking the way we shepherd our beloved animals through their last days. 
Dr. Caroline Horn, another veterinarian who offers end-of-life care from her practice in Chittenden County, said the field has grown during her time in it. When Horn attended her first conference of the International Animal Hospice and Palliative Care Society in 2018, she estimated fewer than 100 people were there. At the latest one she went to, hundreds of people from around the world attended.
“I’ve had to say goodbye to many of my own animals. It is just brutal,” Horn said. “But I want it to be so peaceful that owners can more quickly heal from this tremendous loss, and that’s the space that most mobile vets try to fill.”
“It was just peace and calm”
Tippy the cat had traveled around the country in a trailer with her owner, but she was terrified of strangers. 
“She wasn’t a huge fan of the vet for sure,” said her owner, Patrick White, of Williamstown. “For me, she was super snuggly, super close.”
White lost his other cat, Tippy’s travel mate Mary J, several years ago. He and his partner had opted to put down Mary J in the more traditional way at the vet’s office. He said the staff worked hard to make the process gentle and unhurried, but ultimately it still felt rushed and stressful. 

Tippy the cat with her owner Patrick White, left, and his partner. Courtesy of Patrick White.

So when Tippy began to show signs of kidney failure a few months ago at 16 years old, White thought back to a friend in Chicago who had put down their dog at home. White called Bruner, head of Heart of Vermont Vet in Washington County, and started to make arrangements for when it was time for Tippy to go. 
Bruner said her work usually starts with a conversation about the animal’s health, behavior and day-to-day life to help guide owners to their decision about when to put down their pet. 
“You’re not telling them what to do. They’re telling you what they’re seeing and what they’re feeling,” she said. “And most of them already know what the best thing for them is going to be. But they just need some reinforcement that their decision is a good one.”
When that time came for Tippy, White said, Bruner talked the couple through every stage in the process, giving them the option to go at their own pace. 
“As soon as she walked into the room, it was just peace and calm,” White said. 
Bruner’s service also allowed Tippy to pass away in a comfortable spot on her owners’ bed.
Horn’s work also starts with a conversation or a visit, but she has a slightly different emphasis as a vet who offers hospice and palliative care. When a pet is declining but not yet ready to die, she provides owners with comfort kits, pain and nausea medications, and a plan for worsening symptoms. 

Tippy the cat. Courtesy of Patrick White.

She also advises owners to take advantage of the time to fill out the pet’s bucket list. 
“I don’t think any dog in Vermont should pass away without a creemee — or two or three,” she said. “We want them to go through the McDonald’s drive-in if that’s what their pet likes.”
Horn’s staff at her practice, Paws at Home, checks in with owners regularly as they care for their pets at home. Sometimes she has had to guide owners to recognize the reality in front of them. 
“We can say, ‘Look, do you remember when we first came out, and your pet was doing this and this and this, and they’re not doing any of that anymore?’” she said. 
Bruner said she didn’t think there was such a thing as a perfect time to say goodbye. 
“There’s a time when it’s clearly too early, and a time where it’s obvious what the decision should be,” Bruner said. “And then in between, there is a gray area where it seems to me that as long as the person feels like the bad is outweighing the good, like it doesn’t have to be the right day or the right moment.”
“The most valuable job I’ve ever done” 
Horn came to end-of-life pet care through an indirect route. She spent years as a conventional veterinarian then switched to human medicine and worked in anesthesia for two decades. 
Seeing the growing prominence of hospice and palliative care for people opened her eyes to the “huge need” to bring that to the veterinary world. 
“When I got out of school, I never thought I’d be doing this,” she said. “But I do think it’s probably the most valuable job I’ve ever done.”
The rise of at-home end-of-life care might provide an unexpected benefit to veterinarians’ mental health, too. Vets report high rates of burnout and depression, and one factor is the emotional toll of difficult procedures like euthanasia, according to an analysis of research studies by Nature. 
Horn said some vet clinics have begun referring euthanasias to her practice to avoid the stress on their staff. 
“There’s an emotional toll on everybody in the building, and this just brings it out and makes it a very safe thing,” she said. 
The clearest downside of these services is their cost. Amid rising vet bills and other cost-of-living expenses, some pet owners struggle to afford euthanasia at all.
The Central Vermont Humane Society provides low-cost in-office euthanasia to some low-income pet owners on a case-by-case basis. Erika Holm, the shelter’s co-executive director of programs and operations, said one Vermonter who reached out for help had been quoted $600 by a veterinarian to put down their very large dog because the cost of the drugs rises by weight. 
“We completely understand when people truly can’t afford it, and we do not want animals to suffer and pass away at home,” she said. 

Duffy the cat and owner Laura Cadmus. Photo by Laura Cadmus

She advised Vermonters to call their local shelters to get a list of low-cost clinics and other resources in their area. 
Holm said she’s seen a growing understanding of the impact that losing a pet can have on a person. 
“There’s the people that go, ‘It’s just a dog, you know, or it was just a cat. Why are you so upset?’’’ she said. But “think about what happened during the pandemic. Shelters emptied because people were home, and they wanted a companion there with them. People recognized how meaningful it would be.”
Holm believes that losing a pet can be as difficult, or more difficult, than losing a person in your life. 
“I don’t think unconditional love exists for people toward people, but … animals don’t hold us to the standards that we hold people to, and we also pour our hearts and souls into them in ways we are often more guarded toward people,” she said.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: ‘Not enough data or expertise’: Oklahoma lawmakers consider future of data centers
description: OKLAHOMA CITY — Nearly a dozen state lawmakers heard from operators, developers, environmental agencies, local elected officials and concerned Oklahomans Tuesday as they weigh the best way to regulate the rapidly changing data center industry.  Oklahoma lawmakers held the study in hopes of finding a legislative solution that balances the needs of data center[...]
text:
House lawmakers on Sept. 29, 2026 listened to presentations at the state Capitol on the impacts data centers have on Oklahoma. (Photo by Emma Murphy/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY — Nearly a dozen state lawmakers heard from operators, developers, environmental agencies, local elected officials and concerned Oklahomans Tuesday as they weigh the best way to regulate the rapidly changing data center industry. 
Oklahoma lawmakers held the study in hopes of finding a legislative solution that balances the needs of data centers operators with the growing concerns of residents. Residents in Oklahoma and across the country are concerned about the impact the massive facilities, which house and maintain the physical equipment needed to process digital information, will have on their utility bills and how much water they consume.
Some Oklahoma governments, like in Oklahoma City and the Seminole Nation, have enacted moratoriums on new construction as the demand for data centers increases with growing use of artificial intelligence. 
Rep. Mark Chapman, R-Broken Arrow, on Sept. 29, 2026, led an interim study at the state Capitol on the impacts data centers have on Oklahoma. (Photo by Emma Murphy/Oklahoma Voice)
Rep. Mark Chapman, R-Broken Arrow, who hosted the study, said state lawmakers need to look at the issue from multiple perspectives and figure out how to be as fair as possible to both data centers and Oklahomans when regulating the industry. 
“Some people may be completely on one side or the other of this issue,” he said. “But I would like to think that, as with most things, the truth may fall somewhere in the middle.”
Chapman said data centers are coming to Oklahoma either way and the state needs to decide how it wants to participate. 
“I’m not saying any of this to be a cheerleader for the data center industry,” he said. “I’m simply pointing out that regardless of where you stand on future data center development, we already use them all the time.”
He said he and other lawmakers should be wary of “one-size fits all” solutions.
Kaily Ball, a resident of Kingfisher County, said she began researching data centers when one began being developed five miles from her family’s farm, which they’ve been operating for five generations. 
For Ball, the more than a thousand hours of research she’s done was necessary for her survival and her family’s long-term planning. She said she’d previously dealt with kidney failure as a result of heavy metal poisoning that left her more susceptible to water quality and environmental concerns. 
She said she’s spoken over a thousand concerned Oklahomans as well as elected officials, data center developers and operators, and there’s frustration with the lack of transparency and information available on all sides. 
“What I’ve seen from all sides of the issue is not that there’s not enough data or expertise,” Ball said. “It’s that we’re missing the connective tissue that brings them all together in a way that reduces the administrative burden on everyone.”
Among the concerns on the top of Oklahomans’ minds is water use, Ball said, as well as noise, construction traffic, contaminated natural resources, rising energy bills, and more. 
Water and energy use
Chris Neel, the division chief of Water Rights Administration Division with the Oklahoma Water Resources Board, said the demand for water from data centers is immense, but the board doesn’t always have oversight of its use. 
Google’s data center in Pryor uses an estimated 2.8 million to 3.76 million gallons of water per day, he said. In comparison, Norman, a city serving about 108,000 people, used an average of nearly 24 million gallons of water per day in August. 
Google’s data center in Stillwater is estimated to use 5 million to 6 million gallons per day, Neel said. 
Pryor Mayor Zac Doyle said Google’s data center, located at the MidAmerica Industrial Park, has been there for nearly 20 years and his community has benefitted through reduced utility bills, jobs, partnerships with local businesses and increased funding and grants.
A large data center is pictured in Culpeper County, Virginia. (Photo by Evan Visconti/Virginia Mercury)
He said his constituents in Pryor don’t seem to have an issue with data centers, but there’s some hesitation from private landowners just outside city limits who don’t want a data center built near their homes. 
“In town, we’re used to it and we appreciate it,” Doyle said. 
In addition to the Pryor data center, Google is planning new campuses in Stillwater, Owasso, and the Muskogee County towns of Summit and Council Hill. Data centers with other companies are planned, proposed or being built in other places across Oklahoma, like the recently announced Lambda data center in Chouteau. 
Kimber Shoop, the director of regulatory affairs for OG&E, said the utility company has worked to make sure that large load consumers, like data centers, don’t pass costs onto regular ratepayers through a series of checks and balances. 
Those include long-term commitments, contract termination fees, extra charges if ratepayers are negatively impacted and upfront grid connection costs. 
“If you think about our costs as a big pie, all of our costs, our infrastructure, our capital, our expenses all go into a pie,” Shoop said. “And then when we set rates, we divide that pie up into slices. Residential customers get a slice, industrial customers get a slice, small commercial customers get a slice. But when we add a very large customer like a data center, Google, they take a huge piece of that and everybody else’s slices get smaller. That is the benefit.” 
When data centers are responsibly connected to the grid, it can lower energy costs for consumers, said Matthew Horeled, vice president of commercial and regulatory operations with PSO. 
He said the state should emulate Indiana Michigan Power, which is set up similarly to Oklahoma’s utility companies. They are about two years ahead of Oklahoma in data center growth and development, Horeled said, and have recently filed a rate decrease for their ratepayers because of increased revenue from data centers. 
Lawmakers have previously made attempts to regulate data centers.
House Bill 2992 was signed into law this year to require new data centers to pay for their own infrastructure and the energy they consume, among other stipulations. 
Senate Bill 259 was also signed, requiring data centers that want to use groundwater to implement a closed-loop cooling system, which loses less water than the common alternative of open-air evaporative cooling. 
Passed last year, Senate Bill 480 allows data centers to build their own power plants, bypassing utilities.

name: Georgia Recorder
title: Georgia probes House candidate for allegedly voting in two states
description: Georgia’s secretary of state is investigating allegations that David Dillie, a Democratic candidate for state House District 161, may have voted in two state primaries this year in a violation of state law. Dillie, a 24-year-old mechanic for Gulfstream who lives near Pooler Parkway, has denied the accusation, first reported by The Atlanta Journal-Constitutio[...]
text:
David Dillie addresses 300 people gathered outside the Effingham College & Career Academy to protest the proposed OpenAI data center in Rincon on July 23, 2026. Credit: Justin Taylor/The Current GA/CatchLight/Report for AmericaGeorgia’s secretary of state is investigating allegations that David Dillie, a Democratic candidate for state House District 161, may have voted in two state primaries this year in a violation of state law.
Dillie, a 24-year-old mechanic for Gulfstream who lives near Pooler Parkway, has denied the accusation, first reported by The Atlanta Journal-Constitution, that he voted in both Georgia’s May primary and a month later in a primary in Nevada. Dillie lived in Nevada before returning to Coastal Georgia in 2024.
Dillie, a third-generation Georgian, blamed youth and inexperience for the potential legal trouble. Under Georgia law, double-voting is a felony punishable with imprisonment and fine.
“I thought when you moved, your stuff gets canceled. That is not what happens,” Dillie told The Current GA. “No one mentioned” that the process is not automatic and that I would have to cancel my voter registration in Nevada, he said. “I’m young and, frankly, wasn’t knowledgeable,” he added.
Dillie is challenging Republican state lawmaker Bill Hitchens for the seat he has held since 2012 representing parts of Effingham, Bryan and Chatham counties. Statewide, Democrats have voiced optimism that they can flip the state House of Representatives in November and win control of the chamber for the first time in more than two decades.
Dillie’s outsider status helped him gain traction among voters amid widespread anger at established Republican leaders over the planned $20 billion OpenAI data center near Rincon.
As he jumped into the rigors of campaigning, Dillie said he did not look closely at his own voter registration details before the accusations cropped up.
He was a registered voter in Nevada, where he spent years working in construction in the Las Vegas area, he said. When he moved back to Georgia in September 2024, he registered to vote in the Peach State. But he did not proactively cancel his other registration, he said.
Under a state law passed in 2021, Nevada sends mail-in ballots to every registered voter — and Dillie cited that as the reason why a ballot there with his name on it would have been sent to his old address in the Los Vegas area.
A ballot bearing his name was returned and apparently counted in Nevada’s Republican primary, according to documents obtained by The Current. Dillie, however, says he did not fill out that Nevada ballot and does not know who did. His former residence is a home owned by his godfather.
Dillie said he does not know who submitted his Nevada ballot. “As soon as I know you’ll know,” Dillie said. “I’m glad there is an investigation. I wish it would have been flagged sooner.”
The secretary of state’s office announced its investigation last week, but the press release did not indicate how long it would take to look into the matter.
“Voting in another state’s primary while claiming to be a legal Georgia resident is a very serious allegation,” Secretary of State Brad Raffensperger said in a news release. “My office has opened an investigation to gather all the evidence, determine the facts and take appropriate legal action.”
Raffensperger gave no timeline for the completion of the investigation.
Hitchens, 79, is a retired U.S. Marine and Georgia State Patrol officer, and lives in Rincon, a few miles away from the planned OpenAI data center. He is also a close ally of House Speaker Jon Burns, who is also from Effingham County, something that has attracted ire of local voters mad about the proliferation of data centers in Georgia.
The Republican-led state legislature has failed in two successive years to pass regulation of data centers, despite more than two dozen bills seeking to put guard rails around the industry.
Dillie says he is confident of being cleared of any voter wrongdoing, and won’t be dropping out of the race to represent the district.
“I’m taking this one day at a time,” he said. “I’m not hiding. My opponent wants me to be disqualified. I want the voters to decide.”

title: The pro-Amendment 3 campaign is outspending the opposition by a 33-1 ratio
description: A report shows that the campaign working to see Amendment 3 on the statewide ballot win approval in November is vastly outspending opponents of the measure. The campaign to fund the measure raised $18 million through Sept. 25. All of that financial support came from the Florida Association of Realtors. The two political committees opposing […]
text:
Gov. Ron DeSantis announces his proposal to provide property tax relief in Tampa on May 27, 2026. (Photo by Mitch Perry/Florida Phoenix)A report shows that the campaign working to see Amendment 3 on the statewide ballot win approval in November is vastly outspending opponents of the measure.
The campaign to fund the measure raised $18 million through Sept. 25. All of that financial support came from the Florida Association of Realtors.
The two political committees opposing Amendment 3, Floridians for Shared Prosperity and Vote No on 3 Florida, have raised a combined $537,357. That’s a ratio of more than 33:1 that the pro-Amendment 3 forces have raised so far over the opposition.
That compilation was originally provided by OpenSecrets, the Washington, D.C., independent research group that tracks money in U.S. politics.
The proposal would raise the homestead exemption on non-school taxes to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028. It would lower the annual assessment growth cap from 10% to 5% for non-homestead properties such as commercial buildings and rental units, and would require people moving to Florida after Dec. 31 to wait 5 years in continuous residency before qualifying for the full increased exemption.
State economists have projected that those changes would reduce local government property tax collections by up to $12 billion annually by its fifth year.
Public polling has been split on whether the measure can generate the 60% yes vote required for approval. While a recent St. Pete Polls survey shows the measure losing by getting only 45% support, it also showed that a quarter of the 913 surveyed said they were undecided.
However, a new survey  of 504 registered Florida voters shows Amendment 3 drawing 74% support, according to a Pioneer Institute poll on the housing market released Tuesday. The Pioneer Institute is a Boston think tank that has just launched a research initiative in Florida aimed at studying housing and education.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: Passing Medicaid ballot measure would reduce services and spike insurance costs, opponents say
description: SIOUX FALLS — Opponents of a Nov. 3 ballot measure to end Medicaid expansion if federal funding is cut said Monday that the measure would reduce access to care and shift more health care costs onto people with private insurance. South Dakota’s Republican attorney general and its opponents say Amendment I would automatically repeal Medicaid […]
text:
South Dakota Nurses Association President Deb Fischer-Clemens (left) and Republican Jean Hunhoff, a longtime nurse and former state lawmaker, chat after their coalition encouraging people to vote "No on I" host it's first press conference in Sioux Falls, South Dakota on Aug. 9, 2026. (Photo by Joshua Haiar/South Dakota Searchlight)SIOUX FALLS — Opponents of a Nov. 3 ballot measure to end Medicaid expansion if federal funding is cut said Monday that the measure would reduce access to care and shift more health care costs onto people with private insurance.
South Dakota’s Republican attorney general and its opponents say Amendment I would automatically repeal Medicaid expansion if federal funding falls and no longer covers 90% of the program’s costs. Proponents say the measure allows lawmakers to consider repealing, altering or maintaining it if federal funding falls below that level.
The ‘No on I’ coalition is led in part by Republican Jean Hunhoff, a longtime nurse and former state lawmaker who served 24 years in Pierre, including as chair of the state’s budget committee. 
Hospitals can’t turn people away because they are uninsured, she said. If people lose Medicaid and their ability to pay for care along with it, Hunhoff said, hospitals will need to charge other people more to make up their losses.
“They have to serve those patients, and they’re going to do it,” Hunhoff said. “But they are a business, too, and like any other business, they have to have the finances to be able to continue those services.” 
Medicaid is a federal-state health insurance program for low income people. In 2022, South Dakota voters approved a citizen-initiated state constitutional amendment to extend Medicaid eligibility to adults with incomes up to 138% of the poverty level. The expansion capitalized on a federal law passed during the President Barack Obama administration that covers 90% of states’ expansion costs.
Because the expansion is part of the state constitution, only voters can alter it.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
At a coalition press conference in Sioux Falls, Hunhoff and South Dakota Nurses Association President Deb Fischer-Clemens said Medicaid expansion provides health coverage to more than 31,000 South Dakotans and helps patients get preventive care and treatment before medical conditions become more costly emergencies. 
“It is health insurance coverage for real people, real families and real communities across South Dakota,” Fischer-Clemens said. 
Fischer-Clemens said the financial burden on hospitals would only grow as more preventive care and minor treatments become emergency room visits and surgeries.
Ballot measure could auto-repeal Medicaid expansion, attorney general says in contrast to lawmakers

Expanded Medicaid provides about $400 million annually to hospitals that would otherwise go unreimbursed, South Dakota Association of Healthcare Organizations President Tim Rave said. Without Medicaid reimbursement, more of that care would become charity or unreimbursed care, Fischer-Clemens and Hunhoff said, leaving hospitals to find other revenue sources or cut services. 
“If you take that away, think about the future,” Hunhoff said.
The consequences of undoing Medicaid expansion would be particularly serious in rural communities, Hunhoff said, because those hospitals and clinics often operate on thin margins.
Those costs could ultimately be spread through higher private insurance premiums, too.
“The public will pay for these people’s health care, whether you cut Medicaid or not,” Fischer-Clemens told South Dakota Searchlight. 
The federal government could warn states if it planned to cut the federal match rate, the measure’s opponents argued, giving lawmakers and voters time to address a hypothetical cut. But if they didn’t, Hunhoff said. programs would need to be cut or new taxes would be needed to pay for them.
Republican former Rep. Will Mortenson, of Fort Pierre, sponsored the bill to put Amendment I to a public vote. The issue is fundamentally about budget priorities, he said. If federal funding declines, lawmakers should have the flexibility to decide whether Medicaid expansion should continue, rather than protecting it ahead of other budget priorities, he said.
“This is about whether able-bodied people receiving welfare is a higher priority than, say, K-12 education,” Mortenson said.

title: A bear broke into my kitchen. Then I watched him die.
description:
As bear encounters rise across Vermont, how do we share the woods and the yard without harm to either side?
Read the story on VTDigger here:  A bear broke into my kitchen. Then I watched him die..
text:
This commentary is by Rachel Lee Stoll, an antiquarian bookseller.
There is much conversation right now about bears in Vermont, about their increasing numbers and how and when we hunt them down. I have a dog in this bear fight, because my son and I came home a few weeks ago to find that our house had been visited in our absence by a hungry bear.  
The bear — terrifically nimble — opened a window I had not firmly latched, fell into my son’s room, clambered all about the house and found the glory hallelujah that is the kitchen. His paw hit a knob on our electric stove and turned on a burner. A sturdy old teapot took the heat. The bear opened our fridge and, in what I hope were the best damn hours of his life, slashed and spilled and feasted. He came in and out more than once, started taking food outside, to-go bags; why not? The house was, to put it mildly, a mess. At least the bear was gone when we arrived. But he came back the next morning.  
I hollered at him, airhorn bleating, old dog barking. I did not want him dead; I wanted him gone. He left, but slowly, so forlornly. And he came back again, unafraid of us. I called the wardens, who were excellent, kind and professional. While they set up a huge bear trap, I saw him coming back yet again, moving in that thick, silent manner, slipping through trees, and I pointed him out and said, “Do what you need to do.” They shot him. I started shaking. I think about that bear every day. He has entered my dreams. I have not cleaned his not-so-big prints off our walls.  
I do not want what happened at our house to be used as an argument for shooting more bears out of trees or while asleep in their dens. But there will be more dangerous encounters. Before the bear reached our house, he had been at neighbors’ houses — battering one family’s door and windows while they were inside baking cookies. He was not afraid of people. A few years back, a woman in Winhall was mauled by a bear. I fear we will hear more such stories.  
I had a close encounter with a grizzly while hiking in Montana long ago. I have had two brain surgeries and an adrenal crash alone in a car. I know what to fear in life, and, generally speaking, black bears are not high on that list. But that is a far cry from saying they are not dangerous at all, nor that I want a bear in my kitchen, gobbling up the cheese and peanut butter and buttermilk and 17 Clif Bars — though not the shimmering jar of honey left on the counter. 
What can we do? What should we not do? I am not against hunting when it is done properly. Hunting can be honorable: an animal living its life wild and free until the moment it is killed. But unlike other states such as Colorado and California, Vermont allows hounding: Many dogs are let loose against a bear that runs up a tree and then, terrified, is shot out of the tree, and often shot again when he falls if he is still alive. I despise bear hounding, as do many I know who are hunters. There is no honor in it. We owe the bears more than that.  

READ MORE

If bear season is extended, we need absolute clarity: Killing denned bears should be clearly prohibited. No fuzzy, vague language. What Vermonter wants a bear shot while sleeping in its den? Who are we? What are we made of?  
We do have a problem with too many bears. Everyone in our area who has lived here for decades, as we have, has noticed the uptick. Mother bears leave cubs up trees along our driveway. One cub this summer would sit on a sturdy branch and dangle his legs and chatter on, adorable as all babies are, and I wished he were not there. I told his mother not to trust us so much. Told her I am a bear killer, to no avail. We bark, we holler. I do not want that little bear shot next year. Or going into anyone’s house.  
So what do we do besides kill more of them? Resorts and restaurants should use bear-proof garbage containers properly, with serious fines and regulations with teeth. Why can’t resorts keep garbage inside, or build special garbage sheds? What if more Vermonters kept garbage inside?  
And we can use common sense. I used to keep our kitchen windows closed all summer. This summer was too hot, and I opened one. It was open the day a bear walked right by, inches away. I’ll try to keep those windows closed all summer. But what are we to do on hot summer nights when more bears start realizing, as it becomes part of their culture, that so much tasty food is inside every house?  
We can love bears and still know that their numbers, absurdly good sense of smell, strength and dexterity have become an honest-to-God problem without easy answers. 
Rosh Hashana just passed by. I found myself deep in the woods by a stream, with an old piece of Clif Bar in my pocket. Oh, I thought, as the old dog stumbled happily through the cool water, I could do tashlich, the ritual of symbolically tossing our sins into water as the new year begins, a fresh start. 
I thought of those I needed to ask forgiveness. Faces swam into view, but then the bear rushed in, his beautiful face taking up every inch of my mind. I tossed tiny bits of the stale bar into the stream, sunshine glinting off the water and the rocks all around, and I asked for his forgiveness, again and again.  
I’ll keep walking in their woods, slipping between the trees, searching for beechnuts, calling out with that loud sound that is neither friendly nor alarming, the one that says, I am here, and I know you are too, so let’s be careful, please, mindful of each other.
