name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: Accountability strengthens public school choice in South Carolina
description: For 30 years, the South Carolina Charter Schools Act has stood as one of our state’s most consequential public education reforms. Public charter schools are public, tuition-free schools that give families additional options and educators room to create distinctive programs within a framework of public accountability. Generations of South Carolina students ha[...]
text:
A South Carolina law signed May 15, 2026, after passing the Senate unanimously and getting only one "no" vote in the House increased oversight of charter schools, their authorizers and the management companies they hire. (File photo by kali9/Getty Images)For 30 years, the South Carolina Charter Schools Act has stood as one of our state’s most consequential public education reforms.
Public charter schools are public, tuition-free schools that give families additional options and educators room to create distinctive programs within a framework of public accountability. Generations of South Carolina students have benefited from those opportunities.
At Erskine, I see education from an unusual vantage point: as president of a college and as chairman of the board of a statewide public charter school authorizer.
Schools authorized by the Charter Institute at Erskine now enroll nearly 40,000 K–12 students. That experience has shown me that the right educational setting can expand a young person’s possibilities — and that choice and accountability must advance together.
To protect those opportunities and strengthen public confidence, the General Assembly enacted Act 123 of 2026 following years of work across multiple legislative sessions. The law clarifies expectations for schools and authorizers, strengthens oversight and transparency, and creates a firmer foundation for responsible growth.
SC charter schools to face more scrutiny under finalized accountability bill

Authorizing is not a ceremonial role. An authorizer functions as a Local Education Agency and carries serious responsibilities involving academics, finance, governance, special education, and regulatory compliance.
Act 123 therefore requires future higher-education authorizers to undergo a new state application process. The Department of Education will evaluate each application and make a recommendation; the State Board of Education makes the final decision.
Existing authorizers must sign formal assurances and remain subject to annual state review and expanded transparency requirements. That is a sound principle: new authorizers should demonstrate their capacity, and established authorizers should continue earning the public’s confidence.
Act 123 also strengthens the process through which a charter school may transfer from one authorizer to another. Changing authorizers can no longer be used to escape, delay, or reduce accountability. The law preserves a pathway for warranted transfers while ensuring that accountability follows the school.
Good schools also depend on good governance.
New charter school and authorizer board members must complete orientation covering school finance, instructional programs, school law, state ethics requirements, the Freedom of Information Act, and other public responsibilities. After their first year, charter school board members must participate in annual training provided by their authorizer. These requirements give board members stronger tools to carry out the public trust placed in them.
Act 123’s financial transparency provisions will make budgets, audits, transaction registers, and certain contracts easier for the public to review.
We welcome that scrutiny. It will allow South Carolinians to see both how charter schools use public funds and how effectively they stretch the resources entrusted to them.
Because charter schools operate without the same access to local and facilities funding available to traditional districts, doing more with less is part of their daily work. Greater transparency should make that stewardship easier to recognize.
Senate bill boosting oversight for SC charter schools wins unanimous support

That context does not lessen expectations.
Charter schools must be held accountable for academic quality, fiscal integrity, lawful governance, and responsible stewardship. Accountability, oversight, and transparency are not adversaries of public-school choice; they are essential to sustaining public confidence in it.
Legislation of this complexity is strengthened when ideas are tested, debated, and refined.
I am grateful to the members of the House and Senate, their committee leaders and staff, and the educators, authorizers, school leaders, and families who remained engaged throughout the process.
The final measure earned overwhelming support in both chambers. That broad support — and the hard work required to achieve it — deserves recognition.
Act 123 provides a stronger foundation for public charter education in South Carolina.
Our responsibility now is to implement it faithfully and ensure that the public-school choices available to families remain accountable, sustainable, and worthy of their trust.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Raleigh Rescue Mission’s expansion offers more help for homeless women, children in NC
description: A lot of big changes are underway at the Raleigh Rescue Mission, which this month opened a new $41 million campus in Knightdale for women and children experiencing homelessness. The new campus, named The Garden, allows the faith-based nonprofit to increase its capacity to serve as many as 350 women and children daily, which is […]
text:
The Raleigh Rescue Mission's new facility in Knightdale. (Photo: Raleigh Rescue Mission) A lot of big changes are underway at the Raleigh Rescue Mission, which this month opened a new $41 million campus in Knightdale for women and children experiencing homelessness.
The new campus, named The Garden, allows the faith-based nonprofit to increase its capacity to serve as many as 350 women and children daily, which is 290 more than the 60 it served at its downtown Raleigh facility. 
John Luckett (Photo: Raleigh Rescue Mission)
“This is about so much more than a new campus,” John Luckett, the Rescue Mission’s president and CEO said in a statement following last week’s ribbon-cutting ceremony. “The Garden gives us the opportunity to welcome more women and children into a safe, dignified environment where they can heal, find hope, and take meaningful steps toward a different future.” 
The Rescue Mission’s capacity to serve men at its downtown facility also increases as a result of The Garden coming online.  The nonprofit can now serve as many as 120 men, compared to  only 40 men before the new facility opened.  
In an interview with NC Newsline, Luckett stressed that The Garden is not an emergency shelter for women and children looking for a place to spend a night. In those cases, families are referred to traditional shelters, he said. The Garden is focused on longer-term solutions.
“I tell people that if there was such a thing as a boarding school for people experiencing homelessness, we would be it,” Luckett said. “We do an assessment and people move in and they’re individuals who want to be a part of our New Life program that’s focused on getting a job, getting a car and getting an apartment.”
Raleigh Rescue Mission’s facility for women and children in Knightdale. (Photo: Raleigh Rescue Mission)
The New Life Plan to which Luckett referred is a structured, six-phase program that helps participants build the skills and stability needed for long-term  independence. 
The women and children entering the program will move into one of the campus’ 101 private residential rooms. The campus also features an on-site daycare and will offer life skills and job readiness programs. Women looking to return to the workforce will be prioritized. 
“We are a back-to-work program, and that’s very important,” Luckett said. “We’re trying to get people that want to go back to work and need all the support systems in order to make that happen.” 
Luckett estimates it will take about a year for The Garden to reach capacity. It usually takes a woman with children six to nine months to complete the program. Single women can complete it in four to six months, he said.
The idea for The Garden came after the organization identified a critical shortage of transitional housing for women and children looking to escape homelessness, Luckett said.
Study: Hurricane Helene caused spike in homelessness in North Carolina

Wake County’s 2026 Point-in-Time Count (PIT) numbers show more than 1,000 people were living on the street or in emergency shelters in Wake County on a single night in January. The count identified 1,050 people experiencing homelessness in Wake County, including 307 people living unsheltered and 743 staying in shelters or transitional housing programs. By comparison, 1,127 people were counted during the 2025 Point-in-Time Count.
The PIT is an annual effort required by the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development.
The Garden is located within a new Lennar single-family home community on land donated to the Rescue Mission about 25 years ago. Luckett said a donor gave the mission about 60 acres. It sold Lennar 45 acres for its housing development and retained ownership of 15 acres for The Garden.
Mayor Jessica Day (Photo: Town of Knightdale)
Lennar helped with “water, sewer, electrical, bringing that to the whole area,” Luckett said. 
“When we started looking for a place, we kept coming up with the land that we already owned,” Luckett said. “We ended up within proximity of the downtown location and in a good town that was very welcoming of us having this residential model of getting women and children back on their feet.” 
Luckett said The Garden is loosely based on the Purpose Built Communities model, which focuses on mixed-income housing, cradle-to-college education, community wellbeing and economic vitality.
Knightdale Mayor Jessica Day said in a statement that The Garden will be a game-changer for women and children experiencing homelessness.
“The Garden is not only a resource for women and children facing situational homelessness,” said. “I believe it will be a haven of hope for them, and a chance to re-envision the lives they want for themselves.”

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: Lawsuit challenges legality of 4 North Dakota legislative candidates
description: Three North Dakota Republican Party officials are suing the state’s top election official over what they say is inconsistent enforcement of election rules. The state Supreme Court lawsuit comes as absentee voting already is underway in North Dakota. The lawsuit seeks to overturn the election victories of four GOP legislative candidates should any of them […]
text:
Former state lawmaker Brandon Prichard gives a North Dakota Young Republicans update to the NDGOP state convention at the State Fairgrounds in Minot on March 28, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)Three North Dakota Republican Party officials are suing the state’s top election official over what they say is inconsistent enforcement of election rules.
The state Supreme Court lawsuit comes as absentee voting already is underway in North Dakota. The lawsuit seeks to overturn the election victories of four GOP legislative candidates should any of them win in November.
It’s the latest fissure in the state’s dominant Republican Party, highlighting divisions over how some candidates use petition signatures to get on the ballot, a method some Republicans perceive as an affront to the endorsement process.
[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: The info you need to cast your ballot.]
Citizens Alliance of North Dakota, a political organization led by former Republican state Rep. Brandon Prichard, announced the lawsuit Monday. The case appeared in the Supreme Court online docket Tuesday.
The challengers are District 25 GOP Chair Matt Evans, Rep. Jeff Hoverson, R-Minot, and Douglas Pearson, a District 7 GOP Executive Committee member. Evans and Hoverson lost their Republican primary election bids to candidates their lawsuit now challenges.
The lawsuit names Secretary of State Michael Howe.
Court papers allege the nominating petitions of North Dakota House candidates Blaine DesLauriers, Terry Goerger, Timothy Mihalick and Steve Sauter should be invalidated because of irregularities such as incomplete information from petition signers and no political party affiliation listed on petitions. The lawsuit also alleges that some of those candidates could amend their petitions’ missing or incomplete information but others were rejected, such as a Citizens Alliance petition for a special election in Grand Forks-area District 42.
“This unequal administrative scheme grants special privileges to select candidates while penalizing others who commit similar statutory omissions,” the lawsuit states.
DesLauriers and Mihalick are running mates for Minot-area District 3. Goerger is running for Richland County-area District 25. Sauter is a candidate in Bismarck-area District 7. They are all Republicans who won their primary election after getting on the ballot by gathering petition signatures and not by party endorsement – a point of contention by intraparty opponents who have decried the signature path to the ballot.
The lawsuit asks the Supreme Court to force the secretary of state to declare the four candidates’ petitions insufficient under state law and essentially nullify their election victories if any wins. The challengers want the seats declared vacant and filled by the process in state law for legislative vacancies – a method that would favor them – in which the local district party makes an appointment.
Sauter said he followed the law as to his petition signatures, and he trusts Howe and his office.
“I know I did everything following the rules that they gave me,” he said. 
The North Dakota Monitor left phone messages for DesLauriers, Mihalick and  Goerger. Howe declined to comment.
The challengers’ attorney, Fintan Dooley, said the key concerns are disparate treatment “afforded some people but not others,” and inadequately sized petition forms that can’t fit all the information needed from signers.
In a statement, Prichard said, “The Secretary of State holds a mandatory administrative duty to enforce state election laws as written by the Legislature. Secretary Howe cannot invent extra-statutory curing rules for favored candidates while strictly rejecting citizens’ petitions for minor technical omissions. Equal protection and the rule of law require full compliance with the North Dakota Century Code.”
Court papers detail Prichard’s initial queries beginning in July about petitions and signatures submitted by 13 legislative and three statewide candidates, all Republicans, and his later request to Howe to investigate and invalidate “non-compliant” signatures and to remove five legislative candidates from the November ballot “if there is a finding of insufficient valid nominating signatures.”
Former Republican lawmaker challenges North Dakota law on false political ads

Howe told Prichard, “As required, candidates are afforded the opportunity to correct filings within the prescribed deadlines,” in an Aug. 21 letter included in court papers.
State law requires the official who receives candidates’ primary election documents to notify them of corrections to be made before the submission deadline. A candidate’s name may not be placed on the primary ballot “if the filed documents are insufficient and remain uncorrected,” according to state law.
The lawsuit deepens a rift within the state party between ultraconservative and longtime Republicans months after the June primary. In that election, a number of traditional Republicans got on the ballot via petition signatures and won, defeating candidates who had the GOP endorsement. None of the Republican statewide officeholders sought the party’s endorsement at its convention in March, citing tension within party factions.
Sauter called the lawsuit unfortunate, saying the GOP is “a great party, and these small rifts just don’t help move things forward.” 
Prichard was a state rep from 2022 to 2024, when he lost reelection. In a federal lawsuit, he is challenging the North Dakota law that makes it a crime to lie or include intentionally misleading statements in political ads. 
Reach North Dakota Monitor reporter Jack Dura at jdura@northdakotamonitor.com.

title: Trump is coming to Nebraska to campaign for Sen. Pete Ricketts
description: The stop in Grand Island comes as he begins his midterm campaign blitz to shore up red states as Election Day approaches.
text:
President Donald Trump speaks on the first day of the 2026 Republican National Convention at the American Airlines Center on Sept. 9, 2026 in Dallas, Texas. (Photo by Justin Sullivan/Getty Images)LINCOLN — President Donald Trump is coming to Grand Island next week, a Nebraska Republican Party official confirmed to the Examiner. 
The stop in Grand Island comes as he begins his midterm campaign blitz to shore up red states as Election Day approaches. The president has planned trips to Oklahoma and Iowa, Florida, Texas and Alaska. 
The visit to Nebraska State Fair’s Pinnacle Bank Expo Center will be focused on rallying Republicans for Nebraska Sen. Pete Ricketts in a heated race against Dan Osborn. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The last time Trump came to Nebraska was in 2022 for a campaign rally for Charles Herbster in his bid for governor.
Dave Plond, chairman of the Hall County Republican Party, told Central Nebraska Today that the last president to come to Grand Island was former President George W. Bush.
The national political environment for Republicans has worsened — Democrats are fully bullish about their chances of taking both the U.S. House and Senate. 
Democratic Party Jane Kleeb posted a statement on social media about the likely stop, saying, “Trump would be better served doing his actual job instead of breaking every promise he made to Nebraskans. A coalition of voters across party lines is fed up with Trump’s chaos and ready to elect new leaders.”
The general election is Nov. 3.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Water Valley woman’s birthday fundraiser erases millions in medical debt
description: Beth Mayeaux and her wife Robbie Fischer talk with a party guest while their terrier mix, Mike, sits on the porch, on Saturday, Sept. 26, 2026, in Water Valley.
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
WATER VALLEY — “I can’t believe I’m 60 years old,” said Beth Mayeaux to the friends gathered in her Water Valley home’s light-filled, eggshell blue living room. She paused, smiling, as they clapped and cheered.  
The education sales professional from Jackson thanked the assembled guests for supporting her birthday fundraiser for medical debt relief. The eight-week campaign, which ends Wednesday, raises money for north-central Mississippi’s Yalobusha and Calhoun counties. 
A glossy sign next to her proclaimed, “You gave $21,000.” The money will go to Undue Medical Debt, a national nonprofit that buys past-due medical debt from hospitals and debt collectors for a fraction of the amount patients owed. Using donations, they pay off the balances and notify recipients with a letter in the mail. 
Because the debt can be purchased cheaply, the nonprofit says each dollar donated can relieve up to $100 in medical debt. The money Mayeaux raised erased $3.2 million in medical debt, according to the organization.  
The funds from Mayeaux’s “Getting (G)older, Giving Back” campaign will help over 1,600 people, said Marisa Clemente, Undue Medical Debt’s vice president of philanthropy. It’s enough to cover the nonprofit’s already purchased debt holdings in the two counties, and additional money will go to the Mississippi Delta, where Mayeaux’s wife Robbie Fischer is from.  
Beth Mayeaux thanks guests for supporting her 60th birthday fundraiser, a medical debt relief campaign focused around her home county on Saturday, Sept. 26, 2026, in Water Valley. Credit: Anna Hu/Mississippi Today
In Water Valley, a town of  about 3,400, over a quarter of residents live below the poverty line. That’s more than the roughly 18% poverty rate in Mississippi, which also has among the nation’s highest rates of medical debt. 
Water Valley was a setting that made sense for Mayeaux, who  knew she wanted to do something big for her 60th birthday bash. For past decade birthdays, she had taken trips — to Paris and Champagne for her 50th, to New York for her 40th. This time, she wanted to give back to the community that had welcomed her nearly a decade ago.
She remembered having medical debt in her 20s, how a third party that bought her debt “hounded” her and how it  started impacting her credit score. Just before the COVID-19 pandemic, she learned about Undue Medical Debt. The pieces clicked. 
“It’s just so very Beth,” said Kerry O’Donoghue, a Water Valley resident who became friends with Mayeaux and Fischer soon after they moved to the area. O’Donoghue remembers first hearing about the campaign. 
“I was absolutely all in, and also furious that we live in a country where this is needed,” she said.
A big ask, and a broad imagination
Mayeaux first brought her idea to the mission committee at Church of the Nativity, the small Episocopal church where she helped start an on-site food pantry, now restocked twice a day with shelf-stable foods. She spoke in the first part of the meeting, before church treasurer Eddie Woods presented his financial report.
“When Beth finished with her presentation, she said, ‘I would like to have $3,000.’ And the room went silent,” Woods recounted at the party on Saturday.
Eddie Woods, left, and Mary Beth Pulsifer, center, stand with Duncan Gray on Saturday, Sept. 26, 2026, in Water Valley. Credit: Anna Hu/Mississippi Today
“I was thinking, that’s a lot of money,” said the church’s senior warden, Mary Beth Pulsifer, standing beside him.
Wood smiled as he re-enacted the dramatic moment. 
“I said, ‘Well, it all comes down to finances. So in looking at the budget, I don’t see that we can do $3,000.’ And then I paused and I said, ‘I think we need to do $5,000.’” 
Cheekily, he added, “And Beth seconded the motion.”
Pulsifer talked about her motivation for supporting the campaign: imagining what it would be like to get a letter in the mail saying that your debt is erased. Another partygoer, bankruptcy paralegal Jack Barry, said he’s seen people have to declare bankruptcy due to their medical debt. 
Undue Medical Debt identifies people who earn at or below four times the federal poverty level, or $132,000 annually for a family of four, or have medical debt that exceeds 5% of their income. People don’t need to apply for relief, and face no adverse tax consequences, Clemente said. Because they buy bundled portfolios of debt and can only purchase from hospitals willing to sell to them, the organization can’t respond to individual requests for debt relief. 
Mayeaux and Fischer kicked off the campaign in August with $1,966, representing Mayeaux’s birth year. She wrote letters by hand to her network, a sizable one given that her annual Christmas card list includes some 400 people. While some donations came in larger amounts from grants, the majority were raised through individuals and neighbors in a true “people’s campaign,” she said.
“This is the best thing I’ve ever been a part of,” 71-year-old Woods said. 
Out on the spacious porch, guests mingled over bubbly beverages while Mayeaux flitted between friends. Barbara Phillips, a civil rights attorney, waved Mayeaux over and imparted a secret about her birthday gift. 
That business taken care of, she shared a recent moment when  an acquaintance in New York told her that for things to change in Mississippi was “beyond his imagination.” 
“It occurred to me, well, your imagination does not limit our reality,” said Phillips, a Virginian who grew up in Memphis but has since made Mississippi her home. 
Barbara Y. Phillips shares a story about imagination, and how to not be bounded by others’ lack of it on Saturday, Sept. 26, 2026.  Credit: Anna Hu/Mississippi Today
She conjured an image of Mississippi civil rights activist Fannie Lou Hamer, standing up in a cotton field that stretched for as far as the eye could see and imagining that she could change her world. The vision that Hamer and people that went with her to register to vote had still astonishes her, Phillips said.
For her, that spirit is reflected in efforts such as a medical debt fundraiser, where people take a larger issue into their own hands. 
“We’re doing it right here in this house in Water Valley,” she said. 
The party, which fell on Mayeaux’s actual birthday, provided a fitting finale to the monthslong campaign. “Thank y’all so much,” Mayeaux had said earlier in the living room, at the end of her toast. “Let’s just keep on drinking champagne, eating cupcakes, and erasing medical debt.” 
An hour after the stated 5 p.m. ending time, Mayeaux and Fisher waved off the last of their guests and retired with their terrier Mike to the kitchen for a dinner of frozen pizza. A half-empty basket of pink rubber eraser party favors stood by the door — a reminder of the debt that their collective efforts will wipe away.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: USC, Westinghouse sign agreement for nuclear workforce training center
description: USC inked a deal with nuclear giant Westinghouse related to the school’s plans for a nuclear workforce training center.
text:
A conceptual rendering of a proposed nuclear workforce training center on the campus of the University of South Carolina in Columbia. (Photo courtesy of USC)COLUMBIA — The University of South Carolina inked a deal with Westinghouse related to the school’s plans for a nuclear workforce training center within its engineering school.
The agreement signed Tuesday at the South Carolina Nuclear Summit in Columbia kickstarts talks between USC and the nuclear giant. It does not commit Westinghouse to any investment in the training center.
“While South Carolina is already a strong nuclear state, this strategic partnership between USC and Westinghouse will position the state as a national leader,” Luca Oriani, president of new plant delivery at Westinghouse, said in a statement.
“This collaboration will support high-paying jobs and economic growth across South Carolina while strengthening and further developing the workforce needed to deliver the next generation of nuclear power plants and meet the rising demand for electricity,” he continued.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
USC plans to ask state legislators for $100 million in the next fiscal year, starting July 1, 2027, and is seeking private investors willing to match that amount.
The center on the college’s campus in Columbia will be part of the school’s larger plans to renovate and expand its college of engineering and computing. It will train technicians, engineers, specialized construction professionals and operators for both large- and small-scale nuclear reactors.
USC envisions a building containing simulators to train plant operators and university students in a replica nuclear control room, as well as hands-on construction labs and virtual reality stations for nuclear construction and maintenance training.
University of South Carolina President Michael Amiridis, right, and Luca Oriani, president of new plant delivery at Westinghouse, left, sign an agreement Tuesday, Sept. 29, 2026, at Colonial Life Arena during the South Carolina Nuclear Summit. (Photo by Jessica Holdman/SC Daily Gazette)
“Anybody that wants to be building or operating these reactors somehow will have to come through us because we are going to have a unique facility,” Hossein Haj-Hariri, dean of USC’s Molinaroli College of Engineering and Computing, told reporters at the summit.
The agreement with USC comes amid efforts by Westinghouse’s own parent company, Brookfield Asset Management, to restart construction of a pair of partially built Westinghouse-designed nuclear reactors in the Palmetto State.
Work continues on a $2.7 billion deal between South Carolina’s state-owned utility company, Santee Cooper, and the New York investment firm for the purchase of the abandoned reactors at the V.C. Summer nuclear plant in Fairfield County.
Brookfield has until the end of March 2028 to make a final decision on whether or not to go forward with the purchase and reboot.
In June, the U.S. Energy Department also announced $17.5 billion in loans to speed the construction of 10 other Westinghouse nuclear reactors, to be built in pairs at five undisclosed sites across the U.S. by 2030.
The loans will finance the purchase of big-ticket reactor components that typically take a long time to manufacture. Westinghouse and a utility or ​energy company will each invest $500 million to jointly own each project.
Decision on potential $2.7B sale of SC nuclear reactors could be 2 years away

“Each of these reactors, as you know, requires thousands of people to build, and then a couple thousand or so to run and operate. All of these need to start to get trained,” Haj-Hariri said.
“The challenge is incredible. Before you start building, you need the workforce, which means we have to start yesterday,” he added.
However, serial production of nuclear reactors remains ​unproven as 10 reactors of the same model have never been built over such a short period.
A pair of nuclear reactors at Alvin W. Vogtle Electric Generating Plant in Georgia, which started under construction about the same time as South Carolina’s mothballed reactors, are the only new-built nuclear reactors to come online over the past three decades in the U.S.
That project came in seven years behind schedule and $17 billion over budget.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Will CT fugitive Kosta Diamantis lose his Farmington home?
authors: Isabelle Marceles | Connecticut Public, Jim Haddadin | Connecticut Public, and Frankie Graziano | Connecticut Public
description: Federal prosecutors could move this week to seize the Farmington home of Kosta Diamantis, the former high-ranking state budget official.
text:
Federal prosecutors could move this week to seize the Farmington home of Kosta Diamantis, the former high-ranking state budget official who fled to Greece to avoid sentencing on corruption charges.
Diamantis pledged ownership of his property to remain free on bond while a pair of criminal cases against him are pending. A judge is now set to determine Wednesday whether to forfeit his bail in one of the cases after Diamantis failed to appear in court.
Doing so could clear a path for the government to swiftly take title to his three-bedroom, single-family residence.
The town appraises the property at $502,500, based on its most recent revaluation in 2022. However, outstanding claims secured by the Meadow Road house — including appearance bonds totaling $1 million in his criminal cases — far exceed that amount.
Records reviewed by Connecticut Public show the government would be one of several parties seeking to recoup funds from a future sale, raising questions about how much it can recover.
Land records show a bank holds mortgages on the home. After Diamantis was indicted, he also took out loans totaling $120,000 from an acquaintance, despite signing a declaration that he wouldn’t sell the property or allow additional claims against it.
The purpose of such a restriction is straightforward, said Ian Marcus Amelkin, a Hofstra University law professor who spent nearly a decade as a federal public defender. Less equity means less financial leverage, he said.
“If you continue to remove … equity out of the home basically by adding liens, it’d be less of a stick to ensure that you return to court,” he said.
Records show the acquaintance who loaned Diamantis the money was Lee Ferguson, the former longtime owner of Connecticut contracting companies Ferguson Electric and Ferguson Mechanical.
Ferguson relinquished control of the businesses and served time in federal prison after pleading guilty in 2019 to money laundering.
Reached by phone Monday, Ferguson said he previously believed Diamantis would pay him back with interest after being acquitted.
Ferguson “never thought in a million years” Diamantis would flee the country, and wishes now he had “stood back from the whole situation,” he said.
“I thought of him as a friend, and I was looking to try and help him in his needs, when he was trying to get out from under this dilemma he was in,” Ferguson said.
The line of lenders
A jury convicted Diamantis on 21 counts of bribery, extortion, conspiracy and lying to federal investigators in a federal corruption case centered on his work as the director of the state’s school construction program.
Diamantis, whose first name is Konstantinos, is a former state representative, and previously served as director of the state Office of School Construction Grants & Review. For nearly two years in that role, he was also the deputy secretary of the Office of Policy and Management.
He was indicted and arrested in 2024, and signed a $500,000 appearance bond secured by his primary residence in Farmington.
At the time, he had two open-end mortgages with Thomaston Savings Bank. While the remaining balance he owes is unknown, the combined maximum line of credit is $490,000.
Diamantis confirmed in a text message that he still owes money to the bank. A spokesperson for Thomaston Savings Bank declined to provide information regarding the loans, saying as a matter of policy the bank doesn’t disclose information regarding client relationships, accounts or transactions.
Under the bond agreement, Diamantis promised not to sell the property, allow additional claims against it or otherwise reduce its value.
“The takeaway is that if you are to run, they can actually seize the property that you’re putting up,” Amelkin said.
But the following month after he signed the bond, Diamantis borrowed another $100,000 against the house from Ferguson, according to Farmington land records. Ferguson loaned him an additional $20,000 against the property later that year.
During an interview last week with Connecticut Public, Diamantis characterized the loans as an act of support from a friend.
“I think he felt bad that I was in this particular scenario,” Diamantis said. “He’s one of those guys who knew my reputation for all these years, and I think he was someone who believed that I wouldn’t do something like that and was there to help me.”
Diamantis said he worked for Ferguson’s son for a short time, though it wasn’t clear when or in what capacity.
Diamantis didn’t respond to a request to clarify his remarks. He referred additional questions to his lawyer, Norm Pattis. Pattis didn’t respond to requests for comment.
In 2019, Ferguson admitted in federal court to conducting a scheme to defraud employees by deducting fees from their benefits and steering the money to a company he controlled. He paid more than $3.3 million in restitution and was sentenced to 20 months in prison and a year of supervised release. His son has since taken over the companies.
Ferguson, who lives in Florida, said he doesn’t know what role Diamantis might have had with those companies. He said that professional relationship didn’t have any bearing on his decision to loan Diamantis money, which he now regrets.
“I’m truly distraught about the whole thing,” he said.
The two met about eight years ago at a local golf club in Farmington, Ferguson said. After he was arrested, Diamantis asked Ferguson for assistance, and Ferguson granted him loans at an 8% interest rate, secured by Diamantis’ home, he said.
Ferguson said he knew at the time there were existing bank mortgages on the property, but mistakenly believed that his claim would take precedence over the appearance bond secured in court.
“I thought I was … behind Thomaston Savings Bank, but now I find out that there is a $500,000 government lien prior to mine,” he said.
Ferguson said he hasn’t spoken with Diamantis in months. He now believes it’s unlikely he’ll get his money back, and questions how Diamantis managed to leave the country undetected.
“I was really taken back by the fact that the government basically allowed it to happen, quite honestly,” he said. “I mean, I thought for sure … that they were keeping tabs on him.”
‘Someone would have seen it’
In 2025, the government brought additional charges against Diamantis in a separate federal criminal case. He offered the same house as security for a second $500,000 bond, even after new mortgages appeared in the land records.
It’s unclear from court records what court officials knew at that time about the loans Diamantis received from Ferguson, though a mortgage recorded six days later listed both as existing claims on the property.
Stanley A. Twardy Jr., a former U.S. attorney, said prosecutors, the probation office and the defendant’s lawyer typically review the proposed conditions of a bond package before submitting it to a judge for approval.
“You would think that at the time of the second appearance … that someone would have seen it,” he said, referring to the private loans.
A spokesperson for the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Connecticut declined to comment on whether prosecutors involved in the two criminal cases became aware of the loans, or assessed the equity in the home when evaluating bond recommendations.
The Connecticut office of U.S. Probation and Pretrial Services did not respond to messages seeking comment.
Meadow Road home still occupied?
It’s unclear who now resides at the home. No one answered the door when a reporter visited on Sept. 22. A dog was heard barking inside.
A prosecutor said in court this month federal officials visited the property and a “family member appeared to be present,” though Diamantis’ car was gone.
“The agents spoke to at least one family member who it’s not entirely clear that they know exactly where Mr. Diamantis is,” Assistant U.S. Attorney Jonathan Francis said.
Pattis, the defense lawyer, said in court that family members didn’t know about Diamantis’ plans to leave the country. One daughter was en route from New Jersey to Connecticut to attend the Sept. 17 sentencing hearing for her father, Pattis said.
Federal prosecutors said in court they believe Diamantis drove to Florida, took a boat to Nassau in the Bahamas, then flew to London. They believe he booked the flight about three weeks earlier.
Diamantis had surrendered his U.S. passport to probation officials, but later obtained a Greek passport. In court proceedings, Diamantis told a judge the passport wasn’t in his possession because he had mailed it to Greece to facilitate a real estate transaction.
Federal officials believe Diamantis used the Greek passport to travel.
“We don’t know that he is in Greece but we’re willing to believe that that’s the case,” Francis said in court, according to a transcript.
A spokesperson for the U.S. Marshals Service violent fugitive task force in Connecticut said earlier this month the agency received a warrant to apprehend Diamantis and was beginning its investigation.
‘No intentions of ever leaving’
At a hearing Wednesday, prosecutors are expected to present additional evidence that Diamantis voluntarily skipped his court appearance, a showing that’s necessary to move forward with sentencing him — a step they said will aid extradition.
Francis also asked the judge on Sept. 17 to order Diamantis’ bail forfeited. The judge postponed acting on the request until Wednesday’s rescheduled sentencing hearing.
That order would require certain bond documents in the case to be released to the U.S. Attorney’s Office. They are expected to include a pre-signed warranty deed held in escrow, which would immediately transfer title to the government once recorded, subject to any prior mortgages.
A federal judge this week was weighing a request from Connecticut Public to view the records, which have not been released.
In an interview, Diamantis acknowledged feeling an emotional attachment to the Farmington property, which had long been his home.
“I used to joke with the kids saying, ‘Listen, you know, the day comes when I pass away, I was going to be buried in the backyard by the shed,'” he said. “I had no intentions of ever leaving it.”
This story was first published Sept. 29, 2026 by Connecticut Public.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Donlin dam failure could put lives at risk and harm fish habitat, study says
description: A major dam failure at the huge gold mine proposed for rural Western Alaska could unleash catastrophic flooding that would make one village uninhabitable, poison drinking water sources and cause lasting damage to fish habitat, according to a new analysis by federal regulators. The hypothetical disaster is described in a draft supplemental environmental impac[...]
text:
The Donlin Gold mine camp is seen from the air, June 23, 2025. The site holds 40 million ounces of gold, according to Novagold Resources, the majority owner of Donlin Gold. If developed, the mine would excavate gold from an open pit extending more than 2 miles in length, with a waste held by a 471-foot-high dam. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)A major dam failure at the huge gold mine proposed for rural Western Alaska could unleash catastrophic flooding that would make one village uninhabitable, poison drinking water sources and cause lasting damage to fish habitat, according to a new analysis by federal regulators.
The hypothetical disaster is described in a draft supplemental environmental impact statement the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers prepared for the Donlin Gold mine.
The supplemental EIS, released by the Corps last week, was mandated by a court order issued last year. That order followed a 2024 ruling by U.S. District Court Judge Sharon Gleason that found that the Corps’ previous study of Donlin environmental impacts improperly understated the risks of major break in the dam that Donlin proposes to build to hold its mining waste, known as tailings. 
The Corps’ original environmental impact statement, completed in 2018, analyzed a potential release of up to 0.5% of the millions of tons of material held behind the planned 471-foot-high dam. Shortly after that study was released, the Corps and the U.S. Bureau of Land Management gave their approvals for mine construction.
Gleason’s ruling did not overturn the permits.
The new study, launched in January, evaluates potential results from dam breaches releasing 5.4%, 13.3% and 27% of the total tailings volume.
As hypothetical spill sizes increase, potential impacts become more severe, causing special risks to the village of Crooked Creek, about 10 miles from the mine, the draft said.
“Larger spills would generate much larger flood waves, inundate thousands of acres, flood portions of the Village of Crooked Creek, alter stream channels, and deposit large volumes of tailings throughout the drainage,” the document said.
At risk are the health and safety of people living nearby, the draft SEIS said.
“Risks include contaminant exposure, drinking-water concerns, psychosocial stress, displacement, and potential loss of life in heavily affected areas. The 27 percent scenario could render parts of the Village of Crooked Creek uninhabitable and create significant public-safety challenges,” the document said.
There are also risks to fish in the region: “Larger spills could cause population-level impacts lasting years to decades in Crooked Creek, with the 27 percent scenario potentially causing generational effects,” the draft said.
The maximum 27% spill scenario is based on a comprehensive 2022 study of dam failures at mines, the Corps said.
 

A model mounted on a wall of the Donlin Gold camp’s cafeteria, seen on June 23, 2025, shows how the mine would be developed, according to the most recent plan. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)
 

	Comments on the draft will be accepted until Oct. 23, the Corps said.
Mine opponents said the new analysis vindicates their arguments that the mine poses unacceptable dangers in a region in which communities are dependent on salmon and healthy fish habitat.
“The findings in this document are a validation of our deepest fears and a clear signal that this project is far too dangerous for western Alaska. While we implored the federal government to consider a total failure scenario, which they did not do, they are confirming that a dam failure of just 27% could kill people, poison our drinking water for decades, and wipe out salmon for generations. We cannot, and will not, trade the safety of our children and our rivers for a gold mine that will last only 27 years,” Ashlynn Simeon, deputy director of the Mother Kuskokwim Tribal Coalition, said in a statement.
The coalition was founded by Yup’ik tribal members in the region who oppose the mine. 
One of the attorneys representing the tribal mine opponents said the Corps and BLM erred by using the 27% figure as the maximum release scenario.
“We disagree that pulling a figure based on an average from that dataset is the right way to go about this. We think it is important for the Corps and BLM to look at a full spill because a full spill is a foreseeable potential consequence of building this mine. Many tailings dams have failed across the world, and they have spilled up to 100% of their contents,” Hannah Payne Foster of Earthjustice, the environmental law firm representing the tribal plaintiffs, said by email.
While a spill of 27% of the dammed content would be “disastrous” for some communities, a larger spill would affect even more communities, she said. Without analysis of a bigger spill, residents of a wider area would lack some key information, such as the amount of time they would have to evacuate their villages. Additionally, she said, the mine tailings will pose threats long after mining ceases. They “do not go away when mining ends; they must be held in place in perpetuity.”
Donlin Gold said it will evaluate the draft environmental impact study and stay engaged in the public review process.
In a statement, Donlin Gold said it is committed to protective standards “well beyond the regulatory process.” That includes its design for the tailings storage facility is consistent with that approach, the company said.
“The facility will have multiple layers of protection and oversight from our own engineers designing and monitoring the facility, to independent engineering review, Alaska Native landowners, and the State of Alaska engineers and regulators,” Todd Dahlman, Donlin Gold’s general manager, said in the statement. “These layers provide multiple checks on the design, construction, and operation of the facility, as well as ongoing monitoring to help identify and address potential issues before they become a problem.”
 

Bev Hoffman of Bethel, a founder of the Mother Kuskokwim Tribal Coalition, participates in a rally on Oct. 19, 2023, against the Donlin Gold mine and other resource-extraction projects. The protest was held on the street outside Anchorage’s Dena’ina Civic and Convention Center, where the Alaska Federation of Natives annual convention was underway. Sentiment about Donlin is dividend among Alaska Natives. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)
 

	Calista Corporation, the regional Native corporation that owns the mineral rights that Donlin would develop and has partnered with the mining company, said it is also evaluating the supplemental impact statement and will submit comments.
The Donlin Gold project would commercialize gold deposits estimated at 40 million ounces, according to Donlin Gold’s major owner, Canada-based Novagold Resources. It is “one of the largest known development-stage gold deposits today,” the company’s website says.
The scale of the proposed mine is massive.
It would encompass an open pit more than 2 miles long, the tailings facility and its 471-foot-high dam, a natural gas pipeline running more than 300 miles from Cook Inlet, a natural gas-fired power plant, road and port facilities, and airstrip and related items, according to the Corps’ description.
Alaska Native sentiments about the mine are divided. Calista and the Kuskokwim Corp., the Native corporation that owns the surface where the project is located, are partners with Donlin Gold and have described the project as offering much-needed economic opportunity in the state’s poorest region. Donlin revenues would also be shared with Alaska’s other Native corporations, making the project of statewide economic interest.
But many Yup’ik residents in the region oppose the project because of the risks they see to salmon in the Kuskokwim River area and other natural resources that support traditional lifestyles. They argue that the risks outweigh the potential economic benefits.
Development of the Donlin mine has been considered for decades. The gold at the site was discovered in the 1980s.
Last year, the Trump administration selected the Donlin mine for inclusion in a program called FAST-41, in which permitting is streamlined and coordinated.
One of the key investors in the Donlin project is John Paulson, a billionaire hedge fund owner who is close to Trump.
Paulson last year bought 40% of Donlin Gold after Barrick Gold Corporation, an international mining giant, dropped out of the project. In July, Paulson struck an agreement with Novagold to consolidate their ownership. Under the agreement, Novagold will get Paulson’s shares in Donlin and Paulson will have a major ownership stake in the reformulated Novagold.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Trump used impossible foreign labor standards as tariff workaround, small businesses say
description: Small businesses will once again challenge President Donald Trump’s tariffs in the Court of International Trade in New York City this week.
text:
WASHINGTON — Small businesses will once again challenge President Donald Trump’s tariffs in federal court this week as they continue to feel the squeeze of the administration’s roller coaster policy on import taxes.
Spice importer Burlap & Barrel and rare watch importer Collective Horology will argue Wednesday in the Court of International Trade in New York City that the Trump administration did not properly establish forced labor cases against dozens of U.S. trading partners before levying duties on goods that numerous American importers buy.
The Office of the United States Trade Representative announced in late July that products from 60 top U.S. trading partners will be tariffed at 10% or 12.5%, depending on whether governments have or have not developed laws meant to combat forced labor. The new tariffs cover 99.4% of all goods imported into the United States, according to the office.
The plaintiffs, represented by the legal advocacy nonprofit Liberty Justice Center, allege the administration exceeded its tariff authority delegated by Congress under the forced labor statute, Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974. 
The plaintiffs also argue the tariffs are “arbitrary and capricious” because U.S. trade officials relied on “generalized assertions” that labor policies in 60 economies imposed concrete economic harm to the U.S.
Trade law expert blasts Trump usage
Ambassador Alan Wm. Wolff, a former trade official who helped draft the forced labor statute and filed a brief in support of the small business plaintiffs, said Section 301 was “designed for sort of a rifle shot of retaliation against a single foreign country doing some particular act that’s been verified.”
Wolff served in the Carter and Ford administrations, and later as a deputy director-general at the World Trade Organization.
“I sat through the executive sessions of the committees that were drafting the statute,” he said. “No one ever conceived of the idea that you could just create a sort of a fake, bogus test for other countries – 60 of them — that none of them could meet.”
Wolff told States Newsroom in an interview Sept. 21 that the statute has never been used in this way.
“If the U.S. was serious about forced labor being dealt with in this fashion … it would say, ‘Well, we’ll review it every six months, and if you put in a statute that has the following provisions, we would probably lift the tariff,’” he said. 
“There’s none of that because the purpose is to have the tariff, not to combat forced labor,” he continued.
The Department of Justice declined to comment Monday on ongoing litigation.
The White House and the Office of the United States Trade Representative did not respond Monday.
One tariff after another
The legal challenge on behalf of small business plaintiffs is not the first one to be brought by the Liberty Justice Center, a nonprofit that focuses on “high-impact cases that defend individual liberty and challenge government overreach,” according to its website.
In February, the organization secured a victory against the Trump administration when the U.S. Supreme Court ruled the president’s unprecedented executive tariffs under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act, referred to as IEEPA, were unconstitutional.
The organization won the case on behalf of several small business plaintiffs, ranging from an Illinois-based toymaker and New York-based wine importer, to a Utah-based plastics producer and a Pennsylvania-based fishing gear company, among others.
Almost immediately after the high court struck down his emergency tariffs, Trump imposed a new wide-reaching 10% tariff on global imports under a separate statute – Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974. The statute limited Trump to only 150 days.
The administration concurrently opened sweeping trade practice investigations, including under the Section 301 forced labor statute, on nearly all U.S. trading partners. The government announced its forced labor findings just as the earlier tariffs expired at the 150-day mark.
New duties ‘blatantly pretextual’
Sara Albrecht, the Liberty Justice Center’s CEO, described the administration’s new forced labor tariffs as “blatantly pretextual” to replace duties imposed under Section 122.
“And Section 122 was pretextual for the IEEPA tariff that rolled off this year when he lost at the Supreme Court. So we feel like our job wasn’t done because we struck down the IEEPA tariff, and then the administration just did it again,” Albrecht said.
The organization is again representing small business plaintiffs who allege harm to their bottom line because of the administration’s tariff policy. 
Burlap & Barrel, a New York-based company with warehouses in Hagerstown, Maryland, and Las Vegas imports spices from 22 countries. The California-based Collective Horology imports high-end mechanical watches from independent makers in six European nations.
“They are two individual American small businesses that have been swept up in a political kind of debate. We’re arguing this on behalf of every American small business, every American business that is being forced to once again pay illegal tariffs,” Albrecht said.
The organization has asked the Court of International Trade for class status.
“You have to keep in mind that they’re just getting their IEEPA refunds right now, and we’re almost done with that. But they had to start paying Section 122 (tariffs), and then when that stopped, they had to pay Section 301 (tariffs). So a lot of these businesses are effectively loaning all of their working capital to the U.S. government while we kind of sort this out in court,” Albrecht said.
The Liberty Justice Center had also challenged the Section 122 tariffs on behalf of Burlap & Barrel.
U.S. Customs and Border Protection is still in the process of refunding roughly $166 billion worth of tariffs paid by businesses under Trump’s IEEPA import charges.
“We’re a small nonprofit that is, you know, 12 attorneys trying to again strike down the tariffs, and it would be nice if someone else wanted to jump into the fight,” Albrecht said. “So we’re doing the best we can, and I think we’ve done a good job so far.”
Prior to the tariff case win, the organization was most well known for its role in successfully arguing before the U.S. Supreme Court in Janus v. AFSCME, in which its client Mark Janus challenged public sector unions over paying dues.
This story was first published Sept. 28, 2026 by States Newsroom.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Massachusetts state tests are leaving students unprepared for today’s information challenges
description: What gets tested gets taught. Media literacy isn't tested in Massachusetts, so it isn't taught.
text:
MASSACHUSETTS NEEDS TO fix a significant problem with the state tests required of all public-school students: They do not measure many of the skills the state says are important.  
The recently published Vision of a Massachusetts Graduate calls for students to think critically, question assumptions, and thrive in college, career, and civic life. To achieve those goals, assessments must align with the state’s broader expectations. Otherwise, educators and students receive a confusing message about what is important. 
Education research confirms what common sense and experience tells us, namely, that teachers feel pressure for students to perform well on state tests and believe, as students do, that what is tested is what policymakers consider important. 
State tests should let school leaders, teachers, students, parents and others know how important media literacy education is for young people. What gets tested gets taught. Media literacy isn’t tested, so it isn’t taught. Questions about important competencies are missing on the tests, as the following examples demonstrate. 

Multiple requirements in the Massachusetts standards for English Language Arts and Literacy call for media literacy, such as “Integrate multiple sources of information presented in diverse formats and media (e.g., visually, quantitatively, orally), evaluating the credibility and accuracy of each source” [emphasis added].” Yet, we don’t see any items on the ELA practice test for 10th graders that test this vital competency. 


Massachusetts requires an eighth-grade civics class that is supposed to include “the development of skills to access, analyze and evaluate written and digital media as it relates to history and civics.” The state’s civic test might ask questions to rate the trustworthiness of various websites or perhaps include an item quoting an article or web page claiming the 2020 election was stolen and asking how students might check its accuracy. But there is nothing at all about digital media on the practice civics test, even though students spend hours each day on phones and computers, where misinformation is rampant. 


Vision of a Massachusetts Graduate says students should be prepared for civic life. The Massachusetts science and technology framework includes similar language, namely that graduates should “possess sufficient knowledge of science and engineering to engage in public discussions on related issues, and be careful consumers of scientific and technological information and products in their everyday lives.” Yet there is not a single question on the Massachusetts high school biology test about public policy, or about being a careful consumer (e.g., for green energy products, or genetic testing, or nutrition), or about how to evaluate information related to science and technology. 

According to the Vision of a Massachusetts Graduate, students who graduate should be able to “critically examine information to draw connections, question assumptions, infer meaning, and shape solutions.” That is an admirable goal, as are the goals that students have “the skills to be lifelong learners” who can “thrive in college, career, and civic life.” But the Programme for International Assessment (PISA) just tested more than 760,000 students worldwide and found an alarming tendency toward hasty reading. The PISA report notes that “in a world of shrinking attention spans and rising information overload, policymakers have a crucial role to play in shaping an educational culture that nurtures the depth of thought necessary to thrive.” 
However, these goals cannot be achieved in the digital age if students do not learn how to sort information from misinformation wherever and whenever they encounter it, whether on TikTok, Instagram, Facebook, cable news, from friends, or elsewhere. Research shows that young people are generally poor at evaluating information they encounter out of school; basically, young people are not reliably able to sort fact from fiction. What students need to learn in school is a set of competencies known as media literacy. That is an even more urgent need given the role of AI in spreading misinformation. 
Studies show that media literacy instruction in school helps students to better evaluate unfamiliar information. As a result, dozens of states have adopted laws or policies promoting media literacy education. Schools need to teach and test media literacy so that students are prepared to be lifelong learners. Like teaching reading or mathematics, media literacy education requires instruction across multiple grades and across subjects. 
There is no good excuse for these lapses. Relevant items can be found on some state tests. For example, North Carolina’s high school biology test asks which of four policies “could best reduce global climate change” and New York’s high school biology test asks students what parents could do to protect their children after discovering lead levels in local topsoil are high. These examples show that it is no more difficult to create valid items testing media literacy, or applying science knowledge to societal and personal contexts, than it is to test any other competency. 
If state tests were better aligned with important state goals for students, it would be easier to understand how and why the tests could be useful. As legislators consider policies related to testing, and, one hopes, look carefully at the existing tests and the report from The Massachusetts Department of Elementary and Secondary Education, Media Literacy in Massachusetts A Landscape and Policy Scan, now is a perfect time to fix this problem. 
Kyra Brissette is CEO of Media Literacy Now, a Watertown-based national nonprofit organization advancing media literacy education through policy, advocacy, and public awareness. Andrew Zucker is an independent education researcher and member of Media Literacy Now’s National Advisory Council.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Mercer County officials reject regulations to allow data centers next to coal-fired power plant
description: HARRODSBURG — The Mercer County Fiscal Court rejected zoning regulations on Monday that would have allowed the siting of large data centers on land adjacent to a Kentucky Utilities coal-fired power plant. The unanimous vote by county elected officials during a special meeting is the latest development in the rural community following months of contentious […[...]
text:
Many of the attendees at the Mercer County Fiscal Court meeting brought signs expressing opposition to data centers. (Kentucky Lantern photo by Liam Niemeyer)HARRODSBURG — The Mercer County Fiscal Court rejected zoning regulations on Monday that would have allowed the siting of large data centers on land adjacent to a Kentucky Utilities coal-fired power plant.
The unanimous vote by county elected officials during a special meeting is the latest development in the rural community following months of contentious debate over whether the community should allow hyperscale data centers, and if so, where such data centers should be sited.
Republican Mercer County Judge-Executive Sarah Steele told the more than 170 people sitting in chairs and bleachers that the proposed regulations did offer some protections: requiring a data center developer to enter into a community benefit agreement to ensure the developer pays for its own infrastructure and the requirement of environmental studies.
But the regulations needed more work, particularly to align them into the county’s comprehensive plan, or the long-term guide for land use and development.
“I am not completely anti-data center, but we have to get this right before we approve it,” Steele said.
The vote got a round of applause from the audience, many of them wearing blue shirts as a part of the community group We Are Mercer County that has voiced strong concerns over land use and environmental impacts from potential hyperscale data centers.
An even louder round of applause came when Republican Mercer County Magistrate Susan Barrington told the audience she was outright against the construction of any hyperscale data center because of impacts to agricultural land, nearby horse farms and residential neighborhoods.
“The construction of a monstrous hyperscale data center will cause a significant, highly disruptive, irreversible, and permanent damage to the footprint of District 4,” Barrington said, referring to her magisterial district that includes Shaker Village of Pleasant Hill, a historic site preserving structures of the Kentucky Shakers religious community.
Back to planning and zoning
The vote will send the proposed data center regulations back to a planning and zoning commission — currently made up of members appointed by the county and the county seat of Harrodsburg — that has spent since April working on various drafts of ordinances to regulate the siting of impacts of large data centers.
The county had passed a one-year temporary ban, or moratorium, on data center construction in August that would have expired automatically if the fiscal court had adopted the regulations.
The regulations would have established an “industrial technology” district allowing the siting hyperscale data centers on land — including some farmland — adjacent to the coal-fired E.W. Brown Generating Station, operated by Louisville Gas and Electric and Kentucky Utilities along the Dix River.
While no specific data center proposal has emerged to be located adjacent to the coal-fired power plant, the Harrodsburg Herald reported in December 2025 the commission was hiring a consultant to deal with the possibility of a large-scale data center in the community. The Lexington Herald-Leader reported in February a land developer it was marketing a piece of undeveloped land next to the power plant.
Shaker Village of Pleasant Hill CEO Billy Rankin, center wearing glasses, is among those in Mercer County with strong concerns about proposed hyperscale data centers in the county. (Kentucky Lantern photo by Liam Niemeyer)
The location of the new zoning for data centers alarmed the leadership of Shaker Village of Pleasant Hill in particular, the edge of the zone being less than a mile away from the historic site. The nonprofit urged community members to tell the fiscal court to reject the regulations in the days leading up to the meeting.
Shaker Village of Pleasant Hill CEO Billy Rankin told the Lantern the data center zone was an “arbitrary designation” of land next to the power plant.
“It would be disruptive in many ways, whether it’s the sound, the light, the construction process, all of the above,” Rankin said. “We care about Mercer County. We care about land conservation. We care about historic preservation. We care about our tourism in the county. We want to make sure that all of those factors are considered broadly as a county before a decision that’s so impactful would be made anyway.”
Rankin said he hopes for a “collaborative and well-rounded” comprehensive planning process by the commission.
‘Some questions and some unknowns’
But Steele, the judge-executive, also said during the meeting there are still “some questions and some unknowns” including what the small Mercer County city of Burgin will do.
The small city of about 1,000 people has grappled with a proposal to annex land north of the city — a different location compared to the land next to the power plant — for a hyperscale data center pitched by developer Panattoni Data Centers. A Burgin city council member walked out of a meeting earlier this month to prevent a vote to advance consideration of the potential annexation.
Mercer County Magistrate Susan Barrington pauses her comments while the crowd applauds her opposition to data centers. (Kentucky Lantern photo by Liam Niemeyer)
Any data center regulations passed by the county would not affect land within Burgin city limits because the city doesn’t have planning and zoning regulations. But the Burgin city council is meeting Tuesday to vote on potentially joining the county’s joint planning and zoning commission and potentially create its own regulations.
Laura Duhamel, 67, one of the attendees wearing a blue We Are Mercer County shirt, told the Lantern she had strong concerns about data center construction because she wanted to preserve farmland.
“We’re not out of it yet,” Duhamel said. “I think a lot’s going to depend on what happens in Burgin” with upcoming local elections.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: Canada is SC’s 3rd-largest export market. ‘It’s too early’ to gauge impact of tariffs.
description: More than a month after the latest tariffs on Canadian-made products were enacted, the trade war’s impact on South Carolina’s economy is still difficult to assess, even as further restrictions on Canadian imports take effect Tuesday. “It’s hard to speculate on specifically what impacts tariffs will have at this point,” Joey Von Nessen, a research […]
text:
Steel i-beams form a perimeter barrier at Nucor Steel Berkeley in Huger, South Carolina, on Thursday, May 1, 2025, when Vice President J.D. Vance spoke there. (File photo by Mark Susko/Special to the SC Daily Gazette)More than a month after the latest tariffs on Canadian-made products were enacted, the trade war’s impact on South Carolina’s economy is still difficult to assess, even as further restrictions on Canadian imports take effect Tuesday.
“It’s hard to speculate on specifically what impacts tariffs will have at this point,” Joey Von Nessen, a research economist at the University of South Carolina, told the SC Daily Gazette.
“It’s too early to provide any specific outlook on what those individual effects would likely be,” he said last week, adding “it really will depend on how long they last going forward.”
More than $8 billion in goods and services move between South Carolina and Canada each year, and Canada is the Palmetto State’s third-largest export market behind Germany and Mexico, according to the state Department of Commerce.
Among the top commodities Canada exports to South Carolina are plastics, aircraft and car parts. In return, automobiles and rubber are among the top products South Carolina sends to Canada.
The Palmetto State is also a key destination for Canadian travelers, with the Myrtle Beach area one of the most popular vacation choices.
Part of the problem in assessing the impact of President Donald Trump’s most recent 50% tariffs on nearly $28 billion in Canadian goods — enacted Aug. 26 — is that companies have been reluctant to talk about U.S. trade policy.
Spartanburg County-based BMW, for example, last year halted some shipments of X-model SUVs to Canada after that country hit the automaker with counter-tariffs in reaction to Trump’s initial trade salvo. BMW has resumed those shipments but hasn’t issued a public statement about the most recent tariffs. A spokesman for the carmaker did not respond to the SC Daily Gazette’s request for comment.
Volvo looks to energize SC plant with new models amid shifting global trade, market trends

Volvo also did not respond. The automaker, which builds the EX90 SUV at its Lowcountry plant, has also pulled that vehicle from Canada due to tariffs. However, EX90 sales amounted to only 143 units to Canada in 2025.
Automotive News reported this week that the overall share of U.S.-made vehicles sold in Canada dropped to 28.4% during the first half of 2026, down from 35.4% a year ago.
The S.C. State Ports Authority, a quasi-government agency, also did not want to comment directly on trade policy.
Micah Mallace, the authority’s president and CEO, said very little containerized trade moves between the port and Canada, with plastic pellets used to make thousands of consumer goods the largest commodity. Most trade between Canada and South Carolina moves by truck or rail.
South Carolina metal makers like Century Aluminum and Nucor Steel have traditionally praised tariffs and other trade measures designed to reduce foreign dumping of cheap products on the U.S. market, but neither has publicly weighed in on the latest Canadian trade war.
On Monday, Trump announced plans for a $15 billion steel mill in Iowa. He linked Mesabi Metallics’ decision to build the new facility, which he said will be the nation’s largest, with his tariffs on steel imports. The company will use iron ore from its $2.5 billion mine in Minnesota, which opened earlier this month.
SC now requires American-made steel for roads, bridges and other public projects

Timna Tanners, an analyst with Wells Fargo, told Bloomberg that Canada’s counter-tariffs on roughly $20 billion worth of U.S. steel are largely irrelevant because those metal products are already prohibitively expensive due to previous tariffs.
Trump’s 50% tariff on Canadian wood products – and Canada’s retaliatory tariffs on the U.S. – have led to surging costs for plywood, specialized wood panels and other products. That is expected to lead to higher housing costs as interest rates are making homebuying less affordable.
South Carolina’s $23 billion timber and logging businesses, already under considerable stress, are feeling additional pressure. For example, Canada-headquartered Canfor Corp. permanently closed sawmills in Estill and Darlington after last year’s initial round of Trump-imposed tariffs.
More recently, Jones and Sons Logging Inc. told a Greenville television station that the latest tariffs will add $10,000 to the cost of machinery. Company owner Jeff Jones did not respond to the Gazette’s request for comment.
Canada was the state’s largest source of forest product imports in 2025, at $259 million. Solid wood imports were $390 million – a 3.4% increase of 2024 figures. Forest product exports fell by more than $1 billion last year, to $555 million, and the S.C. Forestry Commission is predicting further declines because of tariffs and a weak economy.
Starting Tuesday, another batch of imports from Canada – including some alcoholic beverages, molasses and some dairy byproducts – will be banned from coming into the United States. It’s not clear what impact that could have in South Carolina, as none of those products are major import commodities to this state. Products already on store shelves or in inventory can continue to be sold.
Regardless, consumers will wind up paying the cost, Von Nessen said, and that can snowball into big problems for the economy as a whole.
“Consumers will see an uptick in prices, and that has the potential to weigh on consumer spending as we look ahead to the end of 2026, and higher inflation overall,” he said. “When consumers are losing purchasing power, that will eventually cause them to cut back on their spending, which can cause an overall pullback in economic activity.”
