name: Kansas Reflector
title: Profiles in resistance: Residents of this Kansas town unite in opposition to ICE and CoreCivic
description: LEAVENWORTH — Amid a clash between a new immigration jail and the city that hosts it, residents from Leavenworth and nearby areas gathered last month to talk strategies for protecting people held in the facility. For some, it was just the latest meeting in a long resistance against the jail opened by the private prison […]
text:
Iona Roberts asks Dan McIntosh and Meghan Wieten-Scott a question at an Aug. 29, 2026, meeting at the Leavenworth Public Library attended by more than a dozen people. McIntosh and Wieten-Scott led the meeting to update concerned Leavenworth and Kansas residents on what they know about the nearby ICE jail and the people detained there. (Photo by Baya Burgess/Kansas Reflector)LEAVENWORTH — Amid a clash between a new immigration jail and the city that hosts it, residents from Leavenworth and nearby areas gathered last month to talk strategies for protecting people held in the facility.
For some, it was just the latest meeting in a long resistance against the jail opened by the private prison company CoreCivic.
Leavenworth, a small city in eastern Kansas, is known for embracing its multiple prisons and a military fort. But some residents refuse to accept the city’s latest installation. They often work together and rally others along the way. A few of them are members of Sisters of Charity of Leavenworth, a religious sisterhood leading effort.
The local activists have taken on two contradictory efforts: ensuring quality conditions in the facility and opposing its existence. They are motivated by cases of mistreatment and death in similar institutions across the U.S., and CoreCivic’s track record of previously operating the facility as an understaffed and violent “hell hole,” as a federal judge termed it.
At an Aug. 29 community meeting at the Leavenworth Public Library, Dan McIntosh described reports of delayed release and medical neglect.
“We’re concerned with why it is taking the outside intervention of media, oversight bodies or activist groups in order for detainees to get the care that they need,” he said at the meeting.
The city waged a year-long battle against CoreCivic’s permit request until March. The prison company had leveraged financial pressure to gain city officials’ approval and open the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement jail.
Though Leavenworth commissioners secured oversight during negotiations, CoreCivic sold the facility to ICE in August, potentially voiding the city’s oversight power.
After months of momentum, the sale also disrupted the activists’ efforts to monitor the jail’s conditions, leaving them uncertain but alert for what will happen next.
Kansas Reflector is telling the personal stories of eight community members who gather volunteers, raise money and host meetings for the sake of those in detainment. They don’t share the same strategies or motives, but they all want to kick ICE out of their city.
Kansas Reflector asked Ryan Gustin, CoreCivic’s spokesperson, via email to include perspectives of the facility’s warden and the employees who have previously spoken out in support of the facility. Gustin said he would not make anyone available for comment.
 
Jean Anne Panisko

Jean Anne Panisko (Photo by Baya Burgess/Kansas Reflector)

Sister Jean Anne Panisko serves with the Sisters of Charity of Leavenworth, a women’s ministry focused on community service. She signs up volunteers inside the facility, despite difficult logistics.
She described volunteering inside the jail as teaching inmates individual skills, such as leading yoga or teaching English.
“It’s always looking at what are the needs?” she said. “And then how do each of us who volunteer — through what talents and gifts we have — can meet some of those needs?”
She wants to use her faith background to pray with detainees who want prayer, she said.
“To be able to pray with them,” she said. “To be able to just talk to them, listen to their stories.”
But Panisko has not been able to actually volunteer inside the facility. No one has.
CoreCivic allowed volunteers, and Panisko said they had to file a few rounds of paperwork to be approved. Then they went through training.
“We were trained for 8 hours, filled out all the paperwork, had our photos taken for our badges and were to begin volunteering the end of August,” she said.
The trained volunteers don’t know when the expected tour will take place or the extent of the volunteer work permitted.
 
Justin Young

Justin Young (Photo by Baya Burgess/Kansas Reflector)

Justin Young, a professional mediator, tries to balance daily efforts to improve life inside the facility without benefiting the jail itself.
He said the warden, Misty Mackey, has worked to prevent harmful conditions — such as riots and disease — and follow the regulations of the special use permit.
“That’s a double-edged sword, though,” Young said, “because if she never messes up, if her facility is run well, it won’t ping the violations of the (special use permit). If it doesn’t ping the violations of the SUP, it never gets shut down.”
He aims to address the needs of those detained.
Young serves on the Carceral Accountability Council. The local group, initially formed as an effort to keep CoreCivic out of Leavenworth, fundraises to provide products to detainees, including scented soap and chess sets.
While the facility provides the basics, he said, the group wants to send products “that make you feel like a human.”
He also serves on the oversight board mandated by the special use permit. He mentions the concerns of detainees’ family members, such as needing extra blankets, at the meetings and sometimes directly to the warden.
The warden makes note of his requests and follows up with him when she fulfills it, he said.
 
Michelle Mendiola

Michelle Mendiola (Photo by Baya Burgess/Kansas Reflector)

Michelle Mendiola helped organize one of the first protests against the jail in the summer of 2025.
The march began at her 19th century home in Leavenworth, the house her family left in part because of the facility.
Mendiola, a Leavenworth small business owner, and her husband, a Lawrence physical therapy clinic director, decided to move to Lawrence to be closer to the clinic, she said.
He has worked there since 2020, she said, but the facility opening was their tipping point.
“My husband is Filipino, and my children are half-Filipino,” she said. “As the project started to really take way and immigration was kind of ramping up, my husband was very uncomfortable living that close with that much presence because he is not white American in appearance.”
Mendiola will remain connected to Leavenworth, she said, not only because her businesses are there but because she will keep informing herself and others about local ICE actions by posting on social media, talking to journalists and communicating with advocates.
“Sometimes knowledge can lead to helplessness, feelings of helplessness,” she said. “But also, you never know when sharing that knowledge can reach the right people who can make a difference.”
 
Michael Delores Allegri

Michael Delores Allegri (Photo by Baya Burgess/Kansas Reflector)

Sister Michael Delores Allegri, a Sisters of Charity of Leavenworth member, retired school teacher and former foster parent, said the United States’ response to immigration is “worse than it’s ever been.”
“You have a group of people whose only crime is that they came into this country and don’t have a green card or don’t have the right paperwork,” she said. “If that’s their only crime, then why are they locked into a facility?”
Allegri served on the oversight board with 13 others, including the city manager, the police chief and the facility’s warden.
She toured the facility as a board member and described it as clean and well-functioning.
But she said the board has only met twice, once in May and once in June. She doesn’t know why the July meeting was canceled, but she said the August meeting was canceled because of the sale to ICE.
She said she wishes to know more about the sale, but she remains in the dark about it and the future of the board.
“If CoreCivic was in dialogue with ICE while the Commissioners were in process of deciding, and it was not disclosed that a sale was being discussed, CoreCivic was not being transparent,” she said.
She said that while the employees who work closely with detainees are transparent, she does not necessarily trust the people in charge.
“I find them to be open and wanting to do what’s best for the people there,” she said. “But they get their direction from CoreCivic who gets their direction from ICE so it gets convoluted. Are they, direct staff, given the opportunity to operate with some autonomy or are bound by the higher layers? I’m not sure if we know enough to answer that question.”
 
Meghan Wieten-Scott

Meghan Wieten-Scott (Photo by Baya Burgess/Kansas Reflector)

Meghan Wieten-Scott, a business consultant and military spouse stationed at Fort Leavenworth, talks to concerned city residents about the facility.
Some people in Leavenworth, she said, still don’t know an ICE detention facility moved into their city.
“We are such a prison town that I think people just assume it’s par for the course,” she said.
Since May, she has led two discussions at the Leavenworth Public Library as a member of Leavenworth Community Response, a local group formed to advocate against the jail.
She discovered the group through a private, encrypted group messaging channel designed to document ICE. She and hundreds of others in eastern Kansas receive alerts about ICE activity and can go to the scene and record on their phones.
She became involved in part to find community in Leavenworth.
“As a military spouse, we move so often,” she said. “Sometimes it feels like you’re shouting into the wind, politically. Like nobody’s hearing you when you’re sending letters and you’re calling. And so this was a way for me to do something here and hopefully make a difference right here in my community, and to come together with people.”
 
Mike Trapp

Mike Trapp (Photo by Baya Burgess/Kansas Reflector)

Not long after Mike Trapp settled in Leavenworth in 2023, he dove into fighting CoreCivic’s return. Then he left the efforts he helped established in the hands of fellow advocates.
Since his first social service job in the 1980s, he has jumped from one community project to the next. In 2021, he left Columbia, Missouri, where he served three consecutive terms on the city council. He now lives in Leavenworth and works at a Jackson County, Missouri, organization training court-appointed special advocates for children in foster care.
“I’m a change agent,” he said.
Around the time the commission approved CoreCivic’s permit, he proposed the city place impact fees it earned from the facility into a legal defense fund to protect itself against potential legal action from CoreCivic. The idea continues to develop.
He also helped create the Carceral Accountability Council in 2025. Though he left the group, he remains a resource to advocates as a local government expert and speaks out against the facility to his 3,000 Facebook followers.
Looking forward, he said he feels hopeful about the city’s ability to oversee the facility and prevent inhumane conditions because of Leavenworth’s “strong permit with local controls.”
While he understood the commission’s decision, he would have rejected the permit, he said, because he does not accept the ICE’s growing detainment system, accusing it of violating due process.
“It’s a naked attempt,” he said, “to hold people hostage in poor conditions until they voluntarily deport.”
 
Ashley Hernandez

Ashley Hernandez (Photo by Baya Burgess/Kansas Reflector)

As the lobbyist for Sisters of Charity of Leavenworth’s Office of Justice, Peace, and Integrity of Creation, Ashley Hernandez holds town halls and speaks to residents to fight detention on behalf of the organization.
She described Leavenworth as a politically diverse and compassionate place. While the city’s prisons and military fort promote values of institutions and law and order, she said, that doesn’t keep residents from questioning the ICE facility.
“It doesn’t really matter what background you have,” she said. “Most of our population is going to say we need to stand up for human rights and against a lot of the abuses that we’re seeing.”
Since the jail reopened in Leavenworth, she has focused on preventing harmful conditions inside..
One of her biggest efforts has been organizing volunteers. She said 17 have passed training required to enter the and many more are waiting to be trained, though none have entered.
Looking forward, she hopes the facility closes.
“Maybe when this administration is up, where we get different people into office, we can shut this facility down,” she said, “We don’t want to continue being complicit with the anti-immigration agenda that this administration is pushing because us Catholics, we welcome all.”
 
Dan McIntosh

Dan McIntosh (Photo by Baya Burgess/Kansas Reflector)

Dan McIntosh said he spends as much time advocating against the facility as he does at his day job as a composer. He corresponds with Leavenworth residents and families of people inside the facility,bringing their concerns to city officials.
“I met more people in Leavenworth in the past year than the previous eight years before that,” he said. “I was a little surprised. I wasn’t expecting as many people to care as much.”
Ahead of the Aug. 29 community meeting, he spent much of that week speaking with Katsiaryna Bartko, a detainee from Belarus who previously had thyroid cancer. As he advocated for her at the meeting, he began to cry but managed to continue speaking.
“She’s still at the facility and is declining. Her kidneys are starting to fail. Her creatine levels are going up, and she may have a myxedema coma any day, excuse me, which has a 20-60% mortality rate,” McIntosh said.
She was released on Sept. 16 and said she is recovering, according to multiple reports.
McIntosh also discussed reports of delayed release during the meeting.
“We’ve talked to some detainees who wanted to be deported all the way back in May and June, and they’re still at the facility and haven’t gotten out yet, even though they signed the papers,” he said.
Advocacy efforts exist below the surface, he said, because of political tension in Leavenworth. He said he doesn’t care what people think of him, so he recruits people who want to advocate against the facility.
“One of the reasons we held that community conversation was to try to help funnel people into the right spot where they’re comfortable helping,” he said.
In late August, he opened his home of four to a woman from Kansas City metro whose husband had been detained. He gave her and her two children a free place to stay while visiting their loved one.
His motivation, he said, comes from basic American ideals.
“I think it flies in the face of the principles of liberty that this country was founded on, to detain people who came here looking for help,” he said.

name: Nevada Current
title: Here are the Nevada State Assembly districts to watch this Election Day
description: The Nevada State Assembly is currently composed of 27 Democrats and 15 Republicans. Will that split change this year? Maybe. But if it does, it isn’t expected to shift by much. With the exception of a 2014 “red wave” where only 15 of 42 Assembly districts went blue, Democrats have held between 23 and 29 […]
text:
(Photo: Alejandra Rubio/Nevada Current)The Nevada State Assembly is currently composed of 27 Democrats and 15 Republicans. Will that split change this year?
Maybe.
But if it does, it isn’t expected to shift by much. With the exception of a 2014 “red wave” where only 15 of 42 Assembly districts went blue, Democrats have held between 23 and 29 seats since 1996, according to Ballotpedia.
While Democrats are expected to retain control of the chamber, Republicans hope to make a dent in their power. And given a noticeable division between more progressive members of the Assembly Democratic Caucus and more moderate ones, the outcome of swing districts could prove crucial in passing, or defeating, controversial pieces of legislation.
This year’s 42 Assembly races include eight open seats, the lowest number since 2016. Here’s a look at the dozen or so the Nevada Current finds noteworthy, either because they can be considered competitive or because they will bring a new face to Carson City next year.
 Open Seats

Assembly District 2, which includes Summerlin South and southwest neighborhoods in the Las Vegas Valley, is currently represented by Republican Heidi Kasama, who opted to run for Clark County Commission instead of re-election. Hoping to succeed her are Democrat Kamilah Bywaters and Republican Drew Teitelbaum.
Republicans outnumber Democrats in AD2 but the lack of an incumbent, combined with what many hope will be a blue wave more broadly, make the district one to watch.
Bywaters, a Las Vegas native, spent 20 years as a Clark County School District special education teacher before moving into education policy work. In 2024, she ran for the nonpartisan Clark County School Board but lost to Lorena Biassotti.
Teitelbaum, who moved to Las Vegas in 2021, worked on Trump’s 2016 presidential campaign and previously held jobs at the White House and U.S. Departments of Treasury and Homeland Security, according to his campaign website. He currently works in government affairs for Allegiant, the Las Vegas-based airline company.
Teitelbaum had significantly outfundraised Bywaters as of July 1, according to their second quarter campaign finance reports.
Teitelbaum raised $44,350 in the first half of the year and entered July with $94,371 on hand. More than 40% of his fundraising came from Republican Assembly Caucus members, underscoring the significance of the race to the minority party hoping to keep the majority party from obtaining a supermajority.
Bywaters raised $13,515 in the first half of the year, spending nearly all of it and entered July with $370.
Assembly District 9, in the southwestern part of the Las Vegas Valley, is currently represented by Assembly Speaker Steve Yeager, a Democrat. Yeager is not running for re-election.
Democrats make up 30% of registered voters compared to Republican’s 26%. Nonpartisans make up the biggest percentage of the district at 37%.
Republican Erica Neely, who two years ago came within 2 percentage points of defeating Yeager despite being significantly outfundraised, is hoping to flip the district red. Hoping to keep the district blue is Democrat Ryan Hampton.
Neely is a mom of six who says on her campaign website that she was a Democrat until the Great Recession made her a Republican. A homeschool advocate, she unsuccessfully ran for the nonpartisan Clark County School Board in 2022 and placed fourth in the primary.
Hampton is a former union organizer who founded a recovery advocacy network. He draws from his own experience with addiction with painkillers. Two years ago he ran for Assembly in a different district.
Hampton had $34,000 going into the general election while Neely had $29,000.
Assembly District 41, which includes Silverado Ranch and nearby areas in the Las Vegas Valley, features Democrat Vinny Spotleson and Republican Kelly Chapman. The district is currently represented by Democratic Assemblymember Sandra Jauregui, who opted to run for lieutenant governor instead of reelection.
Jauregui’s 2024 reelection race was one of the last to be called by the Associated Press. She retained her seat that year by less than 1 percentage point, or fewer than 300 votes. That makes AD41 one of the biggest opportunities for a red-to-blue flip.
Spotleson is a social studies teacher at Valley High School, which he began post-pandemic after a career in environmental policy and politics, having worked for Democratic U.S. Rep. Dina Titus, Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid, and the Sierra Club Toiyabe Chapter.
Chapman is a third-generation casino employee who now works as a table games pit boss at the Fontainebleau, according to her campaign bio and disclosure forms.
Chapman and her supporters have painted Spotleson as a far left socialist.
Spotleson has openly acknowledged he joined the Las Vegas chapter of the Democratic Socialists of America and agrees with some of their positions, but he does not self identify as a socialist. His campaign has focused more on his experience in energy and environment, including his role in passing legislation to shutter coal-fired power plants and boost rooftop solar.
One attack ad sent to some voters in AD41 compares Spotleson to New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdami and Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic U.S. Senate candidate in Michigan. (Notably, the attack ads were paid for by GSD PAC, whose largest financial contributor is a PAC affiliated with Clark County Education Association, of which Spotleson is a member.)
Chapman had $45,800 on hand going into the general election while Spotleson had $18,400.
Assembly District 29 is an open seat featuring Democrat Alex Pereszlenyi and Republican Joe Ludwig. The Democratic-leaning district, which includes parts of Whitney Ranch and Green Valley in Henderson, is currently represented by Democratic Assemblymember Joe Dalia, who mounted an unsuccessful campaign for the Democratic state treasurer nomination instead of seeking reelection to the Assembly.
Pereszlenyi is a data analyst who, in the competitive three-way Democratic primary earlier this year, garnered support from more progressive groups.
Ludwig describes himself as “a Henderson husband, a political science graduate, and a Reagan conservative who believes government should work like good customer service.”
Pereszlenyi received just over $39,000 in cash and in-kind contributions during the first half of the year and entered July with $1,800 after a competitive primary. Ludwig, who had no primary opponents, raised $6,000 and had just under $2,600 as of July.
Assembly District 23 will see a new representative after incumbent Danielle Gallant, a Republican, opted to run for Nevada State Senate. The district, in Henderson, has been reliably red, making Republican Denise Daniels Fanning the favorite over Democrat Jan Allen Aspelund.
Assembly District 7, considered a safe Democratic district, is poised to elect a not-entirely-new face as its representative. Cameron “C.H.” Miller, who represented AD7 from 2020 to 2024 before unsuccessfully running for Las Vegas City Council, is running for his old seat. 
Democratic Incumbent Tanya Flanagan, who was elected in 2024, opted not to run for reelection and is instead running for Clark County recorder. Now, Miller faces only Libertarian candidate Anthony Scott Willet.
 Incumbents with notable challengers

In Assembly District 35, which includes parts of Mountain’s Edge and Southern Highlands in the Las Vegas Valley, Republican Assemblymember Rebecca Edgeworth is being challenged by Democrat Joe Spica.
Edgeworth is a doctor who has taken moderate positions, including participating in Nevada Forum, a bipartisan effort designed to identify and address issues that matter to voters across the political spectrum. Edgeworth flipped AD35 red in 2024 when it was an open seat.
Spica works at the Cosmopolitan and is a Culinary union member.
Edgeworth has significantly out-fundraised Spica. She reported having $146,000 on hand as of July 1, compared to Spica’s $29,000.
In Assembly District 37, which includes parts of Summerlin and Lone Mountain, Democratic Assemblymember Shea Backus is facing Republican Jill Douglass.
Backus has represented the district since 2018, with each of her races being one of the most competitive in the Assembly. In 2024, Backus won by less than 3 percentage points over Republican David Brog.
Her opponent this year, Douglass, is chair of the Clark County Republican Party. Douglass in 2024 challenged Senate Majority Leader Nicole Cannizzaro.
Backus reported having $139,800. on hand as of July 1, compared to Douglass’s $41,600.
Three other Assembly incumbents facing notable challenges:

Assembly District 4, Republican Lisa Cole is being challenged by Democrat Eileen Eady.
Assembly District 21, Democrat Elaine Marzola is being challenged by Republican Patsy Carvalho and Libertarian Tighe Galvin. Marzola, currently the Speaker pro tem, is expected to be Assembly Speaker if reelected.
Assembly District 12, Democrat Max Carter is being challenged by Republican Nancy Roecker in a rematch of 2024. Roecker came within 1 percentage point of unseating Carter in the district, which includes parts of east Las Vegas and Lake Las Vegas.

 Assembly-elects

Six Democrats have already secured their seats.
Alexis Esparza in Assembly District 1 and Miguel Davila in Assembly District 15 both emerged winners of competitive primaries and face no Democratic, third-party or independent candidates.
Four Democratic incumbents — Assemblymembers Venise Karris (Assembly District 10), Cinthia Moore (Assembly District 11), Erica Mosca (Assembly District 14), and Linda Hunt (Assembly District 17) — also do not have general election opponents and have automatically won their seats.
All six districts are considered safely blue districts where Democrats outnumber Republicans by safe margins.

name: Nevada Current
title: 2 Republicans face off in nonpartisan Las Vegas City Council race
description: Voters narrowed the field of candidates vying to represent Las Vegas City Council Ward 2 during the June primary, now the top two voter-getters will get a rematch in November.  Former Clark County firefighter Luke McCarthy and former Las Vegas Municipal Court judge Shannon Nordstrom will face off again during the general election after neither […]
text:
Luke McCarthy, Shannon Nordsrom. (Candidate photos)Voters narrowed the field of candidates vying to represent Las Vegas City Council Ward 2 during the June primary, now the top two voter-getters will get a rematch in November. 
Former Clark County firefighter Luke McCarthy and former Las Vegas Municipal Court judge Shannon Nordstrom will face off again during the general election after neither candidate received the necessary votes during June’s three-way primary to avoid a runoff. 
McCarthy led the field in June’s primary with about 35% of the vote, while Nordstrom finished second with about 33% – a difference of 355 votes. However, neither cleared the 50% threshold needed to win the seat outright. 
McCarthy entered the last stretch of the campaign with a significant fundraising advantage, raising about $130,000 in the first half of 2026, compared to Nordstrom’s roughly $50,000, according to financial disclosure records. 
Both candidates are registered as Republicans and spoke to the Nevada Current about economic development, housing, homeless services, education, and data centers. 
The winner will replace Councilwoman Kara Kelley, who was appointed nearly two years ago to serve out the remainder of former Las Vegas City Councilwoman Victoria Seaman’s term. As a condition of her appointment, Kelley agreed not to run for a full term in the next election.
The west valley ward, which covers much of Summerlin, is home to more than 116,000 residents. 
The nonpartisan Las Vegas City Council includes the mayor and six members, who each represent a ward. Positions are four-year terms and members are limited to a total of three terms on the City Council.
 Meet the candidates

If elected, McCarthy said his priorities as a member of city council would include public safety, community development, and economic growth. 
McCarthy is a firefighter and has been with the Clark County Fire Department since 2006.
He holds bachelor’s degrees in political science and fire science administration from Trinity College, Connecticut, and the University of Maryland. He earned a master’s degree in crisis and emergency management from UNLV.
McCarthy has been endorsed by Las Vegas City Mayor Shelley Berkeley, Las Vegas Metropolitan Police Sheriff Kevin McMahill, District Attorney Steve Wolfson, John Piro, the assistant public defender with the Clark County Public Defender’s Office, and several veterans groups. 
If elected, Nordstrom said her priorities as a member of city council would include public safety, planning and permitting, and maintaining a business-friendly environment in the City of Las Vegas.
Nordstrom is currently a pro tempore judge with the Las Vegas Justice Court. She earned her Juris Doctor degree in international law and intellectual property from the University of the Pacific McGeorge School of Law. 
Before serving as a temporary judge, Nordstrom was an appointed hearing commissioner and alternate judge with the Las Vegas Municipal Court in 2018. In 2022, she also served a 5-month appointment as interim municipal court judge in Department 6.
Nordstrom has been endorsed by former Ward 2 City Councilwoman Victoria Seaman. 
 Data Centers

Data centers have become a growing issue in Nevada. McCarthy said would support a city-wide moratorium on data centers in the City of Las Vegas, although he noted that the construction of one is unlikely in Ward 2 due to the high costs of land.
“We need to hit a pause button,” McCarthy said. 
Nordstrom said she believes the city council needs to look at each individual proposal and make decisions on a case-by-case basis. She emphasized the importance of reviewing the data center’s potential impact to water, power, environment, and neighborhood impacts. Nordstrom said she would be open to city-wide regulation on data centers.
“I think there’s a lot of misinformation out there, and I don’t pretend to have all the information,” Nordstrom said. “That’s how I would approach it. Getting the facts, getting the input from the relevant parties, and make a merit-based informed decision.
“That would be my job: to be open minded and consider anything,” Nordstrom said. 
 Housing 

McCarthy said the City of Las Vegas should review restrictive building codes — including elevator requirements and parking minimums — to attract more housing construction across all price points.
“Anything above four stories needs an elevator. As a firefighter, I don’t subscribe to that. I don’t think it’s necessary. I think we need to change the code,” McCarthy said. “We need to look at parking. Parking really does affect how much housing can be built on a specific piece of property.”
McCarthy said he supported pausing the ability of institutional investors and hedge funds from purchasing single-family homes in the City of Las Vegas. 
Nordstrom said the City of Las Vegas could tackle housing shortages and affordability by overhauling and simplifying the permitting process so housing developers can navigate permitting with ease and shorten their building timeframe.
“We could find a way to reduce some of the time between each of the individual steps, that would overall reduce the timeline. That will help reduce the base cost of new homes coming online from the get-go,” Norstrom said. “If we could make the timeline more certain, it would help them get projects online faster and lower the cost.”
 Homeless services 

McCarthy said the government should meet the homeless population where they’re at and address mental health and addiction issues through wrap-around services, including pet management. He said he is a fan of Las Vegas’ transitional housing facility Campus for Hope, which is set to open in 2028 near Charleston and Jones boulevards. 
“I don’t think it’s an issue of money. I think it’s an issue of pushing people towards services that already exist, but people need to be pushed towards those services,” McCarthy said. 
As a pro tempore judge, Nordstrom created two specialty programs to connect homeless individuals with services and treatment. Nordstrom said that work gave her insight on how to more effectively address homelessness and public safety.
“Fresh start” traffic and specialty court programs connect offenders on the verge of homelessness or experiencing homelessness with community service providers, and gives offenders a path to vacating fines, fees, and jail time mandated by the court.
“I believe when we’re addressing those that are unhoused, there needs to be a comprehensive approach. It needs to include wraparound services, all the treatments that are needed, such as mental health, substance use, but it needs to be on an individualized basis,” Nordstrom said. 
 Public Safety

Both McCarthy and Nordstrom said they would advocate for increased funding for the Las Vegas Metro Police Department and first responders to further support public safety.
McCarthy emphasized the need for better regulation of electric bicycles and scooters, including ordinances making helmets and eye protection mandatory for riders under 18, similar to the ordinance passed by the City of Henderson in March.
He also stressed the need for comprehensive planning around wildland firefighting in light of federal funding cuts that could hinder wildfire safety in nearby Mount Charlston. 
“The urban-wildland interface has become a growing problem because wildfires are now burning entire communities,” McCarthy said.
Nordstrom said she would like to tackle public safety needs on a neighborhood to neighborhood basis, adding that some areas require better maintenance of streetlights and fire hydrants, others more security enforcement at public parks, and others emergency preparedness. 
“Public safety also means things that the city does, like street lighting, safe parks, traffic design, code enforcement, and addressing any repeat problems before they escalate,” Nordstrom said.
The Las Vegas City Council and Clark County are currently in discussions to terminate or extend the interlocal agreements between the county and the city. One point of contention are “county islands,” which are pockets of Clark County land surrounded by the City of Las Vegas. Las Vegas Fire & Rescue routinely responds to fire and medical service calls in these pockets, which the city has argued is not fairly compensated. 
Both candidates said they believe the agreement needs to be reviewed and updated to benefit both the county and the city. Both candidates favored dispatching the closest available unit, regardless of city or county boundaries.
  Economic Development

McCarthy said he would like to see the City of Las Vegas attract more sporting events, which he said would attract national and international tourism. McCarthy said he would support using tax abatements to lure more sports teams to the city. 
“This past summer we had WrestleMania, which brought in about 60,000 people,” McCarthy said. “We need more of those. I’d love to see more pro sports here.”
Nordstrom said when it comes to maintaining a business-friendly environment in the City of Las Vegas, city officials should be open to new industries and avoid unnecessary regulations that may limit those new industries.
Nordstrom said tourism to the City of Las Vegas could be improved by improving safety and visitor experience around the Fremont Street Experience. 
  Charter schools

Cities and counties were granted the ability to sponsor charter schools in 2023. The City of Las Vegas has not applied to become a charter school authorizer, however, the city has approved one charter school through an alternative route, which it opened in response to the pandemic. 
McCarthy said he believes the City of Las Vegas should consider additional charter schools if applicants demonstrate funding, land availability, a strong proposal, and a successful track record.
“I’d be happy to look at it, and I’d be happy to consider it. Now, that doesn’t mean it’s going to happen,” McCarthy said. 
Nordstrom said the city’s first charter school grew out of necessity, but that she does not think the City of Las Vegas “should be in the business of running schools on a bigger scale.”
“I wouldn’t entertain the possibility of creating any more city charter schools again, unless and until our reserve fund is fully funded, and those vacancies at City Hall have been filled,” Nordstrom said.

name: Michigan Advance
title: When time becomes a barrier to justice for Michigan survivors
description: For survivors of childhood sexual abuse, coming forward can be a complex process shaped by trauma, fear, shame and the circumstances surrounding the abuse. Survivors may not disclose what happened or fully understand their experiences until years or decades later. But the law does not always give survivors that same amount of time. In Michigan, […]
text:
Survivors of Larry Nassar's sexual abuse, along with some of their parents react to the Michigan State University Board of Trustees voting unanimously to release documents the school has withheld from the state attorney general for years for its investigation into Nassar's abuse on Dec. 15, 2023. (Photo: Anna Liz Nichols)For survivors of childhood sexual abuse, coming forward can be a complex process shaped by trauma, fear, shame and the circumstances surrounding the abuse. Survivors may not disclose what happened or fully understand their experiences until years or decades later. But the law does not always give survivors that same amount of time. In Michigan, statutes of limitations can prevent survivors from bringing civil claims based on abuse that occurred years earlier.
The experiences now coming to light at Michigan institutions show why those time limits can be significant. An independent investigation into Interlochen Center for the Arts documented decades of sexual abuse and institutional inaction. More recently, 16 former University of Michigan hockey players who played for the university between 1984 and 2001 filed a lawsuit alleging they experienced sexual abuse that was normalized as team hazing. In both instances, survivors are coming forward about abuse that occurred years or even decades earlier, underscoring why the amount of time survivors have to seek legal accountability matters.
We approach this issue from different but connected perspectives seeking justice for sexual abuse survivors. As one of the survivors of Larry Nassar’s abuse, Erin has not only openly spoken about being a survivor but also spoke to him directly in court during his sentencing. For over two decades, Megan has represented survivors of sexual assault and institutional abuse, including hundreds of survivors in cases involving powerful individuals and institutions. Our experiences have shown us both the importance of giving survivors an opportunity to seek accountability and the reality that reaching that point can take time.
As survivors of abuse come forward, the Justice for Survivors package offers Michigan lawmakers an opportunity to remove longstanding legal barriers that have kept many survivors from seeking legal accountability.
The opportunity to be heard
For me, Erin, having the opportunity to share my experience and seek accountability was an important part of healing and moving forward from my abuse. I grew up playing soccer and dreamed of one day playing at the collegiate level. When I began experiencing severe back pain at 11 years old, I was referred to Nassar for treatment at his office on MSU’s campus. I later came forward as a survivor of his abuse and had the opportunity to stand in a Michigan courtroom and speak about my experience as part of the legal proceedings against him.
That opportunity did not erase what happened to me, but it allowed me to seek accountability and have my experience heard. Speaking out also gave me the chance to be a voice for survivors who may not be ready or able to speak for themselves. While every survivor’s experience is different, each person should have the ability to decide for themselves whether and when they are ready to seek accountability.
Why time matters in childhood sexual abuse cases
I, Megan, have spent decades representing survivors of sexual assault and institutional abuse. I have seen why survivors may need years or even decades to understand what happened to them, process their experiences, and decide whether they are ready to disclose the abuse. Grooming, fear, shame and power imbalances can make that process even more difficult.
The experiences at Interlochen and those described by former University of Michigan hockey players in a recently filed suit demonstrate that reality. In both instances, years or decades separate when the abuse occurred from when survivors were ready to come forward to seek accountability.
When a statute of limitations expires before a survivor is ready to come forward, they can lose the ability to bring a civil claim and pursue justice. The law should reflect the reality of how survivors experience and disclose childhood sexual abuse.
A path forward for Michigan survivors
The Justice for Survivors package seeks to address those barriers. Among its proposed reforms, the legislation would extend the civil statute of limitations for survivors of sexual abuse to age 48, eliminate the civil time limit when an abuser has been criminally convicted, and create a one-year revival window for civil claims that have already expired.
For survivors, that revival window would allow them to bring claims before a court and have the facts considered rather than being barred solely because too much time has passed.
Justice and accountability can look different for every survivor, and not everyone will choose to pursue a civil claim. What matters is that survivors have the opportunity to make that decision for themselves rather than having an expired statute of limitations make it for them.
The experiences now coming to light at Interlochen and within the University of Michigan hockey program demonstrate why that opportunity matters. By passing the Justice for Survivors package, Michigan lawmakers can better align state law with the realities of childhood sexual abuse and give survivors a meaningful opportunity to seek legal accountability.

name: Nevada Current
title: Attorney and justice of the peace vie for open seat in District Court
description: Las Vegas Justice of the Peace Noreen DeMonte and civil attorney Danielle Tarmu are hoping to win an open seat in Clark County District Court Department 28. Judge Ron Israel, who was first elected to the seat in 2010, is not seeking reelection.  The prospect of running for an open seat attracted Tarmu to the […]
text:
Danielle Tarmu, Noreen DeMonte (Candidate photos)Las Vegas Justice of the Peace Noreen DeMonte and civil attorney Danielle Tarmu are hoping to win an open seat in Clark County District Court Department 28.
Judge Ron Israel, who was first elected to the seat in 2010, is not seeking reelection. 
The prospect of running for an open seat attracted Tarmu to the race.
“We have some great judges on the bench. We’re just lacking in civil litigation experience,” says Tarmu, adding she “didn’t want to try to take anybody out. We also perceived my opponent as weaker than other candidates.” 
DeMonte earned her law degree from the Indiana University School of Law and is an 18-year prosecutor. 
She filed to run for Las Vegas Justice Court in 2016 but dropped out of the race.  She was elected to Justice Court in 2022 in a special election and then ran unopposed in 2024. DeMonte presides over a criminal docket. 
“She has no civil experience,” says Tarmu, noting Dept. 28 hears both civil and criminal cases. “Justice Court is not training wheels for District Court. I’ve been emphasizing that more now that I’ve realized some people don’t understand the difference.”
In the Las Vegas Review-Journal’s Judging the Judges 2025 survey, 79% of the 87 attorneys who rated DeMonte said she should be retained. Her highest score was for administrative skills while her lowest was for her legal ability.
DeMonte did not respond to multiple requests for an interview.  
Tarmu is a native Las Vegan. She worked in the service industry before attending UNLV’s Boyd School of Law and graduating in 2009. She says her trial experience, appellate work, and knowledge of civil procedure make her the best candidate. 
She acknowledges she has no experience in criminal law. “I was trying to make my way into the public defender’s office where I did externships, but when I graduated there was a government hiring freeze that lasted for several years.”
Tarmu says she also worked for the Innocence Project while in law school. 
“I think I can learn criminal law quickly, because my background is researching the law.” 
She began her career doing insurance defense cases at Lewis Brisbois Bisgaard & Smith, and later joined Robert Eglet’s firm, an opportunity she calls “a dream come true because I wanted to do trial work and Eglet’s office has a great reputation.”
Tarmu now oversees the law and motion practice at Maier Gutierrez & Associates. 
As of July, the first-time candidate had raised $346,000 and had just under $270,000 on hand. 
Her endorsements include the Clark County Deputy Marshals Association, the AFL-CIO, Southern Nevada Building Trades Union, Nevada Police Officer Association, Juvenile Justice Supervisors Association, and PLAN Action. 
DeMonte raised $122,000 as of July and had just under $97,000 in the bank. 
She is endorsed by a dozen police and firefighter unions; labor organizations including Culinary Local 226, SEIU Nevada, Laborers Local 720, and IATSE 720; and community and political groups such as Veterans in Politics, Hispanics in Politics,and the Asian American Group of Las Vegas. 
The Third Branch PAC, which is funded by the Nevada Republican Club, also endorsed DeMonte in the nonpartisan race.  
Additionally, DeMonte is endorsed by Clark County Sheriff Kevin McMahill, District Attorney Steve Wolfson, Nevada Gaming Commissioner Richard Schonfeld, his law partner David Chesnoff, and attorney Ross Goodman. 
The Current reported earlier this month that DeMonte was endorsed by Hope for Prisoners founder and CEO Jon Ponder, who faces criminal charges for alleged sexual abuse and unauthorized contact with Nevada prison inmates. 
The endorsement has been removed from her website. 
“Given the seriousness of the allegations, the campaign removed his name after his arrest,” says DeMonte’s campaign consultant Tom Letizia. “That reflects no view on the merits of the case or on the judge’s ability to decide it fairly.”
However, DeMonte is not recusing herself from presiding at Ponder’s preliminary hearing Oct. 6, according to court records. 
The Nevada Judicial Canons say a judge “shall disqualify himself or herself in any proceeding in which the judge’s impartiality might reasonably be questioned,” including when the judge “has a personal bias or prejudice concerning a party or a party’s lawyer, or personal knowledge of facts that are in dispute in the proceeding.”
Tarmu says DeMonte’s potential conflict “goes well beyond” Ponder’s endorsement to include the support of McMahill and Wolfson, who served on the board of Hope for Prisoners and were aware of sexual misconduct allegations against Ponder in 2020 and were advised to terminate him, but took no action.
Additionally, she notes that Chesnoff, who represented Ponder at his initial appearance, is hosting a fundraiser for DeMonte and is a significant donor. 
Letizia says that like many judges, DeMonte “had a professional connection to Hope for Prisoners through its community work, and she addressed that on the record so the parties could raise any concerns.”
Tarmu counters the case is unique because of DeMonte’s ties to the prosecution and the defense, and contends the “nature of this case and the alleged victims’ and public’s interests being utterly unrepresented requires her to recuse herself and not simply disclose her conflicts.”
Early voting begins Saturday, Oct. 17.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: Facing removal, SC school board member refutes accusations in first-of-its-kind hearing
description: Darlene Dunmeyer-Roberson denied the charges of sharing confidential information and getting her campaign manager a job raised in a state inspection.
text:
Darlene Dunmeyer-Roberson and her attorney, Rep. Kambrell Garvin, respond to an inspector general's report during a hearing on Statehouse grounds in Columbia, S.C., on Monday, Sept. 28, 2026. (Photo by Skylar Laird/SC Daily Gazette)COLUMBIA — A Charleston County School Board member at the center of potentially multiple state investigations told a panel Monday she didn’t mean to share confidential information or tip the scales to get a contract for her former campaign manager. Whether her answers allow her to stay on the board remains to be seen.
The hearing, which lasted nearly four hours, was the first of its kind under a 2022 state law that gave the governor the ability to remove any school board member who engages in “malfeasance, misfeasance, chronic unexcused absenteeism, conflicts of interest, misconduct in office, or persistent neglect of duty in office.” By law, the governor must give the school board member a chance to be heard before making that decision.
SC governor moves to oust Charleston school board member after report found possible fraud

And Darlene Dunmeyer-Roberson asked for the opportunity to defend herself against the findings of an investigation by the state inspector general’s office.
The report, released last month, said she may have broken multiple laws and board policies. It was sent to the State Law Enforcement Division and Department of Revenue for further investigation.
Monday’s hearing focused on three claims in the report: that Dunmeyer-Roberson breached confidentiality by sharing information from the board’s closed-door meetings, that she violated attorney-client privilege in emails shared with reporters, and that she helped her former campaign manager get a contract with the school district.
As for other issues raised in the report, Dunmeyer-Roberson declined to answer questions about whether she lived in her district, which includes Edisto Island, Hollywood, Johns Island, and Ravenel. Panelists didn’t ask about potential issues with her taxes, and questions about payment for her work as a contractor came up only briefly.
Prior to the 2022 law, no one had the authority — outside of a courtroom — to remove individual school board members. While it gave the governor sole discretion, Gov. Henry McMaster appointed a three-person panel to hear Dunmeyer-Roberson’s case. The three attorneys have until Oct. 5 to give their recommendation on whether McMaster should remove her.
Attorneys Clarence Davis, Thomas Limehouse and Adair Ford Boroughs make up the three-person panel hearing the case of Charleston County School Board member Darlene Dunmeyer-Roberson in Columbia, S.C., on Monday, Sept. 28, 2026. (Photo by Skylar Laird/SC Daily Gazette)
“The governor has a big decision to make, because this has precedent for how we operate and how we handle elected officials moving forward,” said her attorney, Rep. Kambrell Garvin, D-Columbia. “That’s a big responsibility.”
The panel McMaster created consists of Adair Ford Boroughs, South Carolina’s U.S. attorney during the Biden administration; Charleston attorney Thomas Limehouse, McMaster’s in-house attorney for almost nine years; and Columbia attorney Clarence Davis, an assistant U.S. attorney during President H.W. Bush’s tenure.
Sending emails
Dunmeyer-Roberson, in her first extensive public response to the report, didn’t deny sending the emails included in the report. But she said she didn’t mean to anything wrong.
Every time she sent an email with potentially confidential information, she believed that information was already publicly available, she and her attorney said.
The inspector general’s report found 10 instances of Dunmeyer-Roberson sending confidential emails to local reporters and 28 times when she forwarded emails to another of her email addresses.
Several marked with attorney-client privilege came in response to questions she had asked, so she thought she could send them, she said.
The emails Dunmeyer-Roberson sent to reporters had to do with information already published in opinion articles, included on public agendas or posted about on social media, Garvin said.
“Those things were already being discussed publicly,” Garvin said. “They were already being discussed on social media.”
South Carolina Inspector General Brian Lamkin looks on during a hearing for Charleston County School Board member Darlene Dunmeyer-Roberson in Columbia, S.C., on Monday, Sept. 28, 2026. (Photo by Skylar Laird/SC Daily Gazette)
But one board member doesn’t have the right to break that privilege for the entire school board, Boroughs said.
And all of the emails from attorneys included a note at the bottom telling the recipient not to forward them without permission, Limestone said.
Dunmeyer-Roberson said she never paid attention to that.
“I’m going to be honest: I don’t think any board member reads the boilerplate to pay attention to it,” she said.
Presenting the findings of his report, Inspector General Brian Lamkin also raised problems with Dunmeyer-Roberson forwarding emails from her school district-provided email address to her own.
“Once it goes to a vendor email account or a personal email account, you have no oversight,” Lamkin said. “You have no control over it, and you don’t know where it’s going to end up.”
The forwarding was especially concerning, he said, because Dunmeyer-Roberson used the same email address for her education consulting business, which worked with the school district until she decided to run for the board in 2022.
Dunmeyer-Roberson stopped doing work with the board in March of 2022, but she didn’t receive her last payment until June. She never removed herself from the list of vendors, which meant she was technically still sending confidential information to a school vendor, Lamkin said.
Dunmeyer-Roberson objected to the idea that she was sending herself information for business reasons. She happened to use the same email address for both personal matters and business, she said.
She sent herself emails she wanted to save, since the district’s emails automatically delete after a certain amount of time, she said.
Doing so is a common practice among board members, Dunmeyer-Roberson said, adding she didn’t know she was doing anything wrong.
Rep. Kambrell Garvin hands attorney Adair Boroughs a copy of a letter in Columbia, S.C., on Monday, Sept. 28, 2026. (Photo by Skylar Laird/SC Daily Gazette)
“They’re emails about governance matters, emails about things that I would need to refer to, but it’s nothing that could harm the district,” she said.
Garvin also pointed to a mention in the report that a grand jury indicted former board member Kevin Hollinshead on charges of bribery, wire fraud and bank fraud. The federal indictment accuses Hollinshead, who resigned in March, of sharing confidential information with another, unnamed board member.
But the panel can’t say for certain that person is Dunmeyer-Roberson, Garvin said.
“Before someone can be held responsible for making an improper disclosure, the evidence must first establish that she was the person who made it,” Garvin said. “Here, that foundational connection is missing.”
Conflict of interest
Dunmeyer-Roberson admitted she sent an email introducing her former campaign manager, Aaron White, to a principal in the district. But that’s not why White got a contract with the district to help mentor students, she said.
“An introduction is not a procurement decision,” Garvin said.
White, who addressed the panel virtually, said he didn’t talk to Dunmeyer-Roberson about his business or contract. The two of them spoke about how his cousin, a student at the high school, had been killed in a shooting several days earlier, and Dunmeyer-Roberson offered to introduce White to the school’s principal to talk about ways of helping students, White said.
Dunmeyer-Roberson was not involved in the process of getting the contract for White’s newly established consulting business, she said.
But Lamkin said she had influence over the decision even if she never explicitly told anyone to hire White.
The presence of a board member on an email with a principal might have created pressure for the principal to give White a contract, Lamkin said.
Inspector General Brian Lamkin lays out details from his report on a Charleston County School Board member in Columbia, S.C., on Monday, Sept. 28, 2026. (Photo by Skylar Laird/SC Daily Gazette)
“The effect, the chilling effect, is, ‘If I don’t do this, I’m going to get my boss in trouble,’” he said. “You don’t have to give a directive to do that. It’s just the implied presence of your position as a board trustee.”
Garvin cautioned the panel about making such a determination.
Saying an elected official can’t make any introductions would tie the hands of everyone elected in the state, said Garvin, a legislator since 2018.
“If we’re going to get into the business of penalizing elected officials for doing their jobs, that’s problematic,” he said. “I mean, from the top to the bottom, from the Statehouse to the county council to the school board, you’re going to have a lot of problems.”
The report raised other issues with White’s contract. School officials never did any background checks of his nonprofit, Circle of Life Foundation. And in an email included in the report, a district employee questioned whether Circle of Life offered “anything unique” that existing staff couldn’t do.
Like other issues raised in the report, Garvin said, those are less about Dunmeyer-Roberson and more about a culture at Charleston County School District that needs changing.
The report “does not show that there is a Darlene Dunmeyer-Roberson problem,” Garvin said. “It shows that the problems potentially are greater and that there needs to be a school board issue as a whole.”
