name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: Some Idaho officials say proposed nuclear waste shipments could threaten Eastern Snake Plain Aquifer
description: Editor’s Note: This is the third and final installment of a three-part Idaho Capital Sun series examining a proposal to bring a new Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus to Idaho. Part one focused on Gov. Brad Little’s role in negotiations and his priorities for Idaho. Part two focused on Idaho state legislators who support bringing the […]
text:
A shipment of transuranic radioactive waste leaves the Idaho National Laboratory en route to the Waste Isolation Pilot Plant for permanent disposal in New Mexico in 2009. During the expedited waste removal funded by more than $22 million from the American Recovery and Reinvestment Act, the site's workers safely retrieved, treated, and shipped close to 4,800 cubic meters of radioactive waste — which would fill two Olympic swimming pools — from the Cold War to permanent disposal facilities. (Photo courtesy of the U.S. Department of Energy)Editor’s Note: This is the third and final installment of a three-part Idaho Capital Sun series examining a proposal to bring a new Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus to Idaho. Part one focused on Gov. Brad Little’s role in negotiations and his priorities for Idaho. Part two focused on Idaho state legislators who support bringing the project to the state.
Accepting a deal with the U.S. Department of Energy to bring a new Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus to Idaho could force the state to accept more than 30,000 tons of spent nuclear fuel and radioactive waste, a retired nuclear manager and a current state legislator told the Idaho Capital Sun. 
“When I read the state’s proposal it was like, wait a second. This is kind of a bait and switch,” said Joel Case, a retired federal project manager who worked for the U.S. Department of Energy and at Idaho National Laboratory. 
In nuclear campus talks, Idaho Gov. Brad Little says protecting Snake aquifer is ‘nonnegotiable’ 

In July, Department of Energy officials announced Idaho was one of five states (the list has since grown to six) selected as a finalist to host a new Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus.
Hosting a campus could create thousands of jobs and attract millions or billions of dollars in investment and revenue, Department of Energy officials and supporters say. 
But the deal comes with a catch. The states selected to host an innovation campus must agree to accept shipments of spent nuclear fuel and radioactive waste from other states, according to a memorandum of understanding Idaho Gov. Brad Little signed in July.
 State officials fought for years to keep out-of-state nuclear waste from entering Idaho

Case has a master’s degree in nuclear engineering, came to Idaho in 1981 and retired in 2022. He held various jobs during his career, and a big part of his work involved implementing the 1995 Settlement Agreement that was reached between Idaho, the Department of Energy and the U.S. Navy. 
The U.S. has about 97,000 metric tons of spent nuclear fuel, a Department of Energy official told the Sun last week. If three states are selected as innovation campus sites and Idaho is one of them, Case said that could mean that about 33,000 metric tons of spent commercial fuel could be shipped to Idaho if all three states split the waste evenly. 
“We don’t need to accept 33,000 metric tons of commercial fuel,” Case said. “That was the whole idea of the Settlement Agreement (with the federal government) that precludes this state from becoming the de facto disposal and storage site for commercial nuclear fuel.”
State legislators make the case for a Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus in Idaho

Case was referencing the 1995 Settlement Agreement that the late former Gov. Phil Batt, a Republican, signed after Idaho sued the federal government to prevent the state from becoming the country’s nuclear waste dumping ground. That agreement, which is commonly referred to as the Batt Agreement, limits the amount of spent nuclear fuel that can be shipped to Idaho and establishes timelines for cleaning up and removing the waste that is here. 
Case says Idaho officials can continue to support Idaho National Laboratory and its work without accepting the shipments of thousands of tons of spent nuclear fuel that would come from the innovation campus. 
In these discussions, Case thinks Idaho should leverage the Settlement Agreement and not accept all the spent nuclear fuel.
“I wouldn’t trust the government, and I used to work for them,” Case said. “We made lots of promises, and even some of the Settlement Agreement milestones we haven’t hit.”
The Eastern Snake Plain Aquifer is outlined in orange of this map of Washington, Oregon and Idaho. (Map courtesy of the U.S. Geological Survey)
Case said it is unclear exactly what Idaho would receive in terms of benefits from an innovation campus, and he said the memorandum of understanding the state signed does not promise any federal funding.
Case said Idaho would need new facilities to complete the work of an innovation campus, and it is not clear who would pay for those facilities. 
Idaho National Laboratory officials declined to comment for the Idaho Capital Sun’s series on the proposed new Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus. 
On Sept. 23, Idaho Gov. Brad Little said storing spent nuclear fuel and nuclear waste above the Eastern Snake Plain Aquifer was “a nonstarter.” The governor also said officials have not identified a site yet in Idaho where the spent fuel and radioactive waste would be stored. 
The Eastern Snake Plain Aquifer is considered the lifeblood of Idaho. It provides drinking water for Idaho families and irrigation water for Idaho farmers. 
 Boise legislator said protecting Idaho from nuclear waste is bipartisan issue 

Idaho state Rep. Monica Church, D-Boise, said Idahoans fought for decades to win guarantees from the federal government about nuclear waste storage and disposal, and the state should not give those protections up based on vague promises of jobs and revenue made by the federal government.
Rep. Monica Church, D-Boise, speaks to reporters at a post-State of the State Address press conference on Jan. 12, 2026, at the Idaho Capitol in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)
Church is the granddaughter of the late former Idaho Gov. Cecil Andrus, a Democrat who sued the federal government in 1991 and threatened to use the Idaho State Police to block shipments of nuclear waste from coming into Idaho.  
“Cec Adrus was famous for saying the Idaho economy would collapse the first time somebody found radiation in an Idaho potato,” Church said. “The Settlement Agreement has protected us from doing things that could jeopardize the quality of our water. It’s also the most Idaho thing I can think of. We have a mechanism to hold sovereignty over the federal government. I don’t know of anything more Idaho than having a tool in your toolbelt to stick it to the feds.”
Church said protecting Idaho’s people, water and environment from nuclear waste has been a bipartisan issue for decades.
Andrus’s Republican successor, Batt, continued Andrus’ fight and signed the 1995 Settlement Agreement with the federal government. 
The agreement includes major deadlines in 2035. Little, Church and other state officials told the Idaho Capital Sun the U.S. Department of Energy is not on track to meet those deadlines. 
State Sen. Dave Lent, R-Idaho Falls, works from the Senate floor on March 10, 2025, at the Idaho Capitol Building in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)
Church also said the innovation campus deal could require Idaho to accept about 33,000 tons of spent nuclear fuel. She said it would be “bonkers” for any Idaho official to throw out or weaken the 1995 Settlement Agreement’s protections. 
Idaho state Sen. Dave Lent, a Republican who supports bringing a Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus to Idaho and believes Idaho National Laboratory could do the work safely, said the amount of spent nuclear fuel coming to Idaho could correspond to one football field covered 30 feet high.
“If you look at all of the aspects, and that includes the workforce, the location, facilities and expertise, we are a standout (potential host site) there,” Lent said in an interview. “Our challenge is going to be helping our citizenry understand what high level waste is and how it can be handled safely.”
 Retired Idaho Supreme Court justice says state should leverage nuclear waste protections in 1995 Settlement Agreement 

Jim Jones, who is a retired Idaho Supreme Court chief justice and former state attorney general, said a Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus could work, be undertaken safely and provide many benefits to Idahoans. 
But Jones said he is cornered about the rapid pace at which the project appears to be moving. For example, the Request for Information Response that Little signed in March references an “ambitious schedule in months rather than decades” to bring the initial capabilities of a Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus online in 2027.
Jones has concerns about whether Idahoans’ health, the environment, electric utility customers and water users will be protected if the deal is rushed or one-sided.
Jim Jones (Photo courtesy of Jim Jones)
“In my book, there are more questions than there are answers,” Jones said. “We are talking about the East Snake River Plain, which has a fractured underbelly with all that basalt. It’s close to the Yellowstone Caldera, and it is earthquake prone. These are some of the technical answers that I think that have to be answered before we can truly understand what we are getting into.”
Jones also doesn’t want a sense or urgency or a desire to reap financial benefits to cause Idaho elected officials to weaken the 1995 Settlement Agreement. 
“That agreement is unique in the county,” Jones said. “It is the only binding agreement of its kind the Department of Energy has entered into with regard to the nuclear waste issue, and it gives the state some substantial leverage.”
He said the Settlement Agreement should be left in place because it legally protects Idaho from becoming “a permanent waste repository” and would “prevent any claims of federal preemption with regard to data center issues or the acquisition of additional water” needed to carry out the project.
If Idaho is serious about bringing a Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus to the state, Jones said state officials immediately should begin conducting a series of public hearings and public comment sessions across the state, where officials would take questions, describe the plan in detail and lay out guarantees to protect Idaho’s people, aquifer and environment. 
 



  As innovation campuses move forward, independent oversight agency says its faces most significant access challenges in history 

As the U.S. Department of Energy seeks an accelerated schedule to deploy the initial capabilities of a Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus, an independent oversight agency of the U.S. government that provides monitoring of Department of Energy nuclear sites said it is facing the most significant access challenges in the agency’s 36-year history.
In a July 10 letter to Congress, officials with the Defense Nuclear Facilities Safety Board said the agency has been unable to conduct some safety reviews after experiencing access denials from the U.S. Department of Energy, including revocations of longstanding access to safety information provided to the agency’s staff. 
Additionally, officials with the Defense Nuclear Facilities Safety Board said they have been unable to post all of their technical documents and reports while they wait for the U.S. Department of Energy to review the documents for safety. 
Finally, the Defense Nuclear Facilities Safety Board itself is unable to meet because for the first time in the agency’s 36-year history, it is down to one board member. Because the board only has one member, it cannot establish a quorum to conduct a meeting or issue formal recommendations as it waits for appointments to be made by the president of the United States. 
“The Board is concerned that this significant level of access denial and limitation is occurring simultaneously with a considerable increase in production at defense nuclear facilities and regulatory change,” Defense Nuclear Facilities Safety Board member Patricia L. Lee wrote in the July 10 letter to Congress. 
Defense Nuclear Facilities Safety Board Technical Director Jonathan W. Plaue told the Sun it is unclear whether the board would provide oversight or monitoring of Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campuses. The board does currently provide environmental monitoring at Idaho National Laboratory. 
So far, the changes haven’t resulted in an accident or safety issue, Plaue said, but he is worried that speeding up timeliness, reducing independent oversight and revising safety requirements could create a problem at some point. 
“I wouldn’t expect it to happen on Day One,” Plaue said. “This will happen with time.”

title: Federal judge upholds Idaho law that bans vaccine, medical treatment requirements in daycares
description: An Idaho judge dismissed a lawsuit from a Boise daycare and parents that sought to block enforcement of a state law that bans daycares from requiring vaccines or medical treatment.  The lawsuit claimed that the Idaho Medical Freedom Act was unconstitutionally vague, arguing its language bans a range of routine health protections — including handwashing […]
text:
Susan Hinchcliffe, a volunteer with the Corrales Fire Department, gives Rachel Ralya’s 14-month old son a Moderna COVID-19 vaccine on June 23, 2022, following the FDA authorization of the vaccine for children ages 6 months to 5 years old. (Shelby Wyatt/Source NM)An Idaho judge dismissed a lawsuit from a Boise daycare and parents that sought to block enforcement of a state law that bans daycares from requiring vaccines or medical treatment. 
The lawsuit claimed that the Idaho Medical Freedom Act was unconstitutionally vague, arguing its language bans a range of routine health protections — including handwashing and sending home sick kids. But last week, Chief U.S. District Judge for the District of Idaho Amanda K. Brailsford granted Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador’s request to dismiss the lawsuit, which was brought by Le Soleil Child Care LLC, and three parents whose kids attend the daycare or hope to.
In her ruling, the federal judge wrote she agreed with Labrador’s interpretation of the law’s definition of “medical interventions,” writing that they refer to health actions that are “medical in nature.” 
“The (Idaho Medical Freedom Act) plainly and unambiguously sets out a standard of prohibited conduct that gives a person of ordinary intelligence fair notice of what is prohibited,” Brailsford wrote, ruling that the daycare didn’t show that the state law was unconstitutionally vague. 
“The Court agrees with the AG that Le Soleil is free to promote its beliefs and values about public health and vaccinations …” the judge wrote. “The only thing the (Idaho Medical Freedom Act) prevents is Le Soleil requiring that only vaccinated students hear those values.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
 AG praises court ruling. Parents, daycare consider appealing, lawyer says.

The ruling upholds a state law that bans daycares, businesses, governments and schools from mandating vaccines or “medical interventions,” which are defined as: “a medical procedure, treatment, device, drug injection, medication, or medical action taken to diagnose, prevent, or cure a disease or alter the health or biological function of a person.”
In a statement, Labrador said he was pleased with the court’s decision.
“Parents make medical decisions for their children. A daycare does not,” Labrador said in a statement. “The Legislature protected that choice in the Medical Freedom Act, and the court upheld it. Daycares can tell parents what they believe about vaccines and health, but they cannot turn a child away because of a parent’s medical decision. That decision belongs to families, and I’m pleased the court agreed.”



Need to get in touch?
Have a news tip?


CONTACT US



Idaho has the lowest rate of kindergartners — nearly four out of every five — who are reportedly up to date on their measles vaccine, according to Centers for Disease Control and Prevention data. The state has reported 10 measles cases this year, as nearby states experience outbreaks. 
In a statement, Andrea Carone, an attorney for the daycare and parents who sued, wrote that the plaintiffs are considering appealing to the U.S. 9th Circuit Court of Appeals.
“Our clients are obviously disappointed by the district court’s ruling and the narrow manner in which it interpreted the right at issue,” Carone said. “The Idaho Medical Freedom Act places parents like our individual clients and daycares like Le Soleil in the untenable position of being unable to take reasonable steps to protect their children or children in their care from childhood diseases that vaccines shield against. This is a clear public health issue that we must rely, in the near term, on the Idaho Legislature to address and correct.”
 The daycare’s lawsuit isn’t the first concern that the bill could prevent sending home sick kids

The lawsuit’s arguments echoed a heated debate among lawmakers over the 2025 bill. 
Republican Idaho Gov. Brad Little vetoed an earlier version of it over concerns that it could prevent schools from sending home sick kids. But in April, his spokesperson said the revised bill that the governor signed into law “does not jeopardize the ability of public schools or daycares to send home children sick with contagious conditions.”
Labrador, also a Republican, urged lawmakers to override the governor’s veto. A veto override attempt by the Senate failed. 
In debating the revised bill, several Republican lawmakers worried that it would stop businesses from sending home sick employees or customers. 
The bill’s author, Health Freedom Defense Fund President Leslie Manookian, wants Idaho’s law to become a national model for similar laws, ProPublica reported.

description: Ahead of the 2026 general election, Idaho election officials mailed out hundreds of thousands of informational pamphlets to households across the state. The voter pamphlet includes information about the range of questions on[...]
text:
A voter casts her ballot during the May 19, 2026, primary election at Westside Elementary School in Idaho Falls. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)Ahead of the 2026 general election, Idaho election officials mailed out hundreds of thousands of informational pamphlets to households across the state.
The state’s official voter pamphlet has already started to arrive at some households, the Idaho Secretary of State’s Office announced.
[Voter Guide: 2026 primary election Voter Guide: Dates to know, how-to instructions and candidate surveys for Idaho’s top contested primaries.]
The voter pamphlet includes information about the range of questions on the ballot — such as Proposition 1, a ballot initiative that would end the state’s abortion ban and establish reproductive rights; a proposed constitutional amendment that would only allow the Legislature to legalize drugs, such as marijuana; a constitutional amendment that would declare English as the state’s official language; and an advisory question that solicits a public vote to declare a state gun. That’s along with information about key upcoming election dates, voting options and voter registration. (You can also find information about those issues, along with races for statewide constitutional offices and in select legislative districts, in the Idaho Capital Sun’s voter guide.)
“Election season is underway,” Secretary of State Phil McGrane, a Republican running for re-election, said in a statement. “Every household in Idaho can expect to receive a Voter Pamphlet with the information you need to be ready to vote in November. This special America 250 edition includes some fun nods to our history as we celebrate 250 years of America and make our mark on the future of our state. Make a plan, get registered, and vote!”
To view the pamphlet online and access it in Spanish or an audio format, visit VoteIdaho.gov, a website run by the Secretary of State’s Office. That’s also where voters can see what their ballot will look like, along with other election resources.
The voter pamphlet does not include information about candidates. In 2023 and 2024, the Idaho Legislature did not approve McGrane’s proposed bill to replace the voter pamphlet with a voter guide, which would include information about candidates. According to a 2024 poll in Boise State University’s Idaho Public Policy Survey, 78% of Idahoans favored a state-issued voter guide.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: New center aims to train Alabamians on parole or probation for manufacturing jobs
description: A new facility at a Perry County education center for people on parole and probation aims to train more people for manufacturing jobs and help them understand the situations they will find with employers. The facility at the Perry County Probation and Parole Re-Entry Program Center, which opened last week, will expand welding and heavy […]
text:
Cam Ward, director of the Alabama Bureau of Pardons and Paroles speaks at the opening of a new facility last week at Perry County PREP Center. He said the facility will allow staff to have more opportunities to train people in welding and in operating heavy equipment during bad weather. (Courtesy of Alabama Bureau of Pardons and Paroles)A new facility at a Perry County education center for people on parole and probation aims to train more people for manufacturing jobs and help them understand the situations they will find with employers.
The facility at the Perry County Probation and Parole Re-Entry Program Center, which opened last week, will expand welding and heavy machinery training, part of a broader program to provide training to those on parole or probation in fields where the state sees labor shortages.
“We want to make sure that before they leave us and go back out into society, that we really fine-tune their skills, getting them ready for what will be expected in the world of work,” said David Walters, president of J.F. Ingram State Technical College, which is operating the facility in partnership with the Alabama Bureau of Pardons and Paroles.
Job training is a part of Re-Entry 2030, a rehabilitation program that aims to reduce recidivism in the state.
“The odds of them going back to prison or jail after they get that employment drop dramatically,” said Cam Ward, the director of ABPP, who established Re-Entry 2030.
Walters also said that the facility is meant to increase capacity. Ingram State offers welding, but most of the training is done in a welding box that does not mimic what they will encounter on the job.
“I talked to someone recently who is a welder, and he said he was on his back for eight hours welding, and another gentleman talked about how he welds up on beams 50 or 60 feet or more above the ground,” Walters said. “And he has got people welding above him and people welding below him. So, we try to make sure we emulate that, so we will have scaffolding that will give them different looks of how to weld and do that properly to meet the requirements for the employer on the job site.”
Ingram State also offers a program to train people to work with heavy machinery, but only when the environment is ideal for it. The facility will allow staff to expand the training opportunities.
Staff had been working with people on heavy equipment outside in the elements and had to suspend the training when during bad weather. The facility will address that barrier.
“This facility, we will be able to keep the training going, it doesn’t matter what is going on outside,” Walters said. “Rain, cold or hot weather, whatever it is, we are still able to do the training.”
Most of the area of the building will be barren, dirt floor, for students to practice using heavy machinery such as skid steers, backhoes and even a small bulldozer.
The goal is to train people to operate such equipment so they can be placed on construction sites to help build the infrastructure in the state.
Walters said that businesses throughout the state continue to face a shortage of workers with specific sets of vocational skills. Alabama’s workforce participation rate has lagged the national average for decades.
Alabama had a seasonally adjusted workforce participation rate of 56.8% in August of this year, according to data from the St. Louis Federal Reserve . That is the fourth-lowest among states in the country, with only Mississippi at 54.7%, New Mexico at 56.7% and West Virginia at 53.8% ranked lower.
Walters and Ward said these skills will be sought as the number of jobs that require welding will continue to expand.
Walters said ABPP, as well as Ingram State are partners in a grant received by the Alabama Department of Workforce that totaled $4 million to provide job training for people with a criminal history and recruit them to skilled labor jobs, including shipbuilding.
According to a news release from earlier this month, the grant will enroll 550 adults who are at least 25 years old in Mobile and Baldwin counties in job training for the next 42 months.
One company, Austal USA, received a contract worth $450 million from General Dynamics Electric Boat to expand its facilities to build the components that will be part of a nuclear submarine for the U.S. Navy. It is recruiting people to help with that.
“Those components are very important, so we need to make sure we have got people who can do that,” Walters said. “So, I felt like the justice-involved population is already a population with some barriers, and they are sometimes overlooked for job opportunities, so we wanted to reach out and show them what we do here at Ingram.”

title: Nashville Democrat sues Tennessee lieutenant governor over committee suspension, other restrictions
description: A Tennessee Democratic state senator has sued the chamber leader over her committee reassignment and travel reimbursement restrictions implemented after she protested from the Senate Floor during a recent special session to redraw the state’s U.S. House map. During a special legislative session in May to redraw and gerrymander Tennessee’s U.S. congressional[...]
text:
State Sen. Charlane Oliver, was suspended from a committee and placed under reimbursement restrictions for unfurling a banner during the May special session to redraw Tennessee's U.S. House map. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)A Tennessee Democratic state senator has sued the chamber leader over her committee reassignment and travel reimbursement restrictions implemented after she protested from the Senate Floor during a recent special session to redraw the state’s U.S. House map.
During a special legislative session in May to redraw and gerrymander Tennessee’s U.S. congressional map so Republicans could net an extra seat in this year’s midterm election ​State Sen. Charlane Oliver of Nashville stood on her desk and unfurled a banner in protest.​Republican lawmakers divided the predominantly Black city of Memphis across three congressional seats to create a map in which the party is favored to win all nine of Tennessee’s U.S. House districts.
​Lt. Gov. Randy McNally, an Oak Ridge Republican and also Senate speaker, suspended Oliver from the Government Operations Committee following the session and reassigned her to the less powerful State and Local Government Committee Oliver is also not allowed to receive a per diem for legislative work and is not allowed to use state funds to attend legislative conferences.
​“When I stood on my Senate desk, I did it because the legislature swiftly moved to silence the voices of Black Tennesseans,” said Oliver in a news release. “An injustice of that magnitude demanded an equally urgent response. As the only Black senator representing Nashville, I carry the voices of people who have been pushed to the margins of this state’s policies for generations.”
​The Lookout reached out to a spokesperson for McNally, and he didn’t respond by the time of publication.
​Tennessee lawmakers implemented a midcycle redistricting after the U.S. Supreme Court ruled in April that states with a history of racial discrimination were no longer required to draw majority-minority U.S. House seats.
Democrats face uphill battle in winning any Tennessee U.S. House race

​A seat that included all of Memphis was Tennessee’s last majority-minority district, after Republicans broke up Nashville’s congressional seat in the 2022 redistricting cycle.
​Before 2022, Republicans held a 7-2 advantage over the Democratic Party in Tennessee’s congressional map. The GOP upped its advantage after 2022 to 8-1 and is now expected to win all nine, as each district is a seat President Donald Trump won by at least 20 percentage points.
​Trump won Tennessee in 2024, with Democratic Vice President Kamala Harris winning around 35% of the vote.
​The Campaign Legal Center is representing Oliver in the lawsuit, and she’s a co-plaintiff with four of her constituents.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Chattanooga goes head to head with state attorney over control of airport board
description: The Tennessee Attorney General’s Office argued Monday that politics shouldn’t be considered in deciding whether the Chattanooga airport authority should be run by a locally-appointed board or a board appointed by state officials under a new law. The state’s attorney and legal counsel for the new state-appointed board also said in a hearing before a […]
text:
Lawyers with the the Tennessee Attorney General's office are arguing the City of Chattanooga lacks standing to challenge a state-appointed airport authority.  (Photo: Chattanooga Airport)The Tennessee Attorney General’s Office argued Monday that politics shouldn’t be considered in deciding whether the Chattanooga airport authority should be run by a locally-appointed board or a board appointed by state officials under a new law.
The state’s attorney and legal counsel for the new state-appointed board also said in a hearing before a three-judge panel that the entity in charge of the Chattanooga airport never really changed when the law took effect July 1 enabling the government and Senate and House speakers to appoint a majority of board members and removing members appointed by the mayor.
The state is asking the Hamilton County Chancery Court panel to dismiss a lawsuit filed by Chattanooga and the former airport authority members in the city’s effort to reverse an airport board takeover. 

SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 
The panel led by Hamilton County Chancellor Jeff Atherton is set to rule on the request as the city seeks a temporary injunction to overturn the state-appointed board. 
The court denied the state’s motion to withdraw the Chattanooga airport authority as a plaintiff in the suit and declined to pause the court proceedings. The new state-appointed board voted this summer to remove itself from the lawsuit. A separate federal proceeding before the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit is pending.
During arguments, Atherton raised the question of whether the airport conflict is “purely an attempt” by a “red legislature to intrude on blue cities.”
But Assistant Attorney General Tyler Sanders argued that such a scenario is a political question and not a factor for the court to address.
Lawmakers passed a measure this year giving state leaders the majority of appointments to boards that oversee airports in Nashville, Chattanooga, Memphis, Knoxville and Tri-Cities. The legislation passed after courts ruled a previous state effort to take over appointments to the Nashville airport authority was unconstitutional.
Chattanooga and Nashville, which separately sued the state over control of its airport authority, say federal law prevents the Federal Aviation Administration from recognizing the new boards until the legal dispute over changing the entity that operates the airports is resolved. They also say it’s a violation of the separation of powers between state and local governments, unfairly targeting them.
Chattanooga state-appointed airport board withdraws from lawsuit

Sanders and the new board’s attorney, former federal judge Sandy Mattice, said Chattanooga can show no harm in the state-controlled appointments to the board, noting that the Federal Aviation Administration is confident in the new state-appointed board based on a recent grant for new runway design at the facility.
They also said the city and former airport authority have no standing to sue the state, which granted Chattanooga the ability to set up the airport authority. Sanders told the judicial panel the power to appoint airport board members comes from the legislature and that the Chattanooga Metropolitan Airport Authority is a subdivision of state government, as are all local government entities.
In addition to Atherton’s question, Circuit Court Judge Joseph “Woody” Woodruff of Williamson County raised a hypothetical situation about what would happen if the “People’s Liberation Army of Chattanooga stormed the airport, ousted the board, took over the conference room, declared themselves the lawful incumbents of the metropolitan authority.” By the state’s argument, he said, the controlling entity wouldn’t change even though the people trying to “occupy the premises and run the show would be unlawful.”
Sanders agreed with that scenario.
The Republican-led legislature tried to commandeer Nashville’s airport authority, sports authority, fairgrounds board and Metro Council membership three years ago after the Metro Council declined to bring the Republican National Convention to the city. Since then, lawmakers and the Nashville leaders have been in a political tussle.
Chattanooga attorney John Konvalinka, counsel for the former airport board, countered the state argument by saying the takeover preempts the mayor’s ability to appoint all of the authority members, based on the law the legislature approved four decades ago.
Konvalinka also said the FAA must approve a change in “ownership” or “governance” of the airport when it is disputed. 
In addition, Chattanooga’s attorney said the city sold the airport property to the airport board and that removal of the city-appointed board puts that agreement in jeopardy and could cost the city financially. He added that the contract contains a “reversion” clause that could send the property back to Chattanooga, which has no contract with the state.
Ultimately, the city believes it has the right to make the appointments, based on the state law, he said.

title: Colorado voters could see more poll monitors during the midterm election
description: Common Cause Colorado and its partners are preparing to expand a longstanding, nonpartisan election protection program during the midterm election with around 1,000 volunteer poll monitors, up from around 300 in 2024. “These are neighbors and folks of all political affiliations who are united around one purpose: to support their neighbors to vote, to watchdo[...]
text:
People cast general election ballots at the Adams County Human Services Center on Nov. 5, 2024. (Photo by Andrew Fraieli for Colorado Newsline)Common Cause Colorado and its partners are preparing to expand a longstanding, nonpartisan election protection program during the midterm election with around 1,000 volunteer poll monitors, up from around 300 in 2024.
“These are neighbors and folks of all political affiliations who are united around one purpose: to support their neighbors to vote, to watchdog the process, keep the vibes positive and ensure that voters have the help they need at the polls,” Aly Belknap, executive director of Colorado Common Cause, said.
“The function of a poll monitor is to provide a culture of safety and support at the polls, and this is all part of preventing intimidation and political violence,” she said.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The effort is part of the Election Protection Coalition, which also includes Disability Justice, formerly known as Disability Law Colorado, Mi Familia Vota, the League of Women Voters Colorado and the Colorado Lawyers Committee. Election observers and poll monitors are normal parts of American elections.
The expanded volunteer cohort comes as President Donald Trump and his administration try to interfere with local election administration and cast doubt on whether election results, especially in vote-by-mail states like Colorado, are trustworthy. The U.S. Supreme Court blocked Trump’s bid to restrict mail-in ballots in November.
“We have to look at the overall intentions and rhetoric and political motivations of this president, which has consistently been to terrify voters and to create the impression that there will be law enforcement policing the process of being a voter,” Belknap said. “The concern we have at this time is just the level of fear for folks as they think about going to the polls this year.”
The U.S. Department of Justice also has plans to send 1,000 monitors across the country to watch election activity.



Quotation







We have to look at the overall intentions and rhetoric and political motivations of this president, which has consistently been to terrify voters and to create the impression that there will be law enforcement policing the process of being a voter.


– Aly Belknap, Common Cause Colorado executive director


The coalition plans to respond with a “clear moral voice against authoritarian advances” that could be considered intimidation or interference with Colorado’s elections.
But Belknap said the goal for poll monitors is to have a “boring shift,” ask voters about their experience and report data such as a polling location’s accessibility and crowd size. They can report any issues to a nonpartisan hotline staffed with legal experts, and the response could vary from documenting whatever hiccup might occur, sending lawyers to a polling site or even dispatching faith leaders to diffuse tension.
The volunteers will also be trained to observe and report U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement activity. Common Cause, Latino advocacy groups and the city of Denver sued the Department of Homeland Security and the Department of Justice in September to stop any deployment of federal law enforcement, including ICE, to polling places. Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin has said that ICE officers could conduct routine enforcement operations near polling locations. During California’s primary elections this year, ICE vehicles were spotted in a parking lot at a Ventura County voting center, raising alarm about voter intimidation.
Volunteers in Colorado will be “visible at the polls to support voters if there were to be the threat of ICE nearby,” Belknap said. But she also said there’s no reason right now to expect ICE agents at Colorado voting centers.
“We know that fear is the point. If Trump can make our communities fearful and it keeps people at home and scared to participate, he is accomplishing his goal,” Belknap said. “And so our job is to support our communities to vote and participate without fear.”
County clerks can start mailing ballots to voters Firday, and drop boxes will open around the state Oct. 12. Election Day is Nov. 3. Voters can check their registration and find answers to many common questions at GoVoteColorado.com.

 Catching Our Eye

• The Ohio Trump rally and the Haitian student’s funeral. The Cincinnati Enquirer’s Patricia Gallagher Newberry reports, “Trump Ohio visit to coincide with funeral for Haitian college student.”
The funeral for a Haitian student who reportedly took his own life will be Oct. 3 in Springfield. Pierre Damas Bel’s death has become a flashpoint in the debate over the Trump administration’s immigration enforcement policies.
Later on Oct. 3, President Trump is scheduled to attend a political rally about 25 miles away from Springfield.
• Trump dismantling LGBTQ discrimination protections. The Hill reports, “Education Department formally rescinds Title IX protections for LGBTQ students.”
The Education Department announced Monday it has formally rescinded the Biden-era Title IX interpretation that gave sex-based discrimination protections to students on the basis of sexual orientation and gender identity.
Schools now must go back to the Title IX code as held under the previous Trump administration in 2020, which the department says will protect women’s sports.
• Standing with Trump on Iran. The Statehouse News Bureau’s Karen Kasler reports, “Ohio’s U.S. senators stand behind Trump on Iran war as high gas prices continue.”
Ohio’s two Republican U.S. Senators are standing behind President Trump when it comes to the war with Iran. This comes as American drivers face high gas prices and record-breaking diesel costs.
Their comments come the same week that they and most other Republican U.S. Senators voted against a resolution to order President Trump to halt the war with Iran.
• Big Crypto and the Ohio US Senate race. Signal Ohio’s Andrew Tobias and Jake Zuckerman report, “‘Big Crypto’ behind critical ads of Sherrod Brown again — without talking crypto.”
For the second time in two years, a deep-pocketed political group backed by the cryptocurrency industry is trying to end Sherrod Brown’s political career.
FairShake PAC announced this week it would spend $30 million on new ads targeting Brown. The group’s financial backers include Ripple Labs, which produces a cryptocurrency used for payments and has given $48 million to the PAC. Coinbase, a cryptocurrency exchange, gave the PAC $25 million, according to Federal Election Commission records.

title: Issue spotlight: North Dakota US House candidates differ on solutions to affordability
description: North Dakota’s Republican and Democrat U.S. House candidates agree citizens are battling affordability concerns, but differ on ways to bring prices down. Republican incumbent Rep. Julie Fedorchak partially blamed increasing diesel prices on President Joe Biden for preventing new fuel refineries from being built in the country while defending her votes to con[...]
text:
From the left, Republican U.S. House Rep. Julie Fedorchak and Democratic-NPL U.S. House candidate Trygve Hammer. (Photos courtesy of the campaigns)North Dakota’s Republican and Democrat U.S. House candidates agree citizens are battling affordability concerns, but differ on ways to bring prices down.
Republican incumbent Rep. Julie Fedorchak partially blamed increasing diesel prices on President Joe Biden for preventing new fuel refineries from being built in the country while defending her votes to continue the Iran war. Democratic-NPL U.S. House candidate Trygve Hammer said Congress needs to assert its authority on the Iran war and tariffs to begin turning prices lower.
Fedorchak said some inflation is due to government spending, which she said Congress has taken “some pretty sizable steps” reducing government spending during her first term.
“Obviously, there’s more work to do,” Fedorchak said.
Iran war
Fedorchak said the war has an impact on energy costs, and those costs are baked into everything else in the economy. Congress reformed energy production in the country over the last 21 months, she said, especially oil and gas extraction and power generation.
[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: The info you need to cast your ballot.]
“Those reforms were driving down the cost of energy substantially, but for the war in Iran, Americans would be enjoying the costs of substantially lower energy prices now,” she said. 
On Friday, the average cost for a gallon of diesel in North Dakota was $6.22, according to AAA fuel prices. One year ago, diesel averaged $3.46 per gallon in North Dakota.
Fedorchak has voted against measures requiring congressional approval to continue the war in Iran six separate times, most recently in mid-September.
Economic sanctions and the U.S. embargo of the Strait of Hormuz are “paying off,” she said, and it would be a “big mistake” to withdraw from the region prematurely. 
“I believe we’ll see that war end sooner rather than later,” Fedorchak said. She added Iran was a growing nuclear threat and would have created a problem for the whole world to contend with, which is why President Donald Trump decided to take action in February.
US, Israel strike Iran; Democrats call for immediate vote on Trump war powers

“As a result, I think we will have a much safer world because that threat is going to be neutralized when this is all said and done,” she said.
In April, Fedorchak said she believed the Iran war would “be done and completed successfully” within 90 days.
“I think that was the intelligence at the time, but it’s really impossible to predict out how these things unfold,” Fedorchak said last week. 
Hammer said he would have voted in support of the Iran war powers resolutions that have come before the U.S. House. He added the war hasn’t made the country more secure “financially or physically.”
“Our delegation in the Senate and House are just allowing it to go, and because we aren’t having the proper oversight, we don’t really have a clear goal,” he said. “We need to find a way to end this conflict, to kind of end the infection, and bring down the inflation.”
Hammer said allowing the war to continue just because Americans have already suffered casualties and paid a financial cost is a false argument for continuing operations. Congress had the opportunity to make its concerns known earlier in the engagement and declined to exercise any authority, he said.
“It’s basically a tax at the gas pump and at the grocery store,” Hammer said. “These are self-inflicted wounds that we didn’t have to have, and if Congress had been exercising its authority, being the check and balance that they are supposed to be, then we might not have had those things.”
Tariffs and healthcare
Hammer said the affordability crisis is showing itself in a “K”-shaped economy, where affluent households are doing well while working class North Dakotans struggle to make ends meet with higher prices.
Besides the war in Iran, Hammer said the other major driver of higher costs are the Trump-imposed tariffs, especially with Canada.
He criticized the Trump administration’s adversarial relationship with Canada and worries that continued antagonism with North Dakota’s biggest trading partner will push them into more substantial agreements with other countries or the European Union.
Farmers, businesses and markets need certainty to operate, Hammer added, and not be destabilized by the federal government.
Fedorchak said tariffs have been a tool for the Trump administration to create a level playing field for trade, and Congress’ role is to evaluate the trade deals brought to the legislative branch. Since the U.S. Supreme Court ruled many of Trump’s tariffs as illegal, Fedorchak said the administration has been issuing its new tariffs in the proper way.
US Supreme Court rules against Trump’s tariffs in 6-3 opinion, dealing blow to trade agenda

She said she recognizes Canada is the top trading partner with North Dakota and has communicated with Trump administration officials that trade decisions with the state’s northern neighbor must be resolved “sooner versus later.”
“We don’t want to lose money on both sides with the export and the import of goods from Canada,” Fedorchak said.
The next Congress plans to address increasing healthcare costs, Fedorchak said, which could take the form of expanded health savings accounts and providing federal healthcare insurance subsidies directly to Americans instead of insurance companies.
Hammer said Congress caused healthcare cost inflation for families by not extending the Affordable Care Act enhanced premium tax credits at the end of 2025, leading to more uninsured Americans.
About 3 million fewer Americans signed up for healthcare plans through the ACA Marketplace between 2025 to 2026, according to KFF. 
“Things will get better. We’re going to get wages up and we will eventually get these gas prices down when we make better decisions,” Hammer said. 
Independent candidates Helene Neville and Charles Tuttle are also running for U.S. House.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Morrisey’s plan for West Virginia Military Hall of Fame faces legal scrutiny
description: Gov. Patrick Morrisey is hoping to finally get the state’s Military Hall of Fame up and running, but his administration's draft rules for its operation face legal scrutiny.
text:
Gov. Patrick Morrisey attends an event at the West Virginia Culture Center in Charleston, West Virginia, on Nov. 10, 2025, to celebrate the 250th anniversary of the U.S. Marine Corps. (Photo courtesy of the West Virginia Office of Gov. Patrick Morrisey)Gov. Patrick Morrisey is hoping to finally get the state’s Military Hall of Fame up and running, but his administration’s draft rules for its operation face legal scrutiny.
Four years after lawmakers created the special hall of fame, Morrisey wants to see it come to fruition under his administration. 
Sen. Ryan Weld, R-Brooke, speaks on the Senate floor on Feb. 27, 2026. (Photo by Will Price/West Virginia Legislative Photography)
But Sen. Ryan Weld, a veteran and chair of the Senate’s Military Committee, has raised several “conflicts and inconsistencies” between Military Hall of Fame rules submitted by the governor versus what lawmakers outlined in their 2022 legislation.  
An agency’s proposed rules have to align with the code lawmakers passed.
“You can’t expand statutes,” said Weld, R-Brooke, in a phone interview. “I hope that they realize that legally they cannot do what they’re trying to do with this,”
Weld added that the Military Hall of Fame’s creation should be focused on veterans and their service, and “not on the politics that may be behind any sort of effort involving veterans.”
Morrisey’s proposed draft rules will govern how the Military Hall of Fame operates, including eligibility rules and how a board evaluates prospective honorees.
Former West Virginia Department of Veterans Assistance Secretary Ted Diaz speaks to lawmakers at the State Capitol in Charleston, West Virginia, in April 2022. (Photo by Will Price/West Virginia Legislative Photography)
Former West Virginia Veterans Assistance Secretary Ted Diaz, who served in the role until early 2025, said the Hall of Fame should belong to veterans and citizens — not to a political party or governor. He doesn’t want to see the project delayed by rules issues, but he wants it done correctly to honor veterans for years to come.
He described Morrisey’s new proposed rules as “very much controlled by the executive branch.”
“I’m still extremely passionate about veterans,” said Diaz, who is a veteran. “I care deeply about what happens to us in this state.”
Hall of Fame still in progress after 2022 legislation
Lawmakers created the Military Hall of Fame to honor veterans of West Virginia who distinguished themselves on the field of battle and received Purple Hearts or awards for valor. Gov. Jim Justice signed the bill into law.
Hershel “Woody” Williams speaks with members of the press while celebrating his 98th birthday with friends on Oct. 6, 2021, at Bare Arms Indoor Range & Training Center in Huntington. (Photo by Ryan Fischer/The Herald-Dispatch)
Two initial inductees were named: World War II hero Hershel “Woody” Williams and Army veteran Phill ​​Gene McDonald, who served in Vietnam.
The hall of fame is not officially running and doesn’t have an allocated physical space. Lawmakers hadn’t allocated any funding with the 2022 legislation. Justice previously proposed funding to establish a physical West Virginia Military Hall of Fame inside the West Virginia Culture Center.
“We have such a high number of veterans that have given so much for our country that I think that this represents an absolutely wonderful way to recognize those sacrifices, to recognize that commitment to service,” Weld said. “But again, I want to make sure that we’re doing it in the right way.”
In an August news release, Morrisey said his administration was now entering “the final stretch to officially honoring the state’s military legends.”
As part of launching the Military Hall of Fame, the executive branch was tasked with submitting draft rules for public comments outlining how the nomination and awards process would work.  This is standard procedure for state agencies charged with carrying out lawmakers’ requirements.
“The statutory requirement to promulgate rules for the Military Hall of Fame predates the Morrisey administration, but that rulemaking process was not completed under the prior administration,” said Lars Dalseide, communications director for the governor. “The current administration moved forward with the process to fulfill that requirement.”
The project is spearheaded by Morrisey, first lady Denise Morrisey and Sen. Brian Helton.
“The administration published the revised draft rules on Aug. 12, 2026, creating a clear pathway to celebrate military service and continued community impact,” a news release from Morrisey’s office said. 
The governor’s proposed draft rules for the Military Hall of Fame differ from the legislation, which Weld said inappropriately go beyond the scope of the bill lawmakers wrote.
While Weld thinks the original bill’s induction requirements might have been a bit too restrictive, he said the requirements were “reflective of the wishes of the lead sponsor and some of the co-sponsors at the time.”
Weld sent a letter in August to VA Secretary Ryan Kennedy outlining a number of legal concerns and spelling mistakes found in the new rules. He noted that a Morrisey-proposed rule would remove a strict requirement that the honorees made contributions to West Virginia or their communities following military service. 
“The Code clearly states that ‘significant contributions to their state or their communities following their military service’ is a requirement for induction,” wrote Weld, who is an attorney. “Should the language of [Rule 6.3] be adopted as currently proposed, it would lessen the requirements for induction, and therefore be in conflict with the code.”
Weld also raised concerns about unqualified service men and women being inducted into the hall of fame since the new rules say the VA secretary “may” reject a nominee if they don’t meet the requirements. 
In response to Weld’s concerns, Dalseide told West Virginia Watch, “The (VA) Department will address the legal issues raised by Sen. Weld through that formal process rather than separately litigating (and) debating those questions through the media while its review is underway.”
“Once that review is complete, the Department will submit the rule and its responses to the Legislative Rule-Making Review Committee as required by law,” Dalseide continued. 
The proposed draft rules included a public comment period, and Diaz submitted his own lengthy list of issues and proposed changes. He served as VA secretary from 2021 to 2025 and was in the position when the Military Hall of Fame was created by lawmakers. 
Diaz wants to see safeguards against conflicts of interests within the board evaluating the nominees. The rules must include more transparency about the induction process, he said. 
“The public must know the criteria used, how the nominees are evaluated, who is inducted, and the basis for the induction, while legitimate, confidential deliberations remain protected,” Diaz said. 
The Department of Veterans Affairs did not provide an interview for this story. 
Members of the U.S. Marine Corps celebrate the country’s 250th birthday at an event Nov. 10, 2025, at the West Virginia Culture Center in Charleston, West Virginia. (Photo courtesy of the West Virginia Office of Gov. Patrick Morrisey)
Lawmaker will have final say on hall of fame rules
Weld has recommended that the Morrissey administration amend the proposed rules for the Military Hall of Fame. A second option, he said, was to ask the Legislature to amend the original bill so it reflects what Morrissey wants. 
“I say in a letter that I’m happy to work with them,” Weld said. “I hope that they realize that and then want to work with veterans in the Legislature to accomplish what they’re trying to do, and do so in a way that still makes membership or induction into the military hall of fame a very high standard and a tremendous honor.”
The public comment period on the proposed rules for the Military Hall of Fame ended Sept. 11. 
“State law requires the (VA) department to consider and respond to those comments before submitting the agency-approved rule to the Committee … the department is now completing that review, including determining whether the proposed rule conforms to the statute authorizing it,” Dalseide said. 
He noted that Weld’s comment will be reviewed as part of that process. 
The Legislative Rule Making Committee will have to vet the Morrisey’s administration’s new proposed rules, then it will have to be approved by the full Legislature.

title: $26K profit from grassroots Soybean Festival to be donated to Martin Fire Department
description: More than $26,700 in proceeds from Martin’s Grassroots Soybean Festival will be donated to the Martin Fire Department, according to John Sellers, the festival’s lead organizer.  Sellers and other community members poured thousands of hours of volunteer work into the grassroots version of the traditional festival after the Tennessee Soybean Festival Committee[...]
text:
A dalmatian mascot sits atop a fire department vehicle during the Simmons Bank Soybean Parade on Sept. 8, 2026. The parade kicked off the community-led Martin's Grassroots Soybean Festival. The Festival raised more than $26,000 to purchase equipment for the Martin Fire Department. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)More than $26,700 in proceeds from Martin’s Grassroots Soybean Festival will be donated to the Martin Fire Department, according to John Sellers, the festival’s lead organizer. 
Sellers and other community members poured thousands of hours of volunteer work into the grassroots version of the traditional festival after the Tennessee Soybean Festival Committee announced in May that the event would not happen this year due to the city’s financial challenges. 
The money is intended to help the department purchase new self-contained breathing apparatus equipment that provides firefighters with clean, breathable air.
After Martin’s former mayor, his daughter and the city’s community development director were indicted in November on charges of official misconduct and the combined theft of more than $450,000 in public funds, the city is under orders from the state comptroller to right its finances.
Children collect candy from the street as fire trucks approach during the Simmons Bank Soybean Parade on Sept. 8, 2026. The parade kicked off the community-led Martin’s Grassroots Soybean Festival. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)
Martin Fire Chief Jamie Summers said the city’s financial situation means capital funds aren’t available to replace the nearly 11-year-old equipment. The department needs 22 sets — harness, mask and tank — and each set costs around $10,000.
The department applied for a federal Assistance to Firefighters Grant to help purchase the equipment, and the donations from the festival in addition to another community fundraiser would help cover the grant’s 10% local funding contribution. Summers said the department is “very anxiously waiting” for news on whether Martin will receive the grant. Notices will be sent out by Sept. 30, according to the Federal Emergency Management Agency, which administers the grant.
“Through our sponsors and countless hours invested, our community not only saved the Soybean Festival, it made it profitable, and now $26,727.47 will be donated to the men and women who protect the community,” Sellers wrote in a Sept. 23 Facebook post. 
Combined with $10,665 raised in the Friend of a FireFighter campaign (also led by Sellers and other volunteers) earlier this year, the Martin Fire Department will receive nearly $37,400 in total community contributions.
John Sellers, lead organizer of Martin’s Grassroots Soybean Festival, takes a moment to reflect after the parade that kicked off the festival on Sept. 8, 2026. (Photo:Cassandra Stephenson/Tennessee Lookout)
“It just makes a person’s heart glad to see,” Summers said. 
Sellers had to start a company and insure it in a 90-day timeframe to put on the festival in early September, as the Tennessee Soybean Festival Committee declined to allow the grassroots festival to use its existing nonprofit structure. Sellers said the timeline was too tight to start a nonprofit organization, so he founded a business, making the profit subject to tax. 
Sellers said he is “retiring” from his role as lead director and will restructure the company into an event and consulting business.
The Martin’s Grassroots Soybean Festival collected $92,276 from sponsors, including $30,000 from the city’s tourism fund, according to Sellers. Another $33,750 came in non-cash contributions, like food and labor donated by Tosh Pork and Martin Stockyards to provide free meals to attendees on one of the festival days. The festival’s expenses totaled roughly $65,549.
“This was never about creating a new festival,” Sellers wrote. “The purpose was to adapt and preserve the Tennessee Soybean Festival so that it could survive, become sustainable, and ultimately be given back to the community.”
The grassroots festival also proved the event could be profitable, he wrote. Sellers said he wants the festival to re-center itself on the community and establish a standard of generating a profit that can be reinvested in that community.
“The festival has an opportunity to become more than a celebration,” Sellers wrote. “It can also become a way for the community to show its appreciation for the people who serve it every day.”

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: ‘Spreading like wildfire’: How one KY county is grappling with a national tick-borne scourge
description: OWEN COUNTY, Ky. — She usually had a “stomach of steel.” Most food wouldn’t really bother her. But when Eliza Petzinger had a helping of country ham during her family’s Christmas dinner last year, the strong reaction — stomach discomfort and nausea — came just hours later.  “I was so sick, and so I knew. […]
text:
Eliza Petzinger puts together pieces of clay soap dishes at her studio in Owen County, Kentucky. She and numerous members of her family have been diagnosed with alpha-gal.(Kentucky Lantern photo by Liam Niemeyer)OWEN COUNTY, Ky. — She usually had a “stomach of steel.” Most food wouldn’t really bother her. But when Eliza Petzinger had a helping of country ham during her family’s Christmas dinner last year, the strong reaction — stomach discomfort and nausea — came just hours later. 
“I was so sick, and so I knew. I just knew,” Petzinger told the Lantern earlier this month.
Just days later in January, she had her doctor test her blood for alpha-gal syndrome, an allergic reaction by the body to a sugar molecule found in most mammals but not in humans. A bite from a tick, primarily the lone star tick found throughout Kentucky, can expose a person to the alpha-gal molecule and trigger an immune response. 
The test came back positive. And unlike Lyme disease, a rarely fatal but chronic tick-borne disease she contracted years ago, the potential lethality of alpha-gal scares her. 
The syndrome can trigger a life-threatening allergic reaction to animal products, including eating red meat, but it can also include products such as gel capsules that have gelatin sourced from red meat. For some people, even the fumes of cooking red meat can trigger a reaction. Less severe reactions can mean stomach distress, rashes, hives, shortness of breath and swelling of the lips and throat. 
Each person’s reaction is different, and some people can test positive and have no reaction at all. Petzinger said her reaction is often delayed by hours. 
“You got to think about how late at night you can eat…because you don’t want to wake up in the middle of the night and be having some reaction. And that’s how a lot of people have had serious, even life-threatening reactions,” Petzinger said. “I’m literally scared to eat certain things.’
It’s yet another illness connected to ticks that’s continuing to emerge in Kentucky, yet Petzinger was already well aware of it when she was diagnosed. Her 13-year-old daughter, Iris, was the first of her family to test positive for alpha-gal about two years ago. So has a brother and a 10-year-old niece, though she says her brother attests he doesn’t have symptoms. 
She said her father tested positive after breaking out in hives a couple of times in the middle of the night. Her mother hasn’t gotten tested yet, but she broke out in hives recently at her granddaughter’s ball game after eating some ham. 
Eliza Petzinger has a pottery business in Owen County. She has contracted Lyme disease and alpha-gal from ticks. (Kentucky Lantern photo by Liam Niemeyer)
Much of her immediate family lives on rolling, green farmland next to each other, and her kids sometimes run in between her house and her parents’ cabin. She estimates about five of 10 immediate family members, including herself, have alpha-gal. A neighbor who raises beef cattle also has it; he’s unable to eat the beef he raises. 
Similarly do a growing number of people in Owen County, one of a number of rural communities throughout Kentucky and the nation grappling with a rising number of ticks and the cases of the illnesses they bring, including alpha-gal. 
Petzinger said the ticks on her family’s land, where she has a pottery studio and farm animals, have been relentless, even with the use of the chemical permethrin on clothes to kill them. That includes the lone star tick, a relatively newer tick that’s come to Kentucky and is suspected by health experts to be the main culprit behind alpha-gal transmission in the United States. 
“I grew up on this big farm, and so I take my kids to the creek. We do all these things, and now the first thought is, ‘Oh gosh, I’m gonna get covered in ticks,’” Petzinger said. “I have to adapt to it and just learn to live with it.” 
Local doctors track the rise
It wasn’t until two or three years ago that most people in Owen County had ever heard of alpha-gal syndrome, according to one local family doctor. Cases of other tick-borne illnesses such as Lyme disease, Rocky Mountain spotted fever and ehrlichiosis would sporadically pop up in Larry Johnson’s health clinic. 
But then came the alpha-gal cases. From him diagnosing zero alpha-gal cases in a month has eventually become one to two cases diagnosed a week during some months this spring and summer, a “huge increase” for his health clinic in a county of a little over 11,000 people. 
From left, doctors Doug Smalara, Eric Bauman and Larry Johnson at Triad Health Systems in Owenton, Kentucky. (Kentucky Lantern photo by Liam Niemeyer)
“It just seemed like all of a sudden it was just spreading like wildfire,” said Johnson, who’s worked as a doctor in Owen County since 2001. Johnson said the cases have shown up in people of all ages who work or spend time outdoors “in the brush,” whether that’s farmers or tree trimmers. 
Kentucky joined a minority of states last year to require cases of alpha-gal syndrome to be reported to public health officials. Three Rivers District Health Department, which serves Carroll, Gallatin, Owen and Pendleton counties, has seen an increase in the rate of all tick-borne illness across the four counties since 2021. 
But with alpha-gal cases now being reported, the rate of cases of tick-borne illnesses per 100,000 people across the four counties has skyrocketed — from 83 cases per 100,000 people in 2024 to over 300 cases per 100,000 people in 2025 and 2026. 
It’s not clear to Johnson and other medical practitioners whether they’re finding more local alpha-gal cases because there’s more awareness of the condition and doctors are testing for it more, or if there are other factors increasing the number of cases. 
Burgers are prepped during a September afternoon at Family Billiards, a diner in downtown Owenton. (Kentucky Lantern photo by Liam Niemeyer)
Owen County residents are taking notice. Owen County Judge-Executive Todd Woodyard said he knows people who deal with alpha-gal. The city’s volunteer fire department chief Greg Estes said he had alpha-gal and avoided red meat for months, though he never got tested for it.
Family Billiards, a diner next to the county courthouse that offers burgers and pool tables, has had a few regulars come in and start mentioning alpha-gal; one of the regulars told co-owner Brandi Neal he stopped eating bacon. 
“He said he got bit by a tick. I guess that caused it,” Neal said. “We work around the issues and do our own thing for them. Whatever gets them to eat here safely without getting sick.” 
The unknowns of alpha-gal
The surge of alpha-gal cases hasn’t just been isolated to Owen County, though. A 2023 report by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention found Kentucky to be among several states with a high incidence of suspected alpha-gal cases, with Muhlenberg County in Western Kentucky cited as having among the highest county rates of cases. 
The rates of other tick-borne illnesses have also significantly increased in recent years, with Kentucky Department for Public Health data showing cases of Lyme disease in the state increasing by 275% between 2020 and 2023. 
On the national front, data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention show tick-borne illnesses have more than doubled since 2004.
Kentucky state epidemiologist Kathleen Winter said other nearby states have seen a similar rise in tick-borne illnesses, likely because both disease surveillance and reporting efforts have increased and more people are being exposed to ticks. 
Winter, a University of Kentucky associate professor, also said the ranges of various ticks are expanding both from the north and south into the state. 
“We live in a region of the country where we have a lot of ticks that like to call this their home,” Winter said. “We think the tick population is increasing, and there are seemingly to be more and more exposures to ticks. So, whether that’s just people spending time outdoors or having them more in urban areas.” 
Johnson and Winter point to the prevalence of the lone star tick as a key factor behind the rise of alpha-gal. 
Jonathan Larson, an extension entomologist at the University of Kentucky College of Agriculture, Food and the Environment, told the Lantern the lone star tick — now the most common tick in Kentucky based on survey data, he said — is seen as the primary tick but not the only tick behind alpha-gal transmission. 
Larson said the state is also seeing more ticks in general because of an abundant amount of wildlife hosts in deer and mice, warmer winters allowing for tick populations to rebound and weedy, invasive plants creating an environment for ticks. 
A bite from a lone star tick can cause alpha-gal syndrome, which can make people have an allergic reaction to animal products. (Centers For Disease Control and Prevention)
Owen County is among Kentucky counties that have plenty of deer, with Kentucky wildlife management officials allowing no limit on the number of antler-less deer that can be taken. 
“All of that adds together to create this kind of perfect storm that we’re seeing. The lone star tick has taken full advantage of it,” Larson said. 
But for Johnson and the other doctors he works with, there’s plenty still unknown about alpha-gal. For example, Johnson said there’s no “rhyme or reason” to how strong an allergic reaction someone might have; a person can have a positive test result, showing an alpha-gal immune response, but have no symptoms after eating red meat. 
Hans Otto, a Boone County allergist who previously served as the president of the Cincinnati Allergy and Asthma Society, told the Kentucky Lantern that alpha-gal has probably been around for decades but only widely recognized by medical professionals in recent years. 
Otto said treating alpha-gal is tricky because, like all medicine, “everybody presents differently.” 
“The tough thing is that avid hunter, outdoorsman who lives off the land, raises cattle, and goes hunting for deer — and if I tell them not to eat mammal meat, they blow a fuse,” Otto said. 
Accepting ‘what your cards are dealt’ 
Greg Cole and his wife are among the Owen County people who’ve been told not to eat mammal meat after being diagnosed with alpha-gal. 
That reality is especially stark given his occupation as a beef cattle farmer, or “playing cowboy for a living” as he calls it. He’s the manager of the Eden Shale Farm, a demonstration farm that raises 100 beef cattle to help educate other cattle farmers on best practices. The farm is overseen by the Kentucky Beef Network, a part of the industry group Kentucky Cattlemen’s Association.  
Greg Cole said he’s learned to eat other food beyond mammals, including seafood and poultry. (Kentucky Lantern photo by Liam Niemeyer)
“You can accept what your cards are dealt, or you can be mad about it,” Cole said. “This is what I’ve done all my life, and I’m not going to change that.”
On a cloudy September day, his lifelong work meant corralling cattle on the Owen County farm as a part of the weaning process, a chorus of bellows heard from the cows in the pens. He tested positive for alpha-gal two years ago, while his wife tested positive about a year later.
He’s been able to pivot, learning to appreciate other foods including seafood, chicken, turkey — “I make a mean turkey burger” — even if he occasionally misses beef. He said he and his wife drive about 40 miles north to a Kroger grocery store that’s well-stocked with options including vegan products. He mentioned how some people are raising ostriches as an alpha-gal safe alternative. They’ve also grown accustomed to bringing their own food to local Cattlemen’s Association events as well. 
“So far we haven’t found a treatment. It’s just dealing with it,” Cole said. “I don’t know if we’ll ever see a treatment or cure or not.” 
Greg Cole, right, helps drive cattle at the Eden Shale Farm in Owen County, Kentucky. (Kentucky Lantern photo by Liam Niemeyer)
Winter, the state epidemiologist, said research is still active and ongoing around potential treatments, including ways to mitigate or reduce symptoms, though the current guidance is to avoid exposure to food and other products that could trigger a reaction. Some people have sought out a specific form of acupuncture that some people say helps with symptoms, though Winter said there is “no clear recommended treatment at this time.”  
Adapting to alpha-gal, though, has been a harder challenge to grapple with for some of Petzinger’s younger family who live just down the road from the Eden Shale Farm. 
Petzinger, who was assembling the dark, clay pieces of soap dishes to be put in her kiln, told the Lantern that her 10-year-old niece has had to go to birthday parties where “you can’t have any of the cake or ice cream.” 
Petzinger’s mother will bake “alpha-gal safe cupcakes for her to take to the party.” 
Her own 13-year-old daughter has struggled at times with managing an alpha-gal-safe diet, too. 
“It’s just so hard. They have enough going to deal with as a teenager,” Petzinger said. 
Eliza Petzinger is among several members of her family who have either tested positive for alpha-gal syndrome or have had allergic reactions after eating red meat. (Kentucky Lantern photo by Liam Niemeyer)
